--- Page 8 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication started on the previous page. The text completes the sentence begun at the end of the last page, where the author was explaining his intention to venture onto a path not yet taken by others.</meta>

—ing a path not attempted by others, which is sometimes so enveloped in the clouds of **antiquity** that in certain matters it does not quite reach the monuments and secrets of our **Ancestors**; in others, it fails to recover the strokes of characters that are worn away and escape the sharpness of the eyes. It is a joy to have advanced this far, even if it is not granted to go further. It will be enough for me to have rescued the remaining trophies of our fathers from destruction and to have left certain matters to be refined by a grateful posterity, so that the evidence of noble deeds which still remain with us do not perish entirely. There will one day be someone who, kindled by love for his country, will add more and not neglect these things. Because of the thorny difficulty of our antiquities, the greater part of our countrymen have been deterred from their duty to the fatherland; despising what is at home, they have devoted themselves to foreign things. But to neglect what is near, to look up to the remote, to adore the external, and to loathe the domestic is not a virtue, but a vice. For this reason, the noble deeds of our ancestors—their rituals, customs, institutions, decrees, victories, triumphs, monuments, and infinite other trophies of **Danish** virtue—lie buried in darkness and are overwhelmed by eternal oblivion. And what could we have hoped for until now, when <term>Learning</term><note>original: "Literatura." In this context, it refers to the broader world of letters, scholarship, and historical record-keeping rather than just fiction.</note> itself was almost obliterated? Ruminating on these things often within myself and deploring our lot,

--- Page 9 ---
<meta>This page continues the dedication to the Chancellors. The author, having previously lamented the neglect of Danish history, now declares his intention to provide a clearer path for the study of the nation's ancient monuments and records. Catchword: lar- (likely leading to "largiri" or "largitate," meaning to grant or with abundance).</meta>

I felt that something had to be attempted, so that I might either stir up noble talents born for our country by my example, or, through this work, pave a smoother path toward our **Antiquities**. Encouraged by the favor and kindness of my superiors, I have already presented preliminary efforts in the <term>Fasti</term><note>original: "Fastis." These were historical records, calendars of official events, or annals of the state.</note> and in literature. Since I see that these were kindly received by fair-minded readers, I decided that these <term>specimens</term><note>original: "παραδείγματα" (paradeigmata). Here meaning models or illustrative examples of the monuments being discussed.</note> of **Monuments** should also be added—works produced here with no small amount of toil and expense. In doing so, I aim to ensure that our **Danish Antiquities** receive no less honor than those of other nations, and that they regain their own majesty to be emulated by future generations. 

I humbly ask that you, **Magnificent Chancellors**, do not disdain to look upon these efforts with a kind countenance and to hold them recommended under your protection and patronage. If I wished to list the reasons that impelled me to this task, I would have to compose a lengthy account of your merits across all ranks of dignity—service rendered to the **King**, the **Prince**, the **Fatherland**, the **Church**, and this **Academy**. 

It is enough to mention that distinguished favor and benevolence with which you have embraced me as your <term>client</term><note>original: "clientem." In the seventeenth century, this implied a formal relationship of protection and support between a social superior and an intellectual or subordinate.</note> for many years in no ordinary fashion; I pray and vow that this favor may remain with me always. I worship God with humble prayers, that He might deign to bless your **Illustrious Magnificences**, along with your noble families, with the breath of His blessing...

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER
->Greetings.<-

<image-desc>Decorative woodcut initial 'E' featuring a human figure entwined with foliage and floral motifs.</image-desc>

Behold before you, friend Reader, these specimens of *Danish Monuments and Inscriptions*, promised to you long ago. They were *acquired by me through much labor and sweat, but are now shared with the public so that they may serve as a sort of* finishing touch and validation <note>original: "Coronis & δοκιμασία [dokimasia]." The Greek term refers to a formal test or proof of authenticity.</note> *for those things upon which we previously commented regarding our* ancient literature and Danish Annals <note>original: "Faſtis Danicis."</note>. Perhaps in these pages a more curious investigator of antiquities <term>Antiquities: The study of the physical remains, customs, and documents of the ancient past.</term> will find something that may delight him, and bear witness to Northern glory and the emulation of the virtue of the ancient Danes. The *Greeks* and *Romans* owe it to their famous writers that the legacy they left to the well-deserving has been freed from the storms of time and the tempests of various adversities, placed before the light and the eyes of all, and in many places seen restored to its former brilliance. Such good fortune did not befall our own [monuments]; rather, they have been held in such contempt and covered in filth and squalor until now, that they have sometimes been cast down to block up dung heaps or for I know not what other shameful uses. Indeed, it was thought a "better fate" for those which were snatched from the sacrilegious hands of monstrous stone-cutters <note>original: "Lapicidarum."</note> and used instead to close a fence or support the collapsed foundation of some barn. It is from such places that what we present here had to be fetched at times, and freed from mud and stench, so that they might come more freely into your sight. I no longer wonder why this province of study has remained deserted until now—attempted by many, but cultivated by none. Nor do I anxiously inquire why certain men of great reputation withdrew their hand once applied to the task, forced to exclaim:

*Behold, dear Reader, the specimens of Danish Monuments and Inscriptions <note>original: "Monumentorum & Inscriptionum Danicarū."</note> long promised to you; obtained by me indeed with much labor and sweat, but now shared with the public so that they may serve as a sort of crowning completion <note>original: "Coronis," a Greek term for the finishing touch or flourish at the end of a manuscript.</note> and a trial <note>original: "δοκιμασία" (dokimasia), meaning a test or scrutiny.</note> of those things which we formerly discussed regarding our ancient Literature and the Danish Calendars <note>original: "Fastis Danicis," referring to Worm’s earlier work on Runic calendars published in 1626.</note>. Perhaps even in these things the more curious examiner of antiquity will find something that might delight him, and testify to northern glory <note>original: "septentrionali gloria"</note> and the emulation of the virtue of the ancient* Danes. *The* Greeks *and* Romans *owe it to famous writers that those things which they left behind for the well-deserving—having been freed from the storms of time and various adversities—are now before the light and eyes of everyone, and in many places are seen restored to their pristine brilliance.* Our *monuments have by no means met with such good fortune; instead, they have been held in such contempt and covered in filth and squalor until now, that they have sometimes been pushed aside to enclose dung heaps or for I know not what other shameful uses. Indeed, it was thought to have gone well with some, which a better fate snatched from the sacrilegious hands of monstrous* Stone-cutters <note>original: "Lapicidarum," referring to masons or builders who destroyed ancient runestones for building materials.</note> *and allowed them to either close up a fence or support the collapsed foundation of some barn. From such places, the items we present here had to be fetched and freed from mud and stench, so that they might come more freely into your sight. I no longer wonder why this province of study has remained deserted until now—attempted by many, but cultivated by none; nor do I anxiously inquire why certain men of great reputation withdrew their hand from the tablet they had approached, forced to exclaim:*

# TO THE BENEVOLENT READER
->Greetings.<- <note>original: "S.", an abbreviation for 'Salutem,' a standard Latin greeting wishing the reader health.</note>

<image-desc>Large decorative historiated woodcut initial 'E' depicting a figure, likely a putto or angel, kneeling within a landscape framed by foliage and architectural elements.</image-desc>

Behold before you, friend Reader, these samples of Danish Monuments and Inscriptions, long ago promised to you. They were procured by me indeed with much labor and sweat, but are now shared with the public so that they might serve as a finishing touch <note>original: "Coronis"</note> and a verification <note>original: "δοκιμασία" (dokimasia), a Greek term for an official test or examination of fitness</note> of those things we formerly commented upon regarding our ancient Literature and the Danish Calendars <term>Fasti Danici: Worm’s 1626 work on ancient runic calendars and chronology</term>. Perhaps in these pages the more curious investigator of antiquity will find something that might delight, and testify to the glory of the North and the emulation of the virtues of the ancient Danes. The Greeks and Romans owe it to their famous writers that the merits they left behind—freed from the storms of time and the tempests of various adversities—remain visible in the light and before the eyes of all, and are seen restored to their original luster in many places.

This happiness has hardly fallen to our own monuments. Instead, they have been held in such contempt and covered until now in such filth and squalor that they have at times been cast down to wall off dung-heaps and for I know not what other shameful uses. Indeed, it was thought a good outcome for some that a better fate snatched them from the sacrilegious hands of cruel stone-cutters <term>Lapicidae: masons or stone-cutters who often broke up ancient runestones to use as building material</term> and allowed them either to enclose a fence or to support the collapsed foundation of some barn. From such places we had to fetch the things we give here, freeing them from mud and stench so they might come more freely into your sight. I no longer wonder why this province of study has remained deserted until now—attempted by many, but cultivated by none. Nor do I anxiously inquire why certain men of great reputation withdrew their hand from the task <note>original: "admotam tabulæ retraxerint dextram," a Latin idiom for abandoning a project just as it was begun</note>, forced to exclaim:

<summary>Ole Worm introduces his collection of Danish runic inscriptions, lamenting how ancient monuments have been neglected or reused as common building materials while praising their historical value. He frames this work as a necessary completion of his earlier studies on Danish history and runic calendars.</summary>
<keywords>Ole Worm, Denmark, runestones, antiquities, Fasti Danici, preservation, epigraphy, Northern history</keywords>

--- Page 16 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of Ole Worm’s work. ->Even stones have their own deaths,<-
->And stiff crags heap up ruins for themselves in disaster!<-
<note>original: "Sua sunt qvoq; funera saxo / Et rigidæ cautes cumulant sibi clade ruinas!" These lines are adapted from the Roman poet Lucan, reflecting on the mortality of even the most permanent-seeming monuments.</note>

*Indeed, quite enough obstacles—and in no smaller a heap than those stones face—were thrown in my path in this race. They delayed me so much as I panted toward these steep heights in mid-course that they would have long ago forced me to lose heart and set aside all care for these matters, had not the benevolence of my patrons and the favorable cheers of the leading men of all the best Literature kept me in my lane and happily encouraged me to finish what remained.*

*I owe my primary thanks to the Magnificent Chancellor of his Royal Majesty, Lord* CHRISTIAN FRIIS of KRAGERUP, *a knight and most prudent Senator of the Kingdom of Denmark, the kindest of patrons of blessed memory* <note>original: "P.M.", an abbreviation for 'Piae Memoriae'</note> *who was the first not only to draw me into this arena, but also never ceased to assist me with advice, kindness, and the generous sharing of documents. He continued to spur me on with frequent encouragements until this little work of ours, having reached its finishing touch* <note>original: "colophonem," literally the 'summit' or 'finishing stroke' of a project</note>, *seemed to him worthy of some light. After him, I owe a great deal to the Magnificent, illustrious, and noble Lord* CHRISTIAN THOMESEN <note>original: "Christiano Thomæo," referring to Christian Thomesen Sehested (1594–1657), a high-ranking Danish official</note>, *Lord of* STOUGARD *etc., Royal Chancellor and Knight. Just as he succeeded to the position of my late Patron before our Most Serene King—by his own great merit and for the benefit of the fatherland—so too has he aided my efforts to unearth our national antiquities with his counsel. He brought the matter to the point where, with elegant illustrations* <note>original: "iconibus"</note> *and typeface, these findings could finally be shared with those who study our antiquities, after long and wearying labors. To these great men* <note>original: "Heroibus"</note> *is owed whatever light may be shed upon our labors and the antiquities of our fatherland, and whatever of the North* <note>The text breaks off here at the catchword "mun-".</note>

<summary>In this portion of the preface, Ole Worm reflects on the difficulties of completing his archaeological survey and pays tribute to his powerful patrons, Christian Friis and Christian Thomesen, who provided the political and financial support necessary to publish the work.</summary>
<keywords>patronage, Christian Friis, Christian Thomesen Sehested, Danish antiquities, preservation, archaeology, 17th century scholarship</keywords>

--- Page 17 ---
<meta>This page continues Ole Worm’s preface, specifically his acknowledgments of the scholars and patrons who encouraged his research into runic inscriptions. It follows a section where he credits the Chancellor Christian Friis for his initial support. The catchword from the previous page was "mun-", here beginning the word "mundi" (of the world).</meta>

whatever delight has come to those who search out the wonders of the world, it must be credited entirely to them. For I frankly confess that it was by their authority and protection that I was led here, so that I dared to attempt paths that were unusual and seemed plainly impassable to many, and I did so not without risk to my reputation and standing.

I saw indeed the efforts in this field of the most celebrated man *Bonaventura Vulcanius* <note>Bonaventura Vulcanius (1538–1614) was a Flemish humanist whose work on the Goths and their language provided a foundation for later runic studies.</note> (whose more important works of this kind you will see here outlined, explained, and restored to their original state). His efforts were received with applause and admiration, and held in high regard by all good men; but I was never able to promise myself, nor even hope, that our own works would rise to that level. Meanwhile, however, the kind judgments of great men regarding what I have published so far promise me as much as I could never have dared to wish for.

I cannot, therefore, but give due thanks to my great friend (whom these studies won for me), the generous and noble man *Sir Henry Spelman*, an English Knight well-deserving for his work on ancient literature, for his fair examination of our *Runes* <note>original: "Runarum"</note>. Likewise to the most celebrated *Petrus Scriverius*, who follows our little work with more than abundant affection in his most ingenious treatise on the origin of *Printing* <note>original: "Typographiæ"</note>, and judges it not at all unworthy to be handled by the hands of the learned. 

Nor did it seem out of place to mention that chosen pair of Danish historians; I mean the most illustrious *Johannes Meursius*, public Professor of the Academy of Sorø, and *Johannes Isacius Pontanus*, who once instilled good literature into the youth in the Gymnasium of Harderwijk, and who is now among the saints <note>original: "νῦν ἐν ἁγίοις" (nyn en hagiois). Pontanus had recently died (1639), and Worm uses this Greek phrase as a respectful way to say he has passed to his eternal rest.</note>. These men have honorably received into their writings the things published by me so far regarding these antiquities, and judged them not unworthy of their praises. This finally was the only thing in my wishes...

<summary>Ole Worm acknowledges the influence of prominent European scholars like Bonaventura Vulcanius and Sir Henry Spelman, crediting their encouragement for his courage to pursue the difficult study of runes. He lists several contemporary historians who validated his work, positioning his research within the broader Republic of Letters.</summary>

<keywords>Ole Worm, Bonaventura Vulcanius, Henry Spelman, Petrus Scriverius, Johannes Meursius, Johannes Isacius Pontanus, Runes, antiquarianism, Danish history, Republic of Letters</keywords>

--- Page 18 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of Ole Worm’s *Danicorum Monumentorum Libri Sex* (Six Books on Danish Monuments). The previous page ended with a mention of Petrus Scriverius and his judgment of Worm's work. The catchword "sci-" from the previous page completes the word "scitorum" (learned) at the beginning of this page.</meta>

...of learned men, I have attempted to respond in some way to the expectations they have conceived. To these I could add not a few Germans, Italians, and Frenchmen—and those among the scholars of better character—who, partly through their own letters and partly through others, have not ceased to urge me that I should no longer keep these things to myself alone.

Furthermore, lest anyone complain that anything has been snatched away from them by this small labor of mine, or that they have been defrauded of their exhausted labors, and so that the undeniable reliability of the <term>transcripts<note>original: "apographorum"; these are hand-drawn copies of the inscriptions found on stones.</note></term> which we have used here may be established, I will not conceal the names of those who specifically provided their welcome service to the fatherland—and indeed necessary service to me—in communicating the <term>monuments<note>original: "cippis"; specifically referring to stone pillars or grave markers.</note></term> and their inscriptions. I hope that others, incited by their example, will collect what remains and will freely contribute their own portion to this work in due time.

Besides those things which I myself noted with all possible diligence in Zealand, Scania, and <term>Jutland<note>original: "Cimbria"; the Cimbrian Peninsula.</note></term>, many others provided me with substitute labor: the Reverend Mr. Bertil Knudsen <note>original: "Bertilus Canutius"; he was a local official and pastor in Lødderup.</note>, Provost and Pastor of Lødderup; and Mr. Jonas Skonvig <note>original: "Jonas Schonvigius"; Skonvig was a famous contemporary illustrator of runic stones.</note>, then chaplain to the Royal Fleet, whose singular diligence in delineating older remains I cannot but praise. For the accounts from Oslo <note>original: "Asloensia"</note>, we are indebted to Mr. Peter Adolf, a most skilled Doctor of Medicine. For those of Stavanger <note>original: "Stavangriensia"</note>, we thank the Reverend and most celebrated man Mr. Thomas Conrad Wegner, the most vigilant Bishop of that same Diocese and my old friend. Others who more particularly declared their affection by aiding our efforts and rescuing these things from the shadows, we have praised each in their own proper place.

All these men, however, will testify with me that it is a work of no small effort to win favor for things so greatly despised, to recover the fleeting marks from the hardest rocks, and to resurrect things buried for so many centuries...

<summary>Ole Worm acknowledges the international scholars who encouraged his work and lists the specific local contributors who provided him with hand-drawn copies of runic inscriptions from across Scandinavia.</summary>
<keywords>Ole Worm, acknowledgments, runic inscriptions, Zealand, Scania, Jutland, Jonas Skonvig, Thomas Conrad Wegner, archaeology, transcripts</keywords>

--- Page 19 ---
<meta>This page continues the preface of Ole Worm’s *Danicorum Monumentorum Libri Sex* (1643). The text follows a list of contributors and moves into a discussion of the immense difficulty involved in deciphering weathered runic inscriptions. The catchword "In-" on this page points toward the beginning of the next section, likely the "Introduction" or "Inlustris."</meta>

*...to investigate, and to wage a kind of war against the violence of time and the elements. This was entirely necessary for one who determined to struggle out of this darkness. To render ancient letters into those now in common use, or even into <term>Roman characters<note>original: "Romanis"; referring to the standard Latin alphabet used in early modern printing.</note></term>, is not so very laborious for someone moderately versed in our <term>literature<note>original: "Literatura"; here referring specifically to the study of runes and ancient Northern texts.</note></term>, especially where the marks appear whole and not mutilated or corrupted. But to restore those eaten away by decay, to correct those poorly transcribed, to adapt an <term>archaic dialect<note>original: "cascum idioma"; an old-fashioned or primitive language, referring here to Old Norse or ancient Danish.</note></term> to the modern one, and to draw out the genuine sense of each—that was a work of greater effort. In this, however, we have so toiled that we hope we have achieved a good many things; we have given place to conjecture in many instances, while in others we have scarcely satisfied ourselves, leaving the attempt unfinished so that those who teach better and more certain things might also have their own honor and glory. If the ancients had left the deeds of our <term>ancestors<note>original: "Majorum nostrorum"</note></term> recorded in writing with the same diligence as the <term>Greeks<note>original: "Græci"</note></term> and <term>Romans<note>original: "Romani"</note></term> did theirs, the path to explaining these things would have been clear—a path which now appears rugged, thick with jagged rocks, and worn by no footprints.*

*Therefore, accept these attempts, <term>kind reader<note>original: "benigne Lector"</note></term>, but with the right of changing, adding, subtracting, and correcting reserved to me; while to you is granted the most free opportunity of conferring with me about them, of aiding the endeavor, of introducing, amplifying, and noting things. With the same spirit in which I offer this, I bid you farewell.*

<summary>In this concluding part of his preface, Ole Worm describes the scholarly "war" against time required to decipher decayed runic inscriptions and transform archaic dialects into modern understanding. He contrasts the lack of written records from Nordic ancestors with the well-documented histories of the Greeks and Romans, inviting readers to collaborate in improving this foundational work.</summary>

<keywords>runology, antiquarianism, historical method, translation challenges, Danish history, Nordic ancestors, classical comparison</keywords>

...attempting to respond in some way to the expectations conceived by learned men. To these I could add not a few Germans, Italians, and Frenchmen—and among them scholars of the highest distinction—who, partly through their own letters and partly through others, have not ceased to urge that I should no longer keep these findings to myself alone.

Furthermore, lest anyone complain that anything has been snatched away from them by this modest effort of mine, or that they have been cheated of the credit for their own exhausted labors, and so that the unquestionable reliability of the <term>transcripts<note>original: "apographorum"; refers to hand-drawn copies of the inscriptions.</note></term> which we have used here might be established, I will not conceal the names of those who have performed a service—pleasing to the fatherland and indeed necessary for me—by sharing individual <term>monuments<note>original: "cippis"; literally "pillars" or "gravestones," used here for runic stones.</note></term> and their inscriptions. I hope that others, incited by their example, will collect what remains and will, in due time, voluntarily contribute their own <term>token<note>original: "Symbolam"; a contribution or share toward a common goal.</note></term> to this work.

Besides those things which I myself noted down with all possible diligence in <term>Zealand<note>original: "Selandia"</note></term>, <term>Scania<note>original: "Scandia"</note></term>, and <term>Jutland<note>original: "Cimbria"</note></term>, several men have provided me with assistance. These include the Reverend Master Bertel Knudsen, <term>Provost<note>original: "Præpositus"; a high-ranking ecclesiastical official.</note></term> and Pastor of Lødderup, and Master Jonas Skonvig, then chaplain to the Royal Fleet, whose singular diligence in sketching ancient monuments I cannot help but praise. For the findings from <term>Oslo<note>original: "Asloensia"</note></term>, we are indebted to Master Peder Adolf, a most skilled Doctor of Medicine. For those from <term>Stavanger<note>original: "Stavangriensia"</note></term>, we thank the Reverend and most illustrious Master Thomas Conrad Wegner, the most watchful Bishop of that same diocese and my old friend. Others who more specifically demonstrated their desire to aid our efforts and to rescue these things from darkness, we have praised each in their appropriate place.

All these men, however, will testify along with me that it is a work of no small effort to restore favor to things so greatly despised, to recover the fleeting marks from the hardest rocks, and to [resuscitate] things buried for so many centuries...

<meta>This page continues the preface of Ole Worm’s work on Danish monuments. On the previous page, Worm acknowledged his collaborators across Denmark, Norway, and Europe. Here, he transitions to the specific philological difficulties of the project: the physical decay of the stones and the linguistic distance of the ancient runic language.</meta>

...to rouse [them], and to wage a kind of war, as it were, against the violence of time and the seasons. This was something that entirely had to be done by one who determined to struggle out of this darkness. To render ancient letters into those now commonly used, or even into Roman ones, is not so very laborious for someone moderately skilled in our **alphabet** <note>original: "Literatura"; here referring specifically to the study of runic characters and the Old Norse/Danish language.</note>, especially where the characters appear whole, and not mutilated or corrupted. But to restore those eaten away by decay, to correct those poorly transcribed, to adapt an **archaic language** <term>cascum idioma<note>An ancient, obsolete, or "primitive" style of speech; Worm uses this to describe the difficulty of translating Old Norse into contemporary 17th-century Danish or Latin.</note></term> to the modern, and to draw out the genuine meaning of each, was a task of greater effort. 

In this, however, we have toiled so much that we hope we have achieved a fair amount, though in many places we have given room to conjecture, and in others we have scarcely satisfied ourselves, leaving the attempt unfinished, so that honor and glory might also belong to those who teach better and more certain things. If the ancients had left the deeds of our **Ancestors** recorded in writing with the same diligence as the **Greeks** and **Romans** did theirs, the path to explaining these would have been clear—a path which now appears rough, thick with jagged rocks, and worn by no previous footsteps.

Therefore, kind reader, accept these attempts, but with the right of changing, adding, subtracting, and correcting reserved to me; to you, however, the very free power is granted of conferring with me about them, of helping my efforts, and of introducing, expanding, and noting. In the spirit with which I offer this, I bid you farewell.

# To the most Excellent, most Famous, and most learned Man,
# Lord Doctor OLAUS WORMIO <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), the celebrated Danish physician and antiquarian to whom this work is dedicated.</note>
## Doctor of Medicine and Royal Professor

*The stone pillars <note>original: "Saxorum cippos"; likely referring to runestones, which Worm famously studied.</note> speaking in an ancient tongue,*

# DANISH MONUMENTS

...denied in reality, they attempt to achieve it boldly through the propagation of species, some in one way, others in another, yet by means suited and granted to their own natures.

Among the rest, man himself—the most divine and excellent of animals—perceives by a silent instinct of nature that he was created and born for a participation in divinity and eternity. He walks not only along this most natural path shown by the **Philosopher** <note>Likely referring to Aristotle, who argued that living things seek a share in the eternal through reproduction and intellect.</note> to attain this desired divinity and perpetuity, but also, partly through the irradiation of divine light and partly through the sharpness of his own mind, he never ceases to try other ways by which he may reach this goal and most conveniently enjoy the longed-for eternity. That way is indeed the safest and most certain which celestial wisdom, contained within the pages of Sacred Scripture, demonstrates; by which, through true faith in the **Mediator** <note>Jesus Christ.</note> and the life worthy of a Christian man (which sprouts from it), we tend toward that goal. Less safe, indeed treacherous and slippery, yet pleasing to mortals and not to be entirely rejected for its significant use in common life, is the way devised by those whom the fire for right and honor has raised to the arduous peak of virtue and integrity.

This is the way by which certain **Tokens** <note>original: "Indicia"</note> are placed on these lands by human art and effort for those who have served well, in memory of justice administered, of the fatherland defended by courage and prudence, and of other illustrious deeds. By these, their memory is snatched from the violence of oblivion, and others are encouraged and animated to tread the path of virtue vigorously. For not in vain does Euripides <note>Though the author attributes this to Euripides, these lines are actually from Sophocles’ play, *Ajax*.</note> exclaim in *Ajax*:

> Alas, how quickly the gratitude toward the dead
> flows away from mortals and is caught in betrayal.
> <note>original Greek: "Φεῦ τοῦ θανόντος ὡς ταχεῖα τοῖς βροτοῖς / Χάρις διαῤῥεῖ καὶ προδοῦς’ ἁλίσχεται."</note>

These **Tokens** the Greeks called by the quite convenient term <term>Kenotaphia</term> <note>Cenotaphs; literally "empty tombs," used for monuments that honor the dead without containing their remains.</note> and the Romans called <term>MONUMENTA</term> <note>Monuments; derived from the Latin *monere*, meaning "to remind" or "to warn."</note>, because they remind those present of things past and recall the illustrious deeds of ancestors to the memory of posterity. As the parent of eloquence <note>The Roman orator Cicero.</note> beautifully expressed to Caesar in these words: *But I am reminded by the name itself what the nature of a monument is: that it ought to look more toward the memory of posterity than to the [memory] of the present [time]*— <note>original Latin: "Sed ego quæ monumenti ratio fit, nomine ipso admoneor, ad memoriam magis spectare debere posteritatis, quam ad præsentis tem-"</note>

It draws on both Christian theology and Classical philosophy (Aristotle, Sophocles, and Cicero) to explain the human impulse for "earthly immortality."</summary>

# BOOK ONE. 3

...grace of time. In this same sense, Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar.</note> writes in *On the Latin Language*, Book 5: *The word "to warn" is derived from "memory," because he who warns acts just like memory.* So too are the **monuments** which are on tombs, and placed beside the road for the reason that they may **warn** <note>original: *admoneant*; the author is highlighting the linguistic connection between *monumentum* (monument) and *monere* (to warn/remind).</note> passersby both that those buried there were once mortal, and that they themselves are mortal. And the legal consultant Florentinus <note>A Roman jurist whose works were included in the *Digests* of Justinian.</note> in the seventh book of the *Institutes* says: *A monument, in general, is a thing handed down for the sake of memory for posterity; in which, if a body or remains are brought in, it becomes a tomb.*

Indeed, since there are various things that have the power to recall the sequence of deeds to our memory—namely **Shrines**, **Altars**, **Tombs**, **Inscriptions**, **Forums**, **Obelisks**, **Statues**, **Temples**, and infinite others of that kind—it follows that the word "monument" has been extended to express all of these. This is supported by Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> when he says: *A monument is that which is built for the sake of the dead, and whatever is made in memory of someone, such as shrines, porticos, writings, and poems.* These things, however, were not only fashioned and constructed in various ways and with various workmanship according to the diversity of races and nations, but even in one and the same tract of land, they were allotted a diversity of material, shape, apparatus, and magnificence, according to the variety of the time and circumstances.

Since I see that these matters have been treated eagerly by many, and yet the accounts concerning the **Monuments** constructed in **Denmark** <note>original: *Dania*.</note> have been plainly omitted, I trust that I shall perform a task of no small value if I bring into the light those things of this kind which I have found recorded in writing by our own people or by foreigners, or which I have seen confirmed by trustworthy report and by <term>personal observation</term> <note>original Greek: *αὐτοψίᾳ* (autopsia), meaning to see something with one's own eyes.</note>. I produce these now to be refined by time and further experience, trusting that this endeavor will find favor among good and honest men.

<meta>The previous page concluded with a discussion of the classical Roman definitions of "monument" provided by Varro, Florentinus, and Festus. ->DANISH MONUMENTS<-

[it is clear] to my mind to pursue, by sketching, all those things which can be included under the title of "monument" and are found among us—or at least the principal ones, and those which can attract a curious investigator by way of their rarity, majesty, or singular antiquity.

While I more accurately survey these ruins still existing among us, I find that they were not all of the same kind. For considering the material from which they were fashioned, they present themselves to us as either made entirely of earth, or of stone and rock, or a mixture of both. Regarding their use or purpose, I see some erected to serve the worship of Idols and provide the opportunity for sacrificing victims; these should be distinguished by us by the names *Shrines* and *Altars*. Others are *Tombs*, intended for burying the dead. Others, containing the praises and commendations of the deceased in our ancestral or Runic <note>The Runic alphabet was used by Germanic peoples before the adoption of the Latin alphabet; here the author refers to the Younger Futhark used in Viking Age and medieval Scandinavia.</note> characters, we call *Epitaphs*. As for those which touch upon genealogies and certain principal deeds in a brief and laconic style, we ask for indulgence if we strictly call them "Monuments." There are also ancient *Forums* <note>original: *Fora*; likely referring to the "Thing" or "Ting," the traditional governing assemblies and courts of the Nordic people.</note>, once intended for settling disputes; *Circles* <note>original: *Circi*; likely referring to stone circles used as sites for judicial duels or "holmgang."</note>, assigned for duels and battles; and *Boundaries*, or stone markers, which separated princedoms, territories, estates, and fields with a certain special sanctity. From these we will select the ones of greater importance; some are to be sampled here in this general consideration of Danish Monuments, while the more significant ones will be reserved for a special treatise on Inscriptions.

## CHAPTER THREE.
### On the Shrines and Altars of the ancient Danes.

To begin with sacred matters: I find that our ancestors performed divine service and sacrificed to their Idols primarily in two places. Sometimes they did so in Shrines and temples constructed at great expense; sometimes in the open air, upon altars built in a peculiar way, as the ruins still visible among us teach clearly enough. For the ancients first covered their idols, called **Skurguder** <note>original: *Skurguder*; from the Old Norse *skurðgoð*, literally "carved gods."</note>, with huts and small cottages, thinking it to be lacking in dignity...

### BOOK ONE

[...they did not believe] that the Gods should be enclosed within roofs, especially where they were meant to be appeased with due worship and to manifest their majesty. But as luxury grew, in certain places they built sumptuous **Shrines**, **private chapels**, and **temples** <note>original: *Delubra, lararia & fana*. These terms describe different types of Roman sacred spaces, here applied to northern contexts.</note> for them. This is why Tacitus, in his work *On the Customs of the Germans*, writes that the ancient Germans had no other temples for the Gods than the groves and woods named after their deities.

Indeed, if we are to trust Clement of Alexandria in his *Exhortation to the Greeks*, temples originated from tombs. For he says:
> *Superstition persuaded people to build temples. For those structures which were previously the more magnificently built tombs of men came to be called by the name of temples. In the city of Larissa, in the citadel, within the temple of Pallas <note>The Greek goddess Athena.</note>, was the tomb of Acrisius, which is now celebrated as a sanctuary. In the Athenian citadel as well, as written by Antiochus in the ninth book of his Histories, was the tomb of Ceres <note>The Greek goddess Demeter.</note>. In the temple of Pallas, whom the Greeks call Polias, lies Erichthonius. Furthermore, Ismarus, the son of Eumolphus and Daira, is buried in Eleusis along with the daughters of Celeus.*

He writes this. In a similar way among us, one may observe that near the burial mounds of the Heathen Kings, **Temples** <note>In this context, the author refers to Christian churches.</note> were constructed by their Christian successors so that they might serve as monuments to the deceased. But because they were unable to convert those great burial mounds, heaped up from the earth, into temples, they placed buildings dedicated to Christ near or beside them, as can be seen at **Jelling** in Jutland, at **Hårlev** in Zealand, and commonly elsewhere.

The majesty of these shrines was greater in some places and lesser in others. They say the most sumptuous was at **Uppsala** <note>A major religious center in ancient Sweden.</note>, which glittered entirely with gold; see the illustration of this in Olaus Magnus, book 3, chapter 6. Albert Krantz, in the preface to his first book on Sweden, discusses it thus:
> *The most noble nation of the Swedes had a temple called Uppsala. The metropolitan seat of the kingdom remains there today, not far from the cities of Sigtuna and Birka. In this temple (which glittered entirely with gold), they worshipped the statues of three Gods <note>Thor, Odin, and Freyr.</note> before they believed in Christ.*

And a little later:
> *A huge tree stood near the temple, spreading with wide branches, remaining green in both summer and winter; no one could name its species. A spring bubbled forth at the place of Sacrifices; those about to perform a sacrifice immersed a living man here: if [he disappeared...]*

"So help me Freyr, and Njörðr, and the almighty Ás..." <note>This is a standard Old Norse oath formula often cited in Icelandic sagas. The Runic text here reflects a variation of the oath taken upon a sacred ring.</note>

*Before that footstool of the Gods, situated in the aforementioned shrines, stood a constructed Altar, covered on its upper surface with iron so that it would not be damaged by the fire which was required to be kept perpetual there. Upon the altar was also placed a basin or bronze vessel in which the blood of the sacrificial victims was collected, along with a lustral vessel and a sprinkler for splashing the blood of the victims upon those standing by. Furthermore, a silver ring (or one made of brass) weighing twenty ounces was kept on the altar. Those performing any legal duty, when about to swear an oath, would religiously touch this ring—which had been smeared with the victims' blood—while they were swearing. For the most part, four-footed animals were designated as victims to be turned into feasts for the sacrificers. However, I find (and it is to be lamented) that the blind heathens also used human victims at the aforementioned place* <term>Kialarnes</term> <note>Kjalarnes, a district in southwestern Iceland</note>: *where before the doors of the Shrine there was a very deep pit into which the human victims were cast. This pit was called* <term>Blotfella</term> <note>Likely "Blót-fyllur," meaning sacrificial pit or "Blót-fall," the slaughter of sacrifice.</note> *after the Sacrifice.*

In Denmark (as far as I know) no ruins of such things now remain; perhaps because our ancestors, once imbued with Christian rites, strove with every effort to remove the abomination of such great idolatry. They either utterly destroyed the more prominent places designated for this, or, where they were once seen, they dedicated temples to the true God in their place, changing superstition into divine worship and attempting to root out every memory of the Idols. Thus, it is not uncommon to see the tables of altars, which still exist in the fields and woods, cast down and scattered.

The structure of the altars among us varies. For the most part, they consist of a mound piled up from the earth, upon the summit of which three huge stones support, brace, and hold up a fourth stone—one that is larger, wider, and flatter—so that it stands out like a table resting on three legs <note>The author is describing a "dolmen," a type of prehistoric single-chamber megalithic tomb common in Scandinavia. In the 17th century, these were widely believed to be "giant's altars" for pagan sacrifice.</note>. Beneath this mass, a cavity is seen, quite vast in some cases, while in others it is filled with earth and stones; this is believed to have been designated for receiving the blood of the victims. It is rare if you do not find flints here suitable for striking fires. For they considered it a sin to use any fire for burning the victims other than that struck from flints.

In certain places, they may be seen constructed with even greater preparation,

In Frisia <note>a coastal region covering parts of the modern-day Netherlands and Germany</note>, the most distinguished Stephanus Stephanius, Royal Historian, noted that such altars exist, citing the first book of Ubbo Emmius’s *Frisian History*, page 21. There, Emmius discusses them in this way:

*“It seems worthy of mention, as has also been noted by others, that in this region many stones of immense weight are found piled together—stones so large that you would believe they could not have been transported there by any vehicle or human strength. Their arrangement is such that they appear to resemble altars. For, while some lie flat, other flat stones are placed on top of them, and a narrow opening is left through which a man might crawl. Legend has it that the pagans, who were once accustomed to sacrifice with human victims, forced the men who were to be slaughtered to pass through those openings. While passing through, they were defiled with dung and other filth thrown by the crowd, and then, having been positioned at the altars, they were sacrificed. This rite is said to have lasted until the time of Boniface, Bishop of Utrecht <note>Saint Boniface (c. 675–754 AD), known as the 'Apostle of the Germans,' who led the conversion of the Germanic tribes to Christianity</note>. For this reason, it is thought that a shameful name for those openings still persists among the inhabitants.”*

Many other things of this kind exist among us, which might rightly fill a curious spectator with wonder. But let us briefly consider for which and what kind of gods the sacred rites were performed at these places.

## CHAPTER FOUR.

->Concerning the Gods and Idols of the Ancient Danes.<-

Just as the divine power of the gods to whom our ancestors were accustomed to offer their vows was frivolous, so too is their number uncertain. Nevertheless, histories testify that they were distinguished into those of greater and lesser importance. Let us hear our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), a Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum* (Deeds of the Danes)</note> discussing the principal ones, and explaining in eloquent words by what arts and devices these mortals achieved the glory of divinity among the Northern peoples:

> *“In olden times,” he says, “certain men steeped in the magic arts—namely Thor and Othinus <note>Odin</note> and many others—who were skilled in the miraculous engineering of illusions, began to claim for themselves the height of divinity after they had won over the minds of the simple. Indeed, by inciting Norway, Sweden, and Denmark—which had been ensnared by the traps of the most hollow credulity—to the zeal of paying them worship, they tainted them with the particular infection of their deception. ...for indeed, the effect of their deceptions grew so widespread that others, venerating in them a certain power of the divinities and believing them to be gods or accomplices of the gods, offered solemn vows of sorcery and displayed the reverence due to sacred things to this sacrilegious error. Thus it happened that the legitimate sequence of feast days <note>The days of the week</note> among us is reckoned by their names, just as the ancients among the Latins are known to have adapted names individually either from the names of their gods or from the seven planets.

The *History of Norway* <note>original: *Hist. Norv.*</note> testifies that the idol of Thor was held in great esteem among the people of Nidaros <note>Modern-day Trondheim, Norway</note> during the reign of King Olaf Tryggvason. When the same king (who feigned that he had come to observe their sacred rites) found the statue of Thor magnificently adorned with gold and silver in the temple of the Nidaros idolaters, and placed on a throne in the midst of the others, he shattered it with a mallet and cast it down. His companions vigorously crushed the rest, reproaching everyone for the foulness of their idol-madness.

To these two, they added a third deity, though it remains uncertain whether it was of the male or female sex; although many have assigned it to the female choir. I find this deity called *Fricco* or *Frig* by some, and *Frigga*, *Frea*, or *Freya* by others; some maintain she was the wife of Odin, famous for her adulteries and thefts. From her, the day of Venus is called *Fredag* or *Freitag* <note>Friday</note> by our people; likewise, those whom we now call *Fruer* <note>The Danish word for "Ladies" or "Mistresses of the house"</note> are named from Freya.

Nor should it seem a wonder to anyone that the sex is doubted, since it is abundantly clear to those who have carefully surveyed good authors what other nations decided concerning Venus and the Moon. There is a passage worthy of note in Macrobius’s *Saturnalia*, Book 3, Chapter 8. He asserts that in the *Aeterian* <note>Likely referring to the works of the scholar Atteius Capito</note> it should be read as:

*not Goddess. There is even a statue of it in Cyprus, with a bearded body but in female dress, with a scepter and a masculine stature, and they think the same being is both male and female. Aristophanes calls her Aphroditos* <note>original Greek: Αφρόδιτον; a masculine form of the name Aphrodite</note>. *Laevinus also speaks thus:* "Therefore worshipping nourishing Venus, whether female or [male]..."

# BOOK ONE

...with which Julius Caesar does not at all disagree in Book 6 of his *Commentaries*. <note>original: "Commentariorum"; Caesar’s *Gallic Wars*, where he describes the customs of the Gauls and Germans.</note> Others assert that Cicero, in Book 3 of *On the Nature of the Gods*, says the Egyptians called the God of death *Their*. But Vossius, in *On Idolatry* Book 2, chapter 33, <note>Gerhard Johann Vossius (1577–1649) was a Dutch scholar whose work on paganism was widely cited in the 17th century.</note> seems to establish that our *Tius* was not so much the same as *Teutates*, <note>A Celtic god mentioned by Roman authors.</note> but rather the *Hesus* of the Romans. For he argues as follows: What the Romans pronounced as *Hesus*, among the Germans—without the Roman ending—was *Hees* or *Hies*, with a variation in the vowel. And a little later: from this comes **Hisesdag**, or more compactly **Hissdag**, which in the Roman language is the day of *Mars* <note>Tuesday.</note>. Commonly, the letters *T.* or *D.* are prefixed, as in many other cases, resulting in **Thijssdag** or **Dijssdag**. Unless you prefer that it was first **Thijssdag** from *Chesus* or *Chisus*, for in the old days *H.* and *CH.* were used interchangeably. But here I allow everyone their own free judgment. Lactantius <note>An early Christian author (c. 250–325 AD) who critiqued pagan practices.</note> records in Book 7 that the Gauls appeased *Hesus* and *Teutates* with human blood.

Related to these was **Tyr** (whose genitive form is *Tyrs* or *Tys*), the son of Odin. He obtained the honors of divinity through his boldness, readiness of hand, and wisdom; supplications were made to him for victory (whether the struggle was a duel or otherwise). From him, the Icelanders believe the day called the day of *Mars* by the Romans is called **Thijssdag** by us. Arngrimus <note>Arngrimur Jónsson (1568–1648), an Icelandic scholar and a key correspondent of the author, Ole Worm.</note> recalls that he read it as **Thijssdag**. On these matters, one should consult Book One of the *Danish Fasti*, chapter 15. <note>The author is referring to his own work, *Fasti Danici*, a treatise on the ancient Danish calendar.</note>

Richard Verstegan <note>An English antiquarian (c. 1550–1640) known for his work on Anglo-Saxon origins.</note> reports that the Saxons, our neighbors, had seven primary Idols to which they consecrated the seven days of the week. The first was the day of the *Sun*, from which they called the first day of the week **Sundag**, the day of the Sun (although others prefer **Sondag**, meaning the day of reconciliation or appeasement). This was represented by a statue of a man carved down to the waist and placed upon a column; he was entirely naked, with a face shining with solar rays, holding a wheel in his hands which covered his whole chest, and decorated all around with streaks of flame, indicating the solar course and heat. The second day, he claims, they consecrated to the *Moon*, whose image they ridiculously expressed in this way: they placed a complete statue of a man upon a columnar base, wearing a hood with donkey's ears sewn on, carrying a moon in his hands, and wearing a short cloak brushing his knees, so that in dress he expressed a man rather than a woman. The third Idol, he reports, was **Tuisto**, from whom the third day of the week is **Tuissdag**. His statue, which was bearded, was also placed upon a column,

The formula of the oath includes these words among others: *May Freyr and Njord and the almighty Aesir help me.* <note>original Old Norse: "Hialpi mier suo Freyr og Niordur og Hinn almatke As." The Aesir are the primary tribe of gods in Norse mythology.</note> The *History of Norway* explains at the very beginning the reason why *Niordur* and *Freyr* were raised to the rank of the gods. For these two were of the Scythian nation, held in the highest esteem among their own people, and given as hostages to Odin, by whom they were counted among the Asian gods. <note>The author is following the "Euhemerist" tradition, which argued that the gods were actually historical kings or heroes from the East (Asia/Scythia) who were later deified.</note> *Thor, Heiner* <note>Hœnir</note>, and *Balder* are established as their colleagues, to whom specific seats in Sweden were assigned.

But Northern superstition was not content with this number of idols; instead, following the custom of other nations, it selected many more gods and goddesses for itself, though of lesser value. Among these, *Diisa* or *Thiisa* found a place as the wife of Thor; <note>The author identifies Disa as Thor's wife, though in most surviving Norse myths, his wife is Sif.</note> because she was believed to especially favor Justice, she seemed no less deserving of a place among the goddesses than Frigga, the wife of Odin. Some claim that from her name, the second day of the week <note>Tuesday; the author is debating whether the day is named for the god Tiis/Tyr or the goddess Disa.</note> was called *Thiſs-dag*. Great pomp and solemnity were observed for her annually at Uppsala, in sacred rites called the *Tiſsating*. <note>The "Disting" or "Thing of the Disir" was a great assembly and market held in Uppsala.</note> While attending these, Adels <note>Adils</note>, a petty king of Sweden <unclear>22</unclear>, fell from his horse and struck his head against a stone so severely that he soon after exchanged life for death, as the *History of Norway* attests. A village in Zealand, Denmark, called *Thiſetvelde* <note>Modern Tisvilde.</note>, took its name from her, as there is a spring and fountain there once dedicated to this *Thiisa*. After the madness of idolatry was abolished, the Papal authorities placed St. Helena in charge of it, which is why the spring is now called St. Helena's. Many people afflicted with various ailments still take refuge there today, promising themselves a return to health.

There was also *Tiis*—called *Teves* by the English and *Teutas* by the Latins—of whom Lucan speaks in this manner in the *Pharsalia*, Book 1:

He was depicted armed, as he presided over wars; they attributed victories to him and sacrificed those conquered and killed in battle to him. Standing upon a column, he wore a crown on his head, held a <term>seax</term> <note>A one-edged sword or dagger typical of the Germanic peoples; the text calls it a "Saxon sword."</note> in his right hand and a shield in his left, with his feet clad in shoes. 

The fifth was **Thor**, from whom comes the fifth day of the week, *Torsdag* <note>Thursday</note>. He was considered the highest of the gods and was worshiped by all the Northern peoples. He was depicted reclining elegantly on a bed, wearing a golden crown on his head surrounded by twelve stars, holding a scepter in his right hand, and otherwise dressed in royal attire. 

The sixth was **Frigg**, who was thought to be hermaphroditic, depicted with the organs of both sexes. Standing on a column, she held a sword in her right hand and a bow in her left; from her comes the day of Venus, *Frigedag* <note>Friday</note>. 

The last he calls **Saeter**, who is elsewhere called *Crodo*, from whom comes *Saterdag*, the day of Saturn <note>Saturday</note>. Atop a column, a perch fish was carved, and the idol stood upon its prickly back with a bare head and long hair and beard. In his left hand he held a wheel, and in his right a handled pitcher filled with water and flowers. He wore a toga cinched around his loins with a linen cloth, and his feet were bare. One may see their images engraved in bronze in the same author's work.

Our friend **Arngrímur** <note>Arngrímur Jónsson "the Learned" (1568–1648), an Icelandic scholar who wrote to correct continental misconceptions about the North.</note> also testifies in his supplement to the *Norwegian Chronicles* that **Gói**, the daughter of Nor, was regarded as a goddess by the Swedes, and that sacrifices were made to her annually in February to obtain victory. From her, the second month of the year, which we usually call February, is named *Goea* <note>The Old Norse month Gói.</note>.

For the more daring and ready for crimes anyone was in that age, the more they believed that miserable person had found a shorter path to divine honors. But the belief in his divinity did not flourish for long: for when that second Odin <note>Often identified as the sorcerer Mithothin mentioned in the previous page's context.</note> returned, **having abandoned the aid of magic tricks**, he went to Funen <note>original Latin: "Fioniam"; the author notes his copy spells it "Pheoniam"</note> for the sake of hiding. Some believe that Odense <note>original: "Otthonia"</note> was named after him, as a hiding place built by him.

Kings also, famous for great deeds, were sometimes adopted into the number of the Gods, and their families were inserted into divine lineages by the credulous crowd. For this reason, **Haldan Biargram**, having defeated **Eric** among the Swedes, began to be held in such high regard **that he was thought to be the son of the great Thor**, was gifted divine honors by the people, and was deemed worthy of public libations, as Saxo relates in Book 7.

Aelnoth mentions a certain idol named **Wig** in the *Life of St. Canute*, chapter 23: from which he thinks Viborg <note>original: "Wiberga"</note> in Jutland <note>original: "Cimbriæ"</note> was named; the Schleswig Breviary also mentions this. The Biarmians <note>A people of the far north, often associated with the White Sea region.</note> honored their **Jumala**, whom the history of Olaf the Stout <note>referring to King Olaf II of Norway</note> described.

I also found in a certain manuscript that there was a distinction among our ancestors between terrestrial and aquatic idols. For they invoked one for the fertility of the harvest and abundance of crops, just as the Latins did Ceres, though the manuscript does not state her name. In the sea, they believed a being called **Nocca** held power, like Neptune; hence they spread the word that those drowned in the waters had been snatched away by the Nocca: **"The Nøkke took him away"** <note>original Danish: "Nocken tog hanem bort"</note>. In certain places in Denmark, they call this Nocca **Nicken**, and they say he appears not only in the sea, but also in rivers and deeper streams, like a sea monster with a human head, especially to those wretches over whom the most immediate danger of drowning looms. They also report that drowned people, when lifted from the water, were found with red noses, as if someone had sucked out the blood with a pressed mouth; hence the common saying: **"The Nøkke has sucked him dry"** <note>original Danish: "Necken haffuer sugit hannom"</note>. Whether that specter belonged to this kind, which was seen in the year 1615 from October 13 to 17 at Marburg near the mill of St. Elizabeth above the Lahn River...

They record that **Krodan** here performed the roles of **Saturn**; he was the presiding spirit of malice and wickedness, and from this comes the expression *Krodan the Rogue* <note>original: Krodan Skalck. I believe this report from Thurii refers to him: In the fifteenth year, a most formidable war arose between **Emperor Henry** <note>Presumably Henry V (r. 1106–1125).</note> and **Lothair**, Duke of the Saxons. In this pitched battle, such a great multitude of mortals perished that the blood of the slain flowed into nearby pits. This battle was waged in two places: at the **Cota of the Ascanians** and the little woods of **Velphia Minorun**, where a willow tree called **CAEDUTUM** <note>original: CÆDUTUM. Derived from the Latin "caedere," meaning to cut, fell, or kill. The name suggests a "Slaughter-Tree" or "Hewn-Tree."</note> cried out three times amidst the uncertain combat. Once the Imperial army had been scattered there and their leader **Hojer Manius** slain, the Saxons erected a pillar inscribed with arms, which they named **CAEDUTUM** in memory of the event; the monastery now called **Wiederstedt** <note>original: Viderostadium</note> was established not far away. This passage is in Book 5 of the *Gleanings of Antiquity*. Lilius Gyraldus, in his *History of the Pagan Gods* (near the end of the first section), testifies that the **Saxons** otherwise worshiped a wooden column placed under the open sky; he adds that it was called **Irmensul** or **Irmenseul**, and was either a statue of **Mercury** or a common place of refuge and a **Sanctuary** for all. The same Gyraldus relates in his thirteenth section that he read in the histories of the Saxons that there was a temple there where an image of **Venus** stood, adorned in this manner: the **Goddess** stood in a chariot, naked, her head wreathed in myrtle, carrying a burning torch at her breast, a representation of the world in her right hand, and three golden apples in her left; behind her were the naked **Graces**, with hands joined and carrying apples, their faces turned away from one another.

A cock sat upon its head, and a bear was upon its chest. Whoever desires more details concerning this should consult the author himself. Truly, as to the manner by which these idols were destroyed by the Emperor Charlemagne, Nicolas Thurius <note>A 16th-century historian; his "Deflorationum antiquitatum" (Gleanings of Antiquities) was a common source for Germanic history.</note> teaches in Book 5 of his *Gleanings of Antiquities* in this manner: *At the first available time, he (that is, Charlemagne) cast down from the Mount of Mars—which is the city of the Istaevones <note>The Istaevones were a grouping of Germanic tribes mentioned by Tacitus.</note> on a high ridge—the statue of Mars which they called Armesule, in the year seven hundred and seventy-two. Then, in the year eighty, he took away the image of Saturn, called Croto, from Hercynopolis in a hostile manner; and soon in eighty-one, Venus from Parthenopolis <note>Magdeburg, often referred to by the Latinized Greek name Parthenopolis, or "City of the Virgin."</note>, in which year he also took the Moon from Mount Calcarius <note>Likely the Kalkberg (Lime Mountain) at Lüneburg.</note>.* Verstegan mentions another called **Flynt**, so named because, standing upon a flint stone, it represented death or a human skeleton, holding a lit torch in its right hand. He adds others of this kind which he reviews in passing, such as **Helmsteed** (I believe our people call it **Helmer**), **Prono**, **Fidegast**, **Sive**, and so on. But who could sufficiently enumerate all the abominations of this kind? We cannot give great enough thanks to the immortal and true God that He has utterly scattered the memory of them (which it is a sin to refresh too much) by the brightness of the Gospel light, and driven it completely from the minds of mortals.

# BOOK THE FIRST.

For Rabanus <note>Rabanus Maurus (c. 780–856), a Frankish Benedictine abbot and scholar whose encyclopedic works were standard references in the Middle Ages.</note> in Book 5 of *On the Propriety of Words and the Mystical Significance of Things*, chapter 10, writes:

> *A **Sacrifice** <note>original: "Sacrificium"</note> is, as it were, a "sacred act" [sacrum factum]. A **Host** <note>original: "Hostia"</note> refers to those sacrifices made before proceeding against enemies [hostes]. **Victims** <note>original: "Victimæ"</note> were the sacrifices immolated after a victory, once the enemies were conquered; and "Victims" were considered greater sacrifices than "Hosts." Others have thought the "Victim" was so named because it fell by a struck blow [ictu percussa], or because it was led bound [vincta] to the altars. A **Holocaust** <note>original: "Holocaustum"</note> is where the whole of what is offered is consumed by fire.*

Indeed, when the ancients performed great sacrifices, they were accustomed to consume the entire host in the sacrificial flame, and this was the "Holocaust." So says Rabanus. Regarding the sacrifices among our own people <note>The author likely refers to the Danes or Northern peoples.</note>, I find that two kinds flourished: one greater and more solemn, which was performed every nine years with great ceremony and pomp; the other lesser and more common. Concerning the former, hear the account of Thietmar, Bishop of Merseburg <note>A 10th-century chronicler whose *Chronicon* is a vital source for the history of the Holy Roman Empire and its neighbors.</note>, in Book 1 of his *Chronicle*, page 12:

> *But because I,* he says, *have heard marvelous things concerning the ancient hosts of these same people (the Danes), I do not wish to pass these by unexamined. There is a place in those parts, the capital of that Kingdom, named **LEDERUN** <note>Modern Leire, near Roskilde.</note>, in the district called **SELON** <note>Zealand (Sjælland).</note>, where after nine years, in the month of January—after the time we celebrate the Epiphany of the Lord—they all assemble. There, they immolate to their gods ninety-nine men, and just as many horses, along with dogs and roosters offered in place of hawks <note>original: "pro accipitribus oblatis"</note>, believing for a certainty, as I said before, that they will appease the gods with these offerings.*

So says he. The district which he calls *Selon* is the region of Zealand, the most fertile island of Denmark, once the capital of the Baltic kingdom and the primary province. In this place is seen the location called *Lethra* by Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), author of *Gesta Danorum*.</note>, commonly called **Leire**; today it is a lowly village, but formerly it was a royal city and the primary seat of the Baltic Kings. Concerning this, our Saxo writes in Book 2 in this manner:

> *One proceeds to **Lethra**, a town constructed by **Rolvo** <note>Hrólfr Kraki, a legendary Danish king.</note> and adorned with the extraordinary wealth of the kingdom; by the authority of its royal foundation and its status as a seat of power, it stood far above the other cities of the neighboring provinces.*

But our Huitfeldt <note>Arild Huitfeldt (1546–1609), a Danish historian and state official.</note>, writing of **Dan**, establishes the first King of Denmark, Dan, as the founder of Lethra.

The same Saxo, a little earlier in the same book, testifies that a famous and well-fortified citadel was added to this city, where he shows in what manner Helgo [sent] his son Rol-

# DANISH MONUMENTS

libations <note>original: "libamenta," referring to liquid offerings or the initial part of a sacrifice</note> were slaughtered at the altar for the gods. However, the human whom fate had offered for sacrifice was drowned alive in the spring that bubbled up at the site of the sacrifices; if he breathed out his soul easily, the priests announced the vow to be favorable. Soon after, having been taken out from there, they would hang him in a nearby grove, which they believed to be sacred, and affirmed that he had been translated among the gods.

Originally, indeed, they appeased all the gods together with sacrifices; but after Mithothyn <note>A legendary sorcerer mentioned by Saxo Grammaticus who allegedly usurped Odin's position</note> the sorcerer had attempted to claim divine honors for himself as well, he easily persuaded the credulous common people that each god must be won over individually with a distinct kind of ritual and sacrifice. Saxo clearly hints at this in Book 1: *During his [Odin's] absence, a certain Mithothyn, famous for his sorceries, as if refreshed by a heavenly blessing, seized the opportunity to forge a divinity for himself. Spreading the new darkness of error over barbarian minds, he led them by the fame of his illusions to perform ceremonies in his own name. He denied that the wrath of the gods or the violation of their spirits could be expiated by confused and mixed sacrifices; therefore, he forbade vows to be made to them in common, establishing separate libations for each of the gods.* From this, it seems, arose so many and such diverse cults dedicated to individual idols.

Dudo of Saint-Quentin <note>A 10th-11th century Frankish historian and dean of St. Quentin</note> shows what kind of sacrifices were specifically intended for Thor, discussing them in this sense: *Furthermore, in the fulfillment of these expulsions and expeditions, they once sacrificed in veneration of THUR <note>Thor</note> their Lord, to whom they slaughtered not any of the flocks or herds, but the blood of men, thinking it the most precious of all burnt offerings. For when the fortune-telling priest had predestined it, the yokes of oxen were struck once and cruelly on the head, and for each one chosen by lot, the brain was laid low on the earth with a single blow to the neck. The fiber of the heart—namely the vein—was sought on the left side, and after their blood had been drained according to their custom, they smeared the heads of their own people with it. Then they quickly weighed the linen sails of the ships to the winds, and thinking to appease the gods by such business, they swiftly rose to the oars of the ships.*

Nor did they think these foul and abominable sacrifices of human blood were displeasing to Odin <note>original: "Othino"</note>: for he, believed to preside over wars, was thought to be in no way better appeased,

than with the blood of their enemies and the captives they carried away with them. For so says **Olaus Magnus** <note>A 16th-century Swedish archbishop and historian</note> in Book 3, Chapter 3: *They appeased Odin, who presided over wars, with the blood and death of captives, believing that the ruler of battles was more appropriately appeased by human blood; from him, in turn, they learned every skill of warfare so perfectly that, after conquering the most powerful empires of Europe and Asia, they achieved the highest degree of bravery.* <note>original: "Othinum qui bellis praesidebat... reportarint"</note> Hence, they said that those slain in war were sacrificed to **Odin**, as witnessed by **Arngrimur** <note>Arngrimur Jónsson, an Icelandic scholar known for his work *Crymogaea*</note> in *Crymogaea*, Book 1, Chapter 6. Furthermore, our own **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> in Book 8 introduces **Harald** <note>Harald Wartooth, a legendary Danish king</note> promising that he would dedicate the souls <note>original: "manes"</note> of the defeated as a gift to **Odin**, provided he obtained the desired victory.

The Norwegian history <note>Likely referring to the *Heimskringla* or similar sagas</note> records that the inhabitants of **Värmland** <note>A province in Sweden</note> offered their king, **Olaf Trätelja**—the first ruler of that region—to **Odin** as a sacrifice by burning him in a fire, so that they might turn away the high cost of grain and other hardships from their own necks. Otherwise, in the same history published by us in the vernacular tongue, among the laws brought by **Odin**, this is also read: That there should be a sacrifice three times every year; in the Winter time for the prosperity of the year; in mid-winter for fertility; and around the end of winter for the obtaining of victory.

These horrific and abominable sacrifices of the human race were urged and restored among the Northerners after **Odin** by **Fro** <note>The god Freyr</note>, the leader of the gods, as our **Saxo** taught in Book 2. *Fro,* he says, *the leader of the gods, took up his seat not far from Uppsala, where he changed the custom of ancient sacrifice—used by so many nations and through so many ages—into a grim and unspeakable atonement; indeed, having set about slaughtering victims of the human race, he paid foul offerings to the gods above.* Moreover, when Fro himself was at last recorded among the number of the gods, he wished the credulous to be fully persuaded that he could only be appeased by this kind of sacrifice. Our same Saxo hints at this in Book 1, where he follows the manner in which **Hadingus** <note>A legendary Danish king</note> returned into favor with the gods: *Nor,* he says, *was there a remedy for the evil until he could return into favor with the gods by expiating his crime with sacrifices. For the sake of propitiating the deities, he performed a divine rite to the god Fro with dark victims, leaving this custom of sacrifice—repeated in an annual circuit of festivals—for posterity to imitate.* The Swedes call this the *Fro Blod* <note>original: "Fro Blod," meaning Freyr’s Blood/Sacrifice</note>. From this comes the term *at blotte* <note>original: "at blotte," from the Old Norse "blóta"</note>, meaning to sacrifice and...

pure libations were sacrificed to the Gods at the altar. However, the man whom chance had offered up for immolation was submerged alive into the spring that welled up at the place of sacrifice. If he breathed his last quickly <note>original: "facilè efflaret animam"</note>, the priests announced a favorable omen; soon after, he was snatched from the water and hung in a nearby grove, which they believed to be sacred, affirming that he had been translated among the Gods.

Originally, they appeased all the Gods together with sacrifices; but after **Mithothyn** <note>A legendary figure who, according to Saxo, took over Odin's place during his exile</note>, the sorcerer, attempted to claim divine honors for himself as well, he persuaded the gullible commoners without difficulty that each god must be worshiped individually with a distinct kind of ritual and sacrifice. **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> hints at this clearly in Book 1: *During [Odin’s] withdrawal, a certain Mithothyn, famous for his sorceries, as if invigorated by a heavenly gift, seized the opportunity to forge his own divinity. Surrounding the barbarian minds with the new darkness of error, he led them by the fame of his magic to pay ceremonies to his name. He denied that the wrath of the Gods, or the violation of their numinous power, could be expiated by confused and mixed sacrifices; therefore, he forbade that vows be made to them in common, establishing separate libations for each of the powers above.* <note>original: "Cujus secessu Mithothyn... libamenta constituens"</note> From this, it seems, arose so many and such diverse cults dedicated to individual idols.

What kind of sacrifices were specifically destined for **Thor** is shown by **Dudo of Saint-Quentin** <note>An early 11th-century historian of the Normans</note>, who discusses them in this sense: *Furthermore, at the completion of these expulsions and military expeditions, they formerly sacrificed while worshiping* **THOR** <note>original: "THUR"</note> *their Lord, to whom they offered not cattle or flocks, but the blood of men, thinking it the most precious of all burnt offerings. By the predestination of a priest-diviner, victims were struck cruelly on the head in the manner of a yoke of oxen; with the brain of the chosen victim crushed by a single blow, he was cast upon the ground. Then, the fibers of the heart—specifically the vein—were sought out on the left side; having drained the blood according to their custom, they smeared the heads of their people with it. Then they quickly weighed the sails of their ships to the winds, and believing they had appeased the Gods by such business, they swiftly rose to the oars of their vessels.* <note>original: "Cæterum in expletione... insurgunt remis"</note>

Nor did they think these foul and abominable sacrifices of human blood were displeasing to **Odin**; for he, believed to preside over wars, was thought to be appeased by no better means...

Furthermore, at the instigation of the Devil, the most atrocious enemy of the human race, idolaters began to appease their deities with human victims around the time of Abraham.
