It is therefore likely that **Odin**, the master of abominable **Idolatry** and **Magic** in these regions (whom our ancient histories report came from Asia to the North with his followers), brought this sacred rite along with him; and he appointed his governor, named **Fro**, to oversee it. Since he urged the work forward vigorously and persuaded the inhabitants that this rite was most pleasing to the Gods, he was thereafter regarded by all as the author of such a horrific sacrifice.

Indeed, we have learned that these abominations grew so powerful that even kings did not spare their own sons. For **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note>, in his 10th book, reports that **Haakon**, King of Norway, destined his own sons for sacrifice so that he might secure a victory over **Harald**.

<margin>Book 10:</margin> *Haakon, having surveyed his troops and realizing that an intolerable disaster loomed over his affairs, since he lacked the material means to withstand it—as if despairing of human help and embracing the divine—took care to appease the gods with an extraordinary atonement. Indeed, he brought two sons of the most excellent character to the altars like sacrificial victims, and for the sake of obtaining victory, he slaughtered them in a wicked offering; he chose to lose the name of "father" rather than lose his fatherland.*

**Crantz** <note>Albert Krantz, a 15th-century historian</note> also reports this regarding Harald, the son of Gunnhild, in his *History of Norway*, Book 3, Chapter 3.

When the inhabitants of the **Nidaros** <note>The region around modern-day Trondheim, Norway</note> district refused to embrace Christian rites and threatened to force their king, **Olaf Tryggvason**, back to paganism by force, he replied that he would offer such dark victims to their Gods that, for that purpose, not slaves or men of lower status would be selected, but the **Magnates** and those who ruled over the rest. Terrified by this threat, they were forced to desist from their **idolatry**.

In western **Iceland**, in the district of the **Thorsnes Assembly**, **Arngrimur** <note>Arngrimur Jónsson, a famous Icelandic scholar</note> shows from the **Eyrbyggja Saga** that there was a circle in which they used to sacrifice men; let us hear the words:

Which he translates as follows:
> There was in the middle of the assembly place a **Circle**, into which men appointed to be sacrificed to the Gods were gathered, who were killed by being dashed against a massive stone placed there, etc.

While these sacrifices were performed, various rites and modes of propitiation were employed: magnificent banquets were celebrated, part of the blood was smeared on the doorposts of the houses, and part was offered as a toast to those standing by. They honored the memory of their gods with strong drinks, stating the name of each one and enumerating specifically what they asked for or sought. In the feasts, a portion of the victim was served; they by no means abstained from horseflesh and other abominable things <note>Church authorities in the Middle Ages strictly forbade the consumption of horsemeat as it was a primary marker of pagan ritual</note>, eating these as if they were sacred and choice dishes with wonderful eagerness. They used the cooked meat of the victims for the feasts; for in the middle of the temple, they set up a hearth intended for cooking the victims. Meanwhile, while the boiling was taking place, they indulged in fuller cups by the hearth (they called this <gloss>carrying the cup</gloss> <note>original: "at bæra fult"; Old Norse "at bera full," the ritual of serving the ceremonial toast</note>), with the priest pronouncing good omens for the people and the sacrifices. Soon, the memory of **Njord** and **Freya** <note>The Norse deities of fertility, wealth, and the sea</note> was honored with cups, so that annual prosperity might befall them, and the most abundant yield of crops and other provisions. In **Uppsala**, while sacrificing to their gods, the petty priests would dazzle the eyes and ears of the spectators with effeminate dances and gestures, the clanging of bells, and the bellowing of discordant music, to such an extent that more noble-minded men were so offended by these things that they preferred to be absent rather than present. Hence it is that **Starkad** <note>Starchaterus; a legendary hero and giant of Norse myth known for his traditional warrior ethics</note>, as **Saxo Grammaticus** <note>A 12th-century Danish historian</note> witnesses in Book 6: *while staying at Uppsala during the time of the sacrifices, he loathed the effeminate body movements, the stage-like clapping of the mimes, and the soft tinkling of the bells; he preferred to betake himself to Haco, the tyrant of Denmark, rather than be present at such things.*

Regarding the dark victims and bloody sacrifices, see the learned commentary on the passage we cited above from Book 1 of Saxo, written by the most distinguished man Master **Stephanus Stephanius** <note>Stephen Hansen Stephanius (1599–1650), a renowned Danish historian and professor at the Sorø Academy</note>, Royal Historiographer and public professor at the Academy of Sorø. Particularly worthy of note is the passage from **Tertullian** <note>An early Christian author from Carthage</note> which he cites, showing that the term "blood" <note>original: "sangvinis"</note> was attributed to these bloody libations by Latin writers:

> *They tear the body, and they pour out the gore,*
> *Such is the rite which is called by its true name, BLOOD.*

In expeditions and battles far from their homeland, I find that our **Cimbri** <note>An ancient tribe likely from Jutland (modern Denmark) who famously invaded the Roman Republic</note> had a far different ritual for sacrificing to their gods. For then the women—especially those of advanced age and those excelling in ancient learning and the art of divination, called **Runes** <note>original: "Runæ"; here referring to "wise women" or "völvas"</note>—performed the duties of priests. The victims, however, were captives. **Strabo** <note>An ancient Greek geographer</note>, in Book 7 on the customs of the Cimbri, elegantly teaches the method by which they sacrificed them in these words:

*Some priestesses, skilled in divination, accompanied their husbands when they went to war; these women had grey hair, wore white linen garments with a cloak of fine flax fastened by buckles, were girded with bronze belts, and were barefoot. They would meet the captives throughout the camp with drawn swords, and after throwing them to the ground, they would drag them to a bronze cauldron. Then, lifting them up, they would slit their throats with the blade, and as the blood flowed into the cauldron, they would prophesy the outcome of the war.*

By which sacrifices your **Teutates** <note>original: "Teutates"; a Celtic deity often identified by Roman writers with Mercury or Mars</note> was appeased is related by **Beroaldus** <note>Filippo Beroaldo (1453–1505), an Italian Renaissance humanist and commentator</note> in the passage cited above from **Lucan** <note>A Roman poet whose work *Pharsalia* mentions the bloody rites of the Gauls</note>, in this sense:

Others have statues of immense size, whose limbs, woven from wicker, they fill with living men. When these are set on fire, the men are surrounded by flame and perish. Some they pierce with arrows, and within the sacred buildings they fix them to a cross <note>original: "patibulo"; a gallows or cross-like instrument of execution</note>, as Strabo relates. Hence he is called "merciless" by Lucan.

**Adam of Bremen** <note>An 11th-century German chronicler and geographer</note>, in Book 1, Chapter 6, teaches what the nature of idolatry was among the Saxons, neighbors to the Danes:

> They worshipped, he says, those who were not gods by nature, among whom they especially venerated **Mercury** <note>In Germanic contexts, Mercury was the Roman interpretation of the god Woden or Odin</note>, to whom they were also accustomed to offer sacrifices on certain days. They believed that, due to the magnitude and dignity of the celestial beings, they should not confine their gods in temples, nor represent them in any human likeness. Consecrating groves and woods, and calling them by the names of gods, they contemplated that mystery <note>original: "secretum"; a hidden or sacred thing</note> with reverence alone. They observed omens and lots <note>original: "sortes"</note> very closely. The custom of the lots was simple: they would cut a branch from a fruit-bearing tree into twigs, and having marked them with certain signs, they would scatter them randomly and by chance over a white garment. Soon, if it was a public consultation, the priest of the people; if private, the head of the family himself, having prayed to the gods and looking up to heaven, took up three individual twigs, and interpreted them according to the mark previously impressed: if they forbade it, there was no consultation on that same matter on that day; if it was permitted, confirmation of the outcomes was still required. One can see the methods of bird-signs <note>term: Auguriorum; the practice of divining the future by observing the flight or sounds of birds</note> and omens more fully described by him in that same place, which we intentionally omit for the sake of brevity.

# BOOK ONE

...run to the burials and tombs of Heroes and Great Men, or even sometimes of an entire slaughtered army. Kings chose these sites for themselves for the most part in places where they held their courts and royal residences, especially if it happened that they died at home from illness or in war. Many of this kind are still shown today, such as that of Sigar <note>original: "Sigari"; likely referring to the legendary King Sigar associated with the tragic tale of Hagbard and Signe</note> near the village of Zealand called **Sigersted**, once a great and splendid royal city; and that of Harald **Wartooth** <note>original: "Hyla detand"; Harald Hyldetand, a legendary 8th-century King of Denmark</note> near Lejre <note>original: "Lethram"</note>, and others elsewhere.

Servius <note>A 4th-century commentator on Virgil</note>, in his commentary on the 6th book of the *Aeneid*, states that the Romans did the same. He says, "*Among the ancestors, all men were buried in their own houses*," from which the custom of worshipping the <term>Lares<gloss>household gods associated with the spirits of ancestors</gloss></term> in the home arose. Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar and archbishop whose works preserved much classical knowledge</note> confirms this in *Etymologies* <note>original: "Orig."; refers to his work *Etymologiae* or *Origins*</note>, Book 15, Chapter 11: "*The word for tomb (sepulchrum) is derived from 'buried' (sepulto); previously, however, everyone was buried in his own house.*" But there was once a time when it was forbidden for anyone to be buried in the city. For this law exists in the *Digest* <note>A massive collection of Roman legal rulings compiled under Justinian</note>, Book 47, Title 12, regarding the violation of tombs, paragraph 5: "*The Divine Hadrian, by rescript, established a penalty of forty gold pieces against those who bury in the city, which he ordered to be paid to the treasury; he also ordered the same for magistrates who permitted it, and commanded the place to be confiscated and the body removed.*" The Law of the Twelve Tables <note>The foundation of Roman law, dating to the 5th century BC</note> supports this, as found in Cicero’s second book *On the Laws*: "*Do not bury a dead man in the city.*" Nevertheless, we read of those buried in the city whose virtue had exempted them from the laws, such as Fabricius <note>Gaius Fabricius Luscinus, a Roman general famed for his integrity</note> in the forum, Poplicola, Q. Posthumus, Tubero, the Vestal Virgins, those who celebrated Triumphs, and the Emperors, of whom only Trajan <note>Roman Emperor (98–117 AD)</note> was buried with his bones brought back into the city. For the Spartans, it was permitted to bury in the city near the temples of the gods.

The Great Men, however, desired to be buried on their own estates and fields where they faced the royal highways, provided they had died an honorable death or met their fate among their own people.

And that this was the practice of the ancient Romans <note>original: "Quiritibus"</note> is still attested by the infinite ruins of tombs on the Appian, Aurelian, and Flaminian Ways. Nor does Varro <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BC), a prolific Roman scholar</note>, cited above, disagree in his fifth book *On the Latin Language*. Thus Propertius <note>A Roman elegiac poet</note> writes in Book 2, Elegy 1:

> *If by chance the nearest road leads you to my tomb,*
> *Stop your British chariot with its yoked team.*
> <note>original: "Si te fortè meo, ducet via proxima buſto. / Eſſeda calatis ſiſte Britanna jugis."</note>

<meta>This page continues the discussion of ancient burial customs, shifting from the locations of royal tombs to the specific funerary traditions and epitaphs used by the Danes, specifically focusing on the honor shown even to fallen enemies.</meta>

DANISH MONUMENTS

From this come those solemn formulas: STOP, TRAVELER. LOOK, TRAVELER. BEWARE, TRAVELER. <note>original: "SISTE VIATOR. ASPICE VIATOR. CAVE VIATOR." These were standard Latin phrases carved on tombs to address passersby, as Roman and ancient burials were often placed along roadsides.</note>

Otherwise, if a harsher fate had thrust men toward their very enemies or foes by whom they were deprived of life, they still obtained tombs among them. For it was always a matter of the highest praise to have laid aside a hostile spirit after death and to have practiced hospitable piety in burying corpses. Hence Hading <note>Hadingus, a legendary early King of the Danes mentioned by Saxo Grammaticus</note>, after Uffo had been overcome, laid aside his hatred and **committed his body to a mausoleum of conspicuous workmanship, confessing the greatness of his enemy through the elaborate splendor of the tomb. Thus, the one whom he used to pursue while living with hostile zeal, he decorated after death with the tribute of honor,** as witnessed by Saxo in Book 1. Hence Horvendill <note>Horvendillus, a Jutish chieftain and father of Amleth</note> followed Coller <note>Collerus, a Norwegian King</note>, whom he had killed, **carrying him out with a royal funeral, and following him with a tomb of magnificent workmanship and a great display of funeral rites**, as related by the same author in Book 3. But all of this was done by agreement; for before they entered into battle, they made a pact between themselves that the survivor should honor the slain with proper funeral rites. Our author [Saxo] records that Coller requested this in a truly elegant speech, the words of which I hope it will be agreeable to repeat here:

> Since the outcome remains in doubt, said Coller, we must yield to humanity in turn, nor should we so indulge our tempers that the final duties are neglected. Hatred is in our souls, yet let piety be present, which may finally succeed rigor when the time is right. For although differences of mind separate us, the laws of nature reconcile us. Indeed, we are joined by the fellowship of these laws, however much malice of spirit may divide us. Therefore, let this be our condition of piety: that the victor shall follow the vanquished with funeral rites. For it is certain that the final duties of humanity are contained in these, which no pious man has ever shrunk from. Let both battle lines, having laid aside their rigor, carry out this duty in harmony. Let malice depart after death, and let the feud be put to rest by the funeral. Let a display of such great cruelty be absent from us, that although hatred came between us while living, we should pursue one another's ashes. It will be glorious for the victor if he conducts the funeral of the vanquished magnificently. For he who has paid the due rites to a deceased enemy gains the favor of the survivor for himself, and whoever bestows the effort of humanity on the dead conquers the living with kindness.

But these things are cited at length, though the elegance of both the matter and the speech will excuse it. In Book 8, Hather <note>Hatterus</note> blessed Starkad <note>Starchaterus, the legendary hero and warrior of Norse myth</note>, whom he had killed, with an honorable burial; and lest he should allow such a great athlete to lie without a tomb, he buried his body in the field...

# BOOK ONE

who commonly took care to commit *Rolung* to burial. Indeed, this field in *Scania* <note>Modern-day Skåne, now in Sweden but historically part of Denmark.</note> still enjoys this name today.

If the enemy seemed to neglect this duty, the allies by no means ignored it, even on foreign or hostile soil. Hence, in that bloody battle near *Sigerstadium* <note>Sejerstad</note>, where King *Sigarus* and many other Danish nobles fell—in which also (to quote the words of *Saxo* <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the medieval Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum.</note>) **both sexes were so intent on war that you would not believe the contest lacked female protection**, the proud allies of the leader Hacon, for the sake of burying their Duke, built a hill of remarkable size, which fame even now names "Hacon’s Mound" according to popular belief.

However, just as the honor of burial was granted to those of outstanding merit and distinguished by the praise of their virtues, they decided that tyrants and those marked by some horrendous crime were clearly unworthy of this honor. Thus, in the speech to the soldiers in Book 4 proposed by *Saxo*, *Amleth* <note>Amletus, the legendary figure who inspired Shakespeare's Hamlet.</note> judged the corpse of *Fengo* <note>Feng, Amleth's uncle, whom he killed to avenge his father.</note> worthy of neither urn nor tomb, but ordered that his ashes be scattered to the winds with these words: **I have cremated others; I have left only Fengo's trunk to be burned by your hands, in which you may at least satisfy your desire for a just vengeance. Run forward eagerly, build the pyre, burn the impious body, boil down the wicked limbs, scatter the noxious ashes, and disperse the cruel embers: let no urn, no tomb, enclose the abominable remains of his bones. Let no trace of parricide remain, let no place within the fatherland exist for his contaminated limbs, let no neighborhood contract the contagion; let neither the sea nor the soil be polluted by the hospitality of his damned corpse. I have provided the rest; this duty of piety alone is left to you. With these funeral rites should a tyrant be pursued; with such pomp should a parricide's funeral be led. For it is not fitting that the ashes of one who stripped his country of its liberty should be covered by that country.**

Once the proper rites were completed, they artificially constructed tombs to the size of a hillock or hill by piling up sod and stones, which *Camden* <note>William Camden, a famous English antiquarian.</note> says are called *Barrows* by the *English*. So much diversity in these is still seen among us that they seem to compete with one another in size, roundness, and the various and distinct arrangement of stones. Those that are cruder consist only of earth heaped into a roundness and a cone; those which are encircled at the base by a single row of stones were for commanders of armies and others...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Scandinavian burial customs, moving from the exclusion of criminals from honorable burial to the specific rites and structures associated with high-ranking leaders and kings. ->DANISH MONUMENTS<-

not infrequently, objects are dug up from such mounds. But I believe these mounds were intended for entire families, which is why they also contain altars to receive the communal sacrifices offered for the safety of the entire tribe.

We noted above that if a Leader fell in battle outside his fatherland, he was buried no less magnificently than at home. But some add that trophies made from the spoils of the enemy were placed atop the mounds; they gather this from Jordanes <note>Jordanes was a 6th-century Byzantine historian of Gothic descent, famous for his history of the Goths.</note> regarding the funeral of Attila, leader of the Goths <note>While Attila was King of the Huns, the author follows a tradition associating him with Gothic history.</note>, where he says:

> *After he was mourned with such laments, they celebrated a **STRAVA** over his tomb with a massive feast.* <note>original: "Postquam talibus lamentis est defletus, STRAVAM super tumulum ejus ingenti commessatione celebrant."</note>

By **STRAVA**, they understand it to mean the spoils of the enemy, and this is based on the authority of Placidus Lactantius <note>A 5th or 6th-century commentator on the works of the poet Statius.</note> regarding book 12 of the *Thebaid* by Statius, where he has this to say:

> *A pyre was built for dead kings from the spoils of the enemy, a burial rite which the Barbarians are said to still observe today, which they call **STRABAS** in their own language.* <note>original: "Exsuviis hostium exstruebatur regibus mortuis pyra, quem ritum sepulturæ hodie quoq́; Barbari servare dicuntur, quem STRABAS dicunt lingua sua."</note>

But to speak my mind freely: I could easily believe that the mounds of Kings and Leaders were sometimes decorated with enemy spoils; however, I do not equally concede that pyres were built out of them. For Jordanes says the *Stravas* were celebrated with a massive feast, which does not fit the description of enemy spoils, but rather fits banquets and funeral feasts established in honor of the deceased. Lactantius, however, clearly enough understands *Straba* to mean the funeral pyre on which the body of the deceased was burned, and which consisted of the enemy's plunder. It is one thing to make a pyre from enemy spoils in which they are burned and perish; it is quite another to place them atop a mound as an ornament, so they might remain there and testify to victories. Therefore, *STRAVA* denotes either a trophy or a magnificent banquet celebrated in honor of the deceased.

Related to the *Strava* was that which our ancestors once called the **Arfveøl** <term>Inheritance-ale; from the Old Norse 'arfr' (inheritance) and 'öl' (ale/feast).</term>, namely a solemn banquet which Kings and Nobles celebrated in honor of a deceased parent when the succession of the Kingdom and property was granted. For it was permitted for no one to succeed a deceased parent unless he first hosted the nobles and friends with such a banquet and solemn rites.

### BOOK ONE.

In these ceremonies, a specific custom was especially observed: in honor of the deceased, led by the heir, massive drinking vessels had to be drained, and the successor would bind himself by a solemn vow to perform some memorable and outstanding deed.

A famous example of this can be seen in the deeds of **Haakon Baron** in the *History of Norway* <note>The author refers to his own edited version of a Norwegian chronicle.</note>, published by us in our native tongue on page 131. There, **Sweyn**, nicknamed *Tuisteg* <note>Sweyn Forkbeard (Svein Tjugeskjegg), King of Denmark and England.</note> or Suenotto, King of Denmark, being about to take up the kingdom following the death of his father **Harold** <note>Harold Bluetooth.</note>, invited not only the nobles of the realm but also the **Jomsvikings** <note>The "pirates of Julin" or Jomsvikings were a legendary order of Viking mercenaries. original: "Julinensibus pyratis"</note> to this solemn *Arffueol*. Before he would lay a hand upon the rudder of the kingdom, he ascended his father’s throne and first drank a great draught from a cup dedicated to his father’s memory, offering it to the guests. He then added a vow that within three years he would invade England and either kill or expel **King Ethelred** <note>Ethelred the Unready. original: "Adelradum"</note>. Following him, the Jomsvikings, after draining the vessel, made such vows that they could ultimately only be fulfilled at the greatest risk to their lives. For a more detailed discussion of these events, consult the History itself. <term>Arffueol</term> <note>Inheritance ale.</note> literally means "inheritance beer" in Latin, just as <term>Festensol</term> means "engagement" or "contract beer." <note>original: "hæreditaria cerevisia... locationis aut conductionis cerevisia"</note> Just as a bride is "contracted" to a groom through such a banquet for the coming nuptials, so too is the Kingdom or inheritance solemnly taken over by the son and heir through this same medium.

Burial mounds occur not only in fields and meadows, but also in woods and groves. However, **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century Danish historian.</note> teaches in Book 8 that these were once placed in sunny, open spots:

> *The current thickness of the forest now occupies the hills which the labor of the ancients had built on the plain for the care of burying corpses.* <note>original: "Colles quos in plano humandorum cadaverum cura veterum labor exstruxerat, præsentis silvæ congeries occupat."</note>

He attributes the cause of this change to the desertion of the land by its inhabitants and tillers, which occurred during the migration of the **Lombards** <note>The Longobardi, a Germanic people.</note> in the time of **King Snio**. 

> *Meanwhile,* he says, *as the work of the tillers grew scarce and the traces of the furrows were covered over by neglect, the land of the Danes took on a wild appearance; having lost the beauty of its native soil, it became bristling with the shapeless density of encroaching groves. This is shown by the current face of its fields. For those acres which were once fertile with crops are now seen packed with tree trunks.* <note>original: "Interea, inquit, Danorum tellus rarescente cultorum opera, sulcorumq; vestigiis situ obductis, silvestrem induit vultum... Quæ enim olim feraciā frugum jugera fuerant, eadem nunc arboreo stipite conferta visuntur."</note>

> *where the common crowd makes its busy path.*
> *After death, the tombs of lovers are so defiled;*
> *let a remote earth cover me with its leafy shade.*

->*Either a mound walled in by unknown sand is damp,*<-

->*And the ashes of Kings rest within a constructed mountain.*<-
<note>original: "Et Regum cineres exstructo monte quiescunt."</note>

From this, Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636 AD) was an influential scholar; his *Etymologies* was the standard encyclopedia of the Middle Ages.</note> says in Book 15, Chapter 12: *The powerful were buried either under mountains or in mountains; from this arose the practice of either building pyramids over corpses or erecting massive columns.* Hence those inscriptions on stones: THEY CREATED A MONUMENT BY PLACING A STRUCTURE UPON IT. <note>original: "FECERUNT MONUMENTUM ÆDIFICIO IMPOSITO."</note> Georgius Gvalterus <note>George Walter was a 17th-century scholar of Sicilian history.</note> asserts in his *Tables of Sicily* that ancient mountain monuments are found everywhere throughout Sicily, especially at **Pantalica** <note>A massive necropolis in Sicily with thousands of tombs cut into canyon walls.</note> in the territory of **Cesare Gaetani**, where they were carved into steep hills from the bottom to the very top. *Since these are countless, he believes they were the burial places for mortals of both higher and lower status.* It is well known that the people of **Agrigentum** <note>An ancient Greek city in Sicily, now Agrigento.</note> were so devoted to building tombs that they did not deny them even to certain horses proven in competition, nor to small birds once kept as pets at home, according to Diodorus Siculus <note>A 1st-century BC Greek historian.</note>.

Nor were these mounds constructed with slight effort or small expense. For Norwegian history testifies concerning **Harald Fairhair** <note>The first King of Norway (r. c. 872–930). original: "Haraldo Harfagre"</note> that two petty kings in **Namdalen** <note>A district in central Norway. original: "Naumedal"</note>, who were maternal brothers, labored for three full years at great expense to build a single burial mound. And **Harald Bluetooth** <note>The King of Denmark and Norway (r. c. 958–986) famously credited with the unification of Denmark. original: "Haraldus Blaatand"</note>, son of Gorm, applied his entire army and a huge number of oxen to a massive stone with which he intended to decorate his parents' tomb; our own **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), the author of the first full history of Denmark.</note> recounts this in Book 10 of his history: *After this, Harald called forth the entire fleet of the kingdom so that he would not approach a task of such great weight with small preparation; joining forces of men and oxen, he ordered a stone of unusual size, found on the Jutland shore, to be hauled away to mark his mother's mound, etc.* And this work was so highly valued (as he adds shortly after) that **Harald** himself, occupied with the dragging of the stone, began to ask some of his men arriving from the fleet more closely: whether they had ever seen such a great mass attempted by mortal hands elsewhere. Therefore, our ancestors do not seem to have been surpassed by any nation in making funeral expenditures, and these mounds formerly cost much more than we value them at today.

> *And the ashes of Kings rest in a built-up mountain.*
<note>original: "Et Regum cineres exstructo monte quiescunt."</note>

Hence **Isidore** <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), an influential medieval scholar whose encyclopedic works were standard references.</note> in Book 15, Chapter 12 says: *The powerful were buried either under mountains or in mountains; from this practice it was derived that bodies would be honored by pyramids or massive columns.* From this come those inscriptions on stones: **THEY MADE THE MONUMENT WITH A BUILDING PLACED UPON IT**. **Georgius Gualterus** in his *Tables of Sicily* asserts that ancient monuments near mountains are found everywhere throughout **Sicily**, especially at **Pantalica** <note>A large necropolis in Sicily containing thousands of rock-cut chamber tombs.</note> in the territory of **Cesare Gaetano**, where they are carved into steep hills from the base to their very summits. Since these are innumerable, he suggests they were burial places for mortals of both higher and lower status. It is well known that the people of **Agrigento** <note>An ancient city in Sicily famous for its Greek temples and elaborate funerary culture.</note> were so devoted to building tombs that they did not deny them even to certain horses proven in competition, nor to little birds once held as household favorites, according to **Diodorus Siculus** <note>A Greek historian of the 1st century BC.</note>.

These mounds were not completed with light effort or small expense. For Norwegian history testifies regarding **Harald Fairhair** <note>Harald I (c. 850–932), traditionally considered the first King of Norway.</note> that two petty kings in **Namdal** <note>A district in central Norway.</note>, who were maternal brothers, labored for three whole years at great expense to build a single mound. And **Harald Bluetooth** <note>Harald Gormsson (c. 935–985), the King of Denmark and Norway who oversaw the creation of the famous Jelling Stones.</note>, the son of Gorm, applied his entire army and a vast number of oxen to a massive stone, with which he intended to decorate the tombs of his parents. Our **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), a Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum.</note> follows this account in Book 10 of his history:

> *After this, Harald, putting forth the whole fleet of the kingdom so that he might not approach a weight of such massive bulk with small equipment, joined the forces of men and oxen. He ordered a stone of unusual size found on the Jutland shore, with which he might distinguish his mother's mound, to be dragged away, etc. And this work was so highly valued (as he adds shortly after) that Harald himself, occupied with the dragging of the stone, began to ask those arriving from the fleet more closely: whether they had ever seen such a mass attempted by mortal hand elsewhere.*

Therefore, our countrymen seem not to have yielded to any nation in providing for parental funeral expenses, and these mounds once cost much more than they are now valued by us.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the scale and construction of ancient burial sites, transitioning from the monumental tombs of the Mediterranean to the specific funerary customs and historical eras of the North as recorded by Scandinavian historians and manuscripts.</meta>

<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

Among other nations, a limit was prescribed for the manner of building. Plato, as Cicero testifies in Book 2 of *On the Laws* <note>original: "de LL." referring to De Legibus</note>, forbade any tomb to be higher than what five men could complete in five days; nor could more stone be erected, nor more inscribed, than what would contain the praise of the deceased, in no more than four heroic verses <term>heroic verses: the dactylic hexameter, the standard meter for epic poetry</term>, which Ennius calls "long verses."

What Olaus Magnus <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557) was a Swedish ecclesiastic and writer known for his "History of the Northern Peoples."</note> reports in Book 16, Chapter 37, I have been unable to find in any other writer of our history, nor does it seem to be entirely consistent with the truth. Namely, he claims that it was the custom of the ancients to hang the corpses of princes in leafy trees, especially oaks, as if in sacred places consecrated to the gods. We do indeed read of those chosen as victims <note>Referring to human sacrifice in Germanic paganism, often associated with the god Odin.</note> being hung in sacred places; but that princes who ended their lives either in war or at home by disease were hung after death is something I have not yet happened to read in any author of proven repute.

## CHAPTER SEVEN.

### On the rites of burial.

I shall not recount here the burial rites of various foreign nations, about which others have written excellently; I consider it worthwhile to touch only upon the customs of our own people, at least as far as our antiquities permit.

Christianus Cilicius <note>Christian von Itzehoe, a 16th-century historian who wrote about the wars of the Dithmarschen region.</note> pursues the matter briefly in Book 1 of his *History of the Dithmarscher War*:
> *Their burials, he says, were in forests and fields, and they fortified the mounds by clothing them with gathered stones, a kind of which many are still seen here and there, which are called "Giant's Paths." Some also (but few) wished to be cremated on built-up pyres in the Roman fashion, and their collected ashes kept in an urn, traces of which have been found in several places in our century.*
<note>original: "Erant, inquit, eorum sepulturae in silvis & agris..."</note>

I have learned from the ancients that certain epochs were introduced among the Northern peoples based on burial rites; since these rites varied, the eras were changed accordingly. For thus my manuscript on parchment <note>original: "membrana mea M.S."</note> records: Three ages of men are usually numbered, which received their names from the manner of their funeral offerings. The first is **Roisold** / the second **Høigold** / the third **Christendomsold**.
<note>These terms represent the "Age of Burning" (Old Norse: Brunaöld), the "Age of Mounds" (Haugsöld), and the "Age of Christianity."</note>

# BOOK ONE.

For in the earliest times, when they were about to perform the funeral rites for the deceased, they would form a site in a flat field near a royal road or on the estate of the deceased using stones of a measured size. It was of an oblong shape, sometimes twenty fathoms <term>fathom: translated from the Latin 'orgia,' a unit of measurement based on the span of a man's outstretched arms, roughly six feet</term> in length and three in width. Within this, they would cremate the corpse of the deceased; the collected ashes they enclosed in urns, and having placed these in the middle of the ring, they packed them on all sides with larger rocks, with a wider stone thrown on top to cover the rest. From there, they filled the entire area with stones, sand, and clumps of earth, and from above they built up a hill in the form of a small mound, which they finally covered with sod so that its greenness might refresh the eyes of passersby. They called these tombs **Roiser** <note>original: "Roiser"; likely referring to the Danish 'røser' or cairns</note> and this burial rite **Roise**. They maintain that this honor was at least granted to kings; others were entombed with less pomp.

The structure of these mounds is still inferred from the ruins, especially around the sea shores where the violence of the sea tide has swallowed part of the land but left another part intact.

In rocky and maritime places, they built mounds from heaps of stones and sand; in more fertile areas, they were made from rich earth with fewer stones added, encircling the base like a crown. Not so many years ago, the Reverend and Most Distinguished man, Master Caspar Bartholinus <note>Caspar Bartholinus the Elder (1585–1629) was a renowned Danish physician and theologian, and the author's brother-in-law.</note> of pious memory, my honored kinsman and colleague, when he was serving as the Rector Magnificent of the University, came for business reasons to a village called **Eggerup** near Korsør <note>original: "Crucis-oram," a Latinization of the Danish town name Korsør</note>. There, when he understood there was a hill in the vicinity from which those carrying away clay had several times happened upon certain pots filled with ashes, he went to the place himself to explore what lay beneath. Having dug up a little earth, he found an urn made of blue clay, in which were enclosed ashes and fragments of burnt bones. These he brought to us, and he gave me both a fragment of the pot and a piece of a rib as a gift, which I keep among my rarities <note>original: "rariora," referring to items in a cabinet of curiosities or museum collection</note>. Sometimes, at the summit of these mounds, they constructed a tomb for receiving bones by means of an orderly arrangement of massive stones. # BOOK ONE.
<sig>F 3</sig>
<meta>catchword: com-</meta>

<note>original: "bello Gallico lib. 6"</note> Caesar's *Gallic War*, book 6, and Tacitus's *On the Customs of the Germans*. For what the former reports concerning the Gauls and the latter concerning the Germans (among whom he numbers the Gothini, Marsingi, Osi, etc.), must be understood as applying equally to our own people. This is especially true when he says: *“There is no ostentation in their funerals; they observe only this: that the bodies of illustrious men are burned with specific types of wood.”* And he adds: *“They do not heap the funeral pyre with costly robes or perfumes; to each man is given his own weapons, and for some, even his horse is added to the fire. A mound of turf raises the grave.”* <note>These quotes from Tacitus's *Germania* (Chapter 27) describe the austere military burials of the ancient Germanic tribes, emphasizing honor over material luxury.</note> Others have mentioned this practice here and there, so it would be a waste of effort for me to dwell on these points any longer. Alexander Guagnini <note>A 16th-century soldier and chronicler known for his descriptions of Eastern Europe.</note> asserts much the same regarding the European Sarmatians in his account of Sarmatia, discussing it in this manner: *“Their burials were in forests and fields, and they remained prominent, covering the mounds with heaped stones; this type of grave is still seen everywhere in the regions of Russia.”* Some also followed the Roman custom of cremating the corpses and hiding the collected ashes in urns. This is not surprising, since the Cimbri, Goths, Vandals, Dacians, and Sarmatians all emerged from the same ancestral stock.

But as to why not only our ancestors but also the Romans cremated their dead, Nicolaus Thurius <note>A humanist scholar who wrote on the history of the Heruli, a Germanic tribe.</note> attempts to explain in his *Short Commentary on the Annals of the Heruli*, section S, in this way: *“It was the Roman custom to burn bodies, by which they signaled that the soul—which alone in us is divine—departs to the stars on a fiery chariot.”* For in this way, the body, because it is of the earth, would settle into ashes. Furthermore, the ancients were persuaded that the higher the flame and smoke rose from the cremated bodies, the more beloved the deceased were to their gods; and the more items were cast into the pyres, the wealthier those whose bodies were burned would be in the next life.

The third and final age, the **Age of Christianity** <note>original: "Christendoms old"</note>, is defined by the manner in which we Christians are now accustomed to burying the dead. It is not necessary to say much about this, as it is well known to everyone.

However, the ancients placed into their mounds not only corpses or ashes, but also weapons, spears, horses, gold, silver, and other **precious heirlooms** <term>κειμήλια; treasures or property of great value passed down through generations</term> most dear to the deceased. This method of burial first began at Uppsala <note>The religious and political heart of ancient Sweden.</note> when the funeral rites were prepared for Freyr, the son of Yngvi. But after that high-spirited King of the Danes, **Dan**, had built for himself a mound of remarkable size—into which, after his death, his corpse was to be carried, adorned with the royal crown, dressed in armor, and placed upon a horse equipped with all its trappings, with many talents of gold and silver added—the earlier method of burial began to be abolished and this new one was introduced, which his descendants and friends willingly embraced. And so began the second age called *Høijelsetiid* <note>Old Norse/Danish for "The Age of Mound-Sitting" or "Mound-Burial Age."</note>, or the Age of Mounds. Though in Sweden and Norway, the former age lasted longer.

That various ornaments and <term>heirlooms<note>original Greek: κειμήλια (keimēlia), meaning treasures or precious goods stored away as property.</note></term> were placed in the mounds of kings along with the corpses is clear partly from the preceding sections and partly from what follows.

The history of Olaf Tryggvason, King of Norway, relates that he saw to it that many burial mounds and tombs of his predecessors were demolished so that he might turn the enclosed treasures to better uses. The surviving records testify that he scraped together a great sum of gold and silver from these. Those things which were brought by friends and others along with the corpse were called "gifts" by the Romans. For so says Tibullus in book 2, Elegy 4:

Also, from a certain mound located near the village of Tved, several urns along with scorched bones were shown to me; they were discovered when sand was being removed from the hill to pave a road. The hill so abounded with them that you could hardly set foot anywhere or press down a spade without the remains of urns and bones revealing themselves as the covering earth was removed.”*

A larger version of the same figure occupies the center of the rowel. This crowned letter undoubtedly suggests that the spur belonged to some **King Harald**, but precisely which one is not for us to guess. 

One may also observe here that the bow which grips the foot is no larger than what would fit comfortably on my own heel; from this, it can be gathered that the man who owned it was by no means of giant stature, but rather of average height. 

In my own archives, I also possess a spur, found underground some years ago, which carries the scent of no less antiquity, although its shape differs greatly from the former. The bow intended for encircling the heel ends in a nearly sharp and obliquely widened angle where it joins the shank, which exceeds four inches in length. It does not embrace the foot in a straight line, but with both arms tilted and then raised again, it forms a Roman **V** on both sides. The rowel inserted at the end of the shank is quite small, though marked with twelve rays (some of which are consumed by decay), as you see expressed in the plate by the letter **E**. ->### BOOK ONE<-

...for the citizens, he provided by law that whichever head of a household <term>paterfamilias|The male head of a household</term> fell in that war, he should be committed to a mound with his horse and all the insignia of his armor. If any grave robber <note>original: "vespillonum," referring to those who handle or plunder the dead</note>, driven by wicked greed, should attempt to disturb it, he would pay the penalty not only with his blood, but also by having his own corpse left unburied, deprived of both a tomb and funeral rites. Indeed, Frotho believed it was only fair that a defiler of another’s ashes should be granted no funeral service, and should suffer in his own body the same fate he had inflicted upon another’s. However, he decreed that the body of a centurion or a **Satrap** <note>A term borrowed from Persian to denote a high-ranking governor or official.</note> was to be buried by a pyre constructed from his own ship. Furthermore, he ordered that the bodies of ten pilots should be consumed by the fire of a single ship; while any slain leader or king was to be cremated upon his own vessel. He wished such scrupulous observation to be maintained in conducting the funerals of the slain so that he would not allow indiscriminate <note>original: "promiscuos," meaning mixed or without distinction</note> funeral rites to exist. From these facts, one may easily conclude that even in the time of this king, both methods of burial were in use: since he decreed that heads of households were to be placed in mounds with their ornaments without being cremated, while centurions, leaders, and kings were to be placed upon a pyre.

Nevertheless, Frotho could not prevent posterity, through his laws, from striving to violate the mounds of the great in the hope of profit, nor from attempting to ransack their hollows—often at no small cost to life and health. I shall not repeat more recent stories that are on everyone's lips; I would rather hear what Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the medieval Danish historian.</note> relates in his third book regarding **Harald**, who attempted to dig through the burial mound of **Balder** <note>Balderus, a heroic figure in Saxo’s history based on the Norse god Baldr.</note> in the hope of seizing riches:

> *This mound (namely the hill in which **Balder** was buried), certain men of our time, of whom **Harald** was the chief, attacked by night in the hope of finding money, spurred by the fame of the ancient burial; but they left, seized by a sudden horror. For from the very peak of the broken mountain, a sudden force of a torrent seemed to burst forth with a great roar of water, its rapid mass involving whatever it struck in a headlong fall upon the fields of the island below. Disturbed by this onslaught, the diggers threw down their shovels and fled in different directions, thinking they would be caught in the whirlpools of the rushing water if they tried to continue their task any longer. Thus, a sudden fear struck by the gods who guard that place turned the minds of the youths from their greed to a concern for their safety, and teaching them to be more mindful of their lives, they abandoned their greedy purpose.*

Read more to this effect in Saxo himself. Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, the Roman naturalist.</note> in Book 7, Chapter 54 says: *The practice of cremation itself among the Ro—*

...thinks it was not a custom of the ancient Roman institution, but after they learned that those buried during long-distant wars were being dug up and desecrated, the practice was then established. Others believe the custom of cremating bodies among the Romans was older than Pliny thinks, because in Plutarch’s writings, Numa <note>Numa Pompilius, the legendary second king of Rome, known for establishing religious rites.</note> forbade his own body to be burned, and likewise forbade the funeral pyre to be sprinkled with wine, as witnessed by the same Pliny in Book 14, Chapter 12. Furthermore, Ovid, in the 4th book of the *Fasti* <note>A poetic calendar of Roman festivals.</note> regarding the funeral of Remus, has these lines:

->*He anointed the limbs destined for the fire; so did*<-
->*Faustulus and Acca, with her hair loose in grief.*<-
->*Then the youths, not yet made citizens, wept;*<-
->*The sudden flame of the lamented pyre was the final act.*<-

Moreover, when a body was to be burned, they were accustomed to set aside a finger to offer as funeral sacrifices <note>original: "inferias"</note>. From this comes that passage of Festus: *A limb of the deceased was said to be cut away when his finger was removed, so that the proper rites might be performed with it while the rest of the body was burned.* A bone was also set aside if someone died abroad, so that the family rites <note>original: "parentarentur," referring to the Parentalia festival for ancestors.</note> could be performed at home and the family could be ritually purified. Cicero writes in the second book of *On the Laws*: *It is not necessary for us to explain what the end of a mourning family is, what kind of sacrifice is made to the household gods with rams, or how the set-aside bone is covered with earth.* Varro <note>A prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note> says in Book 4: *Because the earth is "humus," a dead man is "humatus" (inhumed) when he is covered by earth; for those cremated by the Romans, a sod of earth was not thrown into his tomb, unless a piece of the body was set aside for the purification of the family. Until that piece is covered with earth during the purification, as the Priests say, the family remains religiously stained as long as the person remains unburied.* They also report that it was the custom for relatives to open the eyes of the dying person on the pyre as they breathed their last, and then to show them closed to heaven; they also placed a coin—a <term>danake|δανάην: a small Greek coin placed in the mouth of the deceased</term>—into the mouth, from which they might pay the fare to Charon <note>The mythological ferryman who carried souls across the river Styx.</note> when crossing the Stygian marsh. It is also established that it was not permitted for a toothless child to be cremated; instead, religious tradition dictated they be buried in the earth, because it was believed they had departed as divine beings.

The *History of Norway* <note>Likely referring to the "Historia Norvegiæ" or Snorri Sturluson's "Heimskringla."</note> right at its beginning ascribes the rite of cremating corpses to **Odin**. If anyone desires to know more specifically with what pomp or solemnity the funeral pyres of kings were usually constructed, let them consult our frequently praised author <note>Referring to the 12th-century historian Saxo Grammaticus, whose *Gesta Danorum* is the primary source for this section.</note> in Book 8, where he elegantly sets forth all the rites with which Ringo <note>Sigurd Hring, a legendary king of the Swedes.</note> took care to place the body of Harald <note>Harald Wartooth, King of the Danes, who fell at the legendary Battle of Brávellir.</note>, whom he had slain, upon the funeral pyre. Half the day was spent in this task. At last, the club was found with the body. Thinking that he must perform ancestral rites <note>original: "parentandum"</note> for Harald’s hands, he dedicated the horse he sat upon—harnessed appropriately with golden seats to the royal chariot—to Harald's titles. Then he made vows and added a prayer, that Harald, using this transport, might precede those who shared his fate to the underworld <note>original: "tartara"</note>, and might seek peaceful seats for his allies and enemies alike with the warden of the abyss, Pluto <note>The author uses the Roman name Pluto to represent the ruler of the dead, translating Norse mythology into classical terms for his readers.</note>. And when the fire began to consume the body placed upon it, the grieving nobles began to circle around, and he began to exhort them all more intensely to generously pass into the nourishment of the pyre arms, gold, and whatever was most precious, in veneration of a king who had deserved so much and such things from everyone. He also ordered that the ashes of the burnt body, committed to an urn, be carried to Lejre <note>original: "Lethram," the ancient royal seat of the Danish kings on the island of Zealand.</note>, and there be buried in the royal fashion with a horse and arms.* These things are cited at length because I think they contribute much to the illustration of this whole matter. In Book 3, he touches more briefly upon the funeral rites of King Gelderus of Saxony, who was killed in a maritime war: *He carried out the burial of Gelderus, the King of Saxony, with a most beautiful funeral service, placing him on a pyre built from ships, atop the bodies of his rowers; he not only committed his ashes, like the remains of a royal body, to a notable tomb, but also decorated them with funeral rites full of veneration.*

No doubt she fortified the piled-up mass at the sides with stakes and poles, or perhaps crowned the summit with them; our own *Huitfeldt* <note>Arild Huitfeldt (1546–1609), a prominent Danish historian and state official.</note> leans toward this view. The *Julin History* <note>original: "Historia Julinensis"; likely referring to the chronicle of the legendary Viking stronghold of Jomsborg (Wollin).</note> reports that on the southern side of the rampart there was a ditch ten fathoms <term>orgiae</term> <note>An *orgia* is a measurement similar to a fathom, roughly the span of outstretched arms.</note> wide and just as deep. Above it, however, a bulwark was built from beams and wood with very firm joints, so that towers of the same material stood upon it one hundred fathoms apart from each other, from which the defenders could receive the enemy with weapons and strongly defend themselves. This was no doubt the work of Queen *Thyra*, of which *Eric of Pomerania* speaks. From this, perhaps, our own *Lætus* <note>Erasmus Lætus (1526–1582), a Danish scholar and Latin poet.</note> concludes in Book 4 of *Danish Affairs* that *Harald* was the first of all to make this rampart more solid by constructing it of earth, while he sings thus:
> *This is he who first fortified the Cimbrian* <note>The Cimbrian peninsula, referring to Jutland.</note> *fields with a solid rampart,*
> *And from the body of the earth tore up a massive ridge,*
> *Which drives its immense curve across long tracts,*
> *And marches through the middle of the Isthmus,*
> *Joining the shores of the Eastern Sea with the Western coast,*
> *And looks back upon the slender city of Schleswig!*

One part happened by lot to be raised and fortified by Scania <note>The southernmost province of the Scandinavian peninsula, then part of Denmark.</note>, another by Zealand, and a third by Funen. To Scania fell that part which extends from the gate commonly called Kalegat as far as Hollingstedt; to the people of Zealand and Funen came that portion which turns from the gate toward the Schlei <note>A narrow inlet of the Baltic Sea in Schleswig-Holstein.</note>. Most evident traces of this thing still remain, and can be demonstrated to the eye of the student of antiquity. And so that a plenty of food might be available, the Jutes and the people of Schleswig provided and brought supplies to nourish the multitude of those who were digging and performing the work. Moreover, they surrounded and encircled the rampart with a deep ditch, which is still visible everywhere.*

These things have been cited at greater length because they contain the manner and means by which this work was constructed, which I have not found in other authors.

Although these authors expressly assert that Queen Thyra and Harald built the mass of this rampart and brought the work to completion <note>original: "ad umbilicum perduxisse," literally "led to the navel," a Latin idiom for finishing a book or a great task</note> so that they might suppress the insolence of the Saxons, who were attempting frequent incursions into Jutland <note>original: "Cimbriam," the Cimbrian Peninsula</note>; nevertheless, nothing prevents us from determining that its first line was drawn by Godfred <note>A 9th-century King of the Danes who first fortified the border against Charlemagne.</note>, and perhaps a rough work was begun then, which Thyra and her son later enlarged or restored when it had collapsed, while others brought it to its highest perfection. But, as our Hvitfeld <note>Arild Hvitfeldt (1546–1609), a Danish historian and state official.</note> teaches, it was completed in the year 1158 at the request of Bishop Absolon <note>Absolon (c. 1128–1201), the powerful Archbishop of Lund and advisor to the Danish kings.</note> so that they might keep the Saxons and Slavs <note>original: "Sclavos"; likely referring to the Wends, a West Slavic people.</note> from the kingdom. However, it seems to have been begun in the year 1163, if faith is to be placed in the *Chronicle of King Eric*, which recites these words for the said year: *“Then the King, wishing to prevent the malice of the Teutons <note>original: "Teutonicorum"; a general term for Germanic/German peoples.</note>, surrounded the fortification of Danevirke with a wall; for previously that place had been fortified only with wood.”* <note>original: "Tunc Rex malitias Teutonicorum prævenire volens, munitionem Danevirke muro circumcinxit: ante enim lignis tantum munitus erat locus ille."</note>

It is deeply to be lamented that such a great, immense, and admirable monument of human industry and strength has now so fallen that its ruins are barely visible in certain places. For while it stood in its full vigor, there was scarcely anything that could compete with it in strength, so much so that it was considered by all in its age to be the insuperable bulwark of Cimbria <note>The Jutland Peninsula.</note>. We read that sixty thousand men were at times stationed in its garrison. For when Henry the Lion <note>Duke of Saxony and Bavaria (1129–1195).</note>, around the year 1177, was planning an invasion of Denmark, Bernhard of Ratzeburg dissuaded him, because he knew that *“the guard of the Danevirke had been entrusted to sixty thousand Danes,”* <note>original: "Danevirka custodiam Danorum sexaginta millibus mandatam esse"</note> as Pontanus <note>Johannes Isacius Pontanus (1571–1639), a royal historian.</note> reports in Book 6 of *Danish Affairs*, in the *History of Valdemar I*.

Hence, when Sveno <note>Svend III Grathe (c. 1125–1157).</note> saw that he could by no means break through it by force, he was forced to pave a way for himself through trickery and bribes. By what means he accomplished this, Krantz <note>Albert Krantz (c. 1450–1517), a German historian.</note> teaches in *Denmark*, Book <margin>Book 5, chapter 38.</margin> 5, Chapter 38. And when they had arrived, he says, *“at the great rampart which they called the ‘Work of the Danes,’ he sent ahead someone to corrupt the guardian of the gates with a huge sum of money, so that, with the gates unlocked, he might allow passage without a fight. Having agreed on the money, the man accepted it, thinking he had performed a service for a rightful king. But then the Bishop said it was fitting that the perpetrator, along with the very price of his treason, be fixed to the gates with a single noose.”* <note>original: "Sed tum Pontifex dignum esse ait, quod cum ipsa proditionis mercede, autor uno portis laqueo figeretur."</note> It is therefore clear from this that it was once locked with very strong gates and bars. *“There were,”* says Pontanus in Book 5 of *Danish Affairs*, *“towers, or rather watchtowers, built upon this mound, arranged at such intervals that it was easy to notice the enemy approaching from a distance and to prevent their entry.”* <note>original: "Erant... in hoc aggere extructæ turres vel speculæ potius, per intervalla ita dispositæ, ut ex iis eminus adventantem hostem facile esset animadvertere, atq; aditu prohibere."</note> We conclude, therefore, that nothing was lacking here which one could desire for the structure of a proper fortification (according to the standard of that age). At that time, as it appears, this mass was closed by a single gate called Wiglesdor by Thietmar (perhaps named after King Wiglet), which was continually fortified with such firm bars and strenuous guards that the inhabitants of Denmark seemed to themselves safe from every assault of foreigners and the full force of the Roman Empire. ...residence <note>original: "micilium", the conclusion of "domicilium" from the previous page</note> not far from the small village of **Dannevirke**, which is adjacent to and connected with the rampart; and even now, the surviving ruins, the traces of the ramparts, and the ditches clearly show this.

A work of a not dissimilar nature seems to have been that most celebrated wall, the border of the Roman province in Britain, which some of the ancients called the *Barbarian Rampart, the Frontier Defense, and the Enclosure*; Antoninus and Cassiodorus called it the *Rampart* <note>original: "vallum"</note>, Bede called it the *Wall*, and the Britons called it *Gualsever* and *Mursever*. The Scots called it *Sotiswaith*, and the English *The Picts-wall*, the *Pictish Wall*, and *The Keep-wall*—a wall of guard separating England from Scotland. For many labored upon it, among whom Julius Agricola is established as the first; after him, the Emperor Hadrian, whom the biographer Spartianus reports to have led this wall for eighty thousand paces <note>Approximately 80 Roman miles.</note> to divide the barbarians from the Romans. After him, under Antoninus Pius, Lollius Urbicus worked on it. But Septimius Severus built far more firmly, who, as Orosius witnesses: *“drew a great ditch and a most firm rampart fortified with frequent towers for one hundred and twenty-two miles from sea to sea.”* Others then contributed their efforts, until a sixth frontier defense <note>original: "prætentura"</note> rose anew; concerning which, and this whole matter, read William Camden <note>A famous English antiquarian (1551–1623).</note> who discusses it at length in his description of Britain.

Cosmographers also tell of the Chinese kingdom toward the North, girded by mountains and a very long wall so that it might be safe from the incursions of the Tartars. They say a certain King Tzinzoo <note>A reference to Qin Shi Huang, the first Emperor of China.</note> constructed this work, and because of it, the letters and languages of many were raised even to the heavens. How much more justly do we value our own ancestors who dared to undertake such a great fortification, which extended from the British Ocean <note>The North Sea.</note> to the Baltic Sea through the entire width of Cimbria <note>The Jutland Peninsula.</note>? It was of such mass and strength that it was able to shut out the greatest forces of Emperors and Kings and withstand the power of all enemies. But since this work has its own trumpeters <note>i.e., its own famous chroniclers and advocates.</note> among foreign writers, I shall sound the retreat here <note>i.e., conclude this topic</note> so as not to repeat what has already been done, as I am about to approach the wonders of the stones <note>This likely refers to the upcoming section on megaliths and runestones.</note>.

# CHAPTER NINE.
## *On Danish stone monuments.*

Up to this point, we have seen those types of monuments that antiquity constructed either from earth alone, or from stones joined with earth. The logic of our order now requires us to examine those that consist solely of stones. We gather from the ruins still visible today that these existed in two distinct varieties. Some consisted of stones inscribed with ancient letters, commonly called **Runic**, or **Gothic** by foreigners; others consisted of certain rough, uninscribed stones, yet arranged in a specific order and series. 

Of these uninscribed stones, some constituted forums <note>Places of public assembly and legal judgment.</note>, in which justice was administered to each person according to laws and statutes; some designated assembly places <note>original: "loca comitialia"</note> in which the election of Kings and Emperors was also performed with solemn ritual; some enclosed circuses <note>Arenas for physical contests.</note>, in which giants and fighters <note>original: "pugiles"</note> fought bravely in duels; finally, some indicated places where entire armies were routed and defeated—you might call these trophies. According to the *History of Norway*, Odin <note>original: "Othinus"</note> is established as the originator of these monuments among us.

Regarding the evidence of duels, they intended these to be stones arranged in a long row or a straight line; however, sometimes there is only a single stone, though a massive or great one, as is clear from Book 2, Chapter 9 of Adam of Bremen’s history. For the author says in this place:
> *He went up to the ford called Agrimeswedel, where Biurguido fought a duel against a champion of the Slavs, killed him, and a stone was placed in the same spot in memory.*

He uses the word "champion" <note>original: "Campionem"</note> for the person whom the Danes call a **Kempe**, meaning a warrior or giant; the Romans changed this word into *Cimber*. For when they noticed that all the strongest men were called **Kemper** by the Danes, they used the word *Cimber* according to the standard of their own language.

Here, however, it should be noted in passing that the ancient method of fighting, both in duels and in war, was far different from what we see in use in our own century. For in ancient times, in performing these contests, frequent exchanges of blows were not sought, but it was...

## CHAPTER NINE.
### *Concerning Danish stone monuments.*

Hitherto we have seen the types of monuments that antiquity constructed either from earth alone, or from earth joined with stones; the nature of our arrangement now requires us to examine those which consist of stones alone. We gather from the still-visible ruins that these existed in two distinct types. Some consisted of stones inscribed with ancient literature—commonly called **Runic** <note>original: "Runicâ". The runic alphabet was used by various Germanic peoples before the adoption of the Latin alphabet.</note>, but by foreigners **Gothic**—while others consisted of certain rough, unlettered stones, yet arranged in a specific order and sequence.

Of these, some constituted forums, in which justice was administered to each according to laws and statutes; some designated **assembly sites** <note>original: "loca comitialia". These were open-air meeting places where legal and political decisions, such as the election of kings, were made.</note>, in which the election of Kings and Emperors was also performed with solemn ritual; others enclosed circuses, in which giants and fighters fought vigorously in duels; finally, others indicated places where entire armies were routed and defeated—one might call them **Trophies** <note>original: "Trophea".</note>. In our land, Odin <note>original: "Othinus". The chief deity of Norse mythology, credited in medieval histories with establishing burial and monument customs.</note> is established as their originator, as witnessed by the *History of Norway* <note>original: "Historia Norvagica". An anonymous 12th-century account of Norwegian history.</note>.

Regarding the signs of duels, indeed, people intended them to be stones arranged in a long row and a straight line; but sometimes only a single stone, albeit an immense or large one, as is clear from Book 2, Chapter 9 of the history by Adam of Bremen <note>Adam of Bremen (c. 1050–1085) was a medieval chronicler who documented the history and geography of Northern Europe.</note>. For the author speaks thus in this place:

> *He went up to the ford which is called Agrimestwedel <note>A location in modern-day Germany, near the border of the historical Danish and Saxon territories.</note>, where Biurgvido also fought a duel against the Champion of the Slavs, killed him, and a stone was placed in that same spot in memory.*

He calls a "Champion" what the Danes call a **Kempe** <term>Kempe<gloss>A Danish term for a warrior, fighter, or giant-slayer.</gloss></term>: a word which the Romans changed into "Cimber." For when they noticed that all the strongest men were called **Kemper** by the Danes, they said "Cimber" according to the standard of their own language.

Here, however, it should be noted in passing that the ancient method of fighting, both in duels and in war, was far different from what we see in use in our own century: *For in antiquity, in conducting contests, frequent alternations of blows were not sought, but there was*

# BOOK ONE.

It is nine *Zealand* ells <term>ell: A historical unit of measurement. A Zealand ell (Sielandica ulna) was approximately 63 centimeters or 24.8 inches.</term> in height, five quarters wide at the base, and one thick, gradually tapering to a sharp point. If it did not bear an impressed image of a cross and stand in the cemetery of *Gjerde* <note>original: *Gierdis*; referring to the Gjerde churchyard in Etne, Norway.</note>, I would think it was some kind of military trophy. For the common folk's legend about this stone does not differ much from this opinion, as they imagine a certain Giant was buried here, who saw to it that his sword was placed over his burial urn, so that the hilt was held by the earth and the point by the air, which in the course of time was turned into the stone whose image you see here. I judge that this monument was placed for a Pagan by a Christian.

Many more of the same kind can be seen and observed elsewhere in the same Diocese, indeed of various shapes, but crafted for the same purpose. Among which is that one worthy of mention near the parish of *Fjeldberg* near the farm of *Stø*; of which perhaps I shall write elsewhere.

Furthermore, I seem to gather even from our *Saxo* <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), a Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> that a square series of stones is an indicator of duels held there. For in his fourth book, describing the place where *Frotho* II met *Frogerus* in a duel, he says that *Frogerus marked out two square-shaped spaces on the ground with sides measuring a cubit, intending to provide a precedent from the custom of the place. Once these were marked out, each occupied his assigned part,* etc. From which it can be gathered that those about to fight a duel also designated square areas with stones, outside of which if anyone were pushed by the strength of his adversary, he was considered defeated.

But it may also be gathered that the dueling arena was sometimes arranged in a circular shape from those passages in which the same Saxo, in Book III, describes the encounter of *Ubbo* with the *Slav*. Since these things present the matter in vivid colors, it will not be out of place to add them here. Thus he writes:

> Without delay the field is rounded into an arc, the circle is packed with soldiers, the champions clash, a crash arises, the watching crowd roars, divided in their support. Thus the athletes burn with spirit, and with mutual wounds— <note>original: *vulneribus* (completed on the following page).</note>

...rushing in, they met the same end of light and battle. This clearly points to a place for dueling and fighting, and indeed one that was previously circled, or reduced to a circular form by the placement of stones. Among the laws of dueling, this is also placed in Book IV: *To decide with two against one is as unfair as it is disgraceful. Islands were sometimes assigned for duels, especially when a decision had to be made concerning kingdoms or the safety of an entire army. They chose those which were on the border of both kingdoms, to which there was no access except by boat, and small in size, so that from both sides on the opposite bank, the rest of the soldiers could more conveniently watch the manner and method of the fight. Saxo describes such a place in Book IV, in which **Uffo** <note>Uffo, or Uffe Hin Spage, is a legendary Danish hero who, according to myth, saved Denmark from Saxon conquest.</note> won a victory over the son of the King of Saxony and a distinguished champion <term>athlete: Here used in the classical sense of a professional prize-fighter or champion wrestler.</term> who accompanied him contrary to the laws of the duel. The words are these:
> *By agreement, a place for the fight is sought. This the River Eider <note>original: "Eidorus"; the historic border river between Denmark and Germany.</note> walls in with a circuit of waters, so that with the intervening space resisting, access is granted only by boat. When Uffo sought this place without a companion, a champion of remarkable strength followed the son of the King of Saxony, with frequent crowds on both sides filling the winding turns of the banks in their eagerness to watch.*

Similarly, in Book VII, **Olo** fought with Hialto and Scato on an island, so that he might keep Esa, daughter of the minor King of the Vermians <note>original: "Wermorum"; referring to the people of Värmland in Sweden.</note>, safe from abductors. *The island provided a place for the battle,* he says, *occupying the middle of the lake, from which a village is not far distant, which offers a monument of this kind of slaughter by bearing the names of the brothers Hialto and Scato joined together.*

That the place of playful contests was sometimes marked by a blanket or some kind of cloth <term>lodice: A heavy cloth or blanket, used in Icelandic "hólmganga" (island-walking) duels to define the small area within which the combatants had to remain.</term> placed under the feet of the contestants, we shall show below from the *Crymogæa* <note>A history of Iceland published in 1609.</note> by Arngrimur <note>Arngrímur Jónsson (1568–1648), a prominent Icelandic scholar and historian.</note>. Here, at least, our discussion is concerning the circle of those who celebrated serious and momentous contests.

Olaus Magnus <note>Olaus Magnus (1490–1557) was a Swedish ecclesiastic and writer, famous for his "History of the Northern Peoples."</note> follows the other arrangements of stones in this way in his *History*, Book 1, Chapter 29: *A straight and long line of lettered [inscribed] stones indicates the contests of champions; a square, companies of warriors; and a circular one, the burials of families; while a wedge-shaped line indicates that the battle lines of cavalry triumphed there or nearby with greater fortune.* <note>original: "Literato rectoq; & longo ordine pugilum certamina; qvadrato turmas bellantium & sphærico familiarium designantia sepulturas, ac cuneato eqvestrium acies ibidem vel propè fortunatius triumphâsse."</note> Whether this order was strictly observed in every location, I strongly doubt.

In England, stones of this kind are also found erected by the Danes. For **Camden** <note>William Camden (1551–1623), an English antiquarian and author of *Britannia*, a chorographical survey of Great Britain and Ireland.</note> reports that in Cornwall near **St. Neot's** <note>original: "Neotestov."</note> there stands a large heap of rocks upon which a stone is placed, shaped by nature so much like a cheese that it seems to be pressed like a cheese, whence comes the name **Cheesewring** <note>original: "Wringcheese"; a natural geological formation on Bodmin Moor.</note>: several stones, somewhat square in shape, are also seen in the same plain, seven or eight of which are erected at equal distances from each other. Concerning these, it seems right to judge that they were placed in memory of some battle, as a kind of trophy.

Thus, as the same author reports, toward the North, about six miles more or less from **Salisbury**, a monstrous construction is seen. For within a ditch, huge and rough stones—some of which reach twenty-eight feet in height and seven in width—are erected in a triple series in the manner of a crown. Other stones, as if transverse [lintels], rest upon them so that the work appears suspended, whence it is called **Stonehenge** by us, just as it was called the **Giants' Dance** <note>original: "Chorea Gigantum."</note> by ancient historians because of its size. I judge them to have been altars or a forum designated for legal judgments. He reports that others of the same kind exist near **Burford**, called the **Rollright Stones** <note>original: "Rolvonis saxa"; likely the megalithic complex on the border of Oxfordshire and Warwickshire.</note>, and likewise the **Stiperstones**, famous for the victory of **Harold**. All of these are nothing but trophies and monuments of deeds illustriously performed there by the Danes. This is also clearly hinted at by **John Speed** <note>Johannes Speed (1551–1629), an English cartographer and historian.</note> when, in his description of Devonshire, he relates that certain remains of ancient work are seen at **Exmoor**, namely stones, some erected in a triangle, others in a circle, and arranged in order. These are certainly trophies of victories which Romans, Saxons, or Danes obtained. And he reports that one of them is inscribed with **Danish letters** <note>Refers to Runic inscriptions.</note>. I wish he had shared this for the public good; perhaps it would testify to the illustrious deeds performed there by our own people.
