# CHAPTER TEN.
## Concerning the courts of the ancients and various methods of settling disputes.

The places where legal disputes are publicly settled according to the laws and constitutions of the realm, we here call Courts—in our tongue, *Ting* <note>The *Ting* or *Thing* was the governing assembly and court in Germanic societies, made up of the free people of the community.</note>. These are seen constructed in open and sunny places, or even in woods and groves, near the altars of the Gods, consisting of a collection of large stones arranged in a rectangular or oval shape. To this day, near the city and castle of **Vordingborg** <note>original: "Orethinganam." Worm identifies this site with the *Vordingborg* area on the island of Zealand.</note> in **Zealand** <note>original: "Selandia."</note>, the ruins of such a court are shown, from which they claim the castle and city took their name. When I examined its structure and capacity more carefully, I saw that it had been surrounded by forty-six stones of stupendous size, with one rather large stone standing out in its very center; all were arranged in an oval shape, in such a way that on both sides near the middle, a kind of gate or entrance opened toward the south and the north. The length equaled ninety paces, and the width twenty. In the district of **Merløse** <note>original: "Mierlosano."</note> near **Åmuntorp**, a place exists, enclosed on all sides by rocks, still retaining the name of a court, for they call it *Tinget*. Many more of this kind may be seen here and there in other provinces of the realm.

Moreover, I find that more serious controversies were decided in these places in various ways. **Frotho the Great** <note>A legendary Danish King, often identified with Frode Fredegod, said to have reigned at the time of Christ.</note>, who held dominion over the Danes at the time of Christ’s birth, enacted among other laws this one, as our Historian <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian and author of *Gesta Danorum*.</note> testifies in Book 5: *That every controversy should be decided by the sword: judging it more honorable to contend with strength than with words.* <note>original: "Vt de qvalibet controversia ferro decerneretur: speciosius viribus quam verbis confligendum existimans."</note> *If either of the combatants, by stepping back, should go outside the circle of the marked ring, he would lose his case just as if he had been defeated. But if a commoner should attack a professional fighter over any matter, he [the fighter] should receive him fully armed, while [the commoner] would fight with only a club one cubit long.* Thus the same king, when a feud arose between **Hedin** <note>original: "Hithinum."</note> and **Hogni** <note>original: "Hoginum."</note>, because Hedin was thought to have seduced <note>The Latin text cuts off at "stu-", likely for "stuprasse" (to have defiled or seduced).</note> Hogni's daughter before the marriage rites...

...by enticements, had violated [her], which was then considered a monstrous crime by all nations. When he could not settle the matter according to other laws, he allowed them to decide the issue with the sword; our author expressed it thus: *Frotho, having sent messengers to summon them both at once, more scrupulously investigated the cause of their grudge. Having learned it, he pronounced judgment according to the formula of the law he had established. Seeing, however, that they could not be reconciled even thus—the father obstinately demanding back his daughter—he decreed the dispute must be decided by the sword. Indeed, that seemed the only remedy for ending the controversy.*

**Arngrímur Jónsson** <note>A famous Icelandic scholar (1568–1648) who wrote extensively on Nordic history.</note> pursues the laws and rituals of <term>single combat</term> <note>original: "monomachia"</note> at length in his *History of Iceland*, book 1, chapter 9, from which you may take these points: *Those about to enter single combat or a private duel would mark out a certain space or square—called a "scamma"—which they were not to exceed once the boundaries were set. This was done either by laying a cloak or blanket under the feet of the combatants; hence, if either was defeated, he was bound to redeem his life with three marks of refined silver. Whoever first stained the ground with blood was considered conquered, which occurred, it seems, in less serious contests, much like gladiatorial games. Alternatively, that field of Mars was marked out by making a sort of circle with wooden barriers or something similar; these barriers were called* **Hestesteingur** <note>original: "Heſteſteingur." Likely referring to "hestasteinn" or "heslistengr" (hazel-poles), the latter being used to mark the boundaries of a dueling ground (holmganga).</note> *perhaps because hazel-wood was the first material used for these fences.* The victor, however, who put his adversary to death in this bloody contest, became the heir to all the goods of the defeated, which they called <note>Runes: ᚦᛆᚱ ᚢᛆᚱ ᚢᛂᛁᚴᛁᚦ ᛏᛁᛚ ᛆᚱᚠᚠᛋ (*þar var veigið til arfs*).</note> "there it was fought for the inheritance." Immediately after the victory was won, an enormous bull was led out; if the victor did not kill it with a single blow, the relatives of the defeated man had the right to take legal action against the victor. By these laws of single combat, **Egill Skallagrímsson** <note>The protagonist of *Egils saga*, a famous Viking warrior-poet known for his prowess in duels.</note> won more than once and succeeded to the vast possessions of the defeated, concerning which consult the same Arngrímur more fully on page 134 of book 2. It is established that through this kind of duel, legal disputes over estates, inheritances, and dowries were sometimes settled such that at least the property in question went to the victor, while the rest was adjudged to the heirs. Moreover, the law was the same if someone summoned to a duel refused to meet his adversary as if he had fallen while fighting.

Worthy of note are the things **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian.</note> records regarding these laws of single combat in book 4: *He orders him (Athislus) to step forward and, if there be any strength in him, to [fight] him alone...*

...to test him in combat. For even if he were removed from his brother's help, he would act with his own strength so that the fight would not be judged dishonorable because of an unequal hand. Indeed, for two to fight against one was believed among the ancients to be as unjust as it was shameful. Nor was a victory won in this kind of fight held to be more praiseworthy, as it seemed joined to disgrace rather than glory. Surely, for one to be crushed by two was considered a matter of no effort and the greatest shame. *See what was commented regarding the Athletes in Book 2 of Saxo by the most learned Royal Historian, Stephen Stephens, public professor of the Sorø Academy.* <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220) was Denmark's first great historian; Stephen Stephens (Stephanus Stephanius) was a 17th-century scholar who published a famous commentary on Saxo's work.</note>

The weapons with which they proceeded, equipped for this <term>single combat</term> <note>original: "monomachia"</note>, were a helmet, a shield, a sword, and a spear. The one challenged first directed a blow at his adversary, and thus they exchanged blows in turns.

There was also another kind of single combat, which was carried out in a very large vessel closed at the top; in this, they used a club the length of an arm instead of a sword. In this contest, **Thorgils Orrabeinstjup** <note>original: "Thorgisellus Orrabeinius," a legendary Icelandic hero of the Viking Age.</note> overcame a famous Scottish fighter.

The method of settling controversies through duels thrived for a long time in **Holstein** <note>original: "Holsatia," a region in northern Germany then closely linked to the Danish crown.</note>; for concerning this, Christian Cilicius, in his work on the *Dithmarschen War*, book 1, discusses it thus: *If sharper disputes regarding law or honors arose, especially among the nobles, they settled their suits through duels, with Mars as the judge, following the ancient custom of the Romans (or rather, the Danes).* He adds: *They did not pursue the crime of homicide with the ultimate punishment [death], but punished it with a monetary fine, lest two men be removed from the world by one unlucky accident. And this was observed until the time of **Christian III**, King of Denmark.* <note>Christian III (reigned 1534–1559) was the king who transitioned Denmark to Lutheranism and reformed the legal system.</note> *He, being a Prince of wonderful prudence and most observant of what is fair and good, because that custom seemed to differ from both divine and human law, restricted and softened that law—rooted by use and the length of time—not many years ago with the consent of the nobles. He decreed that whoever kills anyone who is unsuspecting or not equipped with weapons for the defense of their body shall pay the penalty with their head [death]; in other matters, the vigor of the ancient custom remains, so that they might refrain from the shedding of blood. I bring these things up so that one may gather even from this how deep these barbaric laws and customs had struck their roots among the northern peoples, so that they could not be uprooted even over such a long stretch of time.*

<header>### BOOK ONE</header>
<sig>A</sig>

Luitprand, King of the **Lombards** <note>The Lombards were a Germanic people who ruled Italy; King Luitprand reigned from 712–744 AD.</note>, attempted to abolish the <term>trial of the duel</term> <note>original: "duelli examen"</note> as if it were impious, but his efforts were in vain, as is evident from the first book of his laws, Title 9, Law 23. *We are uncertain,* he says, *regarding the judgment of God, and we have heard of many losing their case through battle without a just cause; however, because of the custom of our Lombard people, we cannot forbid this impious law.* This same rite was condemned by Bishop **Agobard**, **Pope Nicholas**, the **Lateran Council**, and others; as a result, it gradually began to be abolished among foreign nations. Among us, it seems to have flourished until the time of **Poppo** <note>Poppo was a missionary bishop credited with converting the Danes by performing a miracle with hot iron (another "judgment of God").</note>, as we shall soon discuss. It is remarkable that this superstition grew so strong that even **Monks** and others devoted to divine things (or so they wished to appear) did not hesitate to settle disputes by duel. **Juretus** <note>François Juret (1553–1626), a French jurist and scholar.</note> records from manuscripts two excellent examples occurring in the age of Ivo. In one, a monk of the monastery of **Vendôme** <note>original: "Vindocinensis"</note> arranges a duel with a cleric of the Bishopric of Saintes. In the other, a religious man named **Anselm**, keeper of the treasury of the Church of Laon, strenuously defeated a goldsmith in <term>single combat</term> <note>original: "monomachia"</note>—the guilty man defeating the innocent. **Spelman** <note>Sir Henry Spelman (1562–1641), an English antiquary famous for his legal dictionary, the *Archæologus*.</note> mentions these under the entry *judgment of God*, and he elegantly set forth every requirement for a duel in his *Archæologus* under the entry *Field* <note>original: "Campus," referring to the field of combat.</note>.

**Tangbrand**, a priest to King **Olaf Tryggvason**, was a vigorous soldier and defeated many in duels, as the *History of Norway* testifies. **Arngrim** <note>Arngrimur Jónsson (1568–1648), an Icelandic scholar.</note> considers that this law of duels and single combat lasted in Norway and Iceland until the year of Christ 1006; see Book 1 of his *Crymogæa*, Chapter 9.

Once the duel was abolished as a means far too bloody, the investigation of legal cases was entrusted to **twelve men**, who were to pronounce what was equitable and just by public authority; it was required to stand entirely by their judgment and sentence. **Ragnar**, surnamed **Lodbrok** <note>The legendary Viking hero Ragnar "Hairy-Breeches."</note>, who is thought to have lived around the year 820 AD, seems to have been the first to introduce this method of deciding controversies. Regarding him, our own **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the Danish historian.</note> writes in his ninth book in this manner: *He established that every dispute, setting aside the instruments of legal actions and allowing neither the charge of the accuser nor the defense of the accused, should be entrusted to the judgment of twelve approved fathers. By the benefit of this law, rash litigation was removed, and he believed the slanders of the wicked were sufficiently countered.*

*...to test his strength in an encounter. For, having set aside his brother's help, he would act with his own strength, lest he be seen as disgraceful for fighting with an unequal hand.* <note>original: "manu impari"</note> *Indeed, for two to decide a matter against one was believed by the ancients to be as unjust as it was shameful. Nor was a victory won in this kind of fight considered more praiseworthy, as it seemed joined to disgrace rather than glory. Surely, for one to be crushed by two was considered a matter of no effort and of the greatest shame.* See what the most learned Royal Historian, **Stephanus Stephanius**, a public Professor at the Academy of Sorø, has commented regarding athletes in his notes on the second book of **Saxo** <note>Referring to Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian.</note>.

The arms with which they proceeded, equipped for this <term>single combat</term> <note>original: "monomachia"</note>, were a helmet, shield, sword, and spear. The one challenged directed the first blow at his adversary, and thus they exchanged blows in turns.

There was also another kind of single combat, which was carried out in a very large vessel closed at the top; in which, instead of a sword, they used a staff the length of a <term>cubit</term> <note>A cubit is an ancient unit of length based on the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger, roughly 18 inches.</note>. In this contest, **Thorgisl Orrabeinsstjup** <note>original: "Thorgisellus Orrabeinius," a figure from the Icelandic sagas.</note> defeated **Randidus**, a Scottish fighter.

The method of settling controversies through dueling flourished for a long time in **Holstein** <note>original: "Holsatia," a region in Northern Germany.</note>; for **Christian Cilicius** <note>A 16th-century historian of the Dithmarschen region.</note> discusses it in the first book of his work *On the Dithmarschen War*: *If sharper contentions regarding law or honors arose, especially among nobles, they settled their disputes by the judgment of Mars* <note>The Roman god of war, here used as a metaphor for battle.</note>*, according to the ancient custom of the Romans (or rather, the Danes).* He adds: *Not pursuing the crime of homicide with the ultimate punishment, they punished it with a monetary fine, lest by one unhappy accident two people be removed from the midst. And this was observed until the time of **Christian III**, King of Denmark. For he, as he was a Prince of wonderful prudence and most observant of what is equitable and good, since that custom seemed to differ from both divine and human law, restricted and mitigated that law—which had become ingrained by use and length of time—not so many years ago with the consent of the nobles. He decreed that whoever killed someone unexpectedly, or someone not equipped with arms for the defense of their body, should pay the penalty with their head; in other matters, the vigor of the ancient custom remains, so that they might refrain from the shedding of blood. I bring these things forward so that one might gather from them how deep these barbaric laws and customs have taken root among the Northerners, so that they could not be extirpated even by such a long stretch of time.*

-># OF DANISH MONUMENTS<-

The laws enacted on this matter by **Ethelred** <note>Ethelred the Unready (r. 978–1016), an Anglo-Saxon king whose laws show significant Danish influence due to the Danelaw.</note> in a full assembly, and published by **Lambarde** <note>William Lambarde (1536–1601), an English antiquarian and legal scholar who published 'Archaionomia', a collection of Anglo-Saxon laws.</note>, prove that this twelve-man jury system flowed from the Danes to the English. Among other things, these words appear:

> *In individual <term>hundreds</term> <note>A 'hundred' was a historical administrative division of a shire or county.</note> let there be assemblies, and let there be twelve men of free condition, senior in age, who, together with the <term>reeve</term> <note>A local administrative officer or magistrate.</note>, shall hold the sacred objects and swear that they will never condemn any innocent man, nor acquit any guilty one.* <note>original: "In singulis centuriis comitia sunto atq̄ liberæ conditionis viri duodecim, ætate superiores, una cum præposito sacra tenentes; jurento se adeo virum aliquem innocentem haud damnaturos, fontemve absoluturos."</note>

**Christian Cilicius** <note>A pseudonym for Christian von Ditmar (1533–1601), a chronicler of the Dithmarschen region in modern Germany.</note> proposes a different, but I believe more recent, method of resolving disputes in the first book of his *Dithmarsch War*, stating the following: They had this custom of speaking the law and exercising judgment.

> *The entire territory was divided into certain parishes or courts. These met at stated times, each for itself in its own place, with their weapons, in the open air in the fields. Noblemen of the same place were present to sit as witnesses to the judgment. There, those who believed they had a grievance against others stepped forward. Once the actions and defenses of both parties had been heard and understood, the entire assembly went into council. The period of time spent in deliberation they called the* **CURAM** <note>original: "CURAM". This likely relates to the Germanic 'Küre' or 'Kora', meaning a choice, election, or legal decision.</note>. *After the controversies had been carefully weighed and argued for both sides, they returned to the session, called the litigants, and pronounced the law. If anyone did not wish to abide by the judgment, he was permitted to appeal to twelve appointed men—either judges or arbitrators—and from these to the assembly of the entire territory. This custom of reducing lawsuits and exercising judgment was observed once a year. Even to this day, there is a place not far from **Rendsburg** which still retains the name* **THE YEARLY BEAM** <note>original: "ANNUÆ TRABIS".</note> *from that judicial custom. Meetings are still sometimes held there now for ending controversies, and there were furthermore similar places in other parts of the <term>Chersonese</term> <note>The Cimbrian Peninsula, modern-day Jutland and Schleswig-Holstein.</note>, the memory of which has vanished over the long passage of time.*

In this case, a matter already discussed is ultimately referred to the twelve men, who impose an end to the dispute by their decision, though the right of appeal is preserved. But by the constitution of **Lodbrok** <note>Ragnar Lodbrok, the legendary Viking hero and king mentioned on the previous page as the reformer of the legal system.</note>, all legal maneuvering between the plaintiff and defendant seemed to be removed, and no room for appeal was left once a sentence was passed.

*...if that turf arch did not collapse while no one was supporting it, he earned trust; but if it did, he was condemned for the crime of falsehood.* <note>The author is describing the "passing under the turf" (Icelandic: *ganga undir jarðarmen*), a ritual ordeal where a strip of turf was sliced from the ground but left attached at the ends, forming an arch. If it stayed up while the person passed under, they were cleared of charges.</note>

*But if in the same oath* (I repeat the words of **Arngrimur** <note>Arngrimur Jónsson (1568–1648), an Icelandic scholar who provided Worm with much of his information on Norse antiquity.</note>) *there was a treaty, they placed a spear under the turf arch as a support, under which two, three, or more who were to be allied stood together, mixing blood drawn by a blade from their hands or elsewhere, to seal their mutual faith by this pact: for which reason the **alliance** <note>original Greek: "τὸ συμμαχικὸν"</note> was especially sanctioned and sworn by this rite, so that those so allied were like certain **defensive and offensive allies**. <note>original Greek: "συμμαχικοί καὶ ἐπιμαχοί"</note> In this, it was especially incumbent upon each (besides the mutual help by which one was bound to another in life) that if one were killed, the remaining survivors—whether one or many—should avenge the death of the **ally** <note>original Greek: "τοῦ συμμάχου"</note> by any means. The blood drawn from the body signified that their own blood, and thus their life, was to be spent for their mutual safety or vengeance.* Our own **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish chronicler.</note> outlines the formula of the treaty slightly differently in Book 1. *The ancients about to enter a treaty,* he says, *were accustomed to sprinkle their footsteps with the exchange of mutual blood, intending to confirm the pledge of friendship by the exchange of each other's blood.* He tells in the same place that **Lyserus** and **Hadingus** entered a treaty in this way and declared war on **Lokerus**, the tyrant of the Curonians.

Arngrimur adds in the same place that the rite proposed above is also found used in place of a certain punishment, subjection, or satisfaction, when some sin or offense had to be atoned for by this pact; namely, that someone should pass once or twice under an earthen arch, though in this case supported in some way (because then no sacred oath was involved). <note>In this context, passing under the turf was a sign of humility or "bowing" to an opponent to settle a feud.</note> **"He thought that everything would become right."** <note>original Runic: ᛘᛅᚾ ᛅᛚᛚᛁ ᚦᛁᚾᚴᛁ ᚦᛁᚦ ᛅᚦ ᚢᛅᚱᚦᛅ ᚱᛁᚦᛁᚴ (*Man alli thingi thith ath vartha rithik*)</note> Hence, a certain man to whom satisfaction was made for an offense through this pact boasted that his adversary was cast down below the pigs: **"The man was called gentle/mollified."** <note>original Runic: ᚢᚦ ᚴᛁᚦᛁ ᚢᛅᚱ ᛒᛚᛁᚦᛁ ᚴᛅᛚᛚᛁᚾ (*Uth kithi var blithi kallin*). The author explains the "below the pigs" insult because pigs root in the earth with their snouts rather than their heads.</note> For pigs enter the ground only with their snout, not their head. These things are from the **Vatnsdæla Saga**. <note>original: "vatzdalu," referring to the medieval Icelandic saga of the People of Vatnsdal.</note>

But since we suggested above that before the aforementioned decree of **Harald** regarding the clearing of oneself through the sacrament of an oath, the method of deciding controversies flourished among us in Denmark through the **ordeal** <note>The *ordalium* was a "judgment of God," such as the trial by fire.</note> or the carrying of hot iron, some things must be explained a little more fully regarding that.

# CHAPTER ELEVEN.
## *On the ordeal.* <note>The term "ordeal" (*ordalium*) refers to a medieval judicial practice where the guilt or innocence of the accused was determined by subjecting them to a painful task, such as carrying hot iron; if they healed without infection, they were judged innocent by God.</note>

After it pleased the eternal God to lead this northern region of the world to the recognition of His Son, having abolished the darkness of idol-worship, and after He had instilled in King **Sweyn Forkbeard** <note>original: *Svenottoni*</note> the mind that—once he had received the washing of rebirth [baptism] and was restored to his kingdom—he should take diligent thought for promoting the salvation of his subjects, the work of **Poppo**, a man equipped with piety, eloquence, and all virtues worthy of a messenger of the Gospel, was provided as if from heaven. For when this man had labored long and much in vain with words to instill a healthy religion regarding the true God into the minds of the inhabitants, he finally, in order to win greater credit for his words, placed his hand into glowing-hot iron in a great assembly of the nobles, and carried it for some time without injury—and not without the greatest admiration from those standing by. By this, he not only achieved his desired goal, but it was also decreed that, with the duel <term>trial by combat; *duellum*</term> abolished, the accused should henceforth clear themselves by the carrying of glowing iron. This event is recorded by some to have happened around the year 1000 from the birth of the Savior. However, the history of the Kings of Denmark, written in the vernacular rhymes <note>Referring to the *Danske Rimkrønike*, the first book printed in Danish (1495).</note>, records that the decision of more difficult cases by duel was abolished and the method of clearing oneself by carrying glowing iron was introduced by **Sweyn** around the year of Christ 986. Receive the full account of the event from our own **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century chronicler of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> here:

> *To the author [Poppo] who was eager but ineffective in bringing the religion, God, the illustrator of His own power, added a partner in the noble work: Poppo, a man conspicuous for talent and holiness and excellent in the special knowledge of letters. After holding a public assembly of the Danes at the harbor to which the frequency of ice gave its name (commonly called **Isefiord**), when he could not bend them by speech from their desire to worship at shrines, he provided a most certain proof of his assertion by a clear sign, and published the truth of his teaching by a conspicuous miracle of holiness. For having asked whether they would obey his warnings if they saw his hand free of injury at the touch of glowing iron; and everyone responding that they would undoubtedly obey, he ordered a glowing iron plate, having the form of a glove, to be prepared,*

Seeing this, the King was baptized with many others, and Poppo was promoted to the Bishopric.* This **Alradus** was made King of Denmark, being the 90th in the line of Kings, in the year of our Lord 950—that is, in the 15th year of the reign of **Otto the Great**. These details do not differ much from what **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), a famous Danish historian</note> reports. He whom this author calls Alradus was actually **Harald**, called "Klack," the father of Sweyn, who indeed began the work of reformation but, hindered by others, could not lead it to the desired end. Consult Saxo on this matter, who handles all these things in his elegant style.

as is clear from the passage of Ranulf de Glanvill <note>A 12th-century English Chief Justiciar and author of a major legal treatise on English law</note> cited below. Some maintain that its use was at least in doubtful cases, where the matter could not be proven by clear and indubitable testimony. It is sometimes taken so broadly that it encompasses four types of proof: the first is that which is performed by *duel* <term>trial by combat</term>; the second by *red-hot iron*, the third by *hot water*, and the fourth by *cold water*. But here it is used more strictly, as will appear from the following testimonies of authors.

William Lambarde, in his *Archæonomia Anglica* <note>original: *Archæonomia*, a 16th-century collection of Anglo-Saxon laws</note> under the entry for Ordeal, explains the whole matter with many clear words in this sense:

> The Ordeal <note>original: *Ordæl*</note> was a method of purging a crime, of which there were two types: one was called the Ordeal of fire, and the other the Ordeal of water. The fire ordeal was usually performed in this way: the accused either walked a few paces carrying a glowing iron in his bare hand, or, while running, stepped with his foot upon certain red-hot plowshares. That iron was sometimes one pound in weight, which they called the Simple Ordeal, and sometimes three pounds, and this they called the Triple Ordeal. They pronounced him innocent (if he happened to escape unharmed); but if they found him burned by the fire, they condemned him of the crime. Likewise, there were two types of water Ordeal: namely, of cold and of boiling water. For either the accused was plunged entirely into ice-cold water, and then (as their strong belief held) the one pure of crime sank to the bottom, while the water immediately rejected from itself the one conscious of guilt <note>Based on the medieval belief that the pure element of water would "reject" a sinner, causing the guilty to float and the innocent to sink</note>; or finally, they immersed their hand up to the elbow in boiling water, and they judged concerning the guilty and the innocent (just as we have said above). Only to noble and free-born men was the power granted to purge themselves by the examination of the fire Ordeal. But peasants and commoners were thrust into the water Ordeal.

You will find more details which were required here in his own work, where he discusses each point more extensively.

What he asserts—that the purgation of the fire ordeal was imposed only on noblemen, but the water ordeal on peasants—is confirmed by Ranulf de Glanvill in Book 14, Chapter 1. *He is bound,* he says, *to purge himself...*

...the one who is accused is tried by the judgment of God <note>original: *Dei judicium*</note>, namely by hot iron or by water according to the different social status of the men: by hot iron if he were a **Free man**, by water if he were a **Peasant**. However, a contrary example from the second book of *Hoveden’s* <note>Roger of Hoveden, a 12th-century English chronicler</note> *Annals* is brought forward by *Selden* <note>John Selden, a prominent 17th-century English jurist and polymath</note> in the second book of *The Janus of the English* <note>original: *Jani Anglorum*</note> concerning *John Senior*, a noble and wealthy man. During the reign of *Henry II*, when John was accused of the murder of the brother of the Earl of *Ferrers*, he failed to clear himself by the judgment of water and suffered the punishment of the gallows. Furthermore, our *Scanian laws* <note>The medieval laws of Scania, then part of Denmark, now southern Sweden</note> impose the investigation of the ordeal of fire upon everyone indiscriminately, both the noble and the commoner, as the text of the laws itself will soon demonstrate more fully. This also seems to be confirmed by that memorable story cited by our *Saxo* <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> in his 14th book, concerning a woman of *Rügen* <note>An island in the Baltic Sea</note>. When she was forced to clear herself of a charge of adultery by this benefit, she was declared innocent in a miraculous way. It will not be unpleasant to recount the story here in his exact words:

> *A certain matron, undeservedly accused of adultery by her husband, offered her right hand to the glowing metal plate for the sake of clearing her reputation. Suddenly, the iron which she was about to receive, as if fleeing the touch of an innocent hand and disregarding its own weight, lifted itself up high. Accompanying the gait of the walking woman with a swinging motion, it fell to the ground by its own impulse when it was meant to be cast upon the altar, amid the pious admiration of the bystanders. This event both lifted the woman’s infamy and made the minds of the spectators more inclined toward religion.* So says Saxo.

The first type of Ordeal, which consisted of carrying glowing iron, was performed in such a way that, once the Mass was finished, the accused would take up the iron to be carried for a measure of nine feet. Once this was done, his hand was covered and sealed for three days. When it was unsealed, if a raw, festering discharge <note>original: *sanies crudescens*</note> was seen in the mark left by the iron, he was held guilty of the crime; but if no sign of injury appeared, he was acquitted as innocent. To this first type we must refer the method by which *Poppo* converted the *Danes*, as witnessed by *Saxo* cited above. To this also pertains the eighth chapter of the Ecclesiastical Laws of *King Athelstan*, enacted around the year 920 AD, published by the most illustrious *Sir Henry Spelman* in the first volume of the *British Councils* <note>original: *Conciliorum Britannicorum*</note>, page 404, which reads as follows:

BOOK ONE.
<header>LIBER PRIMUS.</header>

We command in the name of God and by the instruction of the Archbishop and of all my Bishops, that no one shall enter the Church after the fire is brought in, where the judgment <note>original: *judicium*; here referring to the physical apparatus of the ordeal</note> must be heated, except for the priest and the person who is to undergo the judgment. And let nine feet be measured from the stake <note>original: *staca*</note> to the mark, according to the measure of the feet of the person who must undergo the judgment. And if it be the judgment of water, let it be heated until it is stirred to a boil, and let the vessel <term>alfetum<gloss>a cauldron used in the ordeal of boiling water</gloss></term> be of iron or bronze or lead, or of clay; and if it be a single ordeal <note>original: *anfealt thyla*, an Old English legal term for a simple accusation</note>, the hand shall be immersed after the stone or the test-object <note>original: *examen*</note> up to the **wrist** <note>original: *Wyrste*</note>; and if it be a triple accusation, up to the elbow. And when the judgment is ready, let two men from each side enter and be certain that it is as hot as we have prescribed, and let an equal number from both sides enter and stand on either side of the judgment along the length of the Church. Let them all be fasting and have abstained from their wives that night; and let the priest sprinkle holy water over all of them, and let each of them bow down to the holy water. Let him give to all of them the text of the holy Gospel and the sign of the holy cross to kiss. No one shall tend the fire any longer once the blessing begins, but let the iron lie upon the coals until the last collect; afterward, let it be placed upon the supports <note>original: *staplas*</note>. There shall be no other speaking there than to pray diligently to God the Father Almighty that he deign to manifest his truth in this matter. Let the accused drink holy water, and then let the hand of him who must carry the judgment <note>the hot iron</note> be sprinkled with it, and so let him approach. The nine measured feet shall be divided into three sections: at the first mark by the stake he shall hold his right foot; at the second he shall move his right foot; and at the third mark, he shall throw the iron and hasten to the holy altar. Then his hand shall be sealed <note>wrapped and bound with a bandage</note>, and it shall be inspected on the third day to see whether it be "clean" or "unclean" <note>healed or infected</note> within the sealing. Whoever breaks these laws, let him be subject to the **ordeal** <note>original: *ordalium*</note>: that is, the judgment or test is failed in his case, and he shall pay to the King a fine <note>original: *witæ*</note> of one hundred and twenty shillings.

...is covered with a shroud and led with bare feet across nine glowing ploughshares <note>original: *vomeres*; the heavy metal blades of a plough</note> that have been consecrated with purifying prayers and placed at a fixed distance. If the person passes over them unharmed, they are acquitted. By this type of trial, Edward, King of England—called the Confessor and numbered among the Saints after his death—wished to investigate the chastity of his mother, and he endured feeding the eyes of the bystanders with this spectacle, as British history attests. By this same proof, Harald of Ireland proved that he was born of a Great parent <note>referring to Magnus Barefoot, King of Norway</note> in the writings of Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a medieval Danish historian</note>, Book 13. Harald, he says, originating from the regions of Ireland, struck the most flourishing state of Norway like a lightning bolt. When he asserted that he was fathered by Magnus, the ravager of Ireland, he was ordered to provide evidence of his claim through the argument of divine examination. He walked with bare soles over glowing metal plates (for that was the test demanded of him), and since his feet were not harmed in any part, he led many of the Norwegians to believe his assertion through the clear miracle of his safety. It is well-established, therefore, that this type of trial was specifically assigned to nobles and those born of illustrious lineage.

From a third source, I believe, is drawn the method of testing witches <note>original: *sagas*</note> through cold water. Many have argued about this at length, and not without reason has it long since been eliminated from well-ordered Republics, so that there is no necessity to say more words about it here.

There exists in the *Archaeonomia* <note>a 16th-century collection of Anglo-Saxon laws by William Lambarde</note> a law of Athelstan, King of England, concerning the Ordeal <term>Ordalio<gloss>the "Judgment of God," a legal trial by fire or water</gloss></term>, formulated a little differently than what we cited above from Spelman <note>Sir Henry Spelman, an English antiquary</note>, which I think is not out of place to recount here.

Furthermore, let him be present at Mass on those same days and offer his gift. On the very day he is to undergo the Ordeal, let him receive the bread of the Eucharist, and let him swear an oath that he is pure and not at all conscious of the crime for which he is accused. Then, if the inquiry is to be made by cold water, let him be submerged in the water to a length of a cubit and a half <note>original: *sesquiulnam*; approximately 27 inches or 68 centimeters</note> of rope. > „ This iron, once heated, after the adversary has first taken the oath called the **Oath on the Spot** <term>Aasvoren Eed</term> <note>original: *Aasvoren Eed*; a formal oath taken by the accuser at the site of the ordeal to affirm the legitimacy of the charge</note>, the accused himself must take from the sticks with his bare hand and place it into the basin. > „ There is also a third judgment of iron <term>ferri judicium</term> <note>The "ordeal by iron," a physical test where the accused's innocence was determined by their ability to withstand or heal from contact with red-hot metal</note> pertaining to those who must carry the iron, to whom the aforementioned judgments do not apply. The accused is bound to carry this glowing iron, taken from the sticks, until he has walked nine paces. And only then must he throw it from himself; because of this throw, the native language calls it **Shot-Iron** <term>Skudsjern</term> <note>original: *Skudsjern*; from the Danish *skud* (shot/throw) and *jern* (iron)</note>. If the adversary claims he carried it insufficiently or unlawfully, the accused must prove with two witnesses that he observed the lawful manner of carrying it.
> „ This, moreover, must be observed concerning any judgment of iron: none of them should be carried out in a week that contains a feast day. For the first two days—namely **Monday** <note>original: *secunda feria*</note> and **Tuesday** <note>original: *tertia feria*</note>—the accused shall fast on bread and water and wear woolen garments, and on **Wednesday** <note>original: *quarta feria*</note> he shall undergo the judgment.
> „ Once this is completed, immediately either the feet (if the **plowshares** <term>vomer</term> <note>iron blades of a plow, used in an ordeal where the accused walked over them</note> were stepped upon) or the hands (if the iron was carried) shall be wrapped in a cloth. Once the cloth is bound tightly, a seal shall also be applied, lest any fraudulent substance be added that might either heal the burn or at least remove the appearance of the burn.
> „ This covering on the feet or hands shall remain until **Saturday** <note>original: *sabbathum*</note>. On that day, the accuser must wait for the adversary until sunset in the afternoon. And if the accuser does not arrive even then, the wrapping is to be removed in the presence of those standing by, who, as soon as they see the bare hand or feet, will judge the accused either innocent or guilty.
> „ And if he is judged innocent, he shall pay the price of his labor to the priest. But if he is found guilty, the payment of that fee will belong to the accuser, according to the custom of the church or the province.
> „ For these reasons, it is decreed that a week of the glowing iron must not have any feast day, so that no insult might seem to be offered to the feast day through fasting or such labors.
> „ Beyond this, it should also be known that in detestation of <meta>catchword: theft [furti]</meta>

[He] died in the year 1182. At the **Lateran Council** <note>The Fourth Council of the Lateran, one of the most important assemblies of the medieval Church</note>, in the 18th year of his papacy—which was the year of Christ 1215, and the 13th year of Valdemar II—**Innocent III** was the first to severely forbid clerics from lending their labor to the consecration or blessing of the glowing iron. For the 18th decree of that same Council states:

*That no cleric shall bestow the rite of any blessing or consecration upon the purification by boiling water or cold water, or by the glowing iron.* <note>original: "Ne clericus quisquam purgationi aquae ferventis vel frigidae, seu ferri candentis, ritum cuiuslibet benedictionis aut consecrationis impendat."</note>

Since **Valdemar II** was a contemporary of this Innocent III, and since he issued the **Cimbrian Laws** <term>Leges Cimbricas</term> <note>Also known as the Code of Jutland (1241), a foundational legal text for medieval Denmark</note> (in which nothing regarding the ordeal appears) in the year 1240, it is necessary that this decree regarding the abolition of the **Ordeal** <term>ordalio</term> among the Scanians <note>People of Scania, then a part of eastern Denmark</note> belongs to him.

But it is well established that this method of self-purification ceased among the Norwegians not long after. For the **Norwegian History** of **Snorri Sturluson** <note>A famous Icelandic historian and poet; the text here likely refers to the Saga of Haakon Haakonsson</note> records among the deeds of **Haakon Haakonsson**, the 29th King of the Norwegians, that **Cardinal William** (who had been sent there by Pope Innocent IV to decorate the aforementioned Haakon with the royal diadem) abolished the Ordeal. He taught that it was nearly an act of impiety to tempt God in this way and to call Him as a witness to human affairs through such means. They record that this was done in the year 1248.

However, even though the Christian authorities abolished the ordeal through laws and edicts, they could not prevent subjects in certain places from using it from time to time to establish trust in doubtful matters. An illustrious and memorable proof of this is supplied to us by **Albert Krantz** in his *History of the Vandals*, Book 8, Chapter 30, in these very words:

*Let us also relate what they say happened during that time in the town of **Wittenburg**: a house fire, secretly caused, was blamed on an innocent man in that town. Swearing most solemnly that he had no part in the fault, he offered the common purification of the glowing iron—a practice which the laymen presiding over the judgment either did not know was forbidden by laws, or simply chose to ignore. Therefore, he carried the glowing iron for a considerable distance; then, shaking it from his hands, he showed no sign of injury. The iron vanished from the eyes of all those watching in wonder. Nearly a whole year had passed when another man, about to pave a public road in the town with stones, turned his hand into the sand of the place and, having found the iron, [it was] still glow-* <note>The text breaks off here; the catchword "tes" suggests the next page continues "ignescentes" or "glowing."</note>

Not inconveniently are joined to these accounts the things which authors report concerning the **judicial morsel** <term>offa judiciali</term> <note>A form of ordeal where the accused had to swallow a piece of bread or cheese; failure to do so easily was seen as proof of guilt</note>, since they seem to rely on the same foundation of superstition, though now entirely dispersed by the brightness of the Gospel light. To summarize the matter in a few words, it was administered in this way: they would present the consecrated bread of the Eucharist <note>original: "consecratum panem Eucharisticum"</note> to the accused to be swallowed with certain fixed and determined rites; if it was received by the stomach without any difficulty, the accused was acquitted: but if he felt difficulty in swallowing, he was condemned. Whoever desires more should consult Lambarde <note>William Lambarde (1536–1601), an English antiquary and legal historian</note> in the place cited, who discusses this morsel at greater length. Henry Spelman <note>Sir Henry Spelman (c. 1562–1641), an English antiquary famous for his glossaries of legal terms</note> refers to this as the **Sign of the Cross** <term>Symbolum crucis</term>, the **Holy Eucharist** (which he distinguishes from the judicial morsel, as the latter was barley bread called *Corsned* <note>From Old English "corn" (grain) and "snæd" (piece/morsel)</note> by the Saxons), **Cursed Cheese** <term>Caseum execratum</term>, and others; regarding these, consult his *Archaeologum* under the headings **Judgment of God** <term>Judicium Dei</term>, **Judgment of the Cross** <term>Crucis judicium</term>, etc.

## CHAPTER TWELVE.
->Concerning the places designated for the election of Kings.<-

In these regions, certain places are found where Kings were once created with solemn pomp; these are still seen today, surrounded by large stones, usually twelve in number, with a larger one standing out in the middle. Upon this central stone, they placed the king elected by the votes of all, receiving him with great applause. Here they also held assemblies and consulted on the affairs of the Kingdom. When they were about to designate a King, the electors stood upon the stones surrounding the court to signify the firmness of the decree. Our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum</note> hints at this in these words: *To choose...*

The ancients were accustomed to have the **King** stand upon stones fixed into the earth while they delivered their votes, intending to omen the stability of the deed by the firmness of the stones beneath them. By this rite, **Humblus** <note>A legendary King of the Danes mentioned in Saxo Grammaticus’s *Gesta Danorum*</note>, upon the death of his father, was created King by a new favor of his country, though by a following malice of fortune he fell from King to a private citizen. You will find this related in so many words—as well as many other things—by **Krantz** <note>Albert Krantz (1448–1517), a German historian</note> in Book 1 of his *History of Denmark*, chapter 3. In a similar manner, from antiquity until the reign of **Charles IV** and that most celebrated **Golden Bull** <note>The Golden Bull of 1356, a decree which fixed the system of electing the Holy Roman Emperor</note> which he published concerning the election of Emperors, elections were typically held in open fields under the sky, as **Bernhard von Mallinckrodt** <note>A German scholar and dean of Münster (1591–1664)</note> reports in his work *On the Arch-Chancellors*, page 185.

Because this Kingdom of Denmark, which now flourishes under the rule of a single King, was formerly divided into three distinct parts—as the triple code of laws and many other things still attest—it follows that most manifest traces of these locations exist in the **Cimbrian** <note>Jutland</note>, the **Baltic**, and the **Scanian** (formerly **Gothic**) territories.

In Baltic **Zealand**, near the city of **Lethra**, commonly called *Leire*—once a royal city—there exists a place called *Kongstolen* or the **King’s Throne**. It is conspicuous among the rest for a great stone which was deputed for this business, and even now it is made famous by the accounts of the elders regarding this matter.

In **Scania** <note>Skåne, now the southernmost province of Sweden, but historically part of Denmark</note> near **Lund**, there is a hill called *Lynebarsshöt* <note>Likely Libers Hill (Libers hög), a historic site for the acclamation of kings</note>, where homage was paid to King **Olaf**, and where even in the time of **Christian I** this business was carried out. The most celebrated royal historiographer, **Johannes Meursius**, testifies to this in his life of that king:

> *It pleased the nobles of Denmark to summon Christian, who had been elected King shortly before. After he had arrived on the IV Kalends of October* <note>September 28th</note> *before Lund at the **Trollebarolbie** hill, the ancient place of election, in a very crowded assembly—having received the oath from everyone and likewise the banner of the Kingdom from Archbishop **Ivon**—he was hailed as King by all of Denmark and Norway.*

The most celebrated **Stephanius** <note>Stephanus Johannis Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish philologist and historian</note> has rightly noted that there is an error here; for he believes that the most celebrated Meursius (of blessed memory), with an eye moving too quickly, misread those words of **Johannes Svaning**, formerly the Royal Historian, in the *Life of King Christian I* (which Meursius used in his writing).

## CHAPTER THIRTEEN.

->On Epitaphs.<-

Above, as far as was possible, we have followed the rites of burying the deceased; it seemed that only one thing remained: to examine the inscriptions with which they adorned the burial mounds. We have deferred this concern to this place so that we might not confuse monuments devoid of characters with those that are lettered and endowed with inscriptions (which must be dealt with specifically hereafter).

Once the pyre was built and the mass of the tomb had been brought to completion <note>original: "ad umbilicum perducta," a Latin idiom meaning "brought to the navel" or finished</note>, they sometimes selected one stone more notable and smoother than the others, also remarkable for its size, on which they inscribed the name of the deceased and of the friends who dedicated this final duty to their own, briefly <note>original: "laconicé," in the brief manner of the Spartans</note> in their native—that is, **Runic**—letters. I believe this was always placed in the very center of the tomb, or at the head, although it may now be found moved to public roads and other places.

Sometimes, if cliffs or crags stood near the estates or dwellings of the deceased, they carved letters and characters into one of the smoother sides, especially one facing the house, sparing themselves the labor of cutting out and transporting pieces; or rather, more surely rescuing the memory of such great men from destruction. Examples of this kind are encountered everywhere. The **Haraldian Rock** <note>The Runamo inscription in Blekinge, which was traditionally associated with King Harald Wartooth</note>, to which **Hilditonn** <note>Harald Hilditonn or "Wartooth," a legendary Danish king</note> committed the deeds of his father, still stands visible with traces of letters in **Blekinge** <note>A province in southern Sweden, then part of Denmark</note>, concerning which **Saxo** writes in Book 7 in this manner: *The same man took care to have his father's deeds committed by craftsmen to a rock in Blekinge, which I mentioned (namely, in the preface). Book...*

# DANISH MONUMENTS
<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

IX teaches that *Ragnar Lodbrok*, after killing the *King of the Biarmians* <note>The Biarmians were a people mentioned in Norse sagas, likely located near the White Sea</note>, left such a monument, about which we shall speak more fully in the following chapter. In *Norway*, such things occur frequently. Especially in the Diocese of *Stavanger*, in the prefecture of *Lister*, a rock of remarkable height is seen in the bed of a lake, upon which Runic characters were impressed with great care; regarding these, we shall provide a more thorough discourse in its proper place.

In *Sweden*, three miles from *Stockholm*, in the parish of *Skånela*, on the road leading to *Uppsala*, they say something similar exists, consecrated to *Inguar* by *Sigvid*, *Inguar*, and *Jerlebeng*, placed upon a rock in the middle of a river.

This was further observed in these matters: that if fathers, sons, friends, and kinsmen had contributed funds toward the construction of a monument, they also wished for this to be expressed in inscriptions of that kind. Nor did they pass over the person who acted as the author of the inscription; rather, by adding his name, they attested that he had completed the task—an act both pious and worthy of eternal memory. And although these inscriptions may now seem rude and unpolished to us, it is clear from the following that in that century they represented a singular artistry: not just anyone was equal to this work, and the author, by the display of his own name upon them, considered himself worthy of eternal memory for this very reason. Indeed, our histories teach that *Hiarnus* <note>Hiarnus was a legendary Danish poet who, according to Saxo, was made king because of the epitaph he wrote for King Frotho</note> was rewarded with an entire Kingdom on this account. *By them, a Kingdom was repaid for an epitaph, and the weight of an empire was granted to a composition of a few letters. Thus, a massive reward stood for a meager expense. The exceptional price of a tiny poem even exceeded the fame of Caesar's rewards,* says our Saxo in Book 6.

It is probable that there was such a scarcity of literate men and those who knew letters in that age, that he who could either read or weave together three words stood then at a higher price than the most famous author of vast and laborious works in this current age.

Furthermore, they decorated the inscriptions with wondrous hieroglyphics <note>Here, "hieroglyphics" refers to the intricate Zoomorphic interlace and knotwork common in Viking-age Runic carvings</note> fashioned from various animal figures and the windings of tangled lines, by which they silently signified either the deeds performed, the offices held, or the character, virtues, and vices of the deceased...

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the symbolism used in ancient Northern monuments and epitaphs, specifically examining whether the sign of the cross appeared on stones before the arrival of Christianity.</meta>

<header>BOOK ONE.</header>

...noted and sketched. They used a wolf to represent a tyrant; a lamb for the peaceful and mild; a pig for the filthy; a horse for the noble; a lion for a king; and an eagle for the strong—infinite examples of this kind occur everywhere.

I am not sure if I can agree with Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish ecclesiastic and historian</note>, who claims that the sign of the cross was expressed among certain people before the religion of the true God and Christ was established, as a way to indicate their goodness and integrity. His words in Book 1, Chapter 30, are these: *“Obelisks and stones belonging to such good Princes, marked with the sign of the cross many centuries before the Catholic faith was planted, are still clearly seen in the northern kingdoms.”* It cannot be denied that the mark of a cross is found on ancient monuments, as visual evidence proves this in many cases. However, it does not seem likely to me that it was carved into epitaphs before any knowledge of the true God and His Christ reached our people—unless, perhaps, it was done to disgrace the person who was meant to be praised and celebrated by such an epitaph. Indeed, the cross was an old form of punishment for the Romans—in fact, according to Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous humanist scholar who wrote a definitive work on the history of crucifixion</note>, it was a very ancient punishment used since the time of the first Kings. Yet, the same author doubts whether it was in use among the Germans or other Northern peoples. Therefore, for this reason, the shape of the cross in paganism <note>original: "paganismo"</note> was either completely unknown to us or appeared only by chance. Consequently, whatever examples of that kind occur, I would rather attribute them to Christian times. The examples Olaus brings forward, such as those of Germundus and Holmstanus, do not prove otherwise; for in them, the mention of the Christian religion is very clear, and the inscription itself indicates they were converted from the worship of idols to the true God.

One may gather that our pagan ancestors used the figure of the cross to represent *Thor’s hammer* <note>original: "Thoronis malleum"</note> from what Snorri Sturluson <note>original: "Snorro Sturlæ filius," the famous Icelandic historian and author of the Prose Edda</note> relates in the history of Haakon the Good <note>original: "Haquini Adelstani," a 10th-century king who attempted to introduce Christianity to Norway</note>. For when the Christian King had made the sign of the cross over the cup before drinking, Earl Sigurd of Lade <note>A powerful pagan advisor to the king</note> reported that the King had dedicated the draught to the god Thor, because he had made the sign of the hammer. Thus, if the sign of a cross carved by a pagan ever occurs in these regions (though I have not yet had the chance to see one), it will either be accidental or represent the idea of Thor’s hammer, by no...

-># DANISH MONUMENTS<-

...in no way the memorial mark of our crucified Savior. <note>original: "lo modo Servatoris nostri crucifixi notam memorialem." This completes the sentence from the previous page: "Consequently, whatever examples of that kind [exist, they are] in no way..."</note>

For no honor or worship of the cross existed anywhere before the birth and suffering of Christ the Lord on the cross, as Caspar Ens <note>Caspar Ens (c. 1570–1638) was a German scholar and historian known for his works on the history of the Americas and the West Indies.</note> correctly discusses in the first book of his *History of the West Indies*.

That which Marsilio Ficino <note>Marsilio Ficino (1433–1499) was an influential Italian Renaissance philosopher who helped revive Neoplatonism.</note> reports in Book 3, Chapter 18 of *On Obtaining Life from the Heavens* concerning the sign of the cross being used by the Arabs and Egyptians before the birth of Christ, does not apply here. He reports that he drew from a certain assembly of Arabs the idea that *“the figure of the cross is to be preferred above all others, because bodies act through a power already spread to the surface, and a primal surface is described by a cross.”* <note>original: "crucis figuram cunctis anteponendam, quia corpora per virtutem agunt, ad superficiem iam diffusam, primav. superficies cruce describitur."</note> These people, therefore, indicated nothing else by the cross than the strength of the stars, as he teaches more extensively in the same place. The Egyptians, indeed, had the cross among their symbols, which, according to their custom, indicated a future life; for this reason, they even carved it on the breast of Serapis <note>An Egypto-Grecian deity representing the sun and the afterlife.</note>. But these things can hardly be adapted to our own people with any appearance of probability. From this, it is gathered that the figure of the cross on the monuments of the ancients is not always an indication of the crucified Christ.

Athanasius Kircher <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680) was a Jesuit polymath and one of the first scholars to attempt to decode Egyptian hieroglyphs.</note>, a man most practiced in the most hidden teachings of the Egyptians, says in the final chapter of his *Coptic Forerunner* that he found in fragments of the "Saracenic Kabbalah" written in Arabic, that the Philosophers and Physicians of the Egyptians, Persians, Indians, and Greeks carved the figure of a cross to signify the Elements. Intending to give the reasons for this, after citing a passage from the Arabic, he adds the following: *“And no wonder, for if the Elements are moved out of their natural places, their own homogeneous parts will teach the observer that they naturally return to those same places along straight lines. Therefore, the so-called wise men were by no means inconsistent when they used these four straight lines, running out in opposite directions from a single point or indivisible center of a circle, to indicate the mystery of the four Elements.”* <note>original: "Nec mirum, Elementis enim extra suas sedes naturales dimotis, ea suos ad easdem reditus naturaliter per rectas facere lineas..."</note> However, among the Egyptians, the figure of the cross or the <term>handled Tau</term> <note>original: "Tav ansati". This refers to the Ankh, which looks like a letter T with a handle or loop on top.</note>, which Serapis and their other gods usually held in their hands, is that *“ineffable image of eternity,”* <note>original Greek: "ἀῤῥητον illud ἄγαλma τοῦ αἰῶνος" — the symbol © in the transcription is a Greek ligature for "os".</note> or the unspeakable sign of the age or century, as Johann Friedrich Herwart demonstrates at length in his *Wonders of Theology*...

## CHAPTER FOURTEEN.
### Concerning other inscribed monuments.

We see that our ancestors not only adorned burial mounds with inscribed stones or epitaphs, but they also transmitted to posterity trophies of victories and outstanding deeds, as well as triumphal arches, so to speak, marked with the characters of their native literature <note>This refers to Runic inscriptions.</note>. This is one of the things that our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), the most famous medieval Danish historian.</note> especially wishes to be observed in his preface, while he brings forth these words: *“Nor do I wish it to be unknown that the more ancient Danes, having performed conspicuous works of bravery and being suffused with an emulation of glory, in imitation of the Roman style, not only summarized the titles of their magnificently performed deeds in an exquisite kind of context, like a certain poetic work, but also took care to have the acts of their ancestors—made common in songs of their native speech—engraved on stones and rocks in the letters of their own language.”* He himself proposes an example of this matter in Book 9, where he commends the zeal of Ragnar <note>Regnerus, commonly known as the legendary Viking hero Ragnar Lothbrok.</note>, King of Denmark, by which he took care to have the battles fought by him and his notable victories engraved on rocks, so that the memory of them might be transmitted more surely and conveniently to posterity. *“After the king of the Biarmians <note>The Biarmians were a people living in the northern parts of modern-day Russia/Scandinavia.</note> was killed, and the Finns put to flight, Ragnar [had] on the rocks...”*

# BOOK THE FIRST.

Those of this category that still remain and have come into our hands, we shall set forth in their proper place; nor shall we, as far as lies within us, allow our labor in explaining them to be found wanting by those who study antiquities.

Indeed, the Holy Scriptures abundantly prove that this ritual of erecting stones in memory of famous deeds originated from God Himself and the people of God. For in the fourth chapter of the Book of Joshua, God commands in express words that Joshua choose twelve men from every tribe of Israel, who should select twelve of the hardest stones and erect them in the place of the camp where the tents of Israel were pitched that night. The text expressly teaches in verses 6 and 7 that they ought to be placed for the purpose of being a monument to the event that occurred there:

> *When, he said, your children ask you tomorrow, saying: "What do these stones mean?" You shall answer them: "The waters of the Jordan failed before the ark of the covenant of the Lord when it passed over it; therefore these stones have been placed as a monument for the children of Israel forever."*

Joshua, seeing that this method of transmitting noteworthy things to posterity was not displeasing to God, soon applied it to other things as well. For of his own accord and not by command (verse 9), he placed another twelve stones in the middle of the bed of the Jordan, where the priests stood who carried the ark of the covenant of the Lord. It is established that this occurred around the year of the world 2495, according to the calculation of Helvicus <note>Christopher Helvicus (1581–1617) was a renowned German chronologist and linguist.</note>, around which time some of our own chronologists maintain that the first king of Denmark, Dan <note>King Dan is the legendary eponymous founder of the Danish people.</note>, held power in these lands.

# DANISH MONUMENTS,
## BOOK TWO.

->Containing the *Monuments* existing in *Zealand* <note>original: *Selandia*; the largest and most populous island of Denmark, where Copenhagen is located.</note>.<-

<image-desc>Ornamental drop cap letter 'M' featuring intricate floral and foliate scrollwork.</image-desc>

That many and indeed illustrious monuments of the heroes of old once existed in Zealand is abundantly proved by the fact that it was not only the royal seat of the Baltic Kings <note>original: *Regum Baltheorum*</note>, from which everything worthy of memory originated, but also that after the unification of the three Danish kingdoms into one, great Kings built their defenses in various places there, constructed citadels, established the Royal throne, and raised countless burial mounds—still standing today—as witnesses to their great deeds, giving their own names to various cities and provinces.

However, regarding the stones and markers (especially those containing the praises of our ancestors crafted in our ancient literature <note>original: *literatura prisca*; a reference to Runic inscriptions, which were often misunderstood by later generations.</note>), there is now such a rare abundance of them to be found. We must attribute this to the "splendor" of new cities, fortifications recently built according to geometric principles, palaces, and other magnificent and massive buildings erected for luxury and display. For since our ancient literature has until now been held in no esteem and has lain utterly despised—indeed, even branded with the infamy of witchcraft and sorcery <note>During the post-Reformation period, Runes were often viewed with suspicion or associated with pagan magic.</note>—no one was found to protect the monuments written in our ancestral style and memory from the violent hands of stonecutters, masons, sculptors, and others of that kind...

# BOOK TWO.

...[of those who] have either wished or attempted to snatch away and rescue those things preserving the memory of brave men for late posterity. For they, searching everywhere for stones for the works they had planned—especially the larger and more elegant ones—had no respect for venerable antiquity or the tombs of heroes; seeking materials that served their purpose without discrimination, they demolished monuments, overturned stones, broke pillars <note>original: *cippos*; small pillars or boundary markers used by historians to describe ancient stone markers.</note>, erased inscriptions, and forced everything to serve their own whims; unless the unsuitability of the location, the hardness of the rock, or a less manageable shape exempted them from their violence. To this was added the base greed of the Farmers <note>original: *Agricolarum*</note>, who buried the stones and monuments existing in their fields and estates. Lest these stones hinder the plow or deprive them of even a tiny portion of land, they dug pits and, by throwing soil over them, buried them.

This same cruelty still occupies those who wish to appear more attentive to business and more diligent than others. It is no wonder, therefore, that monuments marked with elegant inscriptions—from which noble deeds performed here might be fully recovered—are now found more rarely than in the past, not only in Zealand <note>original: *Selandia*</note> but also in other parts of our fatherland.

However, lest we trample upon the crumbs that still remain with equal impiety, we shall strive—drawn by a love of venerable antiquity and even urged by the commands of our superiors—to collect, illustrate, and pass on to posterity the better trophies of the ancients that still survive, as much as the weight of our regular duties allows, beginning with Zealand.

So that the curious reader, who burns with the desire to see the things to be presented, does not wander in vain throughout the entire region, I present all of Zealand divided into twenty-seven provinces or districts <note>original: *principatus*</note>, described by the words of Hans Lyschander <note>original: *Johannis Lyfcandri*; a famous Danish historian and royal genealogist (1558–1623).</note> rather than my own.

For he writes thus in the *Third Discourse of the Danish Antiquities*:
"Zealand is a broad and most fertile land which, being very populous, has many and most beautiful cities around its coast and in its inland areas. This land is inhabited in various ways by ordinary..."

### DANISH MONUMENTS

" ...twenty-seven distinct peoples divided into provinces, as recorded in the catalogs of the provinces. These are Danish Princedoms; we may call them either Prefectures, Princedoms, Provinces, Counties, or Tribes. For they are defined such that each of these has its own judicial courts, its own Provost, its own Legislator and Prefect, its own Chancellor, and they differ from one another in their legal appeals, their boundaries, and their customs."

He then recounts each of these Princedoms in order in this manner:

"On the eastern shore of this island, in view of *Amager* <note>original: *Amageria*</note>, where the crossing to *Scania* <note>original: *Scandia*; the southern part of modern Sweden, then part of Denmark</note> is located, *COPENHAGEN* <note>original: *HAFNIA*</note> is seen. It is the largest colony of the Danes and in modern times the metropolis of the whole kingdom. It was built long ago by the great Bishop *Absalon* at the border of the *Smørum* <note>original: *Smarinorum*</note> and *Sokkelund* <note>original: *Soglotarum*</note> districts, where this land is separated from Scania by a small gap. It is truly a most wealthy city, full of the goods of all nations and the Royal tribute, which eastern and western merchants are obliged to pay to the King of the Danes. To the right follow the people of *Strø* <note>original: *Stryones*</note> as far as the *Isefjord* <note>original: *Sinum Issicum*</note>, having their capital in the city of *Slangerup* <note>original: *Ophiopoli*; literally 'Snake-city' from the Greek *ophis*</note>. But to the north dwell the forest-dwelling people of *Holbo* <note>original: *Holbotæ*</note>; the town of *Søborg* <note>original: *Seburgum*</note> is located there. Soon comes *Halsnæs* <note>original: *Halfnesse*</note>, where the *Isefjord* sea flows in from the *Belt* <note>original: *Baltheo*</note>. The Northern Sea closes these off from behind. Next, stretching to the South, follow the broad fields of the *Sømme* <note>original: *Sæmonum*</note> people and their most famous city, *Roskilde* <note>original: *Roeschildia*</note>, an Episcopal seat. This city was once of such great authority that it was the sole metropolitan seat, so to speak, of the Baltic and Danish empire; while its strength was at its peak, it displayed twenty-seven magnificent churches along with many other riches. Next to these is the Princedom of the *Voldborg* <note>original: *Valobriorum*</note> people, situated between the two bends of the *Isefjord*. For since that fjord flows from the north, it is immediately cut into two branches: the one further to the east receives the city of *Roskilde*, while the other turns toward the west and south. Together they create a kind of peninsula in the middle of the Island. The lower parts of this are held by the *Voldborg* people, but the outer reaches are inhabited by another tribe, the *Horns* <note>original: *Horſuiddarum*</note> people, beneath the *Horns* forest. From there, below the said bay, the *Merløse* <note>original: *Merleſii*</note> people hold the plains near the town of *Holbæk* <note>original: *Holbecum*</note>. The *Tuse* <note>original: *Tuſitæ*</note> people soon..."

...met his fate, we can hardly report anything regarding him that was not put forward by our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), the most famous medieval Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note>, whose words it will not be out of place to cite here.

*Beside the Være bridge of Zealand, they entombed the body with a royal funeral, asserting that Frode had desired the opportunity for death and burial in that place where the most excellent province of his kingdom was held. When Frode had died, the Danes—wrongly thinking that Fridlev, who was being educated in Russia, had perished—considered the kingdom to be failing for lack of an heir, and saw that it could not be continued in the royal line. They judged that man most worthy of the scepter who, for the sake of honoring Frode, would attach a song full of praise to his recent tomb, and would commend the likeness of the deceased King to posterity with a beautiful title. Then a certain Hiarno, most skilled in Danish poetry, was stirred by the greatness of the reward to honor the fame of the man with a notable monument of words. In his own manner, he composed a meter in the native style <note>original: "barbarum condidit metrum"; "barbarous" here refers to the non-Latin, Germanic poetic form</note>, the meaning of which I have transcribed into these words, published as four short verses:*

->FRODE, WHOM THE DANES WISHED WOULD LIVE FOR A LONG TIME,<-
<note>original: "FROTHONEM DANI QUEM LONGUM VIVERE VELLENT"</note>
->THEY CARRIED THROUGH THEIR LANDS FOR A LONG TIME AFTER HE DIED.<-
<note>original: "PER SUA DEFUNCTUM RURA TULERE DIU."</note>
->THIS BODY OF THE GREATEST PRINCE, ENTOMBED IN THIS TURF,<-
<note>original: "PRINCIPIS HOC SUMMI TUMULATUM CESPITE CORPUS,"</note>
->THE BARE EARTH CONCEALS BENEATH THE CLEAR SKY.<-
<note>original: "ÆTHERE SUB LIQUIDO NUDA RECONDIT HUMUS."</note>

*With this song published, the Danes rewarded the author with the crown. Thus an epitaph was repaid by them with a Kingdom, and the weight of the empire was given to a composition of a few letters, etc.*

*In an old Chronicle written in Danish rhymes, this same epitaph of the King stands recorded in these words:*

> The Danes carried King Frode through the land <note>original: "Danske the førthe Konning Frode om Land"</note>
> Long after he gave up his spirit.
> They did this because they held him dear.
> They wished to have had him here in the world.
> The mightiest chieftain who ever gained fame
> Is buried here under the damp sky.

*Anders Vedel <note>Anders Sørensen Vedel (1542–1616), a Danish priest and historian who translated Saxo into Danish.</note> expresses it more elegantly in this manner:*

> The Danes carried the corpse three years through the land,
> King Frode the Peaceful, the good:
> Both woman and man would so gladly have seen
> That he might rule the kingdom longer.

->Here lies buried that giant so strong,<-

->By Være Bridge these stones are seen;<-

The location of the burial mound is still visible and known to nearly everyone in Zealand <note>Selandia</note>; for on the road from Roskilde to Slangerup, about halfway along the route, a bridge stands which those traveling there must cross. It retains the ancient name noted by Saxo <note>The historian Saxo Grammaticus</note>, commonly called **Være Bridge**; nearby, a hill is pointed out by the local inhabitants, collapsed in one part, where they say Frode was entombed. It is called **Frode’s Mound** <note>Frode Høy</note>, and many wonderful and varied tales are told about it by the common people. When the elders were questioned about this matter, they reported that the stone upon which the Epitaph was inscribed was broken by masons and carried away, along with several others, for the repair of the bridge. It is truly a cause for sorrow that a thing bought so dearly and valued so highly by the Kingdom has perished so miserably and suffered such a harsh fate. Why do we wonder that the monuments of nobles of lesser importance are now neglected, cast down, and utterly obliterated in Zealand, when the tombs of such excellent Kings have been so foully violated? But we lament in vain what cannot be changed; rather, let us work so that those things which still remain may be rescued from destruction by our efforts.
