...met his fate, we can report hardly anything of him that has not been set forth by our **Saxo** <note>The 12th-century historian Saxo Grammaticus</note>, whose words it will not be irrelevant to bring here.

Otherwise, they buried the body with a Royal funeral at the bridge of **Være** in **Zealand** <note>Selandia</note>, asserting that **Frode** had desired the opportunity for death and a tomb in that place where the most excellent province of his kingdom was held. When Frode was dead, the **Danes**, falsely believing that **Fridlevus** <note>Fridleif, Frode’s son</note>—who was being educated in **Russia**—had perished, and since the kingdom now seemed to falter for lack of an heir and could not be continued in the royal line, they judged him most worthy of the scepter who, for the sake of honoring Frode, would affix a poem full of praise to his recent tomb, and commend the form of the deceased King to posterity with a beautiful inscription. Then a certain **Hiarnus**, very skilled in Danish poetry, in order to pursue the clarity of the man with a remarkable monument of words, and spurred by the magnitude of the reward, composed a barbarian meter <note>A reference to traditional Old Norse alliterative verse</note> in his own fashion. I have transcribed the meaning of this, published in four short verses, into these words:

-> THE DANES, WISHING FRODE TO LIVE LONG, <-
-> CARRIED HIM, DECEASED, THROUGH HIS LANDS FOR A GREAT WHILE. <-
-> THIS BODY OF THE HIGHEST PRINCE, ENTOMBED WITHIN THE SOD, <-
-> IS HIDDEN BY THE BARE EARTH BENEATH THE CLEAR SKY. <-
<note>original Latin: "Frothonem Dani quem longum vivere vellent / Per sua defunctum rura tulere diu. / Principis hoc summi tumulatum cespite corpus, / Æthere sub liquido nuda recondit humus."</note>

Once this poem was published, the **Danes** rewarded the author with the crown. Thus, an **Epitaph** was repaid by them with a Kingdom, and the weight of an empire was granted for a composition of a few letters, etc.

In an old Chronicle written in Danish rhythms, this same **Epitaph** of the King stands carved in this way:

-> The Danes carried King Frode through the land / <-
-> Long after he gave up his spirit. <-
-> They did this because they held him dear. <-
-> They would have had him here in the world <-
-> The mightiest chieftain who departed from fame / <-
-> Is buried here under the wet sky / <-
<note>original Danish: "Danske the førdhe Konning Frode om Land / Lenge syen han gaff op syn andh..."</note>

-> The Danes carried the body through the land for three years, <-
-> King Frode the Peaceful and Good: <-
-> So gladly would both woman and man have seen <-
-> That he might longer rule the realm. <-
<note>original Danish: "De Danske førde lig try Aar om Land / Kong Frode hin Frede gode..."</note>

The location of the burial mound is still visible and known to many in Zealand <note>Selandia</note>; for where the road goes from Roskilde to Slangerup, about halfway along the journey, there is a bridge which travelers must cross. ...we were received, you asked me during the journey to share my opinion with you regarding the monument seen at Trygvelde (which you oversee with great merit by Royal authority). This was so you could more conveniently satisfy the many visitors who admire the mass and carving of the stone and frequently inquire anxiously about its meaning. I do this now all the more willingly and promptly, as I have frequently experienced your kind affection toward me, and you daily demonstrate through your favor, goodwill, and service how much you value men of letters (being yourself elegantly refined in learning). 

For me, this task was made easier because I have frequently surveyed this monument, and I had already recorded its history to be included in the books of Danish Monuments. Accept, therefore, from this second book dedicated to the antiquities of Zealand <note>Selandia</note>, this outline <note>original Greek: σκιαγραφίαν (*skiagraphian*) — literally a shadow-drawing or preliminary sketch</note> of this pillar, such as our industry has been able to bring to light after the efforts of so many others. Cherish it kindly with the breath of your favor, until a more smiling fortune grants a clearer light to the remaining monuments of our homeland. Continue to busily emulate the merits of your uncle, Tycho Brahe—that great Atlas of Denmark—whose name and omen you bear; thus consecrated to eternity, you shall be celebrated forever among the Brahe-Tychos. The matters concerning our pillar are as follows:

***Trygvelde***, or (to use the name given by Bonaventura Vulcanius) ***Tiraquellum***—the "Safe Valley" <note>Latin: *Tuta vallis*</note> of Lyscander—is a Royal estate, located about one league <note>Latin: *lapide* — literally "at the stone," referring to a milestone</note> from the very pleasant town of Køge in Zealand. To the main courtyard here, from a nearby hill called ***Keiferhøjen***, this stone was moved about seventy years ago by Paul Huitfeldt <note>Latin: *Paulus Wobis* — Huitfeldt was a prominent Danish-Norwegian official</note>, who was then the Governor of that place. It can still be seen there today. It is of rough construction, with a length above the ground of four Zealandic ells <note>An "ell" (*ulna*) was a traditional unit of measurement, roughly 2 feet or 63 cm</note>, and a width of one and three-quarter ells at its widest point (for it is uneven). It is almost pyramidal in shape and gray in color. The strokes of the letters run from the base to the peak, each being about a quarter-ell in size. The stone is also pierced by five holes.

The inscription on this stone has been sought after anxiously by many and published by Bonaventura Vulcanius and others, but he who has examined every single tip <note>Latin: *apices* — referring to the serifs or specific marks of the runes</note> exactly...

That is: I made these mounds, I wished for justice to flourish in these realms, lest anyone should rashly stir up disputes, but that subjects might quietly attend to their affairs. Learn from this to settle disputes, and do not rashly excite discords in a peaceful Kingdom.

**Lyscander** therefore considers this to be the eulogy and epitaph of **Hotterus** <note>Hotterus, or Høther, is a hero-king from Danish legend, famously featured in Saxo Grammaticus's Gesta Danorum as the rival of the god Balder</note>, and he builds upon this in the preceding sections, where he weaves the following narrative: Hotterus perished in war around the year of the world 3464 <note>original: "annum mundi 3464" — a dating system starting from the biblical creation</note>. He is thought to be buried in the eastern tract of Zealand, near the Royal estate of **Trygvelde**: where he took care to have a massive mound raised in a field, in which he was accustomed to hold assemblies. He surrounded its perimeter with large stones, adorning the center with one larger than the rest, which he made pervious with holes around the sides, so that he and his nobles could conveniently tie their horses to them. On this stone, however (which was finally moved to the Trygvelde estate), he took care to have the following carved in Runic letters, etc.

But that this monument was placed for Hotterus, not even the smallest stroke of a letter suggests; indeed, it will soon become clear that the stone offers us a meaning entirely foreign to that which Lyscander proposes, once we have presented a genuine drawing of it. Nor is it asserted with any probability that those five holes—three of which are seen on one side (the east), and two on the other (the west)—were carved by Hotterus for the purpose of tying up his horses with his retinue. For the very strokes of certain letters, destroyed by the cutting of the holes, argue the contrary; Hotterus would by no means have permitted the letters on such a famous monument to be obscured in his own lifetime. For who would believe that monuments consecrated to eternity by the one who [made them...]

<page-num>110</page-num>

### DANISH MONUMENTS

Many others have worn out their intellects trying to extract something consistent with the letters and to clarify this splendid monument; but so far, their efforts have been in vain. Moved by the rarity and difficulty of the matter, the illustrious and noble Lord **CHRISTIAN FRIIS** <note>original: "CHRISTIANUS FRISIUS"</note> of Kragerup—a Knight, the Great Chancellor of His Royal Majesty, and the supreme overseer of the Royal Academy in Copenhagen <note>original: "Haffniæ"</note>—finally dispatched me there on September 7, 1624. My mission was to inspect every detail as accurately as possible, to note even the smallest markings <note>original: "apices"</note>, and to illustrate the entire face of the stone. 

I had, in fact, inspected this stone several times before and noted down the inscription for my own private use (at the time, I was attending to the health of the most noble and never-sufficiently-praised Lord **Knud Urne** <note>original: "Canuti Wrne"</note> of Åshøj <note>original: "Asmark"</note>, the most deserving Governor of the Royal District of Trygvelde, who is now *among the saints* <note>original: "ἐν ἁγίοις"; a Greek phrase indicating the person has died and is in heaven</note>). However, to execute these new commands with even greater care and diligence, I undertook the task with the noble Governor of the place acting as a witness and judge of my industry. I performed the work to the best of my ability. First, after thoroughly cleaning the grooves of the characters of dust, mud, and moss, I traced them with chalk. In places where the worn surface of the stone confused the eyes, I used my sense of touch, inserting my fingers into the man-made tracks to distinguish them from the damage caused by the weather.

The sense of the passage does not object to this; indeed, the very position of the letters seems to support it. For if these two sides are joined in the same way they appear on the stone itself, it will be clear that this specific line is closer to the first line on the southern side than to the other lines on the northern side. ...our [estate], a hereditary estate or farm (for that is what the word *Welde* <note>A term related to the modern Danish 'vælde,' meaning power or domain, but here used for a territory.</note> indicates) belonging to Trygo, perhaps founded here by him long ago. That *Welde* once denoted a Kingdom is clear from this: ᚱᚽᚴᚿᚢᛘ ᚿᚽᛘᛅ ᚢᛁᚦᚿᚽ ᚦᚽᚱᚢᛘ ᛒᚱᚽᛁᚦᚦᚽ ᚢᛁᚴᛁᚿ ᚿᛁᚴᛁᚿ <note>Original Runic and Latin: "Rex accepit vastam terram & magnum Regnum."</note>—that is, "The King took a vast land and a great Kingdom." Thus we find *Danawelde* and *Sviawelde*, the Kingdom of the Danes and the Kingdom of the Swedes. Today, it denotes power and jurisdiction, as in the phrase **Power and Domain** <note>Original Danish: "Magt oc Welde."</note>. We read that a certain King of Norway, Olaf, had a father of this name <note>Likely referring to Tryggve Olafsson, father of Olaf Tryggvason.</note>, but historians are silent as to who this specific man was, just as they are about countless others.

Therefore, it is not without cause that our countryman Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian.</note> is compelled to exclaim in this manner in the fourth book of his history:

> How many of our nation's illustrious men has the lack of writers deprived of the splendor of praise and memory! For if fortune had granted this homeland a Latin tongue, countless volumes of Danish deeds would be worn thin by the hands of readers.

ᚴᛁᚱᚦ <note>Original: "Gierth" or "Gerd"</note> is now sometimes taken to mean **to build** <note>Original OCR "skøø" likely refers to 'skøde' or 'skære,' but the author glosses it as "fabricare" (to build).</note> or to erect.

ᚦᛦᛌᛁ <note>Original: "Dysse"</note> is what they then called mounds heaped up from earth, stones, and turf. **Stone-mounds** <note>Original: "Steendysser"</note> are those which consist of stones alone; the name comes from the verb *Dysia*, which signifies burying corpses in the earth. From this comes *Dysiadur*, meaning entombed with earth and stones, which they otherwise called *Kasadur*.

ᚦᚽᚿᚿᛁ <note>Original: "Thenni"</note> used for ᚦᛅᚿᚿᛁ <note>Original: "Thanni"</note>—**this** <note>Original: "disse"</note>; this was an easy slip for the sculptor to make in the transverse line, which should have been carved in the opposite direction.

ᚴᛁᚱᚦᛁ <note>Original: "Gierthi"</note>—properly, "I surrounded this hill with an enclosure," perhaps a stone one. Even today, **To fence** <note>Original: "At gerde"</note> denotes enclosing fields or land with a fence, to hedge it in, or to construct a barrier. From this come the terms **to enclose/to shut in a field** <note>Original: "indgerde/indlucke en Marck"</note> and **a fence** <note>Original: "Gerde."</note>

ᚽᚴᚿᛅᛐ <note>Original: "Egnet"</note>—this denotes for us "appropriated" or "dedicated." The most illustrious Stephanus <note>Stephanus Johannis Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish royal historiographer.</note> thinks that in this place it is put for **Enclosed** <note>Original: "Heinet"</note>, which signifies to us the surrounding of estates with a ditch, a fence, or other such defenses. From this comes **Enclosed and fenced-in property** <note>Original: "Heinet & indheinet Gods."</note>

*Ratha aimin* (ᚱᛅᚦᛅ ᛅᛁᛘᛁᚿ) is read by some as distinct words. If this is so, *Ratha* will be a proper name, for there were many of this name in these Northern Kingdoms. Our Saxo mentions a certain Rafno in the fifth book of his History, to whom King Gother...

<meta>catchword: incu-</meta>

The man in whose memory it was built is the one we presented earlier from Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century historian and author of *Gesta Danorum*.</note>; we cannot doubt that it was placed around the time of Christ's birth, but we believe the name should be read as *Rasnkel* instead, as was stated previously.

It is clear, therefore, from this entire monument, that it does not contain even a single mark <note>original: "ne apicem quidem," literally 'not even a peak' or 'not a jot.'</note> that could support the opinion of those who believe this was the burial stone of King Hotter. Hotter's name is nowhere expressed, which, as in all other cases, ought to have been done; nor are there any deeds recorded here that correspond to his life. For what some have stuffed into vernacular rhymes <note>Traditional folk songs or oral histories in the local language.</note> about a fight with Odin's son *Boo* <note>Also known as Bous or Váli.</note> is indeed consistent with Hotter’s history, but is entirely foreign to this specific inscription. Saxo indeed reports that:

> *Odin, having recovered the divine insignias, when he learned that his son Bous (whom he had fathered by Rinda) was eager for the labor of war, summoned him and ordered him to be mindful of his brother's slaughter; he told him he should exact vengeance from the killers of Balder rather than oppress the innocent with arms, because a more fitting and healthy fight would be available where a pious cause for war had granted the license for just revenge.* 

And shortly thereafter, he adds this concerning Hotter: *He was killed in a battle encountered with Bous.* However, I find nothing akin to this in the entire context of our stone monument. What, therefore, shall we say drove those men to thrust these things, so foreign to the inscription, upon the gullible public? I believe the neighboring village, noble with the name *Hotter’s*, deceived them. For they had heard by rumor that Hotter’s court was once located here—the name *Hottersles* <note>Likely referring to a local place name like Huttersted or a similar derivation.</note> not being inconsistent with this—and a constant rumor had spread everywhere that he was buried in that very place. This was seemingly attested by a mound of remarkable size, now enclosed by a cemetery wall and an adjacent church; thus, they did not think the stone could have been brought from anywhere else but here. Yet it can be proven by living witnesses that, in our own age, the stone was moved not from there, but from another location not far distant (which today is called **Keyserhøyen** <note>Danish: *Kejserhøjen*, or 'The Emperor's Mound'.</note> by the locals, as we noted above). Nevertheless, I do not doubt that a stone once existed on the Horlev hill upon which Hotter's praise was inscribed. But together with many others...

### THE THIRD
## ORETHING.

In the district of the Boresii, commonly called *Baarse Herred* <note>A district in southern Zealand, Denmark.</note>, there was in ancient times a forum <note>term: *forum* — here used in the Roman sense to mean a public square or assembly place for judicial and commercial business.</note> located not far from the seashore called *Orething*, of which even now quite clear traces remain. To this place, the legal disputes of the entire territory—or as some maintain, of all Zealand—were brought, especially capital cases and those of greater importance. Here the highest law was administered, and here the Goddess of Justice, *Disa* or *Thisa* (from whom the inhabitants believed they received their laws and rights), was worshipped with the highest veneration. This is that same Thisa to whom they consecrated not only the third day of the week, *Thisæ dag* or *Tuesday* <note>original: *Thissdag*. While modern linguistics links Tuesday to the god Tiw or Tyr, 17th-century scholars like Worm often explored connections to the goddess Disa.</note>, but they also dedicated the solemn fairs called *Disting* <note>An ancient Swedish and Danish assembly and market held in winter.</note> in the winter months. 

Just as these fairs were held in Denmark at this location with great celebrity and a frequent gathering of the people, they were likewise held in high esteem in Sweden, particularly at Uppsala. This was described by Olaus Magnus <note>A 16th-century Swedish historian and geographer.</note> in Book 4, Chapter 6: 

> *By this image is demonstrated the most ancient rite of ice-fairs, observed in many provinces and places upon the flat and open ice with a most wealthy gathering of merchants. The most famous location for these is in the Archiepiscopal city of Uppsala in the kingdom of Sweden; through its center passes a vast river which, usually around the beginning of February, [is frozen] with such thick ice...*

# BOOK TWO

A notable stone was once placed in the middle of this marketplace, adorned with a remarkable inscription, which was moved several years ago by uncultured and less curious neighbors to strengthen the foundation of the customs house. It served that purpose for some time, until the noble Lord **CHRISTIAN FRIIS** of Kragerup, a knight bachelor and Grand Chancellor of His Royal Majesty, a distinguished judge of Danish antiquities, happened by chance upon some of its strokes <note>strokes: refers to the carved lines of the Runic characters</note> while passing through here on his way to Falster. When he saw that these carvings represented Runic or ancient Danish writing, he ordered the stone to be removed and transferred to the courtyard of the castle. Having returned home after his journey, he soon sent me to Vordingborg <note>original: *Oretingburgum*</note> to examine each detail more accurately.

When I arrived there, I found the stone to be of a nearly oval shape, except that its sides were somewhat flat, especially the side which featured the more frequent strokes of letters. Its length was two Zealandic ells <note>term: *ell* — a historical unit of measurement; the "Zealandic ell" mentioned here is roughly 63 centimeters</note> plus one and a half "quarters." Where it was widest, it was one ell minus one-third of a quarter; its thickness was half an ell plus two-thirds of a quarter. Every letter was equal in length to two-thirds of a quarter. [The Zealandic ell (let it suffice to note this once in passing) contains two Roman feet, according to the description of Jacques Cappel <note>A 17th-century French scholar of weights and measures</note>, and in addition about two and a half inches, or nearly two Rhineland feet according to Snell <note>Willebrord Snell, a Dutch astronomer and mathematician known for his work on measurements</note> with nearly half an inch.] 

Therefore, with all obstacles removed and the strokes of the letters thoroughly cleaned of dirt and mortar, I set about the task. I was joined by witnesses to the proceeding: the most noble governor of the place, Palle Rosenkrantz, a most learned man, as well as other nobles who happened to be present as companions of the Most Serene Prince Ulrich on his Bützow journey. Being wonderfully delighted by the rarity of this antiquity, they themselves lent a hand and were of no small help to me in my purpose; and thus I found the shape of the stone and the marks of the letters to be as follows.

## SINCE IT IS FITTING THAT THE LAWS OF DISA BE HELD IN HIGH ESTEEM, GRIEVANCES SHOULD BE BROUGHT HERE.

ᛶᛓᛐᚽ *Efthe* instead of *effter*, meaning "Because" <note>original: *Quia*</note>.

ᛑᛁᚠᛆᛚᚮᚵᚽᚱ *Disaloger*, that is, "the laws of Disa," a compound word made from *Dia* [Disa] and *loger* [laws] in the plural number. There is also an example here of an abbreviation or a combination of letters <term>bind-rune: *combinationis literarum*; a Runic ligature where two or more characters are joined into a single glyph</term>; for they have fused the letters ᛚ [L] and ᚮ [O] into one. The letter ᛚ [L] is presented inverted, as if it were expressing an *l*, but the word itself here does not allow for a consonant, since the letters *l*, *f*, and *g* cannot form a syllable without a vowel; nor does it entirely represent an *l*, wherefore it must necessarily be read as ᚮ [O]. Any person who examines these monuments more curiously will observe quite a few such inversions of letters made by unskillful craftsmen <note>the author suggests the ancient stone-carver made a mistake or used a non-standard style</note>; however, concerning these laws of Disa, we have already said above what needed to be said.

The *Dyser* were otherwise goddesses similar to the Fates, who were believed to be sent by Odin to those about to die, so that they might carry their souls to the hall destined for the dead <note>Valhalla</note>. For this reason, Ragnar Lodbrok sings thus in the epilogue of his funeral song: <note>original runes: ᚼᛁᛅᛘᛒᛁᛅᚦᚢ ᚦᛁᚱ ᚦᚼᚢᛁᛅ ᚢᛁᛦ ᚦᚱᛅ ᚼᛁᚱᛁᚢᚼᚢ ᚼᛅᚢᚼᛅ ᚼᛁᚦᚿᛁ ᛅᚦᛁᚱ ᚦᛁᚼ ᚼᛁᚱᚦᚼᚼ</note> that is: "the *Dyser* invite me, whom Odin sent to me from the hall of the Gods." From this comes *Disablot* <term>Disablót: a sacrificial festival or ritual held in honor of the female deities or spirits known as dísir</term>, the worship of these goddesses: as in the proverb <note>original runes: ᛚᚢᛁ ᛁᚱᚿ ᛅᚿᚿᛅᚿ ᚼᚢᛁᚿᚦ ᚼᛅᚿᚦᛅᚼ</note>. Not all oracles have perished. I wonder if the word *dysia* comes from this, which means to bury corpses in the earth, from which we get *Dyß* <note>Modern Danish: *dysse*</note>, a burial mound in which the dead are buried.

TR. Very often a preceding vowel is absorbed by the letter R; this occurs not only with this letter, but also with others, so that it is often necessary to understand a vowel included within the consonant when reading. This particle, moreover, is augmentative, increasing the meaning of the following word: TR ᚦᛁᚿ <note>transliterated: TR thin</note>, that is, "held in the highest price" or "of greatest value."

*Kære*, a word still very common among us for accusing, bringing complaints, etc. Thus *at kære nogen*, to accuse someone, and *Kæremaäl*, an accusation or grievance.

Furthermore, the interpretation of this inscription has been made quite difficult by the lines of the letters, which in many places were covered with lime and cement and could only be cleaned with great difficulty; also by the roughness of the stone and its substance, which has been eaten away by rain and storms. Therefore, we wish to put forward this explanation, produced according to our understanding, while deferring to the judgment of those more skilled.

# BOOK TWO.

ᛁ ᚦᛒᛅᛁᚴᛁᚢᛋᚢ ᛅᚠᛏᛁ ᛋᚢᛋᚢᚱ ᚠᛅᚦᚢᚱ
*I Spaikiusu in memory of Susur, his father.*

The complete meaning is not established, as this is merely a fragment: "I Spaikiusu in memory of a dear father." What if it should be read in this manner?
ᛋᛏᛅᛁᚾ ᛋᛁᛏᛁ ᚦᛒᛅᛁᚴᛁᚢᛋᚢ ᛅᚠᛏᛁ ᛋᚢᛋᚢᚱ ᚠᛅᚦᚢᚱ ᛋᛁᚾ.
*Stain seti Spaikiusu eyfti susur fadur sin.*
->SPAIKIUSU PLACED THIS STONE IN HONOR OF HIS DEAR <note>or "of Susur"</note> PARENT.<-

In a triple border, these words remain:
ᛋᚤᛚᚠᛅ ᚱᛁᛋᛏᛁ ᚦᛁ ᛒᚱᚢ ᚦᛁᚠ ᛁ ᚴ ᛁ ᚦᚢᚱᛁᛚᛋ ᛒᚱᚢᚦᚢᚱ ᛋᛁᚾ.
*Sylfa restidi Bru dif ik i Durils Brdur sin.*

The meaning is hidden from us, partly by a quite vast gap in the stone, and partly by the labyrinthine tangles in which the remainder is involved and variously arranged, so that it is scarcely clear where the beginning should be taken from or where it should end. If the ability were given to me to fill in the missing parts <note>original Latin: *supplendi facultas*</note>, I would read it thus:
ᛋᚤᛚᚠᛅ ᚱᛁᛋᛏᛁ ᛋᛏᛁᛁᚾ ᚦᛁᛋ ᚢᚴ ᚴᛁᚱᚦᛁ ᛒᚱᚢ ᚦᛁᛋ ᛁᚠᛏ ᚦᚢᚱᛁᛚᛋ ᛒᚱᚢᚦᚢᚱ ᛋᛁᚾ.
*Sylfa resti stein dis og gerdi bru dis ist Durils brudur sin.*
->SYLFA PLACED THIS STONE AND CONSTRUCTED THE BRIDGE IN MEMORY OF HIS BROTHER DURILDS.<-

The letter **I** <note>the rune ᛁ (Isa)</note> placed in the first position clearly proves that other words preceded it, but what they were is not so clear. From a comparison of the following letters with the inscriptions of other monuments of the same kind, I have set forth my conclusions for consideration, offering some sense to us until someone suggests more suitable or better readings.

**ᚦᛒᛅᛁᚴᛁᚢᛋᚢ** <note>Spaikiusu</note> seems to be a proper name; I find no meaning corresponding to it as a common noun in our language. Observe that the **B** <note>the author is referring to the second character in the name</note> is carved with strokes protruding on both sides to distinguish it from the standard **B**, for here it represents the Latin **P**. However, in the words **ᛒᚱᚢ** <note>bridge</note> and **ᛒᚱᚢᚦᚢᚱ** <note>brother</note>, the figure does not differ from the Latin **B**, which it also represents by its own phonetic power.

**ᛅᚠᛏᛁ** <note>afti</note> stands for **ᛅᚠᛏᛁᛦ** <note>aftir, meaning "after" or "in memory of"</note> by a peculiar local idiom <note>original: *idiotismo peculiari*</note>. It occur—

...here are two dotted letters: **I**, to note **E**; and **ᚢ** with a "stabbed" belly <note>original Latin: *ventre Dagessato*; referring to a 'stung' or dotted rune</note>, so that it corresponds to the value of **Y** and is distinguished from the simple **U**.

**ᚦᚢᚦᚢᚱ** and **ᚠᚢᚦᚢᚱ** <note>Fadur / Father</note> are clear in themselves; for with a few changes, we call a sweet or dear father a **Sødefader** <note>Danish for "sweet-father"</note>. Meanwhile, I do not think it absurd to consider the word *Susur* as the proper name of a certain nobleman, from whom the River *Susa* took its name. This is the opinion of the most famous Stephanius <note>Stephen Hansen Stephanius (1599–1650), a noted Danish historian</note>, who also believes this stone was once placed as a bridge over the Susa river.

**ᛋᚢᛚᚠᛅ** <note>Sulfa/Sylfa</note>: I do not know if this is a man's or a woman's name. If it is a woman's name, see how much kinship it has with *Zilpah* <note>original: *Sylpa*</note>, the handmaid given to Leah by Laban in Genesis 29:24.

**ᚱᛅᛋᛏᛁ** <note>Rasti/Resti</note> abundantly indicates a gap, as does the last syllable of another word, **ᛏᛁ**. The sense indicates that "placed [this stone] and made [this bridge]" <note>original: *Resti hoc gerdi*</note> should be read; but it is clear that something in between is missing, and it is for you to judge if I have filled it in correctly.

**ᛒᚱᚢ** <note>Bru</note> among us denotes both a bridge over a river or watercourse and a road or street paved with stones. Hence, "To bridge" <note>original Danish: *At brolegge*</note> means to pave a place with stones. If you take this word in the first sense, it can be gathered that a bridge was built over the aforementioned river by this *Sylfa*, with this stone inscription in honor of a brother. For there exists in the vicinity a bridge called *Vetersløv bridge* <note>original: *Vetersløff broe*</note>, named after the adjacent village. It is quite strong and large, consisting of huge stones, providing a convenient passage for travelers. But it does not display such great antiquity that we should believe it was built by this *Sylfa*. Nevertheless, nothing prevents us from believing that he or she once built another one, either in the same spot or nearby.

We know it was also a custom among the Romans to build not only burial mounds and underground vaults, but also other proud and magnificent structures in memory of their friends. Thus *Trajan*, in the Roman Forum where he chose a tomb for himself and his kin, [erected] a column...

**BOOK TWO**

The Emperor raised a structure of astounding size and remarkable craftsmanship, which still stands in the same place today, as Xiphilinus <note>John Xiphilinus was an 11th-century monk who wrote an influential summary of Cassius Dio’s Roman History</note> testifies concerning his life in this manner: <note>original Greek: Καὶ ἔσησεν ἐν τῇ ἀγορᾷ καὶ κίονα μέγισον, ἅμα μὲν ἐς ταφὴν ἑαυτῷ, ἅμα δὲ εἰς ἐπίδειξιν τοῦ κατὰ τὴν ἀγορὰν ἔργου.</note> "He also erected a very great column in the forum, both to serve as his own tomb and as a monument to the work performed in that forum." In the same way, Augustus created a <term>Mausoleum</term> <note>A grand, stately tomb, named after the famous tomb of King Mausolus</note> for his own burial, which is now called the **Castel Sant'Angelo** <note>The author here identifies the Castel Sant'Angelo with the Tomb of Augustus; historically, however, the Castle was originally the Mausoleum of the later Emperor Hadrian</note>. Some decorated their tombs with marble statues, as an ancient inscription attests:

->THE MOTHER EMILIA LUCIA DECREED<-
->THE BURIAL PLACE AND A STATUE.<-

->And another:<-

->HERE HE PLACED A TOMB WITH A STATUE<-
->AT THE SECOND STADION FROM THE CITY.<-

Some, like the Egyptians, decorated the burial chambers of Kings and Nobles with massive Pyramids, about which Lucan <note>A Roman poet of the 1st century AD</note> writes in his eighth book:

> *While the Macedonian <note>Alexander the Great</note> is preserved for you in a sacred vault,*
> *And the ashes of kings rest within a hollowed mountain,*
> *While pyramids and unworthy Mausoleums enclose*
> *The spirits of the Ptolemies and their shameful line.*

Others used skillfully constructed buildings; concerning which an old stone inscription reads:

->MARCUS AURELIUS ROMANUS AND ANTISTIA CHRESEME<-
->HIS WIFE MADE FOR THEMSELVES, THEIR FREEDMEN,<-
->AND THEIR POSTERITY A MONUMENT WITH<-
->A BUILDING CONSTRUCTED UPON IT.<-

Why then should our own people not have sought the same thing in the construction of bridges that the Romans sought in other buildings? This opinion is supported by the convenience of the location, the necessity of the bridge, and the force of the river flowing past.

If you take the word in the latter sense, you would say it is by no means foreign to the customs of our ancestors: for visual inspection abundantly teaches us that the monuments of the great men in these regions are surrounded on all sides by stone enclosures, which

# OF DANISH MONUMENTS

The Greeks call them *foundations* <note>original Greek: Κρηπῖδας (krepīdas)</note> and *surrounding walls* <note>original Greek: περιοικομίδας (perioikomidas)</note>, as I have explained regarding the Strö monument <note>The Strö stone is a famous runic monument in Skåne</note>. Because these stone piles resemble the construction of roads or bridges, our people call them **Broer** <note>Danish for "bridges"</note>; perhaps this is what the historians Marcellinus and Juvenal were referring to when they spoke of the "foundation of a bridge" during their discourses.

**IYI** <note>A runic sequence being analyzed by the author</note>: I do not fully grasp what this is meant to signify. If I had not examined the stone most carefully myself, I would think it was an error committed by the scribe and judge that it should be read **IPUIR** <note>Likely the runic formula "after" or "in memory of"</note>, which would yield a clear meaning. Whether the former version means the same thing, I cannot say for certain. Although the final **I** is placed quite far from the other characters, the punctuation marks placed after each word show that it is intended as a single word. Or should it be read with the latter part of the other edge, so that one reads **IYI PNRIU** and so forth?

**BRPNR**: this should be read as **BRUPNR** <note>Likely the Old Norse word "brōðir," meaning "brother"</note>. The first **u** was omitted through the sculptor's carelessness.

Concerning the location of this stone: the situation itself shows it was moved from elsewhere. Its top has been cut off so it could fit more conveniently into a wall. But I have not been able to discover where it was originally placed. It has suffered the same fate as others of this kind in **Zealand** <note>The largest and most populous island of Denmark</note>. I have not yet happened to see any that occupy their original place; instead, they have been forced to accommodate the structures of churches, fortresses, or palaces, or put to other uses, with no pious regard for venerable antiquity.

It is not clear when this monument was made. That it cannot be counted among the most ancient is evident from the fact that it contains several "dotted letters" <term>Dotted Runes</term> <note>A later system of runes where dots were added to existing characters to distinguish sounds, such as 'k' from 'g'</note>, which our people attribute to **Valdemar II**, King of the Danes <note>Valdemar the Victorious, reigned 1202–1241</note>, as I showed in my work *Runic Literature*. Furthermore, it is more elegant and shows the strokes of the characters to be less worn away than others of a greater age. Nevertheless, the reality of the matter shows it is older than the church itself. But as for who those people were, and of what rank, for whom it was placed...

## FIFTH MONUMENT.
### *THE SECOND SANDBY STONE.*

This lay hidden for a long time, buried in the bowels of the earth; it was first dug up in the year 1636. For when they were preparing a pit in the church <note>original: "templo" — while often meaning "temple," in this context it refers to the local parish church</note> for burying a corpse, and the earth had been removed to a depth of nearly two cubits <term>ulnas: an old unit of measurement, roughly equivalent to a Danish "alen" or 2 feet</term>, they struck this large stone. It had to be completely excavated so they could more conveniently finish the work they had started. Once dug up, it was kept for a while leaning against the church wall; from there, the local pastor moved it to the structure of his oven, so that it might serve as a base for the opening. Having been informed by the most Noble Lord Ronnovius Bilde of *Sandby-gaard*, I traveled there and found the structure of the stone in this condition:

## SEVENTH MONUMENT
### THE ALSTED STONE

By the same river, but where it intersects the province of the Ringsteders <note>Ringsted</note>, there exists a village commonly called *Alsted*. In Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note>, Book 12, it is called *Villa Axelstada*, made famous by the battle joined between Sivaldus, son of Sigarus, and Hacon the Boisterous. In this battle—to use Saxo’s words—"the slaughter of Sigarus and the affection for Sivaldus so incited the common minds of the people that both sexes devoted themselves to the war, and you would not believe the contest lacked the support of women." <note>original Latin: *adeò Sigari clades Sivaldiq; charitas promiſcuos plebis animos incitabant, ut uterq; ſe bello ſexus impenderet, nec certamen crederes fæmineis caruiſſe præſidiis.*</note>

It is clear that this stone was moved here from elsewhere to serve in the construction of the courtyard. But no one among the local inhabitants could be found who could provide certain information about it. The elegance of the carving and the use of dotted runes <term>dotted runes: Runic characters modified with a dot to represent different phonetic values, a practice that emerged in the later Viking Age</term> show it to be of the same age as the preceding one. However, I am unsure whether the attached cross (which does not smack of paganism <note>original Latin: *ethnicismum*</note>) might argue for a more recent date, so much so that I scarcely believe it reaches the year of Christ 800 in age. For, as we said above, we cannot agree with those who believe that Runic monuments decorated with the sign of the cross existed before the birth of Christ. The inscription is this:

->**DANISH MONUMENTS**<-

ᛘᚢᛁᚿ Who this **Eskil** <note>original: *Efchillus*</note> was, or where he came from, who placed this monument out of devotion to his kin, I have not been able to discover. In the family of Archbishop Absalon and Esbern Snare, several people of this name are recorded, but I do not know if this monument pertains to them, as I have found no one among them who had a brother named **Ystin**, from whom came a son named **Migi**. In the meantime, I suspect he was the one whom Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> so highly commends for his agility in Book 14. Saxo records a remarkable deed of his on page 280 of the Frankfurt edition in this manner: *Eskil, a knight most noble in spirit and lineage, though heavily burdened by military arms, pursued on foot one of the Slavs <note>original: *Sclavis*</note> who was unarmed and fleeing at a swift pace through marshy places; though the mud gave way beneath his tracks, he was depressed neither by the flood of the pits nor the weight of his armor, and had an easy success in his running. Indeed, he even overtook and beheaded the barbarian. And only then did he return to solid ground, with not even the soles of his feet stained by the filth.* He seems to be the same man whom Saxo mentions on page 306 as having *asserted that he was so crushed and broken by the greatness of his age that he could not even mount a horse without a helper. But when the enemy came into sight, he leaped upon his horse more swiftly than any youth, so that you would think the strength of his body was in no part shaken.* Thus *virtue commands age.* If this is indeed the man, he must have lived around the year of Christ 1176.

ᛋᛏᛅᚿ. A clear transposition of letters is evident here, committed solely and through the sheer carelessness or negligence of the carver; this should trouble no one, nor provide an occasion to think of any other power for these elements, since the sense itself clearly enough teaches that it should be read as ᛋᛏᛁᚿ **Stan** for **Steen** <note>The name Sten or Stone</note>. For although ᛁ <note>the 'i' rune</note> is frequently used for E, nevertheless in this monument a dotted ᛁ always expresses E, as is evident in ᛘᚢᛁᚿ, ᚠᛚᛁᚱ, and ᛂᚠᛏᛁᚱ, while ᛅ represents A.

ᚠᛚᛁᚱ I interpret this as **Flere**, denoting "more" or "others" as a common noun. However, if anyone contends that this is a proper name, I do not object; then the meaning emerges as: *Eskil placed this stone for Ystin and Flir, his brothers.* This name is no longer in use, nor has it been possible to gather from any Runic monuments that anyone was so named among the ancients.

# BOOK TWO

### THE MONUMENT AT ALSTED (CONTINUED)

. ᛘᛁᚴᛁ . **MIKI**. This indicates that Migo was a man of noble and high-born status, as someone who became famous for some outstanding service performed for the fatherland and was distinguished by the marks of nobility. This alone should make it clear that those who believe the title of "Nobility" was not in use among our ancestors in that age are mistaken. Or perhaps it should be read as . ᛘᛁᚴᛁᛚ . **MIKIL** <term>Mikil: an Old Norse word meaning "great" or "magnificent"</term>, which in the old language signified "much" or "greatly"—meaning "Very Noble" or "Noblest." In Danish, one would say *a very noble man* <note>original: "det var en meget ædel Mand"</note>, or in the Dutch tongue, *a noble fellow* <note>original: "een Nobel Baas"</note>. This can refer to his virtue, integrity, and other gifts of the mind as much as to his lineage and ancestry. I would like to insert here what the most famous Opitz <note>Martin Opitz (1597–1639), a renowned German poet and scholar</note> noted regarding this word *Mikil* in his commentary on the ninth verse of the *Song of Saint Anno*.

<margin>cc cc cc cc cc cc cc cc cc cc cc</margin>
*Michil*. From the excerpts of Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius, a famous Renaissance humanist</note>: *Mikil* means great, many, or copious; *Mikilon* means great; *Mikile* means magnificence. In the Kero glossary <note>One of the earliest Old High German dictionaries</note>: "much more" is *Mikelumer*, and "much less" is *Mikilumin*. In the Song of the Blessed Virgin <note>The Magnificat (Luke 1:46)</note> in the Gothic language: *Mikileid sai wala meina fan* <note>original Gothic: "My soul magnifies the Lord"</note>, which in the ancient High German language is: *Mikiloso min sela Truchtin*. In the most ancient Danish songs:

-> *The land of Spain and Miklagard* <note>original: "Spanic Land oc Mycklegaard"</note> <-
-> *They lie so far away from the lee.* <note>original: "De ligge saa langt aff Lee"</note> <-

In this context, *Mycklegaard* refers to our *Meckleburg* (Mecklenburg), known to the Latins as *Megapolis* <note>literally "Great City"</note>. The compiler of those poems observes that Constantinople was also called by this name by the Northern peoples. From this, there can be no doubt that the province on the German coast takes its name. It seems that the word *Michil* or *Mikil*—which the Danes call *Magla*—derives its origin from the Greek *megale* <note>original Greek: μεγαλη</note>, meaning "great."

Because we have encountered this monument, which necessarily makes mention of Alsted <note>original: "Axelstadii"</note> and other surrounding circumstances, we cannot help but point out that the efforts of Johannes Messenius <note>A Swedish historian and rival to Danish scholars</note> are entirely in vain. In his work *The Five Ancient Capitals of Sweden* <note>original: "Sueopentaprotopolis"</note>, he devotes himself to proving—against our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian, whom Messenius frequently and unfairly tries to provoke</note>—that the famous and wonderful example of love and loyalty shown by Hagbard and Signe <note>Legendary lovers in Scandinavian mythology; Signe was a Danish princess</note> did not take place here near Sigersted <note>original: "Sigerstadium"</note>, but rather in Sweden...

### BOOK THE SECOND.

<margin>cc</margin> [Ha]bor <note>Continuing from the previous page: Habor or Hagbart, the legendary hero.</note>, strangled by a noose around the year of salvation 222, was dug up from the earth and shown to many men. Nor does the opinion add a small amount of credibility to our faith, that directly across from the said plain was the royal residence, in which Habor, betrayed, captured, and sentenced to death, was to be hanged across the river.

You see, dear reader, with what battering rams this man attempts to cast down such a great author <note>Referring to Saxo Grammaticus.</note> from the citadel of truth and reputation! Battering rams of fig-wood <note>original: "ficulneis"; a classical Latin metaphor for something weak, brittle, or worthless, as fig-wood was considered poor timber.</note>, to be sure, and plainly inept, which one would hardly consider worthy of examination. But since quite a few things still exist among us that confirm the reliability of our author, let us run through each of his points.

Saxo, he says, *contends that this admirable specimen of love and fidelity happened in his own Denmark, contrary to all likelihood of truth, with the circumstances and the location itself crying out against it.* This man must be remarkably impudent to dare to assert and proclaim such things so boldly about this place—which he has never seen—when an eyewitness inspection teaches the opposite. Let him examine the place cited by Saxo and the circumstances; unless everything corresponds exactly <note>original: "ad amussim"; literally "to the level" or "by the mason's rule," meaning perfectly or precisely.</note> to the history, I would concede the case. 

Come closer, and I will show you even now the city and Royal Palace of Sigar <note>King Sigar, father of Signe, associated with Sigersted in Denmark.</note>; indeed, the burial mound; I will show you the hall of Signe; I will show you Hagbart’s little hill where he was punished by hanging—all things still known by their names to any rural inhabitant. Moreover, in that same place you will see the Susa river <note>The Suså, the longest river in Zealand, Denmark.</note>, the grove from which the soldiers plucked branches, Valbrunna <note>Likely referring to Valbrønd.</note>, the tomb of Haco, and all the other circumstances commemorated by our Saxo. If you can demonstrate these things as clearly on the Sigtuna plain, I will believe that you have probable reasons for this assertion. 

But I marvel that our Saxo foresaw with such a keen eye that there would be someone in the future who would bring a lawsuit against him over this matter, when he bursts forth with these words: *And lest the traces of antiquity be believed by anyone to have utterly vanished, the credibility of the aforementioned matter is displayed by the present signs of the locations, since Hagbart, having died, [gave] his name to the village...*

...brought in, nor does a place far from Sigar’s town <note>King Sigar, the legendary King of Denmark and father of Signe.</note> lie open, where on a plain a slightly higher mound shows the appearance of a protruding piece of earth, much like an old foundation. I shall soon show that all these things are still pointed out by the local inhabitants in our own century, testifying even to this day about the deeds done in that place.

He proceeds to convict Saxo of error based on folk songs <note>original: *cantilenis*</note> composed several centuries ago, and calls to his aid Master Laurentius Nericius <note>Laurentius Petri Nericius (1499–1573), the first Lutheran Archbishop of Sweden and a historian.</note>, who asserts the same thing—though much more modestly, having included an honorable mention of our Saxo. Nericius himself teaches what weight should be given to these songs when he admits they are built upon "wandering rumors" <note>original: *vagabundos sermones*</note> as their foundation, as if they were nothing else. Against these Swedish songs, we oppose Danish ones of the same, if not greater, credibility.

But he adds *that the plain not far from Sigtuna <note>A historic town in Sweden.</note> was named after him, along with the royal hall, proving he was hanged there.* Yet the sequence of the entire history contradicts this. For Sigar was a Dane and his daughter Signe was a Dane, living in Denmark’s Sigersted <note>original: *Sigerstadium*; modern Sigersted near Ringsted on the island of Zealand.</note>. Hagbart, on the other hand, was a Swede (or a Norwegian, as the other author prefers) who came to Denmark—specifically to Sigersted—to see Signe. There he performed the deeds related by Saxo, and there he was captured and condemned to death. How, then, could he have been transferred to Sweden to be punished by hanging? Or how could Signe, while in Sigersted in Denmark, have seen Hagbart on the gallows-steps <note>original: *scalis gemoniis*; a classical reference to the Gemonian Stairs in Rome where the bodies of executed criminals were displayed.</note> near Sigtuna? And how could he, in turn, while in Sweden, see the burning palace in which Signe was trapped, so that they might both perish at the very same moment? Who is so dull-witted <note>original: *bardus*</note> as not to notice these contradictions? There may be a plain in Sweden named after him, perhaps because he was born or raised there, or became famous for his deeds; but it cannot be claimed with any appearance of truth that it was named after his hanging.

He adds his own experience: *that in the "Habor-plain" itself, he received from one of the inhabitants a few years ago a stump of the gallows-post from which Habor <note>Habor is a variant name for Hagbart.</note> was strangled with a rope around the year of salvation 222, having been dug out of the earth.* Who is so "dull-nosed" <note>original: *obtusæ naris*; a Latin idiom for someone lacking discernment or a sense of irony.</note> that they cannot smell the fabrication at the heart of this story? Our Saxo writes: *That someone reported to Absolon <note>Archbishop Absolon (c. 1128–1201), the patron of Saxo Grammaticus and a central figure in Danish history.</note> that he had recovered a beam in that place (near Sigersted in Zealand)...*

### BOOK TWO

...seen it more clearly than a peasant who, probing the soil with his plow-blade, stumbled upon it. This is the basis of Messenius’s account. Even if it were true that someone found a certain piece of wood there a few years ago, it has by no means been proven that this was the beam of Habor’s gallows. He will have to demonstrate that a piece of wood—subjected to rain, rot, and the erosion of the earth—could last for more than fourteen hundred years beneath the ground before I shall give him any credit.

Finally, he thinks he adds great weight to his opinion by claiming that directly across the plain was a royal residence where Habor was betrayed, captured, and sentenced to death. We believe there was a palace there, but we deny he was betrayed, caught, and sentenced in that place. He will never prove it, as all the historical circumstances cry out against it, as we have shown above. I rather think this palace supports the opinion of Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), the author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note>, who records that Hagbart was born in Sweden, and perhaps it was in this very palace—from which the plain took its name.

But leaving these most uncertain matters aside, there is one thing I cannot fail to point out, which reveals the truth of Messenius’s entire discourse. He concludes the words of his [source] Nericius with this exclamation <note>original: *epiphonemate*</note>: *How then is it consistent with the truth that Habor paid the penalty for illicit love in the Cimbrian Chersonese?* <note>The "Cimbrian Chersonese" refers to the Jutland peninsula of modern Denmark. Original: *Cymbrica Chersoneso*.</note> With these words, he either tries to pin a lie on our Saxo, claiming Saxo said Habor was hanged in the Cimbrian Chersonese—which Saxo never even dreamed of, as his entire history proves the contrary by describing the location exactly in the middle of Zealand <note>Selandia; the largest island of Denmark.</note>—or he is so childish and ignorant in geography that he does not know how to distinguish between the widely separated provinces of a neighboring kingdom, whose borders he could have learned from any common map.

What trust can be placed in this historian when he writes of more remote things, if he is so dull or blind in those things right before his eyes? But I shall stop shaking out such obvious nonsense, since anyone who even slightly compares our Saxo with this new writer can see abundantly "how far vetch is from lupines" <note>A proverbial expression meaning two things are completely different or of vastly different quality. Original: *quantum distent Erva Lupinis*.</note>. But so that the whole matter may be made clearer, I subjoin a topographical drawing of the said area, which I myself saw with my own eyes <note>original: *autopsia* (αὐτοψεί)</note>, as the local Pastor and the elders of the neighborhood showed it to me when I visited the place diligently not so many years ago...

...in the borders of the Hallandians, Smålanders, and Blekingers. 
Ancient custom declares that two thousand Scythians or archers served the Danish King in war. These, therefore, along with the other peoples of Scandinavia, are said to be the most warlike, the most excellent, and the most invincible of all nations. Nor, when the affairs of the Northern regions were established, were there any who could be easily compared to them, with the sole exception of the Cimbrian Vandals, whom we call the Winnili and Vinuli. These were very close to the Getae <note>A tribe often historically conflated with the Goths in early modern scholarship</note>, but they fought with different methods. For the Getae are all most skilled *Ballistarii* <note>cross-bowmen or artillerymen</note> and Scythians, expert with both the bow and siege engines. But those Cimbrians are "Picts" <note>The author uses "Ficti," playing on the Latin word for "formed" or "shaped," to explain the origin of the Picts</note>, bravely stirring up war with spear, sword, and Vinulian spikes. When we read various histories and migrations, and consider the ancient movements of nations, we believe more readily that from here came the Picts (or "Ficti"), who are called athletes and gladiators, and from there the Scythians, who are archers. 

Closest to these to the west are the Norici <note>Norwegians</note>, related to the Goths and enjoying similar customs. Following them as far as the Baltic Sea, beneath the Hallandic forest, are the Bergenians <note>likely referring to the inhabitants of the Bjäre district</note> near Engelholm <note>Ängelholm</note>. From these, the Austrians <note>original: "Austrii," meaning those to the south</note> are separated to the east and south by the river Rhine <note>original: "fluvio Rhynensi," likely referring to the Rönne Å in Scania</note>, reaching as far as the Austrian forest. These in turn are separated by the Silesian stream from the great province of the Laudani <note>Likely the Luggude hundred in Scania</note>, which has the city of Helsingia as its Metropolis. 

This city is indeed very ancient, and many dispute its etymology, with different opinions pleasing different people. Some seem to derive it from a greeting <note>Latin: "salutatione," perhaps suggesting a place where people were "hailed"</note> and from the custom of merchants of all nations, who in this place honor the Danish name and pay tribute. But we value more the authority of the inhabitants, whose opinion is judged to be more fitting. The "Helsingi," they say, were peoples of Northern Barbary. These once arrived in the Baltic Ocean—perhaps while the Cimbrian and Getic state and policy were struggling—and occupied the narrows of the Oreonic Sea <note>The Øresund</note>. ### BOOK THREE. ###

...it was called Helsingian, as far as the rivers Silesium and Rha; but concerning the time [of this naming], we could find almost nothing certain that we might assert here with consistency. Afterward, however, as the Christian religion became known to men and took hold, this province is said to have been the first of all in Scandinavia to receive the Catholic faith, and from that obtained the name Laudania or Laudeonia <note>The author is referring to the Luggude district</note> *Lougudeherrit*. From here to the South, across the river Rha, follow the Rhonebians, whose capital is in the city of Landskrona <note>original: "Coronensi civitate"</note>. After a space dwell the Turones, near the very ancient and largest city of Lund <note>original: "Lundensem"</note>, celebrated for its metropolitan See of the Archbishop and the distinguished Parliament of Scandinavia. ## FIRST
### *LUND.*

**F**irst, we encounter here in the province of Turonia—commonly called **Torna Hundred** <note>original: "Torneherrit"</note>—the city of Lund, once the august seat of the Archbishop and the Metropolis, now a pleasant city distinguished by its noble Chapter of Canons. In its cathedral church, besides those things worthy of observation recorded by the most celebrated man *Isaac Pontanus* <note>Johannes Isacius Pontanus (1571–1639), a Dutch-born historian and Danish Royal Historiographer</note>, the Royal Historiographer, there was once a bell of stupendous size, about whose manufacture many people devise various stories. However, it is certain that *Birger*, the last Archbishop of Lund <note>Birger Gunnersen, Archbishop from 1497 to 1519</note>, saw to its creation and gave it the name *Mary of Loreto* <note>original: "Mariae Lauretanae"</note>. But when His Most Serene Majesty King *Frederick II* saw that the tower could not hold such a mass, nor was it suitable for practical use, he saw to it that three other sufficiently vast and large bells were made from it, with which he adorned the tower of *Kronborg*. Its height was nearly four cubits <term>cubit: an ancient measurement, usually the length of a forearm</term>, and its circumference was fourteen. The length of the base equaled three cubits, and its thickness was five spans <term>span: the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the little finger</term>.

In this very Church of St. Lawrence, various wonderful specimens of the architectural art are found, in which these characters are also seen: P A I ✱ H B. These were placed there by the German architect **Adam van Düren** <note>original: "Adam von Byren," a famous Westphalian architect and sculptor active in Sweden and Denmark</note>, for the sake of a good omen, as I believe. Among the rest, in the northern part of the church itself, facing the west, a column is visited whose base contains this inscription and an emblem indicating the difficulty of the proposed work. For a man is seen strenuously cleaning a donkey's hide with a scraper <term>strigil: a tool for scraping skin</term>, sitting upon his knees on it; next to him lies the flayed donkey itself, so burdened by weight that, with its legs broken and the internal organs of its belly bursting through, it is forced to succumb and end its life groaning. The clapper <note>original: "Bapsile"; the internal swinging part of the bell</note> equaled three ells in length and was five spans thick <note>A span (spithama) is the distance from the tip of the thumb to the tip of the pinky finger</note>.

Among other things, in the northern part of the temple itself, a column is seen looking toward the west; its base contains this inscription and an Emblem indicating the difficulty of the proposed work. What this emblem means—as well as the others with which [the architect] decorated the font in the hypogeum <note>an underground chamber; here referring to the cathedral's famous crypt</note> or the crypt of the Choir—anyone may easily gather for themselves. Indeed, he saw to it that this Mausoleum was built for his kin at no small expense, and he studiously took care to propagate the memory of his relatives to posterity with such a splendid work.

\* **ᛋᛏᛅᛁᚾ ᚱᛅᛁᛋᛏᛁ** <note>Runes: *stain raisti* — traditionally "raised the stone"</note>. One might easily gather from this that the stone had indeed been placed in the monument beforehand, but only then was it adorned with letters in memory of Asurius; at the same time, the genuine meaning of the word **ᚱᛅᛁᛋᛏᛁ** <note>raisti</note> is drawn out from here, by which it denotes the letters that express the feelings of the mind. In the same sense, we read in another place **ᛋᛅᛏ ᛋᛏᛅᛁᚾ ᚦᛁᚾᛅ** <note>Runes: *sat stain thina* — "set this stone"</note>: that is, he adorned with letters a stone already adapted to the monument. This form of speaking differs from that of **ᚱᛅᛁᛋᚦᛁ ᚦᛁᚾᛅ** <note>raisthi thina</note> etc., which indicates that a stone or rock was placed there where none had been before.

\* **ᚾᛁᚦᛁᛅ** <note>Runes: *nithia* — a term for kin or descendants</note>. It is not infrequent for **ᚾᛁᚦᛁᛅ** <note>nithia</note> to be put in place of **ᚢᚦᚦᛁᛅ** <note>uthia</note>, with the same meaning, as the variety of regional idioms permits.

\* **ᛅᛋᚢᚱ** <note>Runes: *asur*</note> is also a man's proper name, which is now customary for us to call **ASER** <note>The modern Danish name Asser</note>. It occurs not infrequently in the sacred scriptures; in Genesis 10, verse 22, a son of Shem is so named. There was also Assur, the father of Tekoa, who had two wives, Helah and Naarah, in 1 Chronicles 4, verse 5. From this, Assyria is also called the land of Asur in *Isaiah 7, verse 18.* Indeed, in the tenth chapter, verse 5, *Assur is proclaimed the rod of God’s anger, and the staff in whose hand is the indignation of the Lord.* <note>original Latin: "Assur virga furoris Dei proclamatur, & baculus in cujus manu indignatio Domini"</note> Thus, from these and many other things (about which we may speak in their proper place), it is possible to read the undoubted traces of our origins in a not unbecoming way. Furthermore, if you follow the modern pronunciation of this word, you will find express traces of it among the Israelite people. For the son of Zilpah whom she bore to Jacob is called **ASHER** <note>original Latin text uses "ASER"</note>, over whom Leah triumphed so much that for his sake she believed all generations would call her blessed, Genesis 30, verse 12. And to the same Asher, Jacob, already about to die, gave his blessing in chapter 49, verse 20, *pronouncing that his bread shall be fat, so that he shall even provide delicacies for kings.* <note>original Latin: "panem ejus pinguem futurum pronunciat, adeò ut etiam regibus delitias sit præbiturus"</note> From his tribe was born Anna, daughter of Phanuel, a pro- <note>The word continues on the next page as "prophetess."</note>

...prophetess, who publicly proclaimed the newly born Christ, Luke 2:38. These names do not, therefore, merely smell of paganism <note>original: *gentilismum*, referring to pre-Christian religious practices</note>; rather, they provide clear testimony that our nation was brought over from the people of God. And although here it is read as **OSUR**, our ancestors did not make such a careful distinction between A and O in our literacy. This is evident from the fact that **ᚬ** is nothing other than **ᚭ** doubled, or increased by a single line, as has been more fully demonstrated in our *Runic Literacy* <note>A reference to Worm’s 1636 work *Litteratura Runica*</note>.

**ᛏᚦᚱ** indicates Toro, as attested by common pronunciation, to which the ancients paid greater regard than to the orthography <note>standardized spelling</note> now customary for us. Although this name is even now not infrequent among us, and most modern people twist it into Theodore: however, in ancient times it was in much more frequent use among us. For the primary of the Gods was called **Tor**, from whom not only did the name of the fifth day of the week, **Thursday** <note>original: *Torſdag*</note>, take its origin, and the month of March, **Thor-month** <note>original: *Tormanet*</note>: but even towns, forests, pastures, bridges, and men themselves were gifted with this name, as we have more fully demonstrated in our *Calendars*.

Who or what kind of man this **ᛏᚦᚱ** might have been is difficult to gather from these inscriptions; however, if we take as evidence the fame and common talk of the people (which is necessary in these matters), we must conclude that a certain man from the most noble lineage of the Totts, called **TOR TOT**, is buried here. Concerning him, I find the following in a manuscript containing the genealogies of the most prominent families existing in Denmark: <insert>The first Christian man we find in the lineage of the Axelssons was named Sir Tor Tott, who lies buried in Kiølinghøj.</insert> <note>original Danish: *Den førſte vi finde der Chriſten Mand vaar i de Axelſønners Slæct / heed Her Tor Tott / ſom ligger begrafven i Kiøling Høi.*</note> That is: The first of the family of the Axels who gave his name to Christ <note>converted to Christianity</note> was called Lord **TORO TOTT**, who is said to have been buried in the hill of Kiølinghøj. ### BOOK THREE

...began to prepare snares against his life. Among these were *Lennius, Attula, Tottus, and Vithnus*, who, although he held a governorship among the *Slavs*, was of *Danish* origin. Our native chroniclers record that this *Olon* <note>also known as Ole</note> lived around the year of Christ 290, at which time the invasion of the *Lombards* from these northern kingdoms into foreign lands took place.

*Peter Tott* is also celebrated in our histories; he provided distinguished service to *Valdemar I* against the barbarian *Vandals* in the war around the year of Christ 1171. Regarding him, the same *Saxo* writes in Book 18 of his *History*:

> *Peter, also surnamed Tott, when he had damaged his ship by striking it against some stakes and remained behind to repair it while the fleet of his comrades departed, spent the time devoted to the repair alone and thus free from all danger. Having repaired the stern, he followed his companions and, with no one challenging him, reached the fleet through safe and open waters.*

Among the deeds of *Haakon, son of Haakon*, the most powerful King of *Norway*, I find that around the year of Christ 1255 in *Iceland* there was a certain man of this family named *Toro Tott*. A certain *Giffurius* <note>Gissur Þorvaldsson, a powerful Icelandic chieftain</note>, one of the leading men of *Iceland*, entrusted his ancestral goods and estates to him when he was about to set out to the King in *Norway*. You will find this event described more fully in the *History of Norway* recently published in the common tongue <note>referring to a vernacular translation of the Norse Sagas</note>.

*Paul the Deacon* <note>original: *Paulus Varnefridus*, an 8th-century historian</note>, in Book 1, Chapter 5 of his *History of the Lombards*, mentions a certain village of *Toto* in *Belgic Gaul*, perhaps taking its name from the *Totts*—though others read it as *Turonis*. Could it be named after the god *Thor* <note>original: *Toro Deo*</note>, the primary deity of the Northmen? In Chapter 20, the deeds of *Tato* are described, who held the *Lombard* scepter after his father *Claffo* and overthrew the *Heruli*. Let more skilled critics judge whether the name should be read as *Totto*.

In *Norway*, they usually count fifteen generations of men since the introduction of the religion of the true God; which, when applied here, is not far off the mark. Rather, it seems to confirm what is asserted about *Toro Tott*: namely, that he was the first of this family to give his name to Christ <note>original: *Christo nomen dederit*; a standard phrasing for being the first in a line to be baptized</note>.

# DANISH MONUMENTS

Otherwise, this eulogy is also circulated about him, composed—as it appears—by posterity not without reason:

->Dalby Mill and Kielby Meadow,<-
->Bøge Point and the Ringsø catch,<-
->I give to the new Bosø Cloister;<-
->While I myself lie within this mound.<-
<note>original Danish: "Dalby Mølle oc Kielby Vang / Bøge Øre oc Ringsø fang / Giffuer jeg Bosie Kloster ny / Mens selff ligger i denne Høÿ." This refers to Bosjökloster, a Benedictine nunnery in Scania, which was then part of Denmark.</note>

The sense of which is roughly this:

->*Fields, mills, green pastures, and soil,*<-
->*I gave to those devoted to Christ and the cloisters;*<-
->*Yet it pleased me to be buried in this ancestral hill—*<-
->*Say of Tott, I pray, that his bones rest softly.*<-
<note>original Latin: "Campos, pistrinas, viridantia pascua & arva, / Christo devotis cœnobiisq, dedi: / Hocce tamen placuit colle ut tumularer avito / Totti dic, sodes, molliter ossa cubent." The author provides this Latin verse as a scholarly translation of the Danish folk rhyme.</note>

It appears, therefore, that he was a wealthy man, converted from heathen <term>ethnicis</term> superstitions to the worship of the true God. To declare his gratitude toward the Creator, he wished to bequeath so many goods for the founding of monasteries; meanwhile, in the manner of his ancestors, he wished to be buried on his own land among his kinsmen and friends. Indeed, I am of the opinion that the first Christian magnates in these regions were granted an indulgence by the religious authorities so that they could be brought to the monuments of their ancestors after death, provided they bequeathed certain goods to the churches and cloisters. And under this title, our Toro here consecrated the lands enumerated above to the Bosø monastery. 

It is also said that Erik Rosenkrantz <note>a prominent Danish nobleman, died 1503</note>, the first Christian in that family, built the southern hall of the church at Ørsted <note>original: "Orstadense"</note> in Jutland <note>original: "Cimbriâ"</note> for the same reason, although he preferred a hill situated on the Hofringholm estate—ennobled by the tombs of his ancestors and still conspicuous by its massive stones—as the place where his body would be buried with solemn pomp.

That the Romans shared with us this custom of burying the dead on one's own estates can be gathered even from that passage of Martial <note>Roman poet, c. 38–103 AD</note>:

->*Now your seventh wife, Phileros, is being buried in your field;*<-
->*the field gives back more to no one, Phileros, than to you.*<-

### BOOK THREE.

...while nearly 300 citizens owned fields individually, for a common man, his own land was scarcely available for a necessary roof or a place of burial? In a similar way, the historian Appian, in his first book, intending to explain why the wealthy rejected the agrarian law <note>The Roman laws regarding the redistribution of public land to the poor</note>, brings forward these points: *That they considered it unjust not only to be deprived of their fields, but also of the tombs of their ancestors, located in the hereditary soil.*

In ancient times, the highest honor was held for the tombs of magnates (even among the heathens), especially the collective ones in which the bodies of not just one, but the entire family were buried. It is no wonder then that among the early Christian converts <term>neophytes</term> <note>original Greek: νεόφυτοις</note>, quite a few preferred to be buried in the fields and estates of their ancestors rather than choose new burial vaults for themselves in the churches.

INHERITANCE. It was not uncommon for the ancients to choose heirs for themselves from among relatives and friends, to proclaim them publicly, and to testify to this with exceptional monuments for the eternal memory of the matter. This can be gathered not only from this stone, but also from the one located not so many leagues from this one near the village of Hyllie <note>original: Hierup</note>, on which almost the same words and the same name of Toro are found engraved. It appears, therefore, that he was a wealthy man, converted from heathen superstitions to the worship of the true God. To declare his gratitude toward his Creator, he wished to bequeath so many goods for the founding of monasteries, while in the meantime, according to the custom of his ancestors, he wished to be buried on his own land among his kinsmen and friends. Indeed, I am of the opinion that the religious authorities granted this indulgence to the first Christian magnates in these regions, so that they could be brought to the monuments of their ancestors after death, provided they bequeathed certain goods to the Churches and Monasteries. And under this title, this Toro <note>A Latinized form of the Old Norse name Thord or Tord</note> consecrated the things enumerated above to the Bosjö monastery <note>A Benedictine nunnery in Scania, modern-day Sweden</note>. 

Furthermore, Erik Rosencrantz—also the first Christian in that family—is said to have built the southern hall of the church at Ørstad in Jutland <note>original: Cimbriâ</note> for the same reason, although he preferred the mound located on the Hofringholm estate, ennobled by the tombs of his ancestors and still conspicuous by its huge stones, as the place where his body would be buried with solemn pomp.

This rite of burying the deceased on one's own estates was a custom we held in common with the Romans, as may be gathered from that line of Martial:

As was shown above, the ancients built [tombs] on their own estates; I need not mention that the common report, handed down through the hands of our ancestors, constantly asserts the same.

As for the fact that the previously cited manuscript asserts he was buried in *Kiolinghen* <note>modern Kävlinge in Scania</note>, a few leagues distant from here—a document that does not reflect particularly great antiquity—I believe this should be attributed to the ignorance of the writer. Having heard that Toro was entombed in a mound, the writer assumed it was that one. However, the present inscription, the consistent local tradition, and the ownership of the estate all contradict this. Who does not see that more weight must be given to such evident proofs than to the bare report of a writer unsupported by any foundation of reason?

If you object that no surname is attached here, and contend that for this reason any other Toro or Totte could claim this monument for himself: know that it was by no means the custom among our ancestors to insert surnames into epitaphs, as all surviving examples of this kind among us abundantly show. This was either because they favored <term>Laconism</term> <note>A style of speaking or writing using very few words, named after the Spartans of Laconia</note> and simplicity, or because they believed it was sufficient to be known to posterity by their proper name alone, as their fame, the brilliance of their deeds, and the possession of the estate distinguished them sufficiently from other <term>namesakes</term> <note>original Greek: "ὁμωνύμοις" (homonymois); people sharing the same name</note>.

† **BE.** The name Eber is still common among us today, and without changing a single letter they are called **Ebe**. However, his status or rank remains unknown to me. In the meantime, what I remarked upon earlier seems to apply here regarding the relationship between the names of Danish heroes and those who held leadership among the people of Israel. You can see for yourself how little difference there is between Ebe and Heber if you remove the aspiration <note>The "h" sound at the beginning of the name</note>. Regarding Heber and Geber, read, if you please, the 10th chapter of Genesis, verses 24 and 25.

### BOOK THREE

[...customary not only for our own] people, but also for the Romans, as we are taught by various records. ->The mound grew into a shaped circle,<-

->Mindful with constant care.<-

The seventh stone, which occupies the very center of the whole area and has a pear tree growing next to it, has earned a peculiar name from the local inhabitants. It is called *Little Thule*, because while the others are roughly of equal magnitude, this one is smaller; indeed, in height it does not exceed one and a half Zealand ells <term>ell</term> <note>A traditional unit of measurement; the Zealand ell (Selandica) was approximately 63 centimeters or 2 feet</note>, although in circumference it is nearly equal to two, being cylindrical in shape.

It is as follows: A certain bailiff of a nearby village, attracted by the shape of this stone—which seemed fit enough for domestic use—arranged for it to be moved into his house not so many years ago to be used in a building. Soon, on the following night, such a great tumult and noise suddenly arose throughout the whole house that everyone feared the building was about to collapse, as they had never heard such a thing in that place before. When this continued for several nights, the head of the household, anxious for his own safety and that of his family, fled to God in prayer, seeking the causes of such an evil and asking for deliverance with fervent sighs. restored it to its place. Once this was done, those phantoms and terrifying sights vanished, and the entire house was freed from such mockery. These are the tales they tell; moved by them, the people still call this stone "Little Thule," and the mound itself **Thulshøy** <note>literally "Thule’s Mound" or "Thuls-mound"</note>. They still take holy care today to ensure that no one presumes to lay violent hands on this monument in any way.

Concerning the structure of this entire monument, it does not seem at all irrational to believe it was begun shortly before the worship of the true God <note>referring to the Christianization of Denmark</note> was established in these regions, and completed upon the death of our Toro <note>likely a Latinization of the Danish name Tore</note>. Indeed, after that time, cemeteries and churches—rather than fields or estates—were designated for the burial of Christians, though by special indulgence burial on estates was granted to some. Nor does the presence of a sufficiently aged pear tree contradict this, whether it was placed there by design or by chance, adorning the center of the mound with its very wide foliage. Furthermore, the manuscript cited above records that this Toro was among the first in his family to be imbued with Christian rites; and I have found elsewhere that he lived under King Oluf **Hunger** <note>Oluf I of Denmark, who reigned from 1086–1095 and was nicknamed "Hunger" due to several years of crop failure</note>, around the year of Christ 1088. At that time, many places in this kingdom were still destitute of churches and cemeteries, so that some were compelled by the custom of their ancestors to bury bodies on their estates. Others, even if they had churches and cemeteries, preferred the burial places of their ancestors; the evidence itself shows that this is what Toro did.

When I shared these reflections on the Strø <note>a village in North Zealand, Denmark</note> monument, which were published some time ago, with a certain friend of mine who was traveling to England, he showed them to the most noble Palle Rosenkrantz <note>Latinized as Palæmoni Rosæcrantzio</note> of **Krenckerup**, Royal Governor of Aalholm and at that time the envoy of His Most Serene Royal Majesty. He considered it worthwhile to seek the judgment of a man as noble as he is expert in antiquities, Sir *Henry Spelman* <note>a famous English antiquary (1562–1641) known for his works on legal and ecclesiastical history</note>, an *English-British Knight*.
