### To the Most Illustrious Lord PALÆMON ROSECRANTZ, 
### Ambassador of His Serene Danish Majesty to the English, *Henry*
### *Spelman sends his humblest greetings, with every wish*
### *for the increase of his dignity.*

**I**t was very pleasing (Most Illustrious Lord) that the learned youth Axel Juel <note>Latinized as Axilius Julius; a member of the prominent Juel family</note>, from your circle of followers, recently showed me that Danish monument **TULSHÖI**, which was learnedly, splendidly, and ingeniously described by Ole Worm <note>Olaus Wormius (1588–1654), a famous Danish antiquarian and physician</note>. I am not, however, led to believe that the surname "Tott" <note>One of the oldest and most distinguished noble families in Scandinavia</note> was known anywhere in the world around the year of Christ 290, since the Germans, Gauls, Britons, and (to say nothing of others) all the northern peoples followed the custom of the Greeks and Hebrews in using a simple, single name. Therefore, I do not believe that the "Tott" mentioned by Saxo Grammaticus <note>A 12th-century Danish historian</note> in that century should be counted among the ancestors of Toro Tott—who lived 800 years more recently—merely because he was homonymous <note>original: *ὁμώνυμος*; having the same name but a different identity</note>, any more than I would think those Hebrew Asshurs <note>Referring to the biblical Asshur, son of Shem</note> belonged by family kinship to Asshur the brother of Tott. I do not, however, deny that the Danes, Norwegians, and Goths (whom they once called the Getae) are descended from the Hebrews, as Arngrímur Jónsson <note>Arngrimus Jonas (1568–1648), an Icelandic scholar</note> has quite vigorously proven in his *Crymogæa* <note>The first printed history of Iceland, published in 1609</note>.

Certainly, among our historians who have treated the Danes more extensively than the Danes themselves, no "Saxo" or "Dane" occurs, to my knowledge, who relied on a family surname. Nor have I found any such person among the ancient Gauls in Gregory of Tours <note>A 6th-century historian of the Franks</note>, nor in the middle ages in Aimoin <note>Aimoin of Fleury, a 10th-century chronicler</note>, nor among the Lombards in Paul Warnefrid (also known as the Deacon). I admit, however, that in our histories as well as those of other nations, one occasionally finds an individual addressed by two names; yet neither was a family name, but rather something arising from some accidental circumstance, and often used as a taunt (which Plautus <note>A Roman playwright</note> calls an *improperium* <note>original Latin: "insult" or "reproach"</note>, and we call a Nickname), while the other was his genuine and lawful name.

Our own people, whether Anglo-Saxons or Anglo-Danes before the arrival of the Normans, did not use family surnames; nor in my entire home country <note>Spelman refers to Norfolk and East Anglia</note>, which more than others was entirely subject to the Dane, and today teems with the villages and lineages of the Danes, have I [found] any more accurately in—

,, ...descended from the Danes <note>completing the word "daganti" from the previous page's catchword "dagan-"</note> was found to have two names. There exists a certain old story in memory of this matter: that a Norman noblewoman rejected a marriage with an Englishman because he was not honored with a double name <note>A surname in addition to a Christian name</note>. Shortly thereafter, everyone rushed into the Norman custom, adopting surnames for themselves either from estates, villas, and towns (which was most common among the Normans and Gauls) or from qualities of mind or body, office, magistracy, craft, deeds, and the like, and spreading these same names to their grandsons and their offspring. ,, It is of the most ancient custom to bury in the fields, even the whole family together in the same monument. Thus Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob with their wives were buried in the cave that was at the edge of the field called Machpelah <note>A site in Hebron mentioned in Genesis, considered the burial place of the Patriarchs</note> (where even their first parents, Adam and Eve, are buried, if we believe the Doctors <note>Referring to the Doctors of the Church or biblical scholars</note>). Nor is it empty here what is said, "at the edge of the field." For it suggests another most ancient rite, which Cicero mentions from Plato at the end of the second book *On the Laws*: namely, that the dead were not to be buried in cultivated fields. For they once left the edges of the fields uncultivated, which also seems to have been observed in **TULSHØI**, just as it was more sacredly kept by our Danes and Saxons. 

,, For I notice these mounds <note>tumuli</note> have been raised up prominently in various places from piled-up turf: yet not in fruitful fields, but on heaths and at the borders of plains, which are by no means pleasing to Ceres and Bacchus <note>Ceres is the goddess of grain and Bacchus the god of wine; this means the land was not suitable for agriculture or vineyards</note>. Therefore, those who planted a pear tree in a tomb violated the ancient custom; for this practice is much more recent, and we have never seen a fruit tree in cemeteries: but very often wild and forest trees. I am not unaware, however, that the Jews placed monuments and mounds elsewhere in gardens: but I pass over these things which require further discussion. 

,, Yet I wonder why Toro Tott, the founder of monasteries, did not choose a burial place for himself there <note>within his own foundation</note>, since that would be especially pleasing to the primary founders, and a pledge of future blessedness—as if they would not yield their place even to the departing Monks—especially to return from Christian brothers to Pagans, to flee from the faithful to the unfaithful. Perhaps this was another Toro Tott, and lest I be troublesome to him—may his bones rest softly <note>original: *molliter ossa cubent*; a traditional Roman funerary blessing</note>.

„...he was found to have two names. There exists an old anecdote to commemorate this fact: a noble Norman woman is said to have rejected a marriage with an Englishman because he was not honored with a double name <note>A surname or family name</note>. Therefore, in a short time, everyone rushed to adopt the Norman custom, taking for themselves surnames either from their estates, villages, and towns (which was most common among the Normans and the French), or from qualities of mind or body, from their office, magistracy, trade, deeds, and such things, and passing these same names down to their grandsons and their lineage. Thus Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, with their wives, were buried in the cave which was at the edge of the field called Machpelah <note>original: "Machpelach"; a site in Hebron central to Abrahamic tradition</note> (where also their first parents, Adam and Eve, were interred, if we believe the Doctors of the Church). They once left the edges of the fields uncultivated for this purpose, which also seems to have been observed in TULSH⊕I <note>The symbol between H and I is a circle with a cross inside, likely a Runic or local marking</note>, just as it was more sacredly observed by our Danes and Saxons. For I notice that these burial mounds have been raised up quite prominently from piled turf in various places: yet never in fertile fields, but in heaths and at the boundaries of fields that are not at all pleasing to Ceres and Bacchus <note>An idiomatic way of saying the land was unsuitable for grain (Ceres) or grapes (Bacchus)</note>. Those who planted a pear tree upon a grave therefore violated the ancient custom; for this practice is much more recent, and we have never seen a fruit-bearing tree in cemeteries—but very often wild and woodland trees. I am not unaware, however, that the Jews at other times placed monuments and mounds in gardens; but I pass over these things, as they require more discussion.

„I wonder, however, why Toro Tott, the founder of monasteries, did not choose a burial place for himself there, since that was especially pleasing to the first founders and was considered a pledge of future bliss; he, above all, should not have departed from the Christian brothers to return to the Pagans <note>original: "Ethnicos"</note>, nor fled from the faithful to the infidels. Perhaps this was a different Toro Tott—lest I be troublesome to him, *may his bones rest softly* <note>original: "molliter ossa cubent," a common Roman funerary wish</note>.

# BOOK THREE.

<margin>cc</margin>I desire to know more concerning Runic letters: from where the name arises, which region they belong to, and what people used them? Pliny <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the Roman naturalist</note> mentions the "Rinuci," and today authors place them near the Batavians <note>a Germanic tribe from the modern-day Netherlands</note> and the Frisians. They claim that the modern language of the Frisians is very much in harmony with that of those ancient Teutons and Goths. Furthermore, where Tacitus <note>a Roman historian</note> writes of the "Sunici" in *Germania*, some instead read "Runici." Without a doubt, the little book on Runic Literature by the most learned [Ole] Worm would clarify these individual points, if only a copy of it were available.

<margin>cc</margin>In my opinion, the inscription on the monument is clearly carved in Gothic letters. However, there are various types of Gothic scripts and different alphabets. One was provided by an anonymous source through Bonaventura Vulcanius <note>a Flemish scholar known for his studies on ancient scripts</note>, and four others were gathered from friends elsewhere; however, these differ so little from one another that there seem to be only two main types. One of these was devised by Galfila—others call him Gulfila or Ulphila <note>original: "Ulphila"; the 4th-century bishop known for translating the Bible into Gothic</note>—a Gothic Bishop, around the year 415 AD according to the Chronicle of Isidore. Abbot Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius, a German polymath and cryptographer</note> describes another more recent version found by the Normans (whom he traces back to the Asiatic Goths). Among our own records, a type of Gothic writing is occasionally found that is not unlike the monument, yet it differs in various characters and is well worth an explanation by Worm.

»I cannot help, illustrious sir, but deeply admire your great refinement and incredible kindness, with which you honor me—a man unknown to you by sight, who has never earned any favor from you or your kin. You have done this not only by sending me the gift of your learned *Archaeologus* <note>Spelman's *Archaeologus in modum Glossarii*, a massive dictionary of medieval and legal terms</note>, polished by the most laborious effort of your genius, but also by valuing my "Strö trifles" <note>Worm refers here to his work on the Runic inscriptions found at Strö in Scania</note> so highly that you did not hesitate to devote time to examining them. To show some sign of my mutual affection, I am sending you my *Fasti* <note>referring to Worm's *Fasti Danici*, a work on ancient Danish chronology and Runic calendars</note>, which have been brought out from the deepest darkness into the light—more by the will of my superiors than by my own desire.

I ask, my friend, that you freely exercise that same kindness in examining these matters as you did with the Strö monument <note>original: "Stróense monumento"; referring to the runic stones at Strö in Skåne</note>. For these are things that no one has attempted until now; coming from a single man breaking the ice, who is also distracted by countless other daily affairs, they can easily escape even the most diligent care. Regarding the Tulshøj monument <note>original: "Tulshøi"; a prominent burial mound in Denmark</note>, which you surveyed so carefully, know that I published it at the request of a certain friend. I did not want to waste good hours intended for more serious matters by devoting further effort to these things. Thus, I did not think this paper was of such great value as to undergo the scrutiny of yourself and other such leaders in antiquities; nevertheless, I embrace and honor your critique as most welcome. So that you may know your feedback was taken to heart when it was shared by our most noble Axel Juel <note>original: "Axilium Julium"; Axel Juel (1591–1669) was a Danish nobleman and diplomat who facilitated this exchange</note>, I will freely lay before you the great doubts that crept into my mind after reading it, trusting in your humanity. I will say nothing for now regarding the Germans, Gauls, and Britons; however, regarding the Danes, Norwegians, and Swedes, the opposite is proven both by trustworthy histories and by the genealogies of the nobility, and other records extant among us...

<header>OF DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

...clear documents. To say nothing of the Adelingi <note>A term for nobility, particularly among the Lombards</note> of the Lombards, the Amals, and the Balths—the most ancient families of the Danes and Goths—about whom the Archeologist <note>Likely referring to Henry Spelman, to whom this letter is addressed</note> also learnedly discusses: [there are also] the Gungingi, of whom Paul the Deacon writes in Book 1, Chapter 14 of the *History of the Lombards* <note>original: "de gestis Longobardorum"</note>. Consider whether these were our Gungi, whose principality in Scania <note>Skåne, then a part of eastern Denmark</note> still remains intact, and who boast of being the progeny of the ancient Goths, yielding to none in their skill with the bow. The Lithingi are mentioned by the same author in the same work, Chapter 21. *“These were all Lithingi, for so a certain noble lineage was called among them,”* says Warnefridus <note>Another name for Paul the Deacon</note>: though some read "Adelingi," looking to Paul’s own explanation. From Skjöld <note>original: "Skioldo"</note>, the King of the Danes according to Saxo [Grammaticus] in Book 4—who, as our annals relate, is thought to have lived around the year of the world 3006—our historians attest that many subsequent kings were called **Skjöldungs** <note>original: "Skioldungos"</note>. Rolf <note>original: "Rolvo"</note>, who ruled around the year of the world 3379, was surnamed **Krage** <note>Meaning 'The Pole' or 'Lean Tree'</note>. Fridleif I <note>original: "Fridlevus"</note>, holding power <note>original: "fasces tenens"</note> in the year of the world 3871, was called **Snare** <note>Meaning 'The Swift'</note>. Frotho III—in whose 19th year the Goths migrated from Denmark, and who lived at the time of Christ’s birth—was hailed as **Geffimild** <note>Meaning 'The Generous'</note>. Harald II, taking the throne in the year of the Lord 276, was called **Hylletand** <note>Meaning 'Wartooth'</note>.

I shall proceed no further into the History of the Danish Kings. Now consult the Norwegians, not only starting from Harald Fairhair <note>original: "Haraldo Harfagre"</note>, who they say began his rule in the year of Christ 860—from whose time until the era of our ancestors there was hardly anyone who did not enjoy some surname—but look even at the petty kings <note>original: "regulos"</note> who held the rule of provinces before his time; you will find that for the most part, they used not just a single name, but a double one. What use is it to mention **Ivar Vidfamne** <note>original: "Vidfadne", meaning 'Wide-fathomer'</note>, **Åsa Ildraade** <note>'The Ill-ruler'</note>, **Olav Trætelge** <note>'The Tree-feller'</note>, **Halfdan Hvitbeinn** <note>original: "Huidbeen", meaning 'White-leg'</note>, **Halfdan the Mild** <note>original: "den milde"</note>, **Gudrød the Old** <note>original: "den gamle"</note>, and many others? The Swedes will list for you Roric **Slyngeband** <note>'Sling-ring'</note>, Alric **Gestumblindi** <note>original: "Gestblind", meaning 'The Blind Guest'</note>, Eric **the Wise** <note>original: "hin vise"</note>, Halfdan **Bergram** <note>'Mountain-strong'</note>, and others whom I am reluctant to recall to your memory, as you are most well-versed in history. I could review no less a catalog of great men and nobles (at least among the Danes)...

<summary>Ole Worm lists various legendary and historical Northern kings and their epithets (such as "Wartooth," "Fairhair," and "the Generous") to prove that the use of surnames and descriptive titles is an ancient tradition among the Danes, Norwegians, and Swedes. He cites historians like Saxo Grammaticus and Paul the Deacon to support his claim of long-standing noble lineages.</summary>

...catalog, if I knew that the genealogies handed down to us by hand held any weight with you. I have already brought forward the example of the **Rosencrantz** family <note>original: "Rosæcrantziorum"</note> at Tulshøj <note>A burial mound area in Denmark</note>; I could add the examples of the **Urne**, **Banner**, **Brahe**, **Gyldenstierne**, and **Lange** families, and others, if necessity demanded it.

>*Brave men lived before Agamemnon*
>*Many indeed; but all are unmourned*
>*And buried in a long night of obscurity,*
>*Because they lack a sacred poet.*
<note>A famous quote from Horace (Odes 4.9.25-28) suggesting that heroes only "live on" if historians or poets record their names.</note>

What **Camden** <note>William Camden (1551–1623), a famous English antiquarian</note> relates in his description of Cornwall concerning the family of the **Godolphins** is plain to see and is very well known to **Spelman** <note>Sir Henry Spelman, the English historian to whom Worm is likely writing</note>.

Therefore, I shall not exclude **Tott** <note>original: "Tottum"</note>—about whom **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> writes (whose authority must not be rashly rejected)—from the number of the ancestors of **Thord** <note>original: "Toronis"</note>, unless you can prove with evident documents that other "Tottostums" flourished or that this 800-year-old lineage was interrupted.

I have nowhere said that those Hebrew **Ashers** <note>original: "Assuros"</note> were related by blood to **Asher** the brother of Tott; but because the same names of Heroes can be found in our nation as are found in the Hebrew nation, I contend that we are descended from the Hebrews—a point which I am glad you grant of your own accord. <note>In the 17th century, it was a common scholarly theory that Northern Europeans were descended from the "Lost Tribes" or other Biblical lineages.</note>

But because I perceive that this dispute over surnames can produce various difficulties, I must remind you that surnames in certain Danish families have been of the highest antiquity. However, across several centuries they were interrupted in some branches, only to be eventually reclaimed by their descendants. This is shown by the examples of certain most noble men flourishing among us, and even still living, who—although it is abundantly clear from what stock and family they arose—prefer to be addressed by a long series of names, adding at least their father's proper name. This is the same manner in which the **Greeks** placed the father's name after their own, such as **EYGNIS son of EYBIUS** <note>original Greek: "ΕΥΓΝΙΣ ΕΥΒΙΟΥ"</note>, as seen on an altar that stands at Messina in Sicily; and as the **Romans** did on their coins: **JULIA** [the family name], **C. JUL. CÆS. IMP.** <note>Gaius Julius Caesar, Commander. Worm is showing that the family name "Julia" was used alongside the personal name.</note>

...namely, the daughter. That this was much more frequent among us in the past century was left attested by the most noble Historian of Denmark, **Arild Huitfeldt** <note>original: "Arnoldus Huitfeldius" (1546–1609), author of the *Chronicle of the Kingdom of Denmark*</note>, in his *Life of Frederick I*, near the end. There he relates that the said King <note>Frederick I, who reigned from 1523–1533</note> urged the Danish Nobility to revive their family surnames <term>cognomina</term> and the signs on their shields <note>heraldic coats of arms</note>, which had by then almost been forgotten, so that there would be no confusion among the tribes <note>clans or noble houses</note> and their lineages would not slip into an unrecoverable oblivion. Nor do I hide the fact that certain families are found who, although they first acquired surnames not many centuries ago, nonetheless count an uninterrupted series of ancestors from the most remote age. In this sense, someone who lacked other supporting evidence could assert that **Thord** <note>original: "Toronem"</note> was among the ancestors of the **Totts** <note>original: "Tottiorum," a prominent Scandinavian noble family</note>. But for me, the genealogies of this most noble lineage have served as a model for all others.

You know better than I how much weight the negative authority of foreigners who disagree on Danish matters carries. If you were to compare your English, French, and Saxons who treat Danish affairs with our own manuscripts—especially those not yet published—good God, how meager, how crippled, how ignorant they are of all our customs! I could list for you the surnames of our nobles recorded in the French reports of this year, which are so miserably corrupted that we ourselves can scarcely recognize them; unless the sequence of events confirmed our guess, they would be taken entirely for foreigners. From this, you may easily judge how much faith should be placed in such outsiders regarding these matters. But I do not doubt that you have noticed this yourself.

*I will easily concede that the **Anglo-Saxons** or **Anglo-Danes** did not use a family name <note>original: "gentili nomine"</note> before the arrival of the **Normans** in **Britain**, nor will I call your word into doubt; but from this, we cannot rightly argue for the Danes in their own country and all other northerners.*

I am glad that the custom of burying an entire kinship together in the fields in the same monument has returned to us, enriched by the great abundance of your intellect. But I cannot help but note here that I find things among us that differ from what you gather from **Cicero** <note>The Roman orator and statesman</note>. For among us, the burial mounds <note>original: "colles," literally "hills" or "mounds"</note> are not only found in the heaths and the edges of the fields...

You see my conjectures placed before you, and unless the proposed epitaph, the constant tradition of the family, and other similar examples moved me, I would plainly agree with your denial; however it may be, it is necessary that we give credit to these records until the contrary is proved. It is not at all far-fetched to think that monks, greedy for gain, granted many concessions to the great men who were not yet firmly established in the Faith, lest they overturn the foundations of the doctrine just laid by applying too much rigor.

...and you will find very many monuments and burial mounds of this kind, fashioned with such skill that they serve as tombs for great men, which are most frequently encountered among us. However things may be, it is necessary that we give credit to these until the contrary is proven. It is not at all alien to reason that the monks, greedy for gain, granted many concessions to the great men who were not yet confirmed in the Religion, lest they overturn the foundations of the doctrine just laid by too much rigor.

...monument; this will provide a clear explanation for posterity; behold, I send you a sketch <note>original: "Ideam"</note> of it, and I add more fully those things which I thought useful to be published concerning the name of the **Runes** <term>Runes: the ancient alphabetic characters used by Germanic peoples before the adoption of the Latin alphabet</term>, willingly submitting them to your honest and accurate judgment, hoping for their return enriched by some light and addition from you.

You believe the inscription of the monument is carved in **Gothic** letters, and rightly so: for Gothic letters are nothing other than Runic, and that which is called "Gothic" by foreigners—by those who first carried it into foreign regions—is to us the Runic script in truth and by its genuine name, as the fourth chapter of my *Literature* <note>Referring to Worm's 1636 work, *Runir seu Danica literatura antiquissima*</note> will make clear.

The inscription on the headstone of the stone cross at **Bewcastle** <note>original: "Beucastrienfis"; refers to the famous 7th-century Anglo-Saxon cross in Cumbria, England</note> is truly Gothic or Runic, but it was not accurately transcribed by the inexperienced person; for it is neither complete, nor did characters 4, 5, 7, 8, and 12 escape confusion and distortion. I also complain of this regarding the monument in the county of the **Brigantes** <note>original: "comitatu Brigantino"; the territory of the ancient Brigantes, here referring to Cumberland or Yorkshire</note>, drawn by the most illustrious **Camden** <note>William Camden (1551–1623), a famous English historian and antiquarian</note>; otherwise, there would be no need here for any **Apollo** <note>An idiomatic reference to the god of wisdom, meaning the puzzle is so difficult it requires divine intervention to solve</note>. What if it should be read thus?

But if I had such great influence with the most excellent **Spelman** <note>Sir Henry Spelman (c. 1562–1641), an English antiquary and correspondent of Worm</note> that he would see to it that these were drawn somewhat more accurately by someone not entirely unskilled in this literature, I would ensure that he realized nothing is more pleasing to me than to gratify such friends.

You see, most excellent Spelman, for what purpose I have thought these things should be written to you: namely, that I might give due thanks for your distinguished kindness and the affection of love toward me, that I might not leave your hope unfulfilled, and that I might lay the foundations of future friendship and familiarity between us—indeed, that I might devote myself and all my things to you and your studies. I hope you will interpret these things in the best light, since from them you may easily gather that those things which have been published about Northern matters, whether by foreigners or by our own people, are the smallest part of those which still lie hidden in our archives <note>original: "archivis"</note> at home, and which, because of too much familiarity, have been neglected or looked down upon...

Although I am devoted to other, more serious pursuits, it was no desire for fame, nor the heat of popular favor, but pure love of my fatherland that drove me to these diversions <note>original: "lusus"; literally "games" or "playful works," a modest scholarly trope</note> in my leisure hours <note>original: "horis succisivis"</note>. ### FOURTH
## THE GORSTANGE MONUMENT.

The district <term>Nomarchia: a term Worm uses to describe a "herred," a traditional Danish administrative division</term> of Pherostæ, called *Frostherrit* in the common tongue, contains two villages named *Gaarstang*. Of these, the one situated toward the eastern region is commonly called *Øster-Gaarstang* to distinguish it from the other.

In this place, a sufficiently large stone, worked with crude skill into a conical shape, encloses the dung-heap <note>original: "fimetum"</note> of a certain farmer. It is three and a half cubits <note>original: "ulnarum"; the Danish ell was approximately 2 feet or 63 cm</note> in length and two and a half in width. According to the local inhabitants, it was once located on a hill seen between the aforementioned *Gaarstang* and *Hulmby*, but from there it was moved to these filthy uses—though it is worthy, on account of its antiquity, of a far more noble place. The form and the tenor of the inscription are as follows, which you see in the drawn woodcut <note>original: "typo"</note>, rendered according to the position it now occupies in the dung-heap. Long ago, however, while it was the crown and ornament of its small hill, the stone pillar <term>cippus: a Latin term for a memorial pillar or gravestone</term> stood upright, its peak facing the sky, with the sequence and series of marks drawn from the base to the top and then straight back down again; at that time, it was much easier to read and far more splendid to look upon. But take it here as it now presents itself to those who visit it.

ᚦᚢᛚᚠᚱ : ᚢᚴ : ᚢᛚᚠᚱ : ᚱᛁᛋᚦᚢ : ᛋᛏᛁᚾ : ᚦᛁᛋᛁ : ᚢᚠᛏᛁᚱ : ᚢᛋᛘᚢᛏ : ᛚᛁᛒᛅ : ᚠᛁᛚᛅᚴᛅ : ᛋᛁᚾ.
*Dulfr ug Ulfr risdu stino dist uftir Osmut liba filaga sin.*

->DULFR AND ULFR (WOLFGANG) PLACED<-
->THIS STONE FOR OSMUT, THE COMPANION OF HIS LIFE.<-

The name **Dulfr** is now less familiar to us as a proper name, but **Ulfr** is not unusual, for which we are now accustomed to say *Vulf*. This name smacks of the height of paganism <note>original: "Ethnicissimum"; referring to the pre-Christian era</note>; for the noun itself means "Wolf," from which (as with other wild animals) people in the days of paganism did not fear to take names and adapt them for men; many of these have flowed down even to our own age. However, this name is now much more common among the Germans than among us. Indeed, I do not know what Germanic character this inscription does not show at first glance: for the word **liba** <note>ᛚᛁᛒᛅ</note> might denote "dear" to the Germans <note>original: "charum," likely referencing the German "liebe"</note>, for which our countrymen say *fieri*. Unless, perhaps, it denotes the body or life, which we now call **Liff**, to indicate that he was such a comrade and associate that he stood as a guardian, as it were, of his very body, or a companion of his life. 

The most distinguished Stephanius <note>Stephanus Johannis Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish royal historiographer and contemporary of Worm</note> leans toward this view. For he interprets **liba** as "life," signifying that Osmut was the kind of companion in whom one could safely trust during the greatest crises of life and the most heavy dangers—*someone in whom a man must place his reliance* <note>original: "som mand maatte sla sin Lijd til"</note>. By the same reasoning, we call a faithful Achates <note>A reference to the loyal companion of Aeneas in Virgil's Aeneid, used here to mean a devoted friend</note> or a servant who keeps watch over another's life and is ready to defend it a **Liffdreng** <note>literally "life-boy" or life-guard</note>. We call a "sacred anchor" <note>original: "sacram anchoram"; an idiom for the last resort or sheet-anchor</note> a **Liffanker**. 

In this same way, Martin Opitz <note>A famous German Baroque poet</note>, in his *Notes on the Rhyme of St. Anno* <note>The "Annolied," an 11th-century poem</note> (verse 1, regarding the words *wi sich liebin winefcefte* etc.), notes that in the work of Otfrid, a monk of St. Gall <note>Otfrid of Weissenburg, author of a 9th-century Gospel harmony</note>, written in the Frankish language in rhyme 780 years ago, **Lib** is the same as the German *Leben*, the Belgian *Leven*, the English *Live*, and the Danish *Liff* (life). Alternatively, it could be a surname of **Osmut**.

**Filaga** <note>ᚠᛁᛚᛅᚴᛅ</note> is a word also less worn by use among us today, such that I can scarcely say with certainty what it signifies. In the meantime, I have translated it as "companion" or "associate": for we have in use the verb *at fylge*, which [means] to accom— <note>The text cuts off mid-sentence to follow the catchword on the next page</note>

...to trust <note>The text continues the previous page's discussion of the word "filaga" (fellow/companion).</note>, it notes a companion; from which I suspect this name is derived, denoting a comrade or associate: perhaps in wars and more serious expeditions where the body is exposed to various dangers. No one should raise any suspicion of an error; for I myself have most diligently examined every single mark <note>original: "apices"; literally the tips or points of the letters</note>, and the inscription is so neat and clear that one could wish the remaining monuments we encounter could present themselves so easily to our understanding.

ᚴᚱᛁᛋᛏ : ᛘᛅᚱᛁᚮ : ᛋᚢᚿ : ᚼᛁᛅᛚᛒᛁ : ᚦᚽᛘ : ᚽᚱ : ᚴᛁᚱᚴᛁᚢ :

->**O CHRIST, SON OF MARY, BE PRESENT TO THOSE WHO BENEFIT YOUR TEMPLE: ARCHBISHOP ABSALON AND ESBERN MULE.**<-

In the word *Mariæ* [ᛘᛅᚱᛁᚮ], observe that the character ᚮ, which otherwise usually denotes the letter O, here expresses the diphthong Æ. Our ancestors did not have a specific mark suited for designating this diphthong, so they seized upon a character with a similar sound; thus it may be gathered from this that the letter ᚮ sometimes expresses O, sometimes a double A, and sometimes the diphthong Æ.

The name *Absilon* [ᛅᛒᛋᛁᛚᚮᚿ] is written for Absalon. As for who and how great a man this was, our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), the author of the 'Gesta Danorum'</note> follows his story in many places. He was a contemporary and foster-brother of King Valdemar I, from the illustrious family of the "Whites" <note>original: "Candidorum"; referring to the Hvide family, a powerful medieval Danish clan</note>. On account of his eloquence and various gifts of mind and body, he was first appointed Bishop of Roskilde, and then established as Archbishop of Lund. Having performed these duties excellently, he was most dear to King Valdemar I and most highly favored by his son, Canute. In the year 1202 or (as some prefer) 1200, on March 21 <note>original: "XII Kal. April."; the 12th day before the Kalends of April</note>, he died in the monastery of Sorø, which he himself founded at great expense and enriched most generously from his own patrimony.

How much he was also valued among foreigners is abundantly declared by Arnold, Abbot of Lübeck <note>A 12th-century chronicler</note>, who continued the work of Helmold <note>Helmold of Bosau, author of the 'Chronicle of the Slavs'</note>, in this manner: *In this course of days, from this life—*

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

...thus Lord Absalon, Archbishop of Lund, was taken away, a man of religious devotion and great counsel or discernment, and of exceptional integrity. By his industry, all the churches of the whole of Denmark, which were previously discordant, were made uniform in their divine services. In the cathedral seat, he ordered a crucifix to be fixed above, so that to those entering and leaving, reverence would seem to be given to the Crucified one rather than to himself. Furthermore, bestowing his goods liberally upon churches and monasteries, he especially strove to enrich and adorn the cathedral church of *Blessed Lawrence the Martyr in Lund* with precious crowns, very large bells (as is seen now), and various ornaments. And because he was, as has been said, a lover of religious life, he busied himself with building and enriching the monastery of the Cistercian Monks in *Sorø* <note>original: "Sora"; a town in Zealand famous for its Cistercian abbey where Absalon is buried</note>, where also, toward the end of his days, he fell ill, touched by the affliction of the body. Having set the affairs of his Church in order, on the day of *Blessed Benedict the Abbot* <note>March 21, the feast day of the founder of the Benedictine order</note>, he closed his final day. All *Denmark* grieved not a little at his death; and because he had restored many who were at odds to peace during his life, they commended his departure to God, the author of peace. Among other eulogies dedicated to him after his death, this one by *Saxo Grammaticus* <note>A 12th-century Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum</note> also survives:

> *Absalon here is primate; second by right of beauty to* <note>A pun on the biblical Absalom, known for his great beauty</note>
> *Absalon; a Cato in speech, a David in integrity, a Samuel in deed,*
> *Chariot and charioteer, father and patron, the sheepfold*
> *And the Shepherd, Peace and the nation's Leader, lawmaker and law,*
> *To the strong he was a Samson, to the wise a Solomon, an Abraham*
> *To the righteous, a Phinehas to the perverse, he was an anchor for the Danes.*
> *Whatever there was of Achilles, whatever of Plato, in his*
> *Genius it shone, as the glory of his fame bears witness.*
> *Now the retired father of the Danes rests in the dust;*
> *While his fame stands on earth, he rightly stands in the heavens.*

-> S. G. <-

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

The Åsum churchyard, located in the territory commonly called Giersherred <note>Likely Gjers Herred or a similar administrative district</note>, still preserves to this day a stone carved with Gothic characters.

One may suspect that the Åsum church was founded by Absalon and enriched by this Mule <note>Esbern Mule, the grandson of Esbern Snare mentioned on the previous page</note>, which accounts for the pious prayers contained in this epitaph.

One can easily conjecture its age, as the fact itself shows it was placed here in the year 1232 <note>MCCXXXII</note> by the friends of both men or by the patrons of the church. In that era, we see that these Runic letters of ours still found a place on public monuments, though very rarely. Indeed, I believe this is almost the last of its kind.

We find this village of Åsum ennobled even in the records of our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), the most famous medieval Danish historian</note>. In Book Ten, after describing the stratagem by which Ulf the Swede deceived the Danes at the Helgeå River and exposed them to the danger of drowning, he adds: *By order of the King, the bodies of the victims were searched for in the lake with hooks and nets, and once recovered, he provided them with the final rites at Åsum, a town adjacent to the river.* <note>original Latin: "Rex lacu lustrari jussu mesorum corpora uncis & everriculis capta, apud Asum contiguum amni oppidum, supremis procuravit officiis."</note> At that time, therefore, it was a famous town, ennobled by the burial of so many distinguished and brave soldiers; but now, by the fatal turning of the wheel of fortune, it has been reduced to the narrow bounds of a humble village.

### EIGHTH MONUMENT
## BJERESJÖ II.

Another monument is seen in the same village, enclosing the fence of a certain garden next to the road leading to Gunderslev. It is certain that this stone originally stood on a nearby hill, and from there it was moved to this place by the steward of a certain Consul from Ystad, within the memory of our fathers; but not with impunity. For he was punished with the loss of his bodily health and led a miserable life from then on, as the constant report of everyone maintains. He teaches by his example that the monuments of our fathers—even those of well-deserving heathens—are not to be rashly violated, as they were consecrated for eternity with great expense and pious zeal. The <term>stele: a carved stone slab or pillar</term> itself resembles a pyramid in shape with a pointed apex, being three <term>ells: a traditional unit of measurement, roughly 24 inches</term> in length and one and a half in width. **THINSI** <note>ᚦᛁᚾᛋᛁ</note> can be explained in two ways: it may either denote "this," namely the stone, or the mound which was called a <term>Dysse</term> <note>a type of prehistoric megalithic tomb</note> or *donsi* in ancient times, so that the meaning would be: Ohgi built a stone mound. But the first opinion is more pleasing to me, which the word **SEITI** <note>ᛋᛁᛁᛏᛁ</note> seems to confirm. For stones are said to be "placed," while mounds are said to be "made" or "erected." On the Tryggevælde stone <note>a famous 10th-century runestone from Zealand</note> it is written as *thirthi* <note>original: ᚦᛁᚱᚦᛁ</note>.

**HIRTHO KUTHIN** etc. What the sense of these words might be, I confess I cannot grasp for certain. Whether **HIRTHO** <note>ᚼᛁᚱᚦᚩ</note> here denotes "Lord," or **KUTHIN** <note>ᚴᚢᚦᛁᚾ</note> means "God" or "good," or **TRUK** <note>ᛏᚱᚢᚴ</note> means "Trygg" or "faithful," let others judge. I have referred these to Ulf; as if it indicates that he, now deceased and entombed, was handed over to the protection of the gods by all...

**Vrister's son** <note>original: ᚢᚱᛁᛋᛏᚱ ᛋᚢᚾ</note>: whether there were two people who saw to the placing of this stone, or actually only one, can be doubted. For **Meti** <note>original: ᛘᛅᛏᛁ</note> corresponds with Metta, which is a woman’s name, so it is uncertain whether Vrister is the name of the father and Meti the name of the mother of that son whose own name is not expressed, but is at least suggested by this <term>periphrasis</term> <note>a roundabout way of naming someone by their parentage rather than their proper name</note>. 

However, I deem it more probable that there were two individuals, as I have not yet seen an example in which both the father’s and the mother’s names are expressed. The word **ristu** <note>original: ᚱᛁᛋᛏᚢ</note> seems to indicate the same, as it is a plural verb <note>meaning "they raised" or "they carved"</note>, whereas the singular is **risthi** <note>original: ᚱᛁᛋᚦᛁ</note>. That plurals end in *-u* will be clear even from what follows, where **sunir** <note>sons</note> is also plural. That these stones are truly described by the parents—

I discovered it first in a meadow between Skotby and Gusnabe <note>Modern Skivarp and Gussnava in Scania</note>, though it is now moved; it was formerly seen in an elevated position, three cubits <term>ulna<gloss>a unit of measurement, approximately 2 feet or 60cm</gloss></term> in length and one and a half in width. ->Keulfr and Autir. This stone. After. Tufi.<-
->Son. His.<-

->*Keulfr and Autir, who set this stone after Tufi, their son.*<-
->KEULFR AND AUTIR PLACED THIS<-
->STONE IN MEMORY OF THEIR SON TUFI.<-

Some read ᚴᛁᛘᛚᚾ as *Geltan*, *Galtan*, or *Galto* <note>meaning "boar" or "hog"</note>, for the value of A and E are equivalent, and likewise, the letter ᚾ denotes either a double N or an O; however, those who have examined the stone more accurately find *Keulfr* (perhaps once Chilian, now *Kield*).

Although ᚦᛁᚾᛅ <note>thina</note> might seem to mean "after," the sense here sufficiently indicates it is a proper term, as does the plural word ᛋᛏᛁᚾᚦᛅ <note>stinstha</note>, which signifies "to place" or "to set" <note>original Danish: "at sette"</note>, and because ᛁᚠᛏᛁᚱ <note>eftir - after</note> immediately follows, expressed not with a ᚦ but with an ᛁ.

The carving displays something unique to us; I believe the wolf denotes that this Tufi was born from a great family and noble lineage, displaying an image no doubt acquired through warlike virtue. Whether it relates to the lineage of the Ulfstands <note>A prominent Danish noble family whose name means "Wolf's Tooth"</note>, I leave for others to investigate.

The characters seen around the top of the stone can indeed be rendered into as many Roman letters, but one could not easily extract any meaning from them. They are as follows:

->ᚦᛁ. ᛁᚼᚠᛒ. ᛁᛚ. ᛘᛁ. ᛘᚢ.<-
->DIS SHEB IE LI MU.<-

## THE SJÖRUP STONE.

The second monument in this district stands not far from Sjörup church; it is located in a certain stream where this stone was fitted with others so that it might serve as a bridge for those traveling on foot. It is three and a half cubits <term>ulna<gloss>a unit of measurement, approximately 2 feet or 60cm</gloss></term> in length and two in width.

<note>This is Worm’s 17th-century transliteration of the runes. A modern reading would be: "Saksi satti stēn þessi æftiʀ Ābiǫrn, sin fēlaga, Tōfa/Tōka sun. Sā flō æigi at Uppsala, en vāpnum øfði."</note>

->SAXO PLACED THIS STONE FOR ESBERN HIS COMPANION, THE SON OF TUFA, WHOM I RAISED AT UPPSALA; ANUA ADDED THE INSIGNIA AND ORNAMENTS.<-
<note>original Latin: "SAXO LAPIDEM HUNC POSUIT ESBERNO SOCIO SUO, TUFÆ FILIO, QUEM EGO UPSALIÆ ENUTRIVI: ANUA INSIGNIA ET ORNAMENTA ADDIDIT." Worm interprets "Anua" as a personal name, though modern scholars often read this section as "He did not flee at Uppsala, but fought as long as he had weapons."</note>

ᛋᛅᚼᛋᛁ, now *Saxe*, in Latin *Saxo*; a name made famous by the merits of our Grammarian and Historian <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the author of the Gesta Danorum</note>. Because our ancient alphabet lacks double-consonant letters <note>referring to the letter 'X'</note>, ᚴ and ᛋ <note>k and s</note> are used in place of 'X'.

ᚬᛋᛒᛁᚢᚱᚾ now *Esbern* or *Esbernus*, whose name appears twice in the following monument, but here he seems to have been a grandson of the same name. For ᛅ <note>the 'a' rune</note>, ᚼ <note>the 'h' rune</note> is placed here, as it is in ᛒᚱᚬᚦᛁᚱ <note>brother</note>; for I find it carved in both ways in these monuments.

ᚠᛁᛚᛅᚵᛅ <term>felaga<gloss>a companion, partner, or comrade-in-arms</gloss></term> I judge to have been a comrade and companion in war, derived from the verb *Jeg følger* <note>original Danish: "I follow"</note>. I find the same word in the third Aarhus monument, but with the letters slightly changed to ᛋᛁᚵᚠᚢᛚᚵᛁᚱ <note>sigfulgir</note>. So too in the manuscript history of King Canute the Great <note>original: "Canuti Regis M.S."</note> in our ancient tongue: ᚦᛅ ᛏᛁᛗᛁ ᚦᚬᚱᚬ ᚦᚬ ᛋᚴᚬᚱᛁ ᚢᛁᚦ ᛏᚬᛚᛅ ᚢᛁᚱᛒᛁᛚ ᚠᛁᛚᛅᚵᛅ ᛋᛁᚾ. "Then Thoro Skori said to Tolar Verpil, his companion." From this is derived ᚠᛁᛚᛅᚵᚼᛅᛒ <term>felagshab<gloss>fellowship or society</gloss></term> in the history of Sven Estridsson: ᚦᛅᚱ ᛋᛅᚼᚢ ᛅᚠ ᚼᛅᚱᛅᛚᚦᚢ ᚦᛁᚱᛁᚦ ᚠᛁᛚᛅᚵᛅᚼᛅᛒ ᛋᛁᚾ, where Sven and Harald had entered into a fellowship. It seems to be derived from ᚠᛁᚼ <note>fe</note>, which denotes goods, money, or resources, and ᛗᛅᛏ <note>mat</note> meaning a contribution: for those who enter into a fellowship are accustomed to bring their goods into a common fund, so that whatever they undertake is done at shared expense.

ᛏᚢᚠᛅᚾ <note>Tufa</note> leads one to suspect that this Esbern was the son of that Tufa to whom the brothers placed a monument mentioned above. A certain Tufa is mentioned by Ricobaldus of Ferrara in his *Orchard of the Church* <note>original Latin: "Pomœrio Eccleſiæ"</note>...

### THE THIRTEENTH MONUMENT:
### HUNESTAD.

**E**legant and remarkable is the site visited near Hunestad, composed of eight conspicuous and large stones. Two of these bear elegant Runic characters, and one of them features an accompanying image of a female figure <note>This refers to the Hyrrokkin stone (DR 284), depicting the giantess from Norse mythology who rode a wolf</note>. Three others show monstrous images of a she-bear, a rider, and a wolf, made of intricate knots; the remaining three are without any markings. Two of these are still seen standing, but two have collapsed. It is a monument worthy of being seen. Ruins of a hall or some royal palace are seen nearby; however, what kind it was, or by whom it was built or destroyed, the inhabitants do not remember...

<note>This is Worm's Latin translation rendered into English. As noted above, his interpretation of the phrase "did not flee" as "nourished" is considered incorrect by modern runologists.</note>

ᛋᛅᚼᛋᛁ, now *Sachse*, in Latin *Saxo*; a name made noble by the merits of our Grammarians and Historians <note>A reference to Saxo Grammaticus, the famous 12th-century Danish historian</note>. Because our native alphabet lacks double letters <note>meaning the letter 'X' which represents the 'ks' sound</note>, the runes ᚼ and ᛋ are used in place of X.

ᚬᛋᛒᛁᚢᚱᚾ now *Esbern* or *Esbernus*, whose name appears twice in the following monument; but here it seems to have been a grandson of the same name. In place of ᛁ [the 'i' rune], the ᛂ [the 'e' rune] is used here, as also in ᚦᛂᚾᛋᛁ [this]; for I find it carved in both ways across these monuments.

ᚠᛁᛚᛅᚴᛅ [Partner/Comrade]: I judge this to have been a comrade and companion in war, derived from the verb *Jeg følger* <note>Danish: "I follow"</note>. I find the same word on the third Aarhus stone, but with the letters slightly changed to ᚠᛂᛚᛅᚴᛅ. Likewise, in a manuscript history of King Canute the Great, written in our ancient idiom: ᚦᛅ ᛘᛂᛚᛏᛁ ᚦᚬᚱᚦᚬ ᛋᚴᚬᚱᛁ ᚢᛁᚦ ᛏᚬᛚᛅᚱᚢᛗ ᚢᛂᚱᛒᛁᛚ ᚠᛂᛚᛅᚴᛅ ᛋᛁᚾ. "Then Thoro Skori spoke to Tolarus Verpil his companion." <note>original: "Tunc dixit Thoro Skori ad Tolarum Verpil socium suum."</note> From this is derived ᚠᛂᛚᛅᚴᛋᚴᛅᛒ [partnership/society] in the history of Sven Estridsson: ᚦᛂᚱ ᛋᚢᚾᚦᚱᚢ ᛅᚠ ᚴᛅᚱᚦᚢ ᚦᛂᚱᛅ ᚠᛂᛚᛅᚴᛋᚴᛅᛒ ᛋᛁᚾ, where Sven and Harald had entered into a partnership. It seems to be derived from ᚠᛂ [fe], which denotes goods, money, or resources, and ᛚᛅᚴ [lag], which denotes a contribution: for those who enter into a partnership usually bring their goods together in common, so that whatever they undertake may be done at common expense.

ᛏᚢᚠᛅᛋ: This gives us reason to suspect that this Esbern was the son of that Tufa for whom the brothers placed the monument described above. A certain Tufa is mentioned by Ricobaldus of Ferrara in the *Orchard of the Church*...

### THIRTEENTH MONUMENT
### *THE HUNESTAD MONUMENT.*

Elegant and remarkable is that which is seen near Hunestad, composed of eight conspicuous and large stones, two of which contain elegant Runic characters, and one of those includes an accompanying image of a female. Three others show monstrous images of a bear, a rider, and a wolf made of intricate interlacings; the remaining three are without any markings. Two of these are still seen standing, but two have collapsed. It is a monument worthy of being seen. The ruins of a hall or some palace are glimpsed nearby; however, what sort of place it was, or by whom it was built or devastated, they do not recall—

> There were once women among the Danes who, transforming their appearance into a masculine style, devoted almost every moment of their time to cultivating military skills. They did not allow the strength of their virtue to be dulled by the contagion of luxury, for they loathed a delicate way of life and were accustomed to hardening their bodies and minds with endurance and labor. Casting off all the softness of female frivolity, they forced their womanly nature to adopt a manly ferocity. They sought knowledge of military affairs with such care that one would think they had shed their womanhood; especially those who possessed either vigor of mind or a noble tallness of body were accustomed to enter this way of life. These women, therefore, just as if they had forgotten their natural condition and preferring sternness to charms, intended wars instead of kisses, and tasting blood rather than embraces, they practiced the duties of arms rather than of love. The hands they ought to have applied to the looms, they offered for the service of weapons, so that now they no longer...

On its northern side, it features a rider dressed in a floor-length tunic <note>original: "tunica talari"</note> sitting upon a monstrous animal; he holds reins in his left hand, while his right hand holds various and intricate weaves that creep over the peak of the stone. One may indeed hunt for its "hieroglyphic" <note>In the 17th century, "hieroglyphic" referred generally to symbolic or mystical meanings in art</note> sense from the literature of the Egyptians; however, whether this is consistent with the traditions of our ancestors, I cannot easily say. Why the ancients noted military commanders and cohorts by means of a dragon may be seen in Pierius’s *Hieroglyphica*, book 15. The Royal Prophet David seems to have indicated this in Psalm 74, where *by the heads of the dragons crushed in the waters* <note>original: "per draconum capita in aquis contrita"</note> he understands the soldiers, leaders, and centurions of Pharaoh. I am not displeased by what Aldrovandus <note>Ulisse Aldrovandi (1522–1605), a renowned Italian naturalist</note> notes in his *Ornithology*, book 10, concerning the symbolism of Griffins: *“That the soul or nature of the buried person was such as the thing depicted appears to be. Namely, if a tomb has a sheep or a lamb carved upon it, you may understand the person to have embraced gentleness, their ferocity having been destroyed; if a bull, temperance; if a snake, prudence; or something of this sort, according to what the significance of the animal depicted requires.”*

On the seventh and eighth stones, there are no tracks or linings; they are scattered and collapsed at the sides, all quite rough and of neglected shape.

What I might add concerning the age of this monument, I do not have; I am prepared to be taught by others.

<note>original: "tionem haud parum faciant"</note> ...[they] contribute in no small measure [to the explanation], I shall add here. In the year 1638, in the month of August, among other things, the most learned **Mr. Spelman** <note>Sir Henry Spelman (1562–1641), a famous English antiquarian</note> wrote the following to me:

A certain noble Knight here, and of the highest eminence in the Royal Treasury <term>fisco Regio: The Exchequer, the office responsible for collecting and managing royal revenues</term>, **Sir Peter Osborne**, requests through my mediation that he might receive your opinion on the questions he sends. He is indeed worthy of your satisfaction, and I earnestly ask this in his name.

The questions, recorded on a separate sheet of paper, were these:

> "**Olaus Wormius**, in his book *On Runic Literature* <note>original: *de Literatura Runica*</note>, chapter 28, page 168, includes among other Gothic or Danish names (which, as he says in the same place, are ancient and meaningful) the following, which are names of families among us in England and seem to be derived from there:
> **Alf, Lother, Olafr, Orm, Osbiurn, Rolf, Rudl, Skibern, Svein, Tuke, Tume, Ulf.**
> I ask this favor: that I might understand their derivation and what meaning they have, and likewise whether among those people [the Danes] they have also passed into surnames, just as they have among us in England.
> Among the names of the Poets, whom he calls **Scalds** <term>Scaldros: Old Norse poets, storytellers, and court historians</term>, I find **Thorbiorn, Thorbern, Halbiorn, Biorn**, which seem to have some affinity in their derivation with **Osburn**. In this especially I desire to understand if my conjecture is correct.
> If by chance he has in his possession an image of some ancient monument inscribed with the name **Osbiurn**, I desire to obtain this favor from him: that he send me a transcript together with an interpretation."

To these inquiries of the most Noble **Sir Osborne**, I replied in the following year in this manner:

By the encouragement of the most distinguished **Sir Henry Spelman**, my most honored friend, I shall gladly attempt to answer the inquiries of the most Noble **Sir Peter Osborne**: not because I hope to be able to satisfy his wishes in every respect, but...

...so that he may recognize my spirit is prompt and ready to serve friends, and that the breeze of his favor may never cease to breathe upon my endeavors. If he should ever see me stray from the right path, I ask that he ascribe it to the difficulty of the matter and to the darkness of recalling an almost obliterated antiquity back into the light. Indeed, lest I leave anything untried, I shall repeat each item in the order they were proposed to me, weigh their significance, and note what can be said about them in harmony with our antiquities. I have no doubt that the most Noble Lord will interpret everything in the kindest spirit.

First, he states that in Chapter 28 of my *Runic Literature* <note>original: *Literatura Runica*, Worm's 1636 treatise on runes</note>, page 168, among other ancient and meaningful Gothic or Danish names, I include the following which are family names in England and seem to be derived from our language.

The words from *Runic Literature* from which the most Noble Osborne collected these, on the cited page, read as follows:

> There still exist traces (of proper names) taken from magnanimity, service, bears, wild beasts, bulwarks, and other things, etc.

The meaning of this is not that *all* ancient proper names are of that kind—indeed, not even all those listed in that place—but a great many of them. For many were given by chance, and many at the whim of parents, for which no explanation can now be given; however, many are truly meaningful, as will soon be shown in the examples for which the most Noble Lord requests an explanation. Furthermore, regarding the fact that the names of families in England are derived from those of our countrymen, he can in no way doubt this if he more diligently considers the history of both nations: the common rule we shared for a long time <note>A reference to the Danelaw and the North Sea Empire of Cnut the Great</note>, the marriages of our people who settled there with the English, and their alliances and commerce. Therefore, I am clearly of the same opinion as Mr. Osborne. Your countryman Richard Verstegan <note>Richard Verstegan (c. 1550–1640), an English antiquarian who argued for the Germanic roots of the English people</note> attempted to demonstrate this in some way in his *Antiquities* <note>original: *Restitution of Decayed Intelligence in Antiquities*, 1605</note>, page 303, but he did not penetrate as deeply into the matter as he might have, due, I believe, to a scarcity of our local antiquities and documents.

...history. ### II. Alf, Doral, Lother, Olafr, Orm, Osbiurn, Rolf, Rudl, Skibern, Svein, Tucke, Tume, Vlf.

**ALF.** This was an ancient proper name for nobles among us, but of that kind which we consider primitive <term>primitive: in this context, names that are foundational roots and do not have a secondary descriptive meaning in the language</term>, and which hold no other significance among us. Saxo, the most celebrated writer of Danish history <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), author of the "Gesta Danorum" or "Deeds of the Danes"</note>, reports in Book V that a certain man of this name held command in Hedmark <note>original: "Hetmarchia," a region in Norway</note>. His words are these:

> At that same time, Alf reigned in Hedmark, having a son named Asmund.

### II. *Alf, Doral, Lother, Olafr, Orm, Osbiurn, Rolf, Rudl, Skibern, Svein, Tucke, Tume, Ulf.*

**ALF.** This was an ancient proper name among our nobility, belonging to the class of names we call primitive <term>primitive: names that are root words and not derived from other terms in the language</term>, having no other meaning in our tongue. Therefore, *Osbiurn* is the "Bear of the rivers" or "Bear of the sea"; or one who, in maritime wars, shows himself to be as strong and vigorous as a bear. This word **Biurn** is a root <term>primitiva: a primary word from which others are derived</term> that has produced many compounds from itself, such as *Osbiurn*, *Skibiurn*, *Thorbiurn*, *Halfbiurn*, and many others. Furthermore, what the ancients called *Osbiurn*, those who favor Roman refinement <note>original: *Romanorum mollitiei studentes* - Worm is poking fun at those who prefer "soft" Latinized names over "rugged" Old Norse ones</note> now call *Esbernus*. **ROLF** is a primary proper name of no descriptive meaning that I know of, although the Kings of Denmark have rejoiced in this title, as is clear from the second and third books of *Saxo* <note>Saxo Grammaticus, author of the 12th-century *Gesta Danorum*</note>; now they prefer *Rudolph*.

Regarding **RUDL**, I have nothing else to say, for it is not descriptive but was imposed at the whim of the namer.

**SKIBERN** or *Skibiurn* is composed of *Biorn* and **Skib**, as I mentioned above; with **Skib** denoting a ship and **Biurn** a bear. They gave this name to one who attacked enemies in ships or in naval battle no differently than a bear attacks a hunter or other prey.

**SVEIN** is a primary and simple name; as a common noun <term>appellativè: a word used as a general description rather than just a name</term> it signifies a distinguished, practiced, and industrious youth, who having passed the years of apprenticeship deserved to be numbered among the veterans. It is called *Sveno* by *Saxo*, in whose work many of this name may be found. Indeed, it is still in frequent use today.

**TUKE** descriptively marks one who is thick or fat, but it was used as a proper name both then and now. Moderns prefer *Tycho* <note>Such as the famous astronomer Tycho Brahe</note>.

**TUME** is purely a proper name for both women and men. You will find it assigned to the male sex in *Saxo* Book VIII; our monuments inscribed with Runic letters on stones attribute it to women.

**ULF** denotes a Wolf, from which—no differently than from **Biurn**—various derivatives and compounds exist. From this come *Ranulf* and *Vlfvilda*, of whom *Saxo* writes, who also uses *Ulvo* for *Vlf*. From those who were granted surnames from his teeth <note>Likely referring to a family crest or the name "Wolf's tooth"</note>, the noblemen of the ancient lineage of the *Ulfflands* <note>The Ulfstand family</note> flourish among us. Our *Runic Literature* <note>Worm refers to his 1636 work, *Runir seu Danica literatura antiquissima*</note> asserts: The proper names of the ancients were derived partly from roles of service, such as **Svein** <note>original: *Svein* - meaning a youth, lad, or servant</note>, partly from bears, such as **Biorno**, **Osbiurn**, and **Skibiurn**, and partly from other wild beasts, such as **Ulf** <note>original: *Ulf* - wolf</note> and **Orm** <note>original: *Orm* - serpent or dragon</note>; however, this is not the place for a more extensive discussion of these.

III. Regarding the third question, I believe it has been mostly satisfied. I have explained the derivation of these names in as few words as possible, along with their proper meanings. However, not all of these developed into surnames <note>Worm uses *cognomina* to describe the transition from temporary descriptors to hereditary family names</note> among us in the same way. In ancient times, our countrymen rarely used surnames other than those of their parents <note>referring to patronymics</note>, such as **Alf Thoralſon**, who was the son of **Thorald**, or **Lother Olafrſon**, who was the son of **Olaf** [Latin: *Olai*]; unless, in war or elsewhere, some attribute was given to them due to famous deeds, a memorable event, or some notable physical blemish. Yet we still read traces of some names by which the oldest families were distinguished; among those listed, I believe none should be counted in this category except **Orm**, **Tuke**, and **Ulf**.

IV. Regarding the fourth doubt, the most noble Lord **Osburn** judges most correctly. For these names of the <term>Scaldrorum: Skalds, the ancient Scandinavian poets and historians</term> listed by us—**Thorbiurn**, **Thorbern**, and **Halbiurn**—are derived from **Biurn** or **Biorno** in the same way as **Osbiurn**. For **Biurn** and **Biorno** are the same: the latter being a Romanized form, while the former is recognized as the ancient Danish. **Thorbiurn** and **Thorbern** are synonyms denoting the "Bear of the god Thor," or if you prefer, the "Bear of the Gods." **Halbiurn** denotes a "Half-Bear," or one who has not yet reached the perfection of a true bear. The conjecture is therefore sound.

To satisfy the final request in some way, two previous examples from Book 3 of our *Monuments* have been brought forward in which mention is made of **Osburn**; both are located in **Scania** <note>modern-day Skåne, Sweden, which was part of the Danish Kingdom in Worm's time</note>, one near the village of **Siórup** and the other near **Hunneſtadium**, which have already been sufficiently discussed.

# BRODER PLACED THIS STONE FOR ROSA, HIS BROTHER, THE MOST FAITHFUL JUDGE OF THE GODS. <note>original Latin: "Broderus lapidem hunc posuit Rosæ fratri suo, fidissimo numinum arbitro"</note>

Others read **BRUÞUR** as **BRUÞIR**, not without reason, so that a distinction is made between **BRUÞUR**, which signifies "brother" (as seen in this very monument), and **BRUÞIR**, which is a proper name (like **ÞAÞI** on the Strö stone) designating Broder.

I have translated **RUSA** as Rosa; others read it as **UUSUM**. Whichever it may be, it is clearly established that it is the name of Broder’s brother.

* **ÞREI ÞAÞA TRAÞ** <note>A runic phrase being analyzed for its meaning regarding "faithfulness" or "dearness"</note>: a similar form of speaking appears in monuments VIII and X of this book, and almost exactly in the Rhyme of St. Anno, Archbishop of Cologne, verse XLIII:

> *He said: "Comfort yourself, noble dear one of God."* <note>original German: "Her sprach; trosti dig heiro Godis drut."</note>

Opitius <note>Martin Opitz, a 17th-century German poet and scholar</note> explains this in the following way: "Friend of God," from **trouu** (*trew*), meaning faith. From the Winsbeke <note>A Middle High German didactic poem</note>:

->Dear child, may you be of high spirit,<-
->And live within it with discipline.<-
<note>original German: "Trut Kind, du sin hoch gemut / Vnd darunter in zuchten leben."</note>

Willeram, Abbot of Ebersberg, in his Paraphrase of the Song of Songs, chapter V: *Such is my beloved* <note>original German: "Sulich is min drut"</note>, which Merula translates as *Such is my dear one*. The most learned Spelman <note>Sir Henry Spelman, an English antiquary</note> rightly noted in his *Archaeologus* regarding this word: that foreigners very often change **T** into **D**. These **Drudes**, he adds, are not merely "faithful" in a simple sense, but are a type of vassal who are called *faithful* in Feudal law—and perhaps a more specific category among them. The Councils of the provinces of Rheims and Rouen addressed King Louis in the year 818: *Without the solace and company of the Drudes and Vassals, your soul shall go forth naked and desolate.* <note>original Latin: "Sine solatio & comitatu Drudorum atq; Vassorum..."</note> The author of the *Life of Saint Ulrich*, on page 139, says: *He sought to please his "Drudes" with appropriate gifts.* From this comes *Druchte* or *Druthe* for a betrothed woman. In the Salic Law, Title 14, paragraph 10: *If anyone [assaults] a betrothed girl who is being led to her husband as a Druthe.* <note>original Latin: "si quis puellam sponsatam quæ Druthe ducitur ad maritum."</note> From this come the proper names *Drude*, *Drudhuit*, *Drudholi*, and *Drudprecht*. Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the Danish historian</note> seems to me to have elegantly expressed this turn of phrase in Book VII, where he renders it as "the most faithful judges of the gods." For he says: *Those who were indeed the close companions of the god Frey and the most faithful judges of the gods.* <note>original Latin: "Qui quidem Fro Dei necessarii erant & fidissimi numinum arbitri."</note> He was speaking of the bravest of the Swedes who flocked to the Battle of Bråvalla. <note>A legendary battle between the King of Denmark and the King of Sweden</note>

There are some who imagine strange and rare things to be present on this stone, entirely foreign to its actual content. Regarding this, I found the following in certain papers written by Hermann Chytraeus of Vejle <note>A 16th-century humanist and historian from Vejle, Denmark</note>: *“This monument, in my own judgment, seems to have been erected in the time of King Snio <note>A legendary King of Denmark, said to have ruled during a time of great famine</note> (who lived, as some believe, around the year of Christ 600) during that universal migration of the Cimbri and Goths caused by a most violent famine. It is indeed likely that the parents accompanied their children all the way to the ships; and that part of the inscription, which in Latin sounds like:* **Tell the gods their glory** <note>original Latin: "Dicite Diis suam gloriam"</note>, *seems to belong to the parents. However, even a one-eyed man <note>An idiom meaning "even a person with the poorest vision/judgment"</note> can see that this is entirely alien to the actual inscription.

It seems that someone less skilled in our ancient literature read the characters this way:
->ᛋᛁᛅᚱ ᚴᚢᛏᛅᚱ ᛋᛁᚾ ᛅᚱᛅ: ᚴᚢᛏᛅᚱ ᚢᚬᚱ ᛁ ᚴᚱᛁ.<-
->*Give the gods their honor: Gods be with us in war.*<-
<note>original Danish/Lower German: "Sier Guder sin ære: Guder vor i Kri."</note>
->**GIVE HONOR TO THE GODS, OUR GODS IN WAR.**<-
<note>original Latin: "DIIS DATE HONOREM, DII NOSTRI IN BELLO."</note>

But this is in vain, as all the forms of the letters cry out against it.
A fuller explanation of this stone was once promised to us by the most celebrated man, Master Andreas Vedel <note>Anders Sørensen Vedel (1542–1616), a famous Danish historian and translator of Saxo Grammaticus</note>, the Royal Historiographer, in his notes to the 20th song; but having been prevented by death, he was unable to bring either these or other noble praises of our fatherland to completion.

## THE FIFTEENTH MONUMENT
### *OF TULSTRUP.*

In the same province, in the southern wall of the Tulstrup church, they have fitted a nearly square stone, four ells long and three and a half ells wide. It is distinguished by the figure of what I believe to be a wolf; a border surrounds it, consisting not only of letters but also of other ornaments and certain intricate windings, a small toothed column, and other things of that kind carved into the hard stone. The accompanying illustration will show all these things to you more accurately than a long series of words.

### GLIBER AND OSA RAISED THIS MONUMENT FOR ULF.

It is apparent that the original and proper location of this stone was not a church wall, but rather a certain burial mound or hill, which is expressly mentioned in the text. It is well-established that the stone was moved from that site, and from this we can infer the reason for the rarity of ancient monuments. For later generations, when constructing churches and fortresses, held no reverence for antiquity; they took whatever materials they found that suited their purpose, partly breaking them and partly adapting them for foreign uses. In doing so, they mostly enclosed the inscribed faces within the walls, thus foully hiding the memory of their ancestors from view. <note>The author is describing the common practice of "spolia," where ancient runestones were used as cheap building blocks for medieval churches, often with the writing turned inward or plastered over.</note>

GLIBER is still a female name familiar to us in the form <term>Gleborg</term> <note>A name derived from Old Norse roots meaning "Fortress of Joy"</note>: as if you were to say "the citadel of joy." In the word ᚢᛋᛅ (Osa), the letter ᚢ is inverted, denoting either an O or a double A; so that it may be read as Osa or Aasa, for these vowels possess a certain affinity of sound...

The ancients used these names interchangeably among those who held them. The name **Osa**, indeed, was quite common among the ancients.

**HUL** <note>original runes: ᚼᚢᛚ. Worm is here discussing the word *kumbl* (monument/mound), which he transliterates or finds written as *hul*.</note> See how aptly it corresponds to the Latin *cumulus* [a heap or mound], with plainly the same meaning; it indicates that the hill, or rather the heap or burial mound, was constructed by these two for the burial and memory of **Ulf**.

**ULF** <note>original runes: ᚢᛚᚠ</note> We now say **Wolfgang** or **Ulf**. Based on the evidence of this name, I conjecture that the figure of a **Wolf** carved into the stone represents both the name of the deceased and perhaps his heraldic insignia. Alternatively, following the tradition of hieroglyphics to represent qualities of the soul, I believe they wished to indicate that the man was fierce and strenuous in war and conflict, after the manner of a wolf. This name was especially made famous by that **Ulf** <note>Ulf the Earl (d. 1026), a major figure in Viking Age politics.</note> who was the brother-in-law of Canute the Great, and who fathered King Sweyn—known as **Sweyn Estridsson**—by Estrid (or Margaret, as some prefer). Nor do I dislike the conjecture of our countryman **Pontanus**, who establishes that this Ulf was descended from the ancient English lineage of the Cimbrian Peninsula <note>The Jutland peninsula</note>, and thus bestowed a long line of ancestors upon the Danish King Sweyn Estridsson.

The inscription seems to have been recorded somewhat inaccurately; therefore, we think it should be restored in the way we have done here, so that the meaning remains consistent.

You will notice that the engraver has rendered the figure of the stag a little more elegantly here than it actually appears on the monument itself.

The local inhabitants say those crosses were formerly the insignia of the Dalby Monastery <note>original: Cœnobium Dalbyense</note>, and that the neighboring village was assigned to the jurisdiction of that same monastery. For this reason, some are of the opinion that the crosses denote what has been said, but that the figure of the stag and the hunting scenes relate to the king. Perhaps this stone was marked with these letters long before the foundation of that monastery, and placed in that same spot, not as a boundary marker but as a monument. In the course of time, however, because it seemed to stand in a location suitable for a boundary, the images of the cross and the stag were added for the purpose mentioned above.

*Thununk* <note>original runes: ᚦᚢᚿᚢᚿᚴ</note>. For the word *thununk* is completely unknown to us, nor can any conjecture reach what it ought to signify.

### BOOK THREE.

ᚢᛁ: ᛏ. ᚢᛁᚴ *vien* or *ven* signifies a friend to us, thus the meaning is consistent.

*ᚼᛅᛚᚴ is either a proper name or, if taken as a common noun, signifies "holy." This is what we now call *hellig* <note>Danish: hellig</note>, what the English and perhaps even our ancestors once called *holy*; thus they call a festival day a *holy-day*.

ᚦᚢᚱᚦᚢᚱ *Thurder* I think indicates Thor [Thoro]. The dotted rune [ᚦ] carries the value of *Th*. But who this Thor [Thoro] is, or to whom he belongs, is unknown to us.

ᚱᚽᚢᛏᛁ instead of ᚱᛁᛏᛁ <note>meaning "raised" or "carved"</note>.

ᚴᛅᚱᚠ still signifies carvings or signs to us; hence *Kerffstock* <note>original: "Kerffstock" — a tally stick or piece of wood decorated with notches</note>, a piece of wood decorated with carvings.

᛭ᚱ᛭ In this word, two peculiarities occur which have not been observed in what has been presented so far. The first is [᛭] which represents the letter *G*, perhaps as a capital. Although it is more commonly written as [ᚠ] or in older texts without a dot, we have shown that this mark has the same value in our literature. The second is the combination of the two letters <term>ᚦᚱ</term> <note>the runes Thorn and Raido</note> and ᚱ, which is also worthy of notice.

If there were room for conjecture here, I would understand that *Thurder* to be the person our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century Danish historian</note> calls Torchillus, and [King Gorm] to be the first king of that name, a tireless searcher of nature. Having perceived the filthiness of his idols through Torchillus, he died of grief and left the kingdom to Gotricus. Saxo pursues his deeds at length in the 8th book of his history. Among other things, he narrates the cause of his death as follows:

> *Unable to endure hearing the filthiness of Utgarda-Loki being reproached, he so grieved over the loss of his dignity that he surrendered his spirit, unable to bear the words, even while they were being recited.* <note>original Latin: "Exprobratam Vgarthiloci fœditatem exaudire non sustinens, adeò indignitatis ejus vicem doluit, ut impatientem dictorum spiritum inter ipsa recitamenta deponeret." Utgarda-Loki is a giant in Norse mythology; King Gorm was reportedly devastated to learn his gods were so base.</note>

If this Gorm is the one to be understood here, it is probable that he was called Torchillus by Christians, but addressed as Thor by the pagans. He constructed this monument for his king, for whom he had suffered so many hardships, around the year of Christ <term>747</term> <note>original: DCCXLVII</note> according to the calculation of our annals; although he devoted his life to so many troubles and wore himself out with so many dangers for the man...

## HALLAND.

Because *Halland* and *Blekinge* (to use the words of our Saxo) emerge from the integrity of *Scania* <note>the southern province of Skåne</note>, like twin branches sprouting from the trunk of a single tree, and are connected to *Gothia* <note>Götaland in Sweden</note> and *Norway* by long stretches of coastline and various coastal recesses: we must further examine the monuments which we have heard exist in those places.

> But let us first survey our Lyscander’s <note>Claus Christoffersen Lyscander (1558–1623), a Danish royal historiographer</note> *Halland*, depicted in these colors: "*Halland is the second region of Minor Scandia:*" And it is further divided in two. For one is called Southern, above the great forest of the Hallanders, closest to the borders of the people of *Bergen* <note>referring to the Bjäre region</note>; the other is Northern, touching *Norway*. But the whole land comprises eight very ample lordships reaching from the *Baltic* Sea and on the left extending to the *Smalanders*. Indeed, that land is equal in length to *Scania*, but much narrower in width, for from the *Scandian* people of *Bergen* where it joins the mainland, it runs all the way to the rocky parts of *Norway*. We shall here record only the cities which are most famous and in no way inferior to others. ## BLEKINGE

Now **Blekinge** remains to be surveyed—the other "arm" of **Scania** <note>modern Skåne; at the time of writing, these regions were part of the Danish Kingdom</note>. Our [historian Claus] **Lyskander** <note>Claus Lyskander (1548–1623) was a Danish Royal Historiographer</note> has left us this description of it: From the eastern region of **Scania**, two lands jut out along the Ocean in the shape of a long, outstretched arm. **Lister** <note>original: *Listria*</note> is inhabited by only one people, having **Elleholm** as its capital. But **Blekinge** stretches over a very long distance between the people of **Småland** and the eastern sea <note>the Baltic Sea</note>, with a moderate width. It is composed of three districts: the East, the West, and the Middle, and it contains just as many principal maritime cities: **Sölvesborg**, **Lyckå**, and **Ronneby**. It is blessed with very convenient and favorable harbors; history and ancient monuments testify that many kings of the **Cimmerians** and **Goths** <note>Worm uses these terms to link Scandinavian history to the prestigious "Gothic" lineages of antiquity</note> once lived there. The inscribed rock of King **Hildetand** <note>original: *Hylletandus*; referring to Harald Hildetand (Wartooth), a legendary 8th-century Danish king. It was there that the **Lombard** peoples, flowing down from the northern regions to grace their migration, established their first encampments.
