> >> Thus, among other things, that most famous man says: On the second side of the Leragra monument, ᚢᚦᛅᚱ <note>Runes for U-TH-A-R</note>, the vowel ᚢ [U] is indeed expressed, which forms a syllable with the following consonant (which is unique in all Runic literature: you might call it neither a mute nor a semivowel). They think the complete word should be read as *Udhar*, because the phonetic power of the letter ᚱ [R] (and not its name *bagal* <note>likely a transcription error for *Hagal* or a specific Icelandic variant name</note>) provides the vowel *a* (as in *ba*). So too the following word in the same place ᚼᛒᚢᚼᛒᛅ <note>Runes for H-B-U-H-B-A</note> would be *habehasbba*. Unless it is so, no word or syllable can be drawn from it. There, just as it includes the vowel *a*, so the letter B includes the vowel *e*; by reason, as was said, of its phonetic power and not its name (*Biarkan* <note>The Runic name for 'B'</note> and *Hagal* <note>The Runic name for 'H'</note>). And thus the rest of that word is clear from these, though meanwhile those words are entirely unknown to us.

Furthermore, this manner of writing, while it consists of common Runes or Runic letters, might cause less trouble to those observing that "eclipse" of vowels (for so one might call that hiding or shutting-in of vowels). But as it summons foreign Runes and plays with a variety of characters, it will turn out inextricable for most people today. Especially if anything is inscribed with an admixture of a foreign language (Hebrew, Greek, Latin, or French), which those eager for concealment and complexity have affected and <meta>catchword: facti- (likely "factitasse," meaning "frequently practiced")</meta>

<header>BOOK THREE</header>

I have no doubt that they practiced this repeatedly: and perhaps the matter itself will speak. Let it be permitted here to interpose a conjecture. It is well established from various monuments that the ancients begrudged their descendants—even their own close and distant kinsmen—their coins, weapons, and treasures, <note>original Latin: *clenodia*; referring to precious jewels or heirlooms</note> indeed even a good supply of gold. They did not always bury these in their own tombs, but dug them in deep enough now here, now there, or sank them in deep wells. I would now ask the wise Reader, and any evaluator of such things, whether the same could not have happened regarding **Runic Literature**? Could they have wished to win for themselves a reputation for high esteem and an opinion of their great knowledge by creating a certain wonder and impossibility of reading, or of understanding what was written?

Regarding what has already been said about the second side of this monument, we wish it to be valid for the first side as well; syllables or words cannot be extracted from there in any other way. That side consists of a quite lengthy inscription with at least two vowels expressed a few times: namely **ᚼ** <note>The *Hagall* rune, here likely representing an 'a' or 'h' sound</note> seven times, and a simple **I** only three times, and a dotted one repeated six times—since a heap of bare consonants would exist as something mute and irrational. <note>original Greek: *alogos*; meaning without reason or speech</note>

But just as that first side was contrary to the nature of **Danish Runes**—that is, possessing that more frequent (and elsewhere continuous) omission which I have called an **ellipsis** <term>the grammatical omission of letters or sounds, a common feature in these inscriptions</term>—it throws two further obstacles in the Reader’s path: 1. A foreign and perhaps corrupt language (certainly as far as the spelling is concerned) and 2. quite a large number of characters that are entirely unknown to the common person. I add a third obstacle, one familiar to all **Runes**, which is the mother of entanglement and obscurity, and therefore most hateful to the Reader: this is the negligence or ignorance regarding distinctions and sub-distinctions, such as commas, colons, and periods. Furthermore, there is no observation of capital or lowercase letters—nothing worthy of praise—which must be excused by the example of I know not what kind of literature.

Therefore, we read the first side thus: **RHAMDHAT, BEHARUT, MUTI, HAMPLET,** <note>This is a significant early reference to the legendary figure Amleth, the inspiration for Shakespeare's Hamlet</note> **HEHADEM** (they think these mean "the same") **MIHAM** (they think this means "mine"); we are forced to leave the following little word untouched. **HALHAM MIHA RUX**

# TWENTY-FIFTH
## OF LISTERBY.

In another of the villages we mentioned above, namely *Listerby*, there is a church in which a wooden screen <note>original Latin: *tabulatum*; referring to a screen or partition made of wooden planks</note> of skillfully crafted latticework is seen. From this, one may gather that this place was once greatly ennobled not only by the graves of many great men but also by their deeds. Whether this monument is truly to be ascribed to the aforementioned Villandson, or to some other person, remains unclear. It is certain that this region was celebrated for many and various exploits of our people and for the dwellings of great men. For among others, Johann Lyschander <note>Claus Christophersen Lyschander (1558–1624), the Royal Danish Historian</note> reports in the third sermon of his *Antiquities* that the city of Sölvesborg was once most famous, *at which the Lombard tribes, flowing together from the northern regions, celebrated their first encampment while preparing for their passage and migration.* It is likely, therefore, that they left many monuments of themselves here, of which this may perhaps be one.

...whether it carves through the heights or passes through the depths of the valleys, it is known to maintain the traces of letters in the same sequence. King **Valdemar**, the blessed offspring of the holy **Canute** <note>Valdemar I, known as the Great (reigned 1154–1182), son of Canute Lavard</note>, desiring to know their meaning out of wonder, sent men to cross the crag and gather the series of characters lying open there with careful investigation, and afterwards to mark them down with rods beneath the tips of those same shapes. They were unable to grasp any interpretation of them for the reason that the hollow of the carving itself—partly smeared with mud and partly worn away by the footsteps of passersby—had confused the appearance of the drawn figures on the worn-down path. From this it is clear that even the cracks of solid stone, soaked for a long time with moisture, grow over either by the accumulation of filth or the constant dripping of rain clouds.

Thus writes **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), the primary medieval chronicler of Denmark. # BOOK THREE.

> Alas, what does devouring time, what does the longest decay of the age not consume? <note>original: "Heu quid tempus edax, quid non longissima secli / Absumit caries?" This is a poetic sentiment on the ravages of time, common in Renaissance scholarship.</note>

### BORNHOLM.

<margin>cc cc cc cc cc cc cc cc</margin>**Bornholm** <note>original: "Boringholmus"</note> is an island located closer to the shores of **Scania** <note>The southernmost part of modern Sweden, which was a Danish province at the time of writing</note>, looking toward **Ystad** <note>original: "Eiistadium Veminiorum"</note> in a straight line to the west. This island contains four provinces and has recognized the **Gothic kingdom** <note>Referring to the legendary and historical Geats or Goths of Scandinavia</note> in every age; it had specific princes from Denmark, until it finally passed into the authority of the **Archbishop of Scania** from **Lund**, which led to many disputes. It offers convenient harbors for the Danish Admiral's fleet, which are most useful for maintaining command of the eastern sea. **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century historian</note> calls it *Boringia*; **Adam of Bremen** calls it *Holmia*; and **Paul the Deacon** <note>original: "Paulo Warnefrido", the 8th-century historian of the Lombards</note> calls it *Scoringa*. For I judge this to be the region of which he speaks in Book 1, Chapter 7 of the *History of the Lombards*, where the **Winili** <note>The early name for the Lombards</note>, having departed from Scandinavia, settled for several years. Indeed, he calls it an "island of no great size" shortly after, near the end of that chapter.

### I. THE AAKIRKEBY INSCRIPTION.

In roughly the middle of the island is a village called **Aakirkeby**, approaching the size of a modest town and endowed with exceptional privileges. Here, a stone fragment adorns the courtyard of a certain inhabitant; it is nearly two cubits in length, one in width, and a quarter-cubit in thickness, with a reddish <note>original: "puniceo", literally Punic-wax or purple-red</note> color. It exhibits certain traces of letters, though they are so interrupted that it is now scarcely possible to gather anything certain from them. You have its likeness here, in the drawing as I received it.

# BOOK THREE

The stone which, in the parish of **Aaker**, serves as a bridge for those crossing the river near the estate called **Møllegarden**, is indeed rough, but so flat that it appears more like the lid of a tomb than a traditional memorial pillar, and seems to have been moved there from elsewhere for this purpose. It measures nearly five ells <term>ell: a historical unit of length, roughly 2 feet or 60cm</term> in length, exceeds two ells in width, and is barely a quarter-ell thick. Its color is a faded gray, as is common for stones of this rough type. It was brought to my attention in the form presented above.

-> Ogmund and Fruburn set up this stone in memory of <-
-> Isrgor, their father; may God help his soul. <-

<note>original Old Norse/Danish: "Ogmund aug Fruburnr satu stein eftir Isrgori fadur sin, Gud hialpi siolu hans."</note>

-> OGMUND AND FRUBURN PLACED THIS STONE FOR ISRGOR THEIR FATHER, MAY GOD AID HIS SOUL. <-
<note>original Latin: "OGMUNDUS ET FRUBURNUS LAPIDEM POSUERUNT ISRGORIO PATRI SUO, DEUS ANIMAM IPSIUS JUVET."</note>

**FRUBURNAR** can be read either as a single name or as two separate words: Separated, it reads **FRU BURNAR**, or *Lady Burnera*. <note>The transcription uses 'P' or 'R' variants for the transliterated 'FRU BURNAR' context based on the Runic 'ᚠ'</note> But I would hardly believe that in that age our ancestors addressed or honored more distinguished or noble matrons with the title of "Lady." Norwegian history traces this word back to Freja, the daughter of Njord <note>original: "Noronis," referring to the Norse god Njörðr</note>. For since she was illustrious for her beauty and all the virtues belonging to her sex, she wished the title of her name to be derived for other matrons who shone with virtue or the splendor of their lineage. This practice still holds among us today. However, I have not yet seen it carved on older monuments, so I prefer it to be read as a single word representing a man’s name. In the last syllable of this word, there is an elision of the vowel E, which is included within the letter R, according to the custom accepted by the ancients.

The word **GOD** <note>original Runic: ᚴᚢᚦ</note> indicates that this is a Christian prayer; therefore, it can hardly be placed among the most ancient monuments.

### **THIRD BOOK**
<page-num>237</page-num>

*Good Thurfastr, Thura, and Busi, they set this mound-memorial for ...fasti, their brother. May God help this family and may God have mercy on Faster.*
<note>original: "Thurfastr gud Thuru / aug Busi, dir satu kuml dufi ista --- fas burudr. Gud hialpi ætn disa aug Gud Muibfartl fastr." This is the author's transcription of the Old Norse runes into the Latin alphabet.</note>

-> GOOD THURFASTER, [SON] OF THORA, AND BUSI MADE THIS MOUND IN MEMORY OF ...FASTI THEIR BROTHER. MAY GOD HELP THIS FAMILY AND HAVE MERCY ON FASTER. <-
<note>original Latin: "THURFASTERUS BONUS THORI ET BUSI TUMULUM HUNC FECERUNT IN MEMORIAM --- FASTI FRATRIS, DEUS FAMILIAM HANC JUVET ET MISEREATUR FASTERI."</note>

ᚦᚢᚱᚠᛅᛋᛏᚱ <gloss>Thurfastr</gloss> should be read as *Thurfaster* or *Durfaster*, as if "faithful to the God Thor," a name savoring of paganism <note>The author notes that names incorporating "Thor" reflect the older Norse religion, even if the inscription's prayer is Christian.</note>. In the final syllable, the ‘E’ would be absorbed by the ‘R’.

ᚦᚢᚱᚢ <gloss>Thuru</gloss>. The last letter ᚢ [u] seems to denote the complete word *sun* [son]: it should therefore be read as *Thuru sun* (Thura’s son). However, this "Thura" is the woman we are accustomed to calling either Thora or Thyra, a name enjoyed by the most famous Queen of the Danes and wife of Gorm, concerning whom you may consult the Jelling monument <note>The Jelling Stones are massive carved runestones from the 10th century, often called "Denmark's birth certificate." Thyra was the mother of King Harald Bluetooth.</note>.

ᚴᚢᛘᛚ <gloss>Kuml</gloss>. I judge this to denote a "cairn" or a "burial mound." In the Jelling inscription, it is written as ᚴᚢᛘᛒᛚ <gloss>kumbl</gloss> with the same meaning. If it is to be read as ᚴᚢᛘᛚ <gloss>kuml</gloss> here, it comes very close to the Latin word *cumulus* [a heap or mound]. Indeed, there are certain small hills and mounds near this stone, such as were once intended for burials, which this word suggests. Some believe, not without reason, that this monument was originally located in that very spot.

ᛒᚢᚱ <gloss>Bur</gloss>. Because the peak of the stone has been broken off, the name of the person who earned this monument perished along with it; only these three letters remain.

ᚼᛁᛅᛚᛒᛁ <gloss>Hialpi</gloss> [Help]. A prayer worthy of a Christian <note>original Latin: "Christiano dignum votum." The author is highlighting the transition from pagan names to Christian formulas like "God help his soul."</note>.

ᛅᛏᚿ <gloss>Aetn</gloss> [Kin]. This designates a family, lineage, kinship, or progeny. The first letter of this word seems, in this place, to correspond to the value of the diphthong Æ. Otherwise, this formula of intercession and prayer is quite frequent in our antiquities.

ᛘᚢᛁᛒᛅᚱᛏᛚ <gloss>Muibfartl</gloss> etc. Here I am stuck, and I find myself wishing for more care from the person who sketched these runes. The phrasing I have substituted [in the translation] does not contradict the general sense and is consistent with others of its kind. Let it pass, until someone is found who can restore these and other details to us.

*Thurfastr the Good, son of Thora and Busi, they placed this burial mound in memory of... Fasti their brother. ->THURFASTER THE GOOD, SON OF THORA AND BUSI, MADE THIS MOUND IN MEMORY OF... FASTI HIS BROTHER. MAY GOD HELP THIS FAMILY AND HAVE MERCY ON FASTERUS.<- <note>original Latin: "THURFASTERUS BONUS THORI ET BUSI TUMULUM HUNC FECERUNT IN MEMORIAM --- FASTI FRATRIS, DEUS FAMILIAM HANC JUVET ET MISEREATUR FASTERI."</note>

**ᚦᚢᚱᚠᛅᛋᛏᚱ** should be read as *Thurfaster* or *Durfaster*, meaning "faithful to the god Thor" <note>original: "Thoroni Deo fidelis"</note>; this is a name that smacks of paganism. In the final syllable, the "E" would be absorbed by the "R."

**ᚦᚢᚱᚢ ᛋ.** The last letter, **ᛋ**, seems to denote the complete word *sun* <note>meaning "son"</note>; it should therefore be read as *Thuru sun* <note>"Thora's son"</note>. This Thuru is the woman we usually call either Thora or Thyra, a name held by that most distinguished Queen of the Danes and wife of Gorm, concerning whom you may consult the Jelling monument <note>Worm refers here to the famous 10th-century Jelling stones erected by King Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth</note>.

**ᚴᚢᛘᛚ** I believe this denotes a heap or a burial mound. In the Jelling inscription it appears as **ᚴᚢᛘᛒᛚ** with the same meaning. If it is to be read here as **ᚴᚢᛘᛚ**, it comes very close to the Latin *cumulus* <note>meaning a "heap" or "mound"</note>. Near this stone there are certain hillocks and mounds of the kind once intended for burials, which this word signifies. Some people believe, not without reason, that this monument was originally located there.

**ᚠᛅᚦᚱ.** Because the top of the stone was broken off, the name of the person who earned this monument perished along with it; only these three letters remain.

**ᚼᛁᛅᛚᛒᛁ.** A prayer worthy of a Christian <note>meaning "Help," as in "May God help..."</note>.

**ᛅᛏᚦ.** This designates family, stock, kinship, and progeny. The first letter of this word seems to correspond in value in this place to the diphthong **Æ**. Otherwise, this formula of intercession and prayer is quite common in our antiquities.

**ᛘᚢᛁᛒ. &c.** Here I am stuck, and I find the accuracy of the person who drew these runes to be lacking. The formula I have substituted does not contradict the sense and is consistent with others of its kind. Let it pass, until someone is found who can restore these and other parts to us.

### IV.
## THE FIRST ST. NICHOLAS MONUMENT

This purple Oeland marble <note>original: "marmor Oelandicum"; a type of limestone from the Swedish island of Öland, commonly used for high-status grave slabs</note> represents a stone that can be seen in the courtyard of the church dedicated to St. Nicholas. Its broken corners leave us with an uneven shape; where it is longest, it exceeds four cubits <note>original: "ulnas"; an "ell" or cubit, roughly the length of a forearm</note>; where it is widest, it is one and a half; and where it is thickest, one quarter of a cubit. For a long time, it lay buried and ignored in the dirt, but after the renovation of the courtyard, it was placed in its current position—a more prominent spot where it meets the eyes of readers. The carving is elegant enough according to the style of that era, but no one will easily grasp the meaning of the inscription from the reports brought to us. As we received it, we render it here with only a few changes.

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a runic monument. The monument is a roughly rectangular stone slab with jagged edges. A central oval frame contains runic characters, and is bisected horizontally and vertically by a cross. Additional runes are carved along the arms of the cross and within the oval segments. The cross is decorated with simple scrollwork at the ends of its horizontal arms.</image-desc>

The first parts, having been restored in some way, seem capable of being read comfortably as follows:

ᛅᛋᚢᚱ ᛚᛁᛏ ᚱᛅᛁᛋᛅ ᛋᛏᛅᛁᚾ ᛁᚠᛏᛁᛦ ᛁᛚᚢᛅᚱᚦ ᛁᛅᚦᛁᛚᚢ ᛋᚢᚾᛅᚱ
<margin>(lask,</margin> ᚢᚴ ᛁᚠᛏᛁᛦ ᚼᛅᚢᛏᛁ ᛘᚢᚦᚢᚱ ᛅᛋᛚᛅᚴᛦ.
*Asur lit resa stein eftir Alvard jadilu sunar*
*ug eftir Hauti modur A-*
->ASUR HAD THIS STONE RAISED FOR ILVARD, SON OF JADILU, AND FOR HAUTA, THE MOTHER OF ASLAC.<- <note>original Latin: "ASUR LAPIDEM ERIGI CURAVIT ILVARDO JADILU FILIO ET HAUTÆ MATRI ASLACI."</note>

KOBU SVENO PLACED THIS STONE FOR BAVSO HIS SON — GOOD GOD HELP HIS SPIRIT AND MY SOUL.
<note>original Latin translation of the runes: "KOBU SVENO LAPIDEM HUNC POSUIT BAVSO FILIO SUO — BONE DEUS JUVA EJUS SPIRITUM ET ANIMAM MEAM."</note>

Both the style and the depicted cross abundantly prove this to be a Christian monument; furthermore, the shape of the stone is not unlike common grave markers. However, the person who first drew this did not capture every stroke of the letters, which is why we are forced to leave certain parts untouched.

<term>Y‡BN</term>. If there is no error in this word, it is likely the surname of Sveno, in which the letter ‡ represents the value of either a double A or an O.

<term>TRNTIN</term>. This denotes "Lord" or "God" <note>likely a transliteration of the Old Norse 'Drottin'</note>, a word formerly frequent among us, but in its place we now use the German word **Herre**. The Icelanders, still enjoying our ancient language, do not reject it but write it as **Drotten**; the compound **Jorddrot**, meaning "Lord of the Land," is still familiar to us. See Monument XIV in this book, page 199.

## VI.
### THE FIRST ST. CLEMENT MONUMENT
<note>original: "CLEMENTINUM I"</note>

That pillar <note>original: "cippus"; a small pillar or gravestone</note> which is seen in St. Clement's parish, along the royal road toward the North, displays a greater antiquity. For the stone is rough, pointed, and gray in color. When it was whole, its height exceeded three cubits <note>an "ell" or cubit, roughly 18-24 inches</note>, its thickness was nearly a cubit, and it was of the same width. 

They say it once occupied another place, though it is not certain where. It is a story on everyone's lips that a bailiff <note>original: "Villicum"; a farm manager or local official</note> who attempted to move this pillar for his own use was so overwhelmed by its mass that, his sled having broken and his horses being exhausted, he was forced to abandon it in the middle of the journey. Consequently, even now, the broken-off part around its base has cost the inscription quite a few characters; however, by comparing those that come before and after, they are restored with no difficulty.

**BRUN**. Bruno, a name that is not so very uncommon.

**THUIR** <note>original: ÞUIR</note>, I translate as Thorus. For the letter **Þ** <note>the rune "Thorn"</note> is equivalent to "Th," even when it is not marked with a point in the older texts. A man of high standing by the name of Bruno was the counselor to King Harald Wartooth <note>original: Haraldus Hylletandus; a legendary 8th-century Danish king</note> and his envoy to Ringo <note>King Sigurd Hring of Sweden</note>. It is said that Odin <note>original: Othinum</note> assumed this Bruno's appearance and features so that he might more easily sow the seeds of war between these two kings—seeds that would prove fatal for Harald. Regarding him, our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century author of the "Gesta Danorum" or Deeds of the Danes</note> writes thus at the end of the seventh book: *“At the same time, a certain Bruno was considered the sole participant and confidant in all of Harald's plans. Both Harald himself and Ringo, whenever they had need of a more secret message, were accustomed to trust their orders to him. Whom fami-*

...had attained a level of familiarity <note>original Latin: *familiaritatis*; the OCR begins mid-word from the previous page</note> through their shared upbringing and childhood friendship. Thus, the formula of this inscription declares that it was placed for a father and a brother, even though only one person is specifically named to whose memory it is consecrated.

As far as can be gathered from the sequence of the inscription: Sialva, a Christian woman, first placed this monument for her pagan <note>original Latin: *ethnico*; used here to refer to a non-Christian or practitioner of the Old Norse religion</note> husband Gudbjörn as a vow; as a spouse wishing well for his soul, she added the prayers you see. Truly, after the death of Sialva, a daughter or friend named Birgitta, intending to carry out the last will of the deceased woman, had her buried with her husband, attesting to this with a second inscription on the same stone. The context is clear, except for a few things in the last inscription which escape our understanding, either due to the corruption of the letters or the antiquity of the language.

## IX.
# *THE LAURENTIAN STONE.*

A monument of a more recent age appears, which has been fitted into the wall of the eastern courtyard of the church <note>original Latin: *templi*; while literally "temple," in this context it refers to a Christian church building</note> dedicated to Saint Lawrence. It reached us in a very degraded state, but read it here as it has been restored.

## X. THE GYLDENSGÅRD STONE.

<image-desc>A woodcut of a tall, upright runestone. A band containing an inscription in Younger Futhark runes frames the outer edge of the stone, following the shape of the rounded top and descending both sides. The stone is shown set into a small mound of earth at its base.</image-desc>

**Bufa** <note>original: *ᛒᚢᚠᛆ*</note>, a naming very unusual to us, which gives me no small suspicion of an error; such errors have not infrequently crept into these Bornholm <note>original: *Boringholmicis*</note> records, because I have not yet been permitted to survey the island in person.

**Iftir** <note>original: *ᛁᛏᛁᚱ*</note> is a not uncommon word, composed, it seems, from **In** <note>original: *ᛁᚿ*</note> which designates a "fountain" to us, and **Ih** or **In** which denotes an "island," as if you were to say a fountain bubbling up on an island. <note>The author is attempting a "folk etymology" here; modern linguists recognize *iftir* or *eftir* simply as "after" or "in memory of."</note> But **Sin** <note>original: *ᛋᛁᚿ*</note> or **Sihn**, as we now pronounce it, we usually render in Latin as **Chilianus**, to which a particle is prefixed, which perhaps indicates that he lived on the island.

**Fathur** <note>original: *ᚠᛆᚦᚢᚱ*</note> is undoubtedly a superlative form from **Fatha**. <note>The author mistakenly identifies the word for "father" as a grammar-based adjective.</note>

**Krister** <note>original: *ᚴᚱᛁᛋᛏᛁᚱ*</note> savors of the Christian religion. From this, therefore, anyone can make a conjecture regarding the age of the monument: it is certainly not among the most ancient, but is to be numbered among those of the Middle Ages. The rest of the words are clear and transparent enough.

I know that more remains of inscriptions still exist on the same island, which I leave for others to uncover, as I have received these accounts without sufficient accuracy to allow me to bestow the necessary labor upon them.

## BOOK FOUR
### CONCERNING FUNEN.

The most pleasant of the islands, **Funen** <note>original: *Fionia*</note>, now calls us back to itself. Since it fosters within its ecclesiastical bosom <note>The Diocese of Odense historically included the islands of Funen, Lolland, and Falster.</note> two principal islands, **Falster** <note>original: *Falstria*</note> and **Lolland** <note>original: *Lalandia*</note>—much like **Scania** <note>original: *Scania*; modern Skåne</note> contains **Halland** <note>original: *Hallandia*</note> and **Blekinge** <note>original: *Blekingia*</note>, which we find equally suited to our purpose—we shall by no means pass them by with a "dry foot" <note>An idiom meaning to pass over something quickly or without effort.</note>.

*Our Funen, as Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), a Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum.</note> bears witness, looks out toward Jutland from the west and toward Zealand from the east; it is praiseworthy for its conspicuous abundance of necessary resources, surpassing all other provinces of our region in its pleasantness. It is considered to hold the central position of Denmark, separated by equal intervals from the furthest boundaries.* In its praise, **Lyschander** <note>Claus Christoffersen Lyschander (1558–1624), a Danish historian and poet.</note> has this to say:
> *Funen is abundant in wealth, crops, honey, and all necessary things, breeding brave and distinguished warriors; it received its name from the pleasantness of its locations. Its principalities and provinces number thirteen, to recount which would fill an immense volume; but we shall look only at the cities. The head of the land is **Odense** <note>original: *Othonia*</note>, a great city and an Episcopal see; looking toward the east is **Nyborg** <note>original: *Neoburgum*</note>, of great name because of the honor and reverence of the Danish Parliament <note>original: *Parlamenti Danici*; Nyborg was the site of the Danehof, the medieval national assembly.</note>. Further up is **Kerteminde** <note>original: *Giretminda*</note>, and more to the west is **Bogense** <note>original: *Bothonia*</note>, and nearest to this is **Middelfart** <note>original: *Melfartum*</note>. Toward the west and south is **Assens** <note>original: *Asnisum*</note>, then **Faaborg** <note>original: *Foburgum*</note>, but toward the winter sunrise <note>The southeast.</note> is **Svendborg** <note>original: *Suineburgum*</note>. All these maritime cities of Funen are looked upon by Odense, like a mother and Queen from the inland regions, etc.*

*Suti placed this stone for his brother Ranleif, the son of Scavo the Red, the Skald.* <note>original Runic: *Suti sati stain densi eft Ranleif brudur sin, Sunor Skaus raudum Skialta.*</note>

->SUTO PLACED THIS STONE FOR HIS BROTHER RANLEIF, THE SON OF SCAVO THE RED, THE SKALD.<-

Regarding this monument, it is certain that it was by no means placed by its original owners in the location where it is now found. Evident proof of this can be gathered from the local inhabitants, who testify with one voice that it was moved from a nearby hill surrounded by larger stones. It stood upright there, whereas it now lies cast down to provide a better path for those passing by. The locals add that a certain giant named Ronne was buried in that hill, from whom the village took its name; but the inscription contains "Ranleif," which is not far off, and no doubt after the passage of so many centuries the name has been corrupted and degenerated into "Ronne." This Ranleif was the lord of a nearby castle and fortress called **Skafvfbøe** <note>modern Skovsbo</note>, which now, its walls having been demolished, has become the residence of certain nobles. This narrative is not at all foreign to the inscription, as the name of Scavo also occurs here, by whom that castle was perhaps built; for **Skafvfbøe** in the native tongue signifies the "dwelling of Scavo."

ᛋᚢᛏᛁ <note>Suti</note>: The proper name of the one who placed the monument; he was the son of Scavo and the brother of Ranleif, as the inscription abundantly shows.

ᚱᛅᚾᛚᛅᛁᚠ <note>Ranleif</note>: The person to whom the burial mound and stone are dedicated; a name which later, through uncertain storytelling, degenerated into Rónne.

ᛋᚢᚾᚬᛦ <note>Sunor</note>: I believe there is an error here, and it should read *Sunir* <note>original: ᛋᚢᚾᛁᛦ</note>, that is, "sons" in the plural, so that it includes both men and indicates that Scavo was the father of both Ranleif and Suti.

ᚱᛅᚢᚦᚢᛘ ᛋᚴᛦᛅᛚᛏᛅ <note>Raudum Skialta</note>: These words can be explained in two ways. Either they refer to Scavo, so that the meaning is: this Scavo was called by the nickname "the Red" and was also a poet or Skald <term>skald: an Old Norse poet and storyteller, often serving a royal court</term>; or they are to be taken separately, because they are expressed with a separate line and stroke. <header>BOOK FOUR.</header>

The author of this inscription was a certain man called Raudur Scald; "Raudur" signifies the same as "red" (**Rød**). Many people, both among our own ancestors and others, have been distinguished by this cognomen <note>a nickname or third name</note>. Thus **Erik Raudur** <note>Erik the Red</note> was named as the first explorer of Greenland. It should be noted here that the ancients used the letters *Au* in place of the diphthong **Ø** which is familiar to us, and even now the Icelanders express it as **Ø** in their pronunciation; for they pronounce *Raudur* as *Rødur*. He was so named because of his red hair and beard, much like the historical figures Ænobarbus <note>Latin: "Bronze-beard"</note>, Barbarossa <note>Italian: "Red-beard"</note>, and others. As for what kind of people the <term>Scaldri</term> <note>Skalds: court poets and historians of the Viking Age</note> were and what their office entailed, we have shown this more extensively in our *Runica* <note>Literature on Runes</note> and *Fasti Danici* <note>Danish Calendars/Chronicles</note>.

If our later conjecture is valid, the artistry observed in the carving of this stone is by no means to be overlooked. By a recurring line, they expressed the sequence of the inscription concerning the deceased and the heirs; however, the name of the poet is placed separately in a smaller space, as if beginning a new line. It is truly a polished monument, worthy of a better location, and one that could grant no small majesty to the Skovsbo estate.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a runestone, which is a large rock with an arched top. A band of runic inscriptions follows the outer curve of the stone. The center of the stone is uncarved and shows a rough, rocky texture.</image-desc>

The local inhabitants report that this monument has held its current position ever since the church was first built; however, it was not possible to discover <note>literally "to fish out"</note> what the social rank or standing of this man **Dolfus** might have been, or whether the stone was moved to this spot from somewhere else.

ᚱᚢᛏᚢᛚᚠᚱ Some read ᚱᚢᛏᚢᛚᚠᚱ as the name **Rudolphus**, although in the monument at Avenslev <note>original Latin: Avensloensi</note> the name Rudolph is written as ᚱᚢᚦᚢᛚᚠᚱ.

ᚼᛁᚿᛏ *henti*, "carried away"; perhaps he purchased it with his own money and saw to it that it was brought here.

᛭ This single mark is found twice on this stone; I believe it was placed there for the sake of brevity and to save space, serving as the well-known connective word "and" <note>Old Norse: *auk*; runes: ᛅᚢᚴ</note>. For the same reason, you will find *abt* (ᛅᛒᛏ) written here instead of the full *abtir* (ᛅᛒᛏᛁᚱ) <note>meaning "after," often used in the sense of "in memory of"</note>.

ᛏᚢᛅᚿᛅ *tuona*. First, you will note here a combination of two characters joined into one <term>bindrune</term> <note>a ligature or combination of two or more runes into a single figure</note>; for the first character of this word consists of **T** and **U**. Next is the meaning of the word itself, used more emphatically <note>original Greek: ἐμϕατικωτέραν</note>; today *tuenne* signifies "two," and here it undoubtedly— <meta>The text cuts off mid-sentence; the catchword "bio" suggests the next word is "dubio," completing the Latin phrase "absque dubio" meaning "without doubt."</meta>

...of such stupendous strength that he could be overcome by no one of his age in single combat. Having been taken off by poison by his rivals, he chose a burial mound and monument for himself in this place.

**RULFR HARTHI** <note>Runic: ᚱᚢᛚᚠᚱ ᚼᛅᚱᚦI</note>. If this reading is approved, it agrees with the stories of the local inhabitants, that this Rudolf earned the surname **HARTHI** or "the Hard" <note>original Latin: *Duri*</note> because of his remarkable strength. Therefore, **RULFR HARTHI** will be the proper name of the person buried here. Thus, the word **UNT** <note>Runic: ᚢᚾᛏ</note> must refer to other things that are missing, so the sense might be: "Rudolf the Hard laid low [an unknown enemy]." Otherwise, this reading is also not so dissonant: **RULFR THARTHI UNT**, "Rudolf made the mound." In this case, the name would not be that of the buried man, but of the one who had the monument made, as noted above. Regarding the **R** <note>Runic: ᚱ</note>, note its merger with the **A** <note>Runic: ᛅ</note>.

The reader <note>term: *Anagnosta* refers to the assistant or scribe who first transcribed the stone</note> has described some things erroneously here; therefore, in **HATIR** <note>Runic: ᚼᛅᛏᛁᚱ</note> I read **A** <note>Runic: ᛅ</note> instead of **H** <note>Runic: ᚼ</note>. For the addition of a single stroke was easy, as seen above and below in **HTAIN** <note>Runic: ᚼᛏᛅᛁᚾ</note> where it should be read as **ATAIN** <note>meaning "stone"</note>.

## FIFTH MONUMENT
### AT FLEMLØSE.

Within the region of the Baag Hundred <note>term: *Baageherrit*, an administrative district on the island of Funen, Denmark</note>, among other villages is one named Flemløse. In its churchyard is found a rough stone, three cubits <note>original: *ulnas*</note> long and two and a half wide, endowed with an inscription consisting of four lines in the manner set forth below.

->AFTER RULFR'S DAUGHTER ISVASNUR SET THE STONE...<-
->...GUTHI SET THESE RUNES FOR FATHER FUHIR.<-

I read it thus: *After Rudolf's daughter, Isvasnur set the stone, and Guthi set the Runes after Father Fuhir.*

> IN MEMORY OF THE DAUGHTER OF RUDOLF, ISVASNUR PLACED THIS STONE, AND GUTHI PLACED THE RUNES FOR THE FATHER FUHIR.

This stone was moved from a nearby large and high hill, according to the local residents. It is so worn away by age that the violence of rains and storms has ruined many of the strokes; therefore, some parts must be restored in this manner.

# BOOK FOUR.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large, upright runestone (stela) with an irregular, naturally tapered shape. The stone is covered with vertical columns of runic inscriptions. **AFT** <note>Runic: ᛅᚠᛏ</note>, should be read as **EFT** <note>Runic: ᚽᚠᛏ</note> instead of *eftir* <note>The Old Norse word for "after," commonly found in funerary inscriptions</note>.

In the sequence **HUHI** <note>Runic: ᚼᚼᛁ</note> I read **FATI** <note>Runic: ᚠᛅᚦᛁ; meaning "painted" or "carved"</note>, for the context confirms this meaning. It was an easy error to make where a **F** <note>Runic: ᚠ</note> was made from an **A** <note>Runic: ᛅ</note> by the addition of a single line, especially since the surface of this rougher stone is worn away here and there.

Regarding **ISAK** <note>Runic: ᛁᛋᛅᚴ</note>, I wonder if it may be interpreted as the name **Isach** <note>Isaac</note>. It is quite certain that the ancients confused vowels, especially those that have some phonetic relationship; however, this should be joined with **SNURO** <note>Runic: ᛋᚾᚢᚱᚮ</note>. It does not matter that the last letter is transposed to the beginning of the following line, since our ancestors did not maintain a very strict system of orthography <note>term: *Orthographia*; the conventional spelling system of a language</note>.

‡ I believe this character stands for the word **AUK** <note>Runic: ᛅᚢᚴ; meaning "and"</note>, for the Allerup monument, discussed previously, provides examples of this practice.

I read **RUNA** <note>Runic: ᚱᚢᛚᚠᚱ</note> as "the letters" or "the inscription," which is consistent with the general sense of the passage.

# THE SIXTH MONUMENT
## FROM ÅLEBÆK.

In the province of Lund, the parish of **Otterup** <note>a village on the island of Funen</note> contains a river that flows between the villages of **Fremmelev** <note>original: *Fremmerfløff*</note> and **Nislev** <note>original: *Nißløff*</note>; it is called **Ålebæk** <note>original: *Aalebeck*; meaning "Eel-brook"</note> because of its abundance of eels. ### THE MONUMENTS OF LOLLAND

<margin>,,</margin>
Lolland is a Duchy (says Lyscander <note>Claus Christoffersen Lyscander (1558–1623), a Danish historian and royal historiographer</note>), inhabited by four groups of people and distinguished by as many cities: Nakskov <note>original: *Nahesco*</note>, Sakskøbing <note>original: *Saxopinga*</note>, Maribo <note>original: *Mariæonia*</note>, and Nysted <note>original: *Neostadio*</note>.

In the southern territory of Lolland <note>original: *Lalandia*</note> is a village which the inhabitants commonly call *Tirsted* <note>OCR: *Tiletse*</note>. It is adorned with a spacious church and cemetery; in the south-facing wall of this cemetery is found a fitted, gabled stone, somewhat rough, approaching a crimson color, and provided with four sides, each of which is decorated with its own marks and characters. In height it exceeds two Zealand ells <note>A Danish unit of measurement, roughly 63 centimeters or 2 feet per ell</note>, in width one and a half; its thickness is so great that it can conveniently hold two rows of characters, namely about two quarters of an ell. Where it faces east, west, and south, the strokes of our ancient elements <note>The runes</note> are clearer; where it faces north it is rougher, displaying an etched outline of an **eagle's foot** <note>original: *Aquilini pedis*. This is a significant heraldic reference, as the Urne family coat of arms features an eagle's foot.</note>. The furrows of the lettering run from bottom to top, but those facing west are raised slightly higher from the base than the others. The size of the letters is exceptional and conspicuous, corresponding to the size of the stone and representing the strength of that age. On the eastern and western sides, however, they appear somewhat smaller than on the southern side, because those sides were much narrower than the others and did not seem sufficient to hold larger letters. But the visual representation of the monument placed before your eyes will represent the matter more clearly and fully.

The first and more majestic side facing south, endowed with four rows of larger characters, displays these in an unequal series:

ᚦᚢᚱᛁ : ᚢᚾᛁᚦᛅ : ᚼᚼᛋ : ᛘᛁ : ᚱᚼᛁᛋᛁ : ᛋᛏᛁᚾ : ᚦᛁᛋᛁ : ᚼᚠᛏ

**ᛅᛋᚴᚽᛚ . ᛋᚢᛚᚠᚢ . ᛋᚢᚿ.** Just as the name **Eskil** is familiar to our countrymen even in these times, the name **Sulfa** has fallen out of use. <page-num>254</page-num>
<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

...was the architect of this monument; but as a renowned, opulent, and wealthy hero, he took care to have the gathered mass fitted to the place, carved, and erected at his own expense. Certain modes of speaking should be noted here, which frequently occur in these inscriptions; though similar in wording, they differ greatly in meaning: **ᚱᚼᛁᛋᛁ** <note>original: *rhisi* (reisti)</note> means "he placed" or "raised," and is said of the one who physically built it; **ᛘᚼᚱᚴᛁ** <note>original: *marki* (merki)</note> refers to the Lord who provided the funds and commissioned the work; and **ᚱᛁᛋᛏᛁ** <note>original: *risti*</note> refers to the sculptor or carver.

**ᚼᚠᛏ. ᚴᚢᚼᚿᚴᚼ. ᛋᛁᚿ. APT. KUANKA. SIN. In his own memory.** This is quite peculiar. It is customary for heirs and descendants to build monuments for the deceased; however, we rarely perform this duty for ourselves unless there are compelling reasons. Yet the sentiment of Pliny from his *Letters* (Book 6, Letter 10) holds true here:
> *Faith in friendship is so rare, and the dead are so quickly forgotten, that we ourselves ought to build even our own tombs and take upon ourselves all the duties of our heirs.* <note>original Latin: *Tam rara in amicitia fides, tam parata oblivio mortuorum...*</note>
We see that even the greatest emperors were driven by this, preferring to pass down the memory of their merits to posterity while still alive through stupendous monuments and markers <term>cippis: small stone pillars used as landmarks or grave markers</term> that survive to this day, rather than entrusting it to the unreliable loyalty of their grandsons. Thus Augustus Caesar, according to the historian Suetonius, built a Mausoleum for himself while still living, and Hadrian saw to it that a monument was made for him in Rome near the Tiber, commonly called the *Mole of Hadrian*, known today as the **Castel Sant'Angelo**. Not only emperors, but also patricians and citizens frequently did this, as the surviving inscription formulas testify to us. One elegant example is found in the ancient epigrams of the city, once in the Arenula region <note>A district in Rome now known as Regola</note>; but now in Padua <note>Latin: *Patavii*</note> at the house of Torquatus Bembus, according to Schrader.

-> TO LUCIUS VALERIUS ZABDA, SLAVE MERCHANT. <-
-> WHETHER STUPOR OR INSANITY IS THE NAME OF THIS ENDEAVOR, <-
-> ALL MY WORRIES HAVE BEEN RELIEVED BY THIS CONCERN. <-
-> I COMPLETED THIS MONUMENT AT MY OWN EXPENSE, <-
-> SO THAT THE FRIENDLY EARTH MIGHT GIVE A GUEST-CHAMBER TO MY BONES. <-
-> WHICH IS WHAT ALL REQUEST, BUT ONLY THE FORTUNATE OBTAIN. <-
-> FOR WHAT IS MORE OUTSTANDING, OR WHAT IS MORE TO BE DESIRED, <-
-> THAN TO LAY DOWN THE SPIRIT OF FAILING OLD AGE <-
-> IN THE VERY PLACE WHERE YOU RECEIVED THE LIGHT OF LIBERTY? <-
-> WHICH IS THE GREATEST SIGN OF INNOCENCE. <-

<term>ossuarium: a chest, building, or site made to serve as the final resting place of human skeletal remains.</term>

So true is that which Tertullian <note>A prolific early Christian author (c. 155 – c. 220 AD) from Carthage.</note> says in *On the Testimony of the Soul*, Chapter 4:

> Who today does not so strive for their memory to be celebrated after death, that they preserve their name either by works of literature, or by the simple praise of their character, or by the very grandeur of their tombs? <note>original Latin: "Quis non hodie memoriæ post mortem frequentandæ ita studet, ut vel literaturæ operibus, vel simplici laude morum, vel ipsorum sepulchrorum ambitione nomen suum servet?"</note>

Therefore, there is no reason to wonder that our Eskil took care to build a monument for himself, especially if we more carefully weigh the motives by which he was driven to undertake this work, which the inscription shows in the following lines.

**ᚼᛅᚾ** <note>han: he</note> &c. **ᚢᛅᚾ ᛚᛁᚦᛁᚱ** <note>uan lithir: overcame the troop/people</note>. Here you see a long catalog of enemies overcome by Eskil and crushed by his great strength of spirit. Concerning these—lest so splendid a deed be covered by the rust of envy—our hero rightly triumphs through these words. Therefore, I judge this stone to perform a double duty: it both displays a trophy of victory won over enemies and offers a monument placed at the family tomb. Because he distrusted that this tribute could be properly established for him by posterity, he preferred to have it published while he was still alive, conceived in this manner.

**ᚢᛅᚾ** <note>uan</note> comes from the word *Jeg vinder* <note>Danish for "I win" or "I conquer"</note>, meaning to overcome or conquer. Some read this as *Ven* <note>Danish for "friend"</note>, which would give a completely contrary sense, as if Eskil's friends were being listed rather than his defeated enemies. But this is refuted both by the spelling and by the consensus of other inscriptions of this type. Furthermore, nowhere in this entire monument is the letter **E** represented by an **I** with a transverse mark...

<term>ᛋᛏᛁᚢᛒᛅ.</term> <note>original Runic: Stiuba</note> Stiuba is the name of Toko’s mother; the wife (as I believe) of Eschillus, for whom this was placed by her son out of piety.

Concerning the eagle's foot, carved with a somewhat rougher skill (proving the limited ability of the craftsmen of that age) on the final side: while I examine it, I cannot help but think it represents the coat of arms <note>original Latin: insignia</note> of both Eschillus, who is buried here, and of his entire family. For I have been able to observe this in other cases as well. Therefore, when examining the principal and older symbols of the Danish nobility, none occurs that fits better than this one, which is still familiar on the shields of the most illustrious **Urne** family <note>The Urne family was one of Denmark's oldest and most influential noble houses</note>, and has been passed down to posterity through the long memory of ancestors. Thus, I do not hesitate to assert that this Eschillus, and his son Toko or Tycho, were leading lights of the Urne family in that century, and for that reason, this stone should rightly and deservedly be claimed for that same family.

Nor is there reason for anyone to suspect that the name of the **Urnes** is too recent to claim this praise for itself. Indeed, by the constant report of everyone, it is numbered among the oldest families of the Danes; and **Aimoinus** <note>A 10th-century Frankish chronicler</note>, an ancient author, in Book 4, chapter 97, is a rich witness that in the time of **Charlemagne** <note>original Latin: Caroli Magni</note> around the year 810 AD, there existed several of that name and lineage in Denmark, conspicuous for their wisdom, bravery, and deeds famously performed at home and abroad. From among them, a certain man was sent by **King Hemming** to the Emperor to establish a lasting treaty and friendship on both sides; having completed the matter to his satisfaction, he returned home safely. This was also correctly noted by **Gerard Mercator**, that most excellent and famous geographer, in his *Atlas* when discussing Denmark. And finally, from these sources, **Johannes Adolphus Cypræus** in Book 1 of his *Annals of the Bishops of Schleswig* says:

*“When, however,”* he says, *“Charlemagne, having returned from Rome to liberate the Saxons and Frisians, had decided on arms against him, the matter was settled by the advisors of both...”*

...[as the frequency of] the crowd demanded, <note>The text continues from the previous page's final word fragment, likely forming the phrase 'frequentia postulante' (as the frequent demand required).</note> it was forced to form part of a wall by stonemasons and others who had no respect for venerable antiquity. For in the city of Larissa, in the citadel, there was the tomb of **Acrisius** in the temple of **Pallas** [Athena], which is now celebrated as a sanctuary. In the Athenian citadel also, as written by **Antiochus** in the ninth book of his histories, was the tomb of **Cecrops**. Furthermore, **Ismarus**, the son of **Eumolpus** and **Daira**, is buried in Eleusis along with the daughters of **Celeus**."* So it is everywhere among us in our towns and villages: burial mounds are either near the churches or beneath them. Our ancient inscriptions, those noble epitaphs built into the walls, bear witness to the same fact.

If the commentaries of that most noble man, Lord **Lave Urne** <note>original Latin: Lagonis Urne</note>, formerly the most reverend Bishop of **Roskilde** and one who deserved exceptionally well of the **University of Copenhagen**, still existed within your family, I do not doubt that they would bring the most brilliant light to these and many other matters. This Great Consular House is the one in which the Bishop now lives; it was formerly gifted by the King to the University to serve as a public lecture hall <note>original Latin: Auditorium</note>, in which lectures and exercises for [the benefit of] youth...

> *Why should I say more? The Prince is - - -*
> *He is the hope of his father, and the lord of the sea.*

I find that not only was this **Lave Urne** specifically given as a patron to the **University** <term>Academia: The University of Copenhagen.</term> from your family, but I also find that **Niels Urne**, a Danish knight and Provost of Lund, held the scepters of the University and fulfilled the office of **Rector Magnificus** <term>Rector Magnificus: The highest-ranking official or head of a university.</term> with great praise. **Gysbert Longolius** calls him *a most perfect man, most composed in character, most adorned with remarkable learning, not only most noble by birth at home, but also most distinguished by a visible rank of dignity* <note>original: "Virum perfectissimum, moribus compositissimum insigni eruditione ornatissimum, generis conditione domi non solum nobilissimum, verum & conspicuo dignitatis gradu amplissimum"</note> in the preface of his Notes on Ovid’s *Metamorphoses*; he was of such great learning and kindness that he did not disdain to confer through letters with the most literate men of his age on various matters, as asserted by the same author with whom he lived familiarly, as is clear from the dedication of the said work in **Cologne** <note>original: "Coloniæ Agrippinæ"</note>. Also under him, in the year 1529, **Absalon Urne** was granted university citizenship.

Although these matters may seem somewhat distant from our monument to some, they are nevertheless such things as tend toward the praise of your family; and since they are not found everywhere, I could not help but add them here, as they may perhaps be of use in the future to one who contemplates a more particular history of our nation. Farewell, honor of your family, and continue to favor the endeavors of your **Worm** <note>The author, Ole Worm, refers to himself here in the third person.</note>. Copenhagen, July 28, 1630. <note>original: "V Calend. Sextil. Anni MDCXXX."</note>

ᚢᛋᛏᛁᚱᚦᛁ ᚱᛁᛋᚦᛁ ᛋᛏᛁᚾ ᚦᛁᚾᛋᛁ ᛂᚠᛏᛁᚱ ᚵᚢᛏᛆ ᚠᛆᚦᚢᚱ

### OSTERDI PLACED THIS STONE IN MEMORY OF GUTA, HIS FATHER, A LEADER OF A GOOD ARMY.

Legend has it that this rock was transported from a nearby burial mound to the place where it is now seen. For nearby there lies a larger hill rising to the height of a mountain, which is said to be so infested with specters <note>original: spectris infestus — referring to ghosts or supernatural hauntings</note> that it is hardly safe for anyone to cross it at night.

**ᚵᚢᛏᛆ** **Guta** is an ancient name celebrated in the Gothic family; in our antiquities, a certain man is greeted by this name who was the seventh among the Judges of Gotland, and who is said to have first led colonies into Scania and Scanian Gothia. However, it is certain that the man on this stone was someone else.

**ᚼᛁᚱᚦᛁᚾ ᚵᚢᚦᛆᚾ ᚦᛁᚵᚾ.** **A leader of a good army.** Although I have offered a different interpretation of this formula elsewhere, this one occurred to me here, and it seems (in my view) not entirely out of place. We still call an army a *Heer*, and by adding the suffix that indicates a specific one, we get *Heeren*, for which this stone uses *Herden*. Therefore, *Herden guden* means "of a good army." The word **ᚦᛁᚵᚾ** <note>Thegn</note> is derived from the ancient word <term>Diar: a title for a lord, leader, or priest-king</term>, which denotes a Lord, Leader, or Prince. For Norwegian history tells us that when Odin first arrived in these regions, he appointed twelve presiding officers or princes whose duty was to declare the law to the people and take care of the sacrifices; these they called *Diar* or <term>Drotnar: lords or chieftains</term>, whom the rest of the people were bound to serve. From this *Diar*, why should we not say *Diagn* (Thegn) is derived, to express one who holds command over others? Otherwise, in the funeral song of Ragnar Lothbrok <note>original: Epicedio Regneri Lodbrog — referring to the *Krákumál*</note>, I find this word used for a brave man and a strenuous soldier; for among the rest, verse 23 has: *The hero did not shrink before the helmet.* <note>original: Hrökkve ei þegn fyrir hjalm</note>

<page-num>265</page-num>

<header>BOOK FOUR</header>

<sig>Ll</sig>

**A Thegn for a Thegn.** <note>original: degn fyrir degne</note> That is: **A man shall not retreat from another man.** <note>original: Non recedat Vir à Viro</note>. I am informed by Henry Spelman <note>Sir Henry Spelman (1562–1641) was a famous English antiquarian and philologist</note> that the word **Degen** appears in the laws of King Canute the Great, written in the Saxon language, and is commonly translated as "man," though by some as "Baron." From this, one may conclude that the word denotes a man, but specifically one distinguished by strength and courage, or one established in a certain rank of dignity. Should he be considered of equal rank to the one whom Vegetius <note>Publius Flavius Vegetius Renatus, a writer of the later Roman Empire known for his treatise on Roman warfare</note> calls a **Decanus** <note>literally a "leader of ten"</note> in Book 2, Chapter 13? Again, the words of Vegetius are: *the centuries themselves were divided into messes <note>original: contubernia</note>, so that one man would preside over ten soldiers living under one tent; he was known as the Decanus, the head of the mess.* <note>original: ipse Centuriæ in contubernia divisæ sunt, ut decem militibus sub una papilione degentibus, unus quasi præesset Decanus, qui caput contubernii nominatur.</note> Certainly, neither the word itself sounds out of place, nor does the meaning contradict it.

The origin of the word seems to be this: in the past, if anyone acquired enough by honest and lawful means that he could bequeath something to pious uses or devote himself to the King's service with honor, he was considered by the English as a **Degn** or **Thein** <note>Thane</note>. Moreover, **Degn** is what is now called **Tagn** <note>Tegn</note>, from the verb *to take* <note>original: Teatager</note>; because such men were "taken" or accepted by Kings and Princes and endowed with privileges by which they were exempt from all servile business, and could rise by virtue through the ranks to higher dignities. Similarly, one devoted to the liberal arts, when he had reached the point where—having completed the course of the humanities—he was deemed worthy of higher learning and virtue, was honored with the title of **Degn**. Even a merchant who, at his own expense, had sailed three times to foreign lands in a well-equipped ship, was considered worthy of this title upon his return. Thus, it was the first rank of dignity in any station of life. Here, the **Degn** seems to refer to a veteran soldier worthy of honor. From this, the word was drawn to designate the sword, which in the Danish tongue we truly call a **Degen**, because we use its service for our defense. Richard Verstegan <note>An English antiquarian (c. 1550–1640) who wrote on Germanic origins</note>, in his explanations of ancient words in Chapter 7 of his *Antiquities* under the letter T, calls **Thegn** or **Theyn** a primary and free servant, from which he derives **Thiene**, which even now signifies "to serve" among the Danes.

I wish to add what the most distinguished Mr. Stephanus Stephanius <note>Stephen Hansen Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish historian and professor at Sorø Academy</note>, Royal Historiographer and public Professor of the Sorø Academy, has contributed regarding this passage: ᚦᚓᚌᚿ, ᚦᛖᚦᛖᚾ, ᚦᚓᚌᚿ <note>Thegn, Thethen, Thegn</note>. This means a minister of the war gods, or those who presided over wars.

<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

...[who] were called **Thegn** by the Danes in ancient times, and **Thegan** or **Degin** by the Germans. Melchior Goldast <note>Melchior Goldast von Haiminsfeld (1578–1635) was a Swiss jurist and historian famous for collecting medieval documents.</note>, in his *Observations on the Advice of Tyro, King of the Scots*, page 364, notes that they called tall and robust men **Risios** (whom we call **Giants** <note>original: *Riser*</note> or **Warriors** <note>original: *Kemper*</note>, as in **Long-legged Giant** <note>original: *Langbeen Riser*</note>, **Bermer Giant** <note>original: *Bermer Riser*</note>, etc.). These men, trusting in their might and strength, inhabited forests and mountains for the sake of banditry; against them, the **Rekii** <note>Heroes or knights; from the German *Recken*</note> were summoned and came to the aid of the afflicted. Because they served those who called upon them, they were called **Degen**, which is to say "servants." For that is the proper meaning of **Thegan**. Otfrid of Weissenburg <note>A 9th-century monk and poet who wrote a famous harmony of the Gospels in Old High German rhyming verse.</note>, in his Preface to King Ludwig:

> **He was truly a servant** <note>original: *Thegan sin in waru*</note>
> **In many a count**
> **Much suffering he endured**
> **For that which God commanded**
> **He overcame it thereafter completely**
> **As was fitting for God’s servant**
> **We possess the goodness**
> **Just as a servant might ride.**

And in Book I, Chapter III of his *Gospels*:

> **The third lineage from there**
> **Those were noble servants.** <note>original: *edil Thegana*</note>

That ancient Paraphraser of the Old Testament says:

> **Enoch was the servant of God.** <note>original: *Enoch der Gotis Degin was*</note>

The same author says of Pharaoh and the Patriarch Jacob:

> **Then the King gave his blessing**
> **He let go the noble servant of God.** <note>original: *Er lie den edilen Gotis degin*</note>

Furthermore, a **Noble Servant** <note>original: *Edil thegana* or *Degin*</note> among men is properly a noble man, outstanding in strength and virtue, prepared for the duties of mankind both in war and at home. Within our grandfathers' memory, they were called **Noble Squires** <note>original: *Edelknecht*</note>; but this is an unequal, not to say degenerate, name. For the former made no distinction between the poor and the rich, being prepared to assist everyone equally. These others, however, are called [servants] of Princes, of Bishops—

# MONUMENTS OF DENMARK

<page-num>266</page-num>

...[they called]. Those whom the Danes in ancient times called **Thane** <note>original: *Dhegn*</note>, the Germans called **Thegan** and **Degin**. Melchior Goldastus <note>A 17th-century Swiss scholar known for collecting ancient Germanic texts.</note> in his *Observations on the Advice of Tyrol, King of the Scots*, page 364, notes that they called tall and robust men *Rifios* (to us, **Giants** <note>original: *Rifer* / *Kemper*</note>, such as **Long-leg Giant**, **Bermer Giant**, etc.). These were men who, relying on their strength and power, inhabited forests and mountains for the sake of robbery; against them, the **Heroes** <note>original: *Rekii*</note> were summoned and came to the aid of the afflicted. Because they were at the service of those who called them, they were called **Thanes** <note>original: *Degen*</note>, which means "servants." For that is the proper meaning of *Thegan*. Otfrid of Weissenburg <note>A 9th-century monk and poet who wrote a rhymed version of the Gospels in Old High German.</note> says in his Preface to King Louis:

->Truly to be His thane<-
->In many a number<-
->Many a sorrow he endured<-
->For that which God commanded<-
->He overcame it thereafter swiftly<-
->As was fitting for God's thane<-
->We possess that goodness<-
->As if a thane were riding.<-

And in Book I, Chapter III of the Gospels:

->The third family from there<-
->That was of noble thanes.<-

That ancient Paraphraser of the Old Testament <note>An anonymous author of an early Germanic biblical translation.</note> says:

->Enoch, who was God’s thane.<-

The same author says of Pharaoh and the Patriarch Jacob:

->The King then gave his blessing<-
->He let go the noble thane of God.<-

Furthermore, a "noble thane" <note>original: *Edil thegana*</note> or **Thane** <note>original: *Degin*</note> among men properly signified a nobleman, outstanding in bravery and virtue, prepared by his duty to mankind for service both in war and at home. In the memory of our ancestors, these were called **Noble-servants** <note>original: *Edelknecht*; at the time, this term denoted a young man of noble birth serving a knight before being knighted himself.</note>; but this was a disparate, if not to say degenerate, designation. For the former made no distinction between the poor and the rich, being ready to assist all equally. But these latter-day men were called those of Princes, Bi... <note>The text cuts off here, continuing as "bishops" on the next page.</note>

...Indeed, <note>original: "enim"</note> piracy was once considered honorable and lawful; in this pursuit, Kings themselves or their children frequently exercised their skills, having joined with them the most famous and strongest warriors. <note>original: "Athletis," here meaning champions or professional fighters.</note> Concerning this, Crantzius writes in *Vandalia*, Book 1, Chapter 7:
> Piracy was held in no less honor than theft once was among the Spartans. Among these pagan barbarians, to whom no laws had been handed down and no warnings of justice were known, it was believed that whatever was sought by force and arms was justly possessed. This opinion has not yet been abolished by many among Christians, especially those following the life of armed military service, whose reasoning is this: that just as among the beasts in the fields and forests, among the fish in the waters, and among the birds in the air, the weaker are always prey for the fiercer, so it must be conducted among men.

History of Norway <note>Likely referring to the *Heimskringla* or a similar chronicle.</note> relates that Saint Olaf devoted himself to this study even at the age of twelve, and for this reason, he was distinguished by the Royal title, even though he then had no Kingdom to rule. For it is reported that it was once the custom to grant the Royal title to the sons of Kings as soon as they began to practice piracy.

But this form of piracy was governed by certain laws. For those who prided themselves on the title of **Vikings** <note>original: "Vikingorum"</note> did not overwhelm just any defenseless people or those seeking a living through simple navigation. Rather, they targeted only enemies, or those they knew to be celebrated and outstanding in this same art, and who had acquired a great force of wealth through maritime warfare. Some believe they were called such from *Vijg*, which in the Danish tongue signifies a bay or cove of the sea; for in these places they would hide, safe from the damage of storms, or lay in wait to set ambushes for enemies. Others think the name is derived from the fact that in ancient times they used this same word to denote homicides and slaughters. For those whom they conquered, they soon deprived of life. Or perhaps the name comes from Vikar, a King of Norway and also a distinguished pirate, whom Starkad <note>Starkad (Starchaterus) is a legendary hero in Norse mythology, often portrayed as an old, powerful warrior.</note> strangled and put to death with a strange ingenuity? Regarding this, our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian.</note> writes in his sixth book in this manner:
> Then Starkad, having made a snare out of willow branches, entangled King Vikar, pretending he would only suffer a show of punishment for a brief moment. But the tightness of the knot, carrying out its own law, snatched away the final breath of the hanging man. From him, while still quivering, Starkad tore out the remnants of life with his sword. At the moment he should have brought a remedy, he revealed his treachery.

It remains now for us to say something about the accompanying hieroglyphics <note>In this context, "hieroglyphics" refers to any symbolic or pictorial carvings rather than Egyptian script.</note>. The image of a small boat, as well as the icon of an arrow, confirms what we said about the Vikings: namely, that Fricco, being outstanding in maritime warfare, defeated so many Vikings. Nor does the added drawing of a human head seem to indicate anything other than that the defeated were subjected to capital punishment <note>Beheading or execution.</note>. Since the remaining ornaments consist of cruder outlines, they are not properly distinguished, nor do they allow for an easy explanation.

# DANISH
# MONUMENTS
## BOOK FIVE.
### *CONTAINING CIMBRIA.*

Cimbria <note>The Cimbrian Peninsula, roughly corresponding to modern Jutland in Denmark and Schleswig-Holstein in Germany.</note> calls to us, our sweetest homeland, greatly ennobled by the writings of historians and geographers, inasmuch as it once brought forth those most brave Cimbri <note>An ancient Germanic or Celtic people who, along with the Teutons, famously invaded the Roman Republic in the late 2nd century BCE.</note> who were formidable to the entire Roman Empire and everywhere famous for so many distinguished victories. Our own Lyscander <note>Claus Christoffersen Lyschander (1558–1624), a Danish royal historian.</note> described it for us in this way:

> The ancients called Denmark on this side of the sea the Cimbrian
> Peninsula <note>original: *Chersonesum*</note>, on account of the Kingdom
> of the Cimmerians or Cimbri, which it distinguishes by its great
> size. We call it either Cimbria, Guttia, or Jutland <note>original: *Jutthiam*</note>.
> It is two-fold: Southern and Northern. The former [Southern],
> extending from the Saxons to the cities of Ribe <note>original: *Ripensem*</note>
> and Kolding <note>original: *Coldingensem*</note>, is bordered further
> up by a vast river, from which the Dukes of the Jutes are called
> Syndriaensian. Today this area encompasses noble and brave peoples
> and the excellent towns of the Jutes. The first is the Duchy
> administered from Schleswig <note>original: *Slesvico*</note> toward
> the Baltic Sea <note>original: *mare Godanicum*, referring to the Codanus Sinus</note>.
> The second is that of the Holsteiners <note>original: *Holsatorum*</note>,
> with whom the Minor Frisians dwell; from there four types of
> Marsh-dwellers <note>original: *Marsorum*</note> emerge: the
> Dithmarschen <note>Teutomarsi</note>, the Stormarn <note>Storemarsi</note>,
> the Wilstermarsch <note>Villemarsi</note>, and the Krempermarsch
> <note>Crempemarsi</note>, for there the borders of Cimbria end
> to the South. The other [Northern part] is more northerly, more
> extensive, and divided into several regions; it rears very great
> and brave peoples. Fifteen most famous local districts <note>original: *Toparchiæ*</note>
> of the Northern Cimbri are numbered there, nine of which are
> more noble than the others, just as many...

The furthest region of all Northern Cimbria is **Wensyssel** <note>Now Vendsyssel, the northernmost district of Jutland.</note>, which some have called *Vinnilia*, and others *Venulia*. But custom has introduced the name *Vandalia*, according to Latin softness <note>Early modern scholars often attempted to link the place name "Vendsyssel" with the "Vandals," the Germanic people who sacked Rome in 455 CE.</note>. We have been informed in our own age by a Vandal man that twenty thousand light-armed warriors could easily be raised from its village bailiffs; from ancient times, their courage and authority were so great that they alone among all the peoples of the Danes in Cimbria are said to be fitly compared to the Goths in Scandinavia in spirit and military science. They also have their own cities, but they are not so well-known. However, **Skagen** <note>original: *Schavenia*; a prominent fishing and trading town at the very tip of the peninsula.</note> has become much more famous because of the great abundance of merchants who pass through here from one ocean to the other. Next are numbered the **Toparchies of Thy** <note>original: *Tythonicæ Toparchiæ*; a district in northwestern Jutland.</note>, first five; then two of the **people of Mors** <note>original: *Morsingorum*; the largest island in the Limfjord.</note> in the inner curve of the Limfjord, formerly under the Bishopric of Børglum <note>original: *Burglanensi*.</note> and now of Aalborg <note>original: *Aalburgensi*.</note>. From this land, many derive the Vandals, whom authors testify once crossed from the Scandinavian islands to the German shore on account of an inundation of the Ocean. But there is another opinion of others, who recount a more remote origin. This city is, as it were, the parent of Cimbria, and the fame has reached us that before the Danish era, and then for more or less six hundred years, it was called Cimmersberga <note>Cimmerian Mountain</note>, until the hero Vigletius <note>A legendary King of the Danes mentioned by Saxo Grammaticus</note>, monarch of the Cimmerians, Getae, and Dacians, restored it after it had been overturned and oppressed following the internal discords of the Cimmerian kings. He enriched it and named it Viborg after himself, which Tacitus <note>The Roman historian (c. 56–120 AD)</note> undoubtedly mentions. From this city, the Cimbri ruled most widely; their great valor in the ancient ages of the world is clear from the Cimmerian deeds, which are celebrated throughout the whole world in the monuments of all nations.

<margin>This is it</margin> Next to this is Obersyssel <note>A historic district in Northern Jutland</note>; they claim this is called Obetria in Latin, which they define as an immense region of thirteen provinces or principalities by the Baltic gulf. It is most rich in all kinds of merchandise because of the convenience of the sea that flows in from the east. In this region, on the border of the Ning and Hasle districts, is the very large city of Aarhus, an episcopal seat, which a huge river also cuts in two, dividing the said provinces. Here, Frotho VI <note>A legendary Danish king</note>, the most powerful King of the Danes, English, Normans, and Vandals, first built a magnificent temple to the Holy Trinity. There are also other notable cities: Horsens, Randers, Mariager, and Hobro, all of which are likewise maritime.

<margin>Note</margin> The fourth is Hersissel; the Cimbri call it Harsyssel in their own dialect, and the name corresponds to Herlia, which is Herulia <note>Referring to the Heruli, an East Germanic tribe</note>. There are eight noble principalities of this place, and it can rightly be compared to either Cimmeria or Vinilia. ...[Um]**bricians** and **Salingians**, we find that traces of all these have been left in *Cimbria* <note>The Jutland peninsula</note>, about which others may judge more fully.
From there, the plain of the **Umbri** or **Umbricians** <note>An ancient tribal group</note> extends, divided into four distinct provinces. And soon after, the land of the **Salingians** <note>A group likely associated with the Salling region of Jutland</note> across the **Salian strait** <note>The Salling Sound</note> is divided into five classes <note>Administrative or social divisions</note>.
Next follow three branches of the **Varini** <note>A Germanic people often mentioned by Roman historians</note> and the city of **Varinia**. Soon after, the land of the **Vilini** is organized into two principalities. Immediately following is the very wide region of the **Lori**, divided into nine prefectures. Equal to this is **Istelia**, believed to be so in both cities and people.
Then comes the excellent nation of **Elmeonia**, smaller than the previous three provinces. These are followed by the **Cimbrian Guttones** <note>Likely referring to the Goths of the peninsula</note> in a very abundant tract toward the south. These, therefore, are the **Cimbrian toparchies** <note><term>Toparchy: A small state or administrative district governed by a local ruler</term></note> and lands, fifteen in number, which include exactly one hundred other smaller ones. It will become clear in the accounts of expeditions that all northern peoples—and especially those who inhabit the **Chersonese** <note>The Cimbrian Peninsula, or Jutland</note> to which a land route lies open—incited by both the narrowness of their lands and the fortune of the **Teutons**, occupied the neighboring coastal regions from the **Elbe** <note>original: "Albis"</note> to the **Vistula** <note>original: "Vistula"</note> through war; where, toward the further regions of the **Tuisconites** <note>People named after the legendary Germanic ancestor Tuisco</note>, we find almost all the peoples whom we have already enumerated in *Cimbria*.

*This Northern Tract* is divided, as has been said, into four bishoprics: **Aarhus**, **Viborg**, the **Vandalic** (formerly **Børglum**), and **Ribe**. Taking these into account, the monuments marked with our ancient letters <note>A reference to runic inscriptions, the primary subject of Worm's book</note> which we have received from here, we will divide into as many classes, giving the first place to those of **Aarhus**. # AARHUS.

Aarhus is a famous and beautiful maritime city. Because of the convenience of its location, the fertility of its fields, its abundance of forests, and the suitability of its port, an Episcopal see was first established there around the year 1014 AD. This see governs thirty-one provinces or <term>Nomarchies</term> <note>Administrative districts or prefectures</note>, seven cities, 304 rural parishes, and five fortresses. In the city itself, there are many things worthy of seeing—the cenotaphs <note>monuments to people buried elsewhere</note> of Bishops, Prelates, and Nobles; a magnificent temple dedicated to Saint Clement <note>The patron saint of sailors, appropriate for this coastal city</note>; and the ruins of the Episcopal court. However, because I found no monument there inscribed with ancient letters, I am forced to pass over many things worthy of praise in silence, lest I seem to wander "outside the olive trees" <note>A Latin idiom meaning to stray from the main subject</note>, and instead turn my attention to the neighboring areas. 

I should first mention that I found in certain papers that a sepulchral stone once stood in the cemetery of the church dedicated to the Blessed Virgin in Aarhus, adorned with our Runic marks. The interpretations of these marks vary. Some read them as follows:

ᚦᚢᚱᛋᛏᚢᚿ. ᛁᛂᚱᛁᚴᛋ. ᚼᛂᚦᛂ. ᛁᛂᚵ.
*I was called Dursta Ieries.* <note>original: "Dursta Ieries hede jeg"</note>
->I WAS CALLED DURSTAN SON OF ERIC.<-

The name ᚦᚢᚱᛋᛏᚢᚿ [Thurstun] would denote either Durstan, or if a woman, Dorothea.
ᛁᛂᚱᛁᚴᛋ [Ieriks] means "of Eric," whether referring to a son or a wife; for it is well known in the Cimbrian <note>The local Danish/Jutlandic dialect</note> idiom that *Ierick* is used in place of *Erick*.

Others report that they read the following on the same stone:

ᚦᚢᚱ. ᛋᛏᚿ. ᚱᛂᛁᛋᛁ. ᛋᛏᛁᚿ. ᚦᛂᚿ. ᛋᛁᚿᚢ. Or perhaps in this way:
ᚦᚢᚱᛋᛏᚢ. ᚱᛂᛁᛋᛁ. ᛋᛏᚢᚿ. ᛋᛁᛁᚿᛋ.
*Durstu raised his stone.* <note>original: "Durstu reisdi stun seins"</note>
->DURSTAN CARVED THE STONE DEDICATED TO HIS KIN.<-

Although I was both born and educated in that city where these things are said to exist, and spent a great part of my youth there...

...you might say. Or, as explained above, **Thoralt** is as if one were "entirely devoted to the god Thor." <note>original Latin: "Thoroni addictus"</note>

ᛅᚢᚴᚢᚦ (**Auguth**) I judge this to be the proper name of a man or woman, although it comes very close to the modern word *Augud*, which signifies an idol; perhaps he was the brother of Thorald.

ᛁᛅᚠᛁᚾ (**Iafin**) is an ancient man's name, which also occurs quite often in monuments. Note here the contraction of two letters, ᛁ [i] and ᚠ [f], into one—a practice not infrequent in other inscriptions—and also used in the word ᚾᚬᚱᛏ [nort] of this inscription, where ᚾ [n] and ᚱ [r] coalesce into one. <note>These are known as "bind-runes," a common scribal shorthand in epigraphy where two characters share a single vertical stroke.</note>

ᚾᚬᚱᛏ (**Nort**) I judge this denotes "Our," to indicate that Ingeld was the father of Thorald and Augut, for whom those parts contained within the outer line of the carving seem finally to have been placed.

ᛋᚢᚾᛁ (**Suni**) I judge to mean "good," for children often commend a parent for their goodness. The outer series of the inscription seems to have been added after the first.

They say this stone was moved from a cemetery; whether that is so, I cannot say for certain. Perhaps evidence is provided by another stone still visible in the same place, which we shall now discuss.

<meta>This page continues the linguistic analysis of the second Hobro monument.
