BOOK FIVE. 283

The character <term>ᛉ</term> <note>the Yr rune</note> is rarely found in our monuments with that specific power. While it is commonly used as a final *R*, here—as in the word <term>ᛏᚱᛉ</term> <note>original: "TRY"</note>—it is placed in the middle of a word and signifies *Y* instead. The Icelanders call it <term>Y R</term>, and it is thought to be one of the oldest runes, as I have discussed more extensively in Chapter XII of my work, *Runic Literature* <note>original Latin: "Literatura Runica"</note>.

A "companion" <note>original Latin: "Comes," which evolved into the title "Count"</note> is defined as one who not only stays indivisibly by someone's side as a comrade, but also acknowledges the other as a superior to whom he is bound in service. Thus, our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the famous 12th-century Danish historian</note> calls himself the "least of the companions" of Bishop Absalon in the Preface to his *History*, and in Book 6, the legendary hero Starkad <note>original: "Starchaterus"</note> calls himself a companion of King Frotho: *“When I was recorded as a companion of Frotho.”* Here, however, it seems to denote a "friend," in the sense that certain people were once called "Companions and Friends of the Emperors" <note>original: "Amici Auguſtorum," referring to the Roman Emperors</note> among the Romans—namely, those who were on the councils and followed the emperors on military expeditions. Spartianus <note>a Roman historian</note> writes of this in the *Life of Hadrian*: *“When he sat in judgment, he had on his council not only his own friends or companions, but also legal experts.”* An ancient stone in Milan records:

->GAIUS SENTIUS<-
->SEVERUS<-
->QUADRATO,<-
->OF SENATORIAL RANK, CONSUL,<-
->FRIEND AND<-
->COMPANION OF OUR AUGUSTUS.<-
<note>Original Latin: "C. SENTIO SEVERO QUADRATO C. V. COS. AMICO ET COM. AUG. N."</note>

Regarding these matters, see the extensive discussion by our countryman Stephen <note>Stephen Hansen Stephanius, a 17th-century Danish scholar known for his commentary on Saxo</note> in his notes on Saxo's Preface. In other contexts, all those who belonged to a Prince's retinue were called "companions" <note>original: "comites"</note>. The retinue <note>original: "comitatus"</note> was the court and the household. From Cicero’s fourth speech *Against Verres*, it seems possible to gather that during the height of the Roman Republic, those who accompanied Proconsuls and Governors going into the provinces for public business—such as prefects, scribes, heralds, physicians, and others—were called "companions."

As for what I truly believe is signified by those characters, you will see in the explanation of the eighth monument from Scania <note>Scania, or Skåne, was then a part of the Kingdom of Denmark</note>.
ᛏᚱᚢᚵ <term>Tryg</term> denotes faith <note>or "trustworthiness," from the Old Norse *tryggr*</note>. From this word, which is elsewhere written with a dotted ᚦ <note>the thorn rune; a "dotted" version often represented a 'd' sound</note>, the power of the ᛏ rune <note>the T-rune, named Tyr</note> is sufficiently clear; for if it were to be expressed by an *R*, three consonants would meet without a vowel, producing no sound; and the same letter would be repeated twice in different forms, which is hardly consistent with logic.

# BOOK FIVE.

Thorir raised this stone for Kunugar, his father. <note>original runes: ᚦᚮᚱᛁᚱ : ᚱᛁᛋᛁ : ᛋᛏᛁᚾ : ᚴᚢᚾᚢᚴᛆᚱ : ᚠᛆᚦᚢᚱ : ᛋᛁᚿ</note>
*Thorir raised the stone for Kunugar, his father.* <note>original Latin-script transcription: "Thorir risdi stin Kunugar fadur sind"</note>
->THORIR PLACED THIS STONE FOR HIS FATHER KUNUGAR.<-

On the same side of the church, a hill can still be seen called **King’s Mound** <note>original: *Kuinar Höj*</note>, from which the local inhabitants claim this stone rolled down. Nearby is the source of a spring, which was once called the **Spring of Thorir**. For they say that in that place a certain Lord named Thorir sacrificed his own son to Idols, and soon after this spring emerged, which retained its name from Thorir until a sounder teaching about the true God began to shine forth. For then, in order to utterly abolish this idolatrous madness, they dedicated the spring to the **three Marys** (so to speak) <note>referring to the Three Marys of the Gospels; a common medieval practice to Christianize pagan sites</note>, and it was believed to have acquired the power to drive away various diseases; that superstition still holds strong roots today. Thus, the earlier account agrees with our inscription, the first word of which, ᚦᚮᚱᛁᚱ, names this Thorir. For the letter ᚦ <note>the thorn rune</note> is to be read as a dotted letter <note>indicating a phonetic shift, likely to a 'D' sound</note>. But I find nothing more about him in our historical records.

**Kunugar** <note>original: ᚴᚿᚴᛆᚱ</note> usually denotes "King" as a title; here it seems to be the proper name of Thorir’s father. It certainly has a great affinity with the word *Kuinar*, from which the hill drew its name. A double combination of letters occurs here which should be carefully noted: for ᚢ is joined with ᚤ, as also with ᚬᚱ, in a not uncommon style of writing.

...bt; <note>original: "dubio"</note> he placed this stone) PRAY TO MARY FOR HIS SOUL THAT SHE MAY HAVE MERCY. NICOLAUS KASONIUS.

Local inhabitants report that these stones were moved from the Giesingholm cemetery to this location, a claim which the inscription in no way contradicts. For the inscription is Christian and does not reflect the style of those usually found on the slopes and hills of open fields <note>the author is contrasting this church monument with ancient, pre-Christian Viking runestones found in the landscape</note>. Nor does it seem to be of particularly great antiquity, as the carved image represents the **habit** <term>habit: the traditional clothing or vestments of a religious order or office</term> of a Bishop, as well as the Lamb of God carrying a cross. I believe this image represents Saint Nicholas, as an allusion to the name written there. Indeed, it is not possible to gather from our histories that any Bishop was buried in that spot. This is further confirmed by the mixture of Roman letters with Runes in the words ᚱᚢᛌ <note>original: "Rus"</note> and ᛘᚢᚾᚢᚱ <note>original: "monur"</note>.

I believe ᚱᚢᛌ <note>Rus</note> denotes a Russian or someone from Russia. It is well known how highly Saint Nicholas is esteemed there; they recognize him as their supreme Patron and diligently offer him divine honors. This person, therefore, was a Russian by nationality, unless the Latin "S" should be read as a "B". Regarding ᚦᚢᚦᚢᛌ <note>Thudus</note>, although it might seem it could be explained by the word "after," in this context it more suitably means "above" <note>original Latin: "supra"</note>, to correspond with ᛘᛅᚦᚴᛅᚱ <note>madkar</note>, or the burial place, which we still call a **Legersted** <term>Legersted: an archaic Danish/Germanic term for a final resting place or grave site</term>.

ᚢᚦᛚ <note>Uthl</note> refers to Uffo or Yffo, for the ᚦ <note>the "thorn" rune</note> in this place stands for "Y," as it also does in the following word ᚦᚢᚱᛁᛚ <note>dyril</note>: meaning dear, precious, excellent, or distinguished.

ᚾᛁᛚ <note>Nil</note> provides abundant evidence that something is missing here and that the entire sequence of letters that occupied the lower part of the stone has been lost; perhaps "nildiss"?

ᛒᛁᚦᛁᚦ <note>Bithith, meaning "pray"</note>: this vow or prayer partly indicates the age of the stone.

ᚴᛅᛅᛌᚢᚾᛅᚱ <note>Kaasunor</note>. Whether this Nicholas may be related to our Kaas family <note>a prominent Danish noble family</note>, let others judge. If there are documents concerning this matter in that family, they would be worthy of a place here. As for the stories some tell of Lave **Brock** being buried here, they are mere fables...

### STENALT.

ᚦᚢᚱᚴᛁᛚ **Thorkil**: The name Turchillus <note>A Latinized version of Thorkil</note> is still familiar to us today; it is composed of ᚦᚢᚱ (**Thor**), whom we call Thor. ᚱᛅᚦ ᛋᛒᛅᚴᛅ <term>Ret spaka: literally "the law-wise" or "truly wise"</term>. This epithet seems to have been earned through praise for the man's wisdom and prudence. This one, however, because it was acquired through singular gifts of the mind, was deemed worthy of being passed down to posterity.

ᛋᚢᚾᛁᚱ <term>Sunir: the plural form of "son"</term>. This word indicates that several brothers contributed their funds toward the construction of this monument.

### THE SECOND
## TORDUP STONE.

In the same province, there exists a very beautiful monument which can now be seen in the Tordrup church. In its entryway, one immediately encounters a rough pillar <term>cippus: a low, square pillar used as a monument or landmark</term> which displays three rows of characters on its smoother side. Two of these start from the bottom left side, run across the top of the stone, and terminate on the right. The third row, placed between the others, does not reach the top of the rock. Its height is two and a half ells <note>An "ell" was a historical unit of length, roughly the length of a man's arm</note>, and its width is one ell.

What has been handed down to posterity by tradition regarding this monument, and what the local surroundings reveal to us, must be weighed before we render the reasons for our interpretation.

This stone is said to have been moved from a certain hill looking eastward toward the church, which a small river also flows past, encircling a certain island called *Fersborg*. This name is taken from a strong castle of the same name that once stood there, whose ruins and remains of ramparts can still be seen to this day. They say that the sea itself once reached this castle with such a deep channel that it even admitted merchant ships; this is confirmed by the remains of anchors and other nautical equipment which are dug up there daily. They say that a certain petty king <term>Regulum: a local ruler or sub-king</term> lived in this castle, who, being buried in that hill, obtained the memory of this epitaph. They add that a certain English prince of great renown—yet a pirate accustomed to plunder—was driven here by a storm, and [deprived] of all his goods and life itself by the [people] of the territory...

**Christ’s man** <note>original runes: ᚴᚱᛁᛋᛏᛁ ᛘᛅᚾᚾ</note>; these two words together signify a Christian, a very common expression for us; just as we say *a Christian man* or *a Christian person* <note>original Danish: "en Christen Man/ et Christen Meniske"</note>. From this, one might perhaps gather that there was a dispute over this temple between pagans <term>Idololatras: literally "idol-worshippers," referring here to the pre-Christian Scandinavians</term> and Christians during the first planting of the young Church; but once the case was heard, it was awarded to the Christians. If the inscription on the other column were available to us, perhaps more things regarding this matter would be brought to light.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of Danish runic monuments, moving from the Vregersløde monument to two others found within church architecture: one in Svogerslev (Børglum Herred) and another in Gellerslev (Thy). <page-num>297</page-num>

In the district <term>Nomarchia: an administrative subdivision or "herred"</term> called Børglum <note>original: Borglumherrit</note>, in the village of Svogerslev <note>original: Swegersløff</note>, the church has a square column in its very center supporting the church’s arch. The base of this column consists of a large, somewhat rough stone; although it has been trimmed so that it might be more conveniently adapted to the work, it has nonetheless preserved these letter-forms intact, though they are very much worn down.

<image-desc>A single line of Runic characters inscribed in a horizontal arrangement.</image-desc>

->*...this stone in memory of his father, Loja*<-
->THE STONE IN MEMORY OF HIS FATHER, LOJA.<-

It is clearly evident that this was moved from elsewhere for these purposes during the first founding of the church, but no one remembers its original location. It is also obvious that both the beginning and the end of the inscription are missing. The remaining parts seem to follow from the word **raised** <note>original runes: ᚱᛆᛁᛋᛐᛁ</note>, meaning he "erected" or "placed" the stone.

The word **his** <note>original runes: ᛋᛁᚿᛁᚱ</note> has a peculiar form of the letter S, which I have not found to be as frequent in Danish inscriptions as in Norwegian ones. Since there is a very short crossing from Vendsyssel <note>original: Vinnilia</note> to Norway, one might suspect either that this stone was transported from there, or that the inscription itself was composed by a Norwegian.

This stone, besides being more polished than other common stones, features crosses, a shield decorated with two roses, and also ancient Roman characters; on the border, it contains two words carved in our Runic script. ## SIXTH
### THE LOVE-WAND <note>original: Virgula Erotica. This refers to a "love-stick" or a small wooden rod inscribed with runes, often used for messages or charms.</note>

<margin>
<image-desc>A vertical rectangular diagram representing a small rod or "writing stick." To the left of the main rectangle is a narrow strip containing Runic characters. The main rectangle is divided into sections: at the top is a small cross (+); below it is the text '95OR' and 'CHID'; in the middle is a heraldic shield containing three roses or five-petaled flowers; below the shield is the text '9E RG' and 'RETO'; at the bottom are two hearts joined over a small cross, with the word 'DEI' (God) beneath them.</image-desc>
</margin>

I remember once reading in the works of Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a famous 12th-century Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> that our ancestors, lacking the use of parchment and paper in former times, chose pieces of wood in their place. Upon these, they would briefly record the thoughts of their minds in their native characters <note>The native characters are Runes.</note> whenever they deemed it necessary to write something to their friends. There is a passage in his fourth book where he describes the letters which the messengers of Fengo <note>In legendary Danish history, Fengo is the murderous uncle of Amleth (the inspiration for Shakespeare's Hamlet).</note> carried to the King of Britain in this manner: *Two of Fengo’s attendants set out with him, carrying letters carved into wood (for that was once a famous kind of writing material), by which the King of the Britons was commanded to kill the youth sent to him.* Whether I should include in this category a certain small rod, marked with elegant Runic characters, I do not know; it was sent to me by the Reverend and most distinguished Master Christian Jensen <note>original: Christiani Johannis</note>, of blessed memory, formerly the most deserving Bishop of Aalborg. I present its inscription here, so that anyone may decide about it what seems consistent with reason.

The rod <note>original: bacillus</note> is square, three inches in length, and a third of an inch in width, having four sides marked with characters. It appears to be fashioned from wild plum wood <note>original: pruno sylvestri; likely blackthorn or sloe wood, known for its hardness.</note>, and is exactly of this length and shape.

## SIXTH: THE LOVE-WAND.
<note>original Latin: "Virgula Erotica"</note>

I remember once reading in the works of Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum.</note> that our ancestors, being formerly without the use of parchment and paper, chose wood in its place. Upon these wooden pieces, they would laconically <note>concisely, in the style of the ancient Spartans</note> commit the feelings of their minds in their native characters whenever they decided something should be written to friends. There is a passage in his fourth book where he describes the letters which the messengers of Fengon <note>A legendary Danish ruler and uncle of Amleth (the inspiration for Hamlet).</note> carried to the King of Britain in this manner:

> *Two of Fengon's attendants set out with him, carrying with them letters carved into wood (for that was once a famous kind of writing material), by which the King of the Britons was commanded to put to death the young man sent to him.* 

Whether I can count in this category a small staff <note>Latin: *bacillus*</note>, marked with elegant Runic characters, sent to me by the Reverend and most distinguished Master Christian Jensen <note>Christian Jensen (1596–1635), a Danish priest and scholar.</note>, of pious memory, formerly the most deserving Bishop of Aalborg, I do not know. I present its inscription here, so that anyone may decide about it as seems consistent with reason.

The staff is square, three inches in length and a third of an inch in width, having four sides marked with characters. It appears to be fashioned from wild plum wood <note>likely blackthorn or sloe wood</note>, in exactly this length and shape.

### SIXTH SECTION
### THE LOVE-WAND <note>original: *Virgula Erotica*</note>.

I remember once reading in Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), a Danish historian famous for the *Gesta Danorum*</note> that our ancestors, formerly lacking the use of parchment and paper, chose wood in its place. Upon this wood, they would concisely commit the feelings of their minds in their ancestral characters <note>Runes</note> whenever they decided something should be written to friends. There is a passage in the fourth book where he describes the letters which the messengers of Fengo <note>Fengo is the uncle of Amleth/Hamlet in Saxo's history</note> carried to the King of Britain in this manner:

> *Two of Fengo's attendants set out with him, carrying letters carved in wood (for that was once a famous kind of writing material) which commanded the King of the Britons to kill the youth sent to him.*

Whether I am able to include this little staff <note>Latin: *bacillum*</note> in this category—marked as it is with elegant Runic characters and sent to me by the Reverend and most distinguished Master Christianus Johannis <note>Christian Hansen</note>, of pious memory, formerly the most deserving Bishop of Aalborg—I do not know. I show its inscription here, so that anyone may decide about it what seems consistent with reason.

The staff is square, three inches in length and a third of an inch in width, having four sides marked with characters. It appears to be fashioned from sloe wood <note>The wood of the blackthorn tree, known for its hardness</note>, in exactly this length and shape.

...the other [letter] A, is hidden from me. It is therefore clearly evident that more mystical meanings lie beneath this than the letters known to us indicate. Furthermore, so as not to hide anything that has come into my hands, the most distinguished Mr. Christian Jensen <note>Christianus Johannis</note> sent me the following: "This truly unique monument, once given to me by my noble patron Otto Skeel, was found in the fields of Viborg several years ago by a certain student, as the most accomplished Mr. Villads, Reader of Viborg and Rector of the school there at the time, related to me. ->*Mentioning various handwritings on useless wood.*<-

Grettir brought the remains, which contained human bones, into the temple, and attached to these was a runic staff on which songs were inscribed.

<header>BOOK FIVE.</header>

Local inhabitants report that this stone was moved from a nearby hill called Runehøy <note>literally "Rune Hill"</note> to the place where it is seen now. This report is confirmed by an experiment conducted by the local pastor. A few years ago, while walking around this burial mound, he happened upon a gap. When he lowered his staff into it, he perceived there were certain pots underneath. Upon digging them out, he found them filled with ashes and the remains of burnt bones. This clearly proves that this man Rada <note>original: *Radanonem*—the subject of the previous stone</note> was entombed in that age when they did not bury bodies but cremated them; thus, this monument should be numbered among those that are truly ancient for this reason alone.

I have nothing further to add to the context, as the lines of the letters are clear and the words are also plain enough, except for that final formula <note>referring to the "faithful shepherd/thegn" phrasing</note> which is repeated in very many instances, and about which there is nothing we can add to what we have said above. I note at least this: that inscriptions marked with this form of words possess great antiquity, a fact which the ashes enclosed in urns also suggest.

->THE THIRD<-
->TORUP MONUMENT.<-

In the pavement of Torup Church, near the altar, a fragment of a long stone with its inscribed face turned upward is seen. It is two and a half ells <note>original: *ulnarum*—an ell was a historical unit of length, roughly 2 feet, making the stone about 5 feet long</note> in length and three-quarters in width, covered on all sides with large characters; except in a certain spot where the feet of those treading upon it <note>Torup Church was a functioning space; runestones were often reused as floor slabs, leading to wear from churchgoers</note> seem to have created a gap, as this true drawing of it will show you.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of a prophetic stone in a valley. <header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>
<meta>catchword: Cor-</meta>

->The Nobleman will sell his wares:<-
->The Clergy will plow in tears,<-
->The farmer will be held in contempt.<-

If there is any truth to this story, it is certain that another stone, entirely different from this one, must have existed in that same place, upon which such things were carved. For our stone displays a clearly pagan <note>original: "ethnicam"</note> inscription, while the other would be Christian, insofar as it prophesies the fate of churches and pastors. This one shows Runic letters in a crude carving; that one supposedly had letters of bronze, and indeed in a sequence too long to be captured in just a few marks.

But they say that in Jämtland <note>original: "Jemptia," a province now in Sweden, but then associated with Norway</note>, there is a valley of the same name about which the inhabitants tell exactly the same story. And because Joannes Messenius <note>A famous Swedish historian (1579–1636)</note> recorded this eloquently in his *Specula Sveciæ*, chapter 19, and confirms the matter with several details, I am pleased to include the sequence of his account here. *In this province,* he says, *namely Jämtland, at the foot of the mountains that separate it from Norway, a massive rock carved with Gothic letters <note>Worm uses "Gothic" here to mean Runic</note> is viewed today with no small wonder in a certain very green valley. It was erected during the reign of Erik Stenkilsson <note>original: "Erici Stenchilli," King of Sweden c. 1066–1067</note>, the most glorious King of the Swedes, by Saint Stephen—the most faithful companion of the elder Saint Adalvard in sowing the seeds of the Divine Word through Sweden and Gothia—after he had instructed the natives in the mysteries of eternal salvation. It contains a remarkable prophecy of certain events, which I have translated into these Latin verses from the inscription on the stone mass itself:*

> <margin>cc</margin> When the Swede adopts foreign customs from every side,
> <margin>cc</margin> And the high-born overturn temples and cloisters,
> <margin>cc</margin> Still the stone stands firm in this green valley.
> <margin>cc</margin> When the lot of the wicked is more flourishing in the world,
> <margin>cc</margin> But a dire cross <note>referring to suffering or persecution</note> and death are inflicted on honest souls,
> <margin>cc</margin> Still the stone stands firm in this green valley.
> <margin>cc</margin> But when the Priest thrives just like a Farmer,
> <margin>cc</margin> And one may rightly marvel at the tiller of the field,
> <margin>cc</margin> Then the stone rests strewn upon the ground in this green valley.

<summary>Ole Worm argues that the prophetic stone described in legends must be different from the pagan runestone he is documenting, and he compares the Danish folklore to a similar "prophetic stone" in Jämtland described by Johannes Messenius.</summary>

Furthermore, that stone fell down not many years ago. It is said that Master Laurentius Petri of Närke <note>original: "Laurentium Petri Nericium," 1499–1573, the first Lutheran Archbishop of Uppsala and a key figure in the Swedish Reformation</note>, the Archbishop of Uppsala, set out shortly after to see and describe it. After his death, when Master Jesper Marci, the pastor of Vadstena <note>original: "Vastenensis"</note>, found a copy of this description in the Archbishop’s library, he published a song in the Swedish language <note>original: "Svetico idiomate"</note> earnestly urging the inhabitants of this kingdom to reform their lives. This song is sung everywhere today by the Swedes and Goths <note>A historical reference to the inhabitants of the Swedish regions of Svealand and Götaland</note> with no small amount of admiration. This is his account.

Since reading these things, I have left nothing untried to discover something certain. I have written several times to the local Bishop regarding this matter, and I have even employed the help of the magistrates, but so far I have been unable to obtain anything reliable. They say that a valley of that name exists in that place, and there is a rumor of the stone; but as of yet, no one has been found who can point out its remains. If I learn anything further, it will find its place elsewhere.

* **Hvager** <note>original runes: ᚼᚢᛅᚴᛦ</note> This name is entirely obsolete in this century. It appears from this single stone that he paid the due funeral rites to both his father and his brother, but it is to be lamented that the father's name has completely perished along with a small piece broken off from the top of this stone.

**Sten** <note>stone; original runes: ᛋᛏᛁᚾ</note> In no other monument have I found such a spelling for this word, and if it were not repeated with the same letters shortly after, I would assert that the **T** <note>rune: ᛏ</note> is clearly redundant.

**Iarbuhfo** <note>original runes: ᛁᛅᚱᛒᚢᚼᚠᚢ</note>. The **F** <note>rune: ᚠ</note> here is superfluous; for it can hardly be expressed comfortably with the rest of the word, unless perhaps someone thinks it is a shorthand mark for the entire word **father** <note>original: "fathur"; runes: ᚠᛅᚦᚢᚱ</note>, so that here Iarbuhfo was not the brother of Hvager, but his paternal uncle. This name is also clearly strange and unusual.

**Smidr** <note>original: ᛋᛘᛁᚦᚱ</note> indeed denotes a blacksmith, but I believe our Tuki did not actually practice this trade, but was instead a nobleman distinguished by this surname. Unless, in former times, craftsmen were held in higher esteem than they are now; perhaps he was also a Poet or "Skald" <note>original: "Scialder"; a traditional Scandinavian court poet</note>, or a master of Runes.

**Eskis** <note>original: ᛅᚠᛏᛁᚱ</note> This name is unusual today. By no means should we overlook what those who have more diligently investigated our ancient literature hold as certain: that the letter **yr** <note>original: ᛦ; a rune often representing a final -r sound</note>, when it takes the power of **R**, only concludes words that end in that sound. However, here you will find the opposite. For in this monument, examples exist in which it both begins a word, as here in **R** <note>original: ᚱ</note>; occupies the middle, as in **raised** <note>original: ᚱᛁᛋᚦ</note>; and ends a word, as in **help** <note>original: ᚼᛁᛅᛚᛒ</note>, **Bianar** <note>original: ᛒᛁᛅᚾᛅᚱ</note>, **sons** <note>original: ᛋᚢᚾᛁᚱ</note>, and **stone** <note>original: ᛋᛏᛁᚾ</note>.

ᚼᛂR <note>original: "HER"</note> This word gives me a suspicion of modern usage. For (excepting God and things devoted to divine service) this title is not usually granted to any others than knights and Barons. Its origin does not carry such great antiquity, since I find **HIR** <note>original: ᚼᛁᚱ</note> or **MIAR** <note>original: ᛘᛁᛅᚱ</note> placed in its stead in older records. It signifies, in fact, "Lord." <term>Lord/Sir: the author suggests the title "Her" was a later medieval development for nobility, rather than an ancient Viking-age term.</term>

ᛒᛁᛅᚿᚿᛂᚱ <note>original: "BIANNER"</note> It is clear that this man was from the illustrious and ancient Banner family. Our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century Danish historian</note> does not remain silent regarding the origin of this family in the tenth book of his history. I judge that passage worthy of being inserted here, both because it is not properly understood by everyone, and so that it may provide a sharper incentive to others for serving their country well. He writes as follows: *When the Danish and English armies were joined in a most fierce battle, Tymo, a Zealander <note>original: "Sialandicus"; from the Danish island of Sjælland</note> by birth, seeing the eagle-standards of his allies greatly faltering under the enemy's attack, took up a light branch that chance had offered on a spear. Using it in place of a banner, and shouting in the manner that King Canute's soldiers were accustomed to cry out for mutual encouragement, this fortunate vanguard turned the opposing troops to flight. Thus, he acted as a life-saving standard-bearer for his people, not so much by the power of the sign as by the virtue of his spirit, and he raised the wavering fortune of the Danes toward victory before it could fall. He not only displayed the fullest courage himself, but also recalled it to the hearts of his comrades from which it had almost fled. For the glory of this deed, he later adopted the NAME, and moreover, by title of his courage, he earned the honor of being granted the rank of "primipilus" <term>primipilus: the highest-ranking centurion in a Roman legion; here used by Saxo to denote a high military honor or chief rank</term> by the King.* Nor were the Danes ashamed, having lost their most splendid standard-bearers, to follow the lead of a common man; though he was obscure in appearance, he was so illustrious in the result that their spirits were revived and they secured the prize of safety. That surname, which this Tymo earned by his courage and noble spirit, was "Banner," which his descendants among us still enjoy today. This occurred under King Canute the Great around the year of Christ 1020. Since this Eskil and Risma were among the descendants of this Tymo, it follows that this monument must be of a more recent date.

I see that this wasted labor has been detected by that most learned man Johannes Isaac Pontanus, the royal historiographer, in Book 1 of his *History of Denmark*. Gaffarus and others maintain that Snio began his reign in the year of Christ 577, and that Biorno followed him in 654. What if this Balder stood between them as the son of Snio? This is a compelling possibility, especially since our official histories do not call Biorno the son of Snio, yet our inscription expressly asserts that Snio was the father of Balder, and Tufa was his mother. Whether this Tufa was the daughter of the King of the Goths, our monument does not say.

I shall add the judgment of our most distinguished Stephanius <note>Stephan Johannes Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish historian and contemporary of the author</note> from his letters to me: "This monument would indeed confirm the opinion of Lyscander <note>Claus Christoffersen Lyschander (1558–1623), a royal genealogist</note> and others who—attempting to fill that gap or 'lacuna' in Danish history thought to exist in Book 8 of Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the famous 12th-century chronicler</note> between Kings Harald and Gorm—list a certain Balder among the kings they substitute for those supposedly omitted by Saxo. That is, unless Lyscander himself stated in clear words in his *Danish Genealogy* (page 174) that King Balder was the son of Biorno, rather than the son of King Snio. Truly, what I think of these intercalary <note>term: inserted to fill a gap in a calendar or chronology</note> and supposed kings, I shall demonstrate shortly in my notes to that passage of Saxo, if the propitious divine power grants me life and health. For I judge these kings were simply recorded twice by foreign writers; Lyscander followed them and was himself greatly deceived, leading others into error with him, as usually happens to those who prefer foreign documents over domestic and more truthful evidence." Perhaps Snio had several children, among whom was this Balder, who was never raised to the royal dignity. Whatever the case may be, the monument expressly teaches that Balder was the son of Snio.

### BOOK FIVE.

...the inscription expressly calls him in the following sections. I believe, therefore, that he who is now called Snio by the Latin writers and by us, was called *Snior* <note>original runes: ᛋᚾᛁᚬᚱ</note> by the natives and the ancients; in the same way they called Olaf *Olafuth* <note>original runes: ᚬᛚᛅᚠᚢᚦ</note> and Haquin *Haqunuth* <note>original runes: ᚼᛅᚴᚢᚾᚢᚦ</note>. You will frequently find in these monuments that proper names end in the letter ᚦ <note>the "thorn" rune, representing a 'th' sound</note>. Read the history and deeds of this man in the eighth book of Saxo. It is especially memorable that under this king's rule, the Lombards <note>A Germanic people who eventually settled in Italy; Saxo identifies their origin as Denmark</note> (called foreigners by others) were driven from Denmark by famine and migrated to seek new homes. As for the occasion on which this occurred, I prefer to relate it in the words of our own Saxo rather than my own. He writes as follows:

> *When—whether because the ground was insufficiently watered or too scorched—the crops lay listless and the fields yielded little fruit, the languor of starvation wasted the region deprived of food. Since no help remained to stave off hunger, it was provided by a public decree, on the initiative of Agon and Ebbo, that the elderly and children should be killed. Every age unfit for war was to be cast out of the kingdom, so that the homeland would be preserved only for the robust; none but those capable of bearing arms or tilling the fields were to retain their ancestral homes and the dwellings of their fathers' gods. When their mother Gambaruc heard this from her sons, she realized that the authors of this wicked decree were placing their safety in a crime. Condemning the council's decision, she denied that necessity should be redeemed by parricide. She asserted that a more honorable counsel, and one more desirable for the strength of soul and body, would be to maintain piety toward parents and children and instead choose those who were to leave the country by lot. If the lot fell to the weak elderly, the stronger should voluntarily offer themselves for exile in their place, taking up the burden for the sake of the frail. Furthermore, she said they were unworthy of life if they chose to sustain it by crime and sacrilege, persecuting parents and offspring with such an unfair judgment, performing acts of cruelty in place of charity. Finally, she argued that everyone deserves poorly of their country if their love for their own breath outweighs their love for parents or children. When this speech was reported to the assembly, most supported it with their votes. Therefore, with everyone’s fortunes cast into the lot, those who were marked out were adjudged to be exiles. Thus it happened that those who had been unwilling to obey necessity by choice were forced to obey the judgment of fortune.*

Thus far Saxo.

Of the word *Father* <note>original runes: ᚠᛅᚦᛁᚱ</note>, only the last syllable remains.

The stone stands three cubits <term>cubit: an ancient unit of length, roughly the distance from the elbow to the tip of the middle finger</term> in height and one and a half in width. ->THURALFUS PLACED THIS STONE FOR TUFA,<-
->THE ELDER SON OF TUKE. MAY GOD<-
->HAVE MERCY ON THEM.<-

It is clearly evident that this stone was moved here from elsewhere; however, no one has yet been found who can point out its original location. It possesses a certain peculiarity compared to others, which must be addressed shortly. The many names clustered together make its meaning quite obscure, so that one may suspect, not without reason, that something in it was not correctly recorded.

**Thuralfs** <note>original runes: ᚦᚢᚱᚼᚠᚢᛚᛋ</note> seems to be composed of *Thor* and *Alf*; this Thuralf appears to have placed this monument.

**Stina** <note>original runes: ᛋᛏᛁᚾᛅ</note> is a plural form <note>the author is noting that "stina" (stones) is used rather than the singular "stin"</note> which indicates several stones, or perhaps an entire monument, was placed by him.

**Tufa, Tufa's son** <note>original: ᛏᚢᚠᛅ ᛏᚢᚠᛅ ᛋᚢᚾ</note>: The first sentence does not end here, even though the outer line of carving concludes with these words. The sense, therefore, is this: *Thuralf placed this stone for Tufa, son of Tuke.*

**Elta** <note>original runes: ᚽᛚᛏᛅ</note>: I judge there to be an error here. Perhaps it should be read as **Ilda** <note>original runes: ᛁᛚᛏᛅ</note>, to indicate that Tufa, son of Tuke, was the eldest by birth. Thus the meaning becomes: Thuralf the poet <term>skald: an Old Norse court poet or historian</term> or the Rune-master <note>original Latin: Runam</note> placed this monument in memory of Tufa, who was the eldest son of Tuke.

**God**, etc. <note>original: ᚴᚢᛏ</note>: This prayer proves that the inscription is Christian.

## THE THIRD
# JELLING MONUMENT.

<image-desc>A faint ghost image of a runic stone is visible through the page from the reverse side. It depicts a figure in a cruciform pose, likely Christ, surrounded by intricate Viking-age ribbon interlace patterns typical of the Jelling style.</image-desc>

The monument we are now about to describe is indeed famous and elegant, as it has attracted the eyes and minds of many; so much so that even foreigners have judged it worthy of their labor. Furthermore, it cost its founder both his life and his kingdom, as can be seen in our writer Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> in Book 10, where he discusses this matter in detail. Therefore, I will first present the judgments of others concerning it, and will soon add my own conjectures.

The first of the foreigners (so far as I know) who applied himself to this task seems to me to be the most celebrated and illustrious man Joseph Scaliger <note>A renowned French scholar and polymath (1540–1609)</note>, son of Julius Caesar Scaliger. He shared this monument with Bonaventura Vulcanius while the latter was contemplating a treatise on the letters and language of the Getae <note>A term often used by early scholars to refer to the Goths or early Germanic peoples</note>, as Vulcanius himself attests on page 44 of my copy, presenting it in this manner:

> *The inscription of the monument of Gorm, placed for his wife Thyra.*
> ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ ᛏᛅᚾᛘᛅᚱᚴᛅ ᛒᚢᛏᚾ ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ ᛏᚼᛅᚢᛚ ᛅᚠᛏ ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ
> ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ.
>
> *The inscription of the monument of King Harald, placed for his parents Gorm and Thyra.*

So says Vulcanius, who faithfully rendered what he received from Scaliger, and adds nothing more.

## THIRD SECTION
### THE JELLING MONUMENT.

**T**he monument we are now about to describe is truly distinguished and elegant. It has captured the eyes and minds of many, so much so that even foreigners have judged it worthy of their efforts. Furthermore, it cost its founder both his life and his kingdom, as can be seen in the writings of our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), a Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*</note> in Book X, where he follows this matter explicitly. For this reason, I shall first present the judgments of others regarding it, and soon after, I will add my own conjectures.

The first of the foreigners (at least to my knowledge) who applied any effort to this was the most celebrated and illustrious Joseph Scaliger <note>Joseph Justus Scaliger (1540–1609), a famous French religious scholar and historian</note>, son of Julius Caesar Scaliger. He shared this monument with Bonaventura Vulcanius <note>A Flemish humanist and professor at Leiden</note>, who was then contemplating a treatise on the letters and language of the Goths <note>original: "Getarum"; in the 17th century, scholars often conflated the ancient Getae with the Goths and Scandinavians</note>. Vulcanius himself attests to this on page 44, presenting it in the following manner:

*Inscription of the monument placed by Gorm for his wife Thyra.*
<note>original Runic: ᚴᚢᚱᛘᛦ ᚴᚢᚿᚢᚴᛦ ᚴᛆᚱᚦᛁ ᚴᚢᛒᛚ ᚦᚢᛋᛁ ᛆᚠᛏ ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ ᚴᚢᚿᚢ</note>
King Gorm made this monument in memory of Thyra, his wife.

*Inscription of the monument of King Harald, placed for his parents Gorm and Thyra.*
<note>original Runic: ᚼᛆᚱᛆᛚᛏᚱ ᚴᚢᚿᚢᚴᛦ ᛒᛆᚦ ᚴᛆᚢᚱᚢᛆ ᚴᚢᛒᛚ ᚦᛆᚢᛋᛁ ᛆᚠᛏ ᚴᚢᚱᛘ ᚠᛆᚦᚢᚱ ᛋᛁᚿ ᛆᚢᚴ ᛆᚠᛏ ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ ᛘᚢᚦᚢᚱ ᛋᛁᚿ ᚢᛏ ᚼᛆᚱᛆᛚᛏᚱ ᚢᛆᚿᚿ ᛋᛂᚱ ᛏᛆᚿᛘᛆᚢᚱᚴ</note>
King Harald ordered this monument to be made in memory of Gorm, his father, and in memory of Thyra, his mother; that Harald who won for himself all Denmark.

Interpretations were subjoined to these inscriptions, though they do not correspond exactly to the text, in the following tenor:
<italic>Gorm King [made] monument this over Thyra wife. Harald King built church <note>The early scholars misread the runes for "monument" (kubl) as "church" (kirke) in some instances</note> monument this over Gorm father his and over Thyra mother his. Harald [won] over Denmark.</italic>

Thus says Vulcanius, who rendered what he received from Scaliger in good faith, adding nothing more.
The second person to transmit anything regarding this monument to posterity via public printing is Petrus Lindebergius, who in his [book] of...

<header>BOOK FIVE</header>

...of memorable commentaries, he <note>Referring to Heinrich Rantzau (1526–1598), a German humanist and Danish viceroy known for his interest in antiquities</note> skillfully arranged for the entire monument to be engraved in copper and published it in this manner.

"It pleased me," he says, "to add the monument of King Gorm of Denmark—who is called 'Caesar' <note>original: *Cæsar*; likely a Latinized interpretation of the Runic title for 'King' or a reference to his imperial-level power</note> in the inscription—built by King Harald, his son. It should be known that the Danes, since they were unable to build Pyramids and Obelisks for lack of [quarried] stones, long ago established a huge mass like a mountain rising high out of piled-up earth in memory of their Kings and Heroes." <margin>cc</margin>

A. A church or sanctuary placed between the two shared burial mounds <note>original: *socialibus bustis*; referring to the mounds of the royal couple, Gorm and Thyra</note> of the spouses, covered in lead. <margin>cc</margin>

B. A sepulchral stone, which is five and a half ells <note>An *ulna* or ell was a historical unit of measurement, roughly the length of a man's arm, approximately 2 feet or 60 cm</note> in height and nine in circumference; on one side it displays the figure of a man, and on the other side the letters shown in the following table. <margin>cc</margin>

C. The mound to the north, which has a height of 46 ells, a width of 360 ells, and a breadth at the top of 112 ells. <margin>cc</margin>

D. A well built entirely of stones, from which water is drawn daily by the surrounding people; it has a circumference of 47 ells. John Adolphus Cypraeus <note>A 17th-century historian of the Schleswig-Holstein region</note> mentions this well in almost the same words in his *Ecclesiastical Annals of Schleswig*, Book 1, chapter 11, in this manner: <margin>cc</margin>
> *For that purpose, a well was built entirely of stones at Gorm's monument, from which water may be drawn daily by the surrounding people.*

E. The mound on the other side toward the south is 37 ells high, 431 ells in circumference, and 157 ells wide at the surface. <margin>cc</margin>

F. Where the letter is marked, there was a stone of remarkable size, slightly smaller than the one placed at the church between the two mounds. And so that all things may be better understood, I have included here a depiction <note>original: *typum*; a diagram or illustration</note> of the whole monument. <margin>cc</margin>

It should be observed, however, that this illustration of ours is not that of Rantzau, but a new one, which the illustrious hero Lord Christian Friis of Kragerup—a Knight of the Golden Spur, Royal Chancellor, and while he lived, the greatest Patron of the University of Copenhagen—recently caused to be expressed in vivid colors and accurately described according to the laws of Geometry.

### BOOK FIVE.

Among our own people, there have also been those who devoted significant effort to rescuing this monument from destruction. Among the first of these, I must rightly mention a man most noble in virtue and military glory, **Caspar Markdanner of Søgård** <note>Caspar Markdanner (1533–1618) was a Danish nobleman and a prominent official under King Frederick II</note>, then the most deserving governor of the fortress of Kolding. Drawn by a devotion to venerable antiquity, he saw to it that the fallen stone was erected at his own expense and strove to ensure that the characters were transcribed as accurately as possible in modern letters. A testimony of his devotion toward venerable antiquity remains to this day in the choir of the Jelling Church, inscribed in golden letters as follows:

In the year 1586, under the reign of **King Frederick II** of Denmark and Norway, etc., **Caspar Markdanner of Søgård**, who at that time was the Governor of Koldinghus, ordered the excavation of the stone in the churchyard that now stands here outside the church door. Upon it is found the following inscription, which **King Harald** <note>Harald Bluetooth (Haraldr blátǫnn), King of Denmark and Norway</note> ordered to be made for his father **King Gorm** and his mother **Queen Thyra**, roughly in the year 960. At that time, the Roman Empire was ruled by **Emperor Otto I** <note>Otto the Great (reigned 936–973), whom the text links chronologically to the Jelling monuments</note>. During that same period, Queen Thyra constructed the wall near Gottorp which is still called the **Dannevirke** <note>A system of Danish fortifications in Schleswig-Holstein, traditionally attributed to Thyra in folklore</note>; it began at the end of the Schlei <note>original: "Slyen"; a narrow inlet of the Baltic Sea</note>, where **Hadeby** <note>The site of the Viking Age settlement Hedeby</note> once stood, and extended to the Western Sea. This was done because the aforementioned Emperor Otto intended to invade Denmark with military force. **King Gorm** lies buried here in one mound, and his Queen, **Queen Thyra**, is buried in the other.

*King Harald ordered to be made*

*this monument in memory of Gorm, his father*
<note>original transliteration: *Kubu bausi est Gurm fadur sin*</note>

ᛅᚢᚴ ᛅᚠᛏ᛬ ᚦᚭᚢᚱᚢᛁ᛬ ᛘᚢᚦᚢᚱ᛬ ᛋᛁᚾᛅ

I cannot express enough surprise that Lindeberg <note>Peter Lindeberg (1562–1596), a historian from Rostock who wrote about Northern antiquities</note> passed over the description of the second stone, upon which the Epitaph of **Thyra** stands. He did indeed follow the sequence of the text in part, but he completely omitted the drawing of the stone itself.

>> The third of the foreigners who devoted some effort to these matters is **Johannes Bureus** <note>Johannes Bureus (1568–1652) was a Swedish polymath and the first royal antiquarian of Sweden</note>, a Swede, who published a table at Uppsala in Sweden in the year 1590, which he titled <term>Runa kanstanis Lere Span</term> <note>original: "Runa kanstanis Lere Span"; This Old Swedish title translates roughly to "A Teaching-Sample of Runic Art"</note>. While that work contains other excellent materials concerning Runic literature, it also includes this monument of **Harald**; however, it is mutilated and incomplete, featuring the very same letter forms used by Lindeberg. Indeed, I believe it was taken directly from him. Furthermore, he did not include the other stone placed for **Thyra** by **Gorm**, nor did he follow through to the final words of Harald's Epitaph, in which the Emperor <note>original: "Cæsar"; referring to the Holy Roman Emperor, likely Otto I</note> is hailed. Cypræus <note>Paulus Cypræus (1536–1609), a jurist and historian</note> also mentions it in passing in his *Annals of the Slesvig Church*, Book 1, chapter 11.

<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

This effort to rescue monuments dedicated to the memory of our ancestors from ruin is praiseworthy and deserves to be celebrated in every age. Through this work, the man has consecrated both himself and his family to eternity. If only others—those who, for the sake of a little sordid profit, have devoted themselves entirely to the destruction of such things—had followed his example! They might have rendered themselves worthy of the praise of posterity and contributed a most commendable service to the illumination of our national history. Therefore, for the benefit of foreigners, I shall not be loath to present these matters in a Roman toga <note>original: "Romana toga"; a metaphor meaning he is writing this account in Latin, the international language of scholars, so that those outside Denmark can read it</note>.

IN THE YEAR 1586, during the reign of the late Frederick II, the most powerful King of Denmark and Norway, etc., Caspar **Markdanner** of **Søgård**, Governor of **Kolding** Castle, saw to it that this stone—which was located near the doors of the church and buried under the sod—was unearthed. Upon it is seen the following epitaph, which King **Harald** placed for his father **Gorm** and his mother **Thyra**, around the year of Christ 960, while **Otto I** held the helm of the Roman Empire. Around that same time, Queen **Thyra** oversaw the construction of the rampart near **Gottorp**, called the **Dannevirke** <note>The Dannevirke is a massive system of fortifications across the Cimbrian Peninsula</note>, which extended from the Schlei <note>original: "Slya"; an inlet of the Baltic Sea</note> (where **Hedeby** <note>original: "Haddeby"</note> once stood) all the way to the western sea. She did this to shut out Emperor **Otto**, who was threatening the ruin of Denmark. King **Gorm** found his burial in one of these mounds, and **Thyra** in the other.

Regarding the interpretation of the monument, let the discerning reader judge once we have offered our own reflections. Others who have labored in this field <note>original: "in hoc... pulvere"; literally "in this dust," a Latin idiom for a place of intense study or struggle</note> until now have produced hardly anything beyond what has already been mentioned.

Enticed by the majesty and beauty of this monument, when I was dispatched to **Jutland** <note>original: "Cimbriam"</note> by his Most Serene Royal Majesty in the year 1621 for other business, I traveled to **Jelling** so that I might delight myself for a short while in so noble a mausoleum of such a great king, and survey each detail more accurately. This is what I found.

**Jelling** is a village in the district of **Tørrild Herred** <note>original: "Torildsherrit"</note>—so named after a certain petty king of the Cimbrians named **Torild**—located four miles from **Kolding** and one from **Vejle** <note>original: "Viella"</note>. In its splendor and elegance, it approaches the size of a significant town. It takes its name from a certain **Ellingo**, a Cimbrian—

# BOOK FIVE #

...built by a leader of the **Cimbri** <note>The Cimbri were an ancient tribe from the Jutland peninsula</note> (as some maintain), and formerly made noble by the continuous residence of Kings. Here, this magnificent monument of King **Gorm** and Queen **Thyra** presents itself for inspection; in its location, size, and other details, it corresponds clearly to the drawing presented by the most renowned man, **Peter Lindeberg**. However, neither a genuine and true visual representation <term>Iconographia|A detailed artistic or technical drawing of an object</term> of the stones—for there are two marked with characters <note>original: "characteribus"; referring here to the runic inscriptions</note>—nor an accurate sequence of the inscription, has yet been clearly put forward by anyone. Therefore, we shall devote a little of our labor to these matters here.

Two stones are seen around this monument. One is larger and grey in color, of the size which **Lindeberg** marked with the letter B, tapering to a blunt point. It measures three ells <note>original: "ulnas"; an "ell" or "alen" was a traditional unit of length, approximately 2 feet or 63 centimeters</note> and three-quarters in height. The side that is wider measures four ells and a quarter; the side displaying the **Lion** <note>A reference to the "Great Beast" carved on one face of the stone</note> measures two ells and three-quarters; and the side showing the **Man** <note>This refers to the famous depiction of Christ on the Great Jelling Stone</note> measures two ells and a half.

It is situated at the base of the southern mound <note>original: "montis"; the two large burial mounds at Jelling were often referred to as "mountains" in early modern Latin texts</note> in the churchyard itself. Its first side is decorated at the top with certain intricate patterns; near the base, however, it contains four rows of characters <note>runic letters</note> which are entwined together at their ends.

The second side displays the figure of a **Lion** <note>Known today as the "Great Beast," this is a centerpiece of the Jelling style of Viking art</note>, fashioned with marvelous skill from various carved strokes, and marked with a single row of letters at its base. The third side exhibits the image of a **Man** <note>The earliest Nordic depiction of Christ, shown here surrounded by interlacing ribbon-work</note>, bound in certain coils; as these crawl here and there, they leave only as much space near the ground as is sufficient for a single line of letters, as is clear from this drawing.

On the third side:

*And made the people Christian* <note>original: "Aug tini folk Kristno"</note>
->AND CONVERTED THEIR INHABITANTS TO THE CHRISTIAN FAITH.<-

**KING HARALD** <note>original: "HARALTR KUNUKR"</note> Although several kings of this name have existed, nevertheless, since he acknowledges himself here as the offspring of Gorm and Thyra, no one doubts that this is the Harald whose history our countryman Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century author of the "Gesta Danorum" or Deeds of the Danes</note> pursues at the beginning of the tenth book, nicknamed **Bluetooth** <note>original: "Blaatand"</note>. He was a man tossed by various turns of fortune: he defeated Haakon, the protégé of Athelstan <note>Haakon the Good, King of Norway</note>, conquered the Slavs, crushed the resistance in the Margraviate of Schleswig, drove the Emperor Otto from the Jutland peninsula <note>original: "Cimbria"</note>, and finally, washed in the saving waters of baptism, he embraced the Christian religion.

One may see his praise in Helmold’s *Chronicle of the Slavs*, chapter 15, where among other things he argues thus: *“Harald, at first indeed a pagan, then converted to the faith of Christ by the teaching of the great father Unni <note>Unni was the Archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen who led missions to the North</note>, exercised such great devotion toward the Lord that there has not arisen one like him among all the Kings of the Danes; he who drew such a vast breadth of the North to the faith of divine knowledge, and [filled] the whole land with Churches...”*

# DANISH MONUMENTS #

...made him distinguished among the priests. The industry of this man in divine matters was indeed exceptional; nevertheless, he also shone so brightly in worldly wisdom—specifically in those matters which seem to pertain to the governance of the Realm—that he established laws and rights which, by the man's authority, not only the Danes but also the Saxons still strive to observe today. Scholars understand these laws to be what are commonly called the **Saxenspiegel** <term>Saxenspiegel: Literally the "Saxon Mirror," one of the most important law books and legal codes of the Holy Roman Middle Ages</term>. They are compelled to attribute these to a Danish author both by the similarity to our own laws and by the trustworthy authority of this historian <note>referring to Saxo Grammaticus</note>.

Driven out of the Kingdom, Harald was treacherously killed by his own soldier, Toko <note>historically known as Palnatoke</note>, near Julin <note>modern-day Wolin</note>, in the year 980. His body, Saxo says, was sent to Roskilde and received a solemn place of burial in the sanctuary he had recently founded there. For his country, once ungrateful for his good deeds, embraced the works of this most pious Leader with a late-arriving realization; what it had denied him during his life, it thought should be fully granted to his funeral. Applying every ounce of human effort to the funeral rites, the nation gently embraced the ashes of the man whose spirit it had haughtily hated.

A certain column in Roskilde still displays his image and Epitaph with this series of words:

> While we wrote nine hundred and eighty years
> after the birth of God, he deserved to climb to the heights of heaven.

Not far from Vejle in Jutland <note>original: Cimbria</note> there exists an estate called **Haralds-**<margin>stier</margin> **kær**, taking its name from this same Harald.

For it is not probable that Harald, a Christian, would have built a sanctuary dedicated to Christ in honor of a pagan father and a most bitter persecutor of Christians. Furthermore, if ᚴᛁᚢᚱᚦᚽ were to be read, it would be necessary for the conjunction ᚬᚢᚴ [and] to be inserted between this word and the following ᚴᚢᛘᛒᛚ [monument], for the sense to be clear. # BOOK FIVE #

...with the word *Jeg Kerver* <note>original: "Jeg Kerver," meaning "I carve" or "I incise"</note> I incise and adorn with marks, so that the meaning is: Harald built this mound, which was distinguished by a sepulchral stone adorned with various marks and carvings. This was done to distinguish it from other mounds to which no such stones are attached. Indeed, if anyone should think that such grave markers were once called **Kirthu Vathra** <note>runic: ᚴᛁᚱᚦᚢ ᚢᛅᚦᚱᛅ; an archaic phrase interpreted here as "monumental stones"</note> by our people, I would think him not entirely far from the truth, provided this interpretation could be confirmed by other inscriptions on monuments.

**Thurui** <note>runic: ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ</note> seems to designate the southern mound at the base of which the stone is placed, or at least the stone itself. For it can be gathered from the inscription on the following stone that the northern mound was built for Thyra by her husband Gorm.

**Thuru** <note>runic: ᚦᚢᚱᚢ</note>. This is Gorm the Third, called *Wormio* by some historians, with the surname *Gamle* <note>meaning "the Old"</note>. Saxo <note>the historian Saxo Grammaticus</note> follows his deeds at the end of the ninth book, saying he was always of a hostile mind toward religion; he desired to extinguish the followers of Christ just as if they were the most foul of men. He did not rest from pursuing all who shared this faith, wearying them with various types of injuries and whatever slanders he could muster. Moreover, in order to restore the ancient worship to the shrines, he demolished a temple founded by religious men on the *Schleswig* estate—treating it as if it were some sacrilegious home of impiety—down to its very foundations. He was defeated and driven from North Albingia by *Henry the Fowler* <note>the East Frankish King</note> (who established the March of *Schleswig* as the border of *Denmark*, and for that purpose ordered the castle of *Oldenburg* to be built). Gorm died in the year 934, or as others prefer 930, or others 931. I think there is an error in the history compiled by *King Eric*, where he asserts this Gorm died in the year of our Lord 950; I believe it should read 930.

**Thurui** <note>runic: ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ</note> is also read in the Norwegian history of *Halvdan the Black*. To Saxo, she is Thyra. She was the daughter of the English King *Hedelradus* according to Saxo, or more commonly *Ethelred*. She surpassed others in dignity and industry, known to our people as **Dannebod** <note>meaning "The Pride of the Danes" or "Denmark's Salvation"</note>. ᛦᚼᚢᚾᚠᚴ <note>Runic inscription fragment</note> **The Commander** <note>original: *Imperator*</note> stands out here with the most clear strokes of the letters. I believe the one called "Commander" is Harald, because he snatched Denmark from the hands of Emperor Otto, and partly scattered, partly laid low his forces, which our historian pursues as follows:

> *The Caesar <note>Emperor Otto I</note>, having traversed Jutland as if it were empty of royal leadership since no one resisted, was prevented from advancing further by the barrier of the Limfjord—which at that time enclosed Wendala <note>Vendsyssel, the northernmost part of Jutland</note> with its waters. Having cast his spear into the waves, he not only turned his path back toward the Eider, but his return was very much like a flight. Indeed, having thrown the spear he was using into the sea's waves for the sake of leaving a monument, he gave his own name to the strait.*

But as he appeared heavy in his initial assault, so he proved empty in his departure. For Harald, following the retreating remnants of the enemy with a most fiery pace, slaughtered Eppo, the leader of the rear guard, along with those he found. I do not doubt that there is discussion of this victory in this place, and perhaps for this reason, in contempt of Otto, he decided he should be hailed as the Commander and Caesar of his own Denmark no less than Otto was of Germany. Or perhaps he was called so because he was the first of the Kings of Denmark to have waged war so successfully against the German Emperor.

ᚼᚠᚴ <note>Runic inscription fragment</note> That is, **he conquered**, or **he recovered**, in the manner already stated. For I do not agree with those who think this is a German word.

...[Empe]ror of Denmark <note>original: "tant ban" interpreted as "Keiser van Danmark"</note>, as if the meaning were: **Emperor of Denmark.** For who would have defiled such an elegant monument with the titles of that nation whose most bitter enemy was Harald?

ᛏᛅᚾᛘᛅᚱᚴ <note>Denmark</note> On the following stone, it is written ᛏᛅᚾᛘᚬᚱᚴ, an orthography further removed from the modern style. However, the Icelanders also express the dotted ᛏ as a Latin D.

ᛅᛚᚦ <note>All</note> This indicates that the whole of Denmark was under his rule. A gap <note>original: *lacuna*</note> appears here in the stone, for which reason some believe it should read ᚢᛒᛋᛅᛚᛅ, **Uppsala**; so that the sense is that Harald had conquered Denmark, Uppsala (by which he means Sweden, which in our ancient records is frequently called the Kingdom of Uppsala), Norway, etc., and converted them to the Christian faith.

ᚢᚾᚾᛁᚦ <note>Won or Conquered</note>, I believe this victory refers to the one he obtained in Norway in the name of Harald, son of Gunnhild <note>Harald Greycloak</note>, after Haakon, foster-son of Athelstan <note>Haakon the Good</note>, was put to flight; by which title Norway was also bound to pay him tribute. Our oft-praised historian <note>Likely Saxo Grammaticus</note> also touches upon this in the following words:

> Therefore, when he had handled barbarian affairs with royal execution, he returned to Denmark. He was met by Harald, son of Gunnhild, who was seeking help against the same Haakon and promising that he would give him tribute if, by the benefit of Danish aid, he obtained effective help for his party. Indeed, Harald Bluetooth showed the most merciful humanity amidst these bitter circumstances. Having received Hevindus and Karlhoftus as helpers in the fight, and being gifted a fleet of sixty ships, Harald Greycloak departed having obtained the protection he sought; and it happened that he placed more hope in the aid of the Danes than fear in his own adversity, etc.

Thus Harald <note>Greycloak</note>, having obtained the fortune of ruling by the unexpected death of his enemy, provided the promised tax to the Danes in good faith for three years. That Norway is understood here is also evidenced by the **Lion** carved above these words, which even now displays the heraldry of Norway.

ᛏᛁᛚ ᚠᚱᛁᚦ <note>To peace/To the people</note> I fill this gap by taking into account the historical deeds performed. For the letters ᚠ and ᚱ <note>F and R</note> still stand out clearly enough in all their strokes. I believe the "inhabitants" are indicated. ...son of Kragerup, etc., are those who read ᛏᛁᚾᚴ ᛏᛁᚴ ᚴᚱᛁᚢᛏ <note>original: "ting tik kriut"</note> so that the sense is that Harald held the new **German Christians** <note>original: "Teutonum Christianos"</note> under his rule. Our own **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> does not conceal this, suggesting the same in these concise words:

> *Truly Harald, having settled matters with the Emperor and embraced the fellowship of the Catholic religion, reconciled divine and human peace to his kingdom.* <note>original: "Verum Haraldus rebus cum Imperatore compositis, consortium catholicæ religionis amplexus, divinam humanamq; pacem regno suo conciliavit."</note>

This is the true representation of this stone and the interpretation of its words in accordance with our history. Here one must admire the sharp wit of our ancestors, who were able to comprise such great deeds in so few strokes of words. It is certainly to be hoped that an equal light from history might reach the rest of our monuments; I have no doubt that they would then be read with greater delight and held in higher esteem.

ᚴᚢᚱᛘᛦ : ᚴᚢᚾᚢᚴᛦ : ᚴᛅᚱᚦᛁ : ᚴᚢᛒᛚ : ᚦᚢᛋᛁ : ᛅᚠᛏ : ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ : ᚴᚢᚾᚢ : ᛋᛁᚾᛅ : ᛏᛅᚾᛘᛅᚱᚴᛅᛦ ᛒᚢᛏ

->KING GORM PLACED THIS MONUMENT FOR HIS WIFE THYRA, WHO ADORNED DENMARK.<-

This stone presents a significant puzzle to our historians, who unanimously assert that **Gorm** died before his wife **Thyra**. If that is the case, who could have placed this monument and inscription for the Queen, since she lived for many years after him? Indeed, after his death, she is credited with building the **Dannevirke** <note>A massive system of Danish fortifications in Schleswig-Holstein, built to protect against southern invasions</note> wall. Unless we conclude that Gorm constructed this monument while he was still alive and intended it for the remains of the Queen—who had not yet passed away—we will hardly find a way out of this difficulty. In a certain sense, the massive size and majesty of the stone explained previously <note>referring to the Great Jelling Stone of Harald Bluetooth described on the previous pages</note> seems to support this idea. For **Harald**, upon the death of his mother and seeing this stone we are now discussing, judged it too lowly to either cover or consecrate the head of Danish Majesty to eternity. Deploying the entire fleet of the kingdom—to use the words of our own **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century author of the Gesta Danorum</note>—lest he should attempt the weight of such a great mass with insufficient preparation...

...that his work might proceed, <note>The Latin 'grederetur' is a fragment of 'progrederetur,' continuing from the previous page's description of Harald's labor.</note> he ordered a stone of unusual size, found on the coast of Jutland, to be dragged away by the combined forces of men and oxen so that he might distinguish his mother's burial mound. Some think this is the very stone we discussed earlier, which, having been polished with such ornaments and so exquisite a style of composed words, he substituted for the previous one. But others believe this is not the stone our **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum</note> speaks of, but rather one even grander and larger, which he was unable to lead to the burial place because he was hindered by his son's rebellion, and was forced to leave it almost midway. This is even now pointed out by many in the place of **Bække** <note>original: "Beckehede"</note>. This latter opinion seems more probable to me, since the stone seen in the Jelling churchyard is not of such mass as to require such immense expense and labor to move it. **Harald** seems to have taken such pleasure in that massive stone that he thought nothing greater or more excellent could ever be placed. Our **Saxo** does not hide this, as he adds shortly after: *Meanwhile, Harald, occupied with the hauling of the stone, began to ask one of his men arriving from the fleet more closely whether he had ever seen such a mass attempted by mortal hands elsewhere?* I therefore deem it probable that **Gorm**, now worn out by old age, had destined these burial places for himself and his wife, and even saw to it that this smaller stone was decorated with an epitaph; this was later converted by **Harald** into that more excellent monument after his mother's death, and he would have illustrated it with an even greater mass had his son, attempting to seize the kingdom by force and guile, not rendered his efforts in vain.

ᚴᚢᚱᛘ ᚴᚢᚾᚢᚴ <gloss>King Gorm</gloss> therefore saw to it that the burial mound was prepared.

ᚴᛁᚱᚦᛁ ᚴᚢᛘᛚ <gloss>Made the monument</gloss> This phrase seems to suggest that the mound was constructed after the death of the Queen. However, as we observe happening today, many living people decorate their own sepulchral stones with epitaphs while they are still alive, which are only then fitted to the tomb after death; we believe the same was done here.

ᚴᚢᚾᚢ <gloss>Wife [Kone]</gloss>; it is surprising that in that age, Queens and other heroines born of royal blood were not decorated with a more honorable title than that by which any woman from the common people is addressed today. <note>Worm is commenting on the word 'Kone,' which in his time—and modern Danish—means a wife or woman, finding it humble for a Queen.</note>

This most excellent woman <note>Queen Thyra, wife of Gorm the Old</note> led the work from the mouth <note>of the Schlei</note> to the western ocean. But I cannot agree with those who say this, since our historical documents expressly assert that after her first husband's death, and after the Emperor Otto <note>likely Otto I, who invaded Jutland in the 10th century</note> had been driven out with his forces following an incursion into **Jutland** <note>original: "Cimbria"</note>, the wall was first enlarged by **Thyra** with a new structure. However, **Gorm**, who is the author of this inscription, died long before her. Therefore, I believe the phrase should be understood as referring to all of Denmark, which was adorned by her with various and noble buildings, and even strengthened by her sound counsel. This is the meaning of the word <term>BVT</term> <note>often translated as "bod" or "improvement/adornment"</note> from the verb *jeg bygger* [I build], which can be applied both to physical structures and to a state restored and, as it were, built anew by sound political wisdom. The conjecture of our colleague **Stephanius** <note>Stephen Hansen Stephanius (1599–1650), a Danish royal historiographer</note> regarding these words does not displease me. For he believes they express a title once granted to **Thyra** because of her merits, by which she was commonly addressed as **Thyra** <term>DANEBOD</term>, that is, as **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus</note> explains, *the peak of Danish majesty*. For he wrote to me thus in a letter dated the year 1632:

> In the inscription of the monument which King <term>GORMO</term> placed for his wife **Thyra**, I interpret those last words <term>TANMARKER BVT</term> as <term>DANMARKES BOTH</term> or <term>BOED</term> <note>Denmark's Salvation or Healer</note>. For the best of queens, **Thyra**, was called by the common and distinguished surname <term>DANEBOTH</term> or <term>DANEBOD</term> due to her outstanding merits toward the fatherland; as one may read in the works of Velleius, Lyscander, and others. Furthermore, the shift from the word <term>BVT</term> to <term>BOTH</term> or <term>BOED</term> is an easy linguistic transition.

These are the matters which seemed necessary to me for the explanation of this noble monument. If I have lingered somewhat longer on these points, I wish it to be attributed to the dignity of the subject and the excellence of the monument itself. In the meantime, I am prepared to change my opinion if anyone can elicit something more certain from more evident documents.

Some read <unclear>H R N N P A</unclear>, thinking that there is a combination of two words here, such that *Haer* or *her* denotes "Lord," and *Rolfer* is the proper name of the man buried here. But I would sooner believe that all these letters constitute a single word, since the title of "Lord" <note>original Latin: "Domini titulus"</note> does not appear in other older monuments of this kind. Unless perhaps you would say that *Her* in this place denotes an "army" <note>original Latin: "exercitum"; in modern Danish and German, "Hær" or "Heer" still means army</note>; for this is also a meaning of this word. In that case, the sense would be: "In this place was, or conquered, the army of Rolf." Regarding him, however, nothing has yet been found recorded in our domestic literary monuments.

It seems to me to be a trophy <term>trophaeum</term> <note>a monument erected to commemorate a military victory</note> rather than an epitaph, and I wonder if this might not be appropriately attributed to **Rollo**, called *Gange Rolf* <note>meaning "Walking Rolf" in Old Norse; legend says he was so large no horse could carry him, forcing him to walk</note> by the Norwegians (whom they claim as their own, while foreigners call him a Dane). The annals report that around the year of Christ 900, he emigrated from Denmark with a very well-equipped fleet to seek new homes, and finally occupied **Neustria** <note>a region in the northwest of the Frankish kingdom</note> in France, where from his lineage **William the Conqueror** <note>original Latin: "Vilhelmus conquestor"</note> and other Kings of Britain eventually drew their origin. Perhaps this pillar was placed in memory of this migration: either because he gathered and reviewed his army in that place, or because he had his fleet's anchorage not far from there. Indeed, an excellent monument to this same **Rollo** also exists in **England**, which they call the **Rollright Stones** <note>original: "Rolrichstones"; a megalithic ritual site in Oxfordshire</note>, which is drawn and described at length by **Camden** <note>William Camden (1551–1623), a famous English antiquarian</note> in his description of **Oxfordshire**, a site most worthy of seeing.

> *For at that time* (says Camden) *when he harassed England with the raids of his Danes and Normans, we read that the Danes engaged in battle with the English near **Hook Norton** <note>original: "Hokenorton"</note> and afterwards fought again at **Sherston** <note>original: "Scierstane"</note> in Huiccia <note>an ancient Anglo-Saxon kingdom in the West Midlands</note>.*

Note here that he, by an easy slip, reads *Scierstane* for *Sejerstane*, which denotes "stones of victory"—from the word *sejer* (victory) and *stene* (stones)—an etymology derived from a completely different matter. For stones of this kind, both among us and the Norwegians, are still designated by this name today.

Nor does **Carion’s Chronicle** <note>a popular 16th-century history book originally by Johannes Carion, later edited by Melanchthon</note>, Book 4, seem to disagree, expressly asserting: *The Normans, under the leadership of Rollo, invaded and plundered a part of the Kingdom of France by fleet from the Cimbrian Peninsula <note>the Jutland peninsula</note>, and later obtained it by a treaty with **Charles the Simple** <note>King of West Francia (r. 898–922)</note>, which because in [the West...]*

Some read the inscription as ***HRNNR***, thinking it is a combination of two words, such that *Haer* or *her* signifies "Lord," while *Rolfer* is the name of the man buried here. But I am more inclined to believe all this forms a single word, since the title of "Lord" does not appear in other older monuments of this kind. Unless, perhaps, you might say that *Her* in this place signifies an "army," for this is also a meaning of that word. In that case, the sense would be: "In this place the army of Rolf stood, or was victorious." However, I have so far been unable to find any record of this Rolf in the written history of our own people. 

It seems to me more like a trophy <note>a monument commemorating a military victory</note> than an epitaph, and I wonder if it might fittingly be attributed to **Rollo**, called **Gange-Rolff** by the Norwegians (whom they claim as their own, while foreigners call him a **Dane**). The annals record that around the year 900 AD, he set out from Denmark with a well-equipped fleet to seek new lands, eventually occupying **Neustria** <note>the region of France now known as Normandy</note>, where his descendant **William the Conqueror** and other Kings of Britain eventually trace their origin. 

Perhaps this stone pillar <term>cippus</term> <note>a small low pillar used as a landmark or gravestone</note> was placed in memory of this migration: either because he assembled and inspected his army in this place, or because he stationed his fleet not far from here. For there also exists a remarkable monument to this Rollo in England called the **Rollright Stones** <note>original: "Rolrichstones"</note>, which is drawn and described in detail by **William Camden** <note>the famous 16th-century English antiquarian</note> in his section on **Oxfordshire**, a site most worthy of seeing.

> For at that time (says **Camden**), when he was harassing England with his Danes and Normans through plundering raids, we read that the Danes joined battle with the English near **Hook Norton** <note>original: "Hokenorton"</note>, and afterwards fought again at **Sherston** <note>original: "Scierstane"</note> in **Hwicce** <note>original: "Huiccia," a sub-kingdom of Anglo-Saxon England</note>. Here, note that he [Camden], by a simple slip, reads **Sherston** instead of **Sejerstane**—which signifies "stones of victory," from the word *sejer* <note>original: "feier," Danish for victory</note> and *stene* (stones)—an etymology derived from something entirely different.

For stones of this kind, both among us and the Norwegians, are still distinguished by this name today.

Nor does the **Chronicle of Carion** <note>a popular 16th-century historical work</note>, Book 4, seem to disagree, stating explicitly: 

> The Normans, under the leadership of **Rollo**, invaded and plundered a part of the Kingdom of France with a fleet from the **Cimbrian Peninsula** <note>the Jutland peninsula</note>, and later obtained it through an agreement with **Charles the Simple**, King of France...

which, because in the west—
