There, having cleared the forests, he chose a home for himself, obtaining the necessities for life from neighbors through his servants, until he had established a territory for himself suitable for any purpose, which he called **Heriuffdal** after his own name; now, however, by contraction it is called **Herdal** <note>This refers to the modern province of Härjedalen</note>; it is located within the Diocese of **Nidaros** <note>The medieval name for the city and diocese of Trondheim, Norway</note>. If it could be proven by clear evidence that this Heriulfer had reached these places during the time of his exile and performed some memorable deed there, I would not hesitate to affirm that this stone pillar <term>cippus</term> <note>A small, low pillar used by the ancients as a landmark or a tombstone</note> was placed in his memory.

**Lindeberg** mentions, in the place cited above, another stone in **Holstein** <note>original: *Holfatia*</note>, carved with Runic letters, of which it has not yet been possible to obtain a drawing.

### SIXTH
## THE GOLDEN DANISH HORN.

Not without reason do I include here that golden Horn, which a certain poor Danish girl found in the Diocese of **Ribe** in the year 1639, and which is now kept among the treasures <note>original Greek: *κειμήλια* (keimēlia) — precious heirlooms or stored valuables</note> of the most serene Prince **Christian V**, etc. I have decided to include its history here, both so that the envious may see it is truly Danish and not sought or begged from foreigners, and because I understand that great minds abroad have judged this worthy of spending not just hours, but several days and many sleepless nights of study.

BOOK FIVE.

## To the Benevolent Reader
->S<-

When not so long ago I had been called to Nykøbing Falster <note>A town on the Danish island of Falster where the royal family often stayed at Nykøbing Castle.</note>, to give my counsel because the Most Serene and Most High Lord CHRISTIAN V, elected Prince of Denmark and Norway, etc., and his Most Illustrious Consort MAGDALENA SYBILLA were lying ill with a contagious epidemic fever spreading among us: among the other signs of favor and kindness shown to me then, by order of the Most Serene Prince, that Golden Horn—which had been found in Jutland <note>original: *Cimbria*, the peninsula comprising mainland Denmark.</note> a year before—was presented to me. It was filled with pure wine and brought by that most noble man, as distinguished in learning as in lineage and virtues, Lord JOACHIM GERSTORFF <note>original: *Gestorfius*; he was a high-ranking Danish statesman and chamberlain to the Prince.</note>, the chamberlain to our same Most Serene Prince. This was done so that I might drink the hospitable liquid from it, and so that I might indicate what the emblems, cast into it with such wonderful and ancient skill, were intended to mean. I obeyed these orders as much as I was able. But since I noticed the "hieroglyphic" characters of a hidden philosophy, which seemed to require an Oedipus <note>In Greek mythology, Oedipus solved the riddle of the Sphinx; here, Worm means the symbols are so complex they require a master riddle-solver.</note> himself, I humbly asked that I be allowed to sketch the structure of such a noble cup and to depict its ornaments and emblems, so that the opportunity for thinking about them might be more convenient. The best of Princes did not reluctantly grant my prayers, but conceded them to my discretion until each detail had been accurately sketched and evaluated by me.

While I was weighing the wonderful structure of the work and especially the excellence of the metal, it occurred to me what I remember reading once in Athenaeus concerning the cup of Enallus, which was fashioned from gold so excellent that gold found among others seemed like bronze compared to it. If you like, because it is pleasant, you may read the account in Athenaeus’s *The Learned Banqueters* <note>original: *Dipnosoph.* or *Deipnosophistae*, an ancient Greek work describing a series of banquets where learned men discuss history and art.</note>, Book 11, Chapter 4, translated here into Latin by Natale Conti <note>original: *Natali de comitibus*, a 16th-century mythographer and translator.</note> from the 16th book of Posidonius: "There are those who tell stories of Methymnean matters and of a girl thrown into the sea: for they say that since one of the leaders loved her, whose name was Enallus, he swam to save the girl herself; yet both, when they had been covered by the waves, were seen no more. Afterward, in following times, when Methymne had begun to be inhabited again, they say that Enallus approached, and [told] the manner of his secret..."

Especially since I shall leave many things behind in which more noble minds might worthily exercise themselves. Grant me your favor, kind reader, and if you know better, share it kindly.

# The Golden Danish Horn,

## CHRISTIAN THE FIFTH

### HISTORY OF ITS DISCOVERY,

<image-desc>A large historiated decorative initial letter 'A' intertwined with scrolling vines and leaves.</image-desc>

**A**round the year 1639, during the reign of the most august King of Denmark, Norway, etc., **CHRISTIAN THE FOURTH**, on the 20th day of the month of July, a certain Danish girl named Kirstine Svendsdatter <note>original: *Christlina Svenonis filia*</note>, from the village of Østerby—which is barely half a mile <note>A Danish mile at this time was approximately 7.5 kilometers, making this discovery site very close to the town.</note> distant from the town of Møgeltønder in the Diocese of Ribe—happened upon this golden horn by chance while she was traveling there. Because she thought it was the protruding root of an aged tree (for what was visible was covered on all sides with filth and mud), she began to poke at it with the walking stick she was carrying in her hands, to see what sort of thing it was that was obstructing her path.

But when this method revealed nothing that caught her eye, she assumed it was a root of no value and continued on her journey, leaving it untouched. After eight days had passed, while she was again traveling from Østerby toward Møgeltønder, accompanied by two other servant girls who were heading to a village named Gallehus not far from there, she once more stumbled upon the same horn at the fork in the road. When she examined it somewhat more carefully—and not without a bit of annoyance—she noticed it was something rare and not merely the branch of a root. 

Since she was without the aid of her walking stick this time, she began to dig the earth with her fingers, trying with great effort to unearth the object in her way. While she was thus intent on her work, the others continued on their journey; however, she did not stop until she held the whole object, excavated with her greatest strength, in her hands. She had progressed some distance—

...her companions, who had gone ahead on the other path of the fork leading toward Gallehus <note>original: *Galfuhaſam*; a small settlement near Møgeltønder where the two golden horns were eventually found</note>, she soon called out happily for them to stop or hurry back, as she had come across a rare sight. Handling the unearthed prize together, they concluded it was nothing other than an old hunting horn <note>original: *caſcum venatorium cornu*</note>; they urged her to throw it away as something useless and of no importance. But she replied: "Since it cost me so much effort, I will not refuse to carry it to the town." 

Moving further along, she came upon a stream of fresh water, where she began to wash the unearthed horn and clean it of the filth and mud with which it was covered. Then, both the massiveness of the workmanship and its weight, as well as the glittering streaks of metal gradually being revealed, dissuaded her from believing it was just a common horn meant for hunting. 

Becoming more encouraged by this (despite her companions’ attempts to dissuade her because its heavy weight would double the burden of the pack she was already carrying), she decided to carry it with her into town. Therefore, she placed it in a sack <note>original: *culeo*; literally a leather bag or sack</note> and carried it to Tønder <note>original: *Tunderam*; a major market town in Southern Jutland</note>. But because she thought it was made of brass at that time, she did not hand it over to anyone to be examined. 

Having returned home, she showed it to the rest of her household; they scolded the girl’s foolishness and rashness for putting so much effort into a worthless thing. But the next day, she set herself to polishing the horn further. While she was busily occupied with this, two men came by and asked about her endeavor. She replied that she was cleaning the horn found yesterday so that she could more easily discover what metal it was made of. Examining the work for a moment, they suggested that a trumpeter <note>original: *Tubicinem*</note> had once used this, and that it would be a profitable matter for her if she were to sell it to a man of that profession. 

The girl argued that they were mistaken because it consisted of so many parts—for while she was violently wrenching it from the earth, she had pulled away some of the rings from those that encircled the inner plate from the rest of the body—stating that she would go to Tønder again, so that she might be more certainly informed by others about the use and material of this horn. When she had gone there again, she gave a small piece of it to a certain woman to offer to a goldsmith for examination; for she feared that if she handled the business herself, she might be deceived by someone concealing the truth...

...the Artisan examining it) She returned, bringing back the Goldsmith's opinion that it was indeed gold. Anyone can easily imagine how much she was refreshed by this answer. From here, the fame of the discovery of the golden horn was spread far and wide, enticing many to travel to *Österby* <note>a small village near the discovery site</note> to see the treasure. 

At last, when the matter was reported to the Governor of Tønder <note>original: *Tunderensem Præfectum*</note>, he sent a messenger to the girl, telling her to hurry to him and bring the discovered treasure with her. Obeying these instructions, she presented herself and the horn, asking for the means and a carriage to be provided so that she might meet His Royal Majesty in person and offer the discovered horn to him. But he insisted that it first be shown to the Royal Governor of the Ribe district <note>original: *territorii Ripensis*</note>. The girl did not object; therefore, they set out together on the journey toward Ribe. 

When they arrived there, they did not find the Governor, for he had departed elsewhere to attend to public business. Therefore, the castle Scribe <note>or clerk</note>, thinking the horn should be kept safe until the Governor's return, sent the girl home, promising that he would handle everything accurately. When the Governor returned, he ordered the girl to be called to him so she could explain what had happened in person and inform him whether more things of that kind could be found in that same place. Speaking clearly about what I have already related, she declared she did not know if more of that kind existed at the aforementioned fork in the road. However, if they wished to make an attempt <note>original: *periculum facere*; to test the ground</note>, she would show them the place. Soon, with the girl as their guide, men were sent out to survey everything more diligently, dig up the earth, and search accurately for treasures. But they found nothing of any significance.

Meanwhile, at *Tychopolis*, commonly called *Glückstadt* <note>a town in Holstein founded by King Christian IV</note> (where our most Christian King was then staying with his son, the Prince), someone arrived who told the story of what had happened among his companions, praising the excellence of this golden horn with wondrous tributes: judging it a sacrilege that such a treasure, worthy only of Kings and Princes, should be handled by unworthy commoners. When this rumor reached the King's ears, an order was given to inquire more diligently whether the man was telling the truth. He proceeded to narrate not only the events as he had heard them from trustworthy accounts, but also the place, the time, the girl, and all other circumstances from the very beginning <note>original: *à primo ovo*; literally "from the first egg"</note>, including where this golden horn was now held...

...she did not hesitate to add further details. Her story earned her trust; she so convinced the magistrate that, as the newcomer confirmed and defended her assertion with even sharper and more evident evidence, a man of proven good faith was dispatched to explore everything more accurately and to immediately bring the discovered horn to His Royal Majesty <note>King Christian IV of Denmark</note>. Upon his return, he brought both the gold itself and a written record of the sequence of events. While those present feasted their eyes on such a joyful sight, His Most Serene Royal Majesty noticed that the Prince <note>Prince-Elect Christian, the King's son</note> was greatly delighted by it. Therefore, with a generous spirit, the King gave it to him as a gift, and he enjoined him to see to it that a drinking cup was fashioned from it in memory of the event and in honor of antiquity, which would serve as a lasting monument to the discovered treasure.

Wise counsel dissuaded the Prince's advisors from destroying or tampering with such a noble <term>treasure</term> <note>original Greek: κειμήλιον (keimēlion), referring to a precious heirloom or highly valued possession</note> of antiquity. Instead, they urged the Prince to have it purged of its grime and converted into a polished vessel for use as a cup, since it is well-established from history that our ancestors in these regions used horns in place of drinking cups in ancient times. These counsels did not displease the Prince; therefore, he not only handed it over to a goldsmith to be cleaned and polished, but he also summoned the young woman who had dug it out of the earth. Once she had accurately explained the event in person, he enriched her with a generous reward. The purified gold now presents a most brilliant and precious cup, upon which various "hieroglyphic" <note>In the 17th century, "hieroglyphic" was often used to describe any mysterious or symbolic figures, not just Egyptian ones</note> figures of humans and animals shine with ancient art; these figures daily exhaust the wits of those who attempt to investigate their mystical meaning.

### THE CONSTRUCTION.

This golden horn of the Most Serene Prince consists of a double plate, of which the interior is solid and whole, with a smooth surface on both sides. The exterior, however, is not continuous like the first, but is composed of eleven contiguous, wide rings, as it were, which are distinct and divided by their joints. Yet, these are not all of the same width or thickness. The larger rings follow the smaller ones in such a way that, although they are tightly closed and united by their joints, they can nonetheless be rotated and removed at will without harming the interior plate. These rings yield to the inner substance in smoothness, for they are adorned with two kinds of figures: some of which are made with small dots...

It is valued at one thousand two hundred Imperial thalers; but for the splendor of its antiquity and its rarity, no treasure is to be compared to it. THIS WAS SKILLFULLY MADE IN THE YEAR 1639 under the care, of course, of the Most Serene Prince CHRISTIAN the fifth <note>Referring to Prince-Elect Christian (1603–1647), the son of Christian IV; he was the fifth "Christian" in the royal line but died before he could succeed his father as King</note>, whose name is displayed by a crowned letter C containing the number five. The gold from which this <term>screw-stopper</term> <note>original: *cochlea*, literally "snail shell," referring here to the threaded mechanism of the plug</note> consists, although it is of a high quality, yet if it were compared to the rest of the horn in terms of color, you would swear that the stopper was <term>brass</term> <note>original: *orichalcum*, a golden-colored alloy of copper and zinc</note> by comparison. The Most Serene Prince saw to it that this globe was fitted for the purpose of preventing any poured liquid from leaking out. The rings of which the outer plate consists are of different sizes and widths, according to the proportions of the horn itself which they form. The largest and widest of all is the one that encircles the lip or the top; the narrowest and smallest is the last one, near the screw-globe; the intermediate ones are arranged according to their proportion and are fitly joined to one another. But what most draws everyone's eyes is the marvelous and—according to the custom of that ancient age—quite crude structure of images and statues, which recommends the majesty of antiquity.

## USE.

For what uses it was once manufactured is investigated no less anxiously than the meaning of the emblems with which it is adorned. There are those who think it served the role of a trumpet or a <term>clarion</term> <note>original: *litui*, a curved military horn</note> in war, to fire up the spirits of the soldiers, to rally a failing line, and to sound the signal. There are those who believe that Kings used it in hunts to summon companions and dogs. There are those who think that in sacrifices our <term>Skalds</term> <note>original: *Scaldros*, the court poets and historians of the Viking Age</note>, <term>Runes</term> <note>original: *Runas*; Worm likely refers here to runic masters or those versed in ancient wisdom</note>, and priests called together and invited the people with its sound and braying. There are those who would have it assigned to holding some precious balsam or oil at the anointing of Kings, so that the oily liquid poured through the larger opening would drip onto the head through the narrower one. Others say it served the purpose of a drinking cup. But so that we may come to a somewhat more certain knowledge of this, we must look a little more deeply into the history of horns, and bring forward those things which concern their nature, types, properties, and use in general, so that finally—

<header>BOOK FIVE.</header>

...at last let us come to our own [subject]. Intending to strengthen our assertions with the testimonies of authors of better reputation, we begin from the word itself.

### WHAT IS A HORN.

"Horn" is called *keras* <note>original Greek: κέρας</note> by the Greeks and *cornus* by Priscian; Varro believes it is named from its "curvature" <note>original Latin: *à curvore*</note>. Others derive it from the Hebrew *Keren* <note>original: קרן</note>, which also denotes a horn. To us, as to the Germans, it is called **Horn**, with the Latin "C" changed into a roughened "H."

It is a part of an animal—for the most part a cloven-hoofed one—that is flexible and capable of being split, matching the skin in color, grown onto the head for the sake of ornament and protection. This is its genuine and proper meaning. Meanwhile, authors of high standing have transferred this word to denote other things that have a similarity or affinity with the horns of animals.

Philostratus, in his *Life of Apollonius*, attributes a "horn" to the sky, calling the western region of the heavens the "evening horn" <note>original Greek: Το εσπέριον κέρας</note>.

Of the Moon, Virgil writes in the 3rd book of the *Aeneid*:
> *Now the third horns of the Moon fill themselves with light.*

Henry II—son of Francis I of the family surnamed Valois and King of the Franks—displayed as his <term>Symbol</term> <note>a heraldic device or personal emblem</note> a triple moon rising into horns; you may see an illustration of this among the *Heroic Symbols* of Paradin, published at Antwerp by Plantin. Because some interpreted that he wore this as a gesture to the Emperor of the Turks (with whom his father Francis had struck a treaty), the physician Balduinus Ronseus cleared him of this suspicion in his *Medicinal Letters*, book 16. For inscribed upon this image was: **UNTIL IT FILLS THE WHOLE WORLD.** <note>original Latin: *DONEC TOTUM COMPLEAT ORBEM*</note>. It is established that he wished to suggest nothing else by this than that he would not cease until he possessed the whole world, as Ronseus interprets it; or rather, until he had filled the whole world with the fame of his name. Or, as Paradin explains by understanding the "Moon" to mean the Church, the King seems to promise it certain help and defense; so that once the Church is finally brought back under one God, one King, and one law, the lovely unity and vastness of the entire flock acknowledging a single shepherd might appear.

Both the Greeks and Latins called the parts of a battle line protruding from either side "wings" or "horns" <note>original Greek: κέρατα (*kerata*); original Latin: *cornua*</note>. Thus Caesar writes in Book 1 of the *Gallic War*: *He himself joined battle from the right horn (wing).* Terence writes in *The Eunuch*: *Into the center of this line; you, Donax, to the left horn (wing), and you, Syriscus, to the right.* And Lucan in Book 7 of the *Pharsalia*:

> The ill-fated battle line stood in a fixed order, 
> Not rashly sent into the fields; the care of the left horn (wing) 
> Was yours, Lentulus.

He used *cornus* in the second case <note>the genitive or possessive case</note>, because those words which now end in **U** once also had the ending *US* in the nominative, as the most famous Bangius <note>Thomas Bang (1600–1661), a Danish philologist and theologian</note> rightly noted in his *Philological Observations*, page 95. For this reason, Pliny took great delight in this specific ending. In Book 20, chapter 9: *It is said they are put to flight by the smell of a horn (cornus), if it be burned.* Chapter 11: *The flour or ash of a goat's horn (cornus), and even more so of a buck's. And a little later: With the ash of a stag's horn (cornus), they anoint their sores.* Also near the end of the same chapter: *Some consider the flour of raw horn (cornus) to be more effective for all these same uses.* From this comes the *Corniculum* [little horn] in the cohorts of a Military Tribune, from which we get the *Cornicularius* <note>a Roman military administrative officer</note> who presides over the cohorts of a military tribune. As seen in Tranquillus <note>the historian Suetonius</note>, chapter 17: *Clodianus the cornicularius and Maximus attacked him while he was wounded and resisting.* Valerius Maximus, Book 6, chapter 1: *To whom Cominius, Tribune of the Plebs, appointed a day before the people because he had summoned his cornicularius for the purpose of debauchery.* Tranquillus, in *On Famous Grammarians* regarding Orbilius: *First he performed the office of an apparitor for the magistrates, then served as a corniculum (adjutant) in Macedonia.* In the first book of Maccabees, chapter 9, the word "horn" <note>original Greek: τὸ κέρας (*to keras*)</note> frequently occurs as a term for a part of a battle line. In verse 1: *And the right horn (wing) with them.* In verse 10: *Bacchides was indeed on the right horn (wing).* Again in verse 15: *And he crushed the right horn (wing).*

The bends of rivers and the curvatures of their channels are also given this name, either because of a certain resemblance, or because rivers were numbered among the Divinities, as Charles Paschalius argues in *On Crowns*, Book 10, chapter 4. In Lycophron, the Ocinarus river is called "well-horned" <note>original Greek: ἐσκεράς (*eskeras*)</note> on account of its violence. Statius, in Book 2 of the *Thebaid*, makes the river Inachus horned.

> of the victor-horse headland 
> leans hard toward the grandmother [the sea].
<note>original Greek: "ἔνθα λαμπέτας / ἱππονίϰου πρηῶνος εἰς τηθὴν ϰέρας / σϰληρὸν νένευϰεν." In the text, "ἱππονίϰου" is written with a ligature for "ου" over the kappa.</note>

It is likely that the ancients called all high points "horns." For this reason, Pindar used the phrase "high-horned rock" <note>original Greek: ὑψιϰέρατον πέτραν (*hypsikeraton petran*)</note> instead of "high summits" <note>original Greek: ὑψηλὰ ἀϰρωτήρια (*hypsēla akrōtēria*)</note>.

Not only the ridges of mountains, but even the winding hollows that lie beneath mountains are called "horns" by Oppian in his <term>Cynegetica</term> <note>a Greek poem on hunting</note> Book 4:

> He who dwelt at the top of the mountain under a horned cave.
<note>original Greek: "Ὅς δ' ὕπατον μὲν ἔναιεν ὄρει ϰεραέσσεν ὑπ' ἄντρῳ."</note>

The very lands projected further into the sea, which they call *Chersonesos* <note>peninsulas</note>, are endowed with this name by the poets. Thus Lycophron says of the Thracian shore:

> The Mazusian [promontory] projecting with a land-horn.
<note>original Greek: "Μαζυσία πρόϰυσα Χερσαίῳ ϰέρῳ."</note>

Hence that elegant response of Demetrius given to Philip is noted by Plutarch in his *Life of Aratus*: *If indeed,* he said, *you have the soul of a prophet, you will leave this place; but if you have the soul of a King, you will hold the ox (meaning the Peloponnese) by both horns.*
<note>original Latin: "Siquidem, inqvit, vatis habes animam deferes locum: si Regis utroq; cornu bovem (id est Peloponesum) retinebis."</note>

It is even clear from Ovid's *Letters from Exile* [Tristia], Book 1, that books also had their own "horns," as he speaks to his book:

> *May you bear neither white horns on your black forehead.*
<note>original Latin: "Candida nec nigra cornua fronte geras." In ancient scrolls, "horns" (cornua) were the decorative knobs at the ends of the rod around which the papyrus was wrapped.</note>

In this same sense, Martial said:

> *A book unrolled for us all the way to its horns.*
<note>original Latin: "Explicitum nobis usq; ad sua cornua librum."</note>

> He who dwelt upon the mountain under a horned cave.
<note>original Greek: Ὅς δ᾽ ὕπατον μέν ἔναιεν ὄρει κεραέσσεν ὑπ᾽ ἄντρῳ.</note>

The lands themselves that project further into the sea, which they call <term>Chersonesos</term> <note>From the Greek for "dry island," meaning a peninsula.</note>, are gifted with this name by the Poets. Thus Lycophron says of the Thracian shore:
> The Mazusian headland projecting from the horn of the land.
<note>original Greek: Μαζουσία πρόχουσα Χερσαίῳ κέρως.</note>

From this, that elegant response of Demetrius given to Philip is noted by Plutarch in his *Life of Aratus*: *If indeed,* he said, *you have the soul of a priest, you will offer up the place; but if the soul of a King, you will hold the bull (that is, the Peloponnese) by both horns.*
<note>This refers to the strategic importance of holding certain fortified heights to control the entire peninsula of the Peloponnese.</note>

It is even evident from Ovid, in the first book of his *Tristia* [Sorrows], that books had their own "horns," as he addresses his book with these words:
> May you not wear white horns on a black forehead.
<note>original Latin: "Candida nec nigra cornua fronte geras." In the ancient world, books were scrolls. The "horns" (*cornua*) were the decorative knobs or ends of the central stick (*umbilicus*) around which the parchment was rolled.</note>

In this same sense, Martial said:
> The book unrolled for us even to its horns.

It demonstrates how ancient Greek and Latin authors used the term to denote any projecting, curved, or powerful extremity.</summary>

<page-num>360</page-num>
# DANISH MONUMENTS
<meta>catchword: sium</meta>

To make these matters clearer, it should be observed that books were once customarily written in a continuous flow, usually on a single page and roll: not as they are now, with cut sheets gathered into <term>quires</term><note>A quire is a set of leaves which are folded together; the ancestor of the modern bound book format.</note> or other forms. Because they were folded together and wound up like a spiral, they were called **volumes** (*volumina*), from the word for "rolling" (*volvendo*). At the very edge of the page, for the sake of stability, a very small rod made of cedar, boxwood, cypress, ebony, or ivory was glued along the width where the parchment had been trimmed. This they called the **umbilicus** <note>literally "the navel" or "center-point"</note>. When the volume was rolled up, the ends of this rod would protrude from either side; these were usually decorated with plates of silver, gold, or gems for ornament, and these are what are called the **horns** (*cornua*) of books. Several examples of such volumes, with their horns elegantly turned on a lathe, may be seen in the Library of the Royal University which is in **Copenhagen** <note>original Latin: "Hafniæ." This refers to the University of Copenhagen.</note>.

Ships also had their own "horns." What the Romans called <term>rostra</term><note>The "beak" or ram on the prow of a warship.</note>, the Greeks called *kerata* <note>original Greek: κέρατα, meaning "horns."</note>. Hence Aeschylus says in *Agamemnon*:
> And they, violently struck by horns, 
> vanished away in the storm, 
> amidst the surge and the crashing rain.
<note>original Greek: αἱ δὲ κερωτυπέμεναι βίᾳ / χειμῶνι, τύφω σὺν ζάλῃ τ’ ὀμβροκτύπῳ / ᾤχοντ' ἄφαντοι. The "horns" here refer to the prows of ships colliding in the chaos.</note>
They called ships *eukeraas* <note>original Greek: εὐκεράας</note> when they were well and strongly equipped with beaks or "horns," as in that line:
> To loose the well-horned ships and the mooring cables.
<note>original Greek: Νῆας ἐϋκεράας, ἀνά τε πρυμνήσια λῦσαι.</note>

The <term>yardarms</term><note>The horizontal poles on a mast that support the sails.</note> of ships were also equipped with their own "horns," regarding which Virgil says in the third book of the *Aeneid*:
> *We turn the horns of the sailed yards.*
<note>original Latin: "Cornua velatarum obvertimus antennarum." Here, "horns" refers to the pointed ends of the yardarms.</note>
And Valerius Flaccus in Book 1 of the *Argonautica*:
> *They hurry across the rowing-benches. These men set the*
> *horns free from the high mast.*
<note>original Latin: "Discurrunt transtris. Hi celso cornua malo / Expediunt."</note>

"Horns of the sails" are cited by Macrobius in Book 5 of the *Saturnalia*, chapter 21, from Asclepiades in this manner: *Asclepiades, a man among the Greeks of primary learning and diligence, thinks that the "carchesia" <note>the upper part of a mast or a type of drinking cup</note> were named from naval matters; for he says that the lower part of a ship’s sail is called the "pterna" <note>the heel</note>, while the part near the middle is called the "trachelon" <note>the neck</note>, and the uppermost part is the "carche-"*

<summary>This page explains the historical application of the term "horn" to the decorative ends of book scrolls (volumes) and the structural components of ships, such as the prows (rostra) and the ends of the yardarms.</summary>
<keywords>scrolls, volumes, umbilicus, Copenhagen, ship construction, rostra, yardarms, Aeschylus, Virgil, ancient seafaring</keywords>

<meta>catchword: Ca-</meta>

...to be called the <note>original: "...fium nominari"</note> and from there to spread out on either side into those parts called **horns**.

It is well-established that altars had their own horns from **Jeremiah 17:1**:
> The sin of Judah is written with a pen of iron, engraved with a point of diamond upon the breadth of their hearts and upon the **horns of their altars**.

In this context, some interpret "horns" to mean simply "either side." Writers of the Middle Ages used the term in the same sense. In the *Collection of Canons* by **Burchard**, Book 2, it says: 
> "Therefore I, Burchard, by God’s favor Bishop of the Church of Worms, establish through this testament of authority that a certain servant of our church named Eberhard, who has been offered for holy orders, shall—at the **horn of the altar** and in the presence of noble men—be from this day and time forward a free man, secure from every bond of servitude." 

Similarly, in Book 1 of the *Capitularies* <term>Capitularies are collections of royal decrees, particularly those of the Frankish kings</term> of **Charlemagne**, from the Pithou Library, Chapter 88: 
> "Whenever a useful member of the church family is found worthy of ordination, let that authority be read before the people in the <term>ambo</term><note>A raised pulpit or lectern used in early churches.</note> and before the priests, or before the faithful laity in front of the **horns of the altar**, as is contained in our decree, etc."

**Cicero** mentions the "horns of syllogisms" in Book 2 of *On Divination*:
> "Let us try, then," he says, "if we can move the **horns** of your disputation." 

**Clement of Alexandria** mentions the "horned syllogism" in Book 5 of the *Stromata* <note>original Latin: "Syllogismi cornuti." This refers to a type of logical dilemma or sophism where every path leads to a "strike" against the opponent.</note>. **Seneca** also discusses this in *Letter 45*: 
> "But he who is asked whether he has **horns** is not so foolish as to feel his own forehead, nor is he so dull or slow-witted that he does not know he lacks what you have persuaded him he possesses through your very subtle argument. Such things deceive without causing harm, just as the cups and pebbles of jugglers <note>Seneca is comparing logical fallacies to a "shell game" or "cups and balls" magic trick.</note> do, in which the very deception delights me."

Consult other authors regarding the **horns** on either side of a litter <note>A portable carriage or bed carried by people or animals.</note> or on buildings. "In the **horn of the portico** there is a very spacious bed-chamber," as **Pliny** says in Book 5 of his *Letters*.

**Charles Paschal**, in Book 4, Chapter 21 of his work *On Crowns*, claims that the two **horns** of the episcopal miters and <term>infulae</term><note>The decorative ribbons or bands on a bishop's miter.</note> signify the sanctity and learning for which a Bishop should be distinguished. **Silius Italicus**, in Book 25, teaches that the miter of **Bacchus** was likewise horned, as was the miter of the Priest of **Ammon Nabidis**.

**Cælius Rhodiginus** <note>Ludovico Ricchieri (1469–1525), a Venetian humanist scholar.</note> reports in Book 30, Chapter 1, that "horns" is found to be used in place of "hair" among the Greek grammarians. <note>original: "Et madido torquentem cornua cirrho." Juvenal uses "horns" here to describe a specific curled hairstyle or perhaps the appearance of hair stiffened with ointment.</note>

Anatomists attribute horns to the wombs of animals. In cows, deer, sheep, goats, and animals of that kind, the womb is bipartite and divided into two "horns," as it were. Some have even attributed horns to the human womb. However, by these "horns," **Varolus** <note>Costanzo Varolio (1543–1575), an Italian anatomist and physician to Pope Gregory XIII.</note> understands the lower ligaments, called <term>kerēathēres</term> <note>original Greek: κηρηαθήρες; referring to horn-like projections or appendages.</note> by some. There is also a type of oblong, curved wart which **Avicenna** <note>The famous Persian polymath Ibn Sina (c. 980–1037).</note> calls a "horn" because of the resemblance it has to a horn. For he discusses this in Book 4, Fen 7, Tractate 3, Chapter 8: *"Horns are thick, nail-like additions growing over the joints at the extremities, caused by the intensity of exertion."* **Scaliger** <note>Julius Caesar Scaliger (1484–1558), a celebrated scholar and physician.</note> seems to have had this passage in mind in *Exercise 199*, Section 5, when he says: *"In man, it is not a monster, but a disease."* Regarding this, when the prince **Aboali** <note>Another name for Avicenna.</note> and the great man **Abumeron** <note>Avenzoar (1094–1162), an influential Arab physician from Al-Andalus.</note> told stories of it, I was indeed led to believe it on their authority, until we ourselves saw one on the back of a certain rower who had been on a Ligurian galley for a long time. <note>This refers to a "cutaneous horn," a hard skin tumor made of keratin that can resemble a small animal horn.</note>

The ancients also used to depict **Sleep** with a horn, according to **Servius** in his commentary on Book 7 of the *Aeneid*. Hence **Seneca** says in his *Apocolocyntosis*:

...specifically, and distinguishing it from Ivory, **Macrobius** <note>Macrobius Ambrosius Theodosius (5th century AD), a Roman provincial and Neoplatonist whose commentary on *The Dream of Scipio* was immensely popular in the Middle Ages.</note> writes in *The Dream of Scipio*, Chapter 3: *When the veil of sleep allows the gaze of the soul to look inward toward the truth during rest, it is believed to come from Horn, the nature of which is such that, when thinned, it is permeable to the sight; but when it dulls and repels the gaze from the truth, it is thought to be Ivory.* <note>original: "Velamen somni cum in quiete ad verum usq; aciem animae introspicientis admittit, de Cornu creditur, cujus ista natura est, ut tenuatum visui pervium sit: cum à verò hebetat ac repellit obtutum, Ebur putatur." This refers to the classical "Gates of Sleep": true dreams pass through horn, while false ones pass through ivory.</note>

**Pierius** <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani (1477–1558), an Italian humanist and author of a famous treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs and symbols.</note> reports in Book 41 that the Crown, which is a royal garment, is named from the word "horn" <note>original: "A cornu Coronam." Horns, rays of light, and the crown seem to correspond with one another. Hence **Moses** is depicted with a horned face, though it ought to have been depicted as radiating light. *Upon his face,* says **Clement of Alexandria** <note>A Christian theologian (c. 150–215 AD) who sought to unite Greek philosophy with Christian faith.</note> in Book 6 of the *Stromata* (Miscellanies), *there rested a certain glorified outward appearance,* <note>original Greek: ἐπίχροιά τις δεδοξασμένη</note> a kind of glorified beauty of color. This is what the Poet seems to wish to express when he says:

> The lawgiver himself, that old man, shows himself to us,
> Balancing fiery lights on his horned face,
> And carrying the sacred laws in his holy books.

In what sense **Tertullian** <note>Tertullian (c. 155–220 AD), a prolific early Christian author from Carthage.</note>, in his book *Against the Jews*, attributes "horns" to Christ is clear from his own words. *For Joseph is also blessed,* he says, by his father with these words: *His beauty is that of a bull; his horns are the horns of a unicorn. With them he shall winnow <note>original: "ventilabit," which can mean to toss with horns or to winnow grain (separating the good from the bad).</note> the nations together to the ends of the earth.* *Certainly, no rhinoceros was intended as the unicorn, nor a Minotaur as the two-horned one: but Christ was signified by that figure. A bull on account of both dispositions: fierce to some, as a judge; gentle to others, as a savior, whose "horns" were valued. For in the yardarm of a ship, which is a part of the cross, its extremities are called by this name [horns]. The "Unicorn," however, refers to the post in the middle of the structure. Finally, by this power of the cross and in this "horned" manner, he even now winnows all nations through faith, lifting them from earth to heaven, and then he will winnow them through judgment, descending from heaven to earth.*

[...radiance upon his face] <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion of Moses.</note> that made it difficult for people to look at him.

In these matters, it is widely acknowledged that horns are properly attributed to animals, specifically to those with **cloven hooves** <term>bisulcis: animals like cows or goats whose hooves are divided into two parts</term>. If horns are granted to others—whether animate or inanimate—great Latin authors rightly assert that this does not happen properly, but rather outside the ordinary course of Nature. Aristotle himself, in Book 3 of *On the Parts of Animals*, chapter 2, demonstrates that *Animals having many-toed feet lack horns, because a horn is provided for the sake of defense, and for the many-toed animals, other defenses are not lacking.* For Nature gave claws to some, fighting teeth to others, and to others yet another part by which they are able to protect and defend themselves. **Single-hoofed** <term>Solipeda: animals like horses with a single, solid hoof</term> animals also lack horns, with the exception of the Indian Wild Ass, which bears a single horn. Some maintain that no animals which have small teeth in the upper jaw possess horns. However, Herodotus is a witness that horned Asses are found among the Africans, and Aelian records them among the Scythians. Pliny writes of horned Wild Boars in India, and Agatharchides mentions them in Ethiopia. Aelian also relates that Caspian goats are without horns.

Regarding those horns attributed to aquatic marine creatures and others of that kind, Pliny denies they are true horns in Book 11, chapter 37. *Horns,* he says, *are given in various ways to many aquatic, marine, and serpentine creatures, but those which are rightly understood as horns belong only to the genus of quadrupeds.*

### HORNED MEN.

And although, based on the same reasoning, Pliny rejects as fabulous the horns of *Actaeon and Cippus Genitius* <note>Actaeon was a hunter in Greek myth transformed into a stag; Genucius Cippus was a Roman praetor who allegedly grew horns on his forehead, which was interpreted as a sign he would become king.</note>—about whom Valerius Maximus writes in Book 5, chapter 6, and Charles Paschal in Book 19 of *On Crowns*, chapter 4—nevertheless, reliable observations teach that Horned Men have been found outside the normal course of Nature. And do not think we are speaking of those whom the Italians call *Becco Cornuto* <note>Italian for "horned goat," a derogatory term for a cuckold, or a man whose wife is unfaithful.</note>. I do not know if that man was among their number who fixed large Aurochs' horns to his house with this attached inscription:

-> I wear the horns, and this I know, <-
-> Many wear them who do not know. <-

The very sharp-witted Owen <note>John Owen (c. 1564–1622), a Welsh epigrammatist famous for his Latin verse.</note> airs a witty problem regarding men of this sort in Book 1, Epigram 163:

> *If ever a wife violates the sacred laws of the marriage bed,*
> *Why does the undeserving husband wear horns? Because he is the Head.*
> <note>original: "Si quando sacra jura thori violaverit uxor / Cur gerit immeritus cornua vir? Caput est." This is a pun on the husband being the "head" of the household, while horns literally grow on a head.</note>

Rather, he means the horns of wild beasts hung upon oaks for the sake of Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt</note>. For Propertius <note>A Roman elegiac poet</note> suggests in Book 2 that horns dedicated to the deities were hung from sacred trees:

> *I myself will hunt; even now it pleases me to undertake*

Symmachus <note>A 4th-century Roman statesman and orator</note> says in Book 5, Epistle 63: *For just as the horns of stags are given to the honor of the gods, and the teeth of boars are fixed to the thresholds; so the offerings of the woods are dedicated to the devotion of friends.*

To return to the Nature of horns: for the most part, they are hollow from the root, insofar as they surround a bone that, arising from the head, is inserted into the cavity and fills it entirely. However, they end in a solid point and consist of a simple part at the extremity, as witnessed by Aristotle <note>The famous Greek philosopher and scientist</note> in Book 3 of *History of Animals*, Chapter 9. Yet he exempts stags, which have horns that are entirely solid and spread into branches, and which fall off every year unless they are castrated. Through stags, moreover, Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century German bishop and philosopher who wrote extensively on nature</note> teaches in *On Animals*, Book 2, Chapter 2, Treatise 1, that the rest of that nature is to be understood. *The horns*, he says, *of all animals are empty near the head, and there enters a certain hard substance, almost bony and porous, except for the horn of the stag and those which agree in similarity with the stag.* Hence the same author, in *On Animals*, Book 12, Treatise 3, Chapter 7, does not hesitate to assert: *The horns of stags are more the "purgings" of Nature than weapons; because they shed them, and females do not have horns because they possess less heat and earthly dryness.* In the cited passage, the Philosopher <note>Commonly referring to Aristotle</note> reports that horns adhere to the skin rather than the bone, whence it happens that in Phrygia <note>An ancient kingdom in the west-central part of Anatolia, modern-day Turkey</note> and elsewhere, there are oxen that move their horns just like ears.

The material from which they are generated is nourishment which they have received partly from the mother and partly from external sources, by which the rest of the body is increased and nourished. For thus he says in Book 2 of *Generation of Animals*, Chapter 6: *Nails, hair, horns, the beaks of birds, spurs, and if there is any other such thing, [come] <term>from acquired and growth-promoting nourishment</term> <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς ἐπικτήτου τροφῆς, καὶ τῆς αὐξητικῆς</note>, which they acquire both from the female [mother] and from the outside.* Aelian <note>A 3rd-century Roman teacher and rhetorician who wrote in Greek about animals</note> does not disagree in Book 12 of *On Animals*, Chapter 20, where [the cause] of the growth of horns...

### THE VARIETY OF HORNS.

How great, indeed, is the variety of horns, and how much Nature sports <margin>,,</margin> in them <note>The concept of *lusus naturae* or "Nature's joke" refers to unusual or playful natural formations</note>, I shall report in the very words of Pliny <margin>,,</margin> <note>Gaius Plinius Secundus, the 1st-century Roman author of *Natural History*</note>, who seems to have investigated the matter most diligently. Thus he writes in Book 11, Chapter 37: <margin>,,</margin>

> Nowhere else <margin>,,</margin> is there greater playfulness. Nature has sported with the weapons of animals. <margin>,,</margin> She spread these into branches, as with stags; to others she granted simple ones, <margin>,,</margin> as with the "spike-bucks" <note>original: *subulonibus*, young deer with unbranched horns resembling a shoemaker's awl</note> in that same genus, so named from the shape. In others, she fashioned them into <margin>,,</margin> palms and sent out fingers from them, whence they call them "Broad-horns" <margin>,,</margin> <note>original Greek: *Platycerotas*, likely referring to fallow deer</note>. She gave branched horns to roe deer, but small ones, and <margin>,,</margin> did not make them deciduous <note>shedding annually</note>; for the ram kind, she twisted them <margin>,,</margin> into a coil so they might endure like a boxing glove <note>original: *caestus*</note>, and made them <margin>,,</margin> dangerous for bulls. In this genus, she granted them even to females, <margin>,,</margin> whereas in many others, only to the males. In chamois, they are hooked toward <margin>,,</margin> the back; in fallow deer, toward the front. Upright, moreover, and twisted <margin>,,</margin> with a circuit of wrinkles, and sharpened to a slight point (so that you <margin>,,</margin> might call them Lyres), she gave to the *Strepsiceros* <note>The "twisted-horn" antelope</note>, which Africa <margin>,,</margin> calls the Addax. These are movable just like ears in the herds of Phrygia. <margin>,,</margin> In the Troglodytes <note>A legendary people of Africa</note>, they are directed toward the ground, for which <margin>,,</margin> reason they graze with their necks tilted. To others, she gave a single horn, <margin>,,</margin> and this in the middle of the head or on the nose. And now, for some they are <margin>,,</margin> robust for charging, for others for striking; some are hooked forward, others <margin>,,</margin> hooked backward; for others, suited for throwing in many ways—upturned, <margin>,,</margin> turned back, joined—all tapering to a sharp point. In a certain genus, they <margin>,,</margin> serve as hands for scratching the body; in snails, for testing the path— <margin>,,</margin> these are fleshy, as in the horned vipers <note>original: *cerastis*</note>; sometimes they are <margin>,,</margin> single, but in snails always double, and able to be extended and retracted. <margin>,,</margin>

Thus far Pliny. That he denies horns are deciduous in roe deer <margin>,,</margin> is something Caelius Rhodiginus <note>A Renaissance scholar</note>, following Pausanias <note>A Greek traveler and geographer</note>, thinks is contrary to experience, because he writes that just like stags, the horns of gazelles <note>original: *Dorcadum*</note> also fall off and regrow. In Africa, Nieremberg <note>Juan Eusebio Nieremberg, a 17th-century naturalist</note> asserts that rams are born already bearing horns; the same author, in Book 7, Chapter 2 of his *Natural History*, recounts <margin>,,</margin> that he saw a horse with a horn in the court of King Philip. ...than that I should think Apuleius <note>Lucius Apuleius, a 2nd-century Roman writer</note> in that passage means horns prodigiously grown out of an oak tree; rather, he refers to the horns of wild beasts, hung upon oaks in honor of Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt</note>. Indeed, Propertius <note>Sextus Propertius, a Roman elegiac poet</note> suggests in Book 2 that horns dedicated to the gods were hung from sacred trees:

> *I myself shall hunt; even now it pleases me to undertake*
> *The rites of Diana, and to offer my vows to Venus.*
> *I shall begin to capture wild beasts, and return the horns*
> *To the pine tree, and I myself shall urge on the bold dogs.*

Symmachus <note>Quintus Aurelius Symmachus, a 4th-century Roman statesman</note> writes in Book 5, Letter 63: *For just as it is granted to the honor of the deities to consecrate the horns of stags, and to fix the teeth of boars to the thresholds; so the offerings of the forests are dedicated to the service of friends.*

To return to the nature of horns: for the most part, they are hollow at the root, insofar as they surround the bone that grows from the head; this bone is inserted into the cavity and fills it entirely. However, they end in a solid point and consist of a simple extremity, as Aristotle <note>The Greek philosopher and scientist</note> testifies in Book 3 of the *History of Animals*, Chapter 9. He excepts stags <note>deer</note>, however, which have horns that are entirely solid and spread into branches, and which are shed every year <note>deciduous</note>, unless the animal is castrated. Albertus Magnus <note>A 13th-century German bishop and philosopher</note> teaches in *On Animals*, Book 2, Chapter 2, Treatise 1, that other animals of a similar nature are to be understood through the example of stags. *The horns of all animals,* he says, *are empty near the head, and there a certain hard substance enters, almost bony and porous, except for the horn of the stag and those which resemble the stag in likeness.* Hence the same author, in *On Animals*, Book 12, Treatise 3, Chapter 7, does not hesitate to assert: *The horns of stags are more the purgings of Nature than weapons; they cast them off, and females—because they have less terrestrial heat and dryness—therefore do not have horns.* In the aforementioned passage, the Philosopher <note>Aristotle</note> reports that horns adhere to the skin rather than the bone, which is why in Phrygia <note>An ancient region in modern-day Turkey</note> and elsewhere, there are oxen that move their horns just as they do their ears.

The material from which they are generated is nutrition, which they receive partly from the mother and partly from external sources, and by which the rest of the body is increased and nourished. For thus he writes in Book 2 of *On the Generation of Animals*, Chapter 6: *Nails, hair, horns, the beaks of birds, spurs, and if there is any other such thing, [are formed] from acquired and augmentative nutrition* <note>original Greek: ἐκ τῆς ἐπικτήτου τροφῆς, καὶ τῆς αὐξητικῆς</note>, *which they acquire both from the female and from the outside.* Aelian <note>Claudius Aelianus, a Roman teacher and rhetorician</note> does not disagree in Book 12 of *On Animals*, Chapter 20, where the cause of the growth of horns...

## THE VARIETY OF HORNS.

<margin>cc</margin>
Indeed, as to how great the variety of horns may be, and how much Nature has played with them, I shall relate in the very words of Pliny <note>Pliny the Elder, a 1st-century Roman author of *Natural History*</note>, who seems to have pursued the matter most diligently. Thus he writes in Book 11, Chapter 37: *In no other place is there greater extravagance; Nature has sported with the weapons of animals. She has scattered them into branches, as with stags; to others she has granted simple horns, as with the young "spike-bucks" <term>subulones; young deer with unbranched horns</term> of the same genus, named for the evidence of their shape. For others, she fashioned them into palms and sent out fingers from them, from which they are called "broad-horns" <note>original: *Platycerotas*; likely fallow deer</note>. She gave branched horns to roe deer, but small ones, and did not make them deciduous <note>shedding annually</note>; they are wound into a coil for the ram kind, so that they might endure like a weighted glove <note>original: *cæstus*; a leather wrap used in ancient boxing</note>, yet they are dangerous to bulls. In this kind she indeed granted them to females, whereas in many others they are only for males. They are hooked toward the back in chamois, and forward in drakes. Moreover, they are upright and twisted with a circuit of wrinkles, and sharpened to a smooth point (so that you might call them Lyres) in the twisted-horn antelope, which Africa calls the Addax. These same horns are mobile like ears in the herds of Phrygia. Those of the Troglodytes <note>An ancient tribe in Ethiopia/Red Sea coast</note> are directed toward the earth, for which reason they graze with their necks tilted. Some have single horns, and this is in the middle of the head or on the nose. To some they are for charging, being robust; to others for striking; some are hooked inward, others bent backward; some for tossing, and in many modes: tilted back, turned, joined together, all passing into a sharp point. In a certain kind, they serve instead of hands for scratching the body; in snails, for testing the path—these are fleshy, just as in the horned viper; sometimes there is one, but in snails there are always two, and they are made to be extended and retracted.* Thus says Pliny.

That he denies horns are shed by roe deer is something Caelius Rhodiginus <note>An Italian Renaissance scholar</note>, following Pausanias <note>A 2nd-century Greek traveler</note>, thinks contradicts experience, because he writes that the horns of the gazelle <note>original: *Dorcadum*</note>, just like those of stags, fall off and grow back. Nieremberg <note>Juan Eusebio Nieremberg, a 17th-century Spanish naturalist</note> asserts that in Africa, rams are born already bearing horns; he also narrates in Book 7, Chapter 2 of his *Natural History* that he saw a horse with a horn in the court of King Philip <note>Philip IV of Spain</note>. Varthema <note>Ludovico di Varthema, an Italian explorer</note> writes that he saw oxen with the horns of stags. In the province of Aden, wethers <note>castrated rams</note> entirely lack ears, in place of which small horns protrude. Even a horned hare and dog have been seen, and examples of these indeed exist here in Copenhagen <note>original: *Hafniæ*</note>.

This horn was certainly of an admirable shape, for it consisted entirely of thick bony scales, arranged like overlapping tiles <note>original: "imbricatim," referring to the way roof tiles overlap</note>; it curved backwards. At the bottom part, where it was joined to the head, it was provided with sixteen rows of scales, which then twisted obliquely from the bottom to the top (following their series from left to right) and reached a total number of sixty-two; the uppermost part had only eight rows. However, following the series from right to left, each row was found to consist of seventy-two scales, because they were twisted more sharply. The color of the scales was partly dark and some were even white; and in the individual gaps between the scales, certain bristles still appeared. Whether the horn was mobile might be doubted, since in its internal and hollow part it still retained certain membranes, which would give proof that this part had not been filled with some solid material or bone, but only with flesh. Thus far Clusius <note>Charles de l'Écluse (1526–1609), a pioneering doctor and botanist whose works were foundational to natural history</note>.

But to frankly state what I think of this horn, saving the judgment of others: I strongly doubt whether this object was the horn of any animal at all. The occasion for my doubt is provided by Clusius himself, when he frankly admits its cavity was not filled with a bony, spongy, or cartilaginous substance, but only with flesh. Whether it is permitted to conclude that it was the tail of some larger serpent or amphibian, hollowed out, cleaned, and dried, let others see. We see the tail of the <term>Beaver (Castor)</term> marked with scales, although it does not end in a point. ### THE USES OF HORNS.

Since Nature plays with the structure of horns in so many and such diverse ways that they can hardly be reduced to certain classes, we will not be overly laborious in reviewing them; instead, we shall proceed directly to investigating their uses, and setting aside those which contribute to Medicine, let us at least pursue others.

The ancients fixed them to the shafts of spears to make them sharper, as Maro <note>The Roman poet Virgil (Publius Vergilius Maro)</note> bears witness in Book 5 of the *Aeneid*:

> They carry two shafts of cornel-wood tipped with iron. <note>original: *Cornea bina ferunt præfixa hastilia ferro*. Note: Worm interprets the Latin *cornea* here as "made of horn," though in Virgil’s context it usually refers to the cornel cherry tree, a hard wood used for spears.</note>

And Quintus of Smyrna <note>original: *Quinto Calabro*, a 4th-century Greek epic poet who wrote the *Posthomerica*</note> in Book 9:

> Before him lay his great bow, 
> fitted together from curved horns. <note>original Greek: Πάρονθε δὲ οἱ μέγα τόξον / Κεῖτε πέλας γναμπτοῖσιν ἀρηράμενον κεράεσσι</note>

By which he teaches that bows were accustomed to be joined together from bent horns. Strabo <note>A Greek geographer (64 BCE–24 CE)</note>, in Book 6, writes that certain Ethiopian tribes use horns as weapons when they must go against an enemy—perhaps in the same manner as the Lapps <note>original: *Lapones*</note> do now. Our Greenlanders, who lack veins of iron, are accustomed to arm their oars, javelins, arrows, and spears with horns. But for the most part, they take the horns of Reindeer <note>original: *Rangiferorum*</note> for these uses, adapted into various forms, and sometimes cut into plates, with which they know how to supply the lack of iron quite aptly. This is abundantly clear from their various instruments which I keep among other rarities in my Museum.

Among the Persians, according to Xenophon's testimony, there were **horn-tipped spears** <term>keratina palta</term> <note>original: κεράτινα παλτά</note>, or horny javelins, used in battle.

It is evident from the surviving monuments of antiquity that our ancestors fashioned shields and other weapons for themselves from horns. Regarding shields made of horn, there is a passage in the *Book of Heroes* <note>original: *Heldenbuch*, a 15th-century collection of Middle High German epic poetry</note> concerning Wolfdietrich:

From this, Opitz <note>Martin Opitz (1597–1639), a German poet</note>, in his notes to verse 27 of the *Rhyme of St. Anno*, relates that Siegfried <note>The legendary hero of the Nibelungenlied</note>, the son-in-law of Gibich, King of the Vangiones, obtained his name. For he was commonly called "Horned Siegfried" <note>original: *Hornin Sufrid*, *corneus Sufridus*</note>, not because he was made of horn himself, but because he carried weapons woven from horn and sinew, as Goldast <note>Melchior Goldast (1578–1635), a Swiss pastoralist and scholar</note> noted.

<margin>Book 1, Scene 1, line 185</margin>
Ox horns, sliced into very thin plates, are placed into lanterns so that they might spread the enclosed light more widely and shut out the blasts of the wind. Hence Plautus says in *Amphitruo*, Act 1, Scene 1, line 185:

> *Where are you walking to, you who carry Vulcan <note>The god of fire, here representing the flame of the lantern</note> enclosed in horn?*

And Lucretius in Book 2:

> *Furthermore, light passes through horn; yet the rain*
> *is rejected.*

Even thinner plates, dyed with various colors, serve those who imitate flowers, herbs, and buds for decoration. In a similar way, the ancients once crafted their <term>Cerostrota</term> <note>A type of decorative inlay work made of horn or wax</note>, about which Pliny wrote in the passage cited above in this manner: *“They are gathered for luxuries, now dyed, now smeared over, now as those things called <term>Cerostrota</term>, a type of painting.”* According to Daléchamps <note>Jacques Daléchamps (1513–1588), a French physician and botanist</note> in his commentary on that passage of Pliny, <term>Cerostrota</term> were actually made from small tiles of horn, painted with various colors and inset into wood. For horns are very compliant in nature, even in the living bodies of the animals themselves, so much so that they can be bent with hot wax and, if cut while growing, can be twisted in different directions so that four horns might grow on a single head.

Large ox horns are also suitable for combs, and for the flasks in which soldiers keep their gunpowder, as well as for inkwells and other items of that kind. In my Museum, images are preserved that were elegantly made from horn reduced to a mass and poured into molds so that they stand out in relief; these compete in color, luster, and lightness with those carved from ebony with a chisel.

Shepherds first used horns to call and gather their flocks and cattle, which is why the poets often use the word <term>Buccina</term> <note>A curved trumpet, originally made from a shell or horn</note> in place of "horn." In this sense, Propertius says:

Bbb

<meta>This page continues the catalog of the various uses of horns in antiquity, transitioning from domestic and decorative uses to their role in summoning assemblies, signaling in pastoral life, and their eventual adaptation for military use.</meta>

<page-num>373</page-num>
<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

->Now within the walls the horn of the slow shepherd<-
->sings.<-
<note>original Latin: "Nunc intra muros pastoris buccina lenti / Cantat."</note>

And Columella <note>Lucius Junius Moderatus Columella (4–70 AD), a Roman writer on agriculture</note> says in Book 4: *“To the sound of the horn, the livestock are accustomed to return to the enclosures.”* So it seems that in ancient times there was no distinction between a horn <note>original: *cornu*</note> and a <term>buccina</term> <note>a curved trumpet originally made from a seashell or horn</note>, even according to the testimony of Lipsius <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606), a famous Flemish scholar</note> in Book 4 of *The Roman Military*. From this, they began to use it to call together the people and the assembly, as Lucilius <note>Gaius Lucilius, the Roman satirist</note> can testify in Book 7:

->Let them gather the assembly with a hoarse sound and curved horns.<-
<note>original Latin: "Rauco conventionem sonitu & curvis cogant cornubus."</note>

Nonnius, in his entry for *Cogere* (To Gather), suggests that it is more correct to read "assembly" <note>original: *concionem*</note> instead of "gathering" <note>original: *conventionem*</note>. Thus Dionysius <note>Dionysius of Halicarnassus, a Greek historian</note> in Book 2 says: *Certain attendants of the common people, sounding ox horns, gathered them for assemblies.* <note>original Greek: "τῆς δημοτικῆς ὑπηρέται τινες κέρασι βοείοις ἐμβυκάνωντες, ἐπὶ τὰς ἐκκλησίας συνῆγον."</note> Propertius <note>Sextus Propertius, a Roman elegiac poet</note> suggests the same:

->The horn used to summon the ancient citizens to hear words.<-
<note>original Latin: "Buccina cogebat priscos ad verba Quirites." The term Quirites refers to the Roman citizens in a peaceful, civil capacity.</note>

Eventually, horns were transferred to use in wars to sound the <term>classicum</term> <note>the signal for battle</note>. Vegetius <note>a writer of the later Roman Empire</note> teaches this in Book 2, Chapter 22: *“It is called a 'classicum',”* he says, *“because the trumpeters blow it through the horn.”* And Seneca in *Oedipus*:

->The signal sounded from the curved horn.<-

Horace in Book 2, Ode 1:

->Even now you graze our ears with the threatening murmur of horns,<-
->even now the trumpets sound.<-

Fabius <note>Quintilian, the Roman rhetorician</note> in Book 2, Chapter 18, expresses the matter clearly: *“But what else,”* he says, *“do the horns and trumpets do in our legions? The more powerful their harmony is, the more Roman glory in war excels over others.”* Hence that line of Catullus:

->And many horns were breathing out hoarse-sounding blasts.<-

Varro, in Book 4 of *The Latin Language*, testifies that <term>tubas</term> <note>straight trumpets</note> and <term>lituos</term> <note>curved trumpets</note> were once made from horns. He says: *“The 'buccina' is a type of twisted trumpet, from which the horn-players were called 'buccanistae'; it is called a horn even if it is made of bronze, because they were first made from actual horns.”* Hence Virgil, shortly into the beginning of Book 8 of the *Aeneid*:

->As Turnus raised the signal of war from the Laurentine citadel,<-
->and the horns shrieked with a hoarse song.<-

The signal for leading out the army and for engaging in battle among the Roman Legions was a harmony of trumpets and horns, as we re-

...delays. Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century Neapolitan scholar known for his work on ancient customs, *Genialium dierum*</note> in Book 4, Chapter 2, adds: *“Tyrrhenus the Pisaean was the first to invent the bronze trumpet <note>original: tuba</note>, whereas previously it was made of ox horn. Among the Persians, the hour for setting out was also signaled by a horn. For the Parthians, horns—and often a massive drum with iron bells—sharpened their spirits for battle, as the same author testifies.”* But the exact distinction between trumpets and <term>buccinae</term> <note>a curved horn or trumpet</note> is noted by Vegetius <note>A 4th-century Roman writer on military matters</note> regarding the signals of the cohort. *“Some signals,”* he says, *“are vocal, some semi-vocal, and others are mute. Vocal signals are those pronounced by the human voice, as in the night watches. Semi-vocal signals are those given by horns, or the trumpet <note>original: tuba</note>, or the buccina. The Tuba is the name for the instrument that is straight; the Buccina is that which is bent back upon itself in a bronze circle; the Horn <note>original: cornu</note> is made from wild ox horns <note>original: uris agrestibus</note> bound with silver, and when tempered by art and the breath of the one playing, it emits a sound that can be heard.”* Ovid says in the first book of the *Metamorphoses*:

> The hollow buccina is taken up by him;
> Twisted into a wide coil, which grows from the bottom of the spiral.
<note>original Latin: "Cava buccina sumitur illi; / Tortilis in latum; quæ turbine crescit ab imo."</note>

Psalm 98, verse 5, commands that we sing to the Lord with the harp and the voice of song, with classical trumpets <note>original: tubis classicis</note> and the sound of the horn.

Even today, a horn is used in war with a terrible bellowing in the Swiss canton of **Uri**, as Gesner <note>Conrad Gessner (1516–1565), a Swiss naturalist</note> testifies in his *History of Quadrupeds* when discussing the ox and the cow.

The most ancient Danes called this type of horn a **Lur** <note>original Runic: ᛚᚢᚱ</note> from its sound; indeed, the very sound produced by the horns was called **Lur-blastr** <note>original Runic: ᛚᚢᚱᛒᛚᛅᛋᛏᚱ</note>. For thus my manuscript lexicon says: *Ludun Hliod* <note>original Runic: ᛚᚢᚱᛘ ᛒᛚᚢᛅᛏ</note>, meaning the "Sound of Trumpets."

Arnórr Jarlaskáld <note>An 11th-century Icelandic "Earl's Skald" or court poet</note>, in his accounts concerning Thorfinn, Earl of Orkney, sings thus:

-> ᛁᛅᚱᛚᛅ ᛅᚱ ᚼᛁᚴᚾᛁ ᛒᛅᚱᛏᛅ <-

-> ᚼᚢᚱᚦᚢᛋᛏᚢᛘ ᚠᚢᚱᛁᚱ ᛒᛚᛁᚴᚢᚢ <-

> *The Earl promotes the war,*
> *The sound of many horns*
> *Was heard among the city’s defenses,*
> *The banners of the brave trembled.*

<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

I believe that *Herehorn* <note>From the Germanic roots *heri* (army) and *horn*; essentially a "war-horn"</note> was the name used by the ancient Germans. From this comes that passage in the *Rhyme of Saint Anno*, the Bishop of Cologne <note>An 11th-century Middle High German poem praising the Archbishop of Cologne</note>:

> Oh, how the weapons clashed
> When the famous ones rushed together,
> The **war-horns** resounded,
> And the brooks flowed with blood.
<note>original Middle High German: "O wi di wisini clungen / Da di marin zisammen sprungen, / Herehorn duzzin / Becche blutin vluzin."</note>

Although Opitius <note>Martin Opitz, a 17th-century German scholar and poet</note> interprets this as referring to shields made of sinews or horns, I believe, after considering all the circumstances, that it must be understood as the horns that were used in place of trumpets in wartime.

Our ancestors truly used these kinds of horns, just like the other nations mentioned previously. Nobles and military leaders sounded the signal <note>original: classicum canebant</note> with them to ignite the spirits of the soldiers, so they would press on more fiercely, bravely withstand the enemy’s assault, and restore a faltering line of battle. Thus tells the very famous history or legend of Charlemagne, published in the native tongue <note>Danish</note> in the year 1501 in Copenhagen by Gotfred af Ghemen <note>The first printer to establish a permanent shop in Denmark</note>: *“The heathens blew more than a thousand horns.”* <note>original Danish: "Hedningen blesse mere end i tusende Luder." The 'Lur' is a traditional Northern horn.</note> The same treatise, as well as the ancient songs of the Icelanders, tell marvelous things about a certain horn belonging to Roland—the nephew of Charlemagne by his sister—who died in the Saracen war around the year 778. Statues of him <note>Known as 'Roland statues,' these were erected in German cities as symbols of civic liberty and judicial rights</note> can be seen here and there in the cities of Saxony. From these songs, let us hear the following:

<page-num>382</page-num>
<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

These <term>horns</term><note>referring to the war-horns or "oliphants" discussed on the previous page</note> were worn around the neck, tied with a cord, by the Kings themselves or those closest to them in rank during war, so that whenever they pleased, they could bring them into use without delay. For thus says that vernacular <term>History</term><note>referring to a medieval Danish chronicle or ballad</note> cited above:

->King Salimon struck King Bordant through the shield and mail, so that he fell dead upon the ground. He had Janemund’s horn at his neck, which was called Olivant; it was heard for fifteen French miles. King Salimon took the horn and swore he would not have given it for much gold. Jatmund saw this and that Bordant fell, and that King Salimon took the horn; he grew very angry and struck with the sharp sword Dyrendal, and cleaved Salimon’s helmet, head, back-armor, and saddle, and the horse through the middle; and he took the horn and hung it upon his neck, etc.<-
<note>Original Danish: "Konning Salimon stack til Bordant Konning giennom Skiolden oc Brynten... Hand hafde Janemuns Horn paa sin Hals, som heet Olivant... oc hug med det huasse Suerde Dyrendal..."</note>

That is to say: King Salimon, splitting the mail and helmet of King Bordant with his sword, killed him; he carried the horn of Janemund at his neck, which was called OLIVANT, the sound of which could be heard for fifteen French miles. King Salimon happily seized the horn and valued it at many talents of gold. Seeing this, Jatmund, enraged, with his sword called Dyrendal, so split the head of Salimon through the helmet that with the same stroke he divided both the armor of his adversary and the body of the horse. Thus having gained possession of so precious a horn, he tied it to his own neck, etc. This horn called *Olivant*, as well as the sword Dyrendal, finally came into the possession of <term>Roland</term><note>A legendary Frankish knight and hero of the "Song of Roland"</note>, the nephew of <term>Charlemagne</term> by his sister, by whom this Janemund was slain, as the same author relates.

Paulus Merula <note>A Dutch geographer and historian (1558–1607)</note> teaches in Part II of his *Cosmography*, Book III, page 429, that the horn OLIVANT is still preserved at Bordeaux, where he discusses the town of Blavia <note>Modern-day Blaye, France</note> in these words:

>*The inhabitants claim that Roland, the Palatine Prefect under Charlemagne of the British shore, was born among them, was their Count, and was finally entombed among them in the Church of St. Romanus with his sword placed beside him, which they call DURANDAL, and his horn at the foot of the tomb. However, it is said this was later moved to the Church of St. Severin in Bordeaux.*

Thus it is also established among the Romans that high-ranking men sounded the trumpet, according to <term>Dio</term><note>Dio Cassius, a Roman historian</note> in Book LVII: *The Consul Norbanus,* he says, *was accustomed to sound the trumpet alone—*

<meta>This page continues the discussion of historical horns, moving from the legendary "Olivant" used by Roland and his peers to a physical specimen in the author's own collection and the various practical roles horns played in music, ritual, and medicine.</meta>

<page-num>383</page-num>
# BOOK FIVE.

...was accustomed and much involved in that matter; yet it performed a marvel, for it sounded on the very Calends <note>the first day of the Roman month</note>, as if it had given the signal for war.

In my own collection <note>referring to the *Museum Wormianum*, the author's famous cabinet of curiosities</note>, I keep a **Horn** which formerly served these very purposes. It is black, elegantly fashioned with great skill, and two feet in length. It runs straight from the tip to the middle, while the outer curved part is decorated with crested ridges. From there, it opens into a wider capacity, adorned around the larger opening with pyramidal ornaments carved from the very substance of the horn itself. Near the middle, a tailed attachment emerges, so crafted from the material that it provides a firm grip for the hand of the person holding it.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration depicting a long, curved musical horn or wind instrument, likely a cornett or zink. The instrument tapers from a narrow mouthpiece on the left to a flared bell on the right. Its upper curved edge is decorated with serrated, crest-like ornamentation. A small, hook-like handle or finger rest is attached to the body of the instrument near the center.</image-desc>

Today, **Hunters and Musicians** apply horns to almost these same uses. Musicians, moreover, take delight in those pipes provided with small holes placed proportionally along their length, which produce a very sharp and pleasing sound. In common speech, they are usually called a **Cornet** or **Zink** <note>original: "Cornet vel Sincke"</note> after their material; some call them a **Trumpet** <note>original: "Buccina," a Roman military horn</note>.

Both sacred and secular history abundantly teach us that horns have served as various kinds of vessels. That oil or balsam with which the Kings of the Israelites were to be anointed by divine decree was kept in a horn, and poured from it onto the head of the one being crowned, as 1 Samuel chapter 16, verse 1 shows. For in that place, God speaks to Samuel:
> "Fill your horn with oil, and come, that I may send you to Jesse." <note>original Latin: "Imple cornu tuum oleo, & veni ut mittam te ad Isai."</note>

Galen <note>a famous Greek physician in the Roman Empire whose work dominated Western medicine for centuries</note> is a witness that many instruments of **Physicians** were made of horn, as seen in his books *On the Composition of Medicines* and *The Method of Medicine*. They used horns to measure liquids, they used them during <term>scarification</term> <note>making small incisions in the skin for bloodletting</note> instead of <term>cupping glasses</term> <note>suction vessels; original: "cucurbitulis"</note>, they administered <term>enemas</term> <note>original: "clysteria"</note> with horns, and they stored liquids in them.
