<meta>This page continues the discussion of the various historical and symbolic uses of horns, transitioning from their use as musical instruments to their significance in ancient religious altars, coinage, mythology, and heraldry.</meta>

<page-num>384</page-num>
# DANISH MONUMENTS

Plutarch, in his life of Theseus, mentions that *altar* around which Theseus danced, which he calls a **horned altar** <note>original Greek: "κερατῶνα βωμὸν" (keratona bomon)</note> because it was constructed entirely from horns.

Various authors recall that the altars of Diana and Apollo were also of this kind. Ovid writes in the *Letter of Acontius*:

> *I marvel at the altar built from countless horns.*

The *Etymologicus* <note>a Byzantine Greek encyclopedia of word origins</note>, under the entry for "to mix" <note>original Greek: "κεράσαι" (kerasai)</note>, states that the ancients once used a horn as a water-vessel.

The scholar Antonio Agustín <note>a 16th-century Spanish antiquarian and jurist</note> teaches in his eleventh Dialogue that horns also served the ancients as coffers or receptacles. He presents coins on which statues of **Abundance** and **Prosperity** are depicted, carrying horns filled with offerings. One coin belongs to the Emperor Trajan, and another to Gallienus. This is further confirmed by the *Edda* <note>the collection of Old Norse myths and legends</note> when discussing the skill and generosity of Hrolf Krake, King of Denmark. It relates that his mother Ursa—the wife of King Adils of Sweden—gave a **horn** full of gold to her son Hrolf, so that he might set aside his grievances and be reconciled with his stepfather. The text says:

"Then Ursa gave to her son Hrolf Krake a horn quite full of gold, so that he would be reconciled with her." <note>original runes: ᚦᛅ ᚵᛅᚠ ᚢᚱᛋᛅ ᛅᛏ ᛋᛁᚾ ᚼᚱᚢᛚᚠᛁ ᚴᚱᛅᚴᛅ ᚼᚢᚱᚾ ᚼᛅᚱᚦ ᚠᚢᛚᛏ ᛅᚠ ᚴᚢᛚᛚᛁ, ᛅᛏ ᚼᛅᚾ ᚢᛁᛚᛏᛁ ᚠᚢᚱᛚᛁᚴᛅ ᚢᛁᚦ ᚼᚢᚾ</note> Shortly after, Ursa gave to Rolf Krake the horn refilled with gold, along with a ring called <term>SVIAGRIS</term> <note>meaning "Sowe of the Swedes" or "Piglet of the Swedes," a legendary heirloom of the Swedish royal house</note>.

The aforementioned Antonio Agustín adds in the cited passage that a horn of **Oil** was a standard measure, and that the name also signifies abundance.

The greater part of our **Nobility** wear horns above their hereditary helmet-crests, sometimes distinguished by various colors; in ancient times, these were real horns taken from animals. This may be gathered from Livy's twenty-seventh book, where he discusses Philip, King of the Macedonians, saying:

> *Carried away by the rush of his horse into a tree, one of the horns of his helmet became caught on a protruding branch.*

> *The ribbon hanging from the horned helmet.*

In the same sense, Virgil writes in his twelfth book:

> *Both the sword and the shield, and the horns of the red crest.*

Diodorus Siculus explicitly confirms this regarding the Gauls, stating: "Bronze helmets..."

## BOOK FIVE

They place bronze helmets upon their heads, which have great projections and crests, and present a magnificent appearance to the onlookers. Plutarch, in his life of the legendary King Theseus, mentions that *altar* around which Theseus danced, which he calls the "horned altar" <note>original Greek: *keratona bomon*</note>, as it was constructed entirely from horns.

Authors record that there were also such altars dedicated to the goddess Diana and the god Apollo. Ovid writes in his *Epistle of Acontius*:

> *I marvel at the altar built of countless horns.* <note>original Latin: *Miror & innumeris structam de cornibus aram.*</note>

The *Etymologicus* <note>A famous Byzantine dictionary of Greek words</note> states under the entry for the word *to pour* <note>original Greek: *kerasai*</note> that the ancients once used a *horn as a water vessel*.

Antonio Agustín <note>A 16th-century Spanish scholar and bishop</note> teaches in his second Dialogue that horns also served the function of small boxes or purses among the ancients. He provides examples of coins in which statues of Abundance and Plenty are depicted, holding horns filled with gifts <note>The "cornucopia" or horn of plenty</note>. One coin belongs to the Emperor Trajan, the other to Gallienus. This is also confirmed by the *Edda* <note>The primary source for Norse mythology and legend</note> when discussing the skill and generosity of Hrolf Kraki, a King of Denmark. It relates that his mother Ursa, the wife of King Adils of Sweden, gave her son Hrolf a horn full of gold so that he might let go of past offenses and be reconciled with his stepfather. For it says: <insert>Then Ursa brought the horn to Hrolf Kraki, and it was filled with gold, that he might be reconciled with the king.</insert> <note>This translates the provided runic text: ᛋᛅ ᚦᛅᚢ ᛅᚱᚼᛅ ᛅᚦ ᚦᛁᚢ ᚼᚱᚼᛚᚠᚴᛁ ᚴᚱᚼᚢᛅ ᛒᛅᚱᚢ ᚼᚼᚱᚱ ᚦᚢᛘ ᛅᚦ ᚦᚢᚦᚦᛁ, ᛅᚦ ᚦᛁᚱ ᚦᛁᚴ ᚼᚱᛁᚿᚴᛁᚴ ᚢᚿᚴᚢᚱᛁᚴ.</note> Soon after, Ursa gave Hrolf Kraki a horn filled with gold and the ring called SVIGRIS.

The aforementioned Antonio Agustín adds in the cited passage that a horn of *oil* was once a standard *measure*, and that the name was also used to signify abundance.

The majority of our Danish Nobles wear horns above the helmet of their ancestral coats of arms, sometimes distinguished by various colors; in ancient times, these were real horns taken from animals. This can be gathered from Livy’s 28th book, where he discusses Philip, King of the Macedonians: *“Hurled against a tree by the force of his horse, one horn of his helmet was broken off by a protruding branch.”* <note>original Latin: *In arborem illatus impetu equi, alterum cornu galeae, ad eminentem ramum perfregit.*</note> To this also seems to point the passage cited above from Silius Italicus in his 15th book:

> *An island hanging from a horned helmet.* <note>original Latin: *Casside cornigera dependens insula.*</note>

In the same sense, Virgil writes in his 12th book:

> *Both sword and shield, and the horns of the red crest.* <note>original Latin: *Ensemque Clypeumque & rubrae cornua cristae.*</note>

Diodorus Siculus expressly affirms this of the Gauls: *Bronze helmets.* <note>original Greek: *Krane chalka.*</note>

<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>
<meta>catchword: vinu</meta>

...[Ulf]stands, Brahes, Lunges, and countless others; about whom I may perhaps write elsewhere.

Propertius teaches in book 4 that the machines of the ancients, which the Romans used to shake enemy walls during the storming of towns, were also equipped with horns:
> And while the ram <note>Latin: *aries*</note> with its bronze horn struck the wall,
> And the long penthouse <note>A *vinea*, or "vineyard," was a movable protective shelter for soldiers</note> protected the advanced work.

Truly, that horns were adapted for no use more frequently than for drinking cups can be proven by infinite testimonies of antiquity. Athenaeus <note>A Greek rhetorician and grammarian</note>, in book 2, chapter 8, proves with many examples that the ancients drank from bovine horns and that horns served the purpose of cups. He thinks this is evident from the fact that even now, when wine is mixed with water, they say "to mix" <note>Greek: *kerasai*</note>, and they call the vessel in which the wine is mixed a "Crater" <note>A large mixing bowl; Greek: *krater*</note> as if from "horn" <note>Greek: *keras*</note>, as if it were a mixing vessel named from "pouring the drink into the horn." <note>The author is highlighting an ancient linguistic theory that the words for mixing wine and the bowls used for it are derived from the word for "horn."</note> From this he also thinks it happened that Dionysus (or Bacchus) is depicted as horned, as one who had horns before he was born, with which he pierced the thigh of his father Jove; to this Euripides alludes:
> And she gave birth when the Fates
> brought to fulfillment the bull-horned god.
<note>original Greek: ἔτεκεν δ' ἁνίκα μοῖραι / τέλεσαν ταυρόκερων θεόν.</note>

He is also called "Bull" by many poets, and is seen with a bull's face in Cyzicus <note>An ancient Greek city in what is now Turkey</note>. To this Ovid seems to have alluded in his 21st Epistle:
> *Take up the lyre and quiver, and you will become Apollo manifest.*
> *Let horns be added to your head, and you will be Bacchus.*

And in book 2 of *The Art of Love*:
> *Purple Love pressed the horns of Bacchus.*

Nor is Tibullus different in book 2, Elegy 1:
> *Come, Bacchus, and let the sweet grape hang from your horns,*
> *and you, Ceres, gird your temples with ears of corn.*

Perhaps it is from this that Nonnus of Panopolis <note>A Greek epic poet</note>, in the *Dionysiaca*, book 12, asserts that Bacchus was the first to use a horn in place of a cup, at line 20:
> And he held the curved horn of an ox as a cup.
<note>original Greek: Καὶ δέπας ἀγκύλον εἶχε βοὸς κέρας.</note>

They think a trace of this also exists in Homer, book 8 of the *Iliad*, line 169.

<meta>This page continues the discussion of horns as drinking vessels, following the linguistic and mythological origins of the practice discussed on the previous page. It transitions from ancient Greek theories to specific historical accounts from Thrace, Macedonia, and Rome, eventually leading to a moral critique by St. Ambrose.</meta>

<page-num>387</page-num>
# BOOK FIVE #

*"Having mixed the wine in the horn to drink."* <note>original Greek: οἶνον ἐγκεράσασα πιεῖν.</note>
*"And mixing the wine with a horn for drinking."* <note>original Latin: Vinumque cornu miscens ad bibendum.</note>
But Diodorus <note>Diodorus Siculus, a 1st-century BC Greek historian</note> maintains that horns were attributed to Bacchus <note>Dionysus, the god of wine</note> because he was the first to teach mortals how to yoke oxen to the plow, and how to use their labor to till and break the soil. Although there are also those who have thought that the horns of Bacchus signify solar rays; but with what probability they think this, I do not see.

Xenophon <note>A Greek historian and soldier</note> is a rich witness that the Thracians <note>People from the region of Thrace, now part of Bulgaria, Greece, and Turkey</note> used horns in place of cups in the 7th book of his *Expedition* <note>The *Anabasis*, an account of the expedition of Cyrus the Younger</note>. For when he is about to describe a banquet celebrated among the Thracians at the house of Seuthes, he says, *"First they greeted one another, then, according to the Thracian custom, they drank toasts of wine from horns."* <note>original Greek: κατὰ τον θρᾴκικον νόμον κέρατα οἶνω προύπινον.</note> So too the Paphlagonians, of whom he says the same in book 6: *"While reclining on straw pallets during the meal, they dined and drank from cups made of horn."* <note>original Greek: κατακείμενοι δὲ ἐνισίβασιν, ἐδείπνων καὶ ἔπινον ἐκ κερατίνων ποτηρίων.</note> Thus Hermippus <note>A 5th-century BC Athenian comic poet</note> says in his *Ointments*:

*"Give me to drink from the horn just once more."* <note>original Greek: ἐκ δὲ τῶ κέρατος ἄυ μοι δὸς πιεῖν ἅπαξ μόνον.</note>
*"Truly, give me to drink from the horn again but once."* <note>original Latin: Verum è cornu rursus semel tantum quod bibam.</note>

Lycurgus the Orator <note>One of the ten canonical Attic orators</note>, in his speech against Demades, relates that King Philip <note>Philip II of Macedon, father of Alexander the Great</note> was accustomed to offer a toast from a horn to those whom he decided to receive kindly and as friends. In the <term>triclinium<note>A Roman dining room, named for the three couches (*tri-clinia*) arranged around a table.</note></term> described by Girolamo Mercuriale <note>A 16th-century Italian physician and antiquarian</note> in Book 1, Chapter 2 of *The Art of Gymnastics*, based on a very ancient stone that was kept in Padua in the Rhamnusian house, it is also clear that the Romans used horns instead of cups at banquets. For among the others whom he shows reclining in the dining rooms, and others serving, a certain man is seen holding a horn high with his hands so that the liquid may be poured into it. Saint Ambrose <note>The 4th-century Bishop of Milan and a Doctor of the Church</note>, in his book *On Elijah and Fasting*, vehemently inveighs against the customs of his age, in which guests challenge one another in drinking with horns and indulge too much in drunkenness. It is pleasing to hear his own words:

> To those dividing the feast, he says, there assist boys with shining hair from the Barbarian tribes, chosen for these purposes, distinguished by their various ages; in their midst is a horn full of wine—not an instrument for a feast, but a trumpet <note>Latin: *buccina*</note> of war. First, they play a prelude with smaller cups, as if in a light skirmish <note>Latin: *velitari pugna*</note>, as if [the opening] of tragedies...

...the participants first raise their voices gradually, until the wine opens the way: as soon as their ears begin to grow warm, they demand larger cups. When the feast is finished, you would think it time to rise, but then they renew their drinking from the start; and lest you think this immoderate, a measure is proposed, they compete under a judge, and it is decided according to a law. Madness itself is the master of the games there; here, if anyone turns his cup away, he is forced to drink. What, I ask, could be said more fittingly regarding our own customs? What Apelles <note>A famous painter of ancient Greece, known for his realism</note> could express our gluttons in more vivid colors than this very passage? And a little later: Wine flows into the throats of men even through a horn; and if anyone takes a breath, it is considered a committed crime, a broken line of battle, a loss of position. <note>original Latin: "actores, primo sensim vocem excitant... per cornu etiam fluentia in fauces hominum vina decurrunt..." This is likely a citation from St. Ambrose’s *De Helia et Ieiunio*, critiquing the drinking bouts of his time.</note>

We have shown that the horns of oxen provided drinking vessels for the Britons in Book 1 of the *History of the Danes*, chapter 18, drawing from Malmesbury and Camden. Of these, the former <note>William of Malmesbury, a 12th-century historian</note> in Book 2, chapter 2, has this: *Those of Pusey, named from Pusey, still hold their land by a horn formerly given by King Canute.* <note>King Cnut the Great, who ruled England, Denmark, and Norway in the 11th century. This refers to a "tenure horn," a physical object used instead of a written deed to grant land.</note> The latter <note>William Camden, an Elizabethan antiquarian</note> relates this from a manuscript: *"Ulphus, son of Thorald, turned aside to York and filled the horn from which he was accustomed to drink with wine, and before the altar of God and Blessed Peter, Prince of the Apostles, he offered all his lands and revenues on bended knees."*

Indeed, that our own people used them is clearer than needs demonstration. Hence so many songs in which they celebrate heroes drinking mead from horns; hence everywhere among nobles and scholars so many kinds of these horns are found, differing in size, ornaments, and material. In my own collection of such things, there are two, of the kind used by Norwegians and Icelanders, elegantly carved; the larger of which, which does not savor of too great antiquity (since an inscription shows it was crafted in the year 1598), holds two and a half <term>sextarii</term> <note>A Roman volume measurement; two and a half sextarii is roughly 1.3 liters or nearly 3 pints.</note>; and it displays the stories of the Wedding at Cana in Galilee, Judith beheading Holofernes, Joab pursuing Absalom, with several others skillfully carved into the substance of the horn itself. We provide an illustration of it here.

<image-desc>Circular institutional stamp in the left margin, containing a faded crest or seal.</image-desc>In my manuscript Lexicon, I find the phrase: *he emptied the horn* <note>original runes: ᚼᚢᚿ ᛐᚢᛘᛑᛁ ᛅᚢ ᚼᚢᚱᚿᛁ</note>. Because they are customarily emptied in memory of God and friends, they are usually called *memorial horns* <note>original runes: ᛘᛁᚿᚿᛁ ᚼᚢᚱᚿ; often referred to as "minni" horns in Old Norse tradition</note>. This means they are to perform the duty of cup-bearers.

The *Edda*, that marvelous unraveler of poetic mysteries among our people, mentions in the 21st chapter or fable a certain horn called the **Giallar Horn**. Every day, Mimir <note>A figure in Norse mythology renowned for his knowledge and wisdom</note> used this like a goblet to drink the liquid from the well of wisdom, with which he soaked himself so that he might surpass all others in prudence. It says: *He drinks from the well with the horn called GIALLAR, for there is wisdom in the well.* <note>original runes: ᚼᛅᚿᚿ ᚼᛅ ᛐᚱᛁᚴᚴᛅ ᚢᚱ ᛅ ᛒᚱᚢᚿᚿᛁᚿ ᛅᛘ ᛐᚢ ᚼᚢᚱᚿᛁ ᛅᛐ ᚴᛁᛅᛚᛚᛅᚱ, ᚦᚢᛁ ᛅᛐ ᚦᛅᚱ ᛂᚱ ᚠᚱᛁᛂᚦᚱ ᚢᚱ ᛒᚱᚢᚿᚿᛁᚿ</note>. It is a memorable thing that is read in the deeds of **Egill Skallagrimsson**, namely that he was received at a banquet by the King of Norway, **Eric Bloodaxe**, in which he showed himself so strenuous in draining horns that, on behalf of both himself and his companion **Olvir**, he exhausted all the drinks offered to them, yet he was not overwhelmed by drunkenness like the other guests. **Bard the Cup-bearer**, taking this poorly, implored the help of Queen **Gunnhild** (**who was a sorceress**). She, grieving that her people were coming away defeated in this contest, prepared a special kind of drink medicated by her art, which she saw was poured into a horn and offered to her guest **Egill**. But he, noticing the fraud, inscribed certain **Runes** upon the offered horn with the edge of his knife; when he had stained these with blood drawn from the palm of his hand, he added these verses in a loud voice:

We carve runes on the horn,
we redden the words in blood,
that which is mixed with wine.

Soon the horn burst into fragments and all the liquid flowed out. From these events, it is clear how greatly the Devil, the enemy of human salvation, has mocked the fierce heathens <note>original: *Ethnicos*</note> under the veil of Runes and the deceptions <unclear>of magical tricks</unclear>.

But it was not enough to have turned common bull horns into drinking vessels; Pliny notes in Book 11, in the chapter on **Aurochs** <term>Urus: a massive, now-extinct species of wild ox</term>, that their horns were highly prized. *The Northern Barbarians,* he says, *drink from the horns of the Aurochs, and the horns from a single head are large enough to fill two urns.* <note>Pliny the Elder, Natural History 11.45</note> Sigismund, Baron von Herberstein, reports the same concerning the **Samogitians** <note>A people inhabiting western Lithuania</note> in his *Commentaries on Muscovite Affairs*. Nor did our own ancestors shrink from such vessels, as shown by a third horn in my own collection; it is the largest of all, and while it is not distinguished by any carvings, it is adorned with gilded copper at both the tip and the rim. It also features a beautiful crystal circlet visible just below the rim and can hold five <term>sextarii</term> <note>Sextarius: a Roman unit of volume. Five sextarii equals approximately 2.7 liters or 5.7 pints.</note>.

Such seems to have been the horn that **Saxo Grammaticus** <note>The primary historian of medieval Denmark</note> mentions in his fifth book as being in the court of the British King, a court furnished with royal magnificence—though that horn was of a **buffalo** <note>original: *bubalinum*</note>. Nor was the use of buffalo horns, for which rewards were given, absent from his third book. Notable for their many ornaments, they were held and stored among great treasures. Our same historian teaches us this in his eighth book, where he describes riches and treasures...

# BOOK FIVE.

When **Agatharchides** <note>OCR reads Agarthilochi; likely referring to the Greek historian and geographer Agatharchides of Cnidus (2nd century BCE)</note> was about to list such things, he offered this: "Adjacent to this was a massive buffalo horn, more elaborately adorned with the exquisite brilliance of gems, and not lacking in the craftsmanship of engraving."

**Philostratus**, in his book on the *Life of Apollonius of Tyana*, having explained that the cups of Kings were once made of horn, adds that in the regions near the **Phasis** <note>A river in the ancient region of Colchis, modern-day Georgia, near the Black Sea</note> river, there are **Asses** <term>One-horned wild asses; a description of the mythical unicorn</term> *which carry a single horn on their forehead, with which they fight bravely against Elephants. From their horns, the Indians fashion drinking cups, asserting that anyone who drinks from such a cup shall not be afflicted that day by any disease, nor the pain of a wound, nor the flame of fire, nor can they be intoxicated by poison.* Almost the same is asserted by **Aelian** in Book 4 of *On the History of Animals*, Chapter 52, whose words I am pleased to include, since he describes that rare animal in greater detail. *I have heard that wild Asses, no smaller than horses, are born among the Indians; they are white in the rest of their body, but have purple heads and blue eyes, and they carry a horn on their forehead a cubit and a half in length, the upper part of which is crimson, the lower part white, and the middle part entirely black.* **I hear that the Indians drink from these variegated horns** <note>original Greek: ἐκ δὴ τῶν δὲ τῶν ποικίλων κεράτων πίνειν Ἰνδοὺς ἀκούω</note>; though indeed not all of them do, but only the more powerful ones, and they decorate them with gold, just as they do their arms. They say that he who drinks from this horn becomes safe from incurable diseases, and is neither seized by convulsions, nor attacked by the **sacred disease** <term>Epilepsy</term>, nor by any poisons. Furthermore, if he has previously drunk anything pestilential, he then vomits it up and returns to health. Because of this, **Mercurialis** <note>Girolamo Mercuriale (1530–1606), a famous Italian physician and classical scholar</note> in Book 1 of his *Various Readings* says it seems likely to him that the ancients used horns for cups, both because of their rustic customs and perhaps because they thought greater safety in drinking was gained from them.

I also believe I can gather that the ancients even offered drink to beasts from horns, based on **Pliny** Book 36, Chapter 5, where he reviews the works crafted by **Arcesilaus**, a noble sculptor. Regarding him, he reports these things: *Varro also praises Arcesilaus, of whom he says he possessed a marble Lioness and winged **Cupids** <note>The Roman god of love, often depicted as a winged child</note> playing with her, some of whom held her bound, others forced her to drink from a horn, others put shoes on her feet—all from a single stone.*

As luxury increased, they first began to plate the rims of the horns with metals and add other ornaments of the same material. The rim and the tip of that horn which comes from the **Aurochs** <term>Urus: the large, extinct wild ox mentioned on the previous page</term> were covered in gilded bronze...

**Agatharchides** <note>A 2nd-century BC Greek historian and geographer</note>, when listing such items, also brings forward this: *Beside this lay a massive buffalo horn, elaborately adorned with the exquisite brilliance of gems, and not lacking in the craftsmanship of engraving.*

**Philostratus**, in his book on the life of **Apollonius of Tyana** <note>A 1st-century philosopher and mystic</note>, where he teaches that the cups of Kings were once made of horn, adds that in the regions near the river **Phasis**: *There are wild asses that carry a single horn on their forehead, with which they fight bravely against elephants. This likely refers to early accounts of the rhinoceros, often confused with the legendary unicorn.</note>

**Aelian** asserts nearly the same in Book 4 of *On the Nature of Animals*, Chapter 52, whose words I am pleased to record here, as he describes that rare animal at greater length: *I have heard that wild asses, no smaller than horses, are born among the Indians; their bodies are white, their heads purple, and their eyes blue. They bear a horn on their forehead a cubit and a half in length, the top of which is crimson, the bottom white, and the middle part entirely black.* <note>original Greek: ἐκ δὴ τῶν δὲ τῶν ποικίλων κεράτων πίνειν Ἰνδὸς ἄνω</note> <note>translation: "From these multicolored horns, the Indian lords drink."</note> *And indeed, not all of them drink from these, but only the most powerful, and they decorate them with gold as they do their own arms. I believe I can also gather that the ancients even offered drink to beasts from horns, based on **Pliny**, Book 36, Chapter 5, where he reviews works crafted by the noble sculptor **Arcesilaus**. ...the end was violently broken off by the girl <note>This refers to Kirstine Svendsdatter, the young lace-maker who discovered the first horn in 1639.</note> when she pulled it from the earth with great effort, especially since several of its rings separated from the inner plate under that same force. If the break had happened this way, leaving jagged and uneven ends, some traces would certainly remain; however, gold is a soft and flexible metal that does not easily snap, but rather allows itself to be bent and curved. The discoverer would have undoubtedly noticed such a fracture before she proceeded further and collected the fragments. Now, the fact that it has been turned into a cup <note>A reference to the horn's temporary use or adaptation after its discovery.</note> does nothing to diminish its original purpose.

It could not have been useful for **Hunters**; for it emits a sound unfamiliar to dogs, far different from the sound produced by bull horns when they are used to call the pack. I say nothing of its weight and length, which would have made it a hindrance rather than a tool. Furthermore, any person of sound mind can easily understand that a hunter could not have carried such a treasure through the harsh thickets, mountain ridges, and pathless forests without great danger.

> *While he wanders through trackless thickets of the woods with hunting dogs,* <note>original: "Silvarum canibus dum invia lustra pererrat"</note>

Moreover, there is no foundation for what some claim: that it could have been used in **sacrifices** to call the people together. Where is this either written or depicted? Consult Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), a Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum.</note>, consult the most ancient writers on Danish affairs, and you will not find so much as a whisper that favors this opinion. In the first book of this work, we outlined the sacrificial methods of the ancient Danes based on proven authors; until now, we have been unable to find anywhere that our ancestors used horns or trumpets to assemble the people.

Saxo does indeed mention in Book XIV, when discussing the sacrifices of the Rugians <note>A tribe living on the island of Rügen.</note>, the Idol of **Svantovit** <note>A four-headed Slavic god of war and harvest.</note>, which held a horn in its right hand from which the priest used to divine the harvest of the following year. But I do not see what this has to do with the sacrificial rites of the Danes. Let us hear the words of our Historian, so that the whole matter may become clearer: *“A massive statue stood in the temple, exceeding the size of a human body in every dimension, a wonder to behold with four heads and as many necks, of which two seemed to look toward the chest and two toward the back. Furthermore, of those positioned to the front and back, one looked to the right...”*

A sword of conspicuous size increased the wonder of these things; its scabbard and hilt were enhanced by the external appearance of silver, in addition to the excellent beauty of the engraving. Here, anyone who does not notice that Saxo is dealing not with Danish idolatry and sacrifices, but with those of the *Rugian Svantovitus* (which were far different from the Danish ones), must surely be blind. But it is clear enough from the cited text that the *Rugian* horn was used neither to summon the people nor for libations in that same place. Therefore, I do not see what this contributes to the use of horns among the **Danes**. But those who insist that the golden horn now held by our Most Serene Prince <note>King Christian IV of Denmark, who took possession of the horn after its discovery.</note> is **that very same one**, or made in the shape of the one held in the right hand of the statue of *Svantovitus*, make themselves look plainly ridiculous. For the horn that the statue held in its hand was adorned with various types of metal; the Prince's horn is not "adorned" but cast from a single type of metal, namely gold. That one [Svantovitus'] was complete, tipped with a point, serving the purpose of a cup; this one [the Gallehus horn] was a trumpet, which, so that it could be more conveniently blown, was open at the tip and at both ends. That one could be drained with great speed in a single draught; this one, capable of holding two and a half *sextarii* <note>A Roman unit of volume; 2.5 sextarii is roughly 1.4 liters or about 3 pints.</note>, is barely emptied in four or five strong gulps even by the most strenuous drinkers. That one is recorded to have been equipped with no contiguous rings or circles; this one, on the other hand...

...which has an interior plate fitly covering and surrounding it. Authors report that the former <note>The horn of Svantovitus described on the previous page.</note> was decorated with no emblems or signs; this one <note>The Golden Horn of Gallehus.</note> is adorned with them everywhere. Who, therefore, does not notice that these two are worlds apart <note>original: "toto cælo distare," a Latin idiom meaning to be diametrically opposed or utterly different.</note> and that those who strive to adapt the "hieroglyphics" <note>Worm uses "hieroglyphics" to refer to the mysterious figures and symbols engraved on the horn.</note> existing on this horn to the Svantovitian idol-madness <note>original: "Idolomania Svantovitianæ"</note> are remarkably foolish?

We concede that other nations indeed used trumpets in sacred rites (but not horns, strictly so called) made of bronze, with a tube that widened toward the opening; but the Danes did not. Hence Festus <note>Sextus Pompeius Festus, a 2nd-century Roman grammarian.</note> asserts that the *Armilustrium* <note>A Roman festival for the purification of arms.</note>, in which armed men performed divine rites, was celebrated not without the sounding of trumpets. And Calpurnius <note>Titus Calpurnius Siculus, a Roman bucolic poet.</note> says in his *Eclogues*:

> *To sound trumpets during sacred rites, not during wars.* <note>original: "Inter facra tubas, non inter bella fonare."</note>

If they think it had other uses in sacrifices, they will undoubtedly claim it was intended for receiving liquid or balsam. They might think our ancestors did as the Romans did, who, after placing whole and solid victims (or parts of them) upon the altar-hearth and casting them into the fire, immediately poured certain liquids such as wine or oil over them. They do not notice that the burnt offerings of our people had little or nothing in common with the sacrifices of the Romans. Nor would anyone say aptly or reasonably that everything used by the Romans regarding sacred matters applies to our people. Indeed, if you believe Stuckius <note>Johann Wilhelm Stucki (1542–1607), a Swiss scholar who wrote "Sacrorum Sacrificiorumque Gentilium Descriptio," a standard work on ancient rituals.</note> on sacred matters: *They did not use a <term>cyathus</term> <note>A small ladle or measure for wine.</note> or a <term>cotyla</term> <note>A cup or half-pint measure.</note> in sacrifices, but they set a <term>crater</term> <note>A large mixing bowl.</note> before the gods, not made of silver, nor distinguished with small stones, but made from Coliad earth <note>A high-quality clay from Cape Colias in Attica.</note>. Whenever they filled this, making a libation to the gods from a <term>phiala</term> <note>A shallow sacrificial bowl.</note>, they afterwards poured the wine, moistening it with wine recently mixed in a <term>cymbium</term> <note>A boat-shaped drinking vessel.</note>. From the mixing bowls, they poured the wines into smaller cups called <term>depada</term> <note>original Greek: δέπαδα; refers to beakers or drinking vessels.</note> by Homer.*

You see not a word about horns, much less golden ones. Stuckius expressly denies that the mixing bowl was decorated with silver or gems; how much more so with gold? Indeed, who would believe it was made entirely of gold? The ancients performed divine rites with mixing bowls, shallow dishes, sacrificial ladles, small scoops, bowls, narrow-necked jugs, and small ladles <note>Worm lists various Roman vessels: crateris, pateris, sympuviis, sympulis, catinis, gutis, and cyathis.</note>, but not with horns, as Stuckius learnedly proves in his description of pagan rites, page 134. Furthermore, the mass and capacity of our golden [horn]...

The horn seems to utterly shrink from such a use, so that if there were nothing else, these points would abundantly prove that it cannot be associated with that practice.

Those who assigned it to the anointing of kings were undoubtedly moved by the passage we cited above from 1 Samuel, chapter 16, verse 1, where Samuel is ordered to fill his horn with oil so that he might anoint David as King, according to the custom of the Jewish people. But it has not yet been demonstrated by anyone that the same ritual for inaugurating Danish Kings through anointings existed as that by which the Israelites were inaugurated. Our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), a Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> teaches us otherwise—a man more skilled in our antiquities than perhaps any other. *The ancients, when about to choose a king,* he says in Book 1, *were accustomed to stand on stones fixed in the ground and cast their votes, intending to omen the stability of the deed by the firmness of the stones beneath them.* Crantzius <note>Albert Krantz (1448–1517), a German historian whose works covered the history of Scandinavia.</note> repeats the same thing in almost as many words. Certainly, in the past, kings were not created with such pomp, such solemnity, and so many symbols as is now customary. Ancient simplicity, content with little, rendered itself worthy of the royal throne through outstanding deeds rather than external pomp. Let it therefore be settled for us that this Golden Cup of the Most Serene Prince was formerly a trumpet or a horn, and not truly a drinking vessel.

## KINDS OF DRINKING VESSELS

However, since it has now been converted to the use of a drinking cup, and since various cups of the ancients existed which took their names from their external shape and ornaments, we must look into where it may best be categorized.

They used to call cups and vessels *chased* <note>original: "caelata"</note> which were decorated with prominent figures, expressed either on the inside or the outside. This comes from the word for a "chisel" <note>original: "coelo"</note>, which is a type of iron tool that they call a *cilio* or *celtes*, according to Isidore <note>Isidore of Seville (c. 560–636), a scholar and bishop whose *Etymologies* served as an encyclopedia for the Middle Ages.</note>. Regarding these, Silius Italicus <note>A Roman poet (c. 28–103 AD) known for his epic on the Second Punic War.</note> writes in Book 10:

> ->*Not a single crowd*<-
> ->*Of servants, but a doubled care to set the feast,*<-
> ->*To tend these hearths, to carry cups in order,*<-
> ->*And with certain ones, thus the chased table is built.*<-
<note>original: "Non una ministri / Turba gregis, posuisse dapes bis addita cura, / His adolere focis, his ordine pocula ferre / Nec non & certis, struitur sic aspera mensa." The "rough" or "harsh" table (aspera mensa) refers to the texture of embossed or engraved silver/gold plate.</note>

They shine with the weight of chased gold from antiquity.

> *The brave deeds of the fathers.*
<note>original: "Ingens argentum menſis, cælataq; in auro Fortia facta patrum."</note>

Therefore, I believe our horn should be classified among these "chased cups" <term>cælata pocula; vessels decorated with relief work or engravings</term>; and I am further confirmed in my opinion when I see Statius describing a chased cup with almost the same figures of snakes and serpents as those on our horn. Indeed, what wonder is it that the chasing on our horn is somewhat cruder, since in Pliny’s age no artist was found who excelled in chasing gold. For he says in Book 33, chapter 12: *It is a wonder that no one became famous for chasing gold, though many did in silver; however, Mentor was the most highly praised.* <note>Mentor (4th century BCE) was the most celebrated silver-chaser of Greek antiquity.</note>

It might also find a place among the *Sigillata* <term>vessels decorated with small raised figures or "seals" (sigilla)</term>. For those things were called "sigillata" which contained images of the Gods, or Heroes, or other subjects. The Greeks call these *statues* and *small images*, and likewise *forms of the gods*. <note>original Greek: ἀγάλματα (agalmata), ἀγαλμάτια (agalmatia), εἴδη θεῶν (eide theon).</note> It is in this sense that Cicero writes in his 6th action against Verres: *While I was sitting sadly at home, a servant of the temple of Venus ran up and ordered me to bring the embossed cups to the Governor immediately.* <note>original: "scyphos sigillatos." Cicero’s "In Verrem" is a series of speeches against a corrupt Roman governor.</note> Because seals of this kind were attached to vessels and cups by the skill of engravers and vessel-makers, they were called "sigillata." For all statues that are smaller than human height were called *signs* <note>original: "signa."</note>, as Pomponius Gauricus testifies in Chapter 2 of *On Symmetry*. Truly, *sigilla* <note>small signs or seals</note> are those within this smallest category—a cubit or a palm in height, or even as tiny as can be made; that is, *small signs*.

I would also refer it to the class of the *footless* <note>original Greek: ἀποδῶν (apodon), meaning "without feet."</note>: so called because they cannot stand or be set down on their own, as they lack feet and supports. Therefore, when it is full of liquid, the one who takes it must either keep it in their hands at all times or drain it dry, unless there is someone to help hold it.

It has now been rendered as a vessel of hospitality, since it is presented as something that must necessarily be drained by a foreigner or guest upon their first arrival, whom the Prince deems worthy of such honor.

Finally, I would call it **crustated** <term>crustatum; plated or incrusted</term>, because its inner layer is covered on the outside by several plates in the form of rings. Regarding such things, Cicero says in his oration *Against Verres*: *The brothers from Cibyra are summoned; they reject few things; from those they approved, the plates or emblems were stripped away.* <note>original: "Cybiratæ fratres vocantur, pauca improbant, quæ probarunt, iis crufta aut emblemata detrahebantur." Cicero refers to the plunder of art by the corrupt governor Verres.</note> Thus the people of Haluntium, their luxuries shaken off, returned home with only pure silver. Hence they are called **Crustarii** <term>platers or chasers</term>, by whose skill vessels were bound with plates. See Turnebus in his *Adversaria*, Book 8, chapter 10, where among other things he says: *Cicero calls the ornaments of vessels "plates" and "emblems," between which there seems to have been this difference: that "plates" (crustae) were a kind of covering, like applied foils or layers of metal, even gilded; while "emblems" (emblemata) were more precious, of more exquisite workmanship, and were removable (exemptilia) when they had been bound or attached. Plates, though they could be torn away, adhered more firmly.* <note>Adrianus Turnebus (1512–1565) was a French classical scholar whose *Adversaria* provided commentary on ancient texts.</note> From this, anyone might easily conclude that it could also be classified among "emblematic" vessels.

But what our plated horn signifies to us by the seals on its plates is a matter of deeper investigation, and no one can easily demonstrate it with certainty. As we grope blindly in such great darkness, if we may guess anything—deferring to the judgment of those better informed—we shall reveal our thoughts in few words. Among the thick clouds of antiquity, to never stumble is a great fortune; to err is forgiven.

### EXPLANATION OF THE EMBLEMS.

Horns were once signs of dignity, power, strength, empire, and authority among all nations, even in sacred matters. From this comes the passage in 1 Samuel 2, verse 1: *My heart exults in the Lord; my horn is exalted in the Lord.* <note>original: "Exultavit cor meum in Domino, exaltatum est cornu meum in Domino."</note> And in verse 10: *The Lord shall judge the ends of the earth, and shall give strength to his King, and shall exalt the horn of his Anointed.* <note>original: "Dominus judicabit fines terræ, & dabit fortitudinem Regi suo, & sublimabit cornu Christi sui."</note> This symbolism is found among secular authors as well; Horace aims at the same meaning in his *Epodes*, saying:
> *For, most fierce against the wicked,*
> *I raise my ready horns.*
<note>original: "Namq; in malos acerrimus Parata tollo cornua."</note>
And Plautus says the same in *Pseudolus*, Act 4, Scene 3, verse 5.

No one desires to rejoice worthily. For just as the Egyptians and other peoples (as one may gather from Philo’s *Life of Moses* <note>Philo of Alexandria (c. 20 BCE – 50 CE), a Jewish philosopher who harmonized Greek philosophy with Hebrew scripture.</note> and Clement of Alexandria’s *Stromata*, Book 1 <note>Clement of Alexandria (c. 150 – 215 CE) was a Christian theologian whose *Stromata* or "Miscellanies" discussed the history of knowledge and philosophy.</note>) possessed a twofold method of transmitting knowledge—one popular and open, exposed to all, through which they shared commonly necessary things such as Geometry, Arithmetic, Astrology, Music, etc.; the other, however, was secret and sacred, called "Hieroglyphic," through which they denoted the most weighty mysteries and dogmas of their Theology, Philosophy, and Politics by means of certain symbols and enigmas—so too did our own ancient Runes educate the people regarding necessary matters in two ways. First, plainly and openly through Runic letters, which we have discussed at length in our *Literature* <note>Referring to Worm's 1636 work, *Danica Literatura Antiquissima*, the first major study of runes.</note>; and second, in a concealed and Hieroglyphic manner through the figures of animals and models of other things. Traces of these still exist today, both in the ruins of stone monuments and on wood, bone, horns, and embroidered tapestries. Therefore, Causinus <note>Nicolas Caussin (1583–1651), a French Jesuit polymath who wrote extensively on Egyptian symbols.</note> does not speak out of turn when he asserts in his work on Horus <note>A reference to his study of the *Hieroglyphica* of Horapollo.</note> that *the system of Hieroglyphics was celebrated most frequently among the Egyptians, but then spread widely to other nations.* Indeed, he even strives to show in that same work that this rule of writing was not unknown to the Northern peoples, nor to the Scythians and Ethiopians. Let no one think we are proposing paradoxes <note>In the sense of absurd or self-contradictory statements.</note> when we attribute our own Hieroglyphics to our ancestors—namely, images and figures determined by human will to signify something specific.

Regarding Scythian Hieroglyphics, there is a memorable account related by Clement of Alexandria in Book 5 of the *Stromata*, taken from Pherecydes of Syros. It tells how Idanthyrsus <note>A king of the Scythians during the 6th century BCE.</note>, the king of the Scythians, sent a symbol in place of a letter to Darius <note>Darius the Great of Persia, during his campaign against the Scythians in 513 BCE.</note>, who had crossed the Ister <note>The ancient Greek and Latin name for the lower Danube River.</note> threatening war. The symbol consisted of a Mouse, a Frog, a Bird, a Javelin, and a Plow. Since a doubt arose concerning these (as was natural), Orontopagus the military tribune said they were offering to surrender their empire; he conjectured this because the mouse represented their dwellings, the frog the waters, the bird the air, the javelin their arms, and the plow their territory. Xiphodres, however, interpreted it quite differently. He said that unless we fly away like birds, or hide in the earth like mice, or [dive into the water] like

<note>original: "ſtitu-ranæ"</note>...if we place water under the frog, we shall not escape their spears. From this, one may easily gather that other nations also had their own Hieroglyphs, distinct from those of the Egyptians and not used in the same sense; one would look in vain among them for Canopus, Isis, Osiris, and other monsters of that kind. From this you will also note that there is not just one single way of interpreting Hieroglyphs, but that different, and indeed sometimes contrary, meanings can be gathered from the same symbols. Orontopagus and Xiphodres <note>These appear to be characters or authorities from a Renaissance-era dialogue or emblematic work, used here to show how symbols can be interpreted differently.</note> have shown this by their own example. Therefore, if anyone produces something else or something different from what we have now extracted from the Hieroglyphs of the golden horn, they will not be opposing us, provided they bring forward interpretations consistent with the objects and images.

What, then, forbids us from concluding that the images, emblems, and figures contained on this golden vessel are our own **Danish Hieroglyphics**, aimed at shaping character, establishing governance, and inciting the pursuit of virtue? To demonstrate this more conveniently, we shall survey each individual ring or circle one by one, examine the Hieroglyphs, and briefly indicate what we hope can probably be gathered from them. We shall produce nothing without reason and the clear testimony of approved authors.

## THE FIRST CIRCLE.

The first circle, near the lip (Suidas <note>The Suda (or Suidas) is a massive 10th-century Byzantine Greek encyclopedia.</note> calls it the *codon* <note>original: "κώδων"</note>; he says, *the "codon" is the name given to the wide part of the trumpet* <note>original: "κώδων καλεῖται τὸ πλατὺ τῆς σάλπιγγος"</note>. Hence Sophocles <note>The famous Greek tragedian (c. 496–406 BCE).</note> says: *as with a bronze-mouthed bell in the Tyrrhenian fashion* <note>original: "χαλκοστόμῳ κώδωνι ὡς τυρσηνικῆς"</note> <note>The "Tyrrhenian" or Etruscan trumpet was famous in antiquity for its distinct shape and sound.</note>), is larger and broader than the rest; it is therefore endowed with a double series of emblems and Hieroglyphs. I believe both series are directed toward placing human misery before our eyes and showing the means by which anyone can struggle out of it and render themselves safe from the attacks of those who assault the soul in various ways and try to lure it toward illicit and less honorable things.

I. Emblem. A naked man appears in difficulties—

# BOOK FIVE.

[He is] positioned with hands and feet spread out, as if mourning his own misery, while he is attacked on both sides by serpents charging at him and ejecting their venom. I do not see what could more aptly express human misery. On the right, the "ancient serpent," the Devil, constantly plucks at man by inspiring wicked thoughts, inciting him to commit evil deeds, and leading him into the greatest danger of soul and body. On the left, a serpent of physical enemies <note>The author distinguishes between spiritual "demonic" attacks and physical "human" threats.</note> threatens with arrows and venom; with these plucking from both sides, he cannot help but show a lament through his external bearing and the lines of his limbs, and implore for aid.

That the ancients indicated ruin, evil, terrors, and other inconveniences of that kind through the serpent is testified by *Pierius, Book 16* <note>Pierio Valeriano’s *Hieroglyphica* (1556) was a massive encyclopedia of symbols used by Renaissance scholars to interpret ancient imagery.</note>. Hence at the oracle at Delphi, a serpent stood out, which seemed to challenge *Apollo* in singular combat: by which *Plutarch* wished to designate nothing other than that ruin is always opposed to health and salvation. Regarding the serpent Python, whom *Apollo*—as *Ovid* sings:

> *Indeed, he pierced him with a thousand arrows, and more.* <note>original: "Mille quidem fodit telis & pluribus"</note>

Certain people designate the force and malignity of sickly poison by this; which man is often forced to endure in this mortality. Some say it is a genus of demons, to whom, as *Adamantius* writes, dragons and other serpents are said to minister. *Diodorus Siculus* asserts that *Evil* is hinted at by a serpent entangled in coils. The *poets* imagine snakes entwined in the hair of the *Eumenides* <note>The Eumenides, also known as the Furies, were Greek goddesses of vengeance often depicted with snakes for hair to inspire fear.</note>, especially *Aeschylus* (who is said to be the first inventor of this fable, according to *Pausanias*), so that they might instill terror in men. Hence we read that *Tiberius Gracchus* <note>A famous Roman reformer; bad omens involving snakes in his helmet were said to have preceded his assassination.</note> feared, not without cause, when he found that snakes had laid eggs and produced formed offspring in the helmet he was accustomed to use in wars, shortly before he was crushed and killed by the multitude of the *Quirites* <note>The *Quirites* refers to the Roman citizens in their civil capacity.</note>. Therefore, I believe that the serpents attacking the naked man from all sides indicate the misery in which he is placed in this mortal life.

Without a doubt, [this figure] suggests a man immersed in the filth of vices and reduced to a beast-like state, whom those standing by try to help; showing by their gestures that help must be sought from the heavens. For although a person may be endowed with a human head and reason, if he allows it to be overwhelmed by the appetite for perverse desires, and if the other limbs "put on the beast" by performing works unworthy of a rational man, he should be called a beast rather than a man. Hence Adamantius <note>Adamantius was a common nickname for Origen of Alexandria (c. 185–254 AD), a prolific early Christian scholar.</note> calls a man prone to lust not a man, but a horse. A man, however outwardly groomed and honored, if he is devoid of wisdom, is a beast of burden; for he is very much like the foolish beasts of burden, upon whom ornamental trappings and gilded studs <term>bullae: decorative studs or amulets worn by Roman children or placed on horse tack</term> are not infrequently placed. The Savior himself in the Gospel calls a man of malicious nature a "brood of vipers" in Matthew 3 and 12, and Luke 3. Such a man should be called a viper. Juan Eusebio Nieremberg <note>A Spanish Jesuit polymath (1595–1658) whose works blended natural history with moral philosophy.</note> writes elegantly in *Sigalion* <note>Referring to his work *Sigalion, sive de sapientia mythica* (1629), which explored hidden meanings in myths.</note>, speaking through the persona of Antisthenes:

> *When men desire the pleasures of brutes, they also acquire the souls of those brutes. Through lust they become dogs and horses; through gluttony, pigs or monkeys or [even] plants. And a little later: It would be better for the body to be changed into a beast while the human mind remains unharmed, than to retain the image of a man with the soul of a beast. Nor should one boast of one's form; a monkey could boast, and so could a statue. It would be better to be a horse or a donkey, or a cedar tree endowed with reason, than a man lacking his mind.* See the rest of his most delightful writings.

Whenever it happens that the wild parts seize tyranny over us, and the heat of desire seizes and oppresses the nobility of the soul and assigns it to its own service, then because of the filthiness of that obedience, man is turned into a beast, as Pierius <note>Giovan Pietro Valeriano Bolzani, whose 1556 book *Hieroglyphica* was the standard Renaissance reference for interpreting ancient symbols.</note> rightly says in Book 4. Therefore, so that a pleasant metamorphosis <note>original: "Metamorphosis"</note> may occur, and so that he may return to sound reason, he needs the help of the Powers Above, which those standing by—arranged in a posture for prayer—advise him to implore tirelessly.

IV. That one must not indulge in lust, greed, and gluttony is warned by the vulture, which makes a most greedy attack upon a fish—I would not easily call it a Rugian herring <note>original: "halec Rugianum." A reference to herring from the island of Rügen in the Baltic Sea, famous in the author's time for its fisheries.</note>—while a serpent seems to egg it on from behind, approving of the deed with its head and open mouth. It is clear from many sources that in ancient times, fish were a symbol of the tavern and the cook-shop. Heraclitus used to say that all flesh was merely "body," or a part of a body, but that the power of sea-creatures was like a "compacted soul," having provided them with grace and pleasure. This was the sole reason why the priests of Egypt abstained from sea-creatures: so that they might live piously and chastely. For since they turned away from all delicacies, they considered fish to be both a luxury food and a rich seasoning.

The priests of other nations, however, devised fish-filled places consecrated to their gods so that they alone might enjoy the delicacies of the fish; for among the common people, it was a sin to fish in those waters. This is told of the Rhiti <term>Rhiti: The Rheitoi were sacred salt-water springs on the border of Attica and Eleusis, dedicated to Demeter (Ceres) and Persephone.</term>, the priests of the Attic region, who established certain places filled with the most delicate fish near the borders of the Eleusinians as sacred to Ceres and Proserpine, and therefore maintained that the fish were owed to the priests alone. They report that when Demosthenes was accusing Philocrates of gluttony and lewdness, he charged him with purchasing both harlots and fish with "treacherous gold" <note>Money received as a bribe to betray his country.</note>. > Whether you "slaughter" fish, or leeks and onions.

V. A man, standing as if in wonder in the middle, grieves that almost the same story is repeated, and seems to restrain a bird (I believe it to be a **Kite** <note>original: *Milvium*</note>) which is attacking a fish with its ravenous beak. Although this might seem to point toward the same meaning <note>i.e., gluttony</note>, yet because the figure of the bird is different and the fish is another kind, if I were to say we are being warned here to avoid **Rapacity**, I hope I have produced nothing contrary to reason. For the ancient philosophers, **Plato** and his commentators, used birds and fish of this sort—which devour the slower and weaker creatures of nature—to denote not only those who are devoted to greed and are ready to plunder the weak through robbery and violent tyranny; but they also established that the souls of such men migrate into birds of this kind. Consult **Socrates**' discussion on this in the *Phaedo* <note>One of Plato's famous dialogues where Socrates discusses the immortality of the soul and reincarnation based on one's earthly character.</note>. **Pliny** says in Book 10, Chapter 10, that this bird is most ravenous and always hungry; hence the Poet writes:

->*Just like the hungry breed of Kites,*<-
->*Whose screeching sharpens a hunger of two days' standing.*<-

**Aristophanes** <note>An ancient Greek playwright known for his comedies.</note> also alludes to this when he calls it a <term>kite</term> <note>original Greek: ἰκτῖνα (*iktina*)</note>, an <term>all-seeing snatcher of food</term> <note>original Greek: παντόφθαλμον ἅρπαγα τρεφῶν (*pantophthalmon harpaga trephon*)</note>. It lies in wait for domestic birds, especially chickens and goslings, which are weak and offer no resistance; it attacks them from ambush and steals them away with a secret rush. It even snatches food from the hands of children in the very cities...

## THE SECOND SERIES OF THE FIRST CIRCLE.

I. The arrangement of the statues and images shows that the second series of this first ring agrees with the first. A man, driving away one snake from himself, does not perceive another threatening him from behind until he is harmed.

The Emblem warns that we ought to be circumspect and cautious in the conduct of affairs. For we are so situated in this mortal life that we are not pressed by only one inconvenience; rather, since we are surrounded by enemies on all sides, it is fitting to be an **Argus** <note>In Greek mythology, Argus Panoptes was a giant with a hundred eyes, symbolizing absolute watchfulness.</note>, and you must be continually vigilant, lest while you resist one, many more overwhelm you from behind when you are off your guard. They say that **Hercules** (by whom the ancients denoted a man preeminent in both mental and physical strength) killed snakes while still in his cradle; wishing to suggest that he who is born for great and noble things must extinguish pleasures from a tender age, so that through the remaining course of his life...

...may learn to resist the remaining snakes of vice more cautiously. To this refers that passage of **Silius** <note>Silius Italicus (c. 26–101 AD), a Roman senator and poet known for his epic on the Second Punic War.</note> in Book 1:

> Go quickly, men, and extinguish the nascent flame,
> Lest late-arriving cares return after the dangers have increased.
> <note>original: *Ocyus ite viri, & nafcentem extingvite flammam Ne feræ redeant, post aucta pericula, curæ.*</note>

For as **Plautus** <note>Titus Maccius Plautus (c. 254–184 BC), a celebrated Roman playwright.</note> says in *The Rope*:

> He who takes heed with deliberation, learning, and shrewdness,
> May long enjoy that which was well-acquired.
> <note>original: *Ille qui confultè, doctè atq; aftutè cavet, Diutinè ei uti benè licet partum benè.*</note>

It is established, even from **Plutarch**, that pleasures and lusts are signified by snakes; he cites a memorable story for this purpose concerning an Aetolian woman who was excessively loved by a snake. It was accustomed to visit her at night, coiling itself around the girl’s body, gliding here and there, yet it never harmed her, whether by choice or by accident; and it would depart opportunely around daybreak. When those who had the care of the girl realized this, they compelled her to move elsewhere. For three or four days, the serpent did not appear, but it went around diligently and accurately searching for her. When it soon found her, having come upon her by chance, it did not act as it was accustomed—mild and charming—but instead, fierce and rough, it leapt upon her. First, with its coils constricted around her body, it lashed her thighs with the remainder of its tail, displaying a light anger which, although mixed with some indulgence, clearly demonstrated a punishment. But these things are mentioned in passing, so that the reason why the ancients wanted pleasures and enticements to be signified by snakes might be clear.

**II.** There follows almost the same image of a man placed in straits <note>The Latin *angustiis* suggests being in a narrow, difficult, or distressing situation.</note> as the one we examined in the first Emblem. This, without doubt, indicates nothing other than what we said above. Indeed, the repetition of these images notes that such warnings can never be sufficiently emphasized, because of both their necessity and their utility. **"Twice and thrice, the good things."** <note>original Greek: *Δὶς καὶ τρὶς τὰ καλὰ*. A common proverb meaning that good things bear repeating.</note> Whether the left hand was cut off by accident or by design, I could hardly say. But if the latter, it suggests that every opportunity for escape has been cut off for the man, unless he frees himself in time and does not surrender his conquered hands to vices.

**III.** Next, the second motto of the first series is repeated: but it is changed slightly and transferred to another place. The <term>Cynocephalus</term> <note>A "dog-headed" figure. For that man, positioned in the middle between two others, is dragged along with his neck twisted by one of those sitting nearby; by the other, a staff is shown, twisted into spirals, with which he seems to threaten the one resisting. I believe this indicates that those whom neither right reason, nor good laws, nor the examples and encouragements of honorable men can keep within the track of honesty, must be coerced by the reins of justice and the staff of punishment. Thus **Solon** says, as found in **Stobaeus** <note>Johannes Stobaeus was a 5th-century compiler of Greek extracts.</note>, discourse 9:

->He who has a wicked heart never stays hidden forever,<-

<note>original Greek: Αἰεί ὔτε λέλιθε διαμπερὲς ὅστις ἀλιτρὸν... This passage from Solon emphasizes that divine justice is inevitable, even if delayed by generations.</note>

Which someone has interpreted thus: *Furthermore, he who has a villainous heart does not always remain hidden forever, but at last is altogether proven guilty. One pays the penalty immediately, another in the future. And if some seem to have escaped, so that the fate of the Gods has not fallen upon them, yet it comes entirely, and the innocent pay for the crimes, or rather the children of the first authors in the future.* For unless the wicked are restrained by the barriers of justice and punishment, morals, law, honor, and faith perish, as **Seneca** says in *Agamemnon*, and:

> The madness of arms looms, and the power of the iron sword
> Confounds all law with violence; and to heinous crime
> The name "virtue" shall be given, and it shall endure for many years.
> <note>original: *Imminet armorum rabies, ferriq; potestas / Confundit jus omne manus...* Seneca, Agamemnon, lines 148-150.</note>

IV. A beast with a human head, treading upon a fish with its feet, signifies a man indulging his own desires. Though he has a human face, he should be numbered among the beasts, since, having neglected sound reason, he lets loose the reins on his lusts and delights. For by fish, luxury, gluttony, and lust are signified, as was said above. See what we noted regarding the fourth symbol of the first order.

V. The final figure shows the inconveniences and dangers of idleness. For the lazy and idle man is continually targeted by the arrows of vice and exposes himself to the poisonous bites of the serpent. For "**Idleness is the Devil's pillow**" <note>original: *Otium namq; pulvinar Diaboli*</note> is a common saying.

->Idleness [has destroyed] kings and once-prosperous [cities]<-
<note>original: *Otium reges, prius & beatas* – A fragment of Catullus 51, warning that leisure and idleness can lead to the downfall of great powers.</note>

Leisure, says **Horace**, has destroyed cities,
"How many evils leisure causes for mortals," <note>original Greek: Ὡς πολλὰ θνητοῖς ἡ σχολὴ ποιεῖ κακὰ; a sentiment often attributed to Euripides regarding the dangers of idleness.</note>

### THE SECOND CIRCLE.

Just as our horn displayed the primary exercises of the mind regarding the virtues in the first class of symbols; so in this second ring, it proposes those things in which the body can be honorably and conveniently occupied, and which are especially conducive to dispelling lazy idleness.

I. The first theme brings **Horsemanship** before our eyes, which has always been held in such high regard by our ancestors that it was preferred over almost all other bodily exercises. **Flavius** writes concerning the **Alans** <note>An ancient nomadic Iranian people.</note> that they were such trained riders that they sometimes covered a hundred miles in a single gallop. The **Scythians**, according to **Hippocrates** in his book *On Airs, Waters, and Places*, rode horses incessantly; because of this, the parts dedicated to generation were completely weakened in them. **Herodotus** in Book 1 reports that the **Lydians** were so powerful in cavalry that **Croesus** wished the **Ionians** would come to fight against the Lydians with cavalry. **Strabo** mentions in Book 14 of his *Geography* that the **Colophonians** <note>Inhabitants of Colophon, an ancient Greek city in Ionia.</note> were vigorous in cavalry. Indeed, wherever in the world a war was waged that could not be settled otherwise, it was resolved with the help of the Colophonian cavalry. Hence the common proverb: *He put a Colophonian to it.* <note>original Greek: Κολοφῶνα ἐπέθηκεν. An ancient idiom meaning to put a finishing touch on something or to end a dispute decisively.</note> Our horn, therefore, not without merit, encourages horsemanship, especially for Princes and magnates, for whom the means of maintaining horses

To that end, *King Solomon* had forty thousand stalls for chariot horses and twelve thousand horsemen (1 Kings 4); <note>original Latin: III Regum iv. In the Vulgate Bible used by the author, 1 and 2 Kings are titled 3 and 4 Kings.</note> he also had fourteen hundred chariots and saw to it that horses were brought out of Egypt (1 Kings 10).

Anyone who thinks this horseman is a priest of Svantovitus <note>A four-headed Slavic deity of war and harvest, whose primary cult center was at Arkona on the island of Rügen.</note> fails to notice that Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian.</note> asserts that a priest of Svantovitus, contrary to the common custom of his country, was distinguished by the great length of his beard and hair. But this figure, while he has a beard, does not have a long one, and is entirely lacking in long hair. A priest is depicted in a tunic extending to his shins; this figure stands with a naked body. The former is endowed with the famous Horn of Svantovitus as his badge; this figure holds a spear or a hunting spear.

II. *The handling of weapons* is suggested by the man wielding swords with both hands. This undoubtedly alludes to the ancient way our people practiced with weapons, by which they handled swords with both hands in such a way that one was always poised in the air, as if suspended, while the other was caught alternately by the right hand. By law, they called this *Hand-sword* <note>original: Handſaxe. This refers to the "seax," a single-edged knife or sword from which the Saxons took their name, and here describes a specific martial exercise.</note>. Alexander ab Alexandro <note>A 15th-century Neapolitan scholar known for his work on ancient laws and customs.</note>, in Book III of *Genial Days*, chapter 21, reports that a game existed among the Germans in which naked youths would throw themselves back and forth between swords and threatening spears <term>frameas|A distinct type of Germanic spear or javelin described by the Roman historian Tacitus.</term>, leaping over them unhurt. Trained in the handling of weapons, they grew accustomed to not fearing hostile encounters, wounds, steel, or blood.

Hence, in the past, according to Biondo <note>Flavio Biondo (1392–1463), a pioneering Renaissance historian and archaeologist.</note> in Book II of *Rome Triumphant*, the work of those handling weapons was voluntary. For some, ordered by their petty kings, offered their names for arms to show a specimen of the courage innate to their nation; others declared they would fight in favor of a Leader. Others were drawn by emulation, so that they might challenge someone, or if challenged, they would not refuse the contest. Some who could not or would not end their controversies by discussion, having agreed among themselves that the matter would follow the victor, decided it with the sword. We read that our ancestors handled weapons with such religious devotion that they did nothing without being armed. They feasted armed, they entered councils armed, and they confirmed agreements by the touch of their weapons. They even swore oaths while armed; either with a weapon in the right hand, or sometimes upon the weapons of an honored person...

of his own, or others'. Hence, the taking away of arms was considered a most serious punishment among all nations.

III. **The practice of hunting** is placed before our eyes by the figure who, equipped with bow and arrows, strives to bring down a wild beast. Since nothing strengthens the body for labor and the mind for resisting the enemy quite as much as hunting—as Xenophon <note>Xenophon (c. 430–354 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and soldier; his treatise *Cynegeticus* (On Hunting) argues that hunting makes men better soldiers.</note> testifies in his work *On Hunting*—it is no wonder that among those things in which it is honorably fitting for a prince to be exercised, hunting is also placed. For we have heard that the Kings of the Persians were accustomed to restore the strengths of mind and body in this manner, not through idleness and drinking-bouts that sap the body's strength, but through the timely exercises and delights of hunting and fowling, as time and business allowed. On this account, Alexander the Macedonian, Cyrus, and others are commended—not for the sake of stuffing themselves, but to cherish and strengthen the body's vigor and natural heat for the sake of health, and to explore the history and nature of birds and beasts and record what they learned for posterity; thus they devoted their efforts to hunting and fowling. When Apollonius of Tyana <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher and reputed miracle-worker of the 1st century CE.</note> asked Phraotes, the King of the Indians, about his diet, he received the reply: *“Exercise is enough for me; the wild beasts caught in the hunt belong to others, to whom I give them,”* as Philostratus relates in the *Life of Apollonius*. Eusebius, in *The Preparation for the Gospel*, Book 8, Chapter 5, did not hesitate to assert: *“Those fierce beasts were produced by divine providence for the sake of military exercise.”* For this reason, even warlike women devoted themselves to this pursuit. Among the rest, Hasbites <note>A fictional North African warrior-queen from Silius Italicus's epic poem about the Punic Wars.</note> is celebrated by Silius Italicus, about whom he sings these lines in Book 1:

> *This woman, ignorant of men and accustomed to an empty bed,*
> *had spent her early years in the hunt and the woods:*
> *Her hand was not softened by wool-baskets, nor busy with the spindle.*
> *She loved Dictynna* <note>original: Dictynnam. An epithet for the goddess Diana, used here to represent the goddess and the hunt itself.</note> *and the glades, and to urge on the panting,*
> *hoofed horse with her foot, and fiercely to strike down wild beasts.*

In our **Emblem**, it should be noted that the hunter is depicted equipped with a bow and arrow seeking wild beasts, and not with a musket or other recently invented engines of war. This provides undeniable evidence of the antiquity of this horn.

Among the Romans, there was a certain kind of hunting, as—

referred to the spectacles, in which wild beasts placed in the theater—such as tigers, elephants, and lions—clashed with gladiators even unto the death and downfall of one of the parties. In these hunts, however, only those hired, or condemned, or those ambitious for a display of their own strength were employed, since the greatest risk to life was imminent. Concerning these, Suetonius <note>Suetonius (c. 69–122 CE) was a Roman historian; this quote describes the lavish games held by Julius Caesar.</note> writes in his *Life of Julius Caesar*: *Hunts were produced over five days, and finally a battle divided into two lines, with five hundred infantry, twenty elephants, and thirty cavalry clashing from each side.* <note>original: "Venationes editæ per dies quinq; ac novissimè pugna divisa in duas acies, quingenis peditibus, elephantis vicenis, tricenis equitibus hinc inde commissis."</note> But these types of hunts have no place here, as they are performed with greater danger to the hunter than benefit. That hunting is considered best which is conducted with horses, dogs, and the strength of the body, as Plato teaches in the seventh book of his *Laws*, although he disapproves of fishing and fowling. Xenophon, in the first book of the *Education of Cyrus*, says that hunting seems to the Persians to be the truest meditation on the affairs of war, by which they also become accustomed to enduring cold and heat. Furthermore, those going out to the hunt do not eat lunch until it is finished.

The hunting festivals of Diana were consecrated at Rome on account of the hunts on the eleventh day before the Kalends of September <note>August 22nd.</note>, as is established from the Roman Calendar.

IV. An elderly man, bearded, in priestly dress, holding a horn in his hands, seems to exhort us to preserve moderation in all things and to lighten the cares of the mind with a more cheerful drink at the proper time, while he attempts to offer the horn, filled with mead <note>original: "mulso," a drink made of wine and honey, or in a Northern context, mead.</note>, to the horseman. For just as too-vehement exercise breaks the body, dissipates natural heat, and exhausts strength, so too does moderate exercise, done with measure, strengthen the same, recall the dissipated heat, restore exhausted strength, and is profitable and opportune for all. Therefore, rest must sometimes be placed between labors. For as the Poet <note>Ovid, in his *Heroides* 4.89-90.</note> sings:

> *What lacks alternate rest is not durable:*
> *This restores strength and lifts weary limbs.*

Furthermore, what has been exhausted must be repaired with food and drink. This wise old man, acting as Physician and Priest, seems to urge this with his horn.

of his own, or belonging to another. Hence, the deprivation of arms has been considered the gravest punishment among all nations.

III. The **exercise of hunting** is brought before our eyes by the figure who, equipped with bow and arrows, strives to strike down a wild beast. Since nothing strengthens the body for labors and the mind for resisting the enemy as much as hunting—as Xenophon testifies in his work *On Hunting* <note>Xenophon (c. 430–354 BCE) was a Greek philosopher and soldier; his "Cynegeticus" argues that hunting produces better citizens and soldiers.</note>—it is no wonder that hunting is placed among those activities in which it is fitting for a prince to be honorably practiced. For in this way, not by idleness and drinking bouts which weaken the strength of the body, but by appropriate exercises and delights of hunting and fowling <note>original: "aucupii"</note>—according to the requirements of time and business—we learn that the Kings of the Persians especially were accustomed to restore the powers of their mind and body. For this reason, Alexander the Macedonian, Cyrus, and others are commended; they devoted themselves to hunting and fowling not for the sake of gluttony <note>original: "faginam"</note>, but to foster and strengthen the body's vigor and natural heat for the sake of health, and so that they might explore the history and nature of birds and wild beasts and record what they learned for posterity. When Apollonius of Tyana <note>A Neopythagorean philosopher and contemporary of Jesus.</note> asked Phraotes, the King of the Indians, about his way of life, he received the response: *that exercise was sufficient for him, but the wild beasts captured in the hunt belonged to others, to whom he gave them*; as Philostratus records in the *Life of Apollonius*. Eusebius, in *The Preparation for the Gospel*, book 8, chapter 5, did not hesitate to assert: *Those fierce beasts were produced by divine providence for the sake of military exercise.* This is why even warlike women have dedicated themselves to this study. Among others, Hasbites is celebrated by Silius Italicus, of whom he sings in book 1:

> *She, ignorant of men and accustomed to an empty bed,*
> *By hunting and the woods, had defended her early years;*
> *Her hand not softened by wool-baskets, nor worked with a spindle.*
> *She loved Dictynna <note>An epithet for the goddess Diana/Artemis.</note> and the glades, and to urge on the panting*
> *Horse with her foot, and to lay low the fierce beasts.*

In our Emblem, it should be noted that the hunter is depicted seeking wild beasts equipped with a bow and arrow, not indeed with a musket <note>original: "bombarda"</note> or other newly invented engines of war. This provides indubitable testimony concerning the antiquity of this horn.

Among the Romans there was a certain kind of hunting, pertaining to
