the spectacles must be recalled, in which wild beasts placed in the theater—such as tigers, elephants, and lions—fought with gladiators even unto the death and fall of one of the parties. In these hunts, however, only hired men, or the condemned, or those ambitious to show off their strength were employed, since the greatest danger to life was imminent. Regarding these, Suetonius <note>Gaius Suetonius Tranquillus (c. 69–122 AD), a Roman historian.</note> writes in his *Life of Julius Caesar*: *Hunts were staged for five days, and finally a battle was divided into two lines, with five hundred infantry, twenty elephants, and thirty horsemen engaged on either side.* <note>original: "Venationes editæ per dies quinq; ac noviſſimè pugna diviſa in duas acies, qvingenis peditibus, elephantis vicenis, tricenis equitibus hinc inde commiſſis."</note> But these types of hunts have no place here, as they are conducted with greater danger to the hunter than benefit. That hunting is considered best which is carried out with horses, dogs, and the strength of the body, as Plato teaches in the seventh book of *The Laws*, although he disapproves of fishing and fowling. Xenophon, in the first book of the *Cyropaedia* <note>Xenophon's "The Education of Cyrus."</note>, says that hunting seems to the Persians to be the truest practice for warfare, by which they also become accustomed to enduring cold and heat. Furthermore, when going out to hunt, they do not eat until it is finished.

The hunting festivals of Diana <note>The Roman goddess of the hunt.</note> were consecrated in Rome for the sake of the hunt on the 11th day before the Kalends of September <note>August 22nd.</note>, as is evident from the Roman Calendar.

IV. An aged man, bearded, in priestly dress, holding a horn in his hands, seems to urge the preservation of moderation in all things and the relief of the mind's cares with a more cheerful drink at the proper time, while he attempts to offer a horn filled with <term>mead<gloss>mulsum: a Roman drink made of wine and honey</gloss></term> to a horseman. For just as too-violent exercise breaks the body, dissipates natural heat, and exhausts strength, so too does moderate exercise done with measure; it strengthens the same, recalls dissipated heat, restores exhausted strength, and is profitable and opportune for all. Therefore, rest must sometimes be placed between labors. For as the Poet <note>Ovid, in his *Heroides* 4.91-92.</note> sings:

> *What lacks alternating rest is not lasting:*
> *This restores strength and relieves weary limbs.*

Indeed, things exhausted must be repaired with food and drink. This is what this wise old man, acting as both Physician and Priest, seems to advise with his horn.

> *Of horn, through which an easy exit is given to true shades;*

See what we have noted above concerning the biform nature of horns. In this sense, the emblem perhaps wishes to suggest that after physical exercises, something should be granted to the mind—to reading, studies, histories, and other things that will serve the governance of Princes—so that we may be instructed by them, as if by dreams brought through the horn, as to what needs to be done.

It is not unworthy of observation that while all the other figures on this horn representing humans are naked, without clothes—undoubtedly to show our nakedness and weakness in the pursuit of integrity and virtue—this figure alone is gifted with an ankle-length robe and a hood with a long train hanging down over the shoulders. This shows what the Teachers and Masters of others ought to be like: namely, covered in the garments of virtue, knowledge, and piety. It is also bearded, to teach that wisdom and prudence are required in him. As for the horn he holds in his hands, because it ends in a sharp point and is held in such a way that it can contain and offer liquid, it has a closer affinity with a drinking cup—with which the old man seems to want to refresh those exhausted by physical exercise—than with a trumpet or bugle. Note also in passing what kind of dress the Runes, Skalds, and our native Priests <note>Worm refers here to the "Runes" (learned men), Skalds (poets), and ancient Germanic/Norse priests.</note> used at the time this horn was fashioned.

> And a thousand forms of death: from here 
> The shed blood stained all the lands, and the sea grew red; 
> Then crimes without end went through every home, 
> No wickedness lacked an example.

II. Aristophanes <note>An ancient Greek playwright famous for comedies.</note> teaches in *The Clouds* that the image of a Centaur denotes a man of rustic manners and a prone-to-anger disposition. And since a Centaur is fashioned with a human face down to the waist and the body of a horse for the rest, the ancients wished to denote by this that soldiers—burning with the heat of war—may appear human in face, yet they possess the soul of a kicking and untamed horse. Such a spirit cannot be restrained by any reins or bars once the path to war, theft, plunder, and banditry has been thrown open. Not without cause, therefore, does Tibullus <note>A Roman poet known for his elegies.</note> exclaim in Book I, Elegy 10:

> *What madness is it to summon dark death with wars?*
> *It looms over us and comes secretly with a silent step.*

See the fable of the Centaurs in Natalis Comes <note>Natale Conti, a famous 16th-century Italian mythographer whose works were standard textbooks in the Renaissance.</note>, Book VI. From these is drawn the proverb: <note>original Greek: νῆφ' κἀν ἔνι κενταύροις / "nēph' kan eni kentaurois"</note> *Be sober, even among Centaurs.* This was said against the foolish and senseless who would attempt what could not be achieved; others claim it was said against the contentious and those who crave the property of others, because the craving for things belonging to others brought destruction upon the Centaurs.

III. The same meaning is intended by the two wolves (or figures with dog-like faces) challenging each other; one of them, armed with a curved sword <note>original: "gladio falcato." A sickle-shaped blade or falchion.</note>, attacks an adversary equipped with an axe. This shows the enormity, foulness, and tyranny of wars and quarrels, which turn rational men into beasts more atrocious than dogs or wolves; for they rage against their own species and think that no unspeakable deed is forbidden to them. Alas, how truly it is said:

> *No faith or piety belongs to the men who follow the camps!*
> <note>original: "Nulla fides pietasq; viris qui castra sequuntur!" A quote from Lucan’s *Pharsalia*, lamenting the lack of morals among mercenary soldiers.</note>

Why then should we not cry out:

> *There is no safety in war; we all demand peace from you!*
> <note>original: "Nulla salus bello, pacem te poscimus omnes!" A variation of a line from Virgil’s *Aeneid*.</note>

<meta>This page continues Ole Worm's interpretation of the figures on the Golden Horn. After discussing the symbols of war and savagery (the Centaur and the Blood Eagle), he now turns to the figures representing the "golden peace" of the ancient North, using livestock and agriculture as primary symbols of prosperity.</meta>

<page-num>423</page-num>
<header>BOOK FIVE</header>

For he introduces a figure feeding herds, driving them to pasture with a staff, and warding off wolves and other fierce beasts with an ax; this is done to more happily express the delight and sweetness of golden peace. It seems to me that he clearly wished to sketch that sentiment of the Comedian <note>Aristophanes, the Greek playwright.</note>:

->Peace nourishes the farmer well, even among the rocks<-
->But war treats him badly, even on the open plain.<-
<note>original Greek: Εἰρήνη γεωργὸν κ᾿ ἀν πέτραις τρέφει καλῶς / Πόλεμος δὲ κὰν πεδίω Κακῶς ἔφει.</note>

->*Peace nourishes the farmer well even in the rocks*<-
->*But war is harmful even in the field itself.*<-
<note>The author provides a Latin translation of the Greek verse above.</note>

In ancient times, the greatest part of wealth and worldly happiness was placed in the possession of herds and livestock, as we are taught even from the sacred scriptures in Genesis 13; hence it follows that peace could not be expressed by a more fitting symbol. The flocks and herds of Abraham and Lot are recounted as being so great and numerous that, when a dispute over pastures arose between their shepherds, they were forced to separate from one another. Job possessed seven thousand bleating sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys. All these things were doubled by God once he had shown proof of his patience. Furthermore, even secular authors have left testimony that a happy possession of peace is found in the abundance of oxen and herds. Homer, in the *Iliad*, relates that Iphidamas, the son of Antenor, gave one hundred oxen to his father-in-law as a wedding gift. Nor do we need to seek far-off examples. Everyone knows that the wealth of the northern islands—Iceland, the Faroes, and others—is situated in the multitude of sheep and cattle. And so:

> This man is to be praised, who, with his family grown,
> Occupies his slow old age in a small cottage.
> He himself follows his sheep, and his son the lambs;
> And his wife prepares warm water for him in his weariness.
> <note>These lines are from the Roman poet Tibullus, Book I, Elegy 10, praising the simple, peaceful life of a farmer.</note>

Plutarch, in his life of Numa, relates that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, credited with establishing many religious and civil traditions.</note>—lest the people rot in idleness—divided the lands and joined to them the god Terminus <note>The Roman god of boundaries and landmarks.</note> to separate the borders of the fields. He appointed men to observe these boundaries individually and to go around the fields, judging the character of the citizens by their labors. From this it happened that, as the Romans diligently cultivated the study of agriculture, they often called not only Consuls, Dictators, and Senators from the fields via messengers, but many even took up rustic surnames.

> *And death in a thousand forms: from here blood spilled*
> *Infected all the lands, and the sea grew red;*
> *Then crimes went without end through every home,*
> *And no wickedness lacked a precedent.*
<note>original Latin: *Et mille formas mortis...* These lines are from Seneca’s tragedy *Hercules Furens*, describing the total breakdown of moral order during conflict.</note>

II. Aristophanes teaches in *The Clouds* <note>A famous Greek comedy.</note> that the image of a Centaur denotes a man of rustic manners and one prone to anger <unclear>iribundum</unclear> <note>likely *irabundum*, "wrathful"</note>. And since a Centaur is fashioned with a human face down to the waist, but with the rest of the body as a horse, the ancients wished to denote by this that soldiers, burning with the heat of wars—though they appear human in face—possess the spirit of a kicking and untamed horse, which can be restrained by no bits or bars once the way has been opened to war, theft, plunder, and robbery. Therefore, not without cause does Tibullus <note>A Roman poet.</note> exclaim in Book I of his *Elegies*:

> *What madness it is to summon black death by wars?*
> *It looms, and comes secretly with silent foot.*

See the fable of the Centaurs in Natalis Comes, Book VI <note>A standard 16th-century reference for mythology.</note>. From these is derived the proverb: *Now there are no Centaurs* <note>original Greek: νῦν οὐκ ἔνι κένταυροι</note>. This is said against the senseless and foolish who might attempt what cannot be achieved; others wish it to be said against the contentious and those greedy for what belongs to others, because greed for the property of others brought destruction to the Centaurs.

III. The two figures with wolf or dog faces, provoking one another in turn, mean the same thing; one of them, armed with a curved sword <term>gladio falcato</term> <note>literally a "sickle-shaped sword," likely referring to a falx or a specific type of curved blade depicted on the horn</note>, attacks an adversary equipped with an axe. They show the enormity, foulness, and tyranny of wars and quarrels, which turn rational men into beasts more atrocious than dogs and wolves; for they vent their rage upon their own kind, and think no unspeakable deed they might commit is unlawful for them.
Alas, how
> *There is no faith or piety in men who follow the camps!*
<note>original: *Nulla fides pietasq; viris qui castra sequuntur!* — a quote from Lucan’s *Pharsalia* regarding the lawlessness of soldiers.</note>

Why should we not then exclaim:
> *There is no safety in war; we all beg you for peace!*
<note>original: *Nulla salus bello, pacem te poscimus omnes!* — a quote from Virgil’s *Aeneid*.</note>

...for he introduces a figure pasturing herds, driving them to their fodder with a staff, and fending off wolves and other monstrous beasts with an axe; he does this so that he might more happily express the delight and sweetness of golden peace. It seems to me he clearly wished to sketch that idea of the Comic poet <note>The "Comic poet" refers to Aristophanes, specifically his play *Peace*.</note>:

-> Peace nourishes the farmer well even among the rocks <-
-> While War does poorly even in the open plain. <-
-> *Peace nourishes the farmer well even among the rocks* <-
-> *But war is harmful even in the field itself.* <-
<note>original Greek: Εἰρήνη γεωργὸν... original Latin: Alit Colonum... These verses emphasize that peace brings prosperity even to harsh lands, while war ruins even the most fertile soil.</note>

Because in olden times the greatest part of wealth and worldly happiness was situated in the possession of herds and cattle—as we are taught even from the sacred scriptures in Genesis 13—it follows that peace could not be expressed by a more suitable symbol. The herds of cattle belonging to Abraham and Lot were so many and so great in number that, when a dispute over pastures arose between their shepherds, they were forced to separate from one another. Job possessed seven thousand bleating sheep, three thousand camels, five hundred yoke of oxen, and five hundred female donkeys. All these things were doubled by God once Job had shown proof of his patience. Indeed, other secular authors have also left testimony of a happy state of peace through an abundance of oxen and herds. Homer, in the *Iliad*, records that Iphidamas, the son of Antenor, gave one hundred oxen to his father-in-law as a wedding gift. We need not look for remote examples: everyone knows that the wealth of the northern islands, such as Iceland, the Faroe Islands, and others, lies in the multitude of sheep and cattle. And so:

> *This man is to be praised, whom, with his offspring ready,*
> *A slow old age occupies in a small cottage.*
> *He follows his own sheep, while his son follows the lambs;*
> *And his wife prepares warm water for him when he is tired.*
<note>These lines are from the Roman poet Tibullus, Book I, Elegy 10, praising the simple, peaceful life of the farmer.</note>

Plutarch, in his life of Numa, records that Numa Pompilius <note>The legendary second king of Rome, known for his religious and peaceful reforms.</note>—lest the people grow weak through idleness—divided the lands and joined to them the god Terminus <note>The Roman god of boundaries and landmarks.</note> to separate the borders of the fields, so that individuals might observe them. He established those who would go around the fields, judging the character of the citizens from their labors. From this it happened that, since the Romans diligently cultivated the study of agriculture, they not only frequently called Consuls, Dictators, and Senators from the fields via messengers <term>viatores</term> <note>Official attendants or messengers of Roman magistrates.</note>, but many also held rustic surnames.

# THE FIFTH CIRCLE.

The entire section seems dedicated to the recommendation of Prudence <note>The Latin *Prudentia* refers to practical wisdom and foresight.</note>. Two men show a mirror, brilliant with various gems of virtue, to a man who has been reduced to a beast-like form by his vices; they do this so that, recognizing his own foulness, he might turn away from the allurements of evil and return to a sounder mind through the help of prudence. There are icons of *serpents*, both large and small, trampling and restraining the *fish* of pleasures and lusts; so that, protected by this fortification of prudence, one might complete the course of life more safely. Pierius <note>Giovanni Pierio Valeriano Bolzani (1477–1558), an Italian humanist famous for his work on hieroglyphics.</note> teaches in book 61 that the mirror of examination was once a Hieroglyph because it detects and reveals hidden blemishes, spots, and wrinkles. For the same reasons, painters usually adorn the statue of Prudence with them. Indeed, the Savior himself attributed prudence to serpents when, in Matthew 10, he commands us to be simple as doves but wise as serpents. For just as the serpent, if it is struck, hides its head under the rest of its body, so Christians—even if subjected to various torments—will take care that their faith, acting as the head, remains uninjured. This is explained by Giulio Cesare Capaccio <note>An Italian historian and emblematist (1550–1634).</note> in book 1 of *The Emblems*, chapter 20. Moses also, in Genesis 3, calls the serpent the most prudent among animals. For it is crafty and ready for its own defense and support. Thus:

-> The mind is a great bridle for the human soul. <-
<note>original Greek: Ψυχῆς μέγας χαλινὸς ἀνθρώποις ὁ νῦς.</note>
-> *The mind possesses prudence as its strongest bridle.* <-

It has already been emphasized many times that pleasures and allurements are understood through *fish*. Hence Horapollo <note>The supposed author of an ancient treatise on Egyptian hieroglyphs, popular in the Renaissance.</note> says in Book 1 of his *Hieroglyphics*, chapter 42, that something wicked and abominable is indicated by a fish. This is why those who are occupied with sacred rites shrink from and curse the eating of them. For there is a certain fish of such a nature that it consumes whatever it happens upon, and even rages against its own kind. Therefore, to avoid the company and the tricks of such men, there is a need for counsel and prudence; he who is destitute of these is truly unhappy.

> Believe me, prudence is the first to leave the wretched,
> And sense and judgment flee along with wealth.
<note>A quote from Ovid's *Letters from the Black Sea* (Epistulae ex Ponto), suggesting that when a person loses their fortune, they often lose their ability to think clearly as well.</note>

They say that Philip, King of the Macedonians, [cared] more for prudence, imperial cunning, and the success he had in winning over men—

...possessed [virtues], than to have boasted of the strength of his forces and auxiliaries. Suetonius is the authority for the fact that it was doubtful whether Gaius Julius Caesar was more cautious or more daring in undertaking his expeditions. So true it is that:

### THE SIXTH CIRCLE.

I. This section seems to me to represent **Justice**. A large head devoid of eyes, placed between two beasts, is an emblem of Justice, or of a just judge. Justice is depicted by many with a veiled face, so that she does not look so much at the litigating persons as she perceives the cases with her ears; so that she may grant to each their own *without passion* <note>original Greek: ἄνευ πάθως (aneu pathos); meaning without emotional bias.</note>. For:
> The man who is just and firm of purpose,
> Not the heat of citizens commanding evil,
> Nor the face of a threatening tyrant,
> Shakes from his solid mind; nor the South Wind,
> The stormy ruler of the restless Adriatic,
> Nor the great hand of thundering Jove.
> If the broken world should fall,
> The ruins will strike him unafraid. <note>This is a famous passage from Horace’s *Odes* (3.3), describing the unshakable nature of a man of integrity.</note>
From the head, curls hang down equally; from the neck, the forks <note>Likely referring to the decorative lines or "divaricationes" in the engraving.</note> incline toward no side; just as the Comic Poet commands, saying:
->*Walk the straight path if you are just.* <note>original Greek: Βάδιζε τὴν εὐθεῖαν ἣν δίκαιος ᾖς.</note><-
->*Step forward in a straight line, you who are just.*<-
It is placed between two beasts, whose accusations and cases it is proper to hear; yet it is not fitting to look upon their tyrannical forms. The Egyptians, in a contrary way, represented Justice by an eye.
->*The eye of Justice sees what is happening,* <note>original Greek: Ὄμμα δίκης καθορᾷ τὰ γιγνόμενα.</note><-
says the Poet. Hence that saying, "the eye of Justice" <note>original Greek: Δίκης ὄφθαλμος (Dikēs ophthalmos).</note>. In this sense, Plato also calls justice "watchful" and "avenging." But they had another purpose in mind. So that he may more conveniently weigh the individual moments of things, it is necessary for a judge to be clear-sighted, and from the naked throne of the Sun to spread his rays through all things, and to see all things just like the Sun itself...

...it is fitting to direct, as Proclus <note>A Neoplatonist philosopher who wrote on the nature of justice and the soul.</note> wishes. But once the facts of a case are known, so that she is not clouded by the splendor of a person's status, or corrupted by hope, fear, or bribes, the administrator of justice here ought to be blind. For Justice is aptly compared to the Sun or a bright star; this seems to be hinted at by that star shining with seven rays (representing the other virtues) which is seen to the right, above the head denoting Justice. For the Latin poets imagine that Justice, hating the crimes of men, left the earth and obtained a place among the stars, where she was worshiped under the title of **Astraea** <note>The celestial virgin and goddess of justice in Greek and Roman mythology.</note>. Thus Seneca says in *Octavia*:

> Neglected, she fled the lands and the fierce customs 
> Of men, her hands polluted by bloody slaughter—
> The virgin Astraea, the great glory of the stars. 
> <note>original: "Neglecta terras fugit & mores feros / Hominum, cruenta cæde pollutas manus / Astræa virgo, syderum magnum decus."</note>

-> Ovid, *Metamorphoses*, Book 1 <-

> Astraea, the last of the celestials, left the lands.
> <note>original: "Vltima cælestum terras Astræa reliquit."</note>

II. The fruit and reward of rightly administered justice seems to me to be indicated by the *flower* that accompanies her, which represents a *Lily*. The Masters of Hieroglyphics <term>Hieroglyphicorum Magistri</term> <note>Scholars of emblems and symbols who interpreted visual images as moral or philosophical lessons.</note> hold that the lily is a symbol of Hope; because it is free from every stain and conspicuous in its snowy whiteness, it bids us to have good hope. This is also shown by the inscriptions on various coins of Alexander, Pius, Augustus, Aemilianus, and Claudius, in which one can see a Goddess holding a lily in her right hand, with this inscription: PUBLIC HOPE, AUGUSTAN HOPE, etc. <note>original: "SPES PUBLICA, SPES AUGUSTA"</note>

In particular, there is a coin of Faustina <note>Annia Galeria Faustina, a Roman Empress known for her charity.</note> in which, beneath the lily and the image of the Goddess (who holds a horn of plenty in her hand), the words FOR GOOD HOPE <note>original: "BONÆ SPEII"</note> are added, spelled with a double "I". Indeed, Hope seems to be correctly signified not only by the lily but by every kind of flower. For just as the fruit is contained within the flowers, so the things hoped for are accustomed to follow from hopes, as Stephanus Zamosius <note>István Szamosközy, a 16th-century humanist historian.</note> says in chapter 12 of the *Annals of the Antiquities of Dacia*.

The whole matter was most fittingly expressed by Menander in Stobaeus's seventh sermon:

When you perform a holy act, set a good hope 
Before yourself, knowing this: that 
God also assists a just endeavor.
<note>original Greek: Όταν τι πράττεις όσιον, ἀγαθὴν ἐλπίδα / Πρόβαλλ’ ἑαυτῷ τοῦτο γινώσκον, ότι / Τόλμῃ δικαία καὶ Θεὸς συλλαμβάνει.</note>

*When you do anything holy, propose to yourself a good hope, certain that God also assists a just attempt.*

> If you could only break through the harsh fates,
> You will be Marcellus; give lilies with full hands.
> <note>original: "Si qua fata aspera rumpas / Tu Marcellus eris; manibus date lilia plenis." These lines from Virgil’s Aeneid (Book 6) refer to the premature death of Marcellus, nephew of Augustus.</note>

King Erik <note>Erik I of Denmark, known as Erik the Good (reigned 1095–1103).</note>, who had succeeded Niels, is celebrated by our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220), a Danish historian and author of the Gesta Danorum.</note> for his devotion to justice in Book 14. Meanwhile, he says, Erik, desiring to adorn the peace sought through arms with the ornaments of Justice, restored the laws established by his ancestors—which were then almost entirely subverted by the great storm of wars—to their former state of vigor. Just as he had been distinguished in courage, so he appeared notable in justice; he compensated for the injuries inflicted on the lower classes by punishing their superiors, and sparing neither friendship nor kinship, he corrected the reckless greed of the powerful with either the sword or the noose.

## THE SEVENTH CIRCLE

The last circle endowed with Hieroglyphics <term>Hieroglyphicis</term> <note>In this context, the author uses "hieroglyphics" to mean symbolic or emblematic images found on the artifact, rather than Egyptian script.</note> also displays the ultimate end of our life: Death. This must be placed before our eyes in all our actions, so that we may do what is right, flee from what is unjust, and sincerely fear God. *Let death and exile and all things held to be evil be before your eyes daily:* and especially, of all things, death. <note>original: "μάλιστα δὲ πάντων ὁ θάνατος"</note> In this way, you will never think of anything humble, nor will you desire anything excessively, says Epictetus in Chapter 28 of the *Enchiridion* <note>A manual of Stoic ethical advice.</note>. For as the same author says in Chapter 10: *Death is not an evil. But the opinion about death is what makes it an evil.* Hence, Cicero, the father of eloquence, rightly says in the first book of his *Tusculan Disputations*: *Death does not deter the wise man, for it looms daily due to uncertain chances, and because of the brevity of life, it can never be far away.*

Two bones placed between two combinations of lizards or snakes warn us that we will be food for worms after death. Nothing is now more common than this same symbol; for we are accustomed to prefigure our state after fate with a human skull and bones entwined with serpents.

> *One night awaits all,*
> *And the path of death must be trodden once.*
> <note>original: "Omnes una manet nox / Et calcanda semel via lethi." From Horace, Odes 1.28.</note>

> *You shall carry no wealth to the shadows of Acheron:*
> *Naked, O fool, you are carried to the infernal rafts.*
> <note>original: "Haud ullus portabis opes Acherontis ad umbras: / Nudus ad infernas, stulte vehere rates." From Propertius, Elegies 3.5. Acheron is one of the rivers of the underworld in Greek mythology.</note>

->Therefore:<-

> ***Live mindful of death, so that you may live mindful of salvation.***
> <note>original: "Vive memor mortis, memor ut sis vive salutis."</note>

# DANISH MONUMENTS

It is fitting to direct it, as Proclus <note>Proclus (412–485 AD) was a Greek Neoplatonist philosopher.</note> wishes. Truly, it must be considered that the administrator of justice here ought to be blind, lest he be dazzled by the splendor of a person, or corrupted by hope, fear, or gifts. For Justice is aptly compared to the Sun or a brilliant star; this also seems to be indicated by that star shining with seven rays (representing the other virtues) which is seen on the right side, above the head of the figure denoting Justice. For the Latin poets imagine that Astraea <note>The "star-maiden," a goddess associated with innocence and purity who was the last immortal to live among humans.</note>, the goddess of Justice, left the earth out of hatred for the crimes of men, took her place among the stars, and was honored under that name. Hence Seneca writes in *Octavia*:

> Neglected, she fled the lands and the fierce customs
> of men, and hands polluted by bloody slaughter,
> Astraea the virgin, the great glory of the stars.
> <note>original: "Neglecta terras fugit & mores feros / Hominum, cruenta cæde pollutas manus / Astræa virgo, syderum magnum decus."</note>

-> *Ovid, Metamorphoses, Book 1* <-

> Astraea was the last of the heavenly beings to leave the earth.
> <note>original: "Ultima cælestum terras Astræa reliquit."</note>

II. The *flower* accompanying her, which represents a *Lily*, seems to me to promise the fruit and reward of justice rightly administered. The masters of Hieroglyphics <term>Hieroglyphicis</term> <note>Here referring to the study of symbolic emblems or "Egyptian secrets" popular in the Renaissance, rather than literal Egyptian script.</note> maintain that the lily is a symbol of Hope because, being free from every stain and conspicuous in its snowy whiteness, it bids us to have good hope. This is also shown by the inscriptions on various coins of Alexander, Pius, Augustus, Aemilianus, and Claudius, in which one may see the Goddess holding a lily in her right hand, with this inscription: PUBLIC HOPE, AUGUST HOPE, etc. <note>original: "SPES PUBLICA. SPE AUGUSTA."</note>

Most notably, there is a coin of Faustina <note>Likely Faustina the Elder or Younger, Roman Empresses known for coins depicting virtues.</note> in which, beneath a lily and the image of the Goddess who holds a cornucopia in her hand, is added: TO GOOD HOPE <note>original: "BONA SPEII"</note>, spelled with a double I. Indeed, it seems that Hope is rightly signified not only by the lily, but by all types of flowers. Because, just as fruit follows flowers, so the things hoped for are accustomed to follow hopes, as Stephanus Zamosius <note>István Szamosközy (1570–1612), a prominent Hungarian historian.</note> says in the *Annals of the Antiquities of Dacia*, chapter 12.

Menander <note>An ancient Greek dramatist.</note> expressed the whole matter most conveniently, as cited in Stobaeus, sermon 7:

> Whenever you perform a holy act, hold out
> a good hope for yourself, knowing this:
> That God also assists a righteous daring.
> <note>original: "Ὅταν τι πράττεις ὅσιον, ἀγαθὴν ἐλπίδα / Πρόβαλλ᾿ ἑαυτῷ τοῦτο γινώσκων, ὅτι / Τόλμῃ δικαίᾳ καὶ θεὸς συλλαμβάνει."</note>

*When you do something holy, propose a good hope for yourself, certain that God also aids a just endeavor.*

King Erik, who had succeeded Nicholas, is celebrated by our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), the medieval Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> for his devotion to justice, in book 14. Just as he had been distinguished in bravery, so he appeared remarkable in justice; he balanced the injuries inflicted on the lesser people with punishments for the higher ranks, and sparing neither friendship nor kinship, he punished the reckless greed of the powerful with either the sword or the noose."

### THE SEVENTH CIRCLE

The last circle endowed with Hieroglyphics <term>Hieroglyphica</term> <note>In this context, the author refers to symbolic or emblematic images used to convey hidden moral truths, a common intellectual pursuit in the Renaissance and Baroque periods.</note> displays also the final end of our life: Death. This must be placed before our eyes in all our actions, so that we may do what is right, flee what is unjust, and sincerely fear God.

> "Let death and exile and all things that are held among evils be daily before your eyes: *but most of all, death* <note>original Greek: "μάλιστα δὲ πάντων ὁ θάνατος"</note>. Thus you will never think anything humble, nor will you desire anything excessively," says Epictetus in chapter 28 of the *Enchiridion* <note>Epictetus was a Stoic philosopher; his *Enchiridion* is a manual of ethical advice.</note>. For as the same author says in chapter 10: "Death is not an evil. But it is the opinion about death that makes it an evil." Hence, the parent of eloquence, Cicero, rightly says in the first book of the *Tusculan Disputations*: "Death does not deter the Wise Man, for it looms daily because of uncertain chances, and because of the brevity of life, it can never be far away."

A pair of bones placed between two combinations of lizards or snakes warns us that we will be the food of worms after death. Nothing is now more common than this same symbol; for with a human skull and bones entwined with serpents, we are accustomed to prefigure our state after destiny.

> *One night awaits everyone,*
> *And the path of death must be trodden once.*
> <note>original: "Omnes una manet nox / Et calcanda semel via lethi." From Horace’s *Odes*, Book 1.28.</note>

---

> *You shall carry no riches to the shadows of Acheron <note>Acheron is one of the rivers of the underworld in Greek mythology, representing the realm of the dead.</note>:*
> *Fool, you are carried naked to the infernal boats.*
> <note>original: "Haud ullus portabis opes Acherontis ad umbras: / Nudus ad infernas, stulte vehere rates." From the Roman poet Propertius, *Elegies*, Book 3.5.</note>

->Therefore:<-

> *Live mindful of death, so that you may live mindful of salvation.*

to cast a work of such great weight from metal; I consider it clearly a royal work and one deposited among the treasures of some very wealthy King. Whether, indeed, any other person has ever appeared more worthy of this treasure <note>original: "κειμήλιω" (keimēlion) — a precious heirloom or object of great value.</note> than Frotho the Great—who at the time of Christ’s birth held empire over the Danes and many other regions—I leave for others to discern.

This is certainly clear from the report of our Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century author of the *Gesta Danorum*.</note> in Book 5: that he was extremely wealthy, and that he fixed one bracelet upon a rock which they call "Frotho’s Stone"; another in the province of Wig, after holding an assembly with the Norwegians, having issued an edict that he was providing a test of innocence; he threatened that if these were removed, he would take action against all the governors of the region. And so, Saxo adds: *At the greatest risk to the prefects, gold fixed in the middle of the crossroads without a guard stood as a great provocation to greed, a ready prey for plunder, provoking minds full of desire.* Whether this golden horn of his was among the number of those objects which he had placed at the crossroads of the Ribe district <note>original: "tractus Ripensis" — the area around Ribe in Jutland, where the first Golden Horn was found in 1639.</note>, and was finally buried untouched by the mud and liquefied by rains, I do not know if I would dare to assert. 

Certainly, I do not hesitate to boldly deny that it was brought from Rügen <note>original: "Rugia" — an island in the Baltic Sea.</note>, since I cannot see it proved by any arguments of any importance or by the testimony of authors more worthy of trust, however much the patrons of Svantovit <note>Svantovit was a four-headed Slavic deity worshipped on Rügen; some scholars apparently argued the horn was a Slavic artifact rather than Danish.</note> may twist themselves. You, reader, assess and judge; I take my hand from this tablet <note>original: "manum de hac tabula" — a Latin idiom meaning to stop working on or finish a task.</note>.

Especially since I understand that the preeminent philosopher and philologist of Italy, Fortunio Liceti <note>A famous Italian physician and polymath (1577–1657) who wrote on ancient rings and artifacts.</note>, in his distinguished work *On the Rings of the Ancients* <note>original: "de Annulis veterū"</note>, has treated this matter more diligently, and has declared by deed that this horn is of such value to him that he does not consider the hours he spent on it to be lost at all; rather, he judges it worthy that he should extract a good part of his time for it. For so he wrote from Bologna to Padua in March of this year, to the most learned young man Thomas Bartholin <note>Thomas Bartholin (1616–1680), the famous Danish physician and anatomist, who was studying in Italy at the time.</note>, a son rivaling his great father. Meanwhile, I find it very difficult to believe that this horn had no other use than for testing the vigilance of the governors. For this could have been achieved just as easily with a raw mass of gold, or gold reduced to some other shape with less effort. I readily grant that it was exposed at the crossroads to test the loyalty of the subjects, but I cannot persuade myself it was fashioned for this end alone. I have discussed these matters with my close friend, as our countryman Bartholin <note>Thomas Bartholin (1616–1680), the renowned Danish physician and anatomist, who was studying in Italy at the time.</note> will describe in full: in which I have noted certain **emblems** from Denmark. If I should learn anything more precise about them hereafter, you may be sure I will share it. My mind is now more closely occupied with the study of the **Venetian Miter** <note>The *Corno Ducale*, the distinctive horn-shaped cap worn by the Doge of Venice, which Rhodius is attempting to trace back to antiquity.</note>: to which I believe some clarity has been added, if the exquisite sketch of my coin has come into your sight. It appears to be **Atys** <note>A Phrygian deity and consort of the goddess Cybele, often depicted wearing a pointed "Phrygian cap."</note>, whose image it bears, though—as often happens—the artist’s haste left the right horn of the Moon <note>A crescent moon symbol often associated with Eastern deities.</note> mutilated, and the characters are worn away by their position. 

You have undoubtedly seen something not unlike this in the exposition of the Tarentine monument, which **Pignorius** <note>Lorenzo Pignoria (1571–1631), an Italian antiquarian and scholar.</note> left to us. Nor is that bronze statue, of which you have now sent a print, foreign to this; for Atys wears similar **breeches** <term>bracas</term> <note>original: "bracas" — trousers or leggings, which were considered "barbarian" or foreign dress by the Greeks and Romans, typical of Phrygian or Persian figures.</note> fastened with clasps, and nearly the same miter in a most skillfully carved marble, which today still adorns the Casia house in Rome, where the Canon Ubaldini, brother of the late Cardinal, lives. From that statue I drew the figure of the **Cymbal**, which will shed no small light on the work of Scribonius Compositus <note>Likely referring to the ancient Roman medical writer Scribonius Largus, or a specific commentary on him.</note>. Here, the youth offers his right hand to the left; in his left, he holds a cymbal, while **Cybele** <note>The "Great Mother" goddess of Phrygia.</note> beats a drum. 

What your own statue might imply, you will easily conjecture by your own wit. However, I do not wish to hide that such a style of dress was common to the Phrygians, especially that head-covering, which even the most elegant marble **Ganymede** <note>In mythology, a beautiful Trojan prince; Rhodius refers here to a specific statue in Venice.</note> wears—the one you remember hanging in the dome of the vestibule of St. Mark’s Library in Venice. Mention is made of this among the statues in Chapter 12 of the *Origins of Padua* by Lorenzo Pignorius, where the clothing of the Trojans is learnedly explained. Therefore, if you wish to call your boy a "darling of Cybele," I do not much disagree. Tomorrow, however, I shall consult my antiquarians, who are famous for their knowledge of such things, more fully about him; you shall have their opinion from me. 

I owe much to your most distinguished father-in-law for receiving my little pages with a gentle judgment. I shall testify to my mutual devotion to your nephews: and I have already secured for Bartholin a closer friendship with Scioppius and Octavio Ferrari <note>Prominent Italian scholars of the 17th century.</note>, than which nothing more convenient could have happened for his education in the more refined letters. For the rest, I watch over them with the same sincerity and faith that I promise you regarding your own affection. Farewell, and dutifully greet both of the Finckes and the others interested in my name. 

Padua, July 11, 1642. Your most devoted,

*Having finally obtained the images of the **Florentine Horns**, I will rejoice—not so much on my own behalf as on behalf of the Republic of Letters—that your Treatise will come forth enriched by this slight external addition of antiquity. If the Republic of Letters were not sustained by the very pillar of venerable antiquity, I would fear its imminent ruin. With you as our **Atlas** <note>In Greek mythology, the Titan who held up the heavens; here used to describe Worm as the support of ancient scholarship.</note>, I hope and predict its safety, for you alone have sustained its majesty amidst the shadows of such a great silence of centuries and were the first to bring it to light. Grateful posterity will speak of what the spite of the envious now bites. This is not new to this century; in every age it has been customary for the **dog-like family** <note>original: "Canina familia" — a metaphor for cynical or biting critics.</note> to hate the efforts of their superiors, whom they either could not equal due to an unhappy nature, or would not due to laziness. Yet, among such base minds, virtue, carried higher, has always successfully escaped and despised the envious, whose miserable fate of condition time will eventually deplore. All men love and venerate you, greatest of men, for this reason: that you have not permitted to remain hidden any longer from our century those things fashioned by our ancestors which testify equally to their genius and your own. I will not call as witnesses so many lights of Belgium, England, and France, whom I have seen in person marvelling at your virtue and fame. We shall not let you remain ignorant of what the refined geniuses of our Italians think of it. Let **Kircher** <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680), the famous Jesuit polymath.</note>, **Ferrari** <note>Giovanni Battista Ferrari (1584–1655), an Italian Jesuit and botanist.</note>, the **Knight Puteanus** <note>Ericius Puteanus (1574–1646), a humanist scholar.</note>, **Liceti** <note>Fortunio Liceti (1577–1657), an Italian physician and philosopher.</note>, and **Naudé** <note>Gabriel Naudé (1600–1653), a French librarian and scholar.</note> speak in their own words—men long destined for immortality, whose judgments on the horn I intend to submit to the public press. But what are these Florentine horns compared to yours? The world will judge the dignity of yours by the unequal workmanship of these. For here is lacking the value of gold, the light of Worm’s genius, and the veneration of true antiquity. I wrote before, based on a reliable report, that both were fashioned from **ivory**. The first author, it seems, was a **King of Portugal** <note>original: "Rex Lusitanicus"</note>, whom we have learned from histories occupied the **Barbary Coast** <note>original: "Barbariam" — the North African coast.</note> and other regions of the East. The carved figures all seem to pertain to hunting, for which purpose it was perhaps first intended. However, in the **Turkish galleys** <term>triremes</term> captured by the Grand Duke of Florence, they were blown instead of trumpets to incite the men to battle. At what time this happened, I have not been able to fish out. The horns themselves do show antiquity, but not dating back many centuries, since knights and hunters are seen depicted here and there urging their horses to run with **spurs**, which spurs were only an invention of later centuries, as antiquarians propose, since the ancients incited their horses by other means. The carvings show that it was primarily a Christian work, which both **Muslims** <note>original: "Mahumetani"</note> and **Jews** have abhorred in every age. Furthermore, a **cross** proves this, the sign of a Christian expedition to the East. Those familiar with that land have reported to me that the coats of arms prominent on the other horn are characteristic of the Kings of Portugal;*

### SECOND FLORENTINE HORN.

<image-desc>A detailed woodcut illustration of an engraved hunting horn, shown in profile. The surface of the horn is divided into decorative bands and panels. Since the drawing sent to us shows that these two horns agree in material, size, and shape, it seems likely that they were crafted by the same artist and once belonged to the same owner. Our friend Bartholin <note>Thomas Bartholin (1616–1680), the Danish physician and scholar who communicated these findings to Worm from Italy.</note> correctly gathers from the coats of arms and the shape of the cross that the owner was one of the Kings or Princes of Portugal, to whom these symbols are proper and familiar.

<margin>291</margin>If we search the histories of that nation, we find that the first to be granted the royal title by the army was Alfonso I <note>Afonso Henriques (1109–1185), the first King of Portugal.</note> of that name. For when he fought successfully against the Saracens in the year 1139 and won a magnificent victory, he was honored with this title. Yet the inscription which the other horn displays in this manner seems to prove that these horns were not his, nor do they possess such great antiquity: **DOM. LUIS. IMFAMTE.** — perhaps **DON. LUIS. INFANTE**, with the letter *M* substituted for *N* in the spelling. This translates to: **LORD LOUIS, INFANTE** <note>original: "DOMINUS LUDOVICUS INFANS." The title "Infante" refers to a royal prince of Spain or Portugal who is not the heir apparent to the throne.</note>. Who this Louis truly was is clear from the same records. For King Manuel <note>original: "Emanuel" — King Manuel I of Portugal (1469–1521), known as "the Fortunate."</note> of Portugal, the fourteenth in order, after he had obtained the Kingdom in the year 1495, successively married three wives. # DANISH MONUMENTS

The fifteenth King of Portugal was John III. His second-born brother was Louis, who did not ascend to the throne; but as long as he lived, he was addressed as an **INFANTE** <term>Infante: A title used in the Iberian kingdoms for a royal prince who is not the direct heir to the throne.</term>. Conestaggio <note>Jerónimo Conestaggio (c. 1530–1616), a Genoese historian who wrote about the union of the Portuguese and Spanish crowns.</note> records that this Louis lived a celibate life, yet Terzera asserts that he had a son, **ANTHONY**, who was stripped of his royal dignity by Philip, King of Castile. Therefore, I am persuaded that this Louis was the owner of these horns, so that it appears they were manufactured around the year 1500. Regarding the title of **INFANTE**, it seems to have been proper to the Princes of Portugal from the very cradles of the Kingdom. For Joseph Terzera teaches in his *Genealogical Exposition of Henry III, King of France*, that Alfonso I, before he was granted the royal title, held the name of "Infante" and "Prince" for twenty-seven years, up until that famous battle in the fields of Ourique <note>The Battle of Ourique (1139), a legendary victory for Alfonso Henriques against the Almoravid Moors, which led to his proclamation as King.</note>, in which he joined battle against Ismarius (or Ishmael) and four other Saracen Kings and obtained the victory. However, much later, King Edward <note>Duarte I of Portugal (reigned 1433–1438).</note> ordained that his first-born son, Alfonso V, be called "Prince," whereas previously the first-born of the Kings was called "INFANTE," just like the rest of the brothers.

Beyond what these accounts sufficiently teach—that these horns recognized a Christian maker and owner—Thomas Bartholin derives firm arguments from the sign of the cross and the insignia of the Portuguese. That sign of the cross is figured in plainly the same way as is seen on those large Portuguese gold coins. The reason why the Portuguese Kings claimed this specifically for themselves is clear from the history of Alfonso I. For when he was about to fight against the five Kings of the Saracens in the year 1139 <note>The text says 1199, but this is a likely error for 1139, the traditional date of the Battle of Ourique.</note>, on a Tuesday, which was the 25th of July and sacred to the Apostle St. James, he saw the Crucified Christ in the air, who called out to him: **"ALFONSO, IN THIS SIGN YOU SHALL CONQUER."** <note>original Latin: "ALPHONSE IN HOC SIGNO VINCES." A reference to the vision of Constantine the Great, here adapted to Portuguese founding legend.</note> And so it happened, the Saracen enemies being utterly destroyed and laid low. Hence his descendants retained this sign and symbol as their own. It is abundantly clear that the ancient insignias of the Portuguese are those seen on the other horn. Resendius <note>André de Resende (1498–1573), a celebrated Portuguese humanist and archaeologist.</note> gives the account of these in Book 4 of his *Antiquities* in this manner: *Alfonso, the newly...*

### BOOK FIVE

The King, following the custom usual for victors, remained in the camps for three days. Having granted the plunder to the soldiers, he himself—who until then had used a snow-white shield—devised heraldic symbols that would represent the deeds accomplished there. First, because he had seen Christ fixed to the cross in the air, he formed a blue cross on a silver shield. Next, because he had defeated five Kings, he distinguished five shields across that same cross. In each one, he depicted thirty silver coins <term>bezants: circular symbols on a shield representing coins; in this context, they refer to the thirty pieces of silver paid to Judas</term>, because the Savior of the world had been sold for that many. This arrangement of coins was changed by later Kings for a more convenient method, so that in each individual shield, five coins were placed crosswise in the shape of the letter X. By counting the one in the middle twice—both when counting from top to bottom and from side to side—the total number of thirty is completed. These were the symbols adopted there at that time. *Joseph Terzera* <note>José Teixeira (1543–1604), a Portuguese historian and advisor to Dom António, Prior of Crato.</note> is of the same opinion, and adds that seven castles were added to the Portuguese insignia during the time of Alfonso III.

Regarding the size of these horns, which B. says is expressed in the painting, it should be understood as the one sent to me from Padua, which I, for the sake of convenience, took care to have reduced into this smaller form. The length of the images brought to me was equal to nearly two Roman feet <term>Roman foot: a unit of length (pes) approximately equal to 29.6 centimeters</term> for each. The circumference of the larger rim fulfilled one foot on one horn, and was one inch smaller on the other. The circumference of the smaller rim on both was about four inches. They were of a straight rather than a curved shape. Concerning the emblems and images carved upon them, there is no reason for us to add anything, since it is obvious to everyone that nothing else is denoted by them than the custom and ritual of hunting represented in various ways.

As for the opinion of the most famous Licetus <note>Fortunio Liceti (1577–1657), an Italian polymath and physician known for his work on ancient artifacts and "monsters."</note>, in which he thinks that the "Eagle punishment" <term>Aquilinarem poenam: likely a reference to the 'Blood Eagle,' a legendary Viking execution method where the ribs were severed and lungs pulled out to resemble wings</term> cannot be understood by the man wounding another in the third circle: he in no way contradicts the things I have brought forward, especially since I never firmly established that point. As the matter itself will show, on page 64 of the first edition and 421 of the second edition of this work, I say: *A man slaying a man and finishing him with frequent wounds shows the cruelty of adversaries and enemies.* This is my assertion. I subjoin a doubt: *And I know not whether it alludes to the ancient custom of our people, etc.* But if...

I do not know whether he is alluding to it; certainly, I could not prove he was jesting. Meanwhile, I will not hide what my intention was when I wrote this. I once read these words in Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), a Danish historian and author of the *Gesta Danorum*, a primary source for early Scandinavian history.</note>, Book 9: *They ordered his back to be marked with a wound in the shape of an Eagle, rejoicing to destroy a most cruel enemy with the mark of a most ferocious bird.* <note>original: "Ipsius dorsum plaga Aquilam figurante affici jubent, sævissimum hostem atrocissimi alitis signo profligare gaudentes." This is one of the earliest descriptions of the "Blood Eagle," a legendary Viking execution ritual.</note> But I did not understand the passage well, nor could I get a sufficient explanation from others I consulted, until, searching more accurately through our own antiquities, I found things that seemed relevant, which I have brought forward here. 

Therefore, since I saw this matter had to be unearthed from our deepest antiquity—a subject not obvious to everyone nor properly understood—I thought it would not be out of place to include it here, if perhaps more light could be shed on it from elsewhere. Hence, I have produced these points with doubt and timidity, hoping to find fair interpreters who would receive them in the spirit they were offered. I do not think certain <term>apodictic: clearly established or beyond dispute</term> arguments can be drawn from the arrangement and circumstances of these images; since in that era, with such unrefined craftsmanship, they expressed things as they were able, not as they should have been. To depict the supine instead of the prone, or many wounds instead of one or two, was within their equal power <note>The author suggests the ancient artists may have taken creative liberties with anatomy or perspective due to a lack of technical skill.</note>.

I thought these few things should be noted regarding my dear Bartholin’s letter, so that what he wrote about the Florentine horns might be clearer; leaving more abundant matters to others.

Since I have gathered from documents of antiquities—sent to me by the Reverend and Most Illustrious Mr. Johannes Burchard <note>Jens Bisgård (1586–1643), the Bishop of Ribe and a correspondent of the author.</note>, the most watchful Bishop of the Diocese of Ribe—that there exist in that same place several monuments inscribed with our Runic letters (which I suggested earlier), it happened conveniently that a noble young man, Mr. Laurentius Bording <note>Laurids Bording (1611–1673), a Danish physician and poet.</note>, a most diligent student of both sacred letters and natural history, and not unskilled in the art of drawing, was traveling home to that region. I therefore gave him this task: to investigate these monuments with all possible industry and to transmit accurate drawings of them to me. This he carried out most promptly. Therefore, the things you see here from the Diocese of Ribe I owe to him; if some details should occur among them that escaped both my diligence and his own, there is no reason to wonder, for anyone who has experienced the disasters that winds, rains, storms, and time itself have brought upon our monuments knows the difficulty. In the meantime, we thought it best to offer them exactly as we received them.

### THE SEVENTH MONUMENT
## AT LÆBORG

In the province called Malt Herred, in the parish of Læborg, situated on the northern side of the church in a level field, there stands an elegant monument. In the effort to fully uncover it, great men before me have toiled in vain, hindered by the sheer difficulty of the task. Besides the smaller stones found in that place, two exist which pertain to our purpose. The smaller of these is grey in color, speckled with certain red and whitish spots; it is rough and oblong, five <term>cubits: an ancient unit of length, here referring to the Danish 'alen' of about two feet</term> in length, one and a half cubits wide in some places, and of uncertain thickness; for it could not be exactly measured because the bulk of the stone was buried in the earth on that side. **RAFN.** It was frequent among the ancients, as it is still among the Icelanders, to add an aspirated letter <term>aspiration: a 'breathing' sound like the letter H</term> to the letter R, which they mostly placed before it, such as ᚼᚱᚢᛚᚠ ᚴᚱᛅᚴᛅ *Hrolf Kraka* <note>A legendary 6th-century Danish king</note>, ᚼᚱᛅᚠᚾ *Hrafn* ("raven" or "swiftly"), ᚼᚱᚢᚾᚴᛚᛅ *Hrungla* ("hoof"), ᚼᚱᛁᚾᚾ *Hrinn* ("pure"), and infinite others. This was not at all unusual for the writers of the Middle Ages in Latin, especially regarding proper names. Thus, they called the Emperor Louis *Hludovicus*. I possess two silver coins, dug up here among us near Lejre <note>original: "Lethra," the ancient royal seat of Denmark</note>, on one of which a cross is seen surrounded by this inscription: + HLVDVVICVS IMP <note>Louis the Emperor</note>. On the reverse side is the figure of a temple, around which is + XPISTIANA RELIGIO <note>The Christian Religion</note>. The other coin similarly has around a cross + HLVDVVICVS IMP; on the other side, in larger characters that do not surround any image but are read from left to right, is + VENECIAS <note>Venice</note>, in this fashion:

2. The second circle shows a central cross with the legend "+ HLVDVVICVS IMP" (Louis the Emperor) around the perimeter.
3. The third circle shows a central cross with the legend "+ HLVDVVICVS IMP" around the perimeter.
4. The fourth circle shows the word "VENECIAS" (Venice) divided into two lines: "VEN" above "ECIAS", with a small cross below the text.</image-desc>

Sometimes they added the aspiration in the middle of other letters, even in the same word, as in the formula of the treaty entered into between Louis the Pious and Charles II <note>Charles the Bald</note>, published by Lipsius and Goldast in Tome I of the *Imperial Constitutions*, page 190. In the words of Louis, among the rest: *And with Lothar I will never enter into any agreement* <note>original: "Et ab LUDHER nul plaid nunquam prindrar"</note> etc. Soon after, in the response of Charles: *In this way, that he [treats] me as a brother, and with Lothar in no such thing* <note>original: "In thiu thaz er mig soso maduo inde med LVTHEREM inno theinni thing"</note> etc. Likewise in the oath of the people: *If Louis [keeps] the oath which his brother...* <note>original: "Si LVDHVVIG sacrament que son fradre"</note> etc. See these words cited and repeated in full in our *Runic Literature*, chapter 27.

**TUFI.** This name also occurs in other monuments in this book. It seems to indicate that there were two people who labored on this monument.

**ᚱᚢᚾᛅ [RUNA].** Regarding this word, consult our work *On Runic Literature* <note>original: "Literaturam nostram"</note>, in which we have shown at length that the letters of the Northern peoples were called by this name.

**ᛏᚱᚢᛏᚿᛁᚿ [TRUTNIN].** It seems that the meaning of this word was once different from what it is in this century. For now, we are accustomed to honoring Queens with this title, but in its genuine nature, it signifies a "Lady" <term>Trutnin: related to the modern Danish "Dronning" (Queen), but here used as the feminine form of "Lord"</term>. For *Trutnin* designates a lord, as can be seen in Book III of this work on the Bornholm monument V: *ᚦᚬᚱ ᛏᚱᚢᛏᚿᛁᚿ ᚼᛁᛅᛚᛒᛁ* (May Lord Thor help) etc.; consult also the fourteenth Scanian monument <note>Skåne, now in Sweden, was then part of Denmark</note> in the same book. Hence, *Trutnin* means "Lady." It appears, therefore, that these two men who set up this monument were clients or subjects of that Lady whose name is not expressed. There is no reason for us to think that this Lady was a Queen, or that Rafn and Tusi were Kings and her husbands, since King Gorm, on the Jelling Monument <note>The famous Jelling stones raised by Gorm the Old and Harald Bluetooth</note>, does not call his wife and Queen *Trutnin*, but rather *ᚦᚢᚿᚢ* [thunu] <note>original: "thunu," a version of "thegn" or "lady/wife"</note>, a word with which we are still accustomed to call even common wives today.

Furthermore, the image of a hammer <note>The Hammer of Thor, a common protective symbol in Viking Age inscriptions</note> can be seen in two places on this stone; whether these were the insignias of these two men, let others decide. The holes running both vertically and across the body of the stone appear more recent than the letters themselves; I believe they were impressed upon it by someone who attempted to split this mass so that he might more conveniently adapt it for a building structure. Thus, by a singular fate, this monument was rescued from destruction.

Adjacent to this stone lies another, oblong, smoother, and twice as large. Since the Magnificent Lord Chancellor Christian Friis of Kragerup, of blessed memory <note>Christian Friis (1581–1639), a high-ranking Danish official and patron of the arts and sciences</note>, suspected there might also be letters carved on the side covering the ground, he arranged for the neighboring farmers to be summoned to put their effort into turning it over. They dug a huge pit around the rock to free it from the earth weighing it down, but they could move such a massive weight by no force, so that all hope of reaching a further understanding of this monument seems to have been cut off. It is suspected—

# THE EIGHTH MONUMENT.
## OF FØVLING.

In the cemetery of Føvling <note>original: "Feulingensi"</note> in the same province, toward the north, a gravestone <term>cippus: a low, round or rectangular pedestal set up as a monument or landmark</term> can be seen cast upon the ground. The first word **Bλ** <note>The author uses Greek letters to represent specific runic or stylized character forms found on the stone.</note> consists of a single letter **B**, into which an oblique line from the **λ** <note>lambda</note> is folded, so that it provides us with the word **Bλ**.

The **η** <note>eta</note> in the following word likewise folds the final curved strokes from the **B**.

The third word in **Y** displays three letters, namely **λ**, **Y**, and **κ**; from the first and last, oblique strokes are joined by a straight line in the **Y**. I believe this includes the surname of the buried person, perhaps from the noble lineage of the Langs <note>The Lang family was a notable Danish noble family.</note> among us.

What remains is clear enough on its own. For **Y** likewise includes **R**, and in the last word **R** includes the vowel **E**. The fact that **η** is omitted in the word **RIΨIIIIIT** <note>The author interprets this as "REQUIESCIT," Latin for "he rests."</note> is to be forgiven the sculptor of that age, and perhaps **Y** was intended to have the power of "QV."

It is clear that this monument is not from a more remote age, because it is Christian and has Latin elements mixed in. What is told by the locals about a "gilded knight" <note>original: "equite aurato"—a knight of high rank, often one who had received the golden spurs.</note>, killed by three peasants and buried here, is not entirely improbable, although the circumstances seem doubtful.

### THE NINTH MONUMENT.
### OF VAMDRUP.

The province of Anst <note>original: "Andstherrit"</note> contains, among others, a church called Vamdrup <note>original: "Wamdrup"</note>. Here, behind the church, two stones decorated with our letters <note>meaning Latin or runic characters familiar to the author</note> can be seen. One is in the wall that surrounds the cemetery toward the east, between the gate through which one enters the church and the eastern corner, near the ground; it is almost one and a half ells <note>An "ell" (ulna) was roughly 24 inches or 60 cm.</note> long and wide. It does not display a very great antiquity. For it was carved by Christians, as evidenced by the image of the Lamb carrying the Cross <gloss>the Agnus Dei</gloss> and an inscription consistent with our religion. So much so that I think it was once fitted either to the structure of the church itself or to someone's grave. It is indeed a rough stone, of a grey color leaning toward purple.

*ᚼᛁᚱ* [HIR]. A broken corner has deprived us of the first letter of this word, which however the sense proves has been correctly restored <note>The author infers the missing 'H' to complete the word "Hera" or "Hir" (Here)</note>.

*ᛏᚱᛁᛏᚽᚴ* [DRITAG]. Here I hesitate, for this word is infrequent among us, so that there is a suspicion of a mistake, especially since the first two letters of this word appear in the first row, and the remaining in the second. See whether it should be read ᚢᚿᚦᛂᚱ [UNDER], meaning "under," so that the sense here is: *under this stone etc.*: so that the buried person's name would be ᛋᚢᚿ [SUN], which however is no less unusual to us. The rest is plain.

## ELEVENTH MONUMENT
### THE FIRST OF LANDERUP.

The district of Almind <note>original: *Almidſyffel*—one of the ancient "syssels" or administrative divisions of Jutland</note> is counted among the remaining provinces it holds, including Brusk Hundred <note>original: *Bruskherrit*</note>, but in my judgment it is more correctly called *Broeherrit* <note>The "Bridge Hundred"</note>; for it is surrounded on all sides by rivers and streams, so that access is not open to it except by bridges. This region, besides the elegant and bright town of Kolding, distinguished by its royal and famous castle, holds a nearby rural estate in the Parish of Wilstrup, which they commonly call Landerup. It was once dedicated to Royal recreations, about which the inhabitants tell various stories that are not appropriate for this place. Toward the north from here, a large stone is seen, of unequal shape, somewhat pointed, three and a half cubits <note>An *ulna* or Danish *alen* is roughly 2 feet; the stone is about 7 feet long</note> in length, two in width, and about one in thickness, now tilted on its side. It displays four rows of characters, but they are so eaten away and corrupted by age and the injuries of the weather that nothing worthy of mention can be extracted from them. Behold here the figure as we received it.

The name of Harald **ᚼᛅᚱᛅᛚᛏᚱ** <note>*Haraldr*</note> follows explicitly, just as on the monument at Jelling. ...[God] <note>This continues the word "God" (Danish: *Gode*) from the previous page's inscription analysis.</note>, although the neglect of orthography <note>The study of correct spelling.</note>, common among the ancients, shows that the author was not particularly skilled in refined literature.

What is to be determined about the age of this monument can easily be gathered from this: it is clearly a modern work, having been engraved in the year of Christ 1597. It shows no true antiquity, and I am surprised that no one exists in that region who can provide the author's name and the reasons for its design. What can be hoped for concerning more ancient monuments when recent ones are shrouded in such darkness? In the cipher characters themselves, I find some discrepancy from those handed down by Trithemius <note>Johannes Trithemius (1462–1516), whose cryptographic work *Polygraphia* was used to decode the stone.</note>. For our author draws **G** as Trithemius draws **I**, and vice-versa, **I** as **G**. Furthermore, the character that denotes **S** differs in position and shape from the Trithemian version, provided that our friend Bordingius <note>Likely a reference to a contemporary scholar or correspondent who provided the transcription.</note> has correctly recorded it.

**AIE**, for *eje* <note>Danish for "to own" or "possess."</note>: to possess, to keep, to guard. For the author asks that God possess, rule, and protect our most serene King, **Christian IV**. **CHRESTEAN** is used for *Christian*. **ON** stands for the German *oc* or *ond* <note>meaning "and".</note>.

**HVS HVD**. Guardian and patron of the house. For *Hud* signified protection and patronage among the ancients.

By the symbol of the hand noted here, I judge it indicates nothing other than that the following things are most worthy of note and should be examined by everyone. I do not know whether the author carved these things in imitation of the previous monument, hoping it would be placed among the most ancient ones that no one could unravel. # GOTLAND.

We shall subjoin certain matters regarding Gotland, based on the reliability with which they reached us and in the same manner they were received; for we have not received them with sufficiently accurate or properly supported circumstances, nor do they possess the antiquity we desire. However, because they consist of our ancient letters, or **Runes**, and find a place here, we grant them such merit as they deserve. Gotland was once celebrated for the royal family of the **Amali** <note>The Amali were a leading dynasty of the Goths, famously associated with the Ostrogoths.</note> and for its abundance of merchandise, being most famous in the eastern ocean. It enjoys a single fortress and likewise a single city, **Visby**, once an emporium <note>A major trading hub or market.</note> illustrious for the gathering of all nations and an abundance of goods. There are one hundred rural churches there, over which a Bishop was appointed by **Frederick II**, a King of most praised memory. The Bishop's authority, which had collapsed somewhat over the passage of time, was recently confirmed and restored by our Most Serene King, **CHRISTIAN IV**—may God bless him from on high and keep him safe for these Realms for a very long time.

> Our countryman **Lyscander** <note>Claus Christoffersen Lyscander (1558–1623), a Danish royal historian.</note> depicts the island elegantly in his usual manner; let us hear him: "The Danes hold Gotland, the largest and most extensive island in view of the Vistula <note>A major river in modern-day Poland.</note>, situated in the Sarmatian marsh <note>original: *Sarmatica palude*. A classical geographical term used here to refer to the Baltic Sea region.</note>. We have seen fit to adorn it here with no other praise (though it is most noble), proclaiming it worthy of much honor, than that in it many monarchs of the Cimmerians, Dacians, and Geats <note>Refers to various tribal groups often associated by early historians with the ancestry of the Scandinavians and Goths.</note> held their royal seat—especially the **Amiraldic** <note>Referring again to the Amali dynasty.</note> Emperors who ruled the ocean. In the number of Gothic provinces, it held the first place after Scandinavia, distinguished in glory and reputation. Indeed, it has preserved the **Amalian lamb** <note>original: *agnum Amalonium*. This refers to the 'Lamb of God' (Agnus Dei), the heraldic symbol of Gotland which features a lamb carrying a banner.</note>—for so we name the emblem of the Goths that was once on their shields—safely until now. Into this island, the entire Northern region, then in labor and fertile with so many peoples, sent forth the Geats and Cimmerians from Scandinavia, destined to enter the East. Furthermore, after the destruction of the great **Vineta** <note>A legendary, wealthy city on the Baltic coast said to have been submerged by the sea as a divine punishment.</note>, Gotland possessed a lovely and most wealthy city..."

Visby, also called Visepolis or Visebyana, was most celebrated for the trade of all nations and served as a general marketplace <term>emporium|A center of commerce or a trading hub</term> for the entire East. # SECOND.
## CONCERNING EISTA.

In the church of Eista <note>Modern Etelhem on the island of Gotland.</note> before the doors of the choir, there stands a stone marked with this inscription:

ᛒᚢᛏᚢᛆᚱᛑᚱ ᛁ ᛋᚿᚽᛑᚢ ᚼᛆᚿ ᛚᛁᛏ ᚵᛁᛆᚱᛆ ᚦᛁᚿᛆ ᛋᛏᛆᛁᚿ ᚤᚠᛁᚱ ᛋᛁᚿᛆ
ᚼᚢᛋᚠᚮᛁᚢ ᛒᚢᛏᛆᛁᛑᚢ ᛏᛁᛚ ᛆᛁᛋᛏᚢ

*Butvardr of Snödu had this stone made in memory of his wife*
*Butaid of Eista.*

->BUTVARD OF SNÖDU<-
->CAUSED THIS STONE TO BE MADE IN MEMORY OF HIS<-
->WIFE BUTAID OF EISTA.<-

Nor is this inscription from a more remote age, which is proven both by the dotted letters <note>Medieval runes where dots were added to distinguish sounds, indicating a later date than the Viking Age.</note> and the style of writing.

<margin>Snedu</margin> He indicates by this that he was the lord of the estate or fortress called Snödu.

<margin>Husfroiu</margin> This word smacks of German influence, for the Teutons <note>German-speaking peoples.</note> call a wife a *Hausfraw* <note>House-wife or lady of the house.</note>, in which sense noble matrons are still called *Husfuer* or *Husfruer* among us. But the final words indicate that this woman was of noble lineage, stating that she was the lady of Eista—namely, of that territory in which this inscription stands; this is the meaning of the words "belonging to Eista."

It is certain that this belongs to the Middle Ages, for besides the fact that it mentions Christ and Christians, it contains "dotted" letters <note>Medieval runes like ᚵ (g) and ᛂ (e) used dots to distinguish them from ᚴ (k) and ᛁ (i).</note> ᚵ and ᛂ, as well as the sign of the cross. It is clear that this is an epitaph intended for an entire family, as it lists the names of those buried here; indeed, the author intended this monument for himself as well.

<term>ᚮᚵ</term> This conjunction <note>meaning "and"</note> is noted in different ways here, sometimes as *ug* (ᚢᚵ) and sometimes as *og* (ᚮᚵ).

Let it at least be noted that the character for the letter S is different from the usual one; specifically, it is written here as ᛌ <note>This is a "short-twig" or "staveless" rune for the letter S, often used in later medieval inscriptions.</note>, which they use at the end of words. After defeating the petty kings, Harald Fairhair stayed with him and wished to have his hair—which he had let grow for many years—cut by him. It was for this reason that he was given the nickname "Fairhair" <note>original: *Harfager* or *Pulchricomus*</note> by Ragnvald. However, because Botvida here claims to be the heir of Ragnvald, he was certainly not his son, for their names are expressly recorded in history; rather, he was either a grandson or descended from grandsons, so that the inheritance passed to him through a third or fourth hand. Therefore, it is quite clear that this inscription was placed many years after the time of Ragnvald.

**1409** <note>original runes: ᛗᚴ ᛒᛁᚱᚠ</note>. **From the birth of Christ.** Note here first that the character which must represent the letter **S** in **1409** <note>original: ᛒᛁᚱᚠ</note> is distinct from ᚼ <note>the standard rune for 'h' or 's' in some systems</note>; it is a version used mostly at the end of words among the people of Gotland, as we noted above. For back then <note>in the year 409 AD</note>, our countrymen believe that **Butli, son of Sivard**, held power, a man who was entirely ignorant of Christian rites. It was also at that time that the Goths abroad killed the **Emperor Valens**, who had strived with all his might to drag them into the Arian sect <note>A branch of early Christianity deemed heretical by the late Roman Church</note>. It is more correct, therefore, to date the stone to the year 1409, during the reign of **Queen Margaret** in Denmark.

**The Golden Number** <note>original runes: ᛒᚱᛦᛗᚾ</note>. This is a word derived from *rim* <note>original: ᛒᚱᛁᛦ</note>, which signifies the **Golden Number** <term>Golden Number: a value used in the Middle Ages to track the 19-year lunar cycle and determine the date of Easter</term>, as we have explained more extensively in our *Danish Calendar*. Consult Book 1, Chapter 20: *The Primstaff <note>a wooden calendar stick</note> established the golden number.*

**ᛯᛁᚱᚠᚿ** <note>runic word</note>. What this word means, I do not sufficiently understand. Because these findings breathe only a faint fragrance of antiquity—and yet we do not doubt that greater and rarer trophies of heroes and princes exist in such a celebrated province of the Goths—whoever communicates such things to others for the public good will be judged to have served his country well. What was not permitted to me to discover, I grant not unwillingly to others to find.

# BOOK SIX
## NORWEGIAN MONUMENTS
->containing them.<-

I have little doubt that in Norway there is a rich and bountiful harvest of monuments adorned with our ancient literature; both because Runes have always been held in high esteem there, and because the people there seem to have been less driven to destroy them than others elsewhere. Furthermore, the region itself is naturally so rocky and stony that a scarcity of stone does not force the inhabitants to repurpose stone monuments for other uses. Meanwhile, although only a few rare examples of this kind have reached us from those parts, I will not hesitate to include whatever they may be here.

## MONUMENTS OF BERGEN.

From the Diocese of Bergen, the Reverend and most Distinguished man, Master Nicolaus Paschasius <note>Latin: "Nicolaus Paschasius," the Latinized name of Niels Paaske (1568–1636), who served as the Bishop of Bergen</note>, Doctor of Sacred Theology and formerly a most vigilant Bishop of that same place, has voluntarily shared these items which we present and explain here, among other illustrious remains of antiquity. For this, great thanks are owed to him by all who study the past.

### THE FIRST.
### THE GJERDE MONUMENT.

In the province of Sunnhordland <note>original: "Sundhorlehn"</note>, in the parish of Etne <note>original: "Ethnes"</note>, at the entrance to the graveyard of the Gjerde church <note>original: "Gierdis"</note>, a threshold stone forms a certain monument of rough rock, three cubits <term>ulna: a traditional unit of measurement, often referred to as an "ell," roughly the length of a man's forearm</term> in length...

It is certain that this stone was moved from elsewhere. There are people still living who report that it was transported from the wall that surrounds the cemetery. If this is true, I would believe it was originally positioned so that the letters could be seen from both sides. However, I suspect it was situated on a certain hill or in a field before it was forced into service for the cemetery, standing like a grave-marker or a pillar. It would have been placed so that access to read both sides was freer and without obstruction, although the addition of a cross <note>referring to the small cross at the start of the inscription</note> testifies that these words were carved after the rejection of idolatry <note>idolatry: here referring to the Norse pagan religion before the arrival of Christianity</note>.
