I suspect the same about this stone as I stated above regarding the one from Gjerde; its shape makes it very similar to a grave-marker or an obelisk. Some of the local inhabitants claim that it was previously placed within the cemetery itself. This is perhaps not unlikely; but as I judge it, it once stood upright, with its tip facing the sky. The transcription of its letters reached me in a somewhat faulty state, but I have no doubt that they ought to be read in this sequence.

The mark by which the letter **S** is expressed is peculiar and different from others. For it is drawn thus: ᛌ, which led the person who first transcribed it into error.

**ᚦᚢᚱᛘᚢᚦ** [Thormud]: We have expressed the first letter of this word with **Th**, for such is its value. So that younger students may learn this more easily, they usually place a "dagesh" <term>dagesh: a diacritic point used in Hebrew grammar to indicate a harder sound; here, Worm uses the term to describe a "dotted" rune</term> or dot in its center. since that was not done here, it can be seen as being from a more ancient age.

<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

In the same province lies the parish of **Strandebarm** <note>original: "Strandbarnes," a village and former municipality in Hardanger, Norway</note>. In its church, a column can be seen in which a niche for depositing alms <term>alms: money or food given to the poor as a religious act</term> was formerly carved in such a way that it formed an integral part of the pillar itself. This column bears an inscription arranged so that it ran across both the stone of the column and the lid or door of the niche. Because this door has now been removed, the sequence of letters is left mutilated and incomplete, with only these few characters surviving.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a cylindrical stone column standing on a broad, rounded base. On the face of the column, a set of runic inscriptions is split by a small rectangular recess or niche. Directly above this niche is a symbol representing a church or chapel with a cross on top. The runes are arranged in two rows.</image-desc>

->ᚼᛚ ᛅᛁᛏᚢᚱᚱ ⛪<-
->ᛒ ᛅᚱᛘᚢᚿᛏᚱ ᛋᚢᚿᚿᚱ : ᛒ<-

->*Viler Artur Ommuntr S.*<-
<note>This is a transcription of the surviving runes into the Latin alphabet.</note>

The meaning, without a doubt, was this: **HERE LIES ARTHUR, SON OF AMUND.** <note>original Latin gloss: "HIC JACET ARTURUS OMUNDI FILIUS."</note>

Several combinations of letters <term>ligatures: characters where two or more letters are joined together</term> occur here, such as ᚼᚱ and R, or ᚼᛚ and ᚠᚢ.

## FOURTH MONUMENT.
# HAUS
<note>original: "Housense," referring to the parish of Haus in the Osterøy municipality, Norway</note>

In the district called **Nordhordland** <note>original: "Norhørlehn"</note>, there exists a certain parish by the name of **Haus**. Here, on the northern side of the churchyard, a sepulchral stone is visible, rising step-by-step to a peak. It is two and a half ells <term>ell: a historical unit of length, roughly 24 inches or 60 cm</term> in length and four quarters <term>quarter: one-fourth of an ell</term> in width. It displays the sequence of its inscription in this manner:

<image-desc>A perspective drawing of a three-tiered rectangular stone monument. A line of runic text is engraved across the top surface.</image-desc>

->ᚦᚱᛦ : ᛁᛅᛏᛁ : ᚴᛁᛒᚱᛁ : ᚦᛁᛋᚢ : ᚽᚠᛏ : ᚦᚬᚱᚱᛅ : ᚴᚬᚾᚢ :<-
->*Orm Iati lit gidri disu euft Thorra Kona.*<-
->**ORMER JETI HAD THIS MADE IN MEMORY OF HIS WIFE THORA.**<-
<note>original Latin: "ORMERUS JETI HOC FIERI FECIT IN MEMORIAM UXORIS SUÆ THORÆ."</note>

Although the word *Iati* may signify a "Jætte" or "giant" <note>a giant from Norse mythology</note> when taken as a common noun, I believe it is used here as a surname for Ormer. The word ᚴᛁᛒᚱᛁ (*gidri*) should perhaps be read as ᚴᛁᛅᚱᛁ (*giari*), from the verb **I make** <note>original Danish: "Jeg giør"</note>. This word, as well as the final ones, was previously read incorrectly; however, by considering the blurred strokes of the characters and the circumstances of the object, we have restored them as you see here.

### FOURTH.
### THE HAUS MONUMENT.

A certain parish in the district called **Nordhordland** <note>original: "Norhorlehn"; a traditional district in western Norway</note> exists by the name of **Haus** <note>original: "Hous"; located on the island of Osterøy</note>. Here, on the northern side of the graveyard, a sepulchral stone is seen, rising in steps toward a peak. It is two and a half ells long and as many quarters wide <note>the ell (ulna) was a historical unit of measurement roughly equivalent to 24 inches or 60 cm; a "quarter" was one-fourth of an ell</note>, displaying the tenor of the inscription in this manner:

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a monumental stone on a tiered base. The top surface of the stone bears a runic inscription preceded by a cross. The runes on the stone read: ᚭᚱᛘ : ᛚᛂᛏ : ᚵᛁᛂᚱᛁ : ᛋᛏᛂᛁᚿ : ᚦᛂᚿᚿᛆ : ᛂᚠᛏᛂᚱ : ᚦᚭᚱᚱᚭ : ᚴᚭᚿᚭ : ᛋᛁᚿᛆ :</image-desc>

->Orm let gieri stein thenna efter Thorra kona<-
->ORM ORDERED THIS TO BE MADE IN ME-<-
->MORY OF HIS WIFE THORA.<-

The word **lati**, <note>referring to a variant reading of the runes</note> although it may denote a **Giant** <note>original: "Jætte"; a being from Norse mythology</note> when used as a common noun, I nonetheless believe to be the surname of Orm in this instance. The word translated as **to be made** <note>Latin: "fieri"</note> should perhaps be read as **gieri**, from the verb **I make** <note>Danish/Norwegian: "Jeg giør"</note>. The word **disu** <note>this</note> was read incorrectly, as were the final words; however, by considering the confused strokes of the characters and the circumstances of the matter, we have restored them as you see here.

This stone was dug up some years ago in the church itself, near the foot of the altar, and from there it was moved to the place where it is now seen. It is the epitaph of a certain **Ketill** <note>original: "Chetilli"; a common Norse name</note>, who without doubt either founded the church or enriched it with singular generosity, by which he obtained such an honored place for his tomb—namely, near the altar. Although the inscription appears Christian, it nonetheless smacks of a notable antiquity.

**ᚦᚢᚦ** <note>The author likely reads this as "Guth" or "God"</note> In the ancient language, this denotes God and Lord, from which we even now derive *Drottning*, which signifies **Queen** <note>original: "Reginam"</note> to us.
**ᚼᛁᛅᛚᛒᛁ** This denotes to save, to heal, or to sanctify. What if **ᚼᛁᛅᛚᛒᛁ** is read as *Hielpe* <note>Danish/Norwegian for "Help"</note>? As in: "Help the soul," etc.
**ᛅᚾᛏᛅ** The person who first transcribed this as **ᛅᚾᛏᛅ** committed a manifest error, arising from ignorance of the first letter, which has a great affinity with **I**; it denotes the **soul** <note>Latin: "animam"; the author is correcting the transcription to read "salu" or "önd/anda"</note>.

HE WAS HIS INTIMATE COMPANION AND OF THE LINEAGE OF LORD STENO.<- <note>This is the author's Latin interpretation of the runic inscription on the previous page translated into English. "Steno" likely refers to the Swedish noble family Sture or a similar regional lord.</note>

The clear meaning of this is denied to us both by a gap <note>original: "lacuna"; a hole or missing section in a physical manuscript or stone</note> in the text and by the foreign nature of the dialect. There is no doubt that this column once stood upright, which even the word *RIITI* <note>Old Norse: "reisti", meaning "raised"</note> seems to indicate. If we may gather anything from the position it now occupies, the letter markings faced south. The local inhabitants indeed report that three brothers were once buried here (which is consistent with the inscription), but there is no one who can teach us who they were or whose sons they were. They add, however, that a fierce battle took place in this spot, in which these Leaders fell along with many others in a great slaughter of men. To these men (since they were of an illustrious family and acted bravely), this honor was held above the rest, so that the memory of them might be propagated to posterity by this stone.

ᚦᛅᚱ <gloss>Up to this point the inscription is clear enough, but a gap takes away certain things from us, upon which the sense of the whole inscription largely depends.</gloss>
ᚼᛁ <gloss>of them or of him.</gloss>
ᚦᚱ <gloss>I do not fully grasp the sense of this; I think it should be read as ᚦᛅᚱ / ᚮᛘ <note>original: "thar / som"</note> meaning "who".</gloss>
ᚦᛅᚼ : <gloss>to be read as ᚦᛅᚱ; for in this entire monument, this mark ᚼ never occurs, but in its place ᚱ <note>the 'r' rune</note> of the same value is always put. For ᚼ, therefore, R must be substituted.</gloss>
ᚦᛅᚦ <gloss>we now say *ætt* <term>ætt: a Norse term for a clan, lineage, or family group</term>, meaning progeny, tribe, and family.</gloss>
ᚠᚱᛅᚿᚦᛁᚱ <gloss>*fra* denotes a friend, *franth* denotes kinship <note>original: "necessitudinem"</note>, to indicate that he was bound by the highest bond of kinship and friendship either to the deceased or to their parent.</gloss>

It is square, one foot in length and four fingers in width; unless one were to notice that it is a fragment broken from a harder rock, one might easily call it a brick. This stone provides us with a marvelous example of the combination and entanglement of letters, which completely escapes our understanding: receive the outlines from me here, and seek the interpretation from others.

# LODENA THE FAIR ARRANGED FOR THIS TO BE ADORNED.
<note>original Latin: "LODENA PULCHRA HOC EXORNARI CURAVIT."</note>

One may consider that this court—which is now inhabited by a certain peasant—was once the palace of a nobleman or some high official of Hadeland <note>a traditional district in Eastern Norway</note>; he likely adorned this small chapel at his own expense, as the inscription testifies. But because the letters seem to testify to a certain "Lodena the Fair," she is undoubtedly the one spoken of in the following monument.

*Ylen* even now indicates to us "fair" or "beautiful." <note>original: "YLEN etiamnum pulchrum nobis indicat, vel formosum." Worm is connecting the name to Old Norse linguistic roots.</note>
*Bylen* signifies "to adorn"; we now say *pynte*, with the first vowel slightly changed. She perhaps restored this collapsed chapel and increased its decorations.

## THE SIXTH.
### AT BILDEN.

There is also another court in the same province called *Bilden*, which also has an attached chapel that is now almost in ruins.

In it, a tapestry was once seen, embroidered with ancient skill and intended for the decoration of the altar. On it, the following inscription was read; although it is not carved in stone like most other things, it nonetheless finds a deserved place here. I show an image of it, but I keep the tapestry itself among my more rare items in my Gallery <note>original: "Pinacotheca," referring to Ole Worm’s famous museum of curiosities, the Museum Wormianum</note>, where the opportunity to view it will be granted whenever desired. It is three <term>Zealand ells<gloss>a unit of measurement used in Denmark, roughly equivalent to 63 centimeters or 2 feet per ell</gloss></term> in length, and one and a quarter in width. It is made from a bluish cloth, onto which various figures are embroidered with woolen thread of diverse colors. On one side of the inscription, a knight is seen sitting upon a white horse, dressed in a reddish cloak, holding a spear in his hand with which he fiercely pursues a yellow-colored stag standing in the middle of the waters, followed by a yellow dog. Meanwhile, an eagle with multicolored feathers attacks a fallen man with its beak. At the feet of the stag, a river is visible in which someone in a green toga is fishing with a spherical instrument: one can see green, yellow, red, spotted, and eel-shaped fish. The other side of the inscription is occupied by an animal with a lion’s head and a horse’s neck,

...st; A coat of bear-skin and fair fringes. <note>original Old Norse: "Feldur af birni og fagrar slæður." This completes the riddle from the previous page.</note> That is: a King, having met a certain man, asked him about his name. He, responding, said: In the Royal court I am called a Ripe Field, a New Reed, a House covered with grass, a Little Hop-plant on a branch, a Bear-skin, and a Green Meadow. The meaning is that he said he was called **LODIN**. Indeed, "Lodin" as a common noun denotes someone shaggy or hairy, as has been said; and since a field covered with mature crops, reed beds, houses roofed with green turf, branches of hops, a bear-skin, and a green meadow are all of this nature, he thought his name could be aptly expressed by each of these metaphors. However, because this name is found attributed to both men and women, it will be difficult to say what it signifies in this specific place.

In the region of Viken in Norway, there was a certain man outstanding in wealth and military skill named **LODEN**. When he had sailed to Estonia for business, he found there **ASTRITH**, the daughter of King Eric and mother of Saint Olaf, who had been captured and put up for sale; he bought her and joined her to himself in marriage. He eventually had by her one son named Thorkell Nefja and two daughters, concerning whom you may consult the vernacular Chronicle of Snorri Sturluson <note>the *Heimskringla*</note>, edited by us, in the history of Olaf Tryggvason.

The same Chronicle mentions another **LODEN** in the history of King **SVERRE**, who was called Loden of Mandvig. He fell in battle alongside Magnus Erlingsson in the year 1184, being held among the primary nobles of the Kingdom. I do not think either of these men is indicated here, but rather a noble woman, who in the inscription above was called ᛚᚢᚦᚽᚿᚨ ᛍᛁᚿᚨ: *Beautiful Lodena*, whose sister's daughter was Ragnilta, who worked this Tapestry with her own hands.

From this, *mark* and *farmark* are the names of the signs and seals with which merchants and others mark their goods so they may be distinguished from others. The pronoun ᚦᚽᚿᚿᚨ ("this") seems to be understood here.

**RAGNILDA.** Since several women of this name occur in histories, it is no less doubtful which of them is the one mentioned here. Saxo, in his *Danish History*, book 1, reports that Haakon, King of the people of Nidaros <note>modern-day Trondheim</note>, had a daughter named **RAGNILDA**...

The *Chronicle of Norway* cited above, in the history of **Harald Fairhair**, <note>Harald Pulchricomus, the first King of Norway.</note> records that the aforementioned King took as his wife **RAGNHILD**, the daughter of **Eric**, King of Jutland; <note>original Latin: "Erici Cimbriæ Regis." A manuscript history of the Kings of Denmark called the ***Knytlinga Saga***, <note>A medieval Icelandic saga detailing the lives of the Danish kings.</note> written in our ancient tongue, records among the deeds of **Sven Estridsson**—whom the Norwegians call the son of **Ulf**—that this Sven had a daughter named **RAGNHILD** (whom our own historians do not mention), who was married to **Sven**, the son of **Eskil Erlingson**. I also find in a manuscript *History of Sweden*, recorded by **Olaus Petri**, <note>A prominent Swedish clergyman and historian (1493–1552).</note> the preacher of Stockholm, in the deeds of **Ingjald**, that he also had a daughter named **RAGNHILD**, who on account of the integrity of her life was numbered among the Saints <note>original Latin: "Divas," referring to canonized or holy women.</note> after her death and buried in Telge. <note>Modern Södertälje in Sweden; the figure is Saint Ragnhild.</note> I believe either of these women could be referred to here.

...by name, whom **Saint Eric** <note>Eric IX of Sweden, also known as Eric the Saint (d. 1160).</note> married; the other, **Margaret**, was taken as a wife by **Nicholas, King of Denmark**. He had two sons by her: **Inge**, named after his maternal grandfather, and **Magnus**, whom they called "the Wicked" by surname on account of his crimes, as witnessed by **Johannes Meursius** in his *Danish History*, book 4. <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639) was a Dutch classical scholar and royal historian to the King of Denmark.</note>

Furthermore, as to the fact that our ancestors entrusted their letters to tapestries and garments, they seem to me to have imitated the **Parthians**, <note>An ancient Iranian empire; the author is comparing Scandinavian textile-weaving traditions to those of the East described in classical literature.</note> of whom **Pliny** <note>Pliny the Elder, a Roman author, in his *Natural History*.</note> reports in Book 13, Chapter 11, that although papyrus grows in the Euphrates near Babylon, the Parthians still prefer to weave letters into their clothes. We have shown elsewhere that our own ancestors long ago marked wood, bark, bones, and whatever else was at hand—horns, stones, brass instruments, and so on—with their own characters. <note>The "characters" referred to here are Runes.</note>

Regarding the emblems and ornaments added to these items, their explanation is quite difficult. If any weight is to be given to my conjectures, I believe that solitary **Lion** represents the coat of arms of the **Kingdom of Norway**, indicating that she <note>Likely referring to Ragnhild, the noblewoman suspected of commissioning the work discussed.</note> was descended from the Royal family. Nor does it stand in the way that the lion does not carry an axe or halberd in its paws, since they report that those were only added to the Lion from the time of **Saint Olaf** <note>King Olaf II of Norway (reigned 1015–1028). The lion with the axe remains the coat of arms of Norway to this day.</note> onward. That **Knight** with a spear following a stag with a dog, and the **Fisherman** catching fish in the water, represent the noble exercises in which the great lords used to delight themselves, and signify their dominion over land and sea. But the **Eagle** tearing a fallen man with its beak and claws will denote the arts of war (as seen on the **Toten** stone, <note>Referring to an archaeological find in Toten, Norway, featuring Viking-age imagery.</note> which depicts eagles, dogs, horses, knights, and other things of that kind). For nothing was more common among the ancients, when they attempted to describe those slain in war, than to sing of them being given as food to vultures and eagles. Hence those lines in the *Death-Song of Ragnar Lodbrok*, <note>original: *Epicedio Regneri Lodbrog*. <header>BOOK SIX</header>

The head of the province called **Borgesyssel** <note>A historical region in south-eastern Norway, now known as Borgarsysla.</note> was once the wealthy and splendid city of **Sarpsborg**, made particularly famous by the court of the Norwegian Kings. Not far from here stands the church of **Tune**, on the western side of whose cemetery a rough stone can be seen, inscribed on both sides. It is roughly square and rises about two ells <note>An "ell" (ulna) was a historical unit of length; in this context, it likely refers to about four feet in height.</note> above the ground. One side of it was formerly hidden by the masonry of a wall, but now that the obstacles have been removed, it is visible to the eyes. I have chosen to present a drawing of it, even though I completely despair of its interpretation. <note>The Tune Stone is now recognized as one of the most important Proto-Norse inscriptions in the Elder Futhark.</note>

I mentioned it in the tenth chapter of my *Runic Literature* <note>Referring to Worm's 1636 work, *Runir seu Danica literatura antiquissima*.</note>, and I included it among those things said to be rarer and more intricate. If any "Daedalus" <note>In Greek mythology, Daedalus was a master craftsman who designed the Labyrinth; Worm uses this as a metaphor for a genius who can solve the "labyrinthine" complexity of the runes.</note> helps us out of this labyrinth, he will earn great gratitude from me. I have frequently consulted with my friends who are experts in this literature—as many as I could find—about it, but in vain. See also the stone of the same class at **Lärkeröd** <note>original: *Leragriense*</note> in **Blekinge**.

### EIGHTH.
### HOVGER.

In the same district is the Parish of **Tegneby**, which includes among the farmers assigned to the **Stala** <note>original: *Staale*</note> church one who inhabits the estate called **Houger**. Here, not far from the buildings in a marshy place, a monument stands out, carved into an uneven, somewhat rough, greyish stone. Its longest part is about six ells, and it is about one ell wide at the base. It now lies cast down and part of it is covered by earth; however, I do not doubt that it once stood upright with its tip raised. The inscription is not clear enough; nevertheless, I seem to perceive these things as best I can.

### NICOLAS TAILN CARVED THESE RUNES IN MEMORY OF HIS FATHER AND MOTHER.

It is certain that this stone was once a grave marker <term>saxum sepulchrale</term>, and was moved from elsewhere to serve as the foundation of this barn. However, none of the local inhabitants were able to give us more certain information regarding its original location. Some say that the buildings it now serves were constructed about sixty years ago. They add that there was once a third stone in this district, exactly like these, which was thrown into a nearby lake; they say it can still be seen there when the waters are calm and the sky is clear.

**ᚢᚱᚦᛁᚱ** <note>urthir</note> comes from the word *at graffue* <note>Archaic Danish: to dig or engrave</note>, meaning to carve or engrave.
**ᚠ. ᛆᚴ. ᛘ.** <note>f. ok m.</note>: because of the narrowness of the stone, the author was forced to use contractions for familiar words, using only the first letter which would be obvious to anyone. Thus, **ᚠ** stands for **father** <note>original: *fathur*</note> and **ᛘ** stands for **mother** <note>original: *muthur*</note>. The reader must turn the stone in various directions to grasp the meaning: one must begin with the horizontal line marked with the cross; when that is finished, the stone must be turned and read from the center toward the edge...

<meta>This page continues the discussion of the oval runic stone described on page 483, specifically addressing the symbolic meaning of circular and oval inscriptions before moving on to a new monument in Hadeland.</meta>

<page-num>484</page-num>
<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

one must proceed from both sides, following the course of the already mentioned ellipse. John Selden <note>John Selden (1584–1654) was a famous English jurist and scholar of antiquities</note>, in his notes on the *Arundel Marbles* <note>A collection of ancient Greek sculptures and inscriptions gathered by the Earl of Arundel</note>, elegantly explains that it was once a custom to write names in a circle when the participants wished there to be no priority of rank or dignity among them; thus, none of them would be first and none last, but the honor would be equal for all. Among these marbles, he depicts one circular monument dedicated to Liber <note>Another name for Bacchus, the god of wine</note>, Sylvanus, and Hercules, which displays an inscription laid out in a similar fashion. He also cites this elegant passage from Ausonius <note>A 4th-century Roman poet</note> in the *Play of the Seven Sages*, where Solon speaks these words among others:

> *Rightly of old the Delphic God made sport of the foolish,*
> *When they asked who among the wise might be the first:*
> *By writing their names in a smooth circle,*
> *Lest any should be first, or any the last.*
> <note>original Latin: "Recte olim ineptum Delphicus lusit Deus / Quærentem quisnam primus sapientum foret / Ut in orbe tereti nomina eorum inscribens / Ne primus esset, ne vel imus quisquam."</note>

A witty story is also told regarding Pope Urban. When he had instructed the Franciscan brotherhood to present him with three names from among themselves, one of whom he would elevate to the dignity of Cardinal, they presented the names in a circular figure. They did this so that none of them would seem more worthy than the others based on the priority of their place in the list. But the Pope said, "You have subverted the order, and I shall subvert the order." Ignoring the members designated in that way, he created the head of the order, whom they call the General, a Cardinal instead. However, in these monuments of ours, no such reason can exist as to why inscriptions were committed to round or oval stones rather than others. For each monument displays the name of only a single author and a single deceased person, in which there cannot fail to be the order that is shown. Therefore, the choice of figure must necessarily depend on the whim of the founder.

As far as I can gather from these details, this monument was placed for Evinus <note>Often Latinized as Eyvindr</note> by his mistress or concubine Juruna. She reports that this Evinus had joined himself in legitimate marriage to a certain Gurda—perhaps a woman named Gunara—from Greece <note>original Latin: "è Græcia"; likely referring to the Byzantine Empire, known in Old Norse as *Grikkjariki*</note>, and she mentions yet another woman named Urala.

ᛁᚢᚱᚢᚿ <note>Iurun</note> is a female name that is still familiar to many in Norway and Iceland today. I find a certain woman of this name in the *History of Harald Fairhair*, surnamed **Skaldmær** <note>literally "Skald-Maid" or "Poetess"</note>, because she was successful and celebrated in the ancient art of poetry. A poem she composed is even cited in Norwegian history concerning the dispute between the brothers Eric **Bloodaxe** and Halfdan the **Black** (the sons of Harald Fairhair), which was happily settled. Indeed, I am led by no small evidence to believe that this was the same woman who placed this monument, both because she was a poetess highly skilled in this art, and because in the same century lived the man called Evindus **Skaldaspillere**, who was considered the prince of all poets then living. It seems likely that this Juruna was his lover, perhaps due to their shared intellectual pursuits.

ᛁᚢᛁᚿ <note>Iuin</note> is, I believe, the same Evindus who, due to the excellence of his poetry, was called **Skaldaspillere** <note>The "Spoiler of Poets" or "Plagiarist," a nickname given to Eyvindr Finnsson because he was said to be so talented he surpassed all others, or perhaps because he imitated older styles</note> or **Spildskalder**. He was born of royal lineage and was a man of great authority; his grandmother was the daughter of Harald Fairhair. He dearly loved Haakon Adelstein <note>Haakon the Good, foster-son of the English King Athelstan</note>, in whose praise he sang various songs. Conversely, he poured out curses upon Eric **Bloodaxe** and his sons, who had deprived Adelstein of his life and kingdom. Because of this, he was sought for execution by Haakon **Graycloak**, but he obtained pardon through the mediation of friends on the condition that he give as a gift to Graycloak his gold ring called **Molde**, and that he thereafter celebrate Graycloak's noble deeds in verse at his court. Various songs of his are cited in Norwegian history. Among others, they recommend one composed in honor of the Icelanders, for which—after each man contributed a silver coin—they rewarded him with a skillfully crafted silver dagger. He wore this constantly in their honor, until, under the pressure of extreme necessity and the high price of grain, ur- <note>The text cuts off here at the catchword; the next page likely describes him selling the dagger to buy food.</note>

## IN MEMORY OF THORALD, AND THIS STONE IS A MEMORIAL TO THEM.

To speak freely about what I think regarding this monument: I believe this inscription—by which Egil <note>Likely Egil Skallagrímsson, the famous Icelandic hero and poet</note> is said to have placed this stone in memory of Thorald and the others mentioned here—is older than the previous one. I suspect the stone itself was originally decorated with these runes and placed here, but over the course of time it collapsed and was later restored to its original site by JURUNA. At that time, it was likely decorated with new characters in memory of Evindus <note>Eyvindr Skaldaspillere</note>; or perhaps it was a joint effort by Egil and JURUNA.

ᛦᛁᚦᛁ <note>Runic inscription fragment</note>. He must have been a man of great esteem, who saw to it that mention of his estate or fortress *Viteholm* <note>original: "Viteholm"</note> was made here at the same time; but where or of what sort this *Viteholm* was is not clear to me.

ᛁᚦᚱᛁ <note>Runic inscription fragment</note> Thorald is mentioned quite often in the histories. Our own Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> in Book 1 names a certain Thorald, the son of the Swedish King Hading, who was sent by his stepmother along with his brother to be entangled in various kinds of dangers, and was eventually put in charge of the royal cattle. The same author mentions another Thorald in Book 10, right at the beginning, whom I might not absurdly link to this place. For he relates that Harald Grey-cloak <note>original: "Haraldum Grafelder"</note> sought and obtained aid from the Danes against Haakon Adelstein <note>Haakon the Good, original: "Haqvinum Adelstanum"</note>. In that war in which Haakon fell, Thoralv <note>original: "Thoralvum"</note> behaved so vigorously that when he was stationed in an ambush to disrupt the enemy’s rear, he rushed upon them, launched an attack on the battle line, and inflicted death upon Karlshosto and flight upon the Danes. 

Egil <note>original: "Egillus"</note>, who is called ᛁᚦᚱᛁ on this monument, was a comrade-in-arms to this Thoralv. The Norwegian history concerning Haakon Adelstein reports that he was known by the nickname *Vlffserck* <note>Old Norse "Úlfserkr," meaning "Wolf-shirt," a term often applied to fierce warriors or berserkers</note>; that while he was a young man, he stood out as a most brave soldier and was the standard-bearer for Harald Fairhair <note>original: "Haraldi pulchricomi"</note>. In the battle that preceded the death of Haakon Adelstein (around the year of Christ 960), he fell in combat. After his death, he was buried by the King in a magnificent pyre constructed from the hulls of enemy ships, with pillars and great stones added to preserve the memory of his deeds forever. These things seem to me to fit together beautifully—

## THIRTEEN.
## THE MIRACULOUS TEMPLE.

IN the province of *Telemark* <note>original: "Telemarchica"</note> within this Diocese, in the parish called *Hollen*, I have learned from trustworthy witnesses who saw and surveyed it that there exists a miraculous temple, specifically because it holds a cemetery on its roof, in which the inhabitants were accustomed to bury the dead. I will touch upon the matter briefly. A certain lake of fresh water called *Nordsjø* <note>original: "Nordsoë"</note>, which flows into the sea through various windings, is seen in the district of *Telemark*, about five miles <note>The original "sesquimilliare" (one and a half miles) refers to old Scandinavian miles, much longer than modern miles</note> distant from the city of *Skien* <note>original: "Sceen"</note>. Adjacent to this is a cliff of wondrous height and vastness, which the locals call *Vear*. This cliff was so skillfully hollowed out around the middle that it once constituted a temple, to be seen with no external columns or imported vaulting, but fashioned out of the living rock, decorated with an altar and other ecclesiastical ornaments, and dedicated to St. Michael; now, however, it is miserably defaced by fire. In the center of the vaulted ceiling, a hole is seen carved somewhat higher up, to which an iron handle is still fitted, intended, as they say, for hanging a small bell. A single entrance through a sufficiently large door opens to it, and admits light through the same. Those who traveled there either sought the cliff by boat across the lake, and were then forced to ascend by means of wooden beams and hanging ladders until the door was reached; or from another mountain...

Regarding the origin and foundation of this temple, nothing certain is established. I suspect it was a pagan <note>original: "Idololatricum"</note> shrine that was eventually converted to Christian use.

## STAVANGER RECORDS.

The monuments that exist in the Diocese of Stavanger <note>original: "Stavangriensi"</note> were collected through the expense and no small labor of the Reverend and most celebrated Master Thomas Wegner <note>Thomas Wegner (1588–1654) was the Bishop of Stavanger and a key correspondent of the author, Ole Worm</note>, the most vigilant Bishop of this province. In order to bring fame to the Stavanger Diocese through his industry in gathering the ruins of ancient inscriptions—just as his predecessor had done with a topographical map of the same area—he left nothing unattempted. However, the fact that the outcome did not fully respond to all his wishes must be attributed to the various injuries of the weather; the storms, which know not how to spare the solidity of the cliffs, have swept away many strokes of the letters, corrupted the stones themselves, or broken them by the impact with the ground, to the great detriment of venerable antiquity. Nor did the scarcity of those who, being instructed in the knowledge of our ancient literature <note>referring here to the study of runes</note>, could have spent their effort on these things, provide a small obstacle to his most laudable endeavors. Meanwhile, with a grateful heart, we receive from this most religious man...

# MONUMENTS OF STAVANGER.

The monuments which exist in the Diocese of Stavanger <term>Diocese: the district or territory under the jurisdiction of a bishop</term> were collected through the expense and no small labor of the Reverend and most distinguished Master Thomas Wegner, the most vigilant Bishop of this province. Just as his predecessor had won fame for the Stavanger Diocese with a topographical map of the same, Wegner left nothing untried in his own diligence to collect the ruins of ancient inscriptions.

However, that the outcome did not respond to all his wishes must be blamed on the various injuries of the storms; these, not knowing how to spare even the solidness of the rocks, have carried away many strokes of the letters, corrupted the stones themselves, or broke them as they struck the ground, to the great detriment of venerable antiquity. Nor did a small obstacle to his praiseworthy attempts arise from the scarcity of those who, being trained in the knowledge of our ancient literature <note>Referring to Old Norse and runic literacy</note>, could have devoted their effort to these matters. Meanwhile, with a grateful heart, [the findings] of this most religious man are to be received...

->KALBIORN RESTORED ME.<-
<note>original Latin: "KALBIORNUS ME REPOSUIT."</note>

From the word ᛒᛁᚢᚱᚿ (*biorn* or bear), many ancient compound names exist; the meaning of this one is perhaps composed of *Kal* (either "calf" or "cold") and *urso* ("bear"). The name *Halbiorn* is more common, and I wonder if it might be suspected that it was originally carved that way here, and the other cross-strokes of the letter \* <note>The author is referring to the Runic 'H'</note> were worn away, leaving only that single stroke. In place of ᛒᛁᚢᚱᚿ (*biurn*), I read ᛒᛁᛅᚱᚿ (*biarn*) in other places. In this word, one should also notice the joining of two letters into one: for instead of ᛅ (*a*) and ᛚ (*l*), you have a single composite character ᛅᛚ <term>bind-rune: a ligature of two or more runes combined into a single glyph</term>.

The strokes of the following small words are much decayed; however, they seem to be easily restored as I have written them. Regarding the final ᚴ ᛚ (*k l*), I remain in doubt; I suspect there were more marks on this stone that were not noticed by the person who recorded them. Nevertheless, the meaning of the inscription may be this: Kalbiurnus restored the stone—which had been placed by someone else but had fallen due to the damage of time—to its original position, so that the memory of such a noble monument would not be erased.

<header>BOOK SIX.</header>

The matter itself shows that there is an error <note>original Latin: "mendum"</note> here—a word upon which the meaning of the entire inscription depends. If it is understood to be derived from the word *I consecrate* <note>original Danish: "Jeg vier"</note>, it signifies to hallow or to dedicate. This would indicate that the two people named on the monument either dedicated the temple, or consecrated and donated the stones from which the temple was built, or, according to ancient custom, laid the first foundation stone and oversaw the construction of the temple. These interpretations are quite plausible.

On the same island of Rennesøy <note>original: "Renneröe"</note>, beneath the structure of the main church, there exists a stone marked with Runic characters. Neither all of its lines nor its full size can be determined, because the largest part of it is covered by the walls of the church. Certain letters have been copied from it, which I have included below, so that it might be clear from them how difficult it is to gather anything certain from such poorly recorded outlines. I received them in this sequence:

<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>

->KALBIORN RESTORED ME.<-
<note>original Latin: "Kalbiornus me reposit"</note>

ᚴᛅᛚᛒᛁᚯᚱᚾ <note>Kalbiorn</note>. From the word *Biorn* <note>meaning "bear"</note> there exist many ancient compound names; the sense of this one is perhaps composed from *Kal*, meaning calf, or cold, and *urso*, meaning bear. The name *Halbiorn* is more frequent, and I wonder if one might suspect it was originally carved that way here, and that the remaining transverse strokes of the letter ᚼ <note>the 'H' rune</note> were worn away, leaving only a single vertical line. In place of *BIᚯRᚾ*, I read *BIᚯRᚾ* in other instances. Also to be observed in this word is a <term>ligature|A combination of two or more letters joined into a single character</term> of two letters into one: for instead of ᛅ and ᚿ, you have one composite character ᚿ.

The strokes of the following short words are much corrupted; however, they seem capable of being conveniently restored as I have written them. Regarding the last ᚴ ᚱ <note>K R</note>, I remain in doubt; I suspect there were more marks on this stone that were not noticed by the person who recorded it. Nevertheless, the sense of the inscription may be this: Kalbiorn restored to its place a stone set by another, which had fallen due to the <note>original: "temporum injuria"</note> ravages of time, so that the memory of such a distinguished monument should not be erased.

In the Provostship called <term>Råbyggelag|original Latin: "Robygdelag"</term>, there exists a waterfall where the waters plunge with great force from the steep cliffs, known in the local tongue as <term>Fennefoss|original: "Fennie fos"</term>. ->Good Arnstein carved this stone in memory of<-
->Bjørn, his son, who died in <note>original: Lidnlis. Likely referring to London or a location in England</note>,<-
->Canute placed the ornaments.<-

-><note>original Latin translation: "BONUS ARKSTINUS SCULPSIT LAPIDEM HUNC IN MEMORIAM BIORNONIS FILII SUI, QVI OBIIT IN LIDNLIS, CANUTUS POSUIT ORNAMENTA."</note><-

Most parts of this monument are clear enough in themselves. The transcript had the name **Arnstein** written as two words (<note>ᚼᚱᚴ- ᛋᛏᛁᚿ</note>), but I have no doubt it is a single name, belonging to the man who saw to the placement of this monument. 
Regarding **Bjørn** (<note>ᛒᛁᚢᚱ</note>), perhaps a letter *n* is missing, but it clearly refers to a man named Bjørn.
As for the phrase <note>ᛁᚴᛚᚮᛏ / iklot</note>: either there is an error here, or the word indicates something now unfamiliar to us. I suspect it alludes to something regarding the completion or decoration of this monument; for this reason, I have rendered it as "ornaments" until someone can extract a more suitable meaning from it. <note>Modern scholars often interpret "sati iklot" as "set in England," suggesting the son died during King Canute's campaigns.</note>

### THE TUNSTAD MONUMENT. <note>Tønjum, in the Lærdal district of Norway</note>

<page-num>499</page-num>
<header>BOOK SIX</header>

## MARY HOLY MOTHER OF HOLY JESUS 
## CHRIST HELP HAKON.

In the first sequence of the text, certain letters were not correctly recorded; however, when the weight and emphasis of the meaning were considered, they allowed for an easy correction. In the first word *BARN* <note>original: "BᛅRᚿ"</note>, the rune ᛦ was substituted for a cross <note>†</note> and the number 1. In the word *MARIA* <note>original: "ᛘᛅᚱᛁᛅ"</note>, he marked a point after the letter 'I', and in place of the runes ᚦ and R, he displayed this mark ᛦR, though perhaps ᚱR should have been written. He divided the word *Tetragrammaton* <note>A Greek term referring to the four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH</note> into three separate sections in this manner: *Tetra. Gramma. Ton*, using three points as separators, due to an ignorance of the Greek language. I will not note the smaller mistakes <note>original: "sphalmata"</note>. In the second sequence, there are fewer errors, but the penultimate word was clearly corrupted. After the first word, the letter 'I' was placed instead of a punctuation point. This is followed by the single letter ᚢ <note>U</note> also with a point; whether this should denote *MESSU* <note>Mass</note>, or *MAGDALENA*, or *MODUR* <note>Mother</note> is not entirely clear. However, I incline toward the latter opinion, so that the sense is: *Mary holy mother of most holy Jesus Christ, help Haakon.*

The runes *ᚼᛅᚴᚢᚿ* <note>HAKUN</note> denote the name Haakon <note>original: "Haqvinum"</note>. The local inhabitants believe that the old church was built by King Haakon of Norway <note>Likely King Haakon V Magnusson, who reigned 1299–1319</note> in honor of Saint Mary, the mother of Christ, which is why even now it is called the Church of Saint Mary. Formerly, a great gathering was held here every year, which they called *MARIU MESSU* <note>Mary’s Mass</note>, distinguished by the dedication of the church, the celebration of the mass, and other rituals customary at that time.

## NINTH MONUMENT.
### THE LUND MONUMENT. <note>Referring to the parish of Lunde in the Lærdal district, Norway</note>

The parish of Tunstad, mentioned above, is annexed to the parish of Lund. This place is also not without its own marks of ancient literature. In this church of Lund, there is a door almost consumed by rot and age, upon which certain marks are seen carved in three places. Their meaning will not be easily grasped by anyone who has not observed our ancestors' various ways of intertwining letters <note>A reference to "bind-runes," where multiple runic characters are combined into a single glyph</note>.

ᚱᛅᛚᚴᚾᛁᛋ <term>RALGNES</term> <note>These are the runes as they appear on the door</note> perhaps **Agnes**; however, according to the second reading, I believe it to be ᚱᛅᚾᚢᛚᚠ **Ranulf**, a common enough proper name. Unless you read the bottom line in reverse, you will gather nothing from it; for ᛁᚱᛅᛚᚴ <note>IRALK</note> perhaps ᚴᛚᛅᚱᛁ **KLARI** should be substituted. In this way, you will draw out the following words by starting from the end: **KLARI RANULF SUN RALGNES**, <note>meaning "The guild of Ranulf, son of Klari"</note> the assembly of Ranulf, son of Klari. This man perhaps dedicated this door to the church at his own expense. Formerly, those societies and assemblies that took their names from the Saints were called *Gilde* <note>Guilds</note>, such as *St. Olaf’s guild*, and so on. Regarding these, **Henry Spelman** <note>An English antiquary (1562–1641) famous for his work on legal and historical linguistics</note> writes as follows in his *Glossary*:

*A **Gilda** (called a **Gildoria** by foreigners) is a society of certain people allied for the sake of charity, religion, or trade. They sometimes hold certain goods and lands in common, as well as a guild hall or meeting house. To the Latins, this is a **collegium** <note>college</note>, **fratria** <note>brotherhood</note>, **fraternitas** <note>fraternity</note>, **sodalitium** <note>fellowship</note>, or **adunatio** <note>union</note>. To Hincmar, it is a **confratria** <note>confraternity</note>. To Aristotle, Plutarch, and the Greeks, it is a **Phratria** <note>original Greek: Φρατρία</note>, because they used a common well (which in Greek is called a **Phrear** <note>original Greek: Φρέαρ</note> or poetically **Phreiar**).*

From this comes the name, because the fellowship is supported by pooled funds; for *geld* and *gild* mean money or payment, and *gildan* means to pay or contribute. He teaches in the same place that under the name of Guilds are contained...

# XIII.
## THE FRAMVARDE MONUMENT.

This monument is mentioned by Peder Claussøn Friis <note>original: "Petrus Claudii Undalensis" (1545–1614), a Norwegian clergyman and historian known for his descriptions of Norway.</note> in the *Description of Norway* which was published by me in the common tongue <note>Referring to the Danish translation of Friis's work edited and published by Ole Worm in 1632.</note> some years ago. In treating the Prefecture of Lister, he has this to say: "To the North (of Lister), among the crags, there lies a freshwater lake called **FRAMVARDE**, of such great depth that in certain places the bottom cannot be found by any skill. Here, on a rock rising above the waters, these characters are read:"

->ΛYIUIIRIPIMHIK.<-

These are so conspicuous and clear that they seem as if they were carved not so many years ago, although it is believable they were placed several centuries past. Furthermore, these characters were not inscribed with iron, but rather rubbed onto the rock as if with another stone—which is a thing of wonder.

A drawing of it was sent by the Reverend Master Thomas Wegner, the Bishop of the region:

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of a large, jagged rock formation. Inscribed horizontally across the center of the rock face is a series of characters, seemingly a mix of runic and Latin letters: "ΛYIUIIRIPIMHIK". Vertical hatching lines provide depth and texture to the rock's surface.</image-desc>

As for the matter itself, I believe that several marks of this kind were once entrusted to this stone, which have either perished through the injuries of the weather or were not noticed by those who described them,

...which can be gathered from the conjunction **ᚦᚢ** <note>Rune: *thu*, meaning "and" or "then"</note> which takes the first place here, and which implies something preceding it. I have obtained this inscription from various sources, but not a single letter was added to it. Some read the first letter not as **ᚦ** [th], but as **R**; and in place of **ᛘᛁ ᛘᛁᚾ** [mi min] they read it this way: **ᚱᚢᛚᚠᛁᛦᛁᚦᛁᚾᚾ ᛘᛁᚾ** [Rulfirithin min]. It is called **Runefield** [Rune-field] by the local inhabitants because of the Runic letters visible here; however, the closer you approach the rock, the less the characters appear.
   If room is given for conjecture, I judge it should be read thus:

->**ᚦᚢ ᛁᚼᚢᚱᛁᚦ ᛘᛁ ᛘᛁᚾ.**<-
->AND TO JAVRIDI, HIS LITTLE HEART<-

In **ᛁᚼᚢᚱᛁᚦ** [Ihurith], two lines must necessarily be joined to form a **ᚦ** [th], for a doubled **I** never occurs in our monuments, and our ancestors were more inclined toward ellipsis <term>ellipsis: the omission of letters or words</term> than toward pleonasm <term>pleonasm: the use of more words than necessary for clarity</term> in their lettering. **JAVRIDI** will therefore be a proper name, perhaps of a woman, to whom this inscription was dedicated.
   **ᛘᛁ** [mi]. A diminutive word implying affection, like *Hierte lit* <note>Danish: "little heart"</note>—"little sweetheart," etc. But concerning these matters, let those who have been granted the opportunity to examine each detail more accurately decide.
   Regarding the art by which these characters were impressed upon the rock, I would like to offer a few remarks, as it is not obvious everywhere; but like many noble inventions of the ancients, it is almost lost. Our ancestors made a certain ink from pitch, seal blood, and other things of that kind, with which they committed letters and characters to stones, bones, and other harder objects, so that they were not erasable by any storm or the ravages of time. They called this *seltiere* <note>likely "sel-tjære" or seal-tar</note>, named after the principal ingredients of this mixture: namely, liquid pitch and seal blood. The most celebrated Arngrimur Jónsson <note>original: "Arngrimus jonas" (1568–1648), a notable Icelandic scholar</note> asserts that these characters were written with such a compound in the second part of his *Historical and Chorographical Apology against Pontanus* <note>A work defending Icelandic history against the claims of Johannes Isacius Pontanus</note>, where he adds that at the isthmus of western Iceland, there are the **Hyttars** cliffs called **Biscops Bode** [Bishop’s Booths], and a marsh stagnating on the same shore called **Liika Tiorn** [Corpse Tarn], in which the bodies of drowned sailors were washed (as if it were a pool of funerals or a fatal marsh). In that same place, the precious or more valuable teeth of whales (per-

...[commonly called] the common unicorn <note>original: *vulgare unicornu*. This refers to the narwhal tusk, which in the 17th century was still widely believed to be the horn of the mythical unicorn</note>) were submerged in a shipwreck, and subsequently, as the tide of the sea disturbed and swept everything from the bottom, they were cast onto the shore and found, inscribed or marked with Runic letters (so that any of the sailors might recognize his own property) with an indelible glue of a reddish color. Note here, that this substance which Arngrim <note>Arngrimur Jónsson (1568–1648), a prominent Icelandic scholar who provided much information on Northern antiquities to the author</note> calls "glue" was not only black, but also reddish, and indeed even ash-colored or of another color; we call it the **Ink of the ancients** <term>Atramentum: the Latin word for ink or any black pigment</term>, because it served the same purpose as our own ink, with which we commonly write or press letters with a printing press.

# BOOK SIX.

The province of Madalenis <note>Likely referring to a district in Northern Norway</note> contains among its others a parish called *Andenes*, in whose churchyard, facing the eastern side of the church, a large upright stone is seen, eight ells <note>An ell is an old unit of measurement, roughly the length of a man's arm</note> in length, three and a half quarters wide, and half of a quarter thick. Its southern face, which makes up the thickness of the stone, contains the following words to be read, starting from its lowest part fixed in the ground and proceeding upwards:

->Arinter built this church over the son of Olaf the Tall, his kinsman.<-
->In his own ancestral estate.<-

->*Arintr built the church of this [place?] the son of Olaf the Tall in his own ancestral estate.* <note>original: "Arintr gard kirkiu desa pa sunr Olafs hin hala aodali sinu."</note><-
->ARINTER BUILT THIS CHURCH OVER THE SON OF SAINT OLAF, HIS KINSMAN.<-

Others have described the history of Saint Olaf, who is mentioned here, at great length; the *Chronicle of the Kings of Norway*, published by us in the vernacular language in Copenhagen in the year 1633, follows the series of his deeds succinctly. The *Aarhus Breviary* <note>A liturgical book containing the public prayers of the Church in Aarhus, Denmark</note>, published in Aarhus by Melchior Blume in the year of Christ 1519, during the 29th year of the pontificate of Niels Clausen, asserts: *Saint Olaf died on the first of August, on a Wednesday, in the year 1028 from the incarnation of the Lord, having been cruelly slain by the enemies of the faith in defense of the faith.* However, it is not entirely clear who this son might be, in whose memory this church was built.

For King Magnus <note>Magnus the Good (r. 1035–1047)</note>, who eventually attained the throne, died in Jutland and was transported to Nidaros <note>Modern-day Trondheim</note> by Einar Tambarskjelve <note>A legendary Norwegian archer and politician</note> so that he might be buried with solemn pomp near his father in the Church of Saint Clement. Indeed, the *Chronicle of Norway* mentions on page 343 that this Magnus had a brother called *Tore af Stegen* <note>Thore of Stegen</note>, who perhaps was the one to whom these honors were granted after his death.

ᚮᚦᛆᛚ **Odal** <term>Odal: an ancient Norse legal term for inherited property that remained within a family and was not subject to feudal service</term> denotes hereditary goods, or free estates subject to no servitude; these are contrasted with Fiefs <note>Land held from a lord in exchange for service</note>, which are subject to servitude. This word corresponds with **Allodium**, which denotes an inheritance that comes to us from our parents.

...inseparable from the family! From this comes the term <term>Allodialists</term> <note>Owners of land held in absolute ownership, known as allodium, which is not subject to a superior landlord</note> who held *Allodia* [freehold estates] and were able to make decisions about their properties without consulting any lords; in our tongue these are called *Odal property* <note>original: "Odals godtz"</note>. *Thurgudr rist stin dena eft Thrunt sun sin.*

->THORGUDERUS PLACED THIS STONE<-
->FOR THROUNDUS, HIS SON.<-

**Thurgudr** <note>original: "ᚦᚢᚱᚵᚢᚦᚱ"</note>. If the word were divided, it could be read as "Thor god" <note>original: "Thor guder"</note>. The god Thor was once worshipped with great devotion by the northern heathens; regarding him, see Book I, chapter VI. However, it is more probable that in this context it is a man's name, taken from Thor. It is spoken as if to say "the good Thor," for *gudr* <note>original: "ᚵᚢᚦᚱ"</note> is an adjective meaning good, now written as *god*.

**Thrunt** <note>original: "ᚦᚱᚢᚿᛏ"</note>. From someone of this name, the famous Norwegian trading center **Trondheim** <note>original: "Trontheim"</note> took its name, as if you were to say the home of Thrundus. Others call it **Nidaros** <note>original: "Nidrosiam"</note>, after the river **Nid** <note>original: "Nidda"</note> that flows past it.

---

## XX.
### STANGELAND

In the Parish of *Hoiland* <note>modern Høyland</note>, on the royal road that leads to Stangeland, an artificially constructed hill or mound is seen. &nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;&nbsp;ᛅᚠᛁ ᛋᛏᛁᚾᚦᚢᚱᛁ ᛋᚢᚾ ᛋᛁᚾ ᚠᚢ ᛏᛅᚾᛘᛅᚱᚴᚢ ᚴᛁᛚᛁᚢ ᚢᚱᚬᛁᚢᛒᛋ ᛋᚴᛅᛚ- ᛏᛁᚱ! ᛋᚴᛅᛚᚦ ᚱᛅᛁᛋᛏᛁ ᛋᛏᛁᚾᛅ.

ᚢᛁᚦ ᚠᚢᚱᛁ <note>original runes: v-i-th f-u-r-i</note> is undoubtedly a single word, though poorly divided into two by punctuation. For names of this kind derived from the god Thor occur frequently; for instance, **Bergthor** <note>Mountain-Thor</note>, **Stenthor** <note>Stone-Thor</note>, and so on.

ᛏᛅᚾᛘᛅᚱᚴᚢ <note>original runes: t-a-n-m-a-r-k-u</note> clearly indicates Denmark.

ᚢᛁᚾᚾ <note>original runes: u-i-n-n</note>—To kill, beat, or strike; this suggests that he was killed in Denmark.

ᛋᚴᛅᛚᛏ <note>original runes: s-k-a-l-t</note>—In the ancient age, this denoted a Poet <note>a Skald</note>. We have spoken at greater length regarding the duties and social standing of these figures in the appendix to our *Runic Literature* <note>original Latin: "Literaturae Runicae"</note>. It was a very illustrious title, held in no less esteem then than that of a Doctor or Master today. This explains why those gifted with the ability to readily and elegantly compose songs in the common tongue, and to craft epitaphs for the well-deserving, did not hesitate to engrave their own names upon these stones for the perpetual memory of the event.

Within the precinct of the church at Klepp, on the northern side, two rows of letters are carved into a plank, running its length from bottom to top; the first of these presents the following:

ᚼᚢᛂᚱ : ᛆ : ᛘᛆᚦᚢᚱ : ᚱᚢᚾᛆᚱ : ᚦᛁᛌᛌ : ᛌᛂᛂᚱ : ᚦᛆ : ᛚᛂᛌᛁ :
ᚠᛆᚦᛂᚱ : ᚾᚭᛌᛐᛂᚱ : ᚠᚤᚱᛁᚱ : ᛌᚭᛚᚢ : ᚼᛂᛁᚦᚾᛆ : ᛘᛆᚾᚾᛆ : ᚦᛂᛁᛘ :
ᚼᛁᛆᛚᛐᛁ : ᚴᚢᚦ : ᚦᛂᛁᛘ : ᛂᚱ : ᛌᚢᛆ : ᚵᛁᛂᚱᛁᚱ .

*Whoever, as a man, sees these runes, let him then say an Our Father for the souls of the heathens; may God help those who do so.*

> WHOEVER BEHOLDS THESE RUNES, LET HIM PRAY 
> AN OUR FATHER <note>original Latin: "Pater Noster"</note> FOR THE SOULS OF THE 
> HEATHENS. MAY GOD HAVE MERCY UPON THOSE 
> WHO DO SO.

ᚱᚢᚾᛆᚱ <note>Runar</note>. Here you have the ancient name of our letters; from its placement in this context, one may gather that not only were those characters used by the ancients for sorcery and incantations called "Runes," but also any Northern letters adapted for pious uses.

ᛌᚭᛚᚢ ᚼᛂᛁᚦᚾᚭ <note>solu heidna - souls of the heathens</note>. Any reader may easily infer the age in which these were carved from this phrase. It was clearly shortly after paganism had been abolished. For the inscription commands that prayers be poured out for the souls of the heathens—meaning those who were still living, so that they might be converted to the Christian religion. Furthermore, the fact that they are commanded to pray the *Our Father* <note>original Latin: "Pater noster"</note>, while the *Hail Mary* <note>original Latin: "Ave Maria"</note> is omitted, proves that in that century the cult of the Saints did not yet flourish among us, in the first beginnings of the tender Church.

The second row presents the following:

ᛆᛚᛐᛁᚦ : ᛂᚱ : ᛁᚾᚵᛁᛒᛁᛆᚱᚵᛆᚱ : ᚴᛆᚱᛆ : ᚦᚭᛐᛂᚱ : ᚦᚱᚢᚾᚭᛘ : ᛂᚠᛐᛂᚱ :
ᚴᚱᚭᛌᛘᛂᛌᛌᚢ : ᚢᛘ : ᚢᛆᚱᛁᛐ .

*The memory of Ingeborg, Kare's daughter, is always recalled after the Feast of the Cross in the spring.*

> THE MEMORY OF INGEBORG, 
> DAUGHTER OF KARE, IS ALWAYS RECALLED 
> AROUND THE VERNAL FEAST OF THE CROSS.

ᚦᚱᚢᚾᚭᛘ ᚢᛘ ᚢᛆᚱᛁᛐ <note>drunom um varit</note>. I do not sufficiently grasp the meaning of these words; in the meantime, the conjecture provided here does not seem absurd. For Ingeborg seems to have either built or endowed the church, so that...

### XXIV.
### THE SECOND TANGER MONUMENT.

There exists in the same district, on the royal road that runs between *Tangershoi* and *Figgen*, a square stone two <term>ells</term> <note>original: "ulnarum"; an ell is a historical unit of length, usually about 24 inches</note> and one quarter in length, two quarters and a half in width, and half a quarter in thickness. It was rough indeed, but it contained these letter-marks around its border, and in the middle, a cross decorated with various lines in roughly this manner:

<image-desc>Woodcut illustration of a rectangular stone slab (gravestone). The stone is oriented vertically. Here rests Sir Ildametter, priest of the Mary [Church] of Rein. Rest in peace. Read an Our Father for his soul. Torstein made me.
<note>original runes: ᚼᛁᚱ ᚼᚢᛁᛚᛁᚱ ᛋᛁᚱᛆ ᛁᛚᛑᛆᛘᛂᛏᛏᛂᚱ ᛒᚱᛂᛋᛏᛂᚱ ᚠᛆᛑᛂᚱ ᛘᛆᚱᛁᚢ ᚱᛂᛁᚾᛁᚱ ᚠᚮᛚᛚᛆᚢᛁ ᚱᚮᛚᛁ ᛆᚴᚴᚢ ᚱᛁᛑᛂᚱ ᛒᛆᛏᛂᚱ ᚾᚮᛋᛏᛂᚱ ᚠᛁᚱᛁ ᛋᛆᛚᚢ ᚼᛆᚾᛋ ᛏᚮᚱᛋᛏᛂᛁᚾ ᛂᚱᛑᛂ ᛘᛁ</note>

*Here rests Sir <note>The title "Sira" was used for priests</note> Ildametter, priest of the Mary [Church] of Rein. Rest in peace. Read an Our Father <note>original: Pater noster</note> for his soul. Torstein made me.*

<header>BOOK SIX</header>

HERE RESTS SIR ILDAMETTER, PRIEST, FATHER <note>In this context, likely a title of respect or referring to his role at the Mary Church of Rein</note> OF MARY REINUR, COMPANION OF ROLVO. EVERYONE PRAY AN OUR FATHER FOR HIS SOUL. THORSTEIN MADE ME.

It is quite clear that this monument is Christian and indeed dates from the Middle Ages. The person who first described it did not fully capture all of its strokes; for this reason, he left us with more than a few doubts. From the word **MARIE** <note>original runes: ᛘᛆᚱᛁᛂ</note> through to **HUN** <note>original runes: ᚼᚢᚿ</note> the transcription is unsatisfactory. We hope that someone else will correct these points and more in their own time.

## SECOND.
### THE TINGVOLL MONUMENT.

Of the same class is that inscription which is carved into a white stone in the Tingvoll church <note>Located in Nordmøre, Norway</note>, and inserted into the wall above the altar, of the following content:

ᛂᚵ ᛒᛁᚦ ᚠᛁᚱᛁ ᚵᚢᚦᚱᛋ ᛋᛆᚴᛆᚱ ᛆᛚᛚᛆ ᛚᛂᚱᚦᛆ ᛘᛂᚿ ᚦᛆᚱ
ᛂᚱ ᚡᛆᚱᚦ ᚡᛂᛁᛐ ᛆ ᛋᛐᛆᚦ ᚦᛂᚿᚢ ᚮᚵ ᛆᛚᛚᛆ ᚦᛂ ᛂᚱ ᚱᛆᚦᛆ
ᚴᚢᚿᚢ ᛒᚮᚿ ᛘᛁᚿᛁ ᛘᛁᚿᛁᛋᚴ ᛋᛆᛚᚮ ᛘᛁᚿᛆᚱ ᛁ ᚼᛂᛚᚵᚢᛘ
ᛒᚮᚿᚮᛘ ᛂᚿ ᛂᚵ ᛂᛐ ᚵᚢᚿᛆᚱ ᛆᚵ ᚵᛂᚱᚦᛁ ᛂᚵ ᚼᚢᛋ ᚦᛂᛐᛐᛂ ᚡᛆ-
ᛚᛂᛐᛂ.

> I pray for God's sake all learned men who serve this place, and all who read my prayer, remember my soul in holy prayers; but I was Gunnar and I made this house. Farewell.
> <note>This is a translation of the Old Norse/Old Norwegian runic text: "Eg bið fyrir Guðs sakir alla lærða menn..."</note>

> I ASK FOR THE SAKE OF GOD THAT OTHER LEARNED MEN WHO SHALL HAVE BEEN ORDAINED TO THIS PLACE, AND MY WIFE RADA ALSO ASKS ALL, THAT THEY MAY REMEMBER MY SOUL IN THEIR HOLY PRAYERS; MY NAME WAS GUNNERUS, AND I BUILT THIS HOUSE. FAREWELL.
> <note>This is the author's Latin interpretation: "ROGO PROPTER DEUM UT ALII VIRI DOCTI..." Gunnar is identifying himself as the builder or architect of the church.</note>

The inscription presents no difficulty; for it seems to have been placed by the architect at the top of the altar so that he might have a place in the Masses and prayers for the departed—the very thing he requests here.

Combinations of letters <note>commonly called bind-runes</note> occur here quite frequently: ᛪ <term>double N</term>, ᚿᚱ <term>the combination ur</term>, ᚯ <term>the diphthong ø</term>, ᛆᛚ <term>the combination al</term>, ᛆᚱ <term>the combination ar</term>, ᚥ <term>the combination Vuu</term>.

### THIRD.
### THE FRÖSÖ STONE.

In Jämtland <note>Historically a Norwegian province, it was ceded to Sweden in 1645, shortly after this book's publication</note>, there is an island called Frösö, which is established with its own parish and church. On this island, near the sea, a stone of this shape is found; I present it here exactly as it was sent to me.

<image-desc>A woodcut illustration of the Frösö Runestone (Frösöstenen). The stone has a rounded top and is densely decorated with carvings. At the top center is a large equal-armed cross with splayed ends. Below the cross, a long serpent (a Lindworm) loops in a complex pattern. Runic inscriptions serve as a border along the upper edge and sides of the stone, and further runes are carved within the serpent's body and on a vertical band in the middle. The surface of the stone is rendered with vertical and horizontal hatching to represent its texture.</image-desc>

->Tryn carved [the runes], Östman, Gudfast’s son, had this stone raised and this bridge made, and he had Jämtland <note>original: "Iotalant," a transcription error in the original woodcut for "Iamtaland"</note> Christianized. Asbjörn made the bridge, and [Sten] carved these runes.<-

<note>The inscription is unique for being the only runic stone to mention the conversion of an entire province to Christianity. It dates to roughly 1050 AD.</note>

# BOOK SIX.
<sig>Vuu 2</sig>
<meta>catchword: Chri-</meta>

->TRYN ERECTED [THIS]; ÖSTMAN, SON OF GUDFAST, CAUSED THIS STONE TO BE PLACED AND THIS BRIDGE TO BE CARVED, AND THEY INITIATED JÄMTLAND <note>original: "Joteimnt," a variant transcription of Jamtaland</note> INTO THE CHRISTIAN RITES. ASBJÖRN MADE THE BRIDGE AND THESE STONE RUNES.<-

The stories and fables that the local inhabitants tell about this stone are mere trifles; namely, that a certain magician, by means of these <term>Runic</term> <note>Worm uses the term to refer specifically to the ancient alphabet and its supposed magical properties</note> incantations, bound a serpent which daily brought many losses upon the inhabitants. I believe the occasion for this fable was taken from the snake-like path carved onto this stone, within which the lines and strokes of this inscription are contained.

Because they say this massive stone is placed near the sea, and mention is made of a certain bridge built at the expense of two or three men, they wish this fact to be spread to posterity by this monument; but above all else, they record that by their labor <term>Joteimnt</term> <note>Jämtland</note> was initiated into the Christian rites.

ᛏᚱᚿᛁᚿ **TRNIN** Now read as Truid.

ᚱᛆᛁ. There is a <term>lacuna</term> <note>A gap or missing part in a text</note> here, which a broken-off fragment of the stone has produced. But it is supplied with little effort, for the sense of the passage teaches us what is missing.

ᚱᛆᛁᚢᚦᚿ ᚼᛆᛘᛁᚿ **They placed the stone.**

ᛒᚱᚿ This denotes a **Bridge**, which without doubt was constructed at the shared expense of these two in this place where this stone mass is located. Otherwise, by ᛒᚱᚿ we have elsewhere said that a stone curb or "crown" is denoted, with which the burial mounds of great men were formerly surrounded in the fields, so that this stone might be called a ᛒᚱᚿ.

ᛁᚼᚦᛁᚿᛏ: I judge this to be the region neighboring Jämtland <note>original: "Jemptiæ"</note>, more distinctly called *Jotum Heimar*, about which I see few have noted anything, except my singular friend Arngrimur Jonsson in the first book, fourth chapter of his *Crymogæa* <note>A famous 1609 history of Iceland</note>, where he discusses giants in this manner: *Add that a certain province bordering Norway or Finmark, called Risaland—that is, Land of the Giants (for "en Rise" and "Rese" signify a giant)—was named so in ancient times. Not far from there is Jotum Heimar, that is, the habitation of giants, from where even now "en Jæt" means a giant.* Therefore, they record that this region was [converted] by these men...

I believe [Jämtland] was converted to Christ; for by changing two of the letter signs, you will most clearly find this word here: ᚱᛅᚦᛚ-ᛅᛚᛅᚾᛐ <note>original: "rath-aland," which Worm is interpreting as a variant of Jämtland</note>. There is no reason to suspect anything here concerning Cimbria or Jutland (formerly called **Jotumland** by the same author), since ᛁᚢᛐ [IUT] is very distant from ᚦᛅᛁᛐ [THAIT]; and our historical monuments teach us abundantly by whom and when these lands were imbued with Christian rites. Furthermore, these [lands in Jutland] abolished the cult of idols and devoted themselves to the true God long before Jämtland.

ᛅᛋᛒᛁᚢᚱᚾ **ASBJÖRN**. This was the third architect and <term>Runista</term> <note>a Runemaster or carver of runes</note>, who drew the lines of the inscription and oversaw the work, while the others contributed the funding.

ᛚᛅᚦᛁᚾ ᚱᚢᚾᛅᛦ **STONE RUNES**. They are called "stone runes" because they are engraved on this stone; otherwise, you will rarely find this <term>epitheton</term> <note>a descriptive title or phrase</note> added in other inscriptions.

It has not yet been granted to me to fish out with certainty from historical records at what time Jämtland and the neighboring regions were converted to Christ; otherwise, we might be able to offer something more certain regarding the age of this monument. However, from the deeds of King Olaf Haraldsson <note>Saint Olaf, King of Norway (r. 1015–1028)</note>—who was eventually numbered among the Saints because he devoted himself entirely to converting the Norwegians to Christ—it is clear that around the year 1020 AD, there were still many in the district of Nidaros <note>the medieval name for Trondheim</note> who sacrificed to idols and excluded the worship of the true God with all their strength. It is certain that this monument was set up in that century, and hardly before then.

These are the things, kind Reader, which I was permitted to share with you at this time from the ruins of our fatherland. If hereafter other things are sent by friends, or more accurately noted from those already presented, I will not be burdened to add them to these, so that your appetite for knowledge may be satisfied. Among foreigners, there exist certain new things of this kind, specimens of which I would have added if I had found friends inclined toward my requests. Specifically the *Italian* ones; those from Volterra and Perugia, the Florentine Chimera <note>a famous ancient Etruscan bronze statue discovered in 1553</note> presented by L. Schrader, and others of that kind, [whether they belong...]

# BOOK SIX
<page-num>525</page-num>
<sig>Vuu 3</sig>

...I do not know how I shall relate these things. If those who have the opportunity would search the Vatican Library, perhaps they would find things that fit here. For I can hardly persuade myself that our **Goths**, who inhabited those tracts for so long, and the **Cimbri**, left behind no memory of their deeds in their own letters. I suspect the same of those dwelling in **Spain** and other provinces. In **Gaul** <note>modern-day France</note>, near the city of Loches in the Abbey of **Beaulieu**, those who have described the memorable things of France report that a pyramid <note>likely an obelisk or tall funerary monument</note> stands twelve cubits <note>original: "ulnarum," a unit of measurement roughly the length of a forearm</note> high, marked with Gothic letters. Although certain people promised me a drawing of this, I have not yet been able to obtain it. I do not doubt that more things are to be found in France; I wish there were some among the illustrious lights of that Kingdom who would devote some effort to this. **William Camden** <note>the famous English antiquarian, author of *Britannia*</note> has produced certain **English** examples; but my very dear friend **Spelman** <note>Sir Henry Spelman, an English jurist and antiquary</note> advised me that more exist at **Beucelstria** <note>likely referring to Bewcastle, famous for its Runic cross</note> and elsewhere. What shall I say of **Sicily**? George Walther, in his ancient maps of Sicily and the adjacent islands published at the public expense of Messina, mentions a certain legal instrument of **William II**, King of Sicily, shared with the people of Messina, to which was attached William’s own seal, *in a round sign with the appearance of Gothic letters, in red color*. I will not touch upon things closer to us, to which I understand a learned man has already applied his hand. It is certainly to be hoped that everyone, in their own place, would keep watch over these things, lest the traces of our fathers left among them perish utterly. I trust this can now be done with less difficulty, because the path has been made smooth and clear by me, and I believe those obstacles which deterred others have been removed.

# DANISH MONUMENTS
<page-num>524</page-num>

I believe it was converted to Christ; for by changing two of the letter-marks, you will find this word most clearly here: J-A-M-T <note>original: "IHTI- ✱ I Y T," Worm's attempt to decipher the name of Jämtland from the runes</note>. There is no reason to suspect anything here regarding Cimbria or Jutland—which was formerly called *Jotumland* <note>Land of the Giants</note> according to the same author—since the letters M-N-F are a very far cry from J-M-T; furthermore, our historical records teach us abundantly by whom and when Jutland was imbued with Christian rites. Moreover, Jutland abolished the worship of idols and devoted itself to the true God long before **Jämtland**.

ᛐᚼᛒᛁᚢᚱᚿ <note>Torbjörn</note>. This third man was the builder and **Rune-master** <term>Runista: a specialist in carving and designing runic inscriptions</term> who drew the lines of the inscription and oversaw the work, while the others contributed the funds for the project.

ᛌᛐᛁᚿ ᚱᚢᚿᛆᚱ <note>Stone Runes</note>. These are called "stony" **Runes** because they are carved into this very stone; otherwise, you will rarely find this descriptive term added in other instances.

It has not yet been granted to me to fish out from historical records for certain at what time **Jämtland** and the neighboring regions were converted to Christ; otherwise, we could offer something more definite regarding the age of this monument. From the deeds of King **Olaf Haraldsson** <note>Saint Olaf, King of Norway from 1015–1028</note>—who was eventually numbered among the Saints because he devoted himself entirely to converting the Norwegians to Christ—it is clear that around the year 1020 AD there were still many in the district of **Nidaros** <note>modern-day Trondheim, Norway</note> who sacrificed to idols and excluded the worship of the true God with all their strength. It is certain that this monument was placed during or after that century, and hardly before it.

These are the matters, kind **Reader**, which I was permitted to share with you at this time from the ruins of our fatherland. If other items are sent by friends hereafter, or more accurately noted from those already brought forward, I will not find it a burden to attach them to these, so that your appetite for knowledge may be satisfied. Among foreigners there exist certain new things of this kind, specimens of which I would have added if I had found friends inclined to my requests. There are **Italian** examples—namely from **Volterra** and **Perugia**, and the **Florentine Chimera** <note>the famous Etruscan bronze statue discovered in 1553</note> produced by **L. Schrader** <term>Lorenz Schrader, a German official and author who documented Italian antiquities</term>, and others of that kind—whether to this...

# BOOK SIX.
<page-num>525</page-num>
<sig>Vuu 3</sig>

...I shall relate, I do not know. If those who have the opportunity would search the **Vatican Library**, perhaps they will find things that fit this subject. For I can hardly persuade myself that our **Goths** <note>Worm uses "Goths" to refer to the ancient Germanic ancestors of the Scandinavians</note> and **Cimbrians**, who inhabited those regions for a long time, left behind no memory of their deeds in their own letters <note>original: "literis," here referring to runes</note>. I suspect the same regarding those living in **Spain** and other provinces. In **Gaul** <note>France</note>, near the city of **Loches** in the Abbey of **Beaulieu**, those who have described the notable sights of Gaul report that a pyramid <note>likely an obelisk or stone pillar</note> stands twelve cubits high, marked with **Gothic letters**. Although certain people promised a drawing of this, I have not yet been able to obtain it. I do not doubt that more could be found in Gaul; I wish that among the illustrious minds of that Kingdom, there were those who would devote some effort to the task. **William Camden** <note>1551–1623, a famous English antiquarian</note> produced some **English** examples: but my very dear friend **Spelman** <note>Sir Henry Spelman, 1562–1641, an English historian</note> advised me that more exist at **Bewcastle** and elsewhere. What shall I say of **Sicily**? In the ancient maps of Sicily and the adjacent islands, published at public expense in **Messina**, **Georg Walther** <note>Georgius Gualterus</note> mentions a certain document of King **William II** of Sicily given to the people of Messina, to which was attached William’s own seal, *in a round sign with the appearance of Gothic letters, in red color.* I will not touch upon things closer to home, as I understand a learned man has already set his hand to them. It is certainly to be hoped that everyone, in their own place, would keep watch over these things, so that the traces of our fathers left among them do not utterly perish. I trust this can now be done with less difficulty, because the path has been made smooth and clear by me, and I believe those obstacles which deterred others have been removed.

<header>DANISH MONUMENTS</header>
<page-num>526</page-num>
<meta>catchword: INDEX</meta>

No one knows what it is made of. One broken foot cannot be repaired by any goldsmith because it does not allow for soldering; as soon as it is placed in the fire (which is the only way to join it), it shatters. When drink is kept in it for any length of time—especially wine—it acquires a foul and highly nauseating taste. I thought these things should be noted because <term>Hammelmann</term> <note>Hermann Hamelmann (1526–1595), a German historian whose work Worm is critiquing here</note>, whom I followed above, expressly states it was crafted from gilded silver. He did this more than once, as does the epigram attached to the image of it in this form:

->See here a silver horn,<-
->Washed with gold, engraved with<-
->Images, and notable for its art, etc.<-
<note>original Latin: "Cornu heic videto argenteum, Auro oblutatum, eiconibus Celatum, & arte insignibus, &c."</note>

There are, moreover, not a few things in Hammelmann’s narrative that might cause a wise reader to have doubts, which I leave for others to examine.

***

->The Klep Monument, page 514.<-
<note>Worm is referring back to a monument located in Klepp, Norway, discussed earlier in his volume</note>

Regarding those words: **MAY OUR FATHER PRAY FOR THE SOULS OF THE HEATHENS.** <note>original: "ORET PATER NOSTER PRO ANIMABUS ETHNICORUM"</note> It should be noted that although in the early church the Kings of both Denmark and Norway worked diligently to convert their subjects to the Christian religion, they could not achieve it for a long period of time. Rather, the more stubborn heathens were tolerated by Christians for a long time, as is clear from the history of **Saint Olaf** and the kings who followed him in Norway. In Denmark, although the Christian religion was planted with happy success under King **Harald Klak** around the year of Christ 827, heathens remained permitted among Christians until the reign of **Harald Bluetooth**, a span of over 160 years, as <term>Alsted</term> <note>Johann Heinrich Alsted (1588–1638), a famous German encyclopedist and chronologist</note> maintains in his *Chronology of the Conversion of Peoples* for the year 989. In **Denmark**, he says, **heathen superstitions were completely rooted out during the reign of Harald V** <note>Harald Bluetooth</note>, **before whose time most Danes worshipped both the Christian and heathen religions indiscriminately.** Indeed, there are those who extend this period to **Canute the Great**, King of Denmark and England, suggesting that for almost 180 years Christians lived here in a state of confusion alongside heathens. It is not surprising, therefore, if prayers and vows were poured out by devout Christians, anxious for the salvation of their ancestors, for their conversion.

*Although in my work **Runic Literature** <note>original: "Literatura Runica," referring to Worm’s 1636 book *Runir seu Danica literatura antiquissima*, which was the first systematic study of runes.</note>, I asserted at the time I published it that I had seen no book written entirely and in every part in our ancient letters—with the exception of those Calendars <note>The "Clog almanacs" or "Runic staffs" used for keeping track of feast days.</note> which we provided explained in Book III of the **Calendars**—since then, however, an extraordinary monument of antiquity has been brought to me.
