Among these, I include this double **Series of Danish Kings** and the description of the borders between the Kingdoms of **Denmark** and **Sweden**. These we now present to you, fair Reader, both to provide a taste of this Codex and so that you may see that entire volumes were once written in our ancient letters. This stands against the opinion of those who judge our Runic literature to have been of little use, believing it only found a place on memorial Stones and rock inscriptions. Furthermore, I hope that if other items of this kind should come across your path, you—mindful of the public good—will not be reluctant to share them with me. I wish for you to be persuaded that doing so will certainly bring you honor and glory. ## TO THE KIND READER
->Greetings.<- <note>original: "S.," an abbreviation for "Salutem," a standard Latin greeting wishing the reader health.</note>

<image-desc>Ornamental woodcut decorative initial 'Q' depicting a seated figure amidst dense foliage.</image-desc>

*Although in my work **Runic Literature** <note>original: "Literatura Runica"; referring to Worm's 1636 publication *Runir seu Danica literatura antiquissima*</note>, at the time I published it, I asserted that I had seen no book written entirely and in every part in our ancient letters, except for those **Calendars** <note>original: "Fastis"; refers to Runic stave calendars used to calculate feast days</note> which we provided in explained detail in Book III of the **Fasti**. Since then, however, a remarkable monument of antiquity has been brought to me: namely, the **Codex of Scanian Laws** <note>original: "Codex Legum Scanicarum"; this refers to the famous *Codex Runicus*, a 13th-century manuscript containing the laws of Scania written entirely in runes</note>, written entirely and elegantly in Runic letters on parchment. Although this book is defective and mutilated in certain places due to the ignorance or malice of those who handled it and removed certain parts, nevertheless, besides the Scanian Laws, it contains other things toward the end that are not unworthy of memory. Among these, I include this double **Series of the Kings of the Danes** and the description of the boundaries between the Kingdoms of Denmark and Sweden. These we now present to you, honest Reader, both to provide a certain taste of this Codex and so that you may see that entire volumes were once written in our ancient letters—contrary to the opinion of those who judge our literature to have been of little use, and think it only found a place in stones and rock inscriptions. Furthermore, I hope that if other items of this kind should come your way, you might not be reluctant to share them with me, being mindful of the public good. I would have you be persuaded that this will certainly result in your honor and glory. For I do not doubt that (although the unfairness of time and the ignorance of many have taken from us many famous monuments of this kind) there still exist—both in our homeland and outside it, among the curious—*

<summary>Olaus Worm announces the discovery of a significant Runic manuscript, the Codex Runicus, which proves that runes were used for complete books and not just stone inscriptions. He explains that he is publishing the lists of Danish kings and national boundary descriptions found within it.</summary>

<meta>This page continues Olaus Worm's preface to the reader. Following the announcement of the discovery of the Runic Codex (the *Codex Runicus*), he now encourages other scholars to bring similar hidden treasures to light and explains the technical orthography of the runes used in the printed version.</meta>

...among those who value antiquity, such treasures <note>original: "κειμήλια" (keimēlia); referring to precious heirlooms or stored-away valuables</note> still lie hidden, which, if they were studied by the hands of the learned and made public, would bring great light to the deeds of our ancestors. I therefore urge and ask them, for the sake of the public good and the glory of our fatherland, to continue to deserve well of as many people as possible. 

Furthermore, concerning the time when this codex was written, as well as the author of the works we provide here, we have received nothing recorded in writing, nor do we have anything to put forward beyond what you will find in the **Notes**. At the end of the book, these words appear:

->ᚦᛅᚱ ᚠᛅᚦᛁᚱ ᚦᛁᚱ ᛁ ᚼᛁᛘᛁᚱᛁᚴᛁ ᚦᛁ ᚠᛅᚦᛁ ᛅᚿᛏ ᚠᚱᛅ ᚦᛁ ᛅᚠ ᛘᛅᚦᚴ<-
<note>This is a Runic transcription of a prayer in Old Danish: "Our Father, thou who art in heaven, defend [him] and [save him] from the worm." Worm interprets the last part slightly differently in his Latin gloss below.</note>

*Our Father who art in heaven, defend Tuli from evil and dangers.* <note>original: "Pater noster qui es in cœlis, defende Tuli à malo & periculis."</note>

Whether this **TULI** <note>A common medieval Scandinavian name, also spelled Toke or Tyge</note> was the author, or the one who saw to it that these things were transcribed, or the scribe himself, it is not for me to judge; although I suspect he was the latter.

Regarding the method of writing, it is unique in certain respects. For this mark **ᛑ** expresses the letter **D**; whereas **ᚦ** expresses **TH**; and **ᚢ** represents **U**. He represents **TS** by **ᛌ** with the right leg shortened, which the **Printer** <note>original: "Typographus"; referring to the person setting the metal type for this book</note> was not able to observe conveniently everywhere due to a lack of specific Runic characters. 

Enjoy these crumbs, kind Reader, until someone arrives to satisfy you with richer feasts of our ancient literature. Meanwhile, farewell and look favorably upon our endeavors.

The Muses love you, Phoebus <note>Apollo</note> loves you; for you, leaving the Pegasean 
   Spring behind, the Grace comes as a companion and follower.
Especially since Chrysippus <note>a Stoic philosopher famous for his sharp logic</note> grants you sharpness,
   And great Aristotle his own genius:
Nor is flowery grace lacking in your pleasant words,
   Everything which Erato <note>the Muse of lyric poetry</note> and Minerva <note>the Goddess of wisdom</note> approve.
The latter [Minerva] reveals all of Olympus to you as you meditate,
   And temples not to be approached by a mortal step.
The former [Erato] teaches you to bring forth these RUNIC MONUMENTS <note>original: "MONUMENTA RUNICA"; referring to Worm's foundational studies of Viking-age runestones</note> 
   Into the breezes of light, works worthy to live for eternal days—
Such as our ancient ancestors once placed for us,
   The skillful signs of your genius and mind.
Honor to your virtue! Thus is the path to Olympus;
   Through praise already earned, your glory stands eternal.
Bright Glory weaves victorious laurels for you,
   Ready to carry your name into the Annals.

# MASTER DR. OLAUS WORM <note>Ole Worm (1588–1654), a Danish physician and antiquary who established the "Museum Wormianum," one of the most famous cabinets of curiosities in Europe.</note>

# FIRST SERIES

->Notes and Observations<-

**CONCERNING** the author of this Catalog, I have nothing specific to say, for he is anonymous to me, nor can I determine to whom it should be attributed through certain conjectures. Meanwhile, it is clear that he lived after the death of Saxo Grammaticus <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160 – c. 1220) was a Danish historian famous for the Gesta Danorum</note>, based on the fact that he presents several Kings who were successors to Canute <note>Canute VI</note> (whose history Saxo did not bring to a final conclusion <note>original Latin: "ad umbilicum," literally "to the navel," a Roman idiom for finishing a book scroll</note>). The last king named by our Author is *Eric Menved* <note>Eric VI Menved, reigned 1286–1319</note>, who died in the year of Christ 1319; it is therefore necessary that the author lived after him. Regarding Eric Menved, Claudius Lyscander <note>A 16th-century Danish historian</note> reports that he collected antiquities and monuments concerning the deeds of the Kings with great zeal; these were called the COMPILATIONS OF MENVED <note>original Latin: "CONGESTA MENVEDI"</note>. Whether our Author’s work held a place among these, I cannot affirm for certain. 

What *Eric of Pomerania* <note>King of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden (r. 1396–1439)</note>, King of Denmark, achieved in this genre is known to all, since his historical narrative on the origin of the Danish people and its Kings was made public long ago. He ends with that same King Menved, just as our author does, and if he did not differ from him in both the number and the naming of the Kings, I would believe that our Anonymous author had borrowed his material from there. It is not at all unlikely that the said Eric of Pomerania, when he had applied his mind to writing Danish history, urged the learned men of the country to contribute whatever they held regarding the Kings of Denmark to the common record; and that on this occasion, our author was prompted to record these things, seeking to win the King's favor. 

The style and diction do not suggest the highest antiquity, but rather the elegances of the Middle Ages and the century in which Eric of Pomerania lived. He occasionally introduces Latinisms to declare that he is not entirely unrefined or lacking in all knowledge of Roman literature. His aim and purpose is not to pursue the history or deeds of the Kings of Denmark in a sprawling discourse, but rather to show their bare names, their sequence, and their marriages, leaving the detailed commentaries to others. Many in that century applied themselves to the task of encompassing the deeds of the Danes in a brief summary—

<meta>This page continues the scholarly commentary on the "Catalog of Kings." The previous page discussed the dating of the manuscript, establishing that the anonymous author must have lived after 1319, the death of King Eric VI (Menved). # KINGS OF DENMARK

...from the fragments in my possession, I gather that all these sources share the same end point, namely the history of King Eric Menved <note>Eric VI, known as "Menved" (reigned 1286–1319). His nickname likely comes from an oath he used, "By all holy men" (ved alle hellige mænd)</note>. A specimen of this history, taken from our own codex, will be provided shortly. I cannot wonder enough why our anonymous authors differ so greatly from Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the most famous medieval Danish historian, author of the *Gesta Danorum*</note>, both in the number of Kings and in their names and deeds—especially since Saxo preceded them by more than a hundred, or even two hundred years if you consider the reign of Eric of Pomerania <note>King of Denmark, Norway, and Sweden (reigned 1396–1439)</note>. This is unless we imagine our historian remained so deeply buried in the cloisters of monks that his work was seen by only a few. But let us look at our anonymous author’s text.

**DAN** <note>original runes: ᚦᚨᚿ</note>. We have already noted that throughout this discourse, the rule of orthography <term>orthography: the conventional spelling system of a language</term> observed is that the rune ᚦ represents the letter D, while a modified ᚦ represents Th, contrary to what is found elsewhere. Therefore, it should be read as *Dan*, not *Than*.

**HUMLER** <note>original runes: ᚺᚢᛗᛚᚱ</note>. Saxo, King Eric, and our other more recent historians establish Humblus, the elder brother of Lother, as the second King of Denmark. However, because he was not famous for any great deeds and did not rule for long, our author omits him, and the second King in order is designated as Lother.

**ULVILDA** <note>original runes: ᚢᛚᚢᛁᛚᚦᚨ</note>. The wife of Lother is called Ulvilda by our author; others, whom Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius (1579–1639), a Dutch scholar and historian of Denmark</note> follows, call her Adela, daughter of Gutto, a prince among the Cimbri <note>An ancient Germanic or Celtic tribe from Jutland</note>.

**SKIOLD** <note>original runes: ᚴᛁᚢᛚᛞ</note>. I wonder why Skiold was omitted here, as he is celebrated by Saxo, Eric, and nearly all our other historians. He was so famous for his deeds that, according to Saxo, *all subsequent Kings of the Danes were called by the common name "Skioldungs"* <note>The Scyldings, the legendary royal family of the Danes</note>. Furthermore, the name of his former royal residence, *Skioldeneffa*, survives to this day. Not to mention the songs composed in praise of the Kings of Denmark by the ancient Skalds <note>Skalds were court poets in medieval Scandinavia</note>, which are still called *Skioldunga visur* <note>Skioldung verses or songs</note>. I would like to include one of these here concerning Hakon and Rolf Krake, although it might seem more conveniently placed alongside their own deeds.

->*KUI. KRAKI. HATHNU. BRATHNU.*<-
->*HLRTH. HLRTH. HITHTHI. NITHTHI.*<-
->*HUTHRR. KHITHR. THITHR. BITHR*<-
->*BAN. UTHNL. BHIN. RHINL.*<-
<note>The original text provides these lines in runic script. They represent a cryptic or poetic arrangement of names and terms associated with the legendary King Rolf Krake and his warriors.</note>

To grasp the sense of this meter, the first word of each line is to be joined with the last, and the second word with the third, in this fashion:

<meta>This page continues the philological analysis of the "Catalog of Kings," moving from the earliest legendary figures to more specific literary and historical comparisons. The previous page established the author's discrepancy with Saxo Grammaticus; here, the translator provides a detailed breakdown of an Old Norse verse about the legendary kings Haki and Rolvo Krage, using runic evidence to explain their epithets.</meta>

# THE FIRST SERIES.

->Haki with sword-points wounded limbs,<-
->Kraki with treasures restored the men,<-
->The giver of fine cloth is called scorched by the pyre,<-
->The user of gold is cut by steel.<-
<note>This four-line verse is written in an Old Norse meter. It contrasts two types of leadership: the purely martial violence of Haki and the legendary generosity of Rolvo Krage.</note>

For a better understanding of these lines, take these notes: **Haco** <note>original runes: ᚼᛆᚴᚬ</note> **wounded** <note>original runes: ᚢᛚᚿᛂᚱᛆᚢᛁᛐ</note> or injured the **shins** <note>original runes: ᛚᛂᚵᚵᛁ</note>, or any human limbs—specifically in war—**with sword-points** <note>original runes: ᛒᚱᚬᛑᛑᚢᛘ</note>. In ancient times, the word *Broddur* signified a sword-point or a spear-tip. By **Krage** <note>original runes: ᚴᚱᛆᚴᛂ</note> the author understands Rolvo Krage, the King of Denmark, who **restored** <note>original runes: ᚿᛇᚱᛑᛂ</note> (from which we get *næring*, meaning "nourishment" or "sustenance") the **men** <note>original runes: ᛚᛂᚵᚵᛁ</note> **with coins** <note>original runes: ᚼᚬᛑᛑᚢᛘ</note>. This last word is the ablative plural and the "instrumental" case derived from *Hodd*, which for the Poets signifies "gold"—a case of the material being used to describe the object made from it. He is the **giver of fine cloth** <note>original runes: ᚢᛂᛁᛐᛂᚱ ᛔᛂᛚᛚᛆ</note>, meaning of fine linen garments. In former times, Kings used to bestow such gifts upon their courtiers. This comes from *Pelli*, meaning <term>byssus: an exceptionally fine cloth, often referred to as "sea silk" or high-quality linen</term>; *pella* is the genitive plural. The author implies King Rolvo was accustomed to giving fine linen clothes to his friends. He **was scorched by the fire** <note>original runes: ᛒᛆᛚᛁ ᚼᛂᛁᛐᛁᛋᛐ</note>; this undoubtedly alludes to the history of Haco proposed by Saxo in Book 7, where among other things, he mentions Haco’s funeral pyre. He is the **user of gold** <note>original runes: ᚿᛂᛁᛐᛂᚱ ᚢᛂᛚᛚᛆ</note>. The word *Nei* signifies gold, just as *hodd* does. From this comes *Vellerikur*, meaning "rich in gold" or "abounding in wealth." It implies Haco was wealthy. Finally, **he is cut by steel** <note>original runes: ᛋᛐᛆᛚᛁ ᛒᛂᛁᛐᛂᛋᛐ</note>, meaning he was wounded and pierced through by steel or a steel sword.

**SVIBDAGER** <note>original runes: ᛋᚢᛁᛒᛑᛆᚵᛂᚱ</note>. Other writers place *Svibdager* and *Guttorm* before this king. However, King Eric does not mention him, perhaps because he was never decorated with the Royal diadem, merely acting in the King's place for a short time. His first wife was **Karnefrida** <note>original runes: ᚴᛆᚱᚿᛂᚠᚱᛁᛑᛆ</note>, daughter of Vagnoptus; the other, whom our author omits, was *Ragnildis, daughter of Haquin*.

**KARALL** <note>original runes: ᚴᛆᚱᛆᛚᛚ</note>. This name signifies "The Shaggy" or "The Strong." Some call him *the Generous* or *the Liberal*, others *Frecker*, meaning "The Bold."

**RATU** <note>original runes: ᚱᛆᛐᚢ</note>. King Eric places *Haldanus* and *Helgon* before him; others omit Haldanus and list only Helgon. Saxo makes no mention of this Haldanus, but explicitly establishes Helgon as the brother of *Roe*.

**KRAGE** <note>original runes: ᚴᚱᛆᚴᛂ</note>. Saxo elegantly pursues the reason for this nickname in Book 2, page 28 of my edition, in this manner: *A certain youth named Wiggo, having contemplated the physical size of Rolvo with more attentive...*

# KINGS OF DENMARK

Having scrutinized [him], and seized with great admiration for the same, he began to ask mockingly who that "Krage" might be, whom the prodigal nature of things had gifted with such a height of stature, following up with a witty kind of mockery regarding his unusual height. For in the Danish tongue, a *Krage* <note>original: *Krage*</note> is said to be a tree trunk with half-cut branches by which the tops are climbed, so that the foot, supported by the service of the cut stumps just like the benefits of a ladder, and gradually carried to the higher parts, attains the shortcut of the sought-after height. 

This man, however, is Wiggo, called Voggur <note>original: *Voggur*</note> in Icelandic antiquities, which give a far different reason for this etymology; which it will perhaps be worth the effort to cite here. The *Mythological Edda* <note>The *Prose Edda*, a 13th-century Icelandic work on Norse mythology.</note>, chapter 63, speaks of him in this sense: **HROLF KRAKA**, King of Denmark, surpassed all his predecessors in generosity, courage, and humanity. A certain poor young man called **VOGGUR** came into his court, looking constantly at the King with fixed eyes. When the King noticed this, he said: "What do you want, young man, that you fix your eyes so sharply on me?" Then he replied: "At home I heard that King Hrolf of Lejre <note>original: *Lethræ*; the legendary seat of Danish kings</note> was the greatest of all men in the whole North; but now, sitting on the royal throne, it seems to me I see a tiny little scrap of a boy." 

ᚼᛅᚾ ᚢᛁᛋᛏ ᛚᛁᚦᚱ ᛅᚦ ᛚᛁᛏᛁᛚ ᚴᚱᛅᚴᛁ ᚼᛅᚾ. <note>original runes: *han vist lidr ad litil kraki han*; translated: "He saw at Lejre that he [the King] was a little pole."</note> (Indeed, they wish *Krake* to denote a crow or a tiny boy). "You, young man," the King replied, "because you have given me a nickname, so that hereafter they may call me HROLF KRAKA; according to ancient custom, it is fitting to add a gift to the name." But because I see you lack anything to give, he who has shall give; and drawing a ring from his fingers, he gifted it to him. "The gift," said **VOGGUR**, "is that of the happiest of all Kings. Since I have nothing to return, I pledge that I shall be the avenger of your death." The King, smiling, replied: ᛚᛁᛏᛚᚢ ᚾᛅᚵᚦᚢᚱ ᚢᚬᚵᚵᚢᚱ ᚦᛁᚵᚵᛅᚾᛏ <note>original runes: *litlu nagdur voggur diggant*</note>, that is: **Voggur is content with a little**; which later passed into a proverb. Hence the song remains:

### FIRST SERIES

**Slyngebond**, the reason for whose nickname he gives in Book 3 in this manner: *While positioned on a ship, he decided to offer arm-rings <note>original: armillas; these were gold rings used as currency and marks of honor</note> to a petitioner, thrown with a great toss, but the magnitude of the gap frustrated his attempt. For the arm-rings, falling with a weak and insufficiently vigorous motion beyond the intended place, were swallowed by the waves; from which the name Rorico Slyngebond became attached to him.* <note>The nickname Slyngebond refers to "slinging the bands" or rings.</note> At this point, three kings in sequence are omitted by our author, who are named by Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, a 12th-century Danish historian.</note> and our other historians and are famous for their deeds: namely **Horvendillus**, **Fengo**, and **Amlethus** <note>These figures are the legendary basis for Shakespeare's Hamlet; Horvendill is the father, Feng the murderous uncle, and Amleth the prince.</note>. Besides Saxo, King Eric and other more recent authors also mention them. **Huitfeldius** seems to side with our author; for although he mentions them, he does not grant them a place among the Kings, as is evident from the number prefixed to their history.

ᚢᛁᚵᛚᚽᚴ **Viglet**. <note>original runes: Viglek</note> Called Viglet by others. Likewise ᚼᚢᚵᛚᚽᚴ **Huglet**, <note>original runes: Huglek</note> who is Huglet to others.

ᛏᚮᚱᚮᛋᚢᛋ **Torosus**. <note>original runes: Torosus</note> Muscular, with strong limbs; called *the Strong* <note>original: hin Stercke</note> or *the Bold* by others. To King Eric, he is *the Valiant* <note>original: hin Freckne</note>. Saxo calls him *vigorous* <note>original: vegetum</note>, as he bore witness to the very appearance of his nickname through the strength of his body and mind.

ᛑᛆᚵᚠᚢᛚᛏ **Dagfullt**. <note>original runes: Dagfullt</note> The origin of this word is not sufficiently clear; unless perhaps he was so called because he "fulfilled the day" <note>A pun on his name: dag (day) and fullt (full/fulfilled).</note> for the payment of the tribute he had agreed upon with the Saxons by means of arms. Lysander calls him *Storplade* by an equally obscure etymology; others call him *the Stately* <note>original: hin stortlatne</note> because he was of taller stature.

ᚠᛆᛚᛏᚼᛆᚿ **Falthan**. <note>original runes: Falthan</note> Huitfeldius calls him Faltham, Lysander calls him Faltam, whom he reports was called Gertham or Gertrude by others. He also had another wife named **Hilda**, the daughter of King Alonis of Uppland.

**S.** A peculiar mark for the letter S occurs here, which I have not observed elsewhere except in this manuscript. It is a mutilated ᛋ <note>The Sowilo rune</note>, with the right perpendicular line broken off. In this place, it seems to represent "DS" in *God's Birth* <note>original: Guds Byrd; meaning Christmas</note>; he understands this as the Nativity of Christ, whom he calls God in an absolute sense. In the series of Kings, **Hiarno** is omitted here, whom everyone records as having been gifted the kingdom because of the Epitaph he wrote for King Frotho.

ᚽᚱᛁᛑᛆ **Erida**. <note>original runes: Erida</note> The wife of Fridlevus is called Erida by our author. Hvitfeldius calls her Frogertha, others Frytha. Lysander attributes two wives to him, the first of whom was **Jurita** (which nearly agrees with Frida), daughter of Grubbus; the later was Gertrude, daughter of Amund of Norway, who is undoubtedly the Frogertha of Hvitfeldius—perhaps *Lady Gertha* <note>original: Frue Gertha</note>, Lady Gertha or Gertrude.

ᚠᚱᚮᚦᛁ **Frothi**. <note>original runes: Frothi</note> This Frotho is called *Frecker* <note>meaning "the bold" or "greedy"</note> by others, or *Gefuemilde* <note>meaning "the liberal" or "generous"</note> according to **Hvitfeldt** <note>Arild Hvitfeldt, a 16th-century Danish historian</note>, and *the Large* <note>original Latin: Largus</note> according to **Lyscander** and **Meursius**. But according to our author, the Frotho who follows—the fifth of that name—is nicknamed *Frogne*, whereas Hvitfeldt calls him *Frechne* <note>both terms imply valiance or boldness</note>.

ᚼᚨᚱᚨᛚᛞ **Harald**. <note>original runes: Harald</note> Some place his brother **Harald** before him, though others believe he had not yet been granted the scepter <note>meaning he had not yet officially reigned as king</note>.

ᚼᛁᛞᛁᛝᚱ **Hiddingr**. <note>original runes: Hidingr</note> Here our author clearly disagrees with the others. For after **Haldanus** <note>Halfdan</note>, he lists **Hidingus** <note>Hadding</note> and **Asmundus** as Kings, whom the others do not know; instead, they place a certain **Harald** in their position. **Lyscander**, citing **Saxo**, reports that Harald fathered **Asmund**, King of Norway, by **Thorilda**; it is from him that the other kings highly value having drawn their origin, tracing the solemn sequence of their lineage back to Haldanus, as Saxo says. From here follows **Unguinus**, who is succeeded by **Svartbane** <note>meaning "Black-Slayer"</note>. Svartbane is unknown to most because in his place is put **Sigualdus**, called **Börnesorg** <note>meaning "Child-Sorrow"</note>. However, Hvitfeldt seems to me to have correctly concluded that this was the same person as Svartbane. For **Sigarus** is called the son of Svartha by our author, and Svartha the son of Unguinus. Therefore, let this King be **Sivardus Svartbane**, or **Svartha**, the one nicknamed *Börnesorg* by others.

<margin>Some place **Alfr** among the Kings, and a certain **Regnerus** who killed Alfr, and whose wife was **Rethæ** (our author calls her **Rathæ**).</margin>

ᚨᛚᚠᚱ **Alfr**. <note>original runes: Alfr</note> After Sigarus, he appoints **Alfr**, son of Sigarus, as King of Denmark, whom others omit, placing in his stead a brother, **Sivardus**, whom our author does not recognize as King. Next, he establishes a certain **Regnerus** as King of Denmark, who supposedly killed Alfr; but there is deep silence about him among other writers, except for our Hvitfeldt (into whose hands I am certain this manuscript of ours must have come), who has these words in his history of Sivaldus: *From these are said to have been born five men, who for some time sustained the roles of Kings.* In the naming of these men, however, our author differs from others. To our author, the first is **Buthar** (**Butharus** in Hvitfeldt), who presided over **Scania** <note>Skåne</note>; the second is **Hundingar** (**Hunding** in Hvitfeldt), governor of **Sielandia** <note>Zealand</note>. The third is **Hanmarck** (**Hanevard** in Hvitfeldt), petty king of **Fyonia** <note>Funen</note>; the fourth is **Hagner** (**Agner** in Hvitfeldt), prefect of **Cimbria** <note>Jutland</note>; the fifth is **Roreck**, Count of **Lalandia** <note>Lolland</note>. Commonly they are called **Ostmarus**, **Hundingus**, **Hanno**, **Roricus**, and **Platterus**.

### FIRST SERIES.

**ARANP.** Others place Haldanus <note>Halfdan</note> first, but because he was unable to restore the empire himself, he is omitted by some. However, why our author calls this man the *son of Hyldetand* <note>original Latin: "Hyldetandi filius"</note> I do not know. It must be an error. For Harald himself is called *Hyldetand* <note>meaning "War-tooth"</note> by everyone, not the son of Hyldetand; **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> gives the reason for this in Book VII: *Wesetus struck his cheek with a club, without causing an open wound, so violently that he knocked out two of his teeth; the loss of these was later repaired by an unexpected eruption of molars. This event gave him the nickname Hyldetand; though some claim he earned it because of a prominent row of teeth.* Our author himself seems to admit this in the following passages where he establishes Ringo <note>Ring</note> as the son of Harald Hyldetand's sister.

**RINK.** This is the one called **Hakan Ring** <note>original: "Haquinus Ring"</note> by Swedish writers. Our other historians grant him no place among the Kings of the Danes. King **Eric of Pomerania** reports that a certain Harald, brother of the following Olaf, succeeded Ring. But the others do not agree.

**AMP.** Called *bin fracker* by some, and *Frochne* <note>meaning "the fierce" or "the brave"</note> by others. For he was so wild in his appearance that what others did with weapons, he did to the enemy with his eyes, terrifying even the bravest with the vibrating flash of his gaze. Our author calls him **RINK BANA** <note>Ring-Slayer</note>, because he killed Ring. Others call him **Amuntr** or Omund.

**BIPER.** I believe this Boterus is the one others call **Broder**; for our author expressly asserts that **IARMUNDR** was the son of *Iarmundus* or (as others say) *Jarmericus* <note>Eormenric</note>. I wonder, then, why he passed over *Siward, Buthlum*, and *Jarmericus* himself, as well as the other *Siward*, whom others place after Broder. I suspect there is a gap or a missing section <note>original Latin: "hiatu aut lacuna"</note> in our author’s text.

**BIARN IARNSIDE.** This man is not mentioned by **Hvitfeldt**, and is known to others by name alone. He undoubtedly acquired the nickname *Iernside* or *Ironside* from his bodily strength and the firmness of his flanks. They say he was called this because he did not fear to expose his bare body to the enemies' weapons and always remained unhurt; or, as **William of Jumièges** <note>a 11th-century Norman chronicler</note> says in Book 1, Chapter 5: *Because no shield was held before him, but standing unarmed in the battle-line, he scorned any force of arms, remaining unharmed, just...*

This undoubtedly refers to sorceries and incantations by which she had made him invulnerable. The English gave the same nickname, **IRONSIDES** <note>original: "IRNESIDES"</note>, or "Iron-side," to Edmund, son of Ethelred, because of his bravery, as is evident from **Orderic** <note>Orderic Vitalis, a 12th-century chronicler</note> in Books 1 and 8, and others. However, our subject **BJÖRN IRONSIDE** is omitted by some of our historians from the *Catalog of the Kings of Denmark*; this is because he was sent away early to foreign lands by his father **Lodbrog**, under the leadership of **Hasting** <note>a famous Viking chieftain</note>, to subdue foreign provinces in war. Consequently, around the year of Christ 860, he invaded Gaul with a huge swarm of northern youths and soldiers, and brought many of its provinces under his power; for this reason, he is better known and more celebrated among French writers than Danish ones.

Some assign this duty to **Harald Klak**, among whose number is our own **Huitfeldt** <note>Arild Huitfeldt, author of the "Chronicle of the Kingdom of Denmark"</note>; but **Meursius** <note>Johannes Meursius, a Dutch classical scholar and historian</note> removes him from the list of kings. **Eric of Pomerania** substitutes Inguar—whom others call Ivar—and Meursius follows him; however, he suggests that his brother **Sigurd** <note>Sivardus</note>, who is our subject here, was substituted shortly thereafter. Our author places Sigurd here, and **Pontanus** <note>Johannes Isacius Pontanus, a royal Danish historiographer</note> agrees with him, asserting that they wish him to be called **SNOGÓIE**, or "Snake-eye" <note>original Latin: "Angvioculum"</note>, because he possessed a snake-like gaze.

Huitfeldt identifies him as the son of **Ring**, placing another Erik, nicknamed "the Child," after him. Our author recognizes only a single Erik, the son of Ragnar.

# FIRST SERIES

I know under whose guidance some interpose **Sweyn** <note>original Latin: "Suenonem"</note> between this **Canute** <note>original: "Canutum"</note> and the following **Frotho**, though he was famous for no great deeds.

**ᚠᚱᚢᚦᛁ** [FROTHO]. This Frotho is called *frishe*—meaning lively and sharp <note>original: "vegetus & acer"</note>—by our author; others call him *Haarde snude*, or "Hard-nose" <note>original: "naris durioris"</note>.

**ᛂᚿ ᛂᚿᛦ** [THE ENGLISHMAN]. I believe he means "the Englishman" here, because he was born and educated in England. **Huitfeldt** <note>Arild Huitfeldt, a 16th-century Danish historian</note> records that he was called *Hadevith* by some, for which he thinks we should read "Son of Harald." However, our author reports him as being born of **Frotho**. According to **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, author of Gesta Danorum</note>, King **Eric**, Huitfeldt, and others, **Harald** succeeds him, though our author makes no mention of him—unless he is the one called **GAMPI**, a word unheard of by our other historians. I would certainly judge there to be an error here, except the same word is repeated shortly after, where the next King, **Gorm, son of Gampi**, is described. Finally, a manuscript called the *Gesta Danorum* <note>The Acts of the Danes</note> removed this doubt when it discussed the matter thus:

> "Then Harald his son was made King, and some say he was called King **Ganupi** because he was lazy and unfit for the kingdom." <note>original Old Danish: "Da var Harald hans Søn Konung oc sommi siger at han hete Ganupi Konung for thi at han var Vtressen."</note>

**ᚵᚬᚱᛘ ᚴᚿᚢᛐᛋ ᛋᚢᚿ** [GORM, SON OF CANUTE]. This is the one they call **Gorm the Elder**, or the ancient, because he extended his life beyond the ordinary term of human existence. Huitfeldt and those who follow him seem to have either omitted this man and the preceding Harald, or confused them with these figures.

**ᚼᛆᚱᛆᛚᛐᚼ ᚴᚿᚢᛐᛋᛋᚢᚿ** [HARALD, SON OF CANUTE]. This Harald, called **Bluetooth** <note>original: "Blatand"</note>, is established as the first King who openly professed Christ in these lands. For although others before him had thought of abolishing idolatry, they labored in vain, as they were unable to bring their good beginnings to the desired end.

**ᚦᛦᚱᛁ** [THYRA]. The first wife of Sweyn is called **Thyra** by our author, and the later one **Emma**. Others do not name the first, and say the second was **Syretha** <note>Sigrid the Haughty</note>, daughter of the King of Sweden. Here, some interpose a **Harald**, whom Saxo and others do not mention among the Kings.

**ᛆᛚᚠᛁᚢᛆ** [ALVIVA]. Called **Alviva** <note>Ælfgifu of Northampton</note> by Saxo and **Alvilda** by some; from her, he [Sweyn] fathered **Harald** and **Sweyn**, among others. But **Emma** <note>Emma of Normandy</note>, daughter of **Richard, Prince of the Normans** (not Robert, as Saxo mistakenly thinks), was left as the widow of **Ethelred** and finally joined to him in legitimate marriage.

# KINGS OF DENMARK

**ᛘᛆᚵᚿᚢᛋ ᚵᚮᚦᛁ** [MAGNUS THE GOOD]. I wonder why our author identifies this **Magnus** as the son of **Eric the Bad** <note>original Latin: "Erici Mali"</note> in Norway (I believe he means **Bloodaxe** <note>original: "Blodóxium"</note>), when all other historians testify with one voice that he was the son of **Saint Olaf**. He is indeed omitted by **Eric of Pomerania** <note>A 15th-century King of the Kalmar Union who authored a chronicle of Danish kings</note> in his Catalog of Kings, although he makes some mention of him.

**ᛋᚡᚽᚿᚮ ᚽᛋᛐᚱᛁᚦ** [SWEYN ESTRIDSSON]. He means **Sweyn Estridsson**. What others call **Estrid**, our author calls **Osrida**. This Estrid was, according to others, **Margaret**, daughter of **Sweyn Forkbeard** <note>original: "Tuiskeg"</note> and sister of **Canute the Great**. She was first married to **Richard, Duke of Normandy**, by whom she was repudiated, and then joined to a certain **Ulf**, whom **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century chronicler</note> considers to be the son of **Thorgils Sprakalegg**, though others say he was born of the highest rank in England. Nearly all our historians record that **Harold** succeeded this Sweyn; but the author, omitting him, places **Canute** next.

**ᛆᛁᚵᚮᚦ ᚡᛆᚱ** [ALWAYS GOOD]. Others say **Eigoth**, as if you were saying "entirely good" <note>original: "quasi totum bonum"</note>; **Eric of Pomerania** gives three reasons for this surname, which anyone who wishes may read in his own work. We shall not overstep the boundaries of these notes. He is also called **Eric the Cypriot** <note>original: "Ericus Cyprius"</note> by some, because he died in Cyprus on his return journey from Constantinople.

**ᚽᛘᚢᚿᛑ** [EMUND]. Here, **Eric of Pomerania** inserts **Magnus**; but because he did not obtain command of the entire kingdom, no mention is made of him by our author or others. **Albert of Stade** <note>A 13th-century German chronicler</note> reports that this **Emund** was called by others **Harefoed**, that is, **Hare-foot** <note>original Latin: "Leporipedem"</note>, because he had escaped so many times by taking flight after being defeated. The surname **Emund**, however, was given to him because he was accustomed to praising his own deeds with such great acclaim that it exceeded belief. But the manuscript history of the Kings of Denmark, called by the Icelanders the **Knytlinga Saga** <note>original: "Knitling sagu"</note>, reports that this name was given to him because he could not be reconciled with those he hated over a long series of years.

ᚦᚽᛋᛋᛁ ᚦᚮ ᚡᛆᚱ ᚡᚽᚱᚦᛁᚱ ᚴᚿᚢᛐᛋ ᛘᛆᚿᚿᛆ ᛘᚽᛋᛐᚢᚱ ᚦᚽᛋᛋᚢᚿ ᚼᚡᛁ ᛋᛁᚿ ᛆᛐ ᚱᛁᚦᛆ ᚦᚱᛁᚿᚵᚱ ᛋᛆᛘᚢᛚᛆ ᚼᛆᚿ ᚡᛆᚱ ᛘᛆᚿᚿᛆ ᚡᚽᛋᛐᚢᚱ ᚽᚱᛁ ᚴᚢᚱ ᚼᚽᛁᛋᚴᛁ.
<note>This runic passage translates roughly to: "Though he was once the most worthy of Canute's men... he was the worst of men, Eric the Foolish." It likely reflects a poetic critique of the king's character or lineage.</note>

**Nicolaus Thurius** thinks he was so named because he killed King **Magnus**. For he says in Book 2, Chapter 37 of the *Annals of the Heruli*: *“But having soon restored his army with the help of auxiliaries, he came out superior when battle was again joined with the enemy; he killed Magnus, and was called Emon from that famous victory as if he were memorable.”* **Huitfeldt** records that he was called the **Thunderbolt of the North** <note>original: "Fulmen septentrionis"</note> on account of his tyranny.

<meta>This page continues the genealogical and historical commentary on the Danish line of succession. While the previous page discussed the immediate successors of Sweyn Estridsson, this section shifts to the complex period of the 12th and 13th centuries, focusing on competing claims to the throne, royal marriages, and the legitimacy of various rulers as recorded by Saxo Grammaticus and other chronicles.</meta>

# FIRST SERIES.

**ᚼᛅᚱᛅᛚᛏ** [HARALD]. **Harald**, the son of **Harald Kesja** <note>Harald Kesja was a Danish prince and pretender to the throne in the 1130s; "Kyfia" is a variant spelling</note>, is not placed among the Kings by others, although **Saxo** <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> follows his deeds in Book 14. He contended for the kingdom with **Eric Lamb**, whose name—according to Saxo—came from his patient nature <note>original Latin: "ex patientia"</note>. Some call this Eric "**Eric the Wise**" <note>original: "Erikur hin spake"</note>; see the ***Knytlinga Saga*** <note>A 13th-century Icelandic saga concerning the kings of Denmark</note>.

**ᛋᚢᛅᚾᚬ** [SWEYN]. This man is called **Sweyn Grathe** <note>original: "Gratenhede"</note>, because he died in that place <note>The Battle of Grathe Heath, 1157</note>. At first, he obtained only a third part of the kingdom; however, after his partners in the kingdom, **Canute** (son of Magnus) and **Valdemar** (son of Canute of Schleswig), were killed, he occupied the whole kingdom alone. This is why our author places only **Sweyn** among the Kings, passing over the others.

**ᛅᚦᛚᛅ** [ETHLA]. The woman whom the author calls **Ethla**, the wife of Sweyn, others name **Albeda**; she was the daughter of **Conrad, Margrave of Meissen**.

**ᛋᚬᚠᛁᛅ** [SOPHIA]. Beyond **Sophia**, the daughter of a Russian King and wife of King Valdemar, **Cypræus** <note>Paulus Cypræus, a 16th-century jurist and historian of Schleswig-Holstein</note> believes that our **Valdemar I** (son of **Saint Canute**) had another prior wife named **Margaret the Black**. She is famous for her restoration of the **Danish Fortification**, commonly known as the **Dannevirke** <note>The massive system of Danish fortifications in Schleswig-Holstein</note>.

**ᚱᛁᚴᛁᛋᛅ** [RICHIZA]. Others maintain that the wife of **Canute** was named **Richiza** <note>original Latin: "Regissam"</note>, daughter of **Henry the Lion** <note>The powerful Duke of Saxony and Bavaria</note>.

**ᚦᚱᛁᚦᛁᛅ** [THE THIRD]. Besides the two wives our author recounts, this **Valdemar II**—called by others **the Great** and **the Victorious**—had a third wife, who was actually his first: **Maria**, the daughter of **Emperor Otto IV**.

**ᚼᛁᚾ ᚢᚾᚵᛅ** [THE YOUNG]. This **Valdemar the Young** <note>Valdemar III, who reigned as co-king with his father Valdemar II</note> is not placed among the kings by other historians because he did not hold the empire alone but reigned alongside his father. The author calls his wife **Meretha**, but other historians call her **Eleanor**, the daughter of **Alphonso II, King of Portugal**.

**ᛅᛒᛁᛚ ᛋᚬᚾ** [ABEL]. He omits **Abel** <note>King of Denmark from 1250–1252</note>, perhaps because he acquired the Kingdom through crimes; being polluted by the murder of his brother <note>Abel is notorious for the murder of his brother, King Eric IV</note>, he held the kingdom for only the space of a year.

---

Whoever the author of this Catalog was, he agrees significantly in the recording of historical deeds with King Eric of Pomerania <note>King of the Kalmar Union (1396–1439), to whom a Danish chronicle is attributed.</note>, although he differs in the number of Kings and certain names; so much so that I do not hesitate to assert that either our author extracted his work from Pomerania, or our author enriched that one. The latter seems more likely to me. And so that this may be more evident, I have rendered our author's words in the same terms (though at times more convenient ones could have been used) in which the famous Master Stephanus Stephanius <note>Stephen Jensen Stephanius (1599–1650), a renowned Danish royal historian.</note>—Royal Historian and public Professor at the Sorø Academy—gave us the Pomeranian chronicle, revised from a manuscript codex and restored to its proper integrity in many places. However, I will not hide in the Notes where our author seems to have a different understanding, so that nothing is omitted which might provide some light on the subject.

**HUNDBAN** <note>original: "ᚼᚢᚾᚦᛒᛅᚾ"</note>. The aspiration <note>the 'h' sound</note> has been omitted; whether it was originally prefixed I cannot say, as all the prior parts have perished to us by some misfortune. Meursius <note>Johannes Meursius, a Dutch classical scholar.</note> translates this as *Thrace*.

**THE FORTRESS** <note>original: "ᚦᛅᛘ: ᛒᚢᚱᚴ"</note>. Properly the fortress of *Dyna*. Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century author of the Gesta Danorum.</note> translates it as the city of *Duna*; more correctly, it seems to me, than *Dymin*, as Eric of Pomerania has it. For the former was located in Thrace or on the Hellespont, as is clear from Saxo’s first book; the latter was in Slavia, as is evident from his fourteenth book.

**BRITAIN** <note>original: "ᛒᚱᛁᚦᚦᛁᚾᚾᛁᛘ"</note>. Our author latinizes [the runes] quite often, as we gather not only from this word, but from many others which the following context will provide: **HATHERO** <note>original: "ᚼᛅᚦᛁᚱᚢ"</note>, **SAINT ANSGAR** <note>original: "ᚼᛅᚾᛋᚴᛅᚱᛁᚢ"</note>, **VISIUS** <note>original: "ᚢᛁᛋᛁᚢ"</note>, etc.

**ROSKILDE** <note>original: "ᚱᚢᛋᚴᛁᛚᛏᚢ"</note>. Our author asserts, along with our other historians, that King Roe first built Roskilde, but Eric of Pomerania explains the manner of it. *He [Roe],* he says, *transferred the city, which was previously called Hagekiöping, from the place called Hagebierg; and building it at the port of Isefjord, he called it Roskilde, a name composed from his own name and from the spring [kilde] next to which it is situated.*

### SECOND SERIES

ᚱᚢ : ᚦᚱᚢᚦᛁ : ᛋᚢᚿ : **ROE: FROTHI’S SON:** <note>original: "RO: FROTHI: SUN"</note> Our author disagrees here with King Eric, who establishes this Roe not as the son of *Frotho* but of *Haldanus*. Saxo seems to side with Eric, as he establishes *Roe* and *Helgo* as the sons of Haldanus. Frotho did indeed have a son named Roe, but he was killed along with his brother Scato by Haldanus before he could reach the height of power, which our author also hinted at above. Saxo speaks clearly in Book 1, where among other things he says: <note>original: "Horum natu maximus Haldanus, Roe & Scato fratribus interfectis, naturam scelere polluit, regnum paricidio carpsit."</note> "The eldest of these, Haldanus, having killed his brothers Roe and Scato, polluted nature with crime and seized the kingdom through parricide." Therefore, this Roe was not the brother, but the son of Haldanus.

ᚼᛁᛚᚴᛁ. **HELGE.** <note>original: "HELGE"</note> He asserts that Helgo was the brother of *Roe*, in which he has Saxo supporting him. "The sons of this man (namely Haldanus) were *Roe* and *Helgo*." But King Eric says Helgo was the son of Roe, to whom he adds a *Haldanus* whom our author ignores.

ᛁᛅᚱᛘᛅᚱ. **JARMAR.** <note>original: "JARMAR"</note> King Eric is silent about this Jarmar, as are our other historians; unless he means *Hiartvar*, who killed *Rolvo* <note>The legendary King Hrolf Kraki</note>.

ᚼᚢᛏᚼᛁᚱ : ᛁ : ᛋᚢᛁᚱᛁᚴᛁ. **HOTHER IN SWEDEN.** <note>original: "HUTHER: I: SUERIKI"</note> He undoubtedly suggests that Hother also presided over Sweden: about which there is deep silence in Eric’s account. Saxo touches on the matter briefly in Book 3: <note>original: "Paulo post Attisli fratris, quem Svetis præesse jusserat, excessu cognito, Svetico Danicum imperium sociat."</note> "A little later, having learned of the death of his brother Attisli, whom he had ordered to rule the Swedes, he joined the Swedish empire to the Danish."

ᚠᛅᛚᛏᛁᚱ : ᛋᚢᚿ. **BALDER’S SON.** <note>original: "BALDER: SUN"</note> Our author asserts that Balder was the son of a certain *Thaunmæ*. But Saxo, in Book 3, expressly calls him the son of Odin. Others say he descended from Odin. Some count him among the Kings of Denmark, toward which Saxo also seems to lean. But the author establishes him as a petty king <term>Regulus: a local ruler of a smaller territory rather than a high king</term> of Zealand, which is consistent with the histories; therefore, he should not be numbered among those who ruled all of Denmark.

ᚼᛅᛘᛚᛁᚦ. **HAMLETH.** <note>original: "HAMLETH"</note> Here many things are compiled and recounted that are unknown to others. Regarding *Slange* and *Vege* whom he mentions, you will scarcely find them elsewhere. *Orvendillus* (called Horvendillus by Eric), who is placed among the Kings of all Denmark by Eric, is to our author only the Prefect of Cimbria <note>The modern-day peninsula of Jutland</note>, which is not at all contrary to Saxo. He who is called *Amlethus* by others is called *Amblude* by our author, and he is not placed among the Kings of all Denmark. He is said to have destroyed *Aterum*, whereas King Eric and others say he destroyed *Fengon* <note>The inspiration for Claudius in Shakespeare's Hamlet</note>, who found a place among the Kings in their accounts; this displeases our author. After *Roric* comes *Vermund*...

# KINGS OF DENMARK
<meta>catchword: of</meta>

...who establishes [it]. Indeed, Saxo in Book 4 claims that **Vigletus** gained power after Roric with these words: <note>original: "Interea defuncto Rorico, Vigletus regnum adeptus."</note> *“In the meantime, Roric having died, Vigletus obtained the kingdom.”*

**THYDISKULANDA.** <note>original: "ᚦᚤᚦᛁᛋᚴᚢᛚᛅᚾᛏᛅ"</note> King Eric translates this as *Teutonia* <note>An old name for Germany</note>, while Saxo translates it as *Saxony*, which at that time was its own distinct kingdom, as the same author testifies in Book 4 when discussing the death of Uffo: <note>original: "Ita Saxoniæ regnum ad Danos translatum."</note> *“Thus the kingdom of Saxony was transferred to the Danes.”*

**HUMTH.** <note>original: "ᚼᚢᛘᚦ"</note> Saxo calls the tyrants of Sweden *Homothus and Hogrinius*; King Eric calls them *Haemothus and Hogrinus*.

**HAR: APA.** <note>original: "ᚼᛅᚱ: ᛅᛒᛅ"</note> These were two distinct words, but now we express them as one. For *Hertug* <note>The modern Scandinavian word for "Duke"</note> signifies a Duke.

**SIXTEEN WINTERS.** <note>original: "ᛋᛁᛅᚦᛅᚾ ᚢᛁᚾᛏᛅᚱ"</note> So say Saxo and all the others; but King Eric puts it as the seventh year, undoubtedly due to the carelessness of the scribes. Formerly, our ancestors counted years by winters, as we have shown in the *Fasti* <note>A reference to Worm's own work on ancient calendars and Runic inscriptions</note>.

This is also attested by legal codes and other older monuments. Among others, our codex of the **Scanian Laws** <note>The laws of Scania, a territory that was part of the Danish kingdom in the Middle Ages</note>, written in Runic letters, contains this: ᚢᛁᚾᚦᛅᚱ: ᛋᚢᛅ: ᛚᛅᚾᚴᛅ: ᛅᚱᚠ: ᚢᛁᚾ: ᛅᚱ: ᛅ: ᚼᛅᚱᛏᛅ: ᚦᛁᚦ: ᛅᚦ: ᚾᛁᛅ: ᚦᛅᛏ: ᛁᚾ: ᚦᛅᛏ: ᛁᚱ: ᛋᛏᚢᚦ: ᛅᚦ: ᛋᛁᛅᚦᛅᚾ: ᚢᛁᚾᛏᛅᚱ: ᚦᛅᚦᛅᚾ: ᚴᚢᛘᚦ: ᚴᚢᚾᚢᚴ: ᚦᛅᚱ: ᛅ: ᚦᛁᚾᚴ: ᚦᛅᚾᚦ: <note>This Runic text discusses inheritance and the age of majority, specifically mentioning the term "sixteen winters."</note> Which Andreas Sunonis, the Bishop of Lund, translates in Book 3, Chapter 1 of the provincial laws of the land of Scania: <note>original: "Bona maris impuberis donec quartum decimum annum compleverit, fæminæ, quandiu innapta permanſe-rit alienationi juris cenſura prohibet ſubjacere."</note> *“The law prohibits the property of a male minor from being sold until he has completed his fourteenth year, and a woman's as long as she remains unmarried.”* One should perhaps read "fifteenth," or "sixteenth," as the Runic text has it.

Also elegant and most worthy of note is the testimony on this matter communicated by the most renowned Master Stephanus Stephanius, Royal Historiographer, from his very ancient manuscript on parchment of the **Zealandic Laws** <note>The laws governing Zealand, the largest island of Denmark</note>. This is noteworthy not only because it frequently counts years by winters, but also because it teaches clearly what has been much disputed and sought with great effort: namely, at what time the Zealandic Laws were established. It reads as follows:

> This law was established at the Mal-moot <note>An assembly or council</note> and announced at the Land-thing <note>A regional assembly</note> on the Wednesday that was before Saint James's Day: both in the **fourteenth winter** of King Waldemar since he became a powerful King, and in the **thirteenth winter** of Archbishop Absalon <note>A famous 12th-century Danish statesman and warrior-bishop</note>...

...and three weeks and three days since Saint Canute <note>Saint Canute Lavard (1096–1131), whose remains were moved to a new shrine in Ringsted in 1170</note> was placed in a shrine in **Ringsted**. And King Canute, the son of King Valdemar, was crowned king and consecrated; and it was three winters and five weeks since **Rugia** <note>The island of Rügen</note> was won for Christianity by King Valdemar and assigned to the Diocese of Zealand by King Valdemar and by **Pope Alexander** <note>Alexander III, who reigned 1159–1181</note>. Since God was born, this Law was established in the year one thousand and one hundred winters, and seventy, and seven months, and twelve days.

These laws were enacted in the assemblies <note>original: "comitiis," referring to the 'Thing' or regional councils</note> and published in the general forum on the Wednesday before the feast of Saint James <note>July 25th</note>, in the fourteenth winter of the coronation of King Valdemar, and the thirteenth winter of **Archbishop Absolon**: one year, three weeks, and three days from the time the relics of Saint Canute were placed upon the altar at Ringsted and Canute, the son of King Valdemar, was crowned and elected as King. Three winters and five weeks had elapsed since Rugia was defeated and converted to the Christian faith by King Valdemar and Pope Alexander. From the creation of the world to this very day on which the laws were enacted, there are counted six thousand winters, three hundred winters, and seventy winters, minus five months and sixteen days. From the birth of Christ to the enactment of these laws, there are one thousand and one hundred winters, seventy years, seven months, and twelve days.

You will observe here, dear reader, the careless indifference of the people of the Middle Ages and that century regarding matters of chronology. This author asserts that in the year of Christ 1170, 6,370 years had passed since the creation of the world; whereas, up to this present day in the year 1642, the more accurate chronologists of our age count only 5,592 years.

# THE KINGS OF DENMARK

...cus, perhaps because he was less famous for his deeds; this one was soon removed by his brother, with whom he was supposed to share the empire.

**HINARP.** Unguin, who was placed among the Kings by King Eric <note>referring to the "Chronicle of Eric," a medieval Danish historical work</note> and others, is also omitted here.

**PHERIP.** Here our author breaks away from the accounts of Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus (c. 1160–1220), the most famous medieval Danish historian</note>, King Eric, and others. After Sivald, Saxo places Sigar, who is followed by his son Sivald, according to King Eric; but our author, omitting Sigar, appoints his son as King, whom he calls *Guthrid*.

**RAVNA.** Our author seems to subscribe here to the fables of Johannes Magnus <note>Johannes Magnus (1488–1544), a Swedish archbishop whose history of the Goths and Swedes included many legendary accounts</note>, which are vainer than "Sicilian trifles" <note>original: "gerris Siculis," a Latin idiom for worthless nonsense</note>. Magnus says in Book 11, Chapter 21: *Many Danish and Swedish histories affirm that a certain Attilus, King of Sweden, burned with such hatred for the Danes that he first assigned to them as king a barking dog, which he called Racho; then, after it was torn apart by dogs, he appointed the giant Laes over them.* This is repeated by a more recent writer, the varnisher of Johannes Magnus's fables, L. Paulinus <note>Laurentius Paulinus Gothus (1565–1646), a Swedish archbishop and historian</note>, in the *Arctic History*, Book 2, Chapter 13. The occasion for this fiction was undoubtedly given to him either by the history recorded by Saxo in Book 8, or the name of Hunding, who was one of the five nobles who occupied Zealand <note>original: "Sælandiam"</note> during an interregnum. Indeed, Saxo, in the passage mentioned, reports: *Gunnar, the King of Sweden, in order to punish the cowardice of the conquered Norwegians with a deformity of status unheard of, saw to it that a dog was put in the place of a Ruler.* See the author himself for a more detailed discussion of this. A similar thing is told by the author of the Norwegian History, Snorri Sturluson <note>Snorri Sturluson (1179–1241), the famous Icelandic historian and poet</note>, concerning Eystein, King of Oppland, who appointed his dog named *Sor* <note>also known as Saurr or Suer</note> over the people of Trondheim; see page 73 of our edition regarding this. Concerning *Hunding*, King Eric says this: *Hunding in Zealand; he always lost by hindering others and won by defending himself, from which originated that proverb: **Hund er Hiemme Rigest**.* <note>Old Danish: "A dog is mightiest at home."</note> *Hund* in the common tongue signifies a dog. Hence, mockers take "Hund" for "Hunding." The vanity of this entire fable is proved by the many contradictions in the narrative itself. Our author records that this happened when five men were in charge of the Kingdom, and he does not name the Swedish King who attempted this. Johannes Magnus reports that Attilus the Swede attempted it while Rolf was reigning in Denmark. A certain manuscript falsely claims that after the death of Helgi, a certain Haakon, King of Sweden, appointed his dog over the Danes. The crowd of those patronizing these trifles is so discordant that, however they try to cloak their lack of self-control with a false front, they nevertheless—

**VANTA.** King Eric translates this as "of the Slavs," undoubtedly meaning the Vandals.

**HUGLIK : SIKI.** For the sixth time; King Eric places it seventh, differing thus: *He was most warlike and made all of Germany tributary for the seventh time now.* After this *Gotric*, whom others call *Gudfred*, he places *Olaf*, *Henning*, and *Sivard*, whom our author ignores, joining *Ragnar Lothbrok* <note>the legendary Viking hero Regnerus Lodbrog</note> immediately to Gotric. The daughter of this Gotric was Geva, wife of Widukind the Great, King of the Saxons, whom H. Hennings reports was buried in the Basilica at Enger, but Henry the Fowler <note>original: "Henricum Aucupem," the 10th-century German King</note> transferred her to Bertelheim.

...he behaved with as much zeal in practicing religion as he had previously shown in scorning it. This is undoubtedly the reason why our Author establishes him as the first of the Kings who embraced the Christian Religion, even though our earlier Catalogue grants this honor to *Harald Bluetooth* <note>Harald "Blaatand" Gormsson, credited with the unification of Denmark and its conversion to Christianity</note>.

ᚼᛅᚱᛅᛏᚱ <note>Harald</note>. Between the two Gormos, Erik of Pomerania and others place a certain *Harald*; however, there is deep silence regarding him in our Author’s work.

ᚦᚢᚱᚢᛁ <note>Thyra</note>. *Thyri*. It is unusual for our Author to join Queens with Kings in this Catalogue; you will see it done only twice. It occurs here, certainly, because of the woman’s remarkable wisdom, by which she had served the Kingdom most excellently; and again at the end, where he also grants a place in this treatise to Ingeburga, the wife of the last King Eric.

ᚼᛅᛁᚾ <note>Hen/Soft</note>. Between *Sven Forkbeard* and *Canute the Elder*, Erik of Pomerania places *Harald Hein* (or "the soft"), whom our author bypasses.

Erik of Pomerania does not count him among the Kings, though he makes some mention of him, substituting *Hartecnut*, or "Canute the Hard," in his place—whom our author also omits. Saxo <note>Saxo Grammaticus, the 12th-century Danish historian</note> is a witness that both should rightly increase the number of Danish Kings. He certainly extols Canute with the highest praises in Book X:
> *He says: "None of our Kings was more splendid, even if others made more lands famous through their victories. For the reliability of his favorable reputation had so increased the magnitude of his works that he excelled in the greatness of his renown those whom he had held as equals in the glory of their deeds." See the rest.*

Regarding Magnus, he has this to say:
> *Magnus took possession of Denmark with the favorable consensus of the people, just as if it were owed to him by the law of a mutual pact and bequeathed by the will of Canute himself.*

ᛅᛁᚴᚢᛘ <note>Oikum / Odense</note>. As if you were to say "Odin's Island." One word seems to be missing here which would indicate that he suffered martyrdom. Furthermore, the Author joins these three Kings—*Harald, Canute,* and *Olaf*—with a conjunction in such a way that he seems to suggest they held power at the same time and simultaneously, whereas others (including King Eric himself) list them separately.

ᛅᛁᚴᚭᚦᚽ <note>Eigode / Always-Good</note>. Others call him *Eigode*, meaning "the Good." I suspect there is a mistake here and it should read ᚼᛁᛅᛚᚦᚽ <note>Hialthe</note>. Again, he joins Nicholas with Eric here, whom others keep separate.

ᛘᛅᚾᚾᛅᚱ <note>Men</note>. In the following sections regarding "Men," <note>referring to the people or the collective rule</note> others relate that *Sven, Canute,* and *Valdemar* reigned together with uncertain fortune, having divided the provinces among themselves. Our Author, however, lists Sven alone.

### BOUNDARIES BETWEEN DENMARK
### AND SWEDEN.

Because toward the end of the often-praised manuscript of the Scanian Law <note>The 'Lex Scanica', the oldest provincial law of Scandinavia, dating to the early 13th century</note>, there also exist accounts of the boundaries between Denmark and Sweden written in Runic letters—set out more extensively than they appear in the printed Laws of Zealand—I thought it would not be unwelcome to add them here, so that the student of Runic literature might have more material to practice with.

ᚼᛁᚱ : ᛒᛁᚱᛁᛅᚿ : ᛚᛅᚿᛘᚽᚱᛁᚿᛁ : <gloss>Here begin the land-boundaries</gloss>

## Notes & Observations.

Although Johannes Magnus <note>Johannes Magnus (1488–1544) was the last Catholic Archbishop of Sweden and a historian</note> in Book 18, Chapter 7, tries his best to make these boundaries a matter of controversy for us, I will not dispute with him at this time. It is enough for us that they exist in this most ancient codex, written in Runic letters many years ago; in the volume of the *Laws of Zealand* <note>Latin: "Legum Selandicarum"</note>, printed by Gotfred af Ghemen in the year of our Lord 1410 on the eve of the Annunciation of the Blessed Virgin Mary; and in the *Danish Rhyming Chronicle* published in Copenhagen in the year 1495. Mention of this is also made in the history of the Swedish Kings by Olaus Petri <note>A prominent Swedish reformer and historian</note> in these words: *This Amund Slemme <note>Amund the Ill-disposed, a Swedish king</note> went out and had border-marks laid between Sweden and Scania.* This Amund Slemme took care to place the boundaries between Sweden and Scania <note>The southernmost province of modern Sweden, then part of Denmark</note>. So too says Erasmus Lætus <note>A Danish national poet and historian</note> in Book 4 of *Danish Affairs*:

> Having fulfilled his duty of faith and piety,
> He turned his mind to the fixed borders of the Kingdoms,
> Together with Amund, Prince of the Swedes: from whose realm
> He separated our parts by an extended boundary:
> Lest any dispute should grow among future descendants
> Over the borders or because of an unknown boundary line, etc.

<margin>BOUNDARY.</margin> The *Laws of Zealand* use the term *Skel*, while the Swede Olaus Petri uses *Raamerke*. Both indicate limits or boundaries.

### BOUNDARIES BETWEEN.

[While King Amund] and Sweden were placing [the stones], at least ten are enumerated by our author. If you compare these with those read at the conclusion of the *Laws of Zealand*, the scribe’s carelessness will become clear enough. It is helpful to cite the passage: **The named from Sweden: Torn from West Gothland / Torsten from East Gothland / Gase from Westmanna-land / Grimol from Södermanna-land / Tole and Totte from Uppland.** <note>original Danish: "Thenefnde aff Sveria / Torn aff Veſter Götland / Torſten aff Øſtre Götland / Gaſe aff Veſtermanna Lande / Grimoll aff Sndermanna Lande / Tole oc Totte aff Oplande"</note> 
ᛘᚯᚱᛂ <note>Möre</note>. Nor do we find any less lack of diligence from the writer here: Among those chosen from Denmark, he omitted *Tosto* from Jutland <note>Latin: "Cimbria"</note> and *Ubbo* from Funen <note>Latin: "Fiona"</note>. 

ᚴᚱᛁᛘᚢᛚᚠ <note>Grimulf</note>. The Zealand Codex calls him *Gunoldum*; Grimulf [calls him] *Grimer*. 

ᚼᛁᚱ <note>Hir</note>. This should be read as ᛘᚯᚱᛂ <note>Möre</note>. For thus the Zealand codex states: **The twelve set six stones between the realms.** <note>original Danish: "The tolf Sette ſex Stene mellin Righen."</note> These twelve men placed six stones between the Kingdoms. 

ᛘᚯᚱᛂ <note>Möre</note>. See with what faith and "sincerity" Johannes Magnus <note>Johannes Magnus (1488–1544) was a Swedish archbishop and historian often accused by Danish scholars of bias or inventing history to glorify Sweden.</note>, in the passage cited above, reads *Norre* <note>Norway</note> instead of *Möre*, and from this most manifest corruption of the text, he breaks out into this sarcasm: *"Unless perhaps it makes an invincible argument for the Danes that the sixth boundary stone was placed between Blekinge and Norway. Anyone who knows the vast distance between those lands knows how foolishly that was said."* Most foolish indeed, my dear Johannes! Because it pleased you, against the evidence of the most ancient codices and the very nature of the geography, to use your "blurred and envious eyes" to seize upon the very clear word *Möre*, or to maliciously corrupt it. 

The Zealand codex reads *Möre*. Our Scanian codex writes ᛘᚯᚱᛂ <note>Möre</note>, not once but twice. Toward the beginning it says: ᛒᚱᛁᛘᛋᛁᛂ: ᛚᛅᛒᛁᛋ: ᛋᛁᛏᚢᛋ: ᛂᛋᛏ: ᛁᚿᛏᛂᚱ: ᛒᚱ: ᛘᚯᚱᛂ <note>Brims stone is situated between Blekinge and Möre</note>. Likewise near the end: ᚼᛅᚱᛅᛚᛏᛋ: ᛋᛁᚴᚿᛁᛘ ᛒᛂᚱᚴᛅᚿᛏᛁ: ᛘᚯᚱᛂ <note>Harald's sign, the eastern sea between Blekinge and Möre</note>. Therefore, if anyone reads it otherwise elsewhere, it is clearly established that it is done by manifest error. 

ᚦᛅᚿᛂᚼᚢᛚᛘ <note>Daneholm</note>. Here the Zealand codex, as well as the Scanian one, adds certain things which our author passes over, as they concern history more than boundaries—namely, the dignity and rank of the three northern Kings of Denmark, Sweden, and Norway among themselves. ### DENMARK AND SWEDEN.

...[of Nor]way, held the reins of the King of the Danes, while the King of Uppsala <note>The "King of Uppsala" refers to the King of Sweden, whose seat was historically at Uppsala.</note> held the stirrup. Johannes Messenius, in *The Mirror of Sweden* <note>Latin: "Specula Sveciæ"</note> chapter 2, did not blush to pervert this passage in his usual manner, twisting it into a contrary meaning. *Denmark Island [Dana Insula],* he says, *is divided into three portions: the King of Uppsala possesses one, the King of Denmark another, and the King of Norway the remainder. There, however, when a meeting of the Kings was held, the Dane applied his right hand to the rein of the King of Uppsala, but the Norwegian King [applied his] to the stirrup, for the purpose of restraining and holding them.* Who would not question the good faith of this man, who so wickedly perverts those things which were publicly published to the whole world in print about one hundred and thirty-five years ago, according to the codex of the *Laws of Zealand* <note>The "Laws of Zealand" (Sjællandske Lov) are medieval Danish legal codes.</note>? He himself cites the *Laws of the West Goths*, though he has not yet shown where in the nature of things they exist or have existed. Certainly, the laws of the Kingdom of Sweden that have been made public—which are undoubtedly excerpted from the particular laws of individual provinces and adapted to the modern state of the Kingdom—show not the slightest trace of this.

**OBSERVATION.** This epilogue seems to suggest that someone by the name of Tuli wrote these things and committed them to letters, or arranged for them to be written; hence he concludes with such a devout prayer for himself. In which, since he implores the protection of Christ alone and truly no Saint, one may suspect that the invocation of Saints had not yet become so prevalent among us in that century.

The rubrics you see inscribed here are found thus in our original manuscript <note>Latin: "Autographo"</note>. Furthermore, every single word was separated by two dots, which the printer was unable to express due to a lack of symbols; meanwhile, it was pleasing to mention this so that the ancient method of punctua-
->ting might be<-
->clear.<-

<meta>This page serves as a geographical and administrative appendix. After discussing historical disputes between Sweden and Denmark on the previous page, the author inserts a passage from the Old Icelandic "Knytlinga Saga" to fill the remaining space, detailing the divisions of Jutland under King Canute the Great.</meta>

So that the pages may not remain empty, it has pleased me to subjoin these extracts from an old Icelandic manuscript, commonly called the **Knytlinga Saga** <note>original: "KNITLINSAGU"; a 13th-century saga detailing the lives of the Danish kings.</note>, concerning the constitution of the Kingdom of Denmark in the time of King **Canute the Great**.

Denmark is a large kingdom and its parts are spread far apart. The largest part of Denmark is called **Jutland** <note>original: "Iotland"</note>; it lies to the south by the sea. There is the southernmost Bishop’s seat in Denmark in **Hedeby** <note>original: "Heida Boe"; also known as Schleswig.</note>, and in that diocese there are three hundred and fifty churches <note>original: "halft fiorda hundrad"; literally "half of the fourth hundred," a traditional Norse way of counting.</note>, and 130 ships for the King’s levy. A second Bishop’s seat is in Jutland, called **Ribe** <note>original: "Ripum"</note>; in that bishopric there are three hundred and twenty-four churches. And 110 ships for the King’s levy. A third Bishop’s seat in Jutland is called **Aarhus** <note>original: "Arosi"</note>. In that bishopric there are two hundred and ten churches. And 90 ships for the King. A fourth Bishop’s seat in Jutland is called **Viborg** <note>original: "Viebiorgum"</note>. In that bishopric there are 250 churches. And 100 ships for the King. **Limfjord** <note>original: "Limafiordur"</note> is a great fjord in Jutland; it runs from the northwest to the south. From the northern part of Limfjord there is a narrow isthmus westward to the sea called **Harald’s Isthmus** <note>original: "Haralds eyd"</note>. There King Harald Sigurdsson <note>King Harald Hardrada of Norway (reigned 1046–1066).</note> had his ships dragged across when he was escaping from the King. West of Limfjord is the realm called

<column-break/>

Denmark is a spacious Kingdom extending toward the East. Its largest portion is called **Jutland**; this looks toward the Southern ocean. In it is the furthest Episcopal seat of Denmark, **Hedeby**, in whose Diocese are 350 parishes; moreover, 130 ships are customarily provided for the King’s use in war. The second Episcopal seat of the **Cimbrians** <note>original: "Cimbriæ"; a classical term for the people of Jutland.</note> is at **Ribe**, containing 324 temples. To the King, 110 ships are owed (elsewhere 120). The third Episcopal seat of the Cimbrians is at **Aarhus**, containing 210 parishes. To the King, 80 ships are owed. The fourth Episcopal seat of the Cimbrians is at **Viborg**, containing 250 Parishes. From it, one hundred ships are owed to the King. The **Limic Gulf** <note>The Limfjord.</note> in the Cimbrian lands is large, turning from the north toward the south. From this gulf, where it looks to the north, a thin Isthmus stretches into the western ocean, called the **Isthmus of Harald**. For through this, Harald, son of Sigurd, took care to have his ship dragged when he was fleeing the King of Denmark. At the western side of the Limic gulf is Vanda- <note>The text cuts off here, continuing with the catchword "da-".</note>

<note>Technical terms used: Knytlinga Saga (The Saga of the Descendants of Cnut), Canute the Great (King of Denmark, England, and Norway), Jutland (the Danish peninsula), Episcopal (relating to a Bishop), Harald Sigurdsson (Harald Hardrada), Limfjord (a shallow part of the sea in Denmark).</note>

...Vendsyssel <note>original: "Vendelfskagi"</note>, and it turns towards the north. There is the fifth Bishop’s seat in Denmark, in the place called **Hjørring** <note>original: "Hordingi"</note>. In that bishopric there are 160 churches and 50 ships for the King. The coast of **Jutland** <note>original: "Iotlands syda"</note> is the name for the entire region from Vendsyssel in the west and south to **Ribe**. Between Jutland and **Funen** <note>original: "Fions"</note> runs the **Middelfart Sound** <note>original: "Medalfarar sund"; now known as the Little Belt.</note>.

On Funen is the sixth Bishop’s seat in Denmark, in **Odense** <note>original: "Odins ey"; literally "Odin's Island."</note>. In that bishopric there are 300 churches, and 100 ships for the King. Between Funen and **Zealand** <note>original: "Siolands"</note> runs the **Belt Sound** <note>original: "Beltis sud"; the Great Belt.</note>.

In the bishopric of Zealand there are 411 churches and 120 ships for the King. North of Zealand is the **Øresund** <note>original: "Eyrar sund"</note>.

And north of the Øresund lies **Scania** <note>original: "Skaney"</note>. In Halland <note>A historical province then considered part of the Scanian lands.</note> in Scania is the Archbishop’s seat in **Lund**, which is the eighth bishop’s seat in Denmark. In that diocese there are 353 churches <note>original: "half fiorda hundrad kyrkna og þriar"; "half the fourth hundred" is the Norse way of saying 350, plus three.</note>, and 150 ships for the King. That is the richest bishop’s seat in Denmark.

Between these lands of Jutland and Scania lie many large islands that have not been named before. **Samsø** <note>original: "Sams ey"</note> is under the Bishop of Aarhus, **Læsø** <note>original: "Hlessey"</note> under the Bishop of Viborg. They lie west of Funen: **Als** <note>original: "Ald ey"</note> is under **Schleswig** <note>original: "Heyda boe"</note>, along with **Lolland**, **Ærø**, **Tåsinge** <note>original: "Thorslund"</note>, **Als**, and **Langeland** <note>original: "Kongsland"</note>. In this there are 160 churches, and 50 ships are owed to the King. The western shores of **Jutland** <note>original: "Cimbriæ"</note> from Vendsyssel south towards **Ribe** are called Vendsyssel-neck <note>original: "Vendilskaga"</note>. Between Jutland and **Funen** <note>original: "Fioniam"</note> is the strait called **Middelfart Sound**.

<meta>This page concludes the geographical and administrative survey of the Danish islands, including Bornholm, before transitioning into a poetic tribute to the legendary hero Holger Danske (Ogier the Dane). It links the historical geography of the Knytlinga Saga with the chivalric myths of the Danish Middle Ages.</meta>

Five islands are under the Bishop of **Odense** <note>original: "Fione"</note>. **Møn** <note>original: "Manu"</note> and **Falster** are under the Bishop of **Zealand** <note>original: "Siolandi"</note>. **Bornholm** <note>original: "Boringhundarholmur"</note> lies to the east in the sea off **Scania** <note>original: "Scäney"</note>. It is a great realm and falls under the Bishop of Scania; there are 12 towns <note>The Old Norse "By" refers to estates or significant settlements.</note> and 14 churches there. These lands now named lie under the King of the Danes and are both vast and populous; in ancient times, these lands were the realms of many kings.

<column-break/>

Five islands are subject to the Bishop of **Odense** <note>original: "Otthonienſi"</note>. But Møn <note>original: "Mona"</note> and Falster are subject to the Bishop of **Roskilde** <note>original: "Rofchildenſi"</note>. **Bornholm** <note>original: "Böringholmia"</note>, in which there are 12 royal estates, looking toward Scania from the southern tract, is a powerful island; it is subject to the Bishop of Scania and has 14 temples <note>original: "templa," here meaning churches.</note>. All these provinces enumerated, great and populous, today acknowledge one King of Denmark, though formerly they were divided into many kingdoms.

---

To this rhythm, written by some anonymous author—though it is less polished—this paper has also given space, lest it perish entirely. Indeed, I owe it to a certain parchment manuscript from the Royal Library of the Academy of Copenhagen, to which several other items of that kind were attached.

->*For the glory of God and in praise of His servant HOLGER, the most Christian Prince of the Danes.*<-

Glory of the Danes
and the honor of **Denmark** <note>original: "Daciæ," a common Latinization for Denmark in the Middle Ages.</note>,
offspring of kings,
Holger the Dane.

Child of Japheth <note>According to medieval tradition, the nations of Europe were descended from Japheth, the son of Noah.</note>,
of serene **Gorm’s** <note>Referring to Gorm the Old, the traditional first king of a united Denmark.</note>
ancient lineage,
the Dane Ogier. <note>original: "Udgerus," a variant of Holger/Ogier.</note>

Comely in face,
tall in stature,
a fearless fighter,
Ogier the Dane.

The splendor of the Geats <note>original: "Gytharū"</note>,
offspring of the Goths,
the faithful Geatish nation
was tamed by his arms.

War trophies
everywhere in the world
the unconquered one displayed,
Holger of the Geats.

<column-break/>

Indians and Tartars,
Turks, and Saracens,
these, defeated in battle,
he brought under Christ's rule.

The entire East
trembled in ruin
at the victorious wars
and the weapons of Holger.

Of the high Indian empire
he was made,
by heavenly virtue,
King and Monarch. <note>In medieval legend, Ogier/Holger was often depicted as a conqueror of far-off lands, sometimes identified with the mythical Prester John or his kin.</note>

The piety of Christ
carried him to the stars,
drawn from the depths
of the Tartarean throne. <note>likely referring to his victory over hellish or pagan forces.</note>

A man from a foreign land,
bearing flowers as his signs, <note>possibly a reference to the fleur-de-lis, which Ogier bears in French chivalric romances.</note>
reaching toward the heavens,
clinging to Christ.

<column-break/>

Having crossed the sea,
the Sepulcher of the Lord
he captured by force of arms,
his enemy having been subdued.

The Arabs and Syrians,
likewise the Palestinians,
while then battling,
he brought under Christ's yoke.

Thus all the other
kingdoms of the East,
obtained by divine help,
he drew to Christ.

Famous in military service
and burdened with merits,
thus he, wealthy, ascends
to the heavenly kingdoms.

**The Songs of HOLGER end.**

---
